1931-03-23.text: BERLIN, March 28. (AP)— Foreign Minister Curtius today received successively the French, British and Italian Ambassadors to explain the intentions of Germany and Austria in agreeing to a virtual customs union. During the next few days, it was announced, the foreign minister will see the ministers of all states bordering upon Germany and Austria to offer similar explanations. In foreign office circles confidence prevailed that Curtius can satisfactorily allay any fear that the proposed union might be in contravention of existing treaties or protocols. VIENNA, Mar. 23. (AP) Austria today answered protests against her proposed customs union with Germany with an invitation to other European countries to join them in an abolition of customs barriers. (By The Associated Press.) New York, Mar. 23—Cancer tissue growing artificially in glass dishes is killed in a few minutes by a new serum developed in the cancer research laboratory of London hospital, England. Unlike other tumor remedies this serum is harmless to living tissues except cancer. These discoveries and their possibilities for experimenting with cancer in man are told in the April issue of the American Journal of Cancer by Thomas Lumsden, M. D., director of the London laboratory. The serum comes from animals which have been inoculated with cancer. It is tested upon cells of cancer, of heart, kidney and other body tissues growing artificially outside of living beings. A few rats have been cured of cancer, and others made immune. “Animals,” Dr. Lumsden says, “are capable of forming anti-bodies having a specially lethal effect upon malignant tumor cells of any variety, but which

LEIGHTON BUZZARD, England, March 22.--(4)--Three passengers and three of the train crew were killed today when the Royal Scot Express, one of the finest and fastest trains in the world, left the rails near here and piled up along the track. One of the dead was Sir George Saltmarsh, grain expert, who was vice chairman of the allied wheat purchasing commission in 1915 and 1916. The engineer, the fireman and a dining car steward were killed and nine other passengers were seriously injured. The cause of the accident was not immediately determined. The accident, which occurred at 12:15 p.m., caused great excitement in this peaceful countryside, 38 miles from London. Tangled wreckage blocked all traffic. There was no fire. The “Royal Scot” is one of the fastest trains in the world and about a month ago averaged 90 miles per hour for a 299-mile run.

LEIGHTON - BUZZARD, Eng., Mar. 23. (AP)——London, Midland and Scottish Line officials today sought to learn the cause of the wreck which yesterday piled up the Royal Scot Express, one of the finest trains in the world, and took six lives. Nine passengers were injured. The train, which frequently has registered a speed of 90 miles an hour on parts of the 400-mile run from London to Glasgow, was proceeding at a rapid rate along a clean straight stretch of steel, when the locomotive left the rails and keeled over on its side. The first two coaches telescoped and the third and fourth, after swinging around, crashed into another coach before turning over. One of the dead was Sir George Saltmarsh, grain expert who was vice chairman of the Allied Wheat Purchasing Commission in 1915 and 1916. Two other passengers and the engineer, the fireman and a dining car steward also were killed. Train offic

London, March 22.—The life of the Labor government as well as the fate of many national and empire issues may be profoundly affected by the British political drama which will be unfolded this week. Indian negotiations and international problems, particularly in reference to world-wide disarmament, are only a few of the questions involved. Never in modern times has the political confusion been greater in this country than at present. A major crisis exists as a result of the fine balance of parties in Parliament and internal party dissension over policies and personalities. The Laborites have their own worries with Sir Oswald Mosley forming a “new party” on the right and the Maxtonites on the left wing causing even more real trouble. But Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's troubles are small compared with those of leaders of the older parties, such as David Lloyd George and Stanley Baldwin.

LEIGHTON BUZZARD, Eng. March 23.—(UP)—Relief crews and doctors labored throughout the night to remove injured and dead from the wreckage of three coaches of the Royal Scot Express, which was derailed at the station here yesterday with a loss of at least six lives. It was feared that more of the wounded might die. The train was one of the fastest in the world and was making about 76 miles an hour when it fouled a switch. Two coaches were telescoped, another was turned over and wrecked and every car on the train was derailed. About 60 persons were injured, most of them slightly. The engineer and fireman were killed. One of the passengers killed was Sir George Saltmarsh, an authority on wheat, who had just returned from Australia.

PARIS—Charlie Chaplin was the guest today of Aristide Briand at a small informal luncheon at the foreign office. Lord Tyrrell, the British ambassador, was there and also Minister of Justice Leon Berard who decorated Chaplin in 1921 with the Purple Rosette, making him "Officer of the Academy."

St. John’s N. F., March 23. ()—The ice floes of White Bay today released their grip on the sealing vessels carrying 127 survivors of the Viking disaster, and the ships headed for St. John’s in bright clear weather. Without further mishap, the sealers locked in blocks and hummocks of ice almost a week, should arrive at this port tomorrow morning. The majority of the survivors are aboard the steamer Prospero, to which they were transferred from the sealer Sagona today after a stiff wind had freed the Sagona from its prison of ice. Only the sick and injured were left aboard the Sagona. When all the rescued men are in port and have rested, Sir Richard Squires, prime minister of Newfoundland, will open an inquiry to determine the cause of the explosion that wrecked the Viking, piling up a casualty list of two known dead, twenty-six missing and many injured. QUESNEL, B. C., Oct. 19. (P)— Nature’s three b’s—bees, bears and beavers—have forecast an early and cold winter for British Columbia. Indians here say the honey makers have built their nests high, wide and ample, for protection against expected deep snows. The bears are rolling in fat, expecting long hibernation. Beaver families already have cut and stored an almost unprecedented store of food against an early freeze-up.

New York, Oct. 19 (#)--After a short chase during which only blank warning shots were fired, the 125-foot British motor vessel “Whichone” was captured off Fire Island today by the coast guard patrol boat Cahoon. The vessel, reputedly supplying rum running craft outside the 12-mile limit, carried $70,000 worth of Scotch whisky malt. Her captain, Chesley Anderson, and the ten members of the crew were taken to the barge office late in the day and then transferred to Brooklyn for arraignment in federal court.

Atlanta, Oct. 19.— (AP) — British delegates today blocked efforts of staunch prohibition advocates within the Methodist church to force a separate pronouncement on the liquor question before the General Ecumenical conference. The liquor issue came to the fore in a group meeting to which several questions had been assigned for discussion. It was the objection of the Rev. C. Ensor Walters of London that finally prevented a division of reports, after Bishop James Cannon, Jr., had addressed the meeting and had been termed “a martyred and persecuted man.” ALLIED FORCES’ CLAM Washington, -Oct. 19. — (-) — Complete success in its first campaign to obtain dry planks in 1932 was claimed by the Allied Forces for Prohibition today as the Democratic National committee pointed to “the wide range of opinion” within the party on the issue. Dr. Daniel A. Poling, chairman, said the Allied Forces attained

LONDON, Oct. 21.—Mahatma Gandhi, who has indicated on several occasions that he is disappointed at the lack of progress by the Indian Round-Table Conference, has made reservations to return to Bombay next month. England, he says, is no more prepared to grant the demands of the Indian Nationalists now than when he left Bombay, and he professed to see no hope that Great Britain's attitude would change. In the absence of any assurance as to what the government intends to do, he said, he feels he is wasting his time here. Other delegates to the conference, discouraged by their failure to settle the Hindu-Muslim communal problem, also are planning to go home within a few weeks.

TOKIO, Oct. 20 U.P)—China has asked both France and Great Britain to send troops into Manchuria and has been refused, the government was informed today. Kenkichi Yoshizawa, Japan's representative at the League of Nations council in Geneva, told cabinet authorities here that the information was given him by Aristide Briand of France, president of the council.

MANCHESTER, Eng., Oct. 20—(P)—Increased activity is reported in many Lancashire and Yorkshire cotton mills as a result of an influx of orders since the gold standard was suspended. Mills in which the spindles had long been silent are now humming with activity executing rush orders, while the nearby Yorkshire district cotton doubling mills are working overtime. One large mill at Rochdale has started a night shift to fill its orders and at Haslingden another cotton mill will operate on a 55-hour week instead of the usual 48 hours. Trade union officials have objected to the overtime work, but the workers are said generally to be glad to earn the extra money. The sudden business pickup is attributed to the suspension of the gold standard inasmuch as the drop in the value of the pound sterling against other world currencies amounts virtually to a reduction in the price of manufactured goods,

TOKYO, Oct. 19—CP—In view of the deadlock between Tokyo and Geneva over the League of Nations recommendations aiming at a peaceful solution of the Sino-Japanese controversy over Manchuria, Japan today became more inclined than ever to look to China for a settlement. New possibilities of negotiations directly with China were foreseen in official circles here as the result of reports that the fall of Chiang Kai-Shek as president of the Chinese republic was imminent and that Chiang’s political foes, the Canton insurgents, would play an important role in the formation of a new government at Nanking. In this connection it was recalled that Eugene Chen, foreign minister of the insurgent Canton government, visited Tokyo last August and conferred with Baron Shidehara, Japanese foreign minister. At that time Chen reputedly clarified Canton’s position in the event that Chiang eventually should be

1931-12-23.text: By The Associated Press. New London, Wis., Dec. 23.—Preparing for the worst the weather might do, Raymond Larson, 23, put on five pairs of trousers and seven shirts. His preparedness probably saved his life, for the layers were an effective cushion when he was struck by a hit-and-run motorist on Highway 26. He was found unconscious in a ditch, but is expected to recover.

TOKYO, Dec. 23. (#)—Japan agreed today there is no need to postpone the world disarmament conference slated to be held next February at Geneva, in replying to a vote from the British government dated December 17. The Japanese government pointed out that its delegation already is on the way to Geneva. PARIS, Dec. 23. ()—Government officials said today France will oppose any postponement of the world disarmament conference at Geneva, even for a few weeks.

Tokio, Dec. 23. (UP)—Advancing across Manchuria in a drive against "bandits," Japanese troops and bombing planes captured two Chinese citadels today and ordered warships into action to head off the beaten defenders. Advices received here from Yinkow said that Japanese occupied the citadel at Tilenchuangtai in South Panshan, disarming Chinese soldiery. From Haincheng it was reported that another wing of the Japanese advance had taken the Niuchuang citadel while airplanes continued a bombing foray westward along the Laito river. A cruiser, two flotillas of destroyers, an aircraft carrier and a special service ship based at Jure and Sasebo, within cruising distance of ports near the Manchurian front, were ordered to prepare to sail for Chinwangtao. The order was believed intended to cut off a retreat by the Chinese. Earlier in the advance, Japanese troops captured Faukumen, one of the large

Istanbul, Turkey, Dec. 23.—(P)— Ten members of the passenger list and a crew of a Turkish boat were drowned today in a heavy blizzard which struck the Black Sea and Sea of Marmora. The boat, which was bringing passengers from Black Sea ports to Istanbul, was keeled over and sunk. A Greek ship grounded near Smyrna, but it can be saved, it was said.

Tokyo, Dec. 23—(2P)—The threat of Japanese action against Chinchow appeared to have been dispelled today with the receipt of press reports that the majority of Japanese troops had returned to the South Manchuria railway zone after three days of operations against bandits.

BASEL, Switzerland, Dec. 22—(A% ~The tenor of the report which the Reparations Committee expects to present as a Christmas present to the world tomorrow, is a veiled threat on the life of the two-year old Young Plan, it was reported tonight in international banking quarters. Just how straightforwardly the document will put the matter remained for tomorrow to reveal. It was expected, however, that the parts treating the Young Plan would be so veiled that the French may contend the text means the changes should be temporary on the theory that they will be valuable during the period of the present depression only. At the same time, it was said, the Germans, backed by Great Britain, the United States and the neutral members of the committee, may interpret the report as meaning death to the Young Plan.

MOSCOW, Dec. 23 (UP) — The newspaper Pravda asserted editorially today that responsibility for the Japanese occupation of Manchuria rests principally with the United States. The editorial laid the American attitude to the policies of Secretary of State Stimson which it described as directed at weakening Japan, excluding Japanese capital from inner China and at the provocation of conflict between Japan and Soviet Russia.

| STUTTGART, Germany, Dec. 22 (P)—With two firemen dead and 45 injured in two days of work, the “Altes Schloss” palace was still burning tonight and the flames were being whipped by a stiff wind. All available apparatus was continuing to fight the blaze but its efforts were ineffective. The damage was unofficially estimated at from four to six million marks.

1931-02-17.text: New Delhi, India, Feb. 17.—(A.P.)—For four hours this afternoon Mahatma Gandhi, gaunt leader of India’s restless millions, and Viceroy Lord Irwin, representative of the British empire, met in one of the strangest peace conferences history has ever witnessed. Neither would say much about what they had talked over but they let it be understood that their meeting had been mutually satisfactory and that they would continue their talk tomorrow. Viceroy Lord Irwin hoped in the negotiations to persuade Gandhi to call off the civil disobedience campaign and collaborate in the working out of a federation and dominion status for India in pursuance of plans evolved at the Indian round table conference.

New Delhi, India, Feb. 17, WA The Mahatma K. Gandhi, leader of the civil disobedience movement against British rule, appeared hopeful today of an early return of peace in India. Gandhi visited the viceroy, Lord Irwin, and they talked for four hours. The civil disobedience campaign, Gandhi's demands for amnesty for all political prisoners, the London round table conference proposals for a new constitution and other issues in the controversy were discussed by the Independence leader and the representative of King George.

London, Feb. 17.--(AP)--The sum of twenty million pounds—about £100,000,000—was added today to Britain's dole fund by the House of Commons, which last night accepted recommendations of Miss Margaret Bondfield, Minister of Labor, for new unemployment loans. The new grant pushed the total of the British unemployment fund from 70,000,000 pounds (about $250,000,000) to 90,000,000 pounds (about $450,000,000). The fund is already about $235,000,000 in debt.
Sydney, N.S.W., Feb. 22. (P)- Dame Nellie Melba, Australian diva who is critically ill here, was gradually sinking tonight.

MADRID, Feb. 16 (%)—King Alfonso today made the daring political gesture in an hour of crisis of inviting the enemies of his regime to help govern Spain and thereby, in the opinion of most political observers, saved the monarchy from the most menacing situation of recent history. The medium of his invitation was Jose Sanchez Guerra, a powerful political opponent of Alfonso himself, who tonight at the king’s request was working to form a ministry to replace that headed by Damaso Berenguer which resigned Saturday. The royal gesture had an immediate effect of restoring confidence. The stock exchange had one of the busiest sessions it has known for months. Values rose generally and bankers and business men expressed an optimism that has been long absent. New Delhi, India, Feb. 16.—(AP)—Peace in India now rests in the hands of Mahatma Gandhi, Lord Irwin, the viceroy said today, for the government is ready to concede most of his demands, if he will agree to call off his civil disobedience campaign and give some evidence of a “change of heart toward the government.” Lord Irwin has set aside all of tomorrow and the next day for conferences with the picturesque little man who is leading India’s campaign for independence, and today he spent several hours talking to three influential Indian delegates to the recent round table conference in London. Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, who is credited with having broken down Gandhi’s resistance to the point of arranging a personal talk with the viceroy, gave Lord Irwin his own ideas of the situation in a meeting also attended by Srimivasa Sastri and M. R. Jayakar. Benares, India, Feb. 16.—(AP)—Fifteen persons

Rome, Feb. 17.—(A.P.)—A panic of spectators at the Morgana theater resulted in injuries to scores tonight when part of the roof of the theater caved in. The building was filled with a crowd of Mardi Gras carnival holiday makers. Firemen tried unsuccessfully to prevent a panic, hacking great holes in the wall as emergency exits, but the crowd stampeded. Three ambulances carried off most of the seriously injured.

MADRID, Feb. 17. (WP)—Don Jose Sanchez Guerra today abandoned his efforts to form a cabinet to succeed that of Premier General Damasso Berenguer, resigned. He advised King Alfonso to ask Melquiades Alvarez to form a new government. Alvarez is leader of the Reformist Party, which like the Constitutionalists of Sanchez Guerra, desires to call an assembly to change the 1876 constitution with restrictions on the king's power. The failure of Sanchez Guerra was a surprise inasmuch as he had announced when he left his home to go to the palace that his cabinet was completed. “Everything now depends on the King,” he had said. However, when the former premier left the palace after about half an hour with King Alfonso, he described his abandonment of efforts to form a cabinet as due to failure “to obtain the support of certain factions.” “I declined to form a government because I am a man of the ri

1931-02-11.text: LONDON, Feb. 11—(#)—The Dole, it is officially estimated, cost the British taxpayer between $250,000,000 and $275,000,000 or even more during the financial year opening April 1, next. The figures are contained in a memorandum submitted by the British treasury to the royal commission on unemployment insurance. The memorandum drew attention to the gravity of the situation. “The increase of expenditure in 1930 over that of 1928 was $125,000,000," says the memorandum, “and the increase of 1931 over 1928 may amount to some $225,000,000. Even in the most favorable conditions so great an increase so swiftly incurred would overtax the budget. “In the present conditions it must be taken in conjunction with the other continuing liabilities of the state, both for the war debt and otherwise, and in these conditions it will not merely disturb but will entirely upset the equilibrium of the budget on t

LONDON, Feb. 11.—(U.P.)—The Stars and Stripes will float from many masts tomorrow and wreaths will be placed at the foot of a beloved statue in Parliament Square. In this simple, yet sincere way will United States citizens in London observe the 122nd anniversary of the birth of Abraham Lincoln. A handful of old, bent men, veterans of Civil War days, will place wreaths at the foot of Lincoln's statue which occupies a conspicuous place in Parliament Square just opposite Westminster Abbey.

SPF FORTE Sees YEW R OCT MT, LONDON, Feb. 11.—Three mysterious SOS signals intercepted by a channel steamer advising of a liner in distress 1,000 miles off the west Irish coast and carrying 300 passengers today puzzled maritime authorities. French and British wireless stations immediately sought to communicate with the stricken vessel, but were unable to establish contact. The operator of the cross-channel steamer Engadine, who intercepted the distress calls, was unable to catch the name of the vessel, distinguishing only the last two letters “us.”

Tokyo, Feb. 11.°-(AP)—Plans for a solo flight by Belja Yoshiwara across the Pacific via the Kurile and Aleutian islands were announced today by the vernacular newspaper ‘Hochi. The flight will be made in April. Yoshiwara plans nineteen stops, expecting to follow the route of the American army found the world fliers in 1924. The announcement said the flight was in the interest of Japanese-American friendship. The newspaper will sponsor the venture. Yoshiwara, 26 years old, studied aviation in Germany three years. He is known as “The Japanese Sea Gull.” He will use a light all-metal Junkers seaplane.

BERLIN, Feb. 11, (4)—The threat of a rump parliament was heard in Germany today from Fascist and Nationalist members of the Reichstag, but was not regarded seriously in government quarters. A spokesman for the two parties, whose Reichstag deputation marched out in a body yesterday shortly before an important address on foreign policy by Dr. Julius Curtius, said the Fascists might call an Opposition sitting at Weimar, birthplace of Germany's constitution. Rumors were current today that the Fascists, who recognize the leadership of Adolf Hitler, had taken night trains for Weimar but inquiry at their hotels brought the information that they were still registered. Even should the Fascists and Nationalists go through the motions of organizing a Reichstag at Weimar, government circles felt the organization would be more than a demonstration meeting. By The Associated Press: Berlin, Feb. 11--The opposition benches were empty this afternoon when the Reichstag convened to resume debate on foreign affairs. Apparently the national socialists and the nationalists were carrying out their threat, made yesterday, just before Foreign Minister Curtis began an outline of his policies, that they would stay out of the chamber until an important vote demanded their presence.

PARIS, (UP).—The French naval building program for 1931-32 has been completed for submission to the Chamber of Deputies late this week, asking for speedy construction of half a dozen formidable warships of the latest fighting type. The program, which totals 42,000 tons of projected ships, and definitely ends the “naval building truce” with Italy as a result of failure of negotiations between the two countries for a limitation agreement, was described to the United Press today as follows: One battle cruiser, a super-ship of 23,300 tons which will outclass the new “pocket battleship” type built by Germany. It will have a high speed and carry heavy armaments. A light cruiser of 7,000 tons. A light cruiser of 6,500 tons. A destroyer of the latest type, about 2,400 tons. KOBE, Japan, Feb 10—(P)—Boats searching the blizzard lashed waters of the Japanese coast last night picked up thirty persons counted as lost in the sinking of the Japanese steamer Kisusui Maru yesterday after a collision with the French steamer Porthos. Reports today from outlying ports said thirty rescued had been landed, leaving nineteen unaccounted for. The Kisusui Maru was bound for Shodo island in the Sea of Harima with Japanese returning to celebrate with their families the old style Japanese New Year when the collision with the Porthos occurred in the dense fog. The Kisusui Maru was sunk. The Porthos rescued twenty-five persons and landed them at Kobe today. Other vessels picked up additional survivors of Hyogo prefecture at the northern tip of Awaji island. The nineteen missing include women and children from factories of Okayama. The storm continued to rage with unabated fury se

1931-09-22.text: London, Sept. 22.—()—Rushed through parliament in record time and signed by a royal commission, the British government's emergency measure suspending the gold standard went into effect today for a period of six months. The stock exchange was closed for the second day. The House of Commons passed it just before closing time last night in spite of half-hearted attacks by labor back-benchers and the House of Lords required only two minutes to give it the necessary three readings. The commission acted for King George, who is in Scotland. There was no division on the final vote but the government won majorities of about 100 on successive closure motions. London, Sept. 22.—Great Britain entered its second day of six months suspension from the gold standard with signs of slow adjustment to new conditions, and the London stock exchange prepared to open tomorrow. Trading on the New York exchange went back to normal proportions with prices rallying slowly from yesterday's reaction to the British step. An official ban against short selling remained in force. The British pound sold at 104 francs ($4.077) and 105 francs ($4.11) at the opening of the official money market in Paris. I know you can't get any gold out of the Bank of England even with a check from the King endorsed by Gandhi. We got all the gold over here and look how pretty we are sitting. "Yeah." LONDON, Sept. 22.—British financial and political leaders today looked hopefully to an international conference to restore economic health to the world through a redistribution of the world’s gold supply. With the budget balanced on paper and suspension of the gold standard for six months approved by Parliament and King George on record time, experts considered a conference for redistribution of gold the next move in untangling the world economic situation. War debts may be included. Speaking of the necessity of a remedy for the conditions under which the United States and France hold 65 per cent of the world supply of By Ween Naser

Out of Great Britain’s decision to suspend the gold standard may come “a new era” in international financial relations, with greater co-operation to solve the world’s economic problems, experts predicted today. An international conference seeking to end the unsettled condition of foreign finances through redistribution of the world’s gold was under consideration in London. Such a conference would also attempt to solve such problems as war debts, reparations, and disarmament, all of which affect present-day conditions. Chancellor of the Exchequer Philip Snowden, in two speeches, urged the calling of an international meeting to end the “dislocation of gold reserves” under which 65 per cent of the world’s supply has been amassed by France and the United States. | LONDON, Sept. 21.—(#)— Unity for action in dealing with Great Britain’s dramatic suspension of the gold standard, latest phase of the national crisis, was pledged today by the House of Commons as factional differences were submerged to meet the emergency. It was three minutes of 11 o'clock when the bill passed its final stage. Eleven o'clock is the time fixed by rule for automatic adjournment of the house. It required two minutes in the House of Lords to give the bill three readings and pass it and immediately after this the members of the Commons were summoned to the House of Lords to hear the bill receive royal assent. TIPTON, Ia. Sept 22 — The rumble of marching men and the clatter of galloping horses heralded the arrival today of 1,800 guardsmen as Cedar county went under martial law in Iowa’s battle to enforce its compulsory Bovine tuberculosis testing law. Mobilized from a score of cities, the guardsmen arrived aboard special trains to quell a farmer revolt that has simmered for months in the courts, and broken into open violence on numerous occasions. Yesterday afternoon the outbreak occurred that led to the decision to call out the guard. Sheriffs and their deputies from many eastern Iowa counties were led by Joe Newell to the farm of Joe Lenker near Willow Junction. There were sixty-five of the officers, well armed and instructed to protect state veterinarians as they carried out the tests on Lenker's cattle. LONDON, Sept 22. (UP)—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald is feeling the effects of the fatigue and overstrain of the last few critical days, it was announced today. He will leave London tonight for several days' rest in the country.

1931-10-14.text: WASHINGTON, July 20—(4)— Ambassador Dawes and Senator Morrow conferred with President Hoover today concerning the German financial situation and the conferences growing out of it. Ambassador Dawes will sail for Great Britain on July 22 but it was said at the White House that Senator Morrow will remain here for several days. The New Jersey senator has been in frequent touch with the President during the negotiations over his moratorium proposal. Acting Secretary Castle of the State Department was summoned to the conference shortly after the President arrived. Coming from the conference later Secretary Castle said the President had talked to Secretary Stimson but there had been no overnight developments of any consequence.

Paris, Oct. 14, (UP) — Premier Pierre Laval said today that he is going to Washington in the hope of checking the world economic crisis. In a speech to the Anglo-American Press Association, an organization of English and American correspondents in Paris, he said: "I dare say because I am naturally optimistic that the gravity of events will not prevent us from finding fundamental solutions. My abilities are simple, like my character, but in order to serve the cause of our civilization with President Hoover, my ambition remains vast and my will firm. I desire my only guide to be that old French virtue, common sense."

Boston, Oct. 13.-Business in many of New England's smaller mills and industrial plants has turned the corner toward prosperity, the New England Council reports. A compilation of business trends from reports of chambers of commerce and boards of trade throughout the six New England States was characterized by the council as “the most encouraging in recent months.”

Seaham Harbor, Durham, England. Oct. 13 (P).—Ramsay MacDonald carried his campaign for re-election into the stronghold of his opposition among the radical miners today. This evening he spoke in halls packed with miners at Seaham Harbor and Murton. In the afternoon he addressed an audience at Dawdon, known as a Communistic center, and with one retort to a young Communist he silenced heckling that made the start of the meeting uncertain. “I'm a Communist and I'm against you,” the heckler shouted. “Of course you're against me,” the Prime Minister retorted, “A Communist is always against the interests of the working classes.” “For you the general election is the protection of Britain from the financial crisis which is going on in nation after nation and which, if it hit Britain disastrously, will leave the wreckage not of your bosses but of you,” he said. DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Oct. 13—-(AP)—-One of the most bitter parliamentary battles in Free State history will be fought out in the Dail Eireann during the next few days. Political observers declare it is not at all improbable that by the end of the week the government of President William T. Cosgrave will find its position untenable and will carry the battle to the country in a general election. The conflict will devolve upon the public safety bill which the government is introducing, when the Dail convenes tomorrow, as a result of disturbance; and terrorism during the last few months. While details of the measure have been kept secret it is understood it would confer extraordinary powers on police to deal with emergencies and would provide for the establishment of military courts for summary trial of persons charged with sedition or outrages.

By MILTON BRONNER European Manager, NEA Service (Copyright, 1931, NEA Service, Inc) London — The great army of British beer drinkers, plus those who prefer stronger beverages, pay approximately one fifth of all the money received in John Bull's treas- ury. Beer consumers enriched the gov- ernment by $340,000,000 during the last financial year, while imbibers of whisky, wine, gin and other liquors paid nearly $200,000,000 more. London, Oct. 13.—Unemployment in Great Britain for the week of October 5 decreased by 33,252 from the previous week. The total was 2,791,520, which was 615,329 more than at the same time a year ago. The popular explanation of the decrease is a revival of British industry because of abandonment of the gold standard.

Madrid, Oct. 14. ()—Niceto Alcala Zamora, for six months president of the Spanish republic, resigned this afternoon and his whole cabinet stepped out also in protest against passage of the chamber of deputies of radical anti-Catholic legislation which the cabinet had disapproved. Alejandro Lerroux, the foreign minister, broke the news to the chamber. In the midst of his announcement he interrupted himself to call for three cheers for the republic. The answer was a rousing demonstration, with the deputies and spectators joining in. Who Is Next? There was wide speculation regarding the choice of a man to form a new government, but the general expectation was that Manuel Azana, retiring minister of war, would be chosen. Stimson returned from abroad today with an optimistic prediction that a lasting structure of peace and economic prosperity will be built on the foundation laid by President Hoover's moratorium and the recent seven-power conference in London. During his two-month stay in Europe, the Secretary of State attended the London conference and held "informal conversations" with the prime ministers of England, France, Germany, and Italy. A Lasting Structure. Asked by newspaper men for his views about the general financial situation throughout the world, Stimson replied: "I think there is now good reason to believe that European statesmen, taking advantage of the respite granted by Mr. Hoover's moratorium as well as the recommendations of the London conference, are beginning gradually to lay the foundations of political goodwill, upon which a last

LONDON, England, Sept. 2.—(AP) The National Cabinet completed its new taxation program at a five-hour meeting today and a call was issued for Parliament to meet in special session September 8, to enact the program into law. The government made it clear there will be no dilly-dallying in the House of Commons by deciding to ask for a vote of confidence the opening day of the session without explaining the economy and taxation program designed to cope with the national financial emergency. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald will ask the House to declare without delay, whether it will place its trust in the three-party administration which he heads. Then, if the expected vote of confidence is forthcoming, Phillip Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer will make a full statement setting forth the entire budget balancing scheme. Snowden will appear before Parliament Thursday, it was learned tonight

CHICAGO, OP. Officials of the Illinois Bank and Trust Company announced Walter Wolfe, a veteran employee, had confessed to embezzling "a substantial but undetermined sum" from the bank's bond department. Lloyds of London, under which the bank employees are bonded, estimated the defalcations at $3 million. The bank, the largest in the city, is protected against loss by insurance. George H. Reynolds, chairman of the bank's executive committee, issued the following statement Tuesday night: "Walter Wolfe, manager of the coupon department of the Continental-Illinois Bank and Trust Company, has confessed to officials of the bank that he has embezzled securities from the bank over a period of years, most of which have been taken in the last two or three years. These securities were used in speculations in the stock and grain market. An audit is now being made and until the audit is completed, t

LONDON, Sept. 3. — Dispatches today to the Exchange Telegraph Company from Advent Bay, Spitzbergen, indicated that weak radio communication had been established with the polar submarine Nautilus. Captain Jaeger of the Steamer Ingertraede reported that he heard "weak and indistinguishable" radio signals, believed to have come from Sir Hubert Wilkins' submarine, at 9:50 p.m., Wednesday. The Nautilus had been out of touch with the world since Saturday.

LONDON, Sept. 2.—(INS)—The great cathedral of Moscow, one of the most historic edifices in Russia, was blown up by the Soviet authorities with appropriate ceremonies today to make room for a new Soviet development, it was stated in an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Berlin. On the site of the cathedral will be built “the palace of the grand plan,” commemorating successful completion of the Soviet government’s five-year plan. The edifice was built by Alexander I to commemorate the defeat of Napoleon at Moscow. Long one of the chief places of worship for Orthodox Russians, the cathedral was capable of holding 10,000 persons.

ARABIA, —— Mahatma Gandhi, clad in a loin cloth, was surrounded by thousands of curious Arabs, Jews, and Somalis when he came ashore here from the Steamer Rajputana Thursday. The Mahatma is en route to London to attend the second round table conference of Indian affairs. Gandhi squatted on a table and discussed India’s national affairs. He re-embarked at 9 a. m.

ADEN, Arabia, Sept. 3.—( Mahatma Gandhi and his arrived here at the entrances the Red Sea today and made a brief visit ashore before resuming their voyage to London for the round table conference: A large crowd of excited Indians wearing Gandhi caps, who had waited since midnight, cheered as the S. S. Rajputana steamed alongside the wharf at dawn. Local Indian merchants presented him a purse containing about $1,625. Asked what his program at the conference would be, Gandhi replied: "I shall strive for a constitution that will release India from all thraldom and patronage. I shall work for an India in which the poorest shall feel it is their country in whose making they have an effective voice; an India in which there shall be no high and no low class of people; an India in which all communities shall live in perfect harmony. ROME, Sept. 2—(P)—A final accord was reached by Pope Pius XI and Premier Mussolini today in their bitter three-month controversy over Catholic action clubs, clarifying the conditions of the Lateran treaty and the concordat. The Pope's youth organizations are allowed to resume their activities but are restricted to purely religious endeavors. It was specifically stated there should be no sports or athletics and no intrusion into the syndical or trades union fields. The Italian government announced an agreement of three parts. They are as follows: 1. Catholic action organizations are essentially diocesan under the control of bishops who appoint club officers and directors, none of whom may be from parties hostile to Fascism. "Solution of the world economic crisis lies in repeal of prohibition laws in the United States and the correction of similar mistakes," Bernard Baruch, American economist and financier, told the United Press today. — Baruch called the economic situation neither desperate nor insoluble. He advised that nations follow the advice of Adam Smith, "all that is needed to raise a nation from the lowest barbarism to happiness and peace is easy taxes and a fair administration of justice." Baruch indicated that a solution might be found in the formation of an organization to address difficulties, particularly Franco-German uneasiness, and by the repeal of prohibition. DOUGLAS, Isle of Man, Sept. 5, —(#)—Sir Hall Caine, who during his life was regarded as one of the wealthiest of Great Britain’s contemporary writers, left a personal estate of $1,000,000. His will was filed today. This does not include his real estate holdings and the value of his literary products. The estate is divided among his widow, his daughter and his two sons. The trustees are directed to continue publication of the author's books and plays as long as there is a demand for them. There are no death duties in the Isle of Man as in England, where they would have taken approximately fifty percent of the estate. Sir Hall died Monday.

(AP)—Sir Hubert Wilkins reported by radio from his polar submarine Nautilus this evening that the craft had been damaged in a dive under the ice pack, but the damage was not of serious nature. OSLO, Norway, Sept. 5. (INS)—With wireless communication re-established after a silence of five days, Capt. Sir Hubert's submarine Nautilus reported today it had safely battled its way out of the arctic ice-pack. Messages received here reported Sir Hubert had succeeded in penetrating far below the ice-caked surface of the polar sea, cruising for long periods in a hitherto unexplored marine world below the pack ice. Approaching to within a few hundred miles of the pole, the submarine dove under the ice-pack and cruised beneath a canopy of ice whose underside had never before been seen by man. BARCELONA, Sept. 5 (P)—The general strike of syndicalists which was called off last night after sanguinary clashes between strikers and police was resumed today. The two-day uprising has cost 23 lives to date. Firing continued throughout the night despite assurances of syndicalist leaders that their men would go back to work today.

Geneva, Sept. 6.—(AP)—The proposed Austro-German customs union, already renounced by the foreign ministers of both countries, was ruled illegal Saturday by a decision of the world court at The Hague, voting eight to seven. The court's decision read: “The regime established between Germany and Austria on the basis of and within the limits of the principles laid down by the protocol of March 19, 1931, would not be compatible with protocol No. 1, signed at Geneva on Oct. 4, 1922.” It agreed with a forecast made during the past week by those in touch with political affairs that Austria would be forbidden to pursue the scheme, a source of alarm to France and nations of the little entente particularly. Frank B. Kellogg, former secretary of state, was among seven judges who joined in a dissenting opinion saying that in their opinion the projected union would be compatible both with article 88 o

TOKIO, SEPT. 4. (AP)—The American embassy revealed today that Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh will continue their vacation flight to China September 10. Their plans were approved by the Japan aviation bureau. An application through the American embassy disclosed that the couple planned to take off from the Kasumigaura naval base near here September 10 for Osaka, near where they will spend a few days at several scenic points.

CALCUTTA, India--From the Jamura river district a message arrived today telling of Moyer Vddin, a native, who swam down the river, hanging on the tail of a man-eating tiger. Cheers of the villagers ashore changed to groans as the animal turned and tried to bite, but Moyer jammed a club in the tiger's mouth and continued downstream until the villagers captured the cat. Moyer found the beast stranded by the flood on a raft of fallen trees and decided to capture him. The animal leaped into the native's craft which capsized.

1931-04-03.text: Malaga, Spain, Apr. 2—(AP)—Thirty-one bodies were recovered today from the wreckage of the French steamer Florida following her collision with the British aircraft carrier Glorious in a dense fog 66 miles off Gibraltar yesterday. Authorities were continuing the search for additional bodies, but because of the confusion it could not be definitely established whether or not others were missing. The bodies which were identified included 17 Italians, five Syrians, four Poles, one Russian, three Slavs and one Spaniard. All of them were steerage passengers, chiefly emigrés returning to their native countries. The Florida was struck between the bow and bridge. It was here that the majority of the casualties occurred. This section of the steerage was occupied chiefly by Italian emigrés. In spite of mist, planes from the aircraft carrier flew overhead and witnessed the accident. The flying deck o

Malaga, Spain, April 2.—(#7)— Victims of a terrific head-on collision between the French steamer Florida and the British aircraft carrier Glorious, more than 30 bodies and upward of 50 injured persons were being brought ashore today from the two vessels. While the wreckage of the Florida still is being searched, the total dead tentatively was placed at 33. They include 17 Italians, four Poles, one Russian, three Jugoslavs, five Syrians and one Spaniard. Most of them were returning to their native lands from Buenos Aires. The collision occurred yesterday in a fog in the Mediterranean about 30 miles west of here. Terror Follows Crash Survivors described the scenes of terror after the crash in which the Glorious ripped through the bow of the Florida, grinding steerage passengers to death, splintering bones and mangling bodies, and twisting the framework of the ship into a tangled mass of st

Buenos Aires, April 3.—Kaye Don, the English speed driver, who set a new world record for motor boats in a dash down the Parana river yesterday, told the United Press before his departure for London today that he would ‘try again’ should his present mark of 103.49 miles an hour be shattered. “I believe Miss England II is unbeatable at present,” said Don. “I am quite willing to make another attempt should Gar Wood (the former record holder) break my record.” The former world record was 102.256 miles an hour, set by Gar Wood recently in Florida. Wood broke the record of the late Major Sir H. O. D. Segrave of England, the original owner of Miss England II.

LONDON, April 2.—(AP)—A Malaga dispatch to the Evening News said today it was impossible to ascertain definitely the number of dead aboard the French liner Florida since they were trapped in the mass of debris of the liner’s smashed port bow. No bodies have been recovered. The dispatch said it was believed between eight and thirty had been killed. It was at first thought only members of the crew were dead but it is now regarded as a possibility that some of them are passengers. The Florida collided in a dense fog for sixty miles east of Gibraltar with the British aircraft Glorious which was participating in maneuvers there. Arrangements were being made, the message said, for landing the passengers and injured. The Glorious reported that she was seaworthy and would proceed from Malaga to Gibraltar, arriving there tomorrow.

LONDON, April 2—-(AP)— Lady Doyle, widow of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, novelist and spiritualist leader, said today she had “one hundred percent proof” that she recently had been in communication with her husband, who died last July. She said of the communication that “anyone can see it is genuine in light of the evidence.” Several times the widow has told of receiving messages from Sir Arthur, but she has always refused to disclose their nature. She indicated she may sell the “evidence” of the communications to help the spiritualist cause.

MADRID, April 3 (P)—A report that King Alfonso might go into voluntary exile was denied emphatically today by Premier Aznar of Spain. "It is too ridiculous to deny such a report," one palace official said. "Undoubtedly the king will again go to London to visit his mother-in-law. He may go soon and the queen may accompany him, although no plans are made and no dates fixed. But to talk about his not returning to Spain is absurd."

New York, April 2 (4)—The bureau for street traffic research at Harvard has put out a manual in an effort to elevate the conversation of traffic cops. The purpose is to induce the cops to cut out the rough stuff and talk English. "Whadda ya think you're driving—a fire truck?" And "this ain't no speedway, lady" are looked upon as very bad form. The proper approach, the manual suggests, is for the officer to say: "I'm sorry, sir, but you were driving 45 miles an hour, and I shall be obliged to give you a summons." Doubtless officers throughout America will mail the suggestion with delight and put into immediate effect.

BUENOS AIRES, April 3 (AP)— A new world’s speed boat record was hailed here today—103.49 statute miles per hour, made by Kaye Don, British racer, in Miss England II on the surface of the muddy, swollen Parana river yesterday afternoon. The mark, which will be certified to the International Racing Association at Brussels by the Argentine Yacht Club, which supervised the timing, beats the record of 102.56 miles per hour set recently by the American, Gar Wood, at Miami Beach. Don’s efforts were made in connection with the British trade exposition, which is in progress here. The Miss England II is the same boat in which Major H. O. D. Segrave met his death.

LONDON, July 23. —A historic Seven Power Statesmen’s Conference ended today with the adoption of measures designed to save Germany from financial ruin. The United Press was informed from a reliable source of unofficial authority that the plenary session approved the report of finance ministers suggesting ways and means of temporarily solving the German crisis. Following the Conference, delegates appeared optimistic expressing opinions of real progress made.

WASHINGTON, July 2. President Hoover said today the London conference had “laid sound foundations for the establishment of stability in Germany.” The program adopted by the conference, he said, supplements the suspension of inter-government debts already in effect. “The combined effect,” he added, “should enable the German people with their resources, industry and courage, to overcome the temporary difficulties and restore their credit.” At the same time the president forwarded telegrams of congratulation to Secretaries Stimson and Mellon, who conducted the American negotiations in London.

(Associated Press Staff Writer) London, July 22 (*)-~-The committee of finance ministers of the seven-power conference announced tonight that it had decided on a plan for economic and financial aid to Germany and that the plan would be presented tomorrow to what may be the final plenary session of the conference. The plan, it was understood, would include measures intended to give Germany at least a 90-day “reprieve” in her struggle against financial and economic difficulties. It includes a proposal for extending for three months the $100,000,000 credit from the World Bank for International Settlements and other measures chiefly concerned with the prevention of withdrawals of foreign investments in Germany and with general aid for Germany's finances and those of the Reichsbank. 1931-09-15.text: BELIZE, British Honduras, Sept. 14—Fire threatened to complete the destruction of storm and flood today as the work of burying and cremating the dead from last week's hurricane, now estimated at more than a thousand, went forward. The suburb of Mesopotamia was menaced by flames that spread rapidly in spite of unceasing efforts on the part of soldiers and civilians to block their path. An inflammable liquor warehouse was in the path of the conflagration and fears of an explosion spurred the fighters to frantic measures. Scores of bodies were burned on five great pyres almost in the center of the once-flourishing city, now in ruins. At least 700 bodies were buried in crude trenches dug in the cemetery by convict labor. Still more bodies floating down river from the interior made an accurate check of the dead impossible. Cremation was resorted to because of the fear of disease. Squads of vo

By The Associated Press. London, Sept. 15.—In the soft, deliberate voice America heard over the radio on Sunday Mahatma Gandhi today presented to the federal structures committee of the Indian roundtable conference his demand for home rule and self-determination in India. Speaking for that teeming mass which he has characterized as “India’s dumb millions,” he declared that he had come to London in a spirit of co-operation and that he was determined to strive to the utmost for an agreement. If at any time he finds that he is not serving a useful purpose, he said, he will withdraw from the conference. He demanded complete self-government for India and granting of all the other conditions enumerated in the Karachi mandate given him by the nationalists of India. India, he said, is willing to remain a partner in the British Empire, but that partnership must be such that it may be terminated a

(By The Associated Press.) London, Sept. 14.— The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, carrying a bottle of goat's milk for his midday meal, went to St. James Palace before noon today to attend as a silent observer the first meeting of the federal structures committee formed to draw up a new constitution for India. Pledged not to talk because Monday is “his day of silence,” he was driven to the palace in a small closed car, along with Mme. Sarojini Naidu and her secretary. He was wearing his customary loincloth and shawl, for the possible injury when the car collided with a stone support as it was entering the yard. He was thrown forward in the seat, but appeared none the worse for his experience. Although Gandhi usually sits on his haunches, today he took a chair just as other delegates. CALSHOT, ENG., SEPT. 14. (AP).—British aviators were surprised and somewhat disappointed today when it was announced that the figures to be submitted for official approval in connection with Lieutenant G. H. Stainforth’s attack on the new speed record yesterday will be 379.05 miles an hour instead of 386.1, as unofficially given out yesterday. The reduced figure still constitutes a new world speed record, however. The error in yesterday's figure was due to the use of stopwatches by the timekeeper. Having won the trophy two years in succession, Great Britain gained permanent possession through the withdrawal of the French and Italian entries at the eleventh hour.

The wholesale burial or cremation of victims without identification made it likely that their exact number never will be known. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald made such a suggestion at the London Naval Conference in 1930, but it was dropped because of American opposition. Now, it was learned, this suggestion has been renewed informally, as a step which would start the Geneva disarmament conference off to a favorable start as happened at the Washington Arms Conference. British statements advance arguments that the battleship has lost its major usefulness, that it is the greatest source of expense in naval budgets, and the best place at which to effect large economies. Gandhi, wearing his loin cloth, addressed the federal structure committee of the round table conference today and offered to withdraw from the negotiations if by so doing he would further the efforts to reach an agreement on India. Gandhi, seated on a chair by the side of Lord Sankey in the red and gold entree room of St. James’ palace, spoke 40 minutes. His tones were quiet, deliberate and low, and he spoke without notes. He said he was participating in the conference “absolutely in the spirit of co-operation” and that he would strive to the utmost to find points of agreement. Be assured the government and the committee that he did not desire to embarrass the conference and promised that whatever different points of view arose, he would not obstruct them. “At any time, if I find I cannot usefully serve the conference,” Gandhi said, “I will not hes

LONDON, Sept. 14—(/)—British and Indian political leaders gathered as the federal structures committee preparing for the second round table conference on Indian affairs today heard numerous diplomatic speeches expressing hope the great Indian problem might finally be settled—but Mahatma Gandhi was wrapped in his dhoti (shawl) and said nothing. During the morning and early afternoon Gandhi fared well, for sunlight poured through the window at his back. But as the day advanced the sun passed, and a short time before adjournment, he got up without a word and departed. The leader of India’s Nationalist millions said nothing today because Monday is his day of silence. Saying nothing, he still dominated the meeting, for behind him are the millions who made possible the civil disobedience movement that crippled British business in India. 1931-03-25.text: LONDON, March 25.—David Lloyd George today was able to promise the labor government of Prime Minister MacDonald probably sufficient labor support to keep it in office indefinitely, provided it asks parliament to do nothing offensive to Liberal principles. The parliamentary liberal party, in an eight hour private meeting last night, voted 33 to 17 in endorsement of a statement of policy drawn up by Lloyd George which must become the keynote of labor legislative policy if labor is to remain in power. The 17 votes cast against the doughty Liberal leader, who many believe engaged in a fight to culminate his brilliant political career with another term as premier marked a highwater mark for the Sir John Simon opposition group, whose watchword has become “turn the rascals out.” The terms of the Liberal statement of policy were withheld for publication but they are understood to involve no depa

Madrid, March 24.—(P—Bullets pattered in the streets of Madrid, Tuesday, as King Alfonso, returned only Tuesday morning from a visit to his mother-in-law in London, sat in his palace worrying over the rats which three days of liberty had brought to his capital. These were the highlights of an exciting day. Aleala Zamora, who proclaimed the republic last December, was released from prison under suspended sentence of six months and a day. Several of his companions in the December movement were liberated with him. Santiago Alba, powerful liberal leader, came home after eight years of self-imposed exile, placed himself at the head of the constitutionalists and in an uncompromising manifesto declared political war on Premier Aznar and called upon the king to take a vacation while a constitutional convention decides whether Spain shall remain a monarchy or become a republic.
