NEW YORK, Mar. 25—(AP)—The net value of the estate of the Princess Von Hatefelt-Wildenburg has been fixed by state tax authorities at $1,595,694. The adopted daughter of the late Collis P. Huntington, railroad builder, died in England in 1928. The estate was left in trust to friends:

LONDON, MAR. 25. (AP) -- Rallying after their recent defeat in attempting to introduce prohibition into Great Britain by act of parliament, the temperance forces today sought to curtail liquor advertisements which flare over town and country through the Isles. The Commons rejected the move by a vote of 127 to 112.

WINDSOR, Eng., April 29. (AP)—The Prince of Wales and his brother George arrived here at one o'clock this afternoon from Le Bourget airport, ending an 18,000-mile tour to South America. Their plane, City of Glasgow, dropped down in Windsor Park near the ancient castle where King George and Queen Mary were awaiting them. They had come home in the same manner as they left, by air. Their arrival was informal and unostentatious, with scarcely a cheer from the waiting crowd. It was as though the heir to the British throne had just returned from one of those week-end hops to the continent instead of one of the most important missions he had performed.

St. John’s, N. F., March 25. (P)— Bernt Balchen and his airplane crew were back at their base at Cornerbrook today after their first flight over the ice-filled waters of White Bay in search of Varick Frissell and others missing from the wrecked sealer Viking. With Merion Cooper of New York, organizer of the airplane search, and his relief pilot, Randy Enslow, Balchen flew to Horse Island yesterday and scanned an area 15 miles eastward of the island. They saw no trace of any of the 26 still missing. The expedition was organized at the behest of Dr. Lewis Frissell, father of Varick Frissell, motion picture producer who was on the Viking with two companions to make pictures of the seal hunt. Another of the missing is A. G. Penrod, cameraman. Robert F. Fogg, another flier, who was marooned on the ice with a companion Monday when the skis of his plane broke, was at Hampden today. He succeeded

MADRID, Mar. 25 (—After a four hour battle in which one policeman was killed and a score of police and students were wounded, rebellious students of the San Carlos Medical school abandoned the fortified building today. Police made no effort to detain the students. Eight police were known to have been seriously wounded and perhaps 20 students. Two of the youths were in a critical condition, one with a bullet in the lung and the other with one in the stomach. The students had barricaded within the school building to repel the attacks of the authorities. The red banner of revolution floated openly above the school and its roofs teemed with students watching the fray. The streets were congested for blocks. Students outside the building threw stones at the police. The government was understood to be prepared to suppress further republican outbreaks. The republican leader, Niceto Alcala Zamora

PARIS, Mar. 25—(4)—The international reaction resulting from the Austro-German customs accord seemed to be eased today with the prospect that the matter would go before the council of the League of Nations, probably next May. The council will be asked, it was indicated, whether the Austro-German accord violates the Geneva protocol and the St. Germain treaty, as the French allege. The first hint of the possible submission of the question to the league council was suggested in a communique issued by the British embassy today. In it Arthur Henderson, British foreign minister, expressed strong hope that before the Austrian and German governments pursued their negotiations the league council, under whose auspices the Geneva protocol of 1922 was consummated, 'would be given an opportunity to assure itself that the proposals were not contrary to Austria’s engagements under the protocol.'

1931-01-19.text: ) LONDON, Jan. 14 (P)—Ramsay MacDonald today brought the round table conference to a close, extending a welcoming hand to India as a dominion in the British Commonwealth of Nations with full responsible self-government. The work begun at London will be continued without interruption, he said, and the new Indian constitution will be passed through the British parliament as soon as it is completed. This pronouncement of British policy pledged liberation to India’s 50,000 political prisoners if “civil quiet is proclaimed and assured” in India. In a long declaration of British government policy, the weight of government support was pledged to the findings of the committees of the round table conference which has been laboring in London for two months. These envisage a national federal government of India along the general lines of the United States Congress, with a Senate and House of Repres

SANTANDER, Spain, Jan. 19 (#) After an exciting trip from Paris, the Prince of Wales and his youngest brother, Prince George, were en route today aboard the liner Oropesa on an 18,000-mile journey which will culminate with their inauguration of the British trade exhibition in Buenos Aires in March. The prince’s trouble began late Saturday night when their train was held up 30 miles below Bordeaux by the derailment of a northbound train from the Spanish frontier. Awakened by the halt, both watched the work of clearing the track. French railroad officials at Bayonne sent a special train north to pick them up and carry them to Hendaye. There, already four hours late, they transferred to motor cars, beginning a dangerous ride over sloppy mountain roads to Santander, watering place of the Spanish kings. At Bilbao the automobile occupied by the Prince of Wales careened into that which Prince G

LONDON, Jan. 19.—(AP)—Ramsay MacDonald, beginning his long awaited pronouncement on British policy in India, today told delegates to the Indian round table conference that he accepted the idea of an all-Indian federation at the desire of the round table delegates. He read a declaration by the government deciding to transfer full responsibility for the government of India to the federal and provincial legislatures. The work of negotiations for the future Indian government will be continued without interruption, he said, but details of the structure are still to be decided on. “It is a great achievement,” he said, “both for India and Great Britain. We are grateful to you.” The Indians, said the prime minister, must settle their own communal disputes, for Britain is ‘neither pro-Hindu, pro-Moslem, nor pro-any section of the Indian population. “The attitude of the British government,” he tol

[United Press Staff Correspondent] LONDON—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, delivering the labor government’s declaration of policy to the India round table conference today, announced readiness to grant amnesty to the thousands of political prisoners in India if civil order were assured. The round table conference, which convened on Nov. 12 in an attempt to form a basis for a new Indian constitution, ended at 4:20 p.m. without having achieved its full purpose but with a record which was generally described as “a successful failure.” 50,000 in Jails There are more than 50,000 political prisoners in India. The prime minister expressed sympathy for the political prisoners and the followers of the imprisoned Mahatma M. K. Gandhi in the Indian civil disobedience campaign. He expressed regret that they had boycotted the round table conference and were not represented in the deliberations of so
MANCHESTER, England, Jan 19.—Two Royal Air Force officers were killed and nine persons were injured today when a Royal Air Force bombing plane crashed at the airdrome at Worthydown.

London, Jan. 18.—(4?)—With re-assembling of parliament on Tuesday, Great Britain’s labor government will face a series of tests, any one of which it is believed in some quarters may result in the overthrow of the government. The battle is expected to start Wednesday over the government’s education bill, now in committee stage.

TUCSON, Ariz., Jan. 19 (PB) — Lady Victor Bruce, British aviatrix en route around the world by ship and airplane, took off for Midland, Tex., at 8:50 a. m. M. S. T. today. She had spent the night here, having flown from San Diego yesterday, with a stop at Phoenix. Lady Bruce said Midland would be her next stop unless she decided to drop in on El Paso.

London, Jan. 15.—(AP)—Joy over settlement of the South Wales coal strike was mixed with gloom tonight over a shutdown in the cotton industry affecting 250,000 weavers. The shutdown occurred at noon yesterday at Lancashire as a result of a lockout declared by the employers after a strike in the Burnley area against a system of having each weaver tend more looms than customary. No Settlement in Sight Most of the employees affected are women and girls, no immediate settlement of the dispute was indicated and grave fears were entertained that the whole cotton industry employing a half million workers might be brought to a standstill within the next few days.

1931-01-28.text: (Copyright 1931, By The Associated Press) Bombay, British India, Jan. 27.— ‘Mahatma Gandhi, toothless, shriveled wraith of a man, sat cross-legged on a stone floor today, serving notice on the British empire that India’s campaign of civil disobedience would continue unabated, while outside a frantic crowd, mad for a glimpse of him, struggled so furiously that a woman was crushed to death. Thirty-one others were injured in the crush. Naked but for a homespun loin cloth, he leaned against a hay mattress in the center of a circle of newspaper men, an expression of deep melancholy on his ascetic face, but an almost spiritual light in his eyes. “We can suspend judgment on Prime Minister MacDonald’s statement to the round table conference at London,” he said, “but we cannot suspend the activities of the Indian congress and of the approaching peace talks with delegates returning from the round

London—Britain’s second labor government, approaching its third year, Wednesday faced a critical commons vote with confidence that its master politician, J. Ramsay MacDonald, had maneuvered the ministry to another victory. The promised abstention of the rank and file of the liberal party from voting in the division on the second reading of the trades dispute bill made it pretty certain that the government would be upheld by a majority of from 15 to 30 votes. A dozen explanations were current today in the parliamentary lobbies for the prospective ministerial victory in what a week ago appeared to offer a probability of government overthrow. The simplest and most plausible of these was that David Lloyd George, liberal leader, considered that, however bad a labor ministry, it was to be preferred to a conservative government and would lend his aid in keeping the labor government in power unt

Baltimore, Jan. 27 (#).— Slightly injured when her plane overturned here late today as she neared the end of a trip around the world, Mrs. Mildred Bruce, British flier, decided to forego a reception at the British embassy at Washington tonight. She escaped with a bruise over the left eye and a cut on her right hand, but was badly shaken, and said she would remain at a hotel here overnight, while repairs were made on the plane. The propeller was broken and one wing bent. The accident occurred in view of a large group of spectators at the Glenn L. Martin airport when the plane’s wheels sunk in mud off the packed runway. Mrs. Bruce said she felt the pull of the mire and turned on more power suddenly in the hope of pulling free in one spurt. The spectators saw the plane flop over and ran up to extricate the flier. But she climbed out alone and displayed concern only over the damage to the sh

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS San Francisco, Cal., Jan. 27.—The British motorship Enton with a crew of 60 to 75 men was aground on a reef near the island of New Caledonia today and leaking badly. New Caledonia is in the South Seas about 1,500 miles northeast of Sydney, Australia. A distress signal was picked up by the Dollar liner President Madison, 4,000 miles away and relayed to the United States naval radio station at Honolulu and to the Mussel Rock station here.

London, Today.— (AP)— Physicians attending Princess Beatrice, 74 year old aunt of King George, who is suffering from a broken arm and acute bronchitis, regard her condition as “not without anxiety.” Queen Victoria, of Spain, her daughter, is hurrying to London to be at her bedside. The physicians said the broken arm of the Princess was making satisfactory progress, but that danger lay in the bronchitis. The medical bulletin issued this morning said: “Her Royal Highness, the Princess Beatrice, has had a fairly restful night. Her general condition remains unchanged.”

LISBON, Portugal, Jan. 28.—(?)— The DO-X, giant German seaplane, made a trial flight this forenoon in preparation for takeoff tomorrow on a transatlantic flight to Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The flight was a complete success, and proved the efficiency of recent repairs to one of the wings, which was burned several weeks ago after the ship came here from Altenrhein. The idea of the trial was to see how the 12 American motors would function with a maximum load of 26 tons of fuel, to accommodate which all furniture, carpets and other ornaments were taken off the ship. Capt. Christiansen said the ship's course would be by way of Madeira, Cape Verde, the Canary Islands and Natal. Stops en route for fueling are

BOMBAY, Jan. 28. (/P)—Leaving behind him a message to India’s nationalist millions that their fight for independence must go on, Mahatma Gandhi today speeded by train toward Allahabad, a Central Indian city, where are gathered most of the nationalist working committee. At Allahabad, India’s “City of God,” located on the sacred Ganges, he will visit the bedside of one of his dearest friends, the aged Pandit Motilal Nehru, father of Jawaharlal Nehru, president of the All India National Congress, and discuss with him Britain's offer of an eventual qualified dominion status for India. He faces in Allahabad, when he arrives there tonight, a welcome probably as enthusiastic and frenzied as that which tens and hundreds of thousands gave him here yesterday upon his arrival from eight months in Yeroda prison. In the crush, which centered about his frail 96-pound body one woman was trampled to dea

Stockholm, Sweden, Jan. 27.—Death today closed the adventurous career of Captain Einar-Paal Lundborg, Swedish airman who rescued General Umberto Nobile after the destruction of the airship Italia on an ice floe in the Arctic. He died this evening from injuries suffered a few hours before in the crash of a plane he was testing at Malmslätt flying field for the Swedish government. Although both arms and legs were fractured in the accident, it was expected that his strong constitution would pull him through. A relapse came, however, and he sank rapidly. Rescued Italia Chief Captain Lundborg had many adventures and served as a soldier under four flags, but his major achievement was the rescue of General Nobile. He was a member of the Swedish rescue expedition and on the night of June 24, 1928, set out in a Fokker machine to seek the survivors of the Italia disaster. He managed to land his ma

1931-11-12.text: Dublin, Nov. 12—(UP)— Civil guards and police established a firm grip in Irish Free State cities today to end violent Republican disorders begun Armistice Day by screaming demonstrators. The streets of Dublin were in turmoil until late last night. Mobs tore down and burned British flags, shouted, “down with the king,” and clashed with heavily armed guard patrols. Government and pro-British buildings were stoned. The disturbances ranged from Republican demonstrations to Communist outbursts. Their gravity was increased by the strong protests against the government of President William T. Cosgrave, which recently enforced a law for public safety which put the Free State under strict semi-military rule. The law was designed to end political terrorism. One of the most serious clashes with civil guards occurred when a large crowd stampeded through the streets, carrying posters inscribed “we pr

NEW YORK, Nov. 12 (AP)—A 73-year-old skipper who once bossed Jack London is repairing his 40-foot yawl at Annapolis, Md., after a terrible adventure in which he lost his sight, sailed blindly through a heavy sea and finally wrecked his craft on a fish trap. Capt. H. E. Raabe, who was a slave and ebony trader in the Solomon Islands half a century ago, left Port Washington, Long Island, several weeks ago, alone in his small craft, bound for the South Seas. Nothing was heard of him here until a letter, dated Nov. 6, was received by a friend, George O’Brien, of Jersey City, N. J. On Nov. 2, he said, he was sailing under half gale from the north in Chesapeake Bay. Loses Eyesight “The sun was sinking,” the letter said, “To my surprise the glare on the water became unbearable. I looked up at the mainsail. What a shock! It had turned from white to black. An optical illusion, of course. “The sky,

London, Nov. 11 (/P)—The movement for tariff protection gained new headway today as the House of Commons was giving the government a majority of 369 in the first vote since it was convened. The only opposition, totaling nine votes, came from labor left-wing members, the regular labor party abstaining from the balloting. The question at issue was a motion to take the time allowed for discussion of bills presented by private members. The tariff question was brought up by Winston Churchill, who declared his constituency was heavily in favor of doing away with free trade and trying a 'substantial experiment' in tariffs. Mr. Churchill said it was his belief most of the members of the house represented electors who wanted protection.

Lexington, Ky., Nov. 12. Lady Mary Heath, English aviatrix, announced today she would be married at noon to George Anthony Reginald Williams, an Englishman, now making his home in New York. Both Lady Mary and Mr. Williams came here to attend the Prince of Wales Steeplechase this afternoon. He talked little but she explained he is the son of the Rt. Hon. George Williams, a government official of the Windward Islands, and said they had been engaged a year. Lady Mary said she and Mr. Williams had not expected to be married here and that she brought no special clothes for the event. “I'm just going to wear an old black dress,” she said. “This is the first time I have ever been married to a young man,” Lady Mary said, alluding to the fact that he is just a year younger. “one near my own age. I was married to my first husband who would be way past 80 if he were living now. He was Elliott Lynn.

Hongkong, China, Ney, 12, (Thursday) (4)—The British minesweeper Petersfield, with Admiral Sir Howard Kelly, commander of the China station, aboard, grounded in a storm today on the island of Tungyung, near Foochow, and was bumping badly against the rocks. Most of the crew were landed by the German liner Der Flinger, which responded to an SOS and stood by.

(Associated Press.) TIENTSIN, China, Nov. 11, (AP)—The Keen school for girls, operated by American Methodist missionaries, and the Nankai school were evacuated today in fear of a renewal of the fighting that has kept Tientsin in uproar the last few days. At the same time troops of the British and French concessions set up an international military patrol on the neutral zone adjacent to the Japanese concession. Reports were circulated that Japan had issued an ultimatum demanding that all Chinese defenders of Tientsin be withdrawn. These rumors could not be confirmed, but a reliable source was authority for the statement that negotiations opened tonight between the Chinese and Japanese and they were so successful in the initial stages that the Chinese authorities believed there no longer was danger of attack. Although the nature of the negotiations was not divulged, it was as- (Continued o

BERLIN, Nov. 12. (AP)—Reports were circulated in well-informed circles today that France and Germany had reached an agreement for handling reparations payments with the Young Plan as a starting point and with an assurance that Germany need agree to nothing until she knows what will happen when her 24,000,000,000 marks of short term private debts expire next March. There was no confirmation from any official source.

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Nov. 12. (a) — Dr. Friedrich Bergius and Prof. Bosch of Ludwigshafen, two German scientists, will share the 1931 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, it was announced today. The 1931 prize for physics is not to be awarded this year.

1931-09-30.text: LONDON, Sept. 2—-(P)—A new world's speed record of 415 miles an hour today stamped Flight Lieutenant G. H. Stainforth as the fastest man on wings. He topped his previous mark of 388.67 miles an hour on the second of four laps over a three kilometer (one and seven eighth miles) course at Calshot yesterday. His average was 408.8 miles an hour as compared with the figure of 379.05 made during the Schneider cup races. The judges officially announced his time for the four laps as calculated by an electric camera as 415.2, 405.1, 409.5 and 405.4. His machine was an S6B seaplane, driven by an especially built Rolls-Royce engine described as the most powerful ever built. Although the weather was considered only barely safe, Lieut. Stainforth took off over the Solent easily and was soon buried in the mist. He made the turns with dexterity and continued around the course with the outlines of his p

London, Sept. 30.—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald announced in the House of Commons today that Parliament would adjourn. The announcement was taken to indicate that the question of a general election would be held temporarily in abeyance. The date for adjournment of the present emergency session, he indicated, probably would be Oct. 7. Lord Reading in the House of Lords also announced that the session would end Oct. 7 "unless something unforeseen occurred."

London, Sept. 30—(AP)—Prime Minister Ramsay McDonald informed the House of Commons today that parliament will adjourn next Wednesday. He did not reply to a question by Arthur Henderson, new leader of the Labour party, as to whether it would be an adjournment or dissolution, but political observers agreed that a general election is likely to be held soon. By Wednesday, Mr. McDonald said, parliament will have completed the emergency program laid out by the national government when it took office. Both the economy bill carrying out retrenchments all along the line of government expenditure, and Chancellor Philip Snowden's supplementary budget will be enacted in the next seven days. The press association said most of the members of the House of Commons have concluded the government has decided to dissolve parliament next Thursday or Friday and call a general election for October 28 or 29.

NANKING, Sept. 30,—-(UP)—The resignation of Foreign Minister T. Wang, who was attacked Monday and severely beaten by rioting students resenting Chinese non-resistance to Japan, was accepted today by the government. Dr. Alfred Sve, Chinese Minister to London, and head of the Chinese delegation to the League of Nations, was appointed to succeed Wang. Wang was still in a serious condition due to the attack upon him. His resignation was believed due to his condition and as to disagreement with other members of the Chinese National Government.

Lendon—A—British unemployed clashed with police again today as eases arising from a demonstration near the House of Commons last night were heard in the Bow Street police court. While the court was sitting, a section of a crowd outside tried to break through a police cordon. Mounted police reinforced the guards, the crowd was pushed back and order restored. Twelve of the persons arrested last night were remanded for trial. Several persons were knocked down and one man was injured by a horse's hoof in today's clash.

London, Sept. 30—(UP)—Police clashed today with mobs in renewed unemployment riots, during which many were injured. Demonstrators were trampled by mounted police who charged crowds outside the British Museum. The unemployed, including many women, reassembled after having been ejected from the vicinity of Bow Street police station. The demonstrators gathered early and sought to force their way into the Bow Street police station where 11 men and one woman were held after an unemployed demonstration before the Houses of Parliament last night. They fought police patrols who blocked their way along the narrow, dingy thoroughfare in the heart of London’s West End. A clash occurred at Oxford Street, but the crowd there moved after a brief altercation. They reassembled in Hyde Park. Police again charged, dispersing the meeting. The clashes followed lively engagements during the night, where crow

London, Sept. 30 (Wednesday) — Flight Lieutenant G. H. Stainforth established a new world's airplane speed record of 408.8 miles an hour over a three-kilometer course at Calshot yesterday, it was officially announced this morning. Lieutenant Stainforth broke his own record of 379.05 miles an hour, made in the Schneider trophy race September 13. He flew a seaplane fitted with special engines. The announcement was not made until 4:20 a. m., following a prolonged examination and comparison of the judges’ checks. The racing seaplane flown by Lieutenant Stainforth was fitted with what is claimed to be the most powerful engine ever built and it was designed for this flight alone, achieving the amazing top speed of 415.5 miles an hour on one of the four runs.

LONDON — (#) — Prime Minister MacDonald's decision as to whether he will dissolve the national government and call for an election on an issue of national unity was awaited today in the House of Commons and by the nation. While he maintained silence, the trend of the most reliable opinion was that yesterday's cabinet meetings and conferences of political leaders had increased the probability that he would lead an appeal to the people on a strictly non-partisan basis. Mr. MacDonald was encouraged by the fact that the commons gave him a majority of 55 votes on the third and final readings of the national economy bill last night and sent it to the House of Lords where it was given its first reading. The bill would empower the government to make drastic cuts in the dole and salaries by orders of council and without further parliamentary action. Sir Stafford Cripps, former solicitor-general,

1931-10-09.text: Mansfield, O., Oct. 9 (R)—Sweeping through the entire plant, a fire which started from an overheated oven, virtually destroyed the large plant of the Martin Steel Products Company here early today, causing damage unofficially estimated at $150,000. City firemen were almost helpless because of inadequate water lines at the plant, which lies on the outskirts of the city. They struggled for more than four hours and succeeded in halting the worst damage about 50 feet from the north entrance of the building, which is 259 by 100 in dimension.

Peiping, Oct. 8. (®)—A report that twelve Japanese airplanes bombed the town of Chinchow, 150 miles south of Mukden, killing at least two people, was received here today. J. G. Thomson, British manager of the Peiping-Mukden railway, reporting the bombing to Chang Hsueh-Liang, Manchurian governor, said the bombs were directed chiefly at the university buildings, in which the Manchurian government is temporarily housed.

Washington, Oct. 5.—(A.B)—A mercury tumble of degrees was registered in thermometers here overnight—the work of a harbinger of old man winter abroad over all the region east of the Rocky Mountains. It was a frosty morning, the weather bureau said, in many points of northern New York, New England and Michigan. Cooler weather that affected the eastern slopes of the mountains and all territory east, as far south as Tennessee, arrived here at 3 p.m. yesterday. The temperature then was 44 degrees. By nightfall the silver thread had contracted 17 degrees, and by 4 a.m. today it was down to 54.

AUSTRALIAN FLYER ASR EP ENDS LONDON—Wing Commander Charles Kingsford-Smith, who failed last week to break the flight record between Australia and England, was grounded today by his doctors for three or four months because he is suffering from nervous strain. He abandoned his plans to lower the record for the return journey and will go back to Australia by steamer, leaving his airplane here until next March when he will have another try.

Sheffield, Mng., Oct. 8. (a’)--A war unlike any conflict in the past was predicted by General Jan C. Smuts, soldier and statesman, in a speech at Sheffield university tonight, unless the world soon establishes a “disarmed peace.” “The armed peace led to the World War,” he said. “Would that it had ended there. But the armed peace continues in an aggravated form and as long as it continues mankind seems to be marching to some horrible doom.” “In the World War we saw only the beginning of the vast difference which science is making in human affairs,” General Smuts said. “In the next great war, if that is ever allowed to occur, science will, like some angry outraged deity, go far to destroy mankind itself. London, Oct. 9 (4°)—Great Britain’s women, as candidates, campaign workers and voters, will play a decisive role in the coming general election to determine the life of the national government. The labor party is expected to run from 20 to 25 women for the House of Commons, and the Conservatives and Liberals about a dozen each, while the number to represent independent groups has not been decided. In the 1929 election, 69 women candidates were put forward by all parties and 14 were elected. Eager To Lend Hand. Political organizations are being besieged by women and girls who are eager to lend a hand in boosting the candidates of their favorite nominees. Under a new register dating from Oct. 15, more women will exercise the franchise than in any previous election. Of approximately 80,000,000 eligible voters, women are expected to outnumber men by about 2,000,000, and it is believed this p

LONDON, Oct. 8.—(AP)—Election fever spread throughout the nation tonight, as local political organizations in 600 constituencies, from north Scotland to Land’s End, met to discuss their candidates and the issues on which the campaign is to be waged. On the national government side some difficult decisions must be made. In several constituencies there are both conservative and “national liberal” candidates, each of whom seeks to secure the pre-emptive right to run as sole representative of the national party. In a few places a fight between the rival national candidates seems inevitable. Elsewhere liberals may be fighting liberals—one as a supporter of Ramsay MacDonald, the other as a member of the “liberal free traders,” who are headed, although not yet officially, by David Lloyd George. The conservatives are aiming to put a total of 500 candidates in the field for the voting October 27,

1931-04-11.text: Port Darwin, North Australia, April 10—Charles W. A. Scott, swooping down upon the airfield here from a flight over the turbulent Timor Sea, set a new record today for a flight between England and Australia. Landing at 5:50 p.m. (8:20 a.m. G.M.T. and 3:20 a.m. E.S.T.) he concluded in 9 days 3 hours 20 minutes a trip of about 11,000 miles over the plains, mountains and forests of Eurasia and the Malay Archipelago. His mark is better by 19 hours and 40 minutes than the record established by Wing Commander Charles Kingsford Smith.

Port Darwin, Australia, April 10.——-(/P)—Flashing over the trail of Wing Commander Charles Kingsford Smith, Charles W. A. Scott, former R. A. F. flier, came to rest here today with a new record for the air lanes between England and Australia. He left Lympne air-drome at midnight on April 1 and brought his plane down here at 3:20 a. m., setting the record at 9 days, 3 hours and 20 minutes. Kingsford Smith’s time was 9 days and 23 hours.

CAIRO, Egypt, April 11. (P)—The Graf Zeppelin, slim gray world traveler, was drawn by British soldiers to a landing at dawn today at Almaza airdrome, near the head of the Nile delta, site of one of the oldest civilizations in the world. An hour later, after debarking and taking on new passengers, it roared aloft again, and allowing those aboard one last look at the pyramids turned toward the rising sun for a visit to the Holy Land. Dr. Eckener’s genial face was at a window of the gondola as the zeppelin drew close to the earth and the crowd gave him an ovation as he stepped to earth after the dirigible had been brought down. The zeppelin will return here tonight, debark its passengers, and take off again for Friedrichshafen, where she will arrive Monday morning.

Lisbon, Portugal, April 10.—(P)—A story of having been held prisoner by rebels at Funchal, Madeira, for three days was brought here tonight by the 177 passengers on the Steamer Carvalho Araujo which arrived from the Azores and Madeira. Captain Pinto told the Associated Press one of the passengers was an American. He and two Frenchmen and several Englishmen filed protests with their consulates against what they considered illegal detention. Merely Formal The "imprisonment" was a formality, Captain Pinto said, and involved only delay to those who wanted to continue their voyage. Thirty lieutenants and sergeants returning as passengers to Lisbon from the Azores after being pardoned by President Carmona for complicity in the last conspiracy, joined the rebels. Colonel Noronha, commanding officer of the Fayal garrison, hid in the ship

Important political changes in the governments of three world powers —Japan, Great Britain and France—were foreshadowed today. In Tokio the press reported Reijiro Wakatsuki scheduled to succeed the stricken Premier Yuko Hamaguchi as premier and leader of the Government party. In London the Labor cabinet of Prime Minister MacDonald was facing a test in the House of Commons on next Thursday when the life of the government will be at stake on a motion of censure. In Paris there were indications of growing opposition to Foreign Minister Aristide Briand’s policies, which may lead to wider nationalistic tendencies that would decrease the veteran statesman’s power.

NEW YORK, April 10—7—A 15-year-old high school boy, Jumor Miron Hess, was indicted by the Bronx grand jury today for murder in the first degree in the holding up of Solomon Balewitz, a tailor during a hold-up last Saturday night. Melvin Harris, 12, who took part in the hold-up, testified under a waiver.

Darwin, Australia, — Port Darwin, Australia, Apr. 10— (‘4P)—C. W. A. Scott, former R. A. F. aviator, landed here at 5:50 P. M. after a flight from England which broke the former nine-and-one-half day record of Wing Commander Charles Kingsford Smith. Scott's time was 9 days, 4 hours, 50 minutes.

The Labor cabinet of Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald was envisaged today by many political observers in connection with the forthcoming vote on a motion of censure in the House of Commons Thursday. A new political crisis has arisen, the observers declared, and the MacDonald government—which has been threatened repeatedly in the last few months—probably will face its most trying test next week as a result of a change in the attitude of the Liberal party. The Liberals, who hold the balance of power in the House of Commons, were understood to have sounded out their constituencies during the present vacation of the Commons and, as a result, decided that the rank and file of the party would control the Liberal attitude in debate on the censure motion, which was proposed by the Conservatives. 1931-10-15.text: Be. Laited Press SHOTTON, Eng., Oct. 15 -- Premier J Ramsay MacDonald was howled down by a hostile audience of miners when he tried to make a campaign speech today. He had to abandon the speech. MacDonald, tired and hoarse from his recent speeches, appealed for quiet. “Howls never cowed me and never will,” he said. Renewed yelling was precipitated and the premier was unable to go on. It was the most open antagonism he has encountered so far.

(By The Associated Press) NEW YORK, Oct. 14—Rudy Vallee is just a restaurant to Rafael Sabatini. The English novelist arrived in America today in quest of historical figures for his writings. “Don't you think Texas Guinan as romantic a figure as any of your heroines?” he was asked. “Never heard of her,” said the author of “Scaramouche.” “How about Rudy Vallee?” “I dined there once, that's all.” “Al Capone?” “He couldn't make a hero. He's doing nothing for good.” Mussolini, said the author, is the most romantic person alive.

Seaham Harbor, England, Oct 15.—(AP)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald was unable to obtain a hearing when he attempted to deliver a campaign speech at the Shotton colliery here today. For fifteen minutes he made an effort to address a meeting in his campaign for re-election to the House of Commons from the Seaham Harbor constituency, but his brief speech was continuously interrupted by hoots and catcalls and he finally abandoned it. His voice rapidly weakening, the prime minister ceased talking and offered to answer questions, but even his answers were met with shouts. "Howls have never cowed me and never will," Mr. MacDonald said as he left the meeting.

Seaham Harbor, England—Although in the midst of a campaign fight which may mean his political existence, Ramsay MacDonald finds time to play. In an interval of speech making he kicked off for a football match between two teams of miners.

Tokio—(?)—The Japanese Foreign Office today instructed its delegation in Geneva to use every effort to see that the proposal for including an American representative in the League of Nations Council during discussion of the Sino-Japanese trouble is dropped. The proposal caused more or less commotion at the Foreign Ministry, which lost no time in sending instructions to its Geneva representatives.

Vancouver, B. C., Oct. 15.—(?)— William Green was re-elected president of the American Federation of Labor by acclamation today. He was unopposed and his nomination and election was attended by a wild outburst of enthusiasm by delegates. The federation reaffirms its stand today for legalization of 2.7 percent beer at the coming session of congress.

MADRID, Oct. 15 ()—Spain's new president, Manuel Azana, picked up the reins of government today in an atmosphere of religious dissension fraught with danger for the future of the republic. Under the provisions of the new constitution, he was designated by the national assembly last night as opposition resigned with his cabinet in protest against anti-church legislation. He reappointed the former cabinet with two changes. President Azana told the Associated Press that “the republic is immovable. We are as strong as if we had held power a long time. Our fundamental mission consists of fabricating a great, strong, prosperous republic with peace and justice for all. The government is republican but the republic is for all Spaniards.” The change in authority was accompanied by vigorous demonstrations against the church and threats of revolt against the government. MADRID, Oct. 14 (F)—Niceto Alcala Zamora, who has served as provisional president of Spain since the ousting of King Alfonso XIII six months ago, resigned with his cabinet today and was succeeded within a few hours by Manuel Azana, his minister of war. The formal transfer of power will take place at noon tomorrow... At the same time the new cabinet, which, with two exceptions, is the same as Alcala Zamora’s will be sworn in. The shift in government resulted from the measures restricting religious orders that have been inculcated by the assembly in the constitution under which republican Spain will be governed, and it was accompanied by spectacular street demonstrations. Bands of Communists and anti-clericals roamed the streets of Madrid tonight, singing the ‘Red Flag’ and shouting, “down with the Catholic Church” and ‘death to all Jesuits.’ Most intense excitement prevailed as a conseque

1931-10-06.text: LONDON, Oct. 5—The Brit- ish cabinet decided unanimously to- night to call an immediate general election, it was announced authoritatively following a late session. No formal official statement was given out at the close of the meeting, which lasted two hours, but it was learned the election campaign will be fought by the national government on the basis of a manifesto to be issued by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. The unanimity of the decision was taken to indicate that Sir Herbert Samuel and the other liberals whose attitude during the last few days has been doubtful have thrown in their lot with the prime minister and will give him their wholehearted support. The cabinet's decision followed closely the announcement that a group of 22 liberal members of parliament, including Sir John Simon, had pledged their unqualified support to the prime minister.

SHANGHAI, Oct. 6.—(#)—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh disembarked from the British aircraft carrier “Hermes” at Woosung late today after having received word of the death of the latter's father, Senator Dwight W. Morrow, and immediately motored 18 miles to the American consulate here. A launch conveyed the couple to shore from the aircraft carrier, which had brought them and their disabled plane from Hankow. The plane was damaged last week when it capsized, after being lowered from the Hermes, and Col. and Mrs. Lindbergh were thrown into the Yangtse river. Asked whether he planned to continue his present aerial tour, Lindbergh said: “Under the circumstances I would rather wait a little while before making any announcement.” Contrasting sharply with the receptions given them, this one was marked by grief. Mrs. Lindbergh, showing evidence of shock, was accompanied to a waiting limousine

London, Oct. 6 (UP)—Crowds of unemployed, including hurled stones at mounted police near the British Museum today. Police answered the outbursts, the third in London within a week, by charging into the throng. Several persons were trampled and injured.

Shanghai, Oct. 5.—-(Tuesday)—(#P)—The British naval wireless carried news of the death of Senator Dwight W. Morrow to his daughter and son-in-law, Anne and Charles Lindbergh, aboard the British aircraft carrier Hermes early today. The Hermes was steaming slowly down the Yangtse estuary from Nanking and was scheduled to arrive at Woosung at the mouth of the Whangpoo river, near Shanghai at 5 p.m. today (4 a.m., E.S.T.). Previously it was planned for the Hermes to remain overnight at Woosung, with the Lindberghs staying aboard, and to proceed to Shanghai tomorrow, but plans were uncertain in view of Senator Morrow’s death. Plane Injured The Lindberghs were bringing their monoplane to Shanghai aboard the Hermes for repairs suffered when it capsized, while being lowered from the deck of the Hermes into the Yangtse river off Hankow, throwing the colonel and his wife into the river.

London, Oct. 6.—(A.P.)—The body of Sir Thomas Lipton, British yachtsman and merchant, will be taken to Glasgow tonight to rest by the side of his family. The funeral will be held tomorrow. The details of his will have not been revealed. The Daily Mail said the executors had decided to sell the racing yacht Shamrock V. and the pleasure yacht Erin.

#London, October 6. — Great Britain’s course of action in her financial crisis will be put directly to the people for decision on Oct. 27. The government announced today that parliament, now in special session, would be dissolved tomorrow in preparation for a general election, and that voting would be on the 27th. Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald and his coalition government will go to the country for a “Doctor's mandate” to solve the nation’s ills. It will be the most unusual election in Britain’s modern history. The government forces will be headed by the solid Conservative party, a strong element of the Liberals who have defied the leadership of David Lloyd George and a Labor element of unknown strength which follows MacDonald, Philip Snowden and J. H. Thomas in their break from the socialist party. The country will be asked to vote for what amounts to a Tory-Liberal government head

SHANGHAI, Oct. 6—(UP)—In a torrential rainstorm Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh arrived here today, obviously much moved by the death of Senator Dwight Morrow, Mrs. Lindbergh’s father. They were taken by a speedboat from the British airplane carrier Hermes, which took them aboard when their plane overturned on the Yangtze last week, to the customs jetty and then went by motor car to the Cathay hotel. Mrs. Lindbergh showed plainly the severe strain which news of her father’s sudden death had brought. Lindbergh was very grave. “Gentlemen, under the circumstances we are unable to make a decision on our future plans,” he told newspaper men. There were no Chinese officials present when the Lindberghs arrived and only members of the American official colony received them and escorted them to the hotel.

BY Associated Press ENGLEWOOD, N. J., Oct. 6.—Mrs. Dwight Morrow is receiving messengers of sympathy on account of the death of her husband yesterday, but has not received any word from her daughter. The Lindberghs are cruising in the British airplane carrier, Hermes, down the Yangtze River toward Shanghai, and are unable to cable. The funeral will be Wednesday, and as simple as possible. The Lindbergh baby will be left at the Morrow summer home in Maine. It will not be taken to the funeral because of the prevalence of infantile paralysis.

1931-06-24.text: LIVERPOOL, Eng., (UP).—Wiley Post and Harold Gatty, after a successful flight across the Atlantic, landed their monoplane ‘Winnie Mae’ at the Sealand airdrome, near Chester Wednesday and proceeded on their way around the world after a brief halt. The daring fliers came down at the airdrome at 1 p.m. But despite the strain of their dash from New York to Newfoundland and across the Atlantic in little more than 24 hours, refused to rest but took off with the intention of flying at least as far as Berlin and perhaps to Moscow. Chester is 16 miles southeast of Liverpool and 20 miles from the Irish Sea. First word that the fliers had made the year's first crossing of the North Atlantic came when they passed over Bangor, Wales, 40 minutes before reaching Chester. Bangor is 50 miles due west of Chester, on the northwest coast of Wales. They were headed on a straight course for Berlin. The fliers

CHESTER, England, June 24 (P)——Wiley Post and Harold Gatty "two young men in a hurry" on a flight around the world, landed safely at the Zealand Royal Air Force Airdrome near here this morning on a flight across the Atlantic, snatched a bite to eat and hopped off for Moscow via Berlin with the possibility that they might land at the Cavriman capital. "Hello, England, we've done it," said Gatty when their machine came to a standstill after a flight of a little over 16 hours at the Zealand Airdrome. As soon as the identification numbers of the machine had been checked, royal air force pilots and the ground staff rushed from the hangar to greet the fliers who had nonchalantly left New York City yesterday, barely turned around at Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, and then hopped over the Atlantic.

Great Britain, Germany, Austria and Italy have accepted President Hoover's proposal for a one-year suspension of war debt payments and the world is waiting upon France, whose attitude is still to be determined. In a radio address broadcast through Germany Chancellor Bruening made a frank bid for a Franco-German conference at which the difficulties bequeathed by the war might be straightened out and the two nations begin working together for their mutual salvation. Ambassador Edge, in a conference with Premier Laval of France, was understood to have received an indication of the nature of the forthcoming French reply to the President's offer although the Premier has said his Government will take no definite stand until it has consulted the Parliament regarding the effects of a one-year moratorium on the Young plan. LONDON, June 24—(UP)—A Calvin Coolidge boom for president and emphatic opposition to revision of war debts were salient points in a signed article by William Randolph Hearst, appearing in the Daily Express today. “I for one declare here and now for Calvin Coolidge as next president of the United States,” Hearst, the American publisher, said in his article, entitled "France, the War Menace." Hearst wrote that the American people already had been taxed heavily enough and desire a vigorous American in the White House. An editor's note on the article explained that Hearst was asked to outline the attitude which he and his newspapers will take toward the plan of President Hoover for a year’s suspension of war debts payments. The newspaper said it did not necessarily associate itself with Hearst's attitude.

Milwaukee —(A%— Large quantities of poison were found in the vital organs of Louis Hoffman, 32, and Henry Kopitzke, 46, stricken while attending a barn dance near New London, Wis., it was revealed in a chemical analysis completed today by Dr. E. L. Miloslavich, Milwaukee pathologist. Kopitzke's stomach contained the larger amount of poison, Dr. Miloslavich said, although the lethal potion was of the acute type which would bring death within a few minutes if administered in much smaller portion than taken by Hoffman. An analysis of a partially filled bottle of liquor found near Kopitzke’s body when he went into convulsions failed to reveal any traces of deadly poison, the pathologist said. “I intend to leave for New London today to submit my findings to the district attorney and assist him in a search for the source of the poison,” Dr. Miloslavich said. “Whether it was administered accide

Chester, England, June 24.—The American airmen Wiley Post and Harold Gatty safely crossed the Atlantic on the first leg of their round-the-world flight and landed at Sealand Royal Air Force airdrome this morning, leaving for Berlin twenty minutes later. The fliers took off from Harbor Grace yesterday afternoon and landed at the airdrome, which is six miles from there at 1:45 p. m. (6:45 a. m., S. T.), and took off for Berlin. Because they had planned to make a non-stop flight from Harbor Grace, at 2:05 p. m. (7:05 a. m., E. T.), they made the 2,000-mile crossing from Harbor Grace to Chester in a little over sixteen hours, averaging about 117 miles an hour for the crossing. The arrival of the American airmen, who have made a rapid-fire trip of their round-the-world project, was a surprise to the personnel of the airdrome. No word had been received of their near approach except an unconfir

London, June 24. (Wednesday) 7) William Randolph Hearst, in an article contributed to today’s Daily Express on war debts, declares for Calvin Coolidge as the next president of the United States. “This plan for revision of war debts,” he writes, “is purely a plan of the international bankers who make their money out of commissions. I pledge unending opposition to this plan to plunder the American people in the interest of foreign nations for which most of these bankers are the spoils. They are sure to learn in a way they will never forget that Americans are not the dupes they are supposed to be asked to pay the price of European war frenzy. “Any American politician who asks them to pay for past European wars or to supply the funds for future wars is committing an outrageous piece of robbery and snobbery. House and they are going to have one, either a Coolidge or a Rockefeller.

POOLE, England, June 24—Rescue workers searched the ruins of a section of the Royal Cordite factory at Holton Heath today for bodies feared buried in a terrific explosion. At least 10 workers were killed. Most of the bodies were destroyed by the force of the blast which alarmed the countryside for miles around yesterday. Nineteen workers were injured badly, and doctors treated about 50 for minor hurts. Windows were broken and the blast was felt over an area extending 20 miles from the factory. A man two miles away was knocked from a chair by the explosion. The bodies of the dead were hurled into the air. Most of them were so badly mangled that they were difficult to identify. A great cloud of red dust and smoke was sent up by the explosion, which settled over the wrecked plant and rescue workers. 1931-03-29.text: LONDON, March 28. — (AP)— Typhoid fever has written a ‘finis’ to the life of Arnold Bennett, one of the world’s leading men of letters, whose works, acclaimed by the scholarly, did not disdain the common touch. The end had been foreseen since Wednesday. Stricken with influenza seven weeks ago, he was thought to be recovering when typhoid fever brought him down again. A blood transfusion yesterday gave him temporary relief but he weakened and early last night passed away peacefully. He was 63 years old. Bennett in his lifetime came to hear his own works, particularly the “Old Wives’ Tale” which he published in 1908, rated as classic. He was most widely known perhaps for that work and the “Five Towns” series, which depicted the drabness of England's pottery district. In less serious works he acted as a guide to what is best in literature, travel and recreation. His works include novels, pl

LONDON, Mar. 28. P)—The death of Arnold Bennett, 63, considered one of the greatest novelists of the post-Victorian era, was mourned today throughout Britain. Bennett died last night after a month’s illness. Death was due to typhoid fever. He appeared somewhat improved Wednesday after a blood transfusion but became unconscious yesterday. A few friends were at the bedside when he died. Bennett was born at Hanley, Staffordshire. He married a French woman, but a legal separation was effected in 1922.

KARACHI, India, March 23.—When Gandhi goes to London for the second round table conference on India his only garb, he has indicated, will be his Hindu loincloth spun by Mirabai, nee Madeline Slade, daughter of an English admiral who is his constant and devoted companion. If the London weather happens to be a little cool he will throw a piece of cheesecloth over his chest; if unusually cold he will wrap a blanket around his fragile body. Otherwise his legs and trunk will be bare. He has a horror of living in hotels, so if Premier MacDonald invites him to stay at 10 Downing Street as his guest the Mahatma will insist upon bringing his own pots and pans and tin cans so that Mirabai may prepare his goat milk, vegetables, cracked corn and dates in orthodox Hindu fashion. If the prime minister offers India’s anchorite a soft downy English bed Gandhi is expected to decline, preferring to sleep

Karachi, India, March 28.— "The day that my inner voice tells me my country no longer needs me I will starve myself to death,” Gandhi told a deputation of hostile red shirt communists who called upon him to demand why he had not saved Bhagat Singh, executed at Lahore for the murder of a British police official in 1929. “I shall not complain if you beat me, I have no bodyguard,” he said. “God alone keeps vigil over me. Some think me crazy, some a fool because of my love for my enemies, but it is the very foundation of my whole life's work and creed. “I have nothing left to sacrifice. I have no worldly possessions. I am a beggar. But the day that India abandons the sacred principle of non-violence I shall let my fragile body perish. If you say that I am doing harm to India you have a right to do so, but it is my duty to turn you to the path of affection and truth. I have no weapon against
LONDON, Mar. 21. WUP—An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from ware tonight said that Crown attack of influenza. He reported the young prince's temperature was rising.

Lendon, March 28—(A.P.)—Although Emilio Scala will actually receive less than a half a million dollars, instead of a potential million and three-quarters as a result of winning with his ticket on the Irish hospital sweepstakes yesterday, he will be thoroughly satisfied as soon as he actually gets the money in his hands, he said today. "When that happens," said the Italian proprietor of a humble coffee house in Battersea, "I will know that I am a really rich man and that it isn't all a wonderful dream." It developed today that Scala actually retained only one-quarter of his ticket for himself and his relatives in Italy, selling a three-quarters share in it to a firm of bookmakers for slightly more than $50,000. Nice, France, March 29.—(AP)— Peggy Davis, 37, former Broadway show girl, gave the Riviera a new tragedy last night when she drove her automobile over a steep cliff in the vicinity of the Vanderbilt estate, and dropped 200 feet to her death. The former actress was the wife of an Australian, David Townsend, who is well known in Wall Street circles. She drove the car to her hotel near the cliff, where she scribbled a note as she drank two brandies. Leaving the note with the proprietor of the hotel, she jumped into the automobile and plunged over the edge of the cliff. The note, addressed to her husband, asked his pardon for her act, and beseeched him to take good care of her 1-year-old daughter. Police have been unable to find a motive for her suicide, as apparently her marital life had been happy.

Berlin, Mar. 28—(A.P.)—Millions of German citizens tonight were studying, in their evening newspapers, one of the most far-reaching decrees ever promulgated in the young German republic. It was “Father” Hindenburg’s ukase for squelching disorder. “Those who read radical papers didn’t know but that this might be the last issue of their paper for some time, for amid the drastic provisions of the decree is one empowering the authorities to suppress for as long as eight weeks, if it were found necessary. Those who belonged to such organizations as Adolf Hitler's brown shirts or the Communist red front did not know whether they could meet with their brethren again, for under the new decree, their organizations may be dispersed with the stroke of a pen. 1931-05-01.text: BERGEN, Norway, May 1. (AP). —Captain Albin Ahrenberg, Swedish civilian pilot, took off from here in a heavily loaded Amphibian plane at 6 a. m. for Thorshavn, Faroe Islands, on the first lap of a flight to Greenland where he will look for the missing British scientist. Ahrenberg will fly to Reykjavik, probably today. It is about 390 miles from Bergen to the Faroe Islands and about 528 miles from the Faroes to Reykjavik. Captain Ahrenberg’s plane is equipped with pontoons and replaceable skis by which it may alight on the snow in the desolate Greenland where he could not locate his camp.

PARIS, May 1—(P)—It was stated unofficially today that France will not accept Great Britain's proposals for ironing out the difficulties in the drafting of the Franco-Italian naval agreement: Great Britain suggested, it is understood, that France and Italy sign the treaty on a limited naval building program which was announced on March 1, leaving the way open for France to outline her replacement needs at a naval conference in 1935. Such a proposal, it is asserted here, would place France in the position of asking permission in 1935 for what she considers now to be her right of replacement. It is not believed such a suggestion would be acceptable.

LONDON, May 1,—Office of anxiety to authorities score of European capitals day seems likely to be quietly today throughout continent. London seldom has fear from celebration of international labor day. The processions of radicals will form on the banks and march under guard. Neither Paris nor Berlin can regard the anniversary with calm. Police are to quell any disorders. Authorities say that every possible precaution has been taken in connection. Rome and Moscow look forward to May day with serenity, the former because it was abolished by the fascists seven years ago and the latter because all such celebrations naturally become matters of state. Moscow will start three days of jubilation Friday with military parades, free theatres and hours of oratory for the enjoyment of the proletariat. Spain to Celebrate... ASHTON-UNDER-LYNE, ENGLAND, May 1—(#)—This traditional laborite constituency has sent a tory to the house of commons after a rousing bye-election which ended last night with Sir Oswald Mosley’s “new party” leader being nearly mobbed. An angry crowd of several thousand laborites swarmed about the meeting place where Sir Oswald, a young aristocrat, Lady Mosley, a daughter of the late Marquis Curzon, and others had gathered to listen to returns—which decisively downed the first “new party” candidate to make the race for the commons. The crowd jeered and hooted Sir Oswald and his group, blaming the entrance of their candidate into the race for the conservative victory, which was by a small margin. Sir Oswald, guarded by police, finally left the hall and went through the crowd to his hotel. The defeated “new party” candidate, A. Young, was smuggled out a side door under a heavy police guard,

LONDON, May 1 ()—The red flag waved in parts of Europe today in celebration of May Day but order generally prevailed under the watchful eye of police, and most of the disturbance was verbal. The principal exception was in Berlin where a group of young communists shot and seriously wounded a policeman on duty. By far the greatest demonstration took place in Moscow where all work was stopped and thousands paraded. Joseph Stalin reviewed red troops in front of the Kremlin. In Paris police arrested dozens for speeches which they believed might incite physical violence. London was quiet as usual. A little army of men, women and even children—some in baby carriages—bore red banners as they marched along the embankment but scores of bobbies walked on either side of the parade and there was no disturbance beyond a few weak shouts against capitalists. LAS PALMAS, Canary Islands, May 1 (#)—Germany's big seaplane DO-X took off from Gando bay today, circled over the city, and headed south in the direction of Rio de Oro, on the West African coast. She is resuming the transatlantic flight to South America which was interrupted last November when fire destroyed one of her wings at Lisbon. She has been here since January and yesterday made her first trial flight since last winter.

Continuing earthquakes in the Sanguezur district of the Soviet republic of Azerbaijan, Transcaucasia, were believed today to have added to the loss of life and property damage already sustained by the area in tremors of the past two days. Unofficial estimates of the dead there and in parts of Armenia reached 500 with many more injured. Residents have deserted the stricken villages and are living in the open. All communications have been disrupted and the victims are suffering greatly from the severe weather. So many victims are still buried under the ruins of their homes that it is impossible to make an accurate estimate of the loss of lives.

Moscow, April 30.—(AP)— Further earthquakes in the Soviet republic of Azerbaijan in Transcaucasia today caused fear that the total number of deaths in the wide-spread disturbances, which started Monday, may mount to more than 500. More than 2,000 persons were injured in the original quake, Monday, which wrought severe damage in the southern Transcaucasia sections of the Soviet Union and was felt most severely in Armenia. Today’s renewal of shocks occurred in the Zanguezur district of Azerbaijan. Great suffering is reported in many sections and in some places residents have deserted their stricken villages and are living in the open. Relief Begun The government has started relief work and provided 500,000 rubles (about $250,000) for immediate use among the sufferers. Food and medical supplies are being rushed to devastated areas. London, Sept. 17. (4)--Mahatma Gandhi today protested that the proceedings of the federal structures committee of the round table conference were leading “practically nowhere.” The committee, the Indian nationalist leader declared, has become a “debating society.” The deliberations are “interminable.” Since Monday the Mahatma has sat with his legs tucked under him during the sessions, listening to much debate, occasionally sipping goat’s milk and saying nothing except for one address. A feeling of oppression has been growing on him from the very beginning and already there has been talk that he considered withdrawing. The Mahatma asserted at today's meeting that the committee seemed to be composed “not of the chosen ones of the nations they should be representing, but of the chosen ones of the government.” Another complaint was against “his majesty's advisers,” who, he said, failed to la

Gandhi said in an exclusive United Press interview today. The leader of millions of Indians in their passive struggle for freedom squatted on a mattress on the cement floor of his cell in Kingsley Hall as he received the correspondent. The bedroom terrace overlooks the mist enveloped, dumpy slum houses and myriads of chimney pots in the direction of the Thames dockland. Washington—(4)—The navy department was advised Wednesday that a transport amphibian plane sent with relief supplies to Belize, British Honduras, this morning from the Panama Canal Zone had crashed and three of its crew were killed. The plane, which left Coco Solo, Canal Zone, at 6 a.m., with a load of medical supplies for the hurricane-stricken city, crashed three miles northwest of David, in the Republic of Panama, at 19:21 a.m. Chief Aviation Pilot Isaac L. Jenkins, of Couch, Mo., and aviation machinist’s mate, Arthur O. Miller, La Salle, N.Y., were killed and Lieut. Creighton K. Lankford, of Plattsburg, Mo., fatally burned. Roy J. Miller, radio man third class, Erwin, S.D., was seriously injured.

London, Sept. 17 (AP)—Any further refusal of men in the British navy to carry out orders will be dealt with under the navy discipline act, Sir Austen Chamberlain, First Lord of Admiralty, announced in the House of Commons today in a statement on naval pay reductions and the unrest which has followed them. In reply to an ironical question whether the pay cuts were among those agreed to provisionally by the late labor government, he said that when he took over the Admiralty for the new national government he found instructions to make the cuts in question. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald added that the labor government had been advised by the Admiralty, when the cuts were under consideration, that the men loyally would accept them, provided there were cuts all around in the public services and that there also was an adequate cut in the unemployment.

LONDON (UP).—An order is being issued to the British fleet assuring the men that the pay reduction hardships which caused them to strike are being investigated, Sir Austen Chamberlain, first lord of the admiralty, informed the house of commons Thursday. He warned the participants in the passive mutiny, however, they must return to discipline and obey orders. “Any further refusals by individuals to carry out orders will be dealt with under the naval discipline act,” he said. Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald told A. V. Alexander, former first lord in the conservative government, that the recent labor government had been advised the navy would accept the pay cuts loyally, provided reductions were general in the country and were accompanied by adequate reduction of dole payments. The commanders in chief of the Atlantic fleet's home ports have been summoned to the admiralty to discuss with the sea

London. — The fighting hulks of Great Britain's restless Atlantic fleet were steaming quietly toward their home ports today on the strength of the admiralty's pledge that any hardships resulting from wage reductions would be adjusted. Twelve vessels left Invergordon, Scotland, Wednesday night for Inverness, Portsmouth, Plymouth and Chatham after their crews had been told of officials' decision. There was some delay in weighing anchors until the men were assured that the ships would not be redirected to distant stations. While the passive mutiny in the Atlantic squadron has temporarily been called off, reports were received of unrest over pay cuts in the air force at Malta and the Mediterranean fleet at Gibraltar. NEW YORK, Sept. 17.—(?)—The world groaned with weather complaint this summer. America had drought and extraordinary heat waves. England had the coldest, wettest summer weather within living memory. Southeast central Europe experienced late spring and a June so hot schools had to be prematurely closed. Germany’s summer was remarkably short and marked by frequent sunless days. Italy alternately shivered and perspired. France had to go back to 1850 to find precedent for chilly wetness. Belgium lost 60 per cent of her wheat and oats crop in unusually persistent rains and her potatoes rotted in the ground. Norway was extraordinarily cold. Denmark changed daily from brilliant sunshine to shivering temperatures and ducked sudden thunderstorms. Sweden was cold and rainy. Turks froze in the northern districts and sweltered in the southern. Iceland got the “breaks”; her summer, usually a matter of

1931-03-10.text: Loss in New England BOSTON, March 10.--New England took account of stock today after a snowstorm had claimed the lives of five fishermen, endangered 10 motorists marooned in White Mountain snowdrifts, and left washed up on Massachusetts shores the battered parts of a plane and a flier’s helmet and goggles. Eight Groveton, N. H., high school students, their basketball coach and a chauffeur were found late yesterday in the impassable drifts of snow that severed Crawford Notch, N. H., from the rest of the world. For 18 hours they were without food as the drifts piled higher and higher. Four of their number, who had gone for help, nearly perished in the attempt and they were finally led to safety by railroad workers and state highway men, who came upon them in an abandoned camp. The four youths led the way back to their automobile, where the other six were huddled together for warmth as the

Suffering teamed with terror and death in the Balkans yesterday as Europe's bitter cold spread over the desolation wrought by earthquakes. Meanwhile, London experienced its worst snow storm of 20 years; Quebec its worst of 50 years; Rochester, N. Y., its worst of 15 years. New England and the Midwest struggled up out of snow drifts. Worried folk in seacoast towns scanned ship reports, expecting fresh intensity in gales north of New York. Quakes Continued Quakes shook the Balkans for the third successive day and geologists expected more. Between 100 and 200 persons were listed as dead and thousands were without shelter against the cold. An earth shock at Hakodate, Japan, crumbled buildings. Rivers of France continued to rise. Low sections of Paris were evacuated as the Seine mounted to a foot over the alarm level. (Continued on Page 7)

Washington, March 9—()—Arthur Woods, head of the president’s emergency committee for employment today said conditions were improving over a considerable portion of the country. New England territory, the southwest, and the southeast were specifically cited, little change being noted in the Pacific Coast zone and in the central portion of the United States bordering the Great Lakes. William Phillips, representing the committee in New England estimated that 1,500 workers had been returned to watch making in Waltham, Mass., and 400 cotton mill employees added to payrolls at Fall River. In the weekly summary of public works activity presented to the committee today, it was estimated that 183 projects of governmental and semi-governmental character, entailing an outlay of $92,014,247, were under contract for the period. Since December 1, the total of such construction contracted for in the en
LONDON, March 10. (AP) — Sir Oswald Mosley was expelled from the Labour Party today for his “act of gross disloyalty” in launching a “new political party.”

Bedford, Eng., March 10—(A.P.)—Alfred Arthur Rouse, man of many loves who last November tried to “die by proxy” in an effort to escape the responsibilities of his amorous adventures, today was hanged for the murder of an unidentified man. He was the first person in 145 years to be executed for the murder of an unidentified victim. The body of the man he killed was kept unburied throughout his trial and subsequent incarceration in the hope that Rouse in a last minute confession would tell who he was. During the trial Rouse said the victim was a hitch-hiker, to whom he had given a lift and who had accidentally, perhaps in lighting a cigarette, set fire to his car while Rouse was outside the vehicle effecting temporary repairs. The case was marked by the unswerving loyalty of Rouse’s wife and one of the three women with whom he loved, the mother of his child. After his arrest the wife and t

BEDFORD, England, Mar. 1—Alfred Rouse, dapper, handsome, 36-year-old bigamist whose tangled love affairs held the attention of England for many days, was hanged today for the murder of an unknown man. Prosecution used circumstantial evidence, convincing a jury that Rouse deliberately killed a passenger in his car then set fire to the car so that he might wipe out his past life and start anew.

LONDON — (4) — Southern England was making up today for the lack of real winter weather during the past three months. A temperature of 22 degrees Fahrenheit prevailed in London this morning, and thousands of erstwhile unemployed were engaged in removing an estimated 9,000,000-ton fall of snow which came down yesterday, the heaviest precipitation in twenty years. The sky today was threatening and continued snow and colder weather were predicted. Roads all over the British Isles were piled high with snow or, more dangerous still, were encrusted with ice which made traffic difficult and hazardous. The railroads brought out their snow plows and train schedules were fairly well adhered to. Cross channel steamers and some air services continued to operate through snow storms. Airplane pilots described the experience as much like that of flying through a fog. Among incoming liners buffeted by t

LONDON, March 10.—(U. P.) — The greater part of Europe and its surrounding seas continued today under the lash of storms which were lessening in intensity but were still severe after four days of blizzards, high gales, floods and earthquakes. The known death toll in the European area was high—close to 200—and thousands were injured and homeless. The material damage was immense, but could not be estimated due to incomplete advices. Snow covered the British Isles from Scotland to Cornwall, and the most severe March snowstorm in 20 years took a toll of eight dead and hundreds injured. The steam trawler Locklong was wrecked off Fifeshire, sailors in the channel reported the blizzard so dense that they could not see from one end of their ships to the other; the Hempstead observatory recorded 13 degrees below freezing—the coldest since 1906—roads in many districts were impassable due to snow d

He was quoted as saying that Europe had bullied, misunderstood and misinterpreted him. Chaplin, interviewed at Juan-Les-Pins, France, struck sharply at persons in England who criticized him for not appearing at a “command performance” in a London variety charity affair tonight. No One Wanted Him “They say I have a duty to England,” the interviewer quoted Chaplin as saying. “I wonder just what that duty is. No one wanted me or cared for me in England 15 years ago. Chairman of the last Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the Idaho Republican said in a radio speech last night that adoption of the gold standard in India had “drastically lowered” the purchasing power of nearly 800,000,000 people. He made no direct reference to a resolution approved last week by the International Chamber of Commerce for a conference on silver but two other Republican members of Congress did answer attacks made at the Congress on American tariff and war debt policies. | Washington, May 10.—(CAP) —Reversal of Great Britain’s gold standard policy in India was demanded tonight by Senator Borah of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The Idaho Republican said it had drastically lowered the purchasing power of nearly 800 million people by depressing the price of silver. British Assailed Borah attacked adoption of the gold standard in India, and said with people “growing dangerously restless, governments can at least afford to undo that which they did and which has proved unwise and hurtful to the people.” He characterized the decline in the silver price during the past two years as “one of the prime factors producing and prolonging” the present industrial depression.
