1931-08-16.text: BOMBAY, INDIA, Aug. 15.—Under dripping clouds and in a melancholy atmosphere, 27 delegates including several princes sailed for England today without Mahatma Gandhi to attend the second round table conference on Indian affairs. Most of them seemed depressed that Mahatma was not a fellow passenger, for despite the fact he holds radically different political doctrines they respect him as the leader of the common people. They will arrive in London in time for the meeting of the federal structures committee on September 5. Gandhi, spurned England's invitation to participate in the conference unless his grievances are satisfied, disappeared overnight to his retreat at Ahmedabad where he announced he would stay until “the government puts me in prison.” Conspicuous among the delegates was Mooltan Sparu Jayakar whose frantic eleventh hour efforts failed to compose the differences between Gandhi

TOKYO, Aug. 15 (/P)—Determined effort of C. C. Chichester, New Zealand aviator, to blaze a new air route from Australia to England, ended in failure at Katsura, Wakayama prefecture, today when his plane fell as he started for Tokyo and he was seriously injured. Physicians at first believed he had escaped with injuries to the head and right leg, but later when Chichester lost consciousness they declared belief he had suffered internal injuries.

BOMBAY, India, Aug. 15—(?)}— Twenty-seven delegates, including several princes, sailed for the second London round table conference without Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi went to retreat at Ahmedabad saying he would stay there until the government would imprison him. His milch goats thus escaped seasickness on the ocean voyage. Asked whether, in the event he did not go to London, he would withhold renewal of the civil disobedience movement until the round-table conference had finished its deliberations, Gandhi said it was difficult to give a conclusive answer. "But the Congress will make every effort not to revive the movement," he added. "Much will depend upon the attitude of the government." The Mahatma said a renewal of the struggle between the government and his followers certainly would result if the second round-table conference failed to grant Nationalist demands, "This time," he added, "

NEW YORK, Aug. 15.—(AP)— Local backers of the Herndon-Pangborn around-the-world flight announced this morning that $2,050 had been cabled the flyers to pay the fine imposed by the Japanese court for photographing fortified areas. The flight headquarters here said this action followed receipt of a cable from Hugh Herndon, Jr., the first message received from the flyers since their arrival in Japan. This message also requested $2,000 to meet the cost of installing an additional fuel tank in the plane for their forthcoming flight across the Pacific Ocean to Seattle.

BERLIN, (AP)—Abolition of the entire rationing system for Soviet consumers in Russia, which would mean immediate restriction of Soviet wheat exports and greater foreign markets for American wheat, is provided in plans disclosed today in authoritative reports from Moscow. The United Press learned that Josef V. Stalin, Soviet dictator, addressing a meeting of leaders of Soviet co-operative societies several days ago, announced the scheme for abolishing the system which has kept the people of Russia on a war-time rations basis. Stalin’s plan as outlined to the co-operative societies hitherto, it was said, has been kept secret. The rations system is to be abolished early next year, the reports said. The immediate effect would be restriction of Soviet grain exports notably wheat, from the 1931 crops. A vast volume of wheat and other cereals, dairy products and finished manufactured articles h

TOKIO, Aug. 16.—(UP)—(Sunday) —The isolated little city of Petropavlovsk on the Siberian shore suspended business today and donned holiday attire to welcome Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and his wife, who were expected at 10 a.m. (5 p.m. PST.). Official welcome to Siberia will be extended by Deputy Governor Gromoff and the secretary of the aviation society, according to the correspondent of the Tokio Hochi Shimbun. The entire populace was prepared to swarm to the waterfront to join in the welcome and reports here are that the Soviet officials had prepared elaborate entertainment for the flying couple. SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 15—(UP)—Completing a perilous flight through dense fog above the Bering Sea, Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh landed at Karaginski Island, off Kamchatka Peninsula of Siberia, at 1:49 a.m., P.S.T., today, according to a radio message received at the navy radio station he

MOSCOW, Aug. 15—Russia today was facing two new crises—a shortage of knives, forks and spoons in public eating places and a toothbrush shortage. The newspaper Evening Moscow today called the cutlery situation acute and complained that patrons in restaurants were forced to stand in line waiting for knives, forks and spoons, with their soup and other dishes chilled. The newspaper demanded that suitable measures be taken immediately to relieve the condition. A writer in the same newspaper demands that severe measures be taken against those responsible for “depriving the proletariat of Moscow of toothbrushes.” The shortage of brushes, it is asserted, is so acute that tooth powder factories have had to reduce the output planned for 1931 from 60,000,000 to 25,000,000 boxes.

TOKIO, Aug. 16—(Sunday)—(AP)—Recovering from their first shock at being fined a total of $2,050 for violation of Japanese flying laws, Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, whose sky journey around the world was interrupted ten days ago by their troubles here, today began to view the situation philosophically. “It could have been worse—I suppose,” commented Pangborn, former circus flyer from Wenatchee, Wash., as he recalled the maximum fine for violation of the civil aviation regulations was 3,000 yen ($1,500) for each offender. “And don't forget,” chipped in Herndon, the former Princeton student, “that the workhouse is just around the corner if we don’t raise 2,000 bones within a week.” The aviators were reassured, however, by press dispatches saying their backers in New York had cabled the necessary money. The two men agreed the fine was just about the biggest jolt they ever had experienced

1931-08-11.text: London, Aug. 11.—(U. P.)—Full agreement has been reached on measures to make the Hoover debt holiday effective. A formal protocol embodying such measures will be signed at once, a foreign office communique said today. The communique said that the conference of experts appointed by the governments of Belgium, France, Great Britain, Ireland, Northern Ireland, Germany, Italy and Japan, which for the last three weeks has been sitting in London, held its final sitting in the treasury department this morning. The experts reached complete agreement, the announcement said. It was expected that signatures would be affixed to the formal protocol this afternoon.

London, Aug. 11.— (AP) — Representatives of five great nations concerned in adjustment of German reparations payments this evening signed a protocol co-ordinating the Hoover moratorium proposals with provisions of the Young plan.

BOMBAY, India, Aug. 11 (P)—Almost on the eve of the departure of delegates, two of the most vital elements in India threatened today to wreck the unity and representative character of the second roundtable conference in London which is expected to give Great Britain’s restless dependency its new charter of freedom... With a dramatic swiftness which must have taken the breath away from Viceroy Willingdon, Mahatma Gandhi served notice on the Simla government that he would not go to London unless he is given positive assurance that during his absence peasants who are in arrears with taxes will not be placed under duress by revenue authorities, nor will there be further evictions for default in land revenue or rents.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Aug. 10.—The whereabouts of Parker Cramer, American flier enroute here from the Shetland Islands, was still unknown at 8:30 a.m. (3:30 a.m., in Salem) today. Military planes were scouting the coastline and radio stations were calling vainly. Receive Wireless Calls The Exchange Telegraph agency reported that the naval dockyard had picked up several puzzling wireless telephone calls in which the speaker cried “Hello, hello” in what was judged to be an American accent. Nevertheless, anxiety was felt as the hours passed without definite word of the flier. The calls were distinct and only the word “Norway” was made out. BERLIN, Aug. 10. (AP)—Prussia’s moderate coalition government, its fate of lately closely identified with Chancellor Bruening’s regime, today stood firm against the legal and illegal onslaughts of its enemies of the right and left. The combined efforts of the communists, national socialists and nationalists to dissolve the Prussian diet and to compel new elections failed by three and a half million votes at a plebiscite yesterday. Though revolutionists dynamiters derailed the Basel-Berlin express and the whole of the east central district of Berlin was in a frenzy of fatal rioting, the police obtained full control of the situation. Two police captains were slain in Buelow Platz, communist center in Berlin, and a steelhelmeter leader was killed in Cologne as a result of conflict between authorities and radicals. A score of persons were believed to be dying in Berlin as the aftermath of a

BERLIN, Aug. 10.—(4%—Padlocks and extraordinarily heavy police guards tonight maintained peace in the Buelow Platz, Berlin communist center, which was the scene of a bloody riot last night. Earlier today the police placed a padlock on the Karl Liebknecht Haus in the Buelow Platz, center of Germany's communistic activities, and suspended for two weeks the communist newspaper Rote Fahne in front of which last night's rioting occurred. At sundown a large reserve police force was taken into the neighborhood, still in an ugly mood, but the temper of the police matched that of the communists, and the loss of two popular officers from their ranks in last night's shooting put them in no mind for pleasantries. Twenty-five communists were questioned today in connection with the wrecking of the Basel-Berlin express Saturday night.

BERLIN, Aug. 11—()—Germany, confident that her financial and political troubles had been solved, celebrated today the twelfth anniversary of the founding of the republic. The Republican black, red and gold flag floated from all official and many private buildings and most officials participated in the festivities. Chancellor Bruening, finance minister Dietrich, the president of Prussia and the Lord Mayor of Berlin were on the program for addresses at the opera house. The Berlin police, smarting under the loss of two of their officers in a battle with Communists Sunday, had a celebration of their own in the Lustgarten in front of the former kaiser’s palace.
Berlin, Aug. 11.—-(2P)—Directors of the Reichsbank today lowered the discount rate from 15 to 10 percent, and the rate on collateral loans from 20 to 16 percent.

As it was forecast, these palliatives were confined to a three months extension of the $100,000,000 loan from the central banks of the world powers, to concerted measures in all countries to maintain existing credits in Germany and to recommendations dealing with Germany’s future needs. The final plenary session at the foreign office in Downing Street ended at noon with felicitous farewells which stressed the inter-dependence of nations and welcomed the participation of the United States, through Secretaries Stimson and Mellon, at the European council table. LONDON, July 24—The statesmen of seven nations were enroute for home today after conversations this week which resulted in at least temporary financial relief for Germany. They left details of their program to be worked out by the financial experts who have been here all week also, waiting until cabinet members of the seven powers decided how far their government could go to aid Germany. The financial experts will work out the details of the Hoover plan for a war debts holiday and make recommendations on how to proceed to put it into effect for a year without disrupting budgets. Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson said he would leave for Berlin tonight. Stimson indicated he wanted to resume his informal talks in Berlin about arms limitation, in preparation for the Geneva arms parley next February. He already has seen Mussolini and the French. The moderate newspapers agree the help accorded the nation's finances by the powers is only a stop-gap. But even the opposition newspapers refrain from violent attacks on Chancellor Bruening for failing to leave London with a couple of billion marks in his grip. Auteuil, France, July 24 — Fred Perry, 21-year-old British tennis player, today defeated Jean Borotra in a bitter five-set match to give England an even break with France at the end of the first day of play in the challenge round for the Davis Cup. The scores were: 4-6, 16-8, 6-0, 8-6, 6-4. In the first singles match of the series Henri Cochet, playing in his old time form, rallied from seeming defeat to crush H. W. MOSCOW, July 24.—(UP)—Serious workers among Soviet leaders were bewildered by George Bernard Shaw, Irish wit and playwright, here on a holiday tour, Shaw and Lady Astor, American member of the British parliament, listened to serious speeches by their Russian friends and their counter remarks left the Russians puzzled, Shaw, blue eyes twinkling at a Russian factory, commented: “The more I see of the proletarians, the more I thank God I am not one of them,”

Washington, July 23. (4)—Led by President Hoover, the American capital tonight hailed the results of the London ministers’ conference as a foundation for German economic stability. Secretary Stimson reported fully by both transatlantic telephone and cable the results of the conference. In a formal statement, Mr. Hoover characterized the conference’s work as a contribution to the recovery from the worldwide depression. He said the conference had laid a “sound foundation for the establishment of stability in Germany.” (Turn to Page Nine)

(By The Associated Press) Provincetown, Mass., June 5— The submarine Nautilus, in which Sir Hubert Wilkins and a group of scientists hope to get to the North Pole, left Provincetown harbor for England at 10 o'clock (e. s. t.) last night. The Nautilus had spent the day here in speed trials. The coast guard cutter Ponchartrain accompanied her out tonight and will act as convoy as far as the Grand Banks.

Hamburg, Germany, June 4.—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening and Foreign Minister Julius Curtius left today for England to engage in a week-end conference with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald concerning Anglo-German problems. Their conversations with the British premier and Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson at Chequers are expected to deal with the matter of reparations, the Austro-German customs treaty and other matters affecting indirectly the whole of Europe. The chancellor's last act before leaving Berlin was to submit to President Paul Von Hindenburg a number of emergency decrees which are believed to embody additional slashes in the budget and in wage schedules. If approved, these are expected to contribute further to the nation’s discontent. Their departure coincided with rioting by communists and unemployed persons near the city hall. 1931-06-23.text: | LONDON, June 22. (AP)—The Prince of Wales will be 37 years old tomorrow—and still a bachelor. Britain seems to have accepted the situation and his final decision for there isn’t even the usual crop of rumors buzzing about his blond head. For one thing, much of the affection which set old ladies to gossiping over their teacups and maidens a-sighing, has been transferred from the Prince to little Princess Elizabeth. For another, Wales has changed in this last year from something of a playboy Prince whose main job was to inherit the British throne to a business Prince who means to help restore Britain’s lost trade. He is an older man, as well, and while even at 37 there is still something boyish about him, he isn’t any kid and his public life reflects this change as well.

CHICAGO, June 22.—(AP)—Summer, in its third-day caprice, slid down the thermometer today. Over-Sunday showers and breezes cooled off most of America, choking the heat wave that was spring’s dying gasp. From New England to California, temperatures were moderate. The middle west, seared by a welter that burned out more than a score of lives, was succored by rains and Great Lakes winds. In Kansas and Texas the heat still ruled but cooler temperatures held sway to the west. Beneficial rains brought a respite to Montana. It rained in Denver and sent the ABV downwards, Washington and its surroundings were visited by showers blown down from Alaska. In New York and other eastern states, the weather changed its mind after reaching the nineties and scampered back into the low eighties. But Maryland and parts of the south still sweltered.

| London, June 23. —The Prince of Wales observed his 387th birthday today, still unmarried. For nearly 20 years, almost every eligible girl in the world has been suggested as his bride. A fairly large section of the public is convinced the Prince will never marry and will never become king. With absolutely no official basis for its theories, it believes that when the time comes the Prince will abdicate in favor of his brother, the Duke of York.

WAREHAM, Dorset, Eng., June 23 (/P).--Three persons are known to have been killed and eight others, it is believed practically certain were blown to pieces, in an explosion which wiped out several buildings of the naval cordite factory at Walton Heath today. Nineteen persons were injured.

POOLE Eng., Jun 23. UP)—The Royal Naval Cordite Factory at Holton Heath, six miles from Poole, was shattered by a terrific explosion today. Eleven men were killed and 19 injured. The explosion which occurred in the nitroglycerine department, was heard for a radius of 20 miles. Its force knocked a man from a chair two miles from the factory.
London, June 23—(#)—Alfred Horn, better known as “Trader Horn,” was critically ill in a mercy home at Whitstable today. He was taken sick at the home of his daughter a few days ago.
LONDON, June 23.—(4)—The admiralty announced ten were killed and 19 injured in an explosion at a naval cordite factory near Wareham.

CORK, IRISH FREE STATE, June 22.—Safe after a buffeting by seas, the submarine Nautilus came slowly into Queenstown harbor today and up the river to this city where it was berthed amid a welcoming din, led by civic authorities. Showing the effects of the strenuous 17-day crossing, unshaven members of the crew said the vessel, in which its commander, Sir Hubert Wilkins, plans to try to reach the north pole under the ice, ran short of supplies. This occurred after it became disabled and was picked up by the U.S.S. Wyoming 800 miles off the coast of Ireland. Wilkins Reticent Wilkins was reticent but members of the crew reported the water in the tanks of the Nautilus had been muddy and almost undrinkable during the past few days. The Wyoming transferred meat and bread to them during the last stages. The crew generally suffered from bad air and cramped quarters made necessary by the battering

1931-03-19.text: London, March 19—(UP)—The steamer, Chang Kiang, struck the rock off Heihan Island near Haimen Monday and sank with a loss of 14 lives, Lloyd’s was advised today from Shanghai. The vessel was a total loss. The French gunboat Marne was standing by taking the surviving crew and passengers on board.

Oslo, Norway, March 19—(UP)—Eight persons were known dead today in the wreck of the steamship Hera which crashed on the rocks of Hammerfest at midnight Wednesday in a snow storm. The missing included an eight year old girl and four stewardesses. At least 56 persons fought their way to safety, most of them swimming to shore despite the freezing water. The Hera, a Norwegian ship of 1080 tons, was going at full speed when it struck the rocks.

PISA (WP)—Col. Umberto Maddalena, famous Italian flier, was killed here Thursday when his seaplane crashed off Marina Di Pisa. Lieut. Fausto Cecconi, who was Maddalena’s companion on many distinguished flights, also was killed in the crash, as was another officer, whose name was not ascertained. It was understood they were testing their seaplane in preparation for a flight from Italy to the Panama Canal this summer. Col. Umberto Maddalena was one of the greatest of Italian fliers. He piloted the plane which first sighted the survivors of the dirigible Italia when it was wrecked on its north pole expedition and carried food to them.

SHANGHAI, March 18—(#)— The slaughter of 3,000 peasants in a Communist uprising along the Hupeh-Szechwan border was reported in Chinese dispatches today. Nationalist government military forces at Shasi, Hupeh province, were reported to have undertaken an expedition against the Reds. The scene of the uprising was designated as north of the Yangtse river in the border area mentioned. The area was said to have been pillaged. Communists and mutinous soldiers severed the Peiping-Hankow railway at the Hupeh-Henan border and ravaged the countryside. The disorders were said to be continuing there.

NICE, France, Mar 18.—Magistrate Vachier indicated today at the close of his first examination of Mrs. Charlotte Nash Nixon-Nirdlinger that the former St. Louis beauty would not be charged with first degree murder for the slaying of her husband in their apartment here a week ago. The American beauty’s attorney said she repeated to the magistrate her story to police that she shot in self-defense when she slew the Philadelphia theatre owner and quoted her as saying to the judge: “I have led a dog’s life, but I will always regret I was in a position where I was forced to take human life.” Sobbing often in the course of the two hours and a half she was questioned, her counsel said, the young wife declared fright and terror caused her to keep firing at her husband and chasing him around the room after one bullet had taken effect. | Nice, France, March 18.—()— Mrs. Charlotte Nash Nixon-Nirdlinger must stand trial for killing her husband, Fred Nirdlinger, Magistrate Vachier admitted today after questioning the former St. Louis beauty queen, but he indicated the charge would not be murder in the first degree. Stylishly dressed, Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger was driven to the chambers of Magistrate Vachier today in a prison wagon and told her story, containing the details of how she shot her husband a week ago in their apartment. She told the judge: “IT have led a dog's life, but I will always regret I was in a position where I was forced to take human life.” In Terror She sobbed frequently during the questioning, which lasted two and a half hours, her counsel said, and declared that fright and terror caused her to keep firing at her husband and chasing him around the room after one bullet had taken effect.

TOKYO, March 19—(AP)—Eleven participants in an anti-government demonstration were injured in a clash with police and several policemen also were hurt when they attacked the demonstrators near the parliament buildings today. The demonstration was arranged by the seiyukai, or minority, party as a prelude to introduce in the diet tomorrow a motion of non-confidence in the minseito (majority) cabinet of Premier Hamaguchi. The demonstrators were attempting to reach the diet after marching through the streets carrying banners reading “Dissolve the corrupted diet,” and “Overthrow the reactionary Hamaguchi cabinet.” About 140 demonstrators were arrested. Simultaneously, the social-democratic and proletarian parties held mass meetings and parades and endeavored to march to the diet to present petitions but, like the seiyukai sympathizers, were unable to get within two blocks of the building, whic

NICE, France, Mar. 19.--The fixing of a date for the trial of Mrs. Charlotte Nash Nixon-Nirdlinger on charges of killing her husband was awaited today by her counsel. A magistrate decided yesterday that the former beauty queen should be tried, but on a lesser charge than that of first degree murder, for the slaying last week of her husband, Fred, Philadelphia theater owner. Her plea will be self-defense. Police Doctor Peaulelieu, who performed an autopsy on Mr. Nixon-Nirdlinger’s body, confirmed today that he found evidences of a cranial operation. It has been indicated the operation might have some bearing on the case.

1931-10-23.text: | Lanarka, Island of Cyprus, Oct. 23.—(AP)—The military and naval power of the British empire was hastening today to quell a revolt in Cyprus, ancient Mediterranean island over which Alexander the Great squabbled with an Egyptian Ptolemy, and where St. Paul, St. Mark and St. Barnabas preached early Christianity. For more than a day most of the island has been in control of revolters who are demanding union with Greece, which aided Cyprus in the struggle against Alexander 2,000-odd years ago. The revolt developed after weeks of growing resentment against a British imperial order imposing tariffs which the Cyprian legislative council had rejected. Late last night a group of revolutionists stopped motor trucks carrying rations for British soldiers at Limasol. The drivers of the trucks were forced to abandon them. The mob overpowered the police and attacked and burned the district commission

Cairo, Egypt, Oct. 22.—British troops were rushed by sea and air tonight to the ancient Isle of Cyprus to suppress riots and to put down a well-advanced movement to link the Cyprian government to Greece. Two cruisers, the London and the Shropshire, and two destroyers, the Achates and the Acasta, with more than 1,400 men and officers, were dispatched from the Mediterranean fleet base on the Isle of Crete after riots at Nicosia, capital of Cyprus, in the course of which Government house was burned. (Continued on Page 2)

Larnaka, Island of Cyprus, Oct. 22 — A strange drama of racial and national passion that reaches back to the heroes of ancient Greece is being enacted tonight, here on this little Levantine Island once sacred to Aphrodite. The climax comes tomorrow with the arrival of four British warships from Crete and of airplanes bringing British soldiers from Egypt. Tonight the island populace hopes to bring about union with Greece, to which Cyprus was bound of old. Since dusk yesterday most of the island has been in the throes of mob rule which followed weeks of resentment against an imperial order in council imposing a reorganization of the tariff which the legislative council previously had rejected. Last night, after addressing a large meeting at Nicosia, several members of the council led a mob to government house to present their resignations and to demand union with Greece. London, Oct. 23—()—Disorders in the island of Cyprus have subsided, the colonial office announced today, and the situation is “smoothing over generally though still unsettled.” Several persons were injured Wednesday night when a section of the people agitating for union with Greece caused serious disturbances at Nicosia. One of the injured was reported to have died. For more than a day most of the island has been in control of revolutionists who are demanding union with Greece, which aided Cyprus (Continued on page fifteen.)

London, Oct. 22,—(#)—Bootlegging in the United States results in the corruption of police and law courts, but that is no reason for doing away with prohibition, George Bernard Shaw told the World Prohibition Federation today. He attacked tipplers who utilize the glass to obtain jollity or courage, saying he should feel ashamed if he had to resort to such measures. And he accused Gilbert Chesterton of being a “secret teetotaler,” because Chesterton “is so very loud” in singing the praises of wine. Prohibition Successful. The direct results of prohibition in the United States have been “eminently successful in every way,” Shaw said, “but some of the indirect results are very curious. “There's an industry called bootlegging in America, and its profits are so large the people who conduct it have immense sums for the corruption of justice. In some of the eastern states this corruption of poli

| WASHINGTON, Oct. 23. (U) -- Probably President Hoover and Premier Laval would like to be alone, but their conversations will always be overheard. All because Mr. Hoover is “not proud of his French” and the premier speaks no English. In his first interview with Washington newspaper men, Laval had Robert Pell, aide to Ambassador Edge in Paris, acting as interpreter. A number of expert interpreters have been provided by the state department and the French embassy to the White House conversations.

New York, Oct. 23.—(AP)—Hitting at the use of British ocean liners for “nowhere” or “whoopee” cruises from American ports, Captain John P. Milliken, secretary of the Neptune association, has written to Secretary of the Treasury Mellon protesting the continuance of the trips. He said the vessels violated the coastwise laws because they did not call or stop at any foreign port before entering New York. He also believes it is a violation of the prohibition amendment as the vessels bring liquor into the port for beverage purposes. The Red Star liner Belgenland and Homeric made such cruises Columbus Day, and the White Star liner Majestic went out yesterday on such a trip. NEW YORK, Oct. 23. (?)—Hitting at the use of British ocean liners for “nowhere” or “whoopee” cruises from American ports, Capt. John F. Milliken, secretary of the Neptune association, has written to Secy. of the Treasury Mellon protesting the continuance of the trips. He said the vessels violated the coastwise laws because they did not call or stop at any foreign port before returning to New York.

(AP).—The terms of the British-Franco-Italian naval accord transferring the London naval pact into a virtual five-power agreement were made public today in the form of a memorandum by Arthur Henderson, the foreign secretary. Its terms covered three outstanding considerations in the armament situation—technical problems of European naval power are swept away; renewal of an armaments race, such as led to the World War, has, it is hoped, been prevented; success of the world disarmament conference at Geneva is brought measurably closer. The agreement is based on the principle of continuance of the present Franco-Italian tonnage ratio until 1936, filling a gap in the London treaty by bringing the French and Italian fleets within the effective operation of the pact signed at St. James Palace last spring. London—AP—There was no sign Wednesday of a break in the bitter winter weather which has gripped most of Europe since last week. France, Germany, Austria and the British Isles continued to experience exceptional low temperatures and heavy snowfalls. Although some places in England reported higher temperatures, others recorded temperatures of below zero Fahrenheit. Renewed snowstorms thickened the already heavy blanket of snow. France is experiencing the coldest late winter in many years. Temperatures vary from 14 to 26 Fahrenheit. Snowfalls have been particularly heavy in Normandy, Brittany, Alsace and Savoy where enormous avalanches have blocked a number of roads.

BY 10S Associated Press Frosty winter bit into the south today, tightened its cold grip over Europe and swept the Balkan quake scenes with chill winds. Snow avalanches descended upon rail and telegraph lines in France. Ice encrusted English roads. Ships tossed on high waves through blinding snow along the continental coast. New England and the Midwest still were digging from under drifts. The Black Forest and Rhine Valley of Germany lay buried in white. Battered fragments of boats and the pieces of an airplane were remnants of coast gales in Massachusetts. The boat fragments indicated five fishermen were lost. The airplane pieces spelled tragic mystery. Dixie frost was felt as far south as Miami, Fla.

Paris, Mar. 11 — Renewal of harmony among the five naval powers of the world is regarded in France as the most important achievement of the Franco-British-Italian naval accord. A spokesman for the foreign office said today that the agreement among these three nations is the sole guarantee for the success of the 1932 disarmament conference upon which the world has staked so much. Aristide Briand’s next move will be to submit to the French parliament the London naval treaty of 1930 which, it is expected, now will be ratified almost unanimously.

Paris, March 11.— (AP) — Dispatches from Barcelona, Spain, today said the new republican catalanist party there had published a declaration expressing Catalonia’s aspiration to full autonomy and consecration to the principle of self-determination. The declaration proclaims complete separation from civil and ecclesiastical powers so far as the schools are concerned. The right to use of the Catalonian language, a guarantee of protection for private property honestly acquired, the right of workmen to sufficient pay, and insurance against illness, old age and unemployment. “The new party,” the proclamation reads, “erects a republic of democracy and catalanism in their general principles. On the twenty-second of March we will accomplish various public acts to inaugurate our activities.”

TURIN, Italy, March 11—-(UP)— Professor Lacchinin of the Pino Torinese observatory announced today the discovery, through astral photography, of traces of a new planet in the solar system. The new planet was named provisionally Ba.

Lomion — () — Approbation, laughter and denunciation were visited upon Lady Cynthia Moseley Friday in the public's answer to her courageous speech last evening, setting her husband's “new party” on its way. Sir Oswald was ill abed with influenza, and could not address a great crowd which assembled at Farrington Hall to hear an outline of his principles, but his wife, a daughter of the late Marquis Curzon and a granddaughter of Levi Leiter, Chicago merchant, served ably in his stead. One section of her hearers cheered her statements but others obviously had come to heckle her. At one point after a series of unusual taunts she answered: “My God, if you had sat in the House of Commons for the last eighteen months you would be here on the platform beside me.” Her message was a warning of the “abnormal dangerous and desperate” national crisis facing Britain, for which she offered as a solutio

BOSTON, March 6 (UP)—Devastation unparalleled in nearly a generation lay today in the wake of three monster tides which rolled in from a turbulent and storm-torn Atlantic Wednesday and yesterday and hammered a 200-mile stretch of the New England coast. Estimates of the damage ranged upward of $2,000,000. Scores of seaside houses were in ruins. Others had been carried to sea. Breakwaters at many points had been destroyed or severely damaged. Rail lines, trolley tracks and highways had been washed out. Hundreds of persons were homeless. One ship had foundered, another had narrowly escaped a like fate, and several others had been imperiled. At least two deaths were attributed to the severe storm which was partly responsible for the near-record tides.

| TRURO, N. S., (P)—Twenty families have been huddled for more than a night and day in upper stories of their home on Devil’s Island while roaring waves, sweeping in from the sea through the hamlet’s streets, seethed below them. Word of the plight of the islanders came in telephone messages here during the night. The messages told of a 90-mile gale which sent the seas racing through the village, pounding structures and weakening their foundations. Blinding snow and sleet added to the discomfort of the marooned families. The growling wind and splashing waves ripped to pieces breakwaters and wharves. Only the lighthouse seemed able to withstand their onslaughts. Many tales of bravery among the fishermen were current here today. One concerned Ben Henneberry, lighthouse keeper, who was rescued by neighbors after he was washed out to sea by a giant wave while attempting to save his little boa

Halifax, N. S., March 6. (P)—Aid was speeding through the stormy north Atlantic tonight to the British steamer Rosalind, lying helplessly halfway between St. John's, N. F., and this port. The vessel, which has 35 passengers, lost her propeller in a squall. Agents of the Furness Red Cross line advised tonight the tug Rhode Zee had sailed from St. John's to pick up the vessel within 24 hours and tow her here.

LONDON (U.P)—There are indications that the long-awaited trade boom will start here this spring. These indications are many. Leaders of industry and members of the government are said to be basing their plans on them. The federation of British industries, in its trade barometer just issued, says: “Spring should see some improvement. Chancellor of the Exchequer Philip Snowden is preparing his budget on the assumption that the trade returns will shortly show a substantial improvement and yield him increased revenue. The trade fair, which opens in the spring, and which is attended by buyers from all parts of the world, probably will provide big orders for British industry. Meanwhile, many huge contracts are being secured, often in the face of world competition. Further evidence of the approaching spring boom is to be found in the announcement that the Wellman Smith Owen Engineering corporat

By United Press AMSTERDAM, March 6—An earthquake at Tjoeklil, Java, killed several persons and destroyed many houses today, reports received here said. Thousands fled from their homes, which were flooded by the bursting of dykes in the River Tjitarcen.

NEW DELHI, India, March 5.—The terms on which John Bull and Mother India will resume a speaking acquaintance were made public today, but the way to the altar was still fraught by bypaths to dissension. Mahatma Gandhi ordered the termination of the civil disobedience campaign, and Lord Irwin moved to revoke the statutes against those who waged it, pending the next turn of the wheel of India’s fate.

1931-07-21.text: London, July 21 () (Tuesday)— Chancellor Heinrich Bruening of Germany decided early this morning, unless something new develops later in the day, to withdraw his plea for a $375,000,000 loan for Germany and to ask, for the present, only for a continuation of the present short-term credits estimated at $125,000,000. The German Chancellor's decision was made on the advice of Prime Minister MacDonald. It would stand, he said, unless entirely new viewpoints developed out of today's sessions of the seven-power conference and any reference to a $375,000,000 loan will not be made until later, at least. The situation, as the British Prime Minister is said to have presented it, is as follows: The only country from which Germany can get a long-term large loan at present is France. BY RENDER, MUN, United Press Staff Correspondent. London, July 21— (UP) —Secretary Stimson is confident big American banks will help Germany. They will cooperate toward maintaining German credits providing banks in other countries act similarly, in his belief. Addressing a seven-power plenary session this morning, he made it clear that American banks have not withdrawn any of their credits in Germany, and some have even increased their credits. American sources were reticent concerning proceedings before the meeting, summoned to aid Germany and to avert possible financial crises throughout Europe. From other authoritative sources, however, it was learned that the American state secretary outlined the United States’ attitude and policy, but made no definite proposal. A communique issued after the morning session adjourned said the conferees had considered “methods of international co-operation whereby confidence in Germany's economic stability may be restored in the immediate future.” It was said in well-informed quarters that the conference has been encountering severe and disturbing difficulties, attributed by some to the insistence of France that Germany pay for outside aid with politics! “At the same time, it was said the United States and Great Britain understand the American and British views are in complete accord, that they regard immediate relief as imperative, but they do not approve of a long-term loan at this time.

WASHINGTON, July 21.—(UP)— The American government, through its representatives at the London conference, today proposed an international agreement of bankers be made to maintain short term credits amounting to $1,200,000,000 which have been extended to Germany. The proposal was made as a means of safeguarding the German economic structure. The plan provides further that European nations eliminate present political friction for the economic benefit of Europe. It suggests that an international committee, probably under the auspices of the Bank of International Settlements, provide the machinery for international cooperation to maintain short term credits for Germany. London, July 21.--7P--Prime minister MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson probably will go to Berlin with Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius when the seven power conference here ends, it was learned today. Mr. MacDonald, who has insisted throughout the recent negotiations that re-establishment of confidence in Germany is the prime need of the moment, wants to make a public demonstration of Great Britain's confidence, it was said, and incidentally to return the visit the German statesmen paid to Chequers recently.

MOSCOW, July 21.—(AP)— George Bernard Shaw reached here today, waved his soft hat at hundreds waiting for him at the railway station and declined the pleas of Lady Nancy Astor, who also was a member of the British touring party, to see the gentlemen of the press. “Oh, but you must see them, George,” said the ‘Ainestens princess. “I'll see them — definitely and categorically damned,” Shaw said and demanded to be taken immediately to the tomb of Lenin in Red Square.

Moscow, July 21 (UP)—George Bernard Shaw, Irish wit and writer, arrived by train today for a visit to Soviet Russia. Lady Astor, American-born member of the British parliament, and Viscount Astor, her husband, were on the same train.

1931-02-25.text: ROME, Feb. 24. (4)—Transformation of the London naval three power pact into a five power treaty, with Italy and France adhering, appeared a distinct probability tonight. Word that British minister Arthur Henderson and A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, had left for home to present a conditional accord reached in Paris was hailed with satisfaction in circles conversant with Italian official views.

By The Associated Press London, Feb 24--Gen Charles G. Dawes, America’s fiery ambassador to the Court of St. James, who has won his way to the hearts of the British people, plans to serve his full term of two more years here, he told the Associated Press today. The ambassador thus silenced rumors that he would return to the United States either for political work or in connection with the World Fair at Chicago. He and his brother made themselves responsible for the opening of the exposition on time. The general, who has a host of friends here, seems perfectly satisfied with his present job, although it was reported to be costing him $160,000 a year out of his own pocket. In announcing his intention to remain here for two more years, unless some unforeseen circumstance arises, he waived his famous under-slung pipe and said: “I am 65 years old. What more should I want to do?”

RANGOON, Burma, Feb. 25.—(P)—Fifteen rebel Burmans were killed and six wounded fighting government troops in the Henzada district today. No troopers were killed. A number of Burmese districts near Tharawaddy have been disaffected since the British put down an insurrection in early January.

NEW YORK, Feb. 25, (AP)—Sax Rohmer, British author of crime stories, is in town with an idea for improving New York and Chicago. He would have the federal government put troops into the two cities, declare martial law and make every person on the streets after a certain hour identify himself.

From the nature of measures adopted and orders issued authorities appeared to anticipate stubborn resistance to orders issued in many countries forbidding demonstrations or indoor and outdoor meetings during the day. Austria, where the influence of the communists on Socialist unemployed is slight, is one of the few countries where such strict bans against public gatherings have not been issued. Washington, Feb. 13.—(/P)—A formal report recommending early passage of a compromise bill to swell the borrowing power of veterans on compensation certificates to $1,740,000,000 was made ready for introduction today by the House Ways and Means committee. Prompt approval for the measure, put forward for depression-relief as well as to aid veterans, was anticipated. House leaders prepared to bring it up next Monday under a rule of procedure precluding amendments. Chairman Hawley called the committee to give formal assent after a unanimous agreement yesterday settled the controversy which has raged for weeks. 1931-06-09.text: LONDON, June 9.—The admiralty announced today that the British submarine, Poseidon, one of the largest in the fleet, had been sunk in a collision near Weihaiwei, on the north shore of the Shantung Peninsula in China. Five officers and 26 men were saved but two died after they were rescued. Eighteen men are still missing.

London, June 9.—(4)—The possibility of suspension of debt payments to the United States occupied a large part Tuesday in newspaper speculation over the results of a week-end conference between German and British officials. The Daily Mail featured a dispatch from the Vossische Zeitung of Berlin predicting that the Reich would demand postponement of the “deferable” payments of the Young plan as soon as Chancellor Heinrich Brüning and Foreign Minister Julius Curtius return from their conference with British officials. On the basis of that, the Mail predicted Germany might suspend reparations payments next fall. The big event in their day was a 20-minute conference with King George V. LONDON, June 9—Premier Ramsay MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson have accepted an invitation for a return visit to Berlin as a sequel to the Chequers conference of last weekend, it was officially announced today. No date for the trip has been fixed as yet. Chancellor Heinrich Brüning and Foreign Minister Julius Curtius, who went to Southampton today to board the Europa for Germany, will be hosts to MacDonald and Henderson, and it is anticipated that there will be a continuation of friendly and informal conversations. As was the case in the Chequers meeting, Germany’s financial problems will be discussed, it was presumed. The United States holds the key to the war debts and reparations problems, it was admitted. It was emphasized in well-informed quarters, however, that no direct approach to the United States was envisaged by any of the powers concerned, although it was indi

LONDON, June 9 (®)—Eight American women will be at Buckingham palace tonight as participants in the third court of the season before King George and Queen Mary. With about 400 others, they were in the hands of their dressmakers and social advisers today. Shimmering gowns were being finished and final instructions given before they begin the long ride up the hall for the presentation.

LONDON, June 8—(AP)—The ancient wailing wall in Jerusalem, over which Moslems and Jews have clashed at times in fatal riots, is owned solely by the Moslems, a special government commission ruled today. The commission, which was created by the British government with the approval of the League of Nations Council, also declared that the Jews should have free access to the wall for devotional purposes at all times, but it outlined certain definite conditions regarding appurtenances of worship. All political speeches and demonstrations are forbidden in the neighborhood of the wall and the Moslems were told not to annoy the Jews when they gathered there for their devotions. Use of benches, carpets and similar belongings is prohibited at the wall, and the Jews were told not to blow the ram's horn in the vicinity. However, on their days of worship they are allowed to place near the wall the cab

LONDON, June 6.--(A’)—Diplomatic London, analyzing today what could be learned of the results of the Anglo-German conversations at Chequers, believed it saw the foreshadowing of immediate activity on a large scale in European foreign offices and at Washington to determine when, and how a new world conference on reparations could be called. Close-mouthed as the four principals in the Chequers conferences have been, enough has leaked out to indicate an official reference to “international collaboration” through the medium of an international conference. It seemed equally certain, however, that the diplomatic activity looking toward such a conference must at present be limited to unofficial feelers until a more definite knowledge is obtained of the reasons which are bringing the Amer- (Continued on Page 2, Col. 3.)

REVERE, Mass., June 9—()— Harold B. Clarke, 29 years old, of New York, was under arrest today, charged with the theft of rare editions worth $50,000 from several New England libraries, Boston police who arrested him said he admitted the thefts. Inspectors took him into custody on a warrant charging theft of books from the Lancaster public library. They said that they found $7,000 worth of stolen books in his possession and that 100 valuable books in his room had been prepared for shipment to New York City. The officers said they found a notebook containing names of customers in Paris, London, Berlin and Buenos Aires in Clarke’s possession. They seized a manuscript allegedly written by Clarke entitled “Staggering Revelations of Wholesale Looting of Priceless Literature from Maine to California.” Clarke told them that a New York publisher accepted the book for publication.

1931-03-14.text: “Washington — The United States may yet take an official, active part in the Franco-Italian naval agreement. It has been invited by Great Britain to join the other five powers signatory to the London treaty in debating the final form of the new settlement. This invitation was taken under consideration by Secretary Stimson. Acceptance was indicated. The suggestion was interpreted here as an effort to enable Japan and the United States to recognize and approve officially the new agreement without the necessity of signing. Heretofore, the state department has followed the theory it would be best for the United States only to approve passively the Franco-Italian agreement; Japan adopted the same attitude. Secretary Stimson can see no necessity for the United States to sign the treaty since it relates solely to Great Britain, France and Italy. Signing would require senate approval and delay t

WASHINGTON, MAR. 14, (AP).—Secretary Stimson announced today that Senator Dwight W. Morrow, now en route to Europe on the Leviathan, had wirelessed him agreeing to a request by the secretary that he stop in London and confer with Ambassador Dawes on the naval question. The secretary said he made his request to the senator by wireless after Morrow had sailed. He asked that the senator explain to Ambassador Dawes the general attitude of the American government toward the recently concluded Franco-Italian naval settlement. There was no comment in the state department on who the United States would designate if it accepted a British invitation to participate in drafting the final agreement embodying the Franco-Italian settlement. Secretary Stimson was hopeful he might secure the senator's service if he accepted the invitation.

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, March 14.—(4)—British industry, sciences and arts were extolled to the Argentine and South America this afternoon by the Prince of Wales in formal dedication of the British trade exposition here. The prince commented that he might have opened the exposition in London through some contrivance based on modern invention, but that he had preferred to come to Buenos Aires “to express my sense of appreciation at the exceptional importance of this exhibition to the future of British trade with the Argentine republic. “If, as we all hope, the response of the Argentine purchasing public to the appeal of the exhibition leads in some measure to the revival of industrial prosperity in Great Britain and consequently to diminution of industrial unemployment, a reciprocal result of increase in British consumption of Argentine wheat and Argentine cereals is certain. “Interchange

WASHINGTON, March 13. (P)— Acceptance by the United States of an invitation to be represented on a committee of the five principal naval powers signatory to the London naval agreement to draft the final form of the Franco-Italian settlement tonight appeared likely. Senator Dwight W. Morrow of New Jersey, en route to Europe, probably will be one of the American representatives if the United States accepts the invitation extended by the British government.

New York, Mar. 14—TA.P.—Dr. James H. Kimball appreciates that acid medal the boys are pinning on him today. Who's Who will tell you in cold English he was consulting meteorologist for Lindbergh, Chamberlin, Byrd, Bertault, Brock, Haldeman, Lotti and Yancey before they charted the elements above the Atlantic. DISCLAIMS CREDIT. Dr. Kimball will peer out under gray locks that fall over his forehead and disclaim any personal credit. "It's the weather bureau, not me," he will say, "Of course, I was the one that came into contact with the boys and they make it personal." The medal to Dr. Kimball is being presented by the International Ligue of Aviators, of which King Albert of Belgium is honorary chairman. He is also being received into the league as an honorary member and will be the first American so honored. PRAISES FLYERS. Flying the Atlantic, to him, is more than heroic. "The boys who do

London, March 14.—(/)—Dame Madge Kendall, famous actress of a generation and more ago, who will be 82 tomorrow, retains her belief in old fashioned girls, and thinks the maids of today are given their latch keys too early. “I was 68 before my husband gave me one,” she said today. “On my birthday I persuaded my husband to give me one. He brought me a little charm to hang it on, so I shouldn't lose it. I wish women would try to retain their old fashioned ways. We have made divorce so cheap marriage has become almost comical.” Old Folks to Gather Dame Madge will preside on her birthday night at a dinner of the Old Players’ club, a noted organization of first nighters.

SOUTHAMPTON, England— a pink bathroom for the Prince of Wales; a green one for Prince George. They were installed on the liner that will return them from Buenos Aires. An apple-green reception room was thrown in.

By The Associated Press. NICE, France, March 14.--Under no circumstances will Mrs. Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger, who killed her husband here last Wednesday night be released without a jury trial, the examining magistrate said today. She will be brought before the ordinary session of the court of assizes which does not meet until August, the magistrate said.

1931-05-24.text: LONDON, May 23—4— Wheat exporting nations of the world followed closely the lines proposed by the United States. The decision was made before adjourning to create a registry house for information on the grain growing industry and "restrict wheat production wherever possible." Reduction of acreage at the source was the chief plan offered by the United States as a solution of the world’s overproduction problem. This scheme was presented at the outset of the conference which began on May 18, by Samuel R. McKelvie, member of the American Federal Farm Board. It drew opposition from Soviet Russia which favored the plan of the Danubian states for an export quota project. In the wake of the conference was left the seed which delegates said they hope would sprout into a workable plan to relieve the glut of international wheat production. This was in the form of a continuing committee to be made u

GENEVA, May 23, (P)—European statesmen today concluded a week of conferences which produced measures looking toward economic relief and sent the difficult Austro-German customs accord problem to the World Court. The Council of the League of Nations adjourned today while the Pan-European commission, which sought to work out the dream of Foreign Minister Briand for a European Union, adjourned Thursday. Leading European statesmen attended both sessions. The Council’s most critical act was to refer the proposed Austro-German customs accord to the World Court for an advisory opinion as to its legality. The European commission whose sessions were attended by 23 foreign ministers, laid out plans for a practical program to relieve the economic crisis. First Relief Plan It launched its first relief plan in a convention providing for the organization of an International Agricultural mortgage credi
PARIS, May 23. (#)—Capt. Frank M. Hawks, American speed flier, today received the honor medal of the International League of Aviators during the fifth annual celebration of the organization.

MADRID, May 23.—(AP)—The Spanish religious situation became more unsettled tonight when it was reported in authoritative circles that Papal Nuncio During the past week Monsignor Tedeschini has been holding frequent secret conferences with President Niceto Alcala Zamora concerning Pope Pius’ note of protest against recent anti-church riots and destruction of church property. In the past such departures of Papal Nuncios have been regarded as a prologue to a rupture of diplomatic relations. This latest development follows last night's cabinet decree guaranteeing equal freedom of worship for all creeds in Spain, generally regarded as the first step toward separating the state and church. Many Catholics consider this decree a direct violation of the concordats signed with the Vatican in

Rouen, France, May 23 (UP)— Mayor John H. Porter, of Los Angeles, who created consternation at Havre yesterday when he walked out of an official ceremony because a toast was being drunk, compromised with his principles today and participated in a toast at which real wine was used. Today's incident occurred at a municipal luncheon given to the party of American mayors, including Rolland B. Marvin, of Syracuse, N. Y., touring France as guests of the government. The red wine of Bordeaux and bubbling champagne were served. When the toasts were proposed, Mr. Porter lifted the glass in front of him and raised it towards his peers. He did not drink any of the wine, however, merely making the gesture. At Havre yesterday, Mr. Porter and his wife left the hall when the other Americans drank wine, explaining: "We won't violate the constitution wherever we go and no matter what the rest do." Mr. Por

VANDALIA, ILL., (UP).—Four men were shot, a dozen others were injured in hand-to-hand fighting, and five state buildings lay in ruins Monday as the result of the latest outbreak in the series of riots that have flamed during recent months in Illinois penal institutions. With the bayonets of national guardsmen bristling around the barbed wire enclosed farm and the “honor” prisoners apparently subdued after a short but mad riot during which they burned their dormitories, officials felt certain all danger of trouble was past at the state farm for misdemeanants about a mile from here. Unlike the riots held in other prisons in recent months in protest to treatment, Sunday night's riot here was said by officials to be directly the result of the failure of four men in an attempt to escape. All the 600 prisoners had known for weeks, Supi. C. J. Metzger said, that the break was planned. He had kn

WASHINGTON, (U.F.)—President Hoover will save about $75,000,000 in three governmental departments in the next three years, if tentative promises of heads of those departments come true. The president returned from the Rapidan River camp today with the assurance of Postmaster General Walter Brown of Toledo, O., that it should be possible to save $593,000,000 in the postal service—$38,000,600 in the year closing June 30, and $15,000,000 the following year. He gave the public indication of how this would be done. Mr. Hoover and his party left the Rapidan at 6:30 a.m. and arrived in Washington at 9:20. They breakfasted at the camp before their departure. Upon arrival here Mr. Hoover went immediately to his office to begin the labors of the day. VATICAN CITY, May 23—The Catholic Church's new chart of labor was given to the world today by Pope Pius XI, who based it on the premise of plain, simple justice and of man’s right to earn enough to keep his family happy. Championing this right, the pope emphatically condemned “economic dictatorship,” degradation of the state by moneyed interests, the present economic life which he described as “hard, cruel and relentless in ghastly measure,” and socialism and communities. The pontiff said that two evils rise from modern industrialism. One is the economic abasement of the workman; the other is the moral degradation of both employers and employees. His mind shudders, he set out, at “the frightful peril to which the morals of workers and the virtue of girls and women are exposed in modern factories.” For the first evil the pope recommended: 1. 1931-05-25.text: New York, May 24.—(#?)—Harry Stein, ex-convict, and Harry Greenberg, were formally charged with the murder of Vivian Gordon, Broadway butterfly, today, and Harry Schlitten, Newark, N. J., chauffeur, and Izzy (English) Lewis were held as material witnesses after the alleged confession of Schlitten at police headquarters. Police said Schlitten told them he drove the car in which Miss Gordon was strangled, February 26, and from which her body was thrown into a thicket in the upper Bronx. Robbery the Motive The police are convinced robbery was the sole motive for the killing. The body was stripped of its coat, the hands of jewelry, the woman's pocketbook was taken and then, the police official said, with Stein holding the shoulders and the chauffeur the feet, the body was dumped into a thicket.

In five southern New England airports tonight were poised observation planes, attack planes, pursuit planes, and mighty bombers, ready to take off tomorrow to repulse the theoretical threat from the sea. At the Bowles airport in Agawam, near here, rested a tremendous array of fighting craft, more than 400 pursuit, bombardment, and observation planes. Here were established the headquarters for the New England maneuvers with Brig. Gen. Benjamin D. Foulois in charge. At Springfield municipal airport was a group of 43 transport planes. At the Brainard airport in Hartford, Conn., were 107 planes of the 22nd observation squadron, national guard planes representing 19 states. While the army was flying planes by the hundreds through New England yesterday with only little difficulty, the score against civilian aviation was a different story. Seven persons were killed and one was injured in various parts of the United States. At Wallingford, Conn., a wing fell off Raymond McCorkle’s passenger plane, plunging the pilot and his two passengers to death. The passengers were not immediately identified. A plane spun Guy Strickland and Wayne Putnam to their deaths at Wayne, Neb., when a down current took it. The most spectacular accident of the day occurred at the top of Nittany Mountain, near Bellefonte, Pa., where an air pilot, James D. Cleveland, met his death. Fog, rain and snow obscured his visibility, and he barely missed clearing the mountain. He was burned to death with a thousand pounds of mail, when the ship hit the peak. Capt. J. H. MOSCOW, May 25.—(#)--The United States is pictured as the villain of the recent wheat conference at London in today’s editorial by the military newspaper Red Star. The American, the editorial says, ‘stood firmly against international marketing pools and refused to compromise on acreage reductions, thus ending the conference “without results as had been expected.” - “The greed of the capitalist knows no bounds,” says the Red Star. “To increase their profits they let millions starve. Soviet Russia was willing to make reasonable compromise but the United States and Canada would consider nothing but their own plan and that plan had to do with dumping huge surpluses in Europe at the expense of other wheat-growing countries. “We were willing to adopt a quota basis but only on the pre-war export figures. No one can say we are over-producing. With the great growth of our urban population we need

ROME, (UP)—Premier Benito Mussolini was thrown from his horse while riding today. He was slightly bruised about the face. Mussolini was taking his customary morning ride in the park when his horse stumbled over a hurdle and fell to his knees, pitching the premier to the ground. Mussolini rose smilingly. His bruises were not serious.

AUTEUIL, France — (AP) — George Lott Jr. and Jehn Van Ryn, of Philadelphia, today won the French hard court tennis doubles championship, defeating Virgil Kirby and Nat Farquharson, of South Africa in straight sets. The scores were 6-4, 6-3, 8-4. The Philadelphia youngsters are the first Americans to win the doubles title since 1926 when Vincent Richards and Howard Kinsey won.

BUDAPEST, Hungary, May 28. W.P—Helene, Princess of Greece, and divorced wife of King Carol of Roumania, has been ruled out from the royal family, the Roumanian newspaper Patria, organ of the National Peasant Party, said. In banner headlines The Patria published a report that military commanders had been ordered to treat Helene, whom Carol only last year proclaimed his Queen, as a private person in future. She is to receive one of the honors accorded only members of the royal family, the dispatch said. The Patria said Premier Nicholas Jorga, of Roumania, had urged Carol to take action. The report followed months of effort to effect a reconciliation between Helene and King Carol. Carol flew back to Bucharest last June and seized the throne. He named Helene his Queen, despite the fact they were divorced, and made effort to get the divorce annulled. Helene, however, could not forgive Prince

Tokyo—(f)—— The cabinet Monday announced a cut in the salaries of all government employees, including army and navy officers and forthwith came face to face with the most serious labor dispute in a half century of government operated railroads. All bureau and section chiefs of the railway ministry prepared their resignations and 219,000 railway employees throughout the country threatened to cease work. As the wage cut applies only to employees receiving more than $42.50 per month, the great majority are not directly affected. In the face of the threat the cabinet refused to withdraw its thrift schedule. The wage cut was designed to save about $4,000,000 annually and becomes effective June 3. About 9,990 railroad workers will have their salaries reduced. 1931-03-08.text: (By The Associated Press) This globe was battered from within and without yesterday by storms, rising rivers and earthquakes. Mariners over much of the Atlantic called up all their skill to fight dangerous gales. Storms raged in the North Sea, flooding flat lands along the English coast and imperiling ships. In the United States, a blizzard swept the prairie states and the Great Lakes region, blocking highways, snapping poles, and slowing traffic of all kinds. Snow covered much of the region. Cold northwest winds, accompanied by rain swept down into Dixie, with promise of more to come. The weather man warned shipping from the Virginia Capes to Jacksonville, Fla. Peasants trembled as earth shocks demolished buildings in Bulgaria, Jugoslavia, Greece and South Siberia. In Siberia a shepherd and 200 of his sheep died in a mountain slide. London, March 7.—(A. P.)—All the prize fights of recent years in Ames Hall put together have not produced so much good scrapping as developed when the Trades Defense Union exhibited a purported "soviet slave" in a mass meeting called to protest Russian economic methods last night. The "slave" voiced an appeal for freedom for the men, women and children working in Russian timber camps, from which he said he escaped a few months ago. Running fights continued between spectators and a crowd of interrupters during the two-hour meeting. The disturbers were ejected. The disturbance began when Winston Churchill and Lord Brentford, formerly Sir William Joynson Hicks, both former conservative ministers, started addressing the meeting. Both were heckled. Lord Brentford said treatment of women in the prison camps was such that he dared not reveal it in a mixed audience. The "soviet slave," whose nam

LONDON, March 7.—(UP)—The worst gale since 1917 swept the British Isles today as Britain received her share of 10,000,000 tons of air rushing from the northern to the southern hemisphere and creating weather havoc throughout the world. “This transference of air occurs every season between January and July,” Sir Napier Shaw, famous British meteorologist, said. “It is not surprising that it does not always cross the equator without immense friction.” The portion of the “friction” received by Britain caused immense damage and discomfort on sea and land. Huge seas in the English Channel sent all shipping rushing for shelter. The Thames rose rapidly and reached its most dangerous state since the disastrous floods of 1928. The river overflowed at Putney and Wandsworth. The south coast was ravaged by waves which swept over the seawall for many miles and flooded many towns and villages. Littlest

LONDON, March 10 (UP), P. Morgan's yacht Corsair, upon which the Archbishop of Canterbury has been invited to join the American financier on a Mediterranean cruise, was forced to seek shelter at Gibraltar during a heavy storm, the Exchange Telegraph company said today. The British cruiser Centaur was slightly damaged, the Exchange report said, by heavy seas. Several ships of the British Atlantic fleet now at Gibraltar got up steam and prepared to put out to the open sea.

Washington, April 25—(A.P.)— President Hoover cleared his desk today preparatory to departing this afternoon by boat for Cape Henry, Va., where tomorrow he is to attend a celebration of the 324th anniversary of the landing of English colonists. The trip to the cape will be made on a 140-foot inspection boat of the Department of Commerce and will be over a route long familiar to Mr. Hoover. He often took fishing trips down the Potomac and the Chesapeake Bay during his term of office as secretary of commerce. The president expected to arrive at Little Creek Inlet, five miles from Cape Henry, about 2 o'clock Sunday afternoon. There he will board a train for the five miles to the Cape Henry church where the celebration takes place.

Rome, March 7, (#)—The formality of signing the naval accord between Great Britain, France and Italy is taking almost as long to arrange as the negotiations out of which the agreement came. It had been understood here today that the ceremony of signing would take place in London next Tuesday, but in official quarters tonight, it was said that the signing had been postponed until the United States and Japan had examined the text. The situation as it was understood here tonight is that publication of the agreement, originally set for last Monday, is still unsettled, but dispatches from London and Paris said the text would be published on Wednesday simultaneously in all the capitals concerned. The agreement, it is understood, has not been even initiated by the men who write its terms, because the British delegates prefer to await the approval of Washington, Tokyo, and the British dominions.

AVAIYU, MATCH 5, WU.F)—A GIRL was born to the Empress Nagako at the Imperial Maternity Villa today, her fourth daughter, leaving the Japanese empire without a male heir apparent. The baby was born at 12:02 p.m., the imperial child weighed 3.365 grammes (7.4 pounds) and was 49 centimeters (19.25 inches) in height. Mother and daughter were reported doing well. The Empress entered the Maternity Villa at 9:50 a.m. She passed her 28th birthday in retirement yesterday. Two of her daughters, Teru and Taka, are living, in addition to the baby born today. The other girl born to the imperial couple died in infancy. For the fourth time the hope of all Japan for an heir to the throne was unfulfilled.

Tokyo, March 7. (AP)—Japan sang praises today to a new member of the imperial family, born to Emperor Hirohito and Empress Nagako at 12:02 p.m., but Prince Chichibu, the emperor's younger brother, continued to be the heir presumptive of the oldest unbroken royal line in the world. Birth of the little princess, the fourth daughter born to the imperial couple, was heralded throughout the empire by the national radiocasting system with broadcasting of the national anthem. In Tokyo citizens were apprised of the event by the municipal sirens while the official Gazette, the government organ, issued one of its rare “extras.” 3 Ceremonies Performed. 1931-03-20.text: NEW YORK, March 19.—(4?)— Miss Christabel Pankhurst, daughter of Emmeline Pankhurst, noted British militant suffragist of the last generation, believes the second coming of Christ is at hand. She is confident it will occur in her lifetime—that she will eventually see him. Is Fulfillment of Prophecies, Her faith, she said today, is based on the fulfillment of prophecies first uttered by Moses and reiterated through the Bible to the end of Revelations. Miss Pankhurst does not hold with those who believe the reappearance will mean the end of the world, but she expects it to be dramatic enough so that there can be no doubt of his identity. “Two thousand years ago,” she said. “He came in poverty and weakness and humility. But this time he will descend to the earth in all his majesty, with demonstrations of divine power more miraculous than any of the miracles of modern science.” Rather than v

LONDON, March 20. — (UP) — Lloyd's correspondent at Alexandria relayed a wireless message today saying the Italian warship Porto Corsini was in distress 30 miles south of Sheduan island. The Lloyd's dispatch said the British steamer City of Dunkirk and the British motor vessel Ortina Shell were proceeding immediately to aid the Porto Corsini. Available atlases do not list a Sheduan island. The island of Shad-Wan is in the Red Sea, near the Gulf of Suez.

LONDON—(#)—Captain A. T. Doff Cooper, husband of Lady Diana Manners, will sit for St. George's division of Mayfair in parliament, having won a bye-election Thursday from Sir Ernest Petter, 17,242 to 11,532. His victory was a vindication of the policies of Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, and a rejection of the insurgent conservative platform of the Beaverbrook and Rothermere press, which took Sir Ernest's part. Liberals and laborites were not represented, the seat being traditionally conservative. The election campaign was marked by unusual animosities. The servant vote in this section of Mayfair outnumbers the vote of the masters.

PISA, ITALY, Mar. 19—(4)—Col. Umberto Maddalena, famous Italian flier and finder of the dirigible Italia survivors, Lieut. Fausto Cecconi and Mechanic Sergeant Damonte were killed today when their seaplane fell into the sea. Maddalena discovered General Umberto Nobile and a group of other survivors of the Italia in 1928 near Spitzbergen and dropped medicine and supplies to them on the ice after the Italian airship had been wrecked on its north pole flight. He and Lieutenant Cecconi formerly held world air records for distance and duration flights and both had recently returned from the Latin-American flight of Air Minister Italo Balbo on which Maddalena was adjutant.

PISA, Italy, March 19.—Three heroes of Italian aviation who would have taken part this summer in a projected group flight from Orbetello, Italy, to New York, plunged to their death today in the sea near here. The dead are: COL. UMBERTO MADDALENA, who in 1925 first sighted Gen. Nobile and the stranded crew of the dirigible Italia. CAPT. FAUSTO CECCONI, former co-holder with Maddalena of the world records for non-refueling endurance and distance flights. SECOND LIEUT. GIUSEPPE DAMONTE, commended with Maddalena and Cecconi on the recent Italian air squadron flight across the South Atlantic to Brazil. The three met death together today as they flew from Sesto Calende to Rome in preparation for an effort to regain the distance and endurance records over a closed circuit, held by Maddalena and Cecconi from last June until less than three weeks ago. Col. Maddalena was piloting the Savoia-Marche

PARIS, March 20.--(UP)—The Paris-Bordeaux express train was derailed at Estampes, 35 miles from Paris, last night in an accident which cost the lives of 9 persons, one of whom died of heart trouble. The accident was one of the most unusual on record. The restaurant and baggage car side-swiped a local train. Then another car of the express was derailed 50 yards further along the track, while still another car was derailed and turned over 760 yards further along. The local train, as well as the express, was seriously damaged, but it carried no passengers.

Shanghai, March 20.—()—(Friday)—Unconfirmed waterfront reports today said 250 persons drowned when the French steamer Chankiang struck a rock and sank in the China Sea off Amoy March 16. The Chankiang carried 300 passengers and crew. Of these, reports said, only 50 were saved. Wireless messages were garbled and reports of the loss of lives may be greatly exaggerated.

PISA, Italy. March 20.—(AP)—A variable propeller of a type which Col. Umberto Maddalena always favored, was blamed today for the disaster which yesterday took the lives of Maddalena and two companions, Capt. Cecconi and Lieut. Damonte. None of the bodies has been recovered. An inquest commission found that the propeller had broken, cutting the fuselage in two when the plane was several thousand feet in the air. The propeller was Maddalena’s specialty. He believed it enabled him to take off with heavier loads of fuel than with an ordinary propeller.
