Whitstable, Kent, England, June 26. -(AP)— Alfred Aloysius Smith, known to the world as “Trader Horn,” died today at a nursing home in Tankerton after a brief illness. He was a “young man of 82,” in his own words. He was stricken with a chill at the home of his sister several days ago and did not rally. With a sparkling eye and a great white beard, he maintained until his death bed the happy, breezy manner that had accompanied a career of adventure. “Trader Horn” came out of the jungles of the dark continent to take a place in the spotlight of the world’s literary capitals. In collaboration with Mrs. Ethelreda Lewis, he wrote “Trader Horn” and entertained England and America with fascinating tales of his experiences with African natives. His travels began in 1871 when he left Lancashire for the ivory coast of West Africa on behalf of a Liverpool steamship company. After assisting the com
WHITSTABLE, Kent, England. Alfred Aloysius Smith, picturesque character in the book, “Trader Horn,” died here today, the Central News reported. Horn had been in ill health for some time. He was 82.

LONDON, June 26.—(Friday)—Reports were printed in this morning’s newspapers on the basis of dispatches from Vienna which said that either Queen Helen of Rumania, or Mme. Magda Lupescu, friend of King Carol, was suffering from an overdose of poison. The Vienna correspondent of the Daily Herald said rumors were current in Bucharest that one of the two women was ill of poisoning, but that it was difficult to obtain confirmation or denial. One of the reports, this correspondent said, was that Mme. Lupescu had been found unconscious 10 days ago but that her condition was not dangerous and that the king's physicians attended her. When she recovered, the report said, she left for Paris at the king's suggestion. The Vienna correspondent of the Daily Express said that Queen Helen had taken poison by mistake and that officials of her household had confirmed reports of her illness. The marital diff

Paris—Andrew W. Mellon, whose visit to England was an important factor in the announcement of President Hoover’s moratorium plan, reached Paris Thursday and plunged immediately in the task of harmonizing the French and American attitudes on the president's proposal. He went direct to the American embassy where for two hours he conferred with Ambassador Edge. Then he called on Minister of Finance Flandin and three hours later went to his hotel. The French reply to Mr. Hoover's proposal, the main lines for which are generally known now, appeared to be a basis for negotiations to work out a formula by which the president's proposal may be translated into action. Today Mr. Mellon will have luncheon with Premier Lavall. Soon thereafter the premier must go into the chamber of deputies prepared to answer nine interpellations regarding the war debt plan and the French reply to Washington. Govern

LONDON, June 26. (AP).—Published reports that Queen Helen of Rumania might have taken poison by mistake and be suffering from the effects were discredited today by the secretary of the British legation in Bucharest. He said over the telephone that she had risen early and taken a horseback ride in the royal gardens. “There is absolutely no truth in the suggestion that Queen Helen is lying ill,” he said. The denial was due to a dispatch to the Daily Express from Vienna that attaches of the queen’s household reported she drank from the wrong bottle on her dressing table by mistake. The Vienna correspondent of the Daily Herald said that either the queen or Magda Lupescu, King Carol’s paramour, had taken an overdose of a sedative but that he was unable to confirm who it was. Elaborating on his denial, the British representative said: “I have just been speaking to her royal highness herself. S

BERGEN, Norway, Aug. 1 (P) - The submarine Nautilus, in which Sir Hubert Wilkins hopes to cruise under the ice across the top of the world, arrived at Bergen from Plymouth, England, today. Sir Hubert said he thought he would be ready to leave for the Arctic on Monday.

1931-08-02.text: PARIS, Aug. 1.—4UR+}—Complete accord between the Bank of France and the Federal Reserve Bank in New York was reached today on a large extension of credits to the Bank of England. The agreement was reached in hurried conferences concluded here at noon, with consultations by transatlantic telephone to New York. It provides for the immediate extension of credits totaling near $250,000,000 to the Bank of England. The Bank of England agreed to pay 3 3-8 per cent interest. The loan will be divided equally between the Federal Reserve Bank and the Bank of France.

London, July 30. (4)—David Lloyd George, who underwent a serious operation yesterday for hematuria, was reported in a satisfactory condition tonight. A bulletin issued early this evening stated: “Mr. Lloyd George has had a fairly comfortable day and has slept at intervals. His strength is well maintained and his general condition continues to be satisfactory.

| KRASNOYARSK, Siberia, Aug. 1. == (UP)—Miss Amy Johnson, British girl flier, landed at 4 a.m. today on her way from London to Tokio in her light Puss Moth plane. She paused but briefly, hurrying on eastward over the Siberian Plains. Miss Johnson said she made a forced landing just beyond Maryinsk yesterday, but was unhurt and continued a little later.

NEW YORK, Aug. 1.—The federal reserve system today concluded in co-operation with the Bank of France, a $250,000,000 credit to the Bank of England. It was explained in high banking circles that the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, in co-operation with the other 11 banks of the federal reserve system, had arranged to purchase from the Bank of England up to $125,000,000 in prime commercial bills, as a measure to aid both American and British trade. Bankers have applauded the aggressive measures taken by the Bank of England to correct the situation arising from the flights of its gold to the continent, primarily to France, and described the credit negotiated today merely as a measure to make the protection of sterling exchange doubly sure. Today's credit is expected to keep the pound sterling close to gold parity, so the British will not have to pay an expensive premium for dollars to pay

BERGEN, Norway, Aug. 1--(UP)— The submarine Nautilus, commanded by Sir Hubert Wilkins, explorer, arrived from England today on its way toward the North Pole. The submarine, which originally left the United States some weeks ago, is to be overhauled here and loaded with fuel and supplies for the northward cruise which is planned to take Wilkins and his crew under the Arctic ice to the pole.

BOMBAY, India, Aug. 1.—()—When Mahatma Gandhi sails two weeks hence as a steerage passenger for the London round table conference he will not even have a suit case, a tooth brush or a coat and hat. His only baggage will be two goats, a spinning wheel, a spare loin cloth and a copy of Thoreau's essay on “Civil Disobedience.” The goats, given him by one of his numerous admirers, will supply the milk, which is his principal article of diet, throughout the three weeks of the voyage and during the conference at London. The steamship company broke a long-standing rule to allow the goats to be brought along. Miss Madeleine Slade, Gandhi's English disciple and attendant, will have charge of the goats, milking them twice a day while he watches. So that he will be in no danger of being swept overboard while he sleeps on the third-class deck, the steamship company will build a special rail around G

BASEL, Switzerland, Aug. 3.—Governors of the Bank of International Settlements met today and renewed the $100,000,000 Reichsbank credit for three months, in accordance with recommendations of the recent London financial conference. The group also studied reports of the financial situation in Hungary and Austria, with a view to taking suitable measures if a crisis develops.

London, Aug. 2—(i)—The Bank of England made two announcements Saturday afternoon which are regarded in British financial circles as of the highest possible importance in connection with the world's monetary position. The first was that the Federal Reserve Bank at New York and the Bank of France each had granted the Bank of England a credit of £25,000,000 (about $125,000,000). The second was that the British Treasury had authorized the Bank of England to increase its fiduciary note issue by £15,000,000 (about $75,000,000) for a period of three weeks. The fiduciary issue, which is that portion of the Bank of England’s note issue against which the bank does not hold gold in its vaults, is thus raised to £275,000,000 (about $1,475,000,000) instead of £260,000,000 (about $1,300,000,000), which up to Saturday was the highest figure authorized by law.

1931-06-27.text: - Columbus, Ohio June 27 (4)—Led by stocky Gene Sarazen, who shot a sub-par 71, the American professional golf stars jumped into the lead over the British team in the first round of play in the 36-hole singles matches today. Sarazen led Fred Robson, 3 up, and Billie Burke was 2 up on the big British star, Archie Compston. Densmore Shute, United States, was three up on Bert Hodson at the end of the first round. Al Espinosa, United States, and Ernest Whitcombe were all even at the end of the second nine. Johnny Farrell, United States, and Billie Davis were all square at the end of 18 holes. Walter Hagen, United States, had Charles Whitcombe 4 down, but the English gained a little hope when Whiffy Cox blew his first nine lead to Abe Mitchell, the gaunt British leading one up. Burke held his 2 up advantage over Archie Compston.

LONDON, June 27. (AP).-- The Reuter’s agency reported today that a revolt has broken out among the members of the Spanish airforce at Tablada, near Seville, Spain. The revolt is said to be headed by Major Ramon Franco, who was dismissed. Many airmen from all parts of the country are reported to have arrived at the airport by air before the outbreak. At midday a column of troops left the Seville garrison, bound for the airdrome.

(By the Associated Press) The boom spirits continued yesterday to grip the stock markets of the world. In New York, London and Paris, securities continued their rise in value, while in Berlin the Bourse was hesitant, but firm. New York—Principal shares showed gains of 82 to $8 a share, railroads leading the advance. London—Trading slowed up in the early hours for profit taking, but later prices continued their upward climb. Paris—The Bourse had one of its most active days, apparently convinced of the success of the Franco-American discussion on the Hoover proposal for a debt moratorium. The trend of the market was indicated in Bank of France stock which rose 800 francs despite announcement of a dividend cut. Berlin—The Bourse was generally firm, but still cautious, awaiting the outcome of the Hoover proposal. At the opening the market was inclined to weakness, but losses were held to one

GLASGOW, June 26.— Representatives of 11 northern and eastern Montana counties will meet here tomorrow to lay before John G. Brown, special representative of the secretary of agriculture, their economic difficulties. County commissioners and county agents of Hill, Sheridan, Daniels, Roosevelt, Phillips, Blaine, McCone, Richland, Dawson, Garfield and Valley counties have been invited.

SHANGHAI, June 27—(?)— Wiley Post and Harold Gatty landed at Blagoveshchensk, Siberia at 5 a.m. Texas time. They landed in a mud hole but the plane was undamaged. They had come 850 miles from Irkutsk. They planned to start for Khabarovsk Sunday morning or Saturday afternoon American time.

GENOA, Italy, June 27. -- Four bombs were exploded here early today, shattering many windows and damaging the walls of several buildings. Police arrested hundreds of suspects. The bombs went off at half-hour intervals, awakening the populace over a wide area in the center of the city and creating a semblance of panic. One exploded near the royal palace, another in the Piazzo Della Nunziata, a third near the streetcar barns and the last near a factory at San Vincenzo.

PMUAUYU VESURASA, pilberia, June 27—(4%— Wiley Post and Harold Gatty experienced the first mishap in their globe-circling flight when their plane bogged down in a mud hole as they arrived here from Irkutsk tonight. The plane’s wheels were buried hub deep and all efforts of the fliers to extricate it proved fruitless, even horses being unable to budge the machine. The fliers planned to obtain a tractor at daylight in an effort to drag the plane from the sticky mud. If this failed they said they would have a gang of men dig the machine out, as they were determined to continue the flight with as little delay as possible. Irkutsk, 850 miles away. Far Ahead of Schedule. UTSK, Siberia, June 27—(Pi— Far ahead of their schedule and well past the halfway point in their 15,000-mile dash around the world, Wiley Post and Harold Gatty sped their monoplane Winnie Mae out of Irkutsk today for an 850-mi

1931-09-23.text: London, Sept. 3.—(JP)—Hope that Parker D. Cramer, American airman, who was lost on a flight from Detroit to Copenhagen, remains alive lingered today. On the request of the American embassy, the British Broadcasting Company appealed to ships in North Sea waters and residents of the barren Orkney and Shetland Islands to keep a sharp watch for Cramer and his radio operator, Oliver Pacquette. The message said that the wreckage of Cramer's plane, recently salvaged by the British trawler Lord Trent, indicated the possibility that the men might have taken refuge on one of the uninhabited islands. The Daily Mail pointed out that what was taken for a flying suit was found in the cockpit of the plane by the master of the Lord Trent, demonstrating to the newspaper that the pilot might have been able to discard the suit and leave the machine before it crashed.

BEVERLY HILLS, Calif. Sept. 23.—The American Legion did themselves mighty proud by giving the President such a fine reception. They made him feel he alone was not entirely responsible for the war in China, England's dole, fog over Alaska and What-a-man's “it.” He told ‘em truthfully that the taxpayers couldn't stand another cash bonus and the boys said “O. K., Chief, we don't want to cause the taxpayers any hardship, but do you think a glass of beer would be asking too much for our service rendered?” Vanre

London, Sept. 23 (#)—Stanley Baldwin, leader of the conservative party, was at the helm of the British government for the first time since 1919 today. As Lord President of the council Mr. Baldwin became acting prime minister yesterday when Ramsay MacDonald left for a secret destination in the country to recuperate from the strain of keeping the pound sterling afloat on the world’s money markets. Mr. MacDonald’s friends and associates were not alarmed over his condition and felt that a few days of golf and rest would restore him to tip-top shape. Some newspapers professed to see in his departure a connection with the growing movement for an early appeal to the electorate on a protective tariff issue. The Herald, Labor Organ, for instance, said he was being offered a bewildering variety of advice and was slipping away to take counsel with himself on a decision.

United Press Staff Correspondent TIPTON, Ia., Sept. 23—(UP)— Embattled farmers from the county in which President Hoover was born were arrayed today against 1,800 men of the Iowa National Guard sent here to enforce the state compulsory tuberculosis test law. Arrival of the troops, who marched unmolested behind their company colors to the Cedar county fairground where they are camped, was the signal for an outburst of jeers and hoots from farmers lining the sidewalks of this peaceful village in the heart of one of Iowa's richest farming districts. The farmers, however, were without the weapons they used Monday when, armed with pitchforks and clubs, they drove 65 special deputies from the farm of J. W. Lenker. The deputies attempted to test Lenker’s cattle. Conferences between leaders of the guard and officials of the state department of agriculture were

LONDON, Sept. 23.—()—Mahatma Gandhi, who leads millions toward liberty, and Charlie Chaplin, who makes millions laugh, today cherished a friendship of mutual understanding. “A very charming man,” said Gandhi of Chaplin. “A most interesting figure,” said Chaplin of Gandhi. At Chaplin’s behest they met for the first time yesterday in the east end home of one of the Indian leader’s friends. Adults and children thronged around the house as the film comedian entered and loaded him down with bouquets of garden flowers. Their talk was terminated by evening prayers. Gandhi and his English disciple, Mira Behn, knelt and clasped their hands as they intoned their supplications to the God of the Hindus. Chaplin sat quietly by and when it was over he said he was glad he had come.

London, Sept. 22 (44)—While the London Stock Exchange made ready to open tomorrow for business as usual, Great Britain tonight was preparing to renew efforts for an international conference to deal with problems of the world gold supply. While the country calmly continued readjustments after its temporary suspension of the gold standard, Lord Reading, Foreign Secretary, let it be known that Great Britain would seek to call such a conference. Meanwhile, the House of Commons again tackled the supplementary budget of Chancellor of the Exchequer Snowden. Stanley Baldwin, Conservative leader and Lord President of the Council, is temporarily helmsman of the National Government. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald today went to the country for a rest after the strain of recent weeks.

(Copyright, 1931, By United Press) Washington, Sept. 23—The administration was represented today by one of its informed spokesmen as willing to carry naval disarmament to levels even lower than those established by the Washington and London treaties. Any steps toward further disarmament, this official pointed out, will depend on the attitudes and proposals of the other powers at the Geneva conference next February. It is significant, however, that the administration is giving considerable thought to the costliness of battleships. Undersecretary of State William R. Castle has compiled figures to show that the “long term” cost of a single battleship is a quarter of a billion dollars. He secured this estimate by totaling the ship's $40,000,000 original cost, its maintenance for 20 years, and 5 percent compound interest on the capital invested in it. Great Britain has informally suggested to

NEW YORK, Sept. 23 (AP).— Active buying of railroad issues sent the stock market scampering upward today in a rally that lifted principal shares $2 to more than $15. With the ban on short selling lifted just before the opening and the London market cheerful after its two-day holiday, New York prices rose in lively fashion. Wall Street heard much gossip concerning possible early relief for the railroads, either through higher freight rates or a wage reduction following the cuts just announced by the steel and some other industries. Active short covering swept the rail shares, boosting Norfolk and Western nearly $7. New York Central, Baltimore and Ohio and Pennsylvania rose to $5. United States Steel common pushed up more than $5.

1931-04-08.text: New York, April 8—(CAP)—Sections of upper New York state, Pennsylvania and New England were covered with snow today, as a result of a storm, which crippled power and light service in several communities and hampered highway traffic throughout the affected areas. A wet, sticky blanket was laid from the foothills of the Adirondacks to Albany, varying in depth from three to eight inches. Salem, N.Y., was thrown into darkness when 12 inches of snow disabled the lighting system. Many telephone lines were down. Traffic in the vicinity of Olean, N.Y., was hampered by the storm. Buses were four and five hours behind schedule. The storm extended as far as Port Allegany, Coudersport, and Emporium, Pa. At Tawanda, Pa. 16 inches of snow fell in 24 hours. Light and telephone wires were down at Sanatoga. In New England, the heaviest fall was reported from southern and western New Hampshire, where hund

By The Associated Press SOUTHAMPTON, Eng. April 8 The giant Cunard liner Berengaria was anchored in a dense fog off Nab Tower, at the entrance of the Spithead today, after spending several hours aground nearby during the night. Bounded by a heavy fog, the liner went aground early in the evening as it proceeded from Cherbourg. There was a jar and a heavy crunching sound, and then the vessel shivered as its engines were thrown in reverse to try to refloat it. These efforts were continued for about two hours, but in vain. Four tugs made futile attempts to release her, but two others and a rising tide were necessary before the ship was refloated. The fog was still too dense to proceed and the ship anchored nearby. All but 75 of the liner's passengers were removed by tender shortly after the accident and taken to Southampton. Others remained aboard, electing to spend the night on the ship rat

WINDSOR, Eng., April 8.—The British public, which had been awaiting not without certain anxiety news from the sickroom of their monarch, was heartened this forenoon by an official statement that there was a slight improvement in the condition of King George. His majesty had been suffering since last Sunday from a chest cold, which yesterday was designated in an official bulletin as an attack of subacute bronchitis.

Chicago, Apr. 8—(AP)—A special newspaper correspondent, F. C. Pockburn, representing a London, England, daily came to Chicago yesterday ready to report any killings resulting from the election. But there were no killings.

LONDON, April 9.—(4)—Defeat of William Hale Thompson, mayor of Chicago, received front page space in almost all London newspapers today. No paper expressed any sorrow at the passing of “Big Bill.” An editorial in The London Standard congratulated the people of Chicago on “having liberated themselves from an influence which dominated their civic life so long.”

SINGAPORE, Straits Settlements April 8—(ADP)—The British airman, A. W. Scott, who is trying to beat Wing Commander Charles Kingsford Smith's nine day record from England to Australia, arrived here at 1:50 p.m. today and left at 2:20 for Palambanga, en route to Port Darwin, Western Australia.

LONDON, ADT B-- Wednesday) —(UP)—The liner Berengaria went aground in the mud east of Nab-tower, off the Isle of Wight, the Central News reported early today. It was refloated at 3 a.m. The Central News dispatches said that the Berengaria had been aground since 12:45 p.m., Tuesday. The majority of the passengers were landed at Southampton on a tender at midnight, after groping through a dense fog. Reports said the first indication of the mishap on board came when the big liner halted, shivered and then shook as the engines churned the muddy waters of the English channel at full speed. The engines were kept at full speed astern off and on for two hours, the reports said, but the ship failed to be.

Boston, Mass—(?)—Old Man Winter, who has been retreating northward in recent weeks, paused long enough last night to throw a monkey wrench into New England's communications system. A storm that laid down a heavy wet blanket of snow ranging in depth up to 19 inches carried down telephone and telegraph lines, in some cases felled poles, isolated whole sections of New Hampshire and Vermont, and delayed railroad trains. Electric power transmission lines and local fire alarm signal systems also suffered. From Concord, N.H., came reports that more than 400 telephone stations were out of order. Although emergency telephone crews were rushed into service, toll service with surrounding areas was disrupted. Electric light service was disrupted in outlying sections around Concord. Member newspapers of the Associated Press in Vermont were being served during the forenoon from Boston by a wire that r

1931-05-06.text: (By The Associated Press) Death, tragedy, hope and ambition reigned yesterday over aviation in the four corners of the world. Death struck three British fliers, on two continents. Among the three was Captain Glenn Kidston, millionaire aviator-sportsman, who set a new record of six and one-half days for a flight from England to Cape Town, South Africa. Kidston was killed at Van Reenen, Natal, Africa, when his plane crashed in a storm. With him, was also killed T. A. Gladstone, pioneer British commercial flier. Other British Casualties In a crash 100 miles east of Port Arthur, Ontario, Canada, Lloyd Newburn, pilot, was killed. At Farnborough, England, Flight Lieut. H. R. D. Waghorn, British Schneider cup winner in 1929, was seriously injured when his plane crashed. Bert Hinkler, noted Australian flier, took off from Toronto on a flight by stages across the Atlantic to Africa. Prepares for

WINDSOR, England, May 6.—The ringing of bells in the royal chapel and Windsor church reminded the people that today was the 21st anniversary of the accession of George V to the throne of England. The king, recuperating from a recent attack of bronchitis, spent the day quietly within Windsor castle.

__ ALDERSHOT, England, May 6. UP)--Two Royal Air Force fighting airplanes collided in flight during maneuvers today at Farnborough, where Flight Lieut. H. R. D. Waghorn crashed yesterday. Pilots of both planes took to parachutes and escaped unhurt while their ships smashed to the ground. Waghorn’s physicians said this morning that his condition, pronounced serious after an operation yesterday, was unchanged after a quiet night.

VAN REENAN, Natal, May 5.—(P)—Glen Kidston, one of England's foremost fliers, wrecked his plane against a mountainside today and was killed. T. A. Gladstone, a pioneer in British flying over Africa, died with him. Their bodies were mutilated almost beyond recognition, but the Orange Free State police at Harrismith said they had confirmed the identification. Kidston was flying Gladstone up from Johannesburg on the way to Pietermaritzburg. A gale was blowing. The theory is that clouds of dust made visibility extremely bad and Kidston failed to see the Drakensberg mountains until too late.

WINCHESTER, Va., May 5, (B)—Queen for a day and made to feel it by the acclaim of thousands of her loyal subjects, Miss Patricia D. Morton, young English girl, today wielded her scepter over a land from which melancholy had been banished. As Queen Shenandoah VII, ruler of the valley where millions of apple trees were in full bloom, she found her every whim gratified and her many subjects eager to serve her. Never was a real queen shown more whole-hearted loyalty. At noon she was to hold court, an official luncheon and reception for the princesses from 15 states. Except for the reception, her majesty was left to her own desires until the hour of the big spectacle of the apple blossom festival, "the trail of pink petals," a monster parade in her honor in which officials announced there would be 32 bands and 50 floats. Queen Shenandoah will ride on a throne atop a gaily decorated float, pre

Hull, England, May 5, (4P)—Major Stanley Cotton sailed for Iceland tonight on the steamer Deitifoss with the airplane in which he will join in the search for Augustine Courtauld, British explorer, missing on Greenland’s ice cap. Cotton expects to reach Reykjavik, Iceland, Sunday. He will make that city his base instead of Angmagsalik, on the border of the Greenland ice barrier, where Captain Albio Ahrenberg already has landed with another rescue plane. The plane in which Major Cotton will search for his fellow countryman is equipped with long range wireless apparatus and the flyer will be able to send and receive while aloft or on the ground. It was not known here today whether Captain Ahrenberg had started to the icy peak where Courtauld has been marooned for weeks.

Reykjavik, Iceland, May 6—Sigurd Johnson, whose airplane expedition in search of Augustine Courtauld, the British scientist in Greenland, failed when his plane developed motor trouble, returned here today in the steamer Odinn with disquieting news for other rescuers. While he was at the edge of the Greenland ice barrier, he made contact for the headquarters of the British Arctic air route expedition of which Courtauld was a member and was told that the chances of locating the ice cap station where Courtauld may be were very small. Landing on that frozen plateau would be practically impossible, he was informed. He brought more cheering news, however, concerning the three men who set out overland to relieve Courtauld two weeks ago. They have not been heard from, but they have enough provisions to last them another month.

Aberdeen, S. D., May 6—Students were “picketed” about classrooms of northern normal and industrial school today as developments were awaited from the state board of regents following dismissal yesterday of two students and a walkout of more than 300 students in protest. The walkout climaxed disturbances on the campus incited by purported “revelations” alleging “incompetency” of unnamed faculty members and attacking the character and morals of Dr. David Allen R.B. Anderson, president. Charges against the teachers and Dr. Anderson were contained in three notices posted on bulletin boards. Petitions circulated among students alleging “bad conditions” at the school were sent to the board of regents asking for an investigation. Expulsion of Alfred Bieber and Miss Bernice O'Grady, students, on the grounds that their “conduct was detrimental to the best interests of the school,” led to a studen

1931-09-28.text: LONDON, Sept. 28.—(UP)—Suspension of the gold standard by Norway and Sweden and increased bank rates in several European countries were effective today, a week after Great Britain suspended the gold standard for six months. The Swedish state council met at Stockholm and decided to suspend the gold standard until November 30. At the same time the bank rate was increased from six percent to eight percent. At Oslo, the Norwegian state council decided to suspend the gold standard temporarily and prohibit the export of gold. The bank rate was raised from six percent to eight percent. Holland stuck by the gold standard. The Netherlands bank issued a statement at Amsterdam saying the gold standard would be maintained unconditionally and that no inflation was expected as the gold position was stronger than ever. The Belgian government, in order to balance its budget, decided to reduce defense ap

LONDON, Sept. 28.—(4)—Premier Ramsay MacDonald told the minorities committee round table conference the Hindus and Moslems must settle their difficulties without the assistance of England. He said he had been the scapegoat too often. At his suggestion the committee adjourned until Thursday for unofficial negotiations by Gandhi and the Agha Khan, leaders of the two factions.

Norway and Sweden have temporarily gone off the gold standard, just a week after Great Britain took similar action. An embargo was placed on the exportation of gold by both countries and the bank discount rates were raised to 8 per cent. The discount rate of Norway went up from 4.5 per cent and that of Sweden from 6 per cent. The decision to follow the action of Great Britain was made at cabinet meetings in Oslo and Stockholm on Sunday. Both countries have been off the gold standard before. Norway suspended the gold standard shortly after the outbreak of the World War and returned to it in 1928, when it again permitted the export of gold. Sweden had restored the gold standard several years earlier. London, Sept. 28, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald informed the House of Commons today that he hoped to be able to announce on Wednesday when the present special session of parliament would be brought to a close. His statement put an end to rumors that he would announce an immediate general election.

Curtis suggested recently, in one of his newspapers, is sometimes useful. “Poor England,” sliding down from a gold basis, automatically inflates her currency. A pound worth less, means more pounds, and more pounds, until inflation goes too far, mean more cheerfulness. London's stock market Thursday was cheerful, British securities rising. Not so here, where we sit in our five billion dollar pile of ‘yellow gold, clinging to our darling gold standard. MANSFIELD, O., Sept. 28 — Three youths who escaped from the Mansfield reformatory last night by making keys which opened two doors and then lowering themselves over a 40-foot wall were being sought today. They were Albert Hasey, 18, Cleveland, serving a sentence for burglary and larceny; Frank Laut, 21, Cleveland, convicted of robbery; and Frank Lewenski, Toledo, imprisoned for burglary and larceny.

LONDON, SEPT. 28. (AP)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald informed the House of Commons today that he hoped to be able to announce on Wednesday when the present special session of parliament would be brought to a close. His statement put an end to rumors that he would announce today an immediate general election.

(United Press Staff Correspondent) LONDON, Sept. 28~-(UP)—Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald appealed to members of the India Minorities committee today to solve their own problems and permit the work of the second India round table conference to proceed unhampered by their domestic difficulties. “I have often been a scapegoat in my life,” MacDonald said at the opening session of the Minorities committee meeting at St. James’ Palace. “I am willing to be again, if necessary, but I think you, yourselves, should become your own scapegoats and take on your shoulders the responsibility of solving this difficult and intricate problem.” The premier said the suggestion that the British government eventually arbitrate in the traditional Hindu-Moslem disputes was “unsatisfactory.” The committee's session was brief and adjourned until 12 a.m. Thursday. 1931-09-24.text: Washington, Sept. 24—America is ready to forego some of her cruiser rights under the London treaty to aid world disarmament. Construction of 11 destroyers on which bids were opened recently is considered necessary, however, to replace obsolete types and help relieve unemployment. Secretary Stimson, indicating acceptance in principle of Italy’s proposal for a year’s naval holiday, specifically excepted the destroyers from any such agreement. Because of America's interest in disarmament, he said, the United States was willing to forego some of its cruiser building rights in its belief an arms truce at this time would favor the success of the disarmament conference at Geneva in February.

By The Associated Press. Tipton, Iowa, Sept. 23.--State veterinarians tonight were ready to continue tuberculin testing of Cedar county cattle under the protection of National Guardsmen, resuming where they left off Monday when 200 farmers defied 65 deputies seeking to protect two veterinarians testing cows on the E. J. Lenker farm.

LONDON, Sept. 24 (P)—Conditional arrangements whereby Parliament would adjourn within a fortnight and not reconvene until February were being discussed today in the lobbies of the House of Commons. Such an eventuality was subject, however, to the possibility of a general election which continued to be the foremost political topic. The Liberals appeared to be divided on the election question and David Lloyd George was said to be annoyed at those members who are willing to support an election on a tariff policy.

(By The Associated Press.) London, Sept. 24—A “holistic” theory of the universe, in which “science is perhaps the clearest revelation of God,” today gave General Jan C. Smuts attention as a philosopher as well as statesman and soldier. The former premier of South Africa has come to the conclusion from long study that material conceptions of space and matter are giving birth to a hypothesis of the unity of mankind's evolution which he calls “holism.” As president of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, he explained to the centenary meeting of that organization yesterday his “scientific world picture of today.” “In other respects,” he said, “it is a strange new universe, impalpable, immaterial, consisting not of material or stuff but of organization, of patterns, or wholes which are unceasingly being woven to more complex or to simpler designs. “In the large it appears t

Tipton, Ia., Sept. 24.—The National Guard, 1500 strong, here to enforce the state bovine tuberculosis test law, moved into action today in Iowa's first cattle-testing “war.” The guardsmen were to protect the 75 veterinarians while the cattle were submitted to tests. The forces of Governor Turner were assembled when Cedar county farmers drove state cattle testers from the farms with pitchforks, stones and eggs. Opposition from the farmers was anticipated but what form it would take was problematical. “I'd rather sell my cows than turn ‘em over to those crooks,” declared J. W. Lenker, who said he had sold his herd to a neighbor. He described as grossly unfair the methods of the state in making the tests. This charge brought from Dr. Peter Malcom, head of the state department of animal husbandry, a reply that the test provided by the law “is 98 per cent efficient.” The state took steps to p

Wendham, Australia, Sept. 24. (P) Wing Commander Charles Kingsford-Smith, conqueror of the Atlantic and the Pacific, left today in the plane Southern Cross, in an attempt to lower the flight record between Australia and England. The record of 5 days, 21 hours and minutes is now held by C. A.

LONDON, Sept 24. — Lord Byng of Vimy, former governor-general of Canada, an outstanding World War figure and commissioner of London police since 1928, informed his officers at Scotland Yard today that he will retire at the end of this month. In 1929 he suffered a severe illness and went to South Africa to recuperate. Recently he became ill again and spent some time in the south of France. There were rumors then that he would resign as the head of Scotland Yard, but these were denied.

London, Sept. 23.—(#)— Squatting in his homespun cotton robes before a big meeting of conservative, liberal and labor members at the House of Commons tonight, Mahatma Gandhi voiced the strongest demand he has yet made in London for Indian independence. In a gentle voice that seemed to soften his bold statements, the Indian nationalist leader declared he would be satisfied with nothing short of complete independence: Would Be Partners Safeguards, such as British control over the army and finance, were unacceptable, he said, but complete independence does not exclude partnership with Britain on a basis of full equality.

1931-10-18.text: BERLIN, Oct. 16—(4)—Germany reverted tonight to a virtual dictatorship under Chancellor Heinrich Brüning when the Reichstag, after giving the chancellor a vote of confidence, voted to adjourn until Feb-23. Adolf Hitler's national socialists and Alfred Hugenberg’s nationalists arose and walked out of the chamber following upon the confidence vote, announcing they had not more interest in what the Reichstag might do. Even with the support of the Communists, the two parties were able to muster only 270 votes against the chancellor. The vote in favor of the confidence motion was 295. The adjournment paves the way for Chancellor Brüning to launch a campaign immediately to put Germany’s economic house in order without parliamentary interference. Friedrichshafen, Germany, Oct. 17 (Saturday) (4).--The German dirigible, Graf Zeppelin took off at 1:05 a.m., today on its third voyage of the year to Pernambuco, Brazil. The ship carried 17 passengers.

Geneva, Oct. 17 (4)—The United States and twelve other nations agreed through their League of Nations council representatives tonight to send a note to Nanking and Tokyo directing the attention of China and Japan to their engagements under the Briand-Kellogg pact. Prentiss G. Gilbert, the American spokesman, and the twelve council members who are not parties to the conflict in Manchuria, participated in the agreement. The step was taken to place the Briand-Kellogg pact, under which the United States is associating itself with the council’s discussions, formally into play as a basis of international action for mediating the trouble in the Far East. The action resulted from a lengthy secret session of the council at which an attempt was made to find a formula which would consider China’s appeal for intervention and at the same time respect Japan’s insistence upon direct negotiations betwee

United Press Staff Correspondent GENEVA, Oct. 17. (U.P)—Chinese charges of Japanese bombing, mining and digging trenches in Manchuria were published here today while the League Council considered the Manchurian conflict in a private session. Two hundred men were reported killed in a battle with Mongolian bandits. Prentiss Gilbert, American observer, attended the session but Japanese and Chinese delegates were not present. Dr. Alfred Sze, Chinese delegate, made public a communication to the Council containing the following charges against Japan: Cinchow, provisional headquarters of Chang Hseuh-Liang, in Manchuria, was bombed Oct. 15. Japanese troops were intrenched around the city walls. Japanese were reported mining a region near Chiliho and digging trenches in the district, also on Oct. 15. Col. BERLIN, Oct. 11—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening’s position at the head of the German government appeared secure for the winter today. The national opposition threat fell, the cabinet received a vote of confidence by a margin of 25 votes, and the Reichstag had adjourned until February 23. Adolph Hitler's fascist-nationalist opposition, which had revoked its policy of abstention from the Reichstag in the hope of defeating Bruening, again admitted defeat and marched stormily out of the chamber, shouting the fascist slogan. The departure of the opposition followed defeat of six motions of misconfidence in the government and various members of the cabinet, and demands for dissolution and new elections.

1931-04-27.text: Cape Henry, Va., April 26.—(AP) A torrential rain and windstorm today drenched President Hoover and his official party and broke up the 324th anniversary celebration of the landing of the first permanent English colonists. After an uncomfortable delay in getting back to the ship on which he came from Washington, the president, who took his wetting good-naturedly, was en route to the White House tonight aboard the Department of Commerce boat Sequoia. Among Sand Dunes Skies were threatening as President Hoover and Governor Pollard walked from the special train to the natural amphitheater among the sand dunes. The president cast apprehensive eyes at the lowering clouds and the wind was blowing the fine sand in clouds as the huge crowd rose to sing “America.” The storm broke suddenly as Bishop A. C. Thomson of the Episcopal Diocese of Southern Virginia began the opening prayer. Presi- (Conti

PARIS, April 27.—(#)—The foreign office and ministry of marine today studied a British foreign office note containing Downing street's answer to French proposals seeking a solution for Franco-Italian-British naval difficulties. While the contents of the British communication were kept a closely guarded secret, there was undisguised pessimism in some quarters today and feeling that the note would mark a breakdown, for the present at least, of negotiations which had looked to completion of a tripartite accord. HUNDON, April 27--Philip Snowden, chancellor of the exchequer, introduced his $4,316,247,800 budget in the House of Commons Monday and assured the poorer classes that they would not be called on to make up out of their incomes the current deficit of $112,888,000. Instead, he made bold proposals for raising the needed revenue. The first and most striking was a tax of one penny in the pound on the capital value of land, a directed challenge to the landed interests of Great Britain and the House of Lords. Legislation making it effective can be put through the House of Commons without the consent of the lords. The second proposal was to utilize 20,000,000 pounds of the 33,000,000 pound fund which Britain maintains in New York for handling debt transactions. The remaining 14,000,000 pounds would be deposited with the Bank for International Settlements in Basel for meeting Britain's internatio

AANA AURA ON, PRE RE he CRE freee” Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer, today announced in his budget week a proposal for taxation of land values at the rate of one pound to the pound. A scheme which is opposed by the House of Lords almost to a man. Compared with this the rest of his speech was unexpectedly mild, with none of the dramatic measures which had been anticipated for the raising of $401,683,000 which is the estimated expenditure for the 1931-32 financial year. The proposed land tax, which cannot be put into force for at least two years because of the need for preliminary valuation, will fall most heavily upon the country nobility, gentry with large estates, many of which are kept exclusively for sporting purposes. These elements of the population are strongly represented in the House of Lords where the proposal is likely to be resisted to the last gasp.

LONDON, April 27. (INS)—Retracing the route by which he set a speed record last year, Wing Commander Charles Kingsford-Smith left Australia for England today with the first air mail cargo to be carried over a newly-opened postal circuit. Piloting his trusty Southern Cross, the famed transatlantic and transpacific aviator hopped off from Port Darwin, Australia, at 7 a.m., Exchange Telegraph messages stated. His first halt will be at Koepang, Timor. From there he will continue to London by way of Burma.

STAINES, Eng., April 26. (?)— Sir Edward Clarke, grand old man of the English bar, died today at the age of ninety. He retired from active practice in 1914. Clarke figured in some of the most sensational cases of the last century, including the famous Baccarat cheating case involving Edward VII, then Prince of Wales. He also defended Mr. Jameson, of “Jameson’s Raid” Boer war fame when he was tried in 1902.

LOS ANGELES, April 27 — Commander Donald B. MacMillan said today he hoped to solve the disappearance four years ago of Capt. Charles Nungesser and Francis Coli, French fliers, when he attempted a round-trip flight from Boston to London this summer. The veteran Arctic explorer said he planned an aerial survey of the northern portion of Labrador, and a side trip to Baffin Land. He added he believed it possible the French fliers, who hopped off from Paris May 7, 1927, for New York, might have been forced down in Labrador. He will keep a close watch for their plane, the White Bird. With Charles F. Docheville of Los Angeles, a former navy flier, MacMillan said he would pioneer a proposed northern air mail and passenger route at the request of Great Northern Atlantic Airways.

Oklahoma City, April 26.—(AP)—Three men, trapped in an empty tank by flames of a spectacular oil fire in the Oklahoma City field, were burned seriously today. Six fire departments, called to the scene when waste oil became ignited on the British-American Oil Producing company’s Jeanette Lewis Holmes lease directly east of the Wheeler school, fought the flames in an effort to prevent their spread. Tanks Flame Four tanks of 1,000 barrels capacity were on the lease, two of them containing oil. As the heat became intense, oil from the two filled tanks boiled over and caught fire, sending flames high into the air. The injured men: Theodore Saulsberry, 30. Lee Overby, 25. T. M. Fisher, 25. 1931-08-12.text: LONDON. (AP). President Hoover's proposals for a year's war debt and reparations holiday were fitted to the Young Plan for reparations payments Tuesday after three weeks’ work by financial experts of the interested nations. Protocols signed Tuesday evening in the cabinet room of the foreign office provide that the suspended payments shall be repaid in ten equal annuities spread over the period from July 1, 1923 to July 1, 1943—in other words, there shall be a year's interim between the expiration of the debt holiday and the beginning of repayments. The suspended payments shall bear interest at the rate of 3 percent, the protocols provide, and shall be “absolute obligations involving no option of postponement.” The report of the experts states that it would have been much better if the procedure of repayment of suspended payments could have been simply a postponement until 1932 of payment

LONDON, AUG. 11. (AP).—Complete agreement has been reached on measures designed to make the Hoover reparation holiday plan effective, it was announced today in an official communique issued by the committee of international experts charged with dovetailing the Hoover plan and the Young plan. Hugh S. Gibson, American ambassador to Belgium, represented the United States as an observer at the commission's meeting. Those who participated will sign an agreement at the treasury office this evening. With the signing of the protocol, President Hoover's proposals may be considered as having gone definitely into effect although as a matter of fact they have been effective provisionally since the middle of July when a German reparations payment fell due.

By The Associated Press. LONDON, Aug. 12.—A foot-long cylinder, four inches in diameter and painted grey was discovered in the water today off the west coast of Jutland. Apparently it had been in the sea but a short time and an investigation was started immediately to determine whether it might furnish a clue to the fate of Parker D. Cramer, American aviator who is missing on a flight between the Shetland islands and Copenhagen.

LONDON, Aug. 12.—(#)—A Reuter’s dispatch from Tokyo Tuesday said the public prosecutor there had decided to order the confinement of Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon Jr., American aviators, pending the outcome of an investigation of charges that they flew over fortified areas in Japan without permission. The two flyers, who failed in an attempt to set a new speed record around the world, have been undergoing questioning by Japanese officials for several days.

LONDON, Aug. 12--(LP)-- Technical measures necessary for the operation of President Hoover's one year war debt holiday were ready today for formal approval of powers involved. The measures, drawn up by the committee of experts in session here, were approved by the ambassadors at a ceremony in the Locarno room of the foreign office late yesterday. The ambassadors and financial experts affixed their signatures to the formal protocol, which is to be effective as of July 1, as soon as ratifications of the government are deposited at Paris. Under these measures, Germany is to re-pay the 1931 war reparations annuities within a 14-year period. Proposal for American participation in an international wheat information service is before the state department for approval. The plan was evolved at the recent London meeting of exporting nations convened by Canadian High Commissioner Ferguson in an effort to relieve the troubles of the world’s wheat farmer. Its purpose is to supplement existing information services on supply and demand in the hope that an adjustment between the two can be effected. Nils A. Olsen, chief of the agriculture department's economics bureau, returned to his office this week after serving as one of the two American delegates to the conference. Samuel R. McKelvie, former member of the farm board, was the other. Olsen remained in London for a meeting of a conference committee in July which drafted the proposal for the information service. VIENNA, Aug. 12-1) Princess Olga, niece of King Alexander of Jugoslavia, Princess Elizabeth of Greece and Patrick Ramsay, British minister to Athens, narrowly escaped death yesterday when their automobile side-slipped and somersaulted on the Wuizen Pass near the Austro-Jugoslav frontier. Newspapers said the car rolled 90 feet down a slope and came to a stop against a tree, averting a catastrophe.

1931-02-18.text: Hollywood, Calif., Feb. 18—(4)— The lure of the films faded and flickered out for Edna Best while homesickness for dear ol’ Lunnon grew. The English girl, brought here for what Hollywood considered her “big chance,” left handsome John Gilbert waiting at the camera yesterday as a result. She just walked out, leaving him, a large cast, an irate director, technicians and all who had gathered at the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer studio to begin work on “Cheri-Bebi.” Director John Robertson tore his hair when Miss Best failed to appear. “A telegram, sir,” said a messenger boy. It was from Miss Best, filed as she passed through Needles, Calif. “Please forgive me. I am on my way back to London and my husband. I am awfully homesick and besides I am just afraid I wouldn't be any good in the picture. Edna Best

Melbourne, Australia. Feb. 18. 1—Relatives of Dame Nellie Melba were summoned to her bedside today when the famous opera singer lost strength after an illness of several weeks. Melba was unable to leave her steamer when she arrived in Australia from England, suffering, it was said, from a skin disease.

(international: News Service) COLDWATER, Mich., Feb. 18.— W. Perkins Bull, K. C., wealthy landowner of Toronto and London, today was suffering from injuries which doctors say may prove fatal as the result of an automobile collision near Quincy, Mich. Bull, accompanied by Bernard Magruder of Racine, Wis., was speeding to Detroit in a rented automobile when it crashed into a motor truck trailer at a terrific rate of speed, according to witnesses. Miss Dorothy Stewart, who was physical director of the local Y. W. C. A. for seven years, is now conducting the gym classes for the business women in the Butler Y.

2 - MADRID, Feb. 17 (#)—A new political crisis, in which loomed the threat of a military dictatorship, was thrust upon Spain today with the failure of Jose Antonio Sanchez Guerra to form a government on a basis of liberal constitutional revision. Sanchez Guerra, designated by King Alfonso yesterday to get together a cabinet, went to the palace at noon today and informed the king that he had been unable to secure the collaboration of the Republicans and Socialists, radical Left groups, and would have to renounce his task. He advised the king to call upon Melquiades Alvarez, another advocate of constitutional revision to limit the powers of the throne, and leader of the “Reformist” group of the Spanish Conservative party. Alvarez, if anything, would be regarded as more radical than Sanchez Guerra, whose designation by the king yesterday was regarded by Monarchists as a surrender to the Ext

Madrid, Spain, Feb. 18—/P— After four days of political turmoil and uncertainty, Spain today had a new monarchist cabinet, avoiding revolution on the one hand and dictatorship on the other. Either of those possibilities had seemed imminent but now it is believed that the tense atmosphere of the past week will be cleared and that the situation is once more tranquil, at least for the time being. The fundamental causes of all the trouble of the past year still exist however, and opposition to the monarchy probably will be renewed when the time is right. Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar, the oldest officer in the Spanish navy and generally regarded as a neutral in politics succeeded where Jose Sanchez Guerra and Melquiades Alvarez had failed. This afternoon he brought a new cabinet to the royal palace and its members were sworn in before the king. It includes General Berenguer, the admiral’s pred

MADRID (U.P) — Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar Y Cabanas became premier of Spain Wednesday, taking the oath of office at the head of a monarchical concentration government. After more than four days of the most serious government crisis during the reign of King Alfonso XIII, the 70-year-old captain general of the navy was suddenly called to the premiership to safeguard the throne against threats of republican upheaval and demands for far-reaching restrictions on the monarch. Within less than three hours Admiral Aznar completed the task which the most influential liberal politicians in Spain had failed to accomplish. The monarchical concentration cabinet will work for parliamentary government as well as a constitutional convention to revise the constitution of 1876, but without such stringent restrictions on the king’s power as proposed by the constitutionalists and liberals who failed to for
ISTANBUL, Feb. 18--(4)—Seven peasants were buried alive in a snow avalanche in the mountains of Eastern Turkey, near Malatia, rescuers finding the bodies. Others are feared lost in the blizzard.

Tokio, Feb. 18 (UP)—Three Japanese naval aviators were killed and the auditorium of an agricultural school was destroyed when a naval seaplane caught fire and crashed in Shizuoka prefecture today. The plane was acting as an attacker in practical exercises when it suddenly burst into flames. It fell directly on the school auditorium igniting the structure.

1931-01-08.text: LONDON, Jan. 8.—(4)—One hundred ships from all ports of the world were held in British ports today by a heavy fog. The Mersey was shrouded and many boats anchored there feared to move. At Manchester a fog of intensity unknown for a generation has persisted for five days. Bronchitis and pneumonia have accounted for many deaths, traffic on land has been greatly impeded. There have been many accidents and injuries.

ROME, Jan. 8—Birth control theories were condemned in an encyclical addressed by Pope Pius XI to Roman Catholic bishops Thursday. The reference to contraceptive methods appeared clearly aimed at the resolutions of the recent Lambeth conference of Anglican bishops in London, who admitted the advisability of birth control under certain circumstances. A Mortal Sin The encyclical said that an act impeding procreation is an offense against God and a mortal sin. "The destruction of an unborn child is murder," the encyclical added. The encyclical quoted Saint Augustine, recalling his statement that "the wife was a mere mistress and the man was the wife's paramour." All relations except conjugal were condemned in the encyclical, which said that any third party was inadmissible. Several Subjects The encyclical, dated Dec 31, contained 16,000 words. Ripon—A)— A volunteer fireman Edward Kopplin, 55, is dead and damage of $55,000 was estimated by school officials as the result of a fire that destroyed Smith Hall at Ripon College. Kopplin, driver of a city fire truck, fell dead apparently from heart disease as the truck careened into a curb at the scene of the fire. About 50 members of Delta Sigma Psi fraternity were made homeless by the fire and two of their number were injured slightly as they attempted to retrieve their belongings from the burning building. Bruno Anderson and George Cunningham, football stars, were the injured students.

Paris, Jan. (.—(@)— the body of Marshal Joffre, hero of the Marne, rested today in Les Invalides, hall of French immortals, whose massive dome shelters the bodies of Napoleon and Foch. Two million Parisians braved freezing weather to stand outside Notre Dame and along the route to Les Invalides for hours while the funeral cortege, in sombre ceremony, proceeded from the cathedral to the temporary resting place of the man who saved France from the invader in 1914. In front of the Invalides, war veterans who had suffered wounds while serving under “Papa” Joffre were given seats of honor while Senator Louis Barihou, minister of war and personal friend of the Marshal, ex-

MELBOURNE, AUSTRALIA, JAN. 8. (AP).—Six men were killed, one is missing and three were injured in the huge tidal wave which swept the coast of New Guinea on December 24, the administrator of that territory reported today. The great wall of water from 25 to 50 feet high swept along the coast for forty miles and rolled 300 yards inland, he said.

PARIS, Jan. 6. (AP)—Frenchmen today gazed for the last time on the familiar, beloved features of “Papa” Joffre, Marshal of France, hero of the Marne, and commander of the French armies in the first two years of the World War. Sixty-five thousand persons were estimated to have filed by the catafalque in the chapel of the Ecole Militaire from 9 a.m. yesterday to 11 p.m. last night and it was believed that many more would view the body today. There can be no extension of the time for doing homage at the dead Marshal’s bier beyond 9 o’clock tonight, for at that time the body will be removed to the cathedral of Notre Dame for the last requiem of the church. (Continued on Page 5)

Paris, France—France, in a final tribute of love and respect to the “Savior” of Paris, gave Marshal Joffre Wednesday a national funeral which in its grandeur reminded of that “day of ashes” when the body of Napoleon Bonaparte was brought back from St. Helena. Wednesday night the body of the victor of the Marne lay, like that of Napoleon, under the great dome of the Invalides, in a disused sacristy of the Chapel of St. Louis, dedicated to the old crusader king. It was placed there so that Madame Joffre might pray beside her soldier husband in silence. Some months from now the body will be transferred to “Chestnut Grove,” the marshal’s country home, where it will be entombed in a mausoleum like that of Washington at Mt. Vernon. Church and state united to make the last rites of France’s loved soldier a full expression of the republic’s gratitude and respect. Thousands of French people fille

ROME, Jan. 8. (UP)—Tragedy dimmed the rejoicing of the Italian people over the South Atlantic flight of General Italo Balbo's seaplane squadron today. Officials announced that five aviators were killed in two accidents that marred the beginning of the flight from Bolama, Portuguese Guinea, approximately 1900 miles over the ocean to Natal, Brazil. Two pilots, two mechanics and one wireless operator were killed. The first accident occurred when the airplane piloted by Captain Enea Silvio Recagno was forced to descend. First Sergeant Louis Fois was killed when the heavily loaded plane struck the water. The left float of the seaplane was damaged. Captain Recagno, Lieutenant Renato Abbriata and Radio Operator Sergeant Mario Mancini were not injured, officials said. The seaplane remained afloat and the four survivors were rescued. The machine later was towed to Bolama. The accident that cost t

1931-02-06.text: (Ivy Associated Press) HAMILTON, Bermuda, Jan. 28.—The Prince of Wales and his brother, Prince George, reached here today aboard the Cropesa en route to Buenos Aires where the heir to the English throne will open the British trade exposition next March. They came ashore for a brief visit before resuming their journey this afternoon. Havana will be their next stop.

DAYTONA BEACH, Fla., Feb. 6.—(4)—Captain Marion Campbell who yesterday lowered the world’s automobile speed record with a speed of 245 miles per hour, announced today he would return to England without further attempts to lower his own record, as he thought yesterday he might do.

(Hy Yheo Associated Press) Daytona Beach, Fla. Feb. 5 — Roaring over the ocean speedway here like a blue streak, Captain Malcolm Campbell, of England, today attained a speed of 215.75 miles an hour on the first of two official trials for the world’s land speed record in his huge Bluebird racing car. The driver flashed by the grandstand at tremendous speed at 3:53 p.m. and quickly disappeared in a haze that hung over the course. Because of the haze, the car was not visible from the grandstand until he entered the officially measured mile. The run was made from north to south.

Colon, Feb. 6.—(A. P.)—Steaming into this harbor this morning, while the coast guns boomed a salute, the steamship Oropesa came alongside her pier and discharged the Prince of Wales and his brother, Prince George. The royal tourists, who are on their way to South America for the British Trade Exposition at Buenos Aires next March, stayed on the pier only long enough to acknowledge the welcome of diplomatic and military officials. Going to France Field, the airport, the brothers climbed into a Pan-American air liner and took off for Panama City. They will board the Oropesa again at the Pacific end of the Panama Canal.

BIRMINGHAM, Eng. and, (UP) — It was spring, the year was 1909 and T. R. Winshull was in love, He wrote his sweetheart asking her to be his bride. She rejected his proposal next day by letter. A year later, it was spring. T. R. Winshull again was in love. He proposed and was accepted. A family was reared. In 1923 Winshull died. Two years later the girl who had rejected his proposal died a spinster. A few days ago T. R. Winshull, Jr., received a letter signed “Lilly” saying she had reconsidered her decision and would marry him. Winshull stared at the letter in amazement. He did not remember proposing marriage to any girl. Then he noticed the date of the missive—March, 1909. The love letter from his father's first sweetheart had been 22 years in arriving at its destination.

LONDON, Feb. 6—(#)—Wilhjalmur Stefansson, writing in the current “Spectator,” lifts a corner of the curtain which enshrouds the death of Salomon August Andree, who “never came back from his polar balloon expedition of 1897. Andree and K. Fraenkel, whose bodies were found in the Arctic wastes last August, were overcome by the subtle fumes of carbon monoxide as they sat about a kerosene stove in their virtually airtight tent, Stefansson believes. He developed his theory from evidence discovered on White Island, where the bodies of the explorers and the remains of N. Strindberg, another member of the expedition, were found. He almost died himself of the same cause, Stefansson writes, in an Eskimo snow house on Coronation Gulf 20 years ago. “Their tent was nearly airtight,” the article says, “for it was made of balloon silk and the floor was sewn to it in one piece. DECISION, rendered by the Italian King Victor Emanuel in favor of France against Mexico may promote better Italian-French feeling. West in the Pacific Ocean, 870 miles west of the Mexican coast, is a little island, called by the English Clipperton Rock and by the Mexicans, La Isla De La Pasion "The Isle of the Passion." France and Mexico claimed it and agreed to let King Victor Emanuel arbitrate. Now, 22 years later, Emanuel gives the land to France, ordering Mexicans to withdraw their little body of soldiers.

HASTINGS, N. Z., FEB. 5. (AP).—Another sharp earthquake rocked the ruins of this town at 10 o'clock last night, throwing the already frightened populace into further panic. Martial law has been declared and no one is permitted to enter the designated district without a permit lest what is left of the buildings may collapse. There has been some looting but armed sentinels were posted at various points throughout the town tonight. NO AMERICANS LISTED AMONG EARTHQUAKE CASUALTIES

1931-08-21.text: London, Aug. 21.—(A.P.)—Resignation of Ramsay MacDonald's labor government became a possibility today as an outgrowth of Great Britain's economic and financial crisis. The situation became more complicated and difficult as the cabinet maneuvered in vain to reconcile widely divergent views as to how the budget is to be balanced and a deficit of half a billion dollars is to be avoided. In the face of a non-committal but clearly hostile attitude of the trades union council toward the government's economy program, the prime minister was placed in the position of facing a special session of parliament and trying to force his proposals through with the support of the opposition parties against a section of his own party. The immediate aspects of the problem became more political than economic or financial this afternoon as the government's predicament was revealed. Word came that Stanley Baldw

- TOKYO, Aug. 21. — Another night on the wave-tossed steamer standing by their plane off Ketoi Island was in prospect for the Lindberghs today. As the afternoon waned, the plane's motor still refused to function satisfactorily and a fog, thick as a London "pea-souper," enveloped the whole scene. Colonel Lindbergh struggled with his motor and Japanese seamen strove to prevent the plane from being dashed on the rocks as gulls cried shrilly and sea lions barked. While her husband remained "on the bridge" to save his ship from foundering if possible, Mrs. Lindbergh whiled away the tedious hours aboard the steamer Shirakawa Maru, turning the pages of Japanese illustrated magazines. The captain on the steamer has turned reporter and has spent much of his time answering requests of Tokyo newspapers for information about the famous couple. In one message he told how at mess, knives and forks bei

| LONDON, Aug. 20.—(#)—The governing committee decided today to open the stock exchange on Saturdays commencing September 19 “in view of the situation in the country and the desirability of affording facilities for dealing.” The exchange has been closed Saturdays since war days. London's decision was followed almost immediately by similar action of the Birmingham exchange and other provincial cities are expected to follow suit. It is likely also that the banks will be called upon to remain open past the usual Saturday closing time at noon.

LONDON, Aug. 31--Great Britain confronted with the gravest financial crisis in her modern history, marshaled her best minds Friday night in an effort to solve the problem. The cabinet, which has been in almost continuous session for several days, was summoned hastily to a special meeting. The meeting was called after hours of consultation between leading members of the government and representatives of the Conservative and Liberal parties. The Conservatives left No. 10 Downing Street, the prime minister's residence, at 6:35 p.m. and the Liberals 16 minutes later. The cabinet was then summoned. It was understood the representatives of the two opposition parties would return to Downing Street to receive the cabinet's reply to their objections to the government's redrafted proposals for national economy.

W. H. (Alfalfa Bill) Murray shut down the wells and stopped production under martial law. Refineries throughout Oklahoma, Texas, and Kansas, figured together, did not have enough crude oil to last three days, and with East Texas and all fields in Oklahoma closed, observers said there was nothing for the refiners to do but meet the $1 price set by Gov. Murray when he called out his national guard. Unofficial offers of $1 a barrel had been made to Murray, and it was reported repeatedly that the Magnolia Petroleum Company, subsidiary of Standard Oil of New York and the fourth largest purchaser in the mid-continent area, was ready to meet the price demand. Nemuro, Japan, Aug. 21.—UVP—The Lindbergh monoplane progressed a short distance toward Nemuro today—at the end of a tow rope. After having been stranded since early Wednesday because of fog and motor trouble off Ketoi island, Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh were forced to accept the aid of a Japanese government steamship in getting their helpless plane to an anchorage safer than the wild little island 410 miles northeast of here. Will Work on Motor; they reported by wireless today they were being towed to Muroton Bay, Shimushiru island, 15 miles southwest of Ketoi. A later message announced the arrival. Colonel Lindbergh said he would spend two or three hours working on the motor and then test it. Incidentally the colonel who never has said much about the perils of his famous solo flight from New York to Paris in 1927 disclosed his first night afloat in his plane in the treacherous

By the ASSOCIATED Press NEMURO, Japan, Aug. 20--Motor trouble and fog held Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh at Keoti Island, one of the world's worst fog zones, again tonight. The flying couple, forced down there late yesterday while on their way from Petropavlovsk to Nemuro, were described in radio reports as rather weary, having spent last night in the cramped quarters of their plane and getting little, if any sleep. In spite of their weariness and an accumulation of trouble during today, the fliers were said to be in good spirits. They decided to taxi their plane to Muroton Bay, 15 miles to the southwest, but the engine trouble developed. Toward evening the treacherous currents of Ketoi began to change and Lindbergh had the plane towed to another nearby anchorage by the Japanese government steamer Shimushiru Maru, which had arrived early in the day.
