1931-08-22.text: LONDON, AUG. 22. (AP).—The Duke of Gloucester was operated on for appendicitis this morning and a subsequent doctors' bulletin said his condition was satisfactory. The Duke, third son of King George, was stricken Wednesday while visiting friends in Leicestershire and was removed to a private nursing home. It was decided an immediate operation was necessary. He is 31 years old.

LONDON, Aug. 22—(AP)—King George has decided to return to London immediately from Balmoral, Scotland, where he went yesterday with Queen Mary, a move which was interpreted by some political observers as foreshadowing the early resignation of Ramsay MacDonald’s labor government. He will travel by special train, reaching London early tomorrow morning. Stanley Baldwin, leader of the Conservative party, which is the second strongest in the House of Commons, is hurrying back from France and will meet again tomorrow with the cabinet on the budget crisis. It appeared the way was being prepared for a change in the government of Great Britain if that eventuality should prove necessary. The king's return, newspapers say, means only one thing—that Prime Minister MacDonald has not been able to obtain sufficient support for his economy plan, either within his own party or from the opposition, and tha

London, Aug. 22—()-—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and his cabinet, winding up their emergency session on the budget today, issued the following communique: "The cabinet has been putting the finishing touches to its scheme which it is believed will meet the situation. The members will assemble tomorrow to hear the results." . The brief communique, which came at the end of a long day of cabinet meetings and conferences with the opposition leaders was the only official statement available of a political deadlock. Causes Sensation News of the king's decision to return caused a sensation and its immediate effect was to create the impression that Mr. MacDonald's government was ready to step out. The cabinet’s communique, however, had a reassuring effect and removed the impression the government already had made its decision. Stanley Baldwin’s return from France was another indication of the

United Press Staff Correspondent LONDON, Aug. 22. (UP)—The labor ministers gathered today for the first Saturday cabinet session since the World War to continue their urgent quest for a solution to the empire’s financial crisis. The meeting assembled at 9:30 a. m., the ministers hurrying to No. 10 Downing Street—the premier’s official residence—after hasty breakfasts and a brief night's sleep. The extraordinary cabinet session was called by Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald last night, after the ministers had been in almost continuous session for two days. Dramatic developments were expected. J. H. Thomas, Secretary of State for Dominions, was among the first to arrive, puffing his pipe. An eager crowd watched the ministers gather. The sun shone fitfully through a cloudy sky as the session convened, symbolizing the political situation’s hourly alternation and bursts of optimism. The crowd, pac

(Associated Press) LONDON, Aug. 21—Prime Minister MacDonald, facing one of the greatest economic and financial crises in the history of Great Britain, tonight was confronted also with definite opposition in trades union ranks to his budget relief proposals and the possibility that his government might be squeezed into a resignation. As an indication of the seriousness of the situation, the cabinet, which had adjourned without expecting to reconvene before tomorrow, hurriedly was recalled for an emergency meeting tonight at No. 10 Downing street. What took place at the emergency meeting was not divulged, but immediately after it was adjourned the prime minister and Chancellor of the Exchequer Snowden conferred with Neville Chamberlain and Sir Samuel Hoare, conservative leaders, and Sir Herbert Samuel and Sir Donald McLean, representatives of the liberals. It was announced that the three-p

London, Aug. 22 (UP)—It was reported this afternoon that the three-party conference with the cabinet had failed to reach agreement, indicating that the government's proposals for dealing with the present crisis were considered inadequate. This report, if substantiated, would indicate probable failure of attempts at united co-operation for putting the government plans into effect. The cabinet adjourned at 3:45 p.m. J. W. Thomas, secretary of state for the dominions, said it would reconvene on Sunday.

London, Aug. 22—(?)—The Brit- ish labor cabinet, summoned to No. 10 Downing street by Prime Minister MacDonald at the unusual hour of 9:30 today continued its efforts to break the deadlock that threatens the life of the government and delays solution of the nation’s financial crisis. With the cabinet in session on Saturday for the first time in many years, the seriousness of the political situation was indicated. The present financial crisis, originating in estimates of a coming $600,000,000 deficit in the budget, developed yesterday into a grave political struggle carrying the fate of the MacDonald government. Faced with stubborn opposition from sections of his own party, particularly the powerful Trades Union Congress whose battle cry is “hands off the dole,” Mr. MacDonald has the difficult task of maintaining unity among his ministers and at the same time securing support for his econ

LONDON, Aug. 22—The Evening News said today it understood King George would arrive in London from Balmoral, Scotland, by special train tomorrow morning in view of the gravity of the political situation. His Majesty has been grouse shooting. For government leaders to interrupt the royal sport would be construed by the public as an indication of an extraordinary crisis, and would presumably be resorted to only because of the most urgent necessity.

1931-07-03.text: LONDON, July 3 (UP)—The United States is the greatest nation on earth in the eyes of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. The Hoover moratorium offer, he believes, is an “action of great wisdom, of great courage and of deep insight.” America and Great Britain are matching strides in the “great moral causes” of humanity in his opinion. He spoke at the Independence Day dinner of the American Society of London last night. The Boston tea party, he said, was a historical incident, that “means you are able to lift up your heads to the world, that you have been able to build up by patient labor, by courage and by self-respect the greatest nation that now exists on the face of this earth.” “I am perfectly certain that to whatever political party you may belong you will excuse me if I say that the recent action of your President to alleviate and soothe the wounds and unhappiness of Europe is an actio

LONDON, July 2—A rough and tumble fight unprecedented for more than a quarter of a century took place today in the staid old house of commons, mother of parliaments, when left wing laborites resisted the suspension of one of their members. Later, after order was restored, the government escaped defeat by only five votes on an amendment to the Snowden land tax bill, which would have exempted garden cities and garden suburbs from the tax. Several liberals voted against the government. When the melee was at its height, with fists flying and members kicking, wrestling and tearing clothes and hair, the speaker was forced to adjourn the session because of the general disorder. This was the first time this action had been taken since the great battles of Irish nationalist days. The trouble was ended after the offending member, J. McGovern, of Shettleston, Glasgow, who had defied the speaker, wa

PARIS, July 3 —P)—A heightened possibility that the French-American debts conversations may lead to a general conference on the entire problem of war debts and reparations was seen today. The conversations, continuing today after another delay, may be enlarged to include Great Britain, Germany, Italy, Belgium and probably Greece, the United Press learned on reliable authority, in the event the Paris parleys now under way are unsuccessful. Optimism was expressed by both French and American statesmen. They admitted that developments had occurred rapidly in the past 24 hours and that the outlook for an agreement was "very promising", but insisted it was premature to say that total accord had been reached. Invitation Refused The government meanwhile refused an invitation from Great Britain to come to Chequers, in England, for a week-end parley. It was explained, however, that France always h

LONDON, July 3—Prime Minister Ramsey MacDonald, speaking last night at the Independence Day dinner of the American Society in London, called the United States “the greatest nation which now exists on the face of the earth.” Referring to the Boston tea party, he said: “That historical incident means that you are able to celebrate this day, that you are able to look back on your history with pride. It means that you are able to lift up your heads to the world, that you have been able to build up by patient labor, by courage and self-respect the greatest nation that now exists on the face of the earth.”

London, July 3—Lloyd George answered the defection of Sir Simon and two fellow liberals from the party ranks today with one of the most bitter personal attacks heard in the House of Commons in many years. Emphasizing his points with an uplifted pince-nez he pointed accusingly at his former lieutenant and co-leader. He mercilessly twitted Sir John and painted word pictures of him which drew shouts of laughter from the labor benches. From the conservative benches came loud protests. When Lloyd George had finished he was given a four minute ovation by the labor benches. Sir John was sitting behind the man who attacked him. At first he appeared to pay no attention but later on observers thought he tolerated the studied sarcastic jibes of the head of the liberal party with difficulty.

DARTFORD, Kent, England, July 3. (*)—Sir William Hart Dyke, a political figure of the golden era of Gladstone and Disraeli, died today at his home. He was 94. Lady Dyke, who is ill, was not informed of his death. He was a great sportsman, owning an estate of 9,000 acres, and was credited as one of the originators of lawn tennis. He represented this division in parliament from 1885-1906, but held his first post from West Kent in 1865.

LONDON, July 3. (U.P)—A profound impression was noticeable here today as a result of Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald's speech at the American Society's Independence Day dinner, in which he said that the "United States today is the greatest nation on the face of the earth." The Labor premier’s sincere friendship for America long has been traditional among his friends and others. However, none had anticipated that he would go so far as to admit that the United States was greater than the British Empire. Premier MacDonald said that Great Britain and the United States were absolutely in hearty agreement and that they were going to "keep step" together. In his address to the 350 guests present at the dinner in the Savoy Hotel, the premier referred to President Hoover's war debts and reparations holiday scheme as "an act of great courage." "His move to alleviate and soothe Europe's wounds and unha

Wimbledon, Stadium, England, July 3.—(A.P.)—Frank X. Shields, who injured his leg Wednesday in a fall in his semi-final match of the men’s singles, today notified officials he would be unable to play tomorrow. The title thus going to his young fellow countryman, Sidney B. Wood, Jr., by default. Wood, not yet 20 years old, thus succeeds to the title held by such noted tennis players as Rene La Coste, Jean Borotra, Henri Cochet, Gerald Patterson, Little Bill Johnston and Big Bill Tilden, the 1930 title holder. Shields fell in the fourth set of his match with Jean Borotra, and was in such pain that it was thought for a time he had been seriously injured. After a short rest, however, he returned to the court to run out the set.

1931-04-07.text: | WINDSOR, Eng, April 7, (AP). England got something of a shock at noon today when it was learned from the issuance of an official statement that King George V, who the country believed was only suffering from a slight cold, actually was a victim of bronchitis. The statement said the attack was of a “sub-acute” nature, and that the patient was progressing satisfactorily, though slowly. The statement brought sharply home to the nation, however, that it is barely two years ago since the monarch was hovering between life and death from a chest disorder which originated in a cold caught on Armistice Day, 1928. The king’s health has been a matter of keen public interest ever since his recovery the following spring.

CHICAGO—(U.P)—Acting Police Commissioner John H. Alcock laughed heartily today over a telephone conversation with a reporter for the Daily Herald in London, England. The London paper called to ask Alcock how many people would be killed in the mayoralty election and if he thought “Big Bill” Thompson would win. Alcock replied that nobody would get hurt and asked if Thompson could depend upon having the moral support of King George. The commissioner got his biggest laugh, he said, when he learned the call had cost the newspaper $33.

NEW DELHI, India, Apr. 6 (AP) — Mahatma Gandhi is considering a visit to the United States, either before or after the second round table conference in London, it was announced today. Gandhi believes, it was said, that India’s liberation movement will receive greater world support if he visits the country which 150 years ago faced much the same problem which he claims now is confronting India.

WASHINGTON, April 7.--(UP) President Hoover held a 25-minute conference today with Montague Norman, governor of the Bank of England. The weekly cabinet meeting was delayed 10 minutes by the president to continue the conference, Afterward Norman said the chief subject of the discussion was the wintry weather that descended this morning on Washington.

WASHINGTON, April 7 (AP)— The Atlantic coast from Florida to New England today experienced its second day of after-Easter rain and snow. The weather bureau, which said snow was falling as far south as Asheville, N. C., held out the hope of fair and warmer weather for the south Atlantic states tomorrow. It predicted continued rain in the middle Atlantic and New England states for another day. The country east of the Appalachian mountains, excepting the Pacific northwest where there was some rain, was experiencing generally fair weather. The heavy precipitation in the east was expected to do much in relieving a shortage of sub-soil moisture in Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania. Washington, D. C., also experienced sleet and snow, which dampened and chilled the lingering Easter holiday visitors.

Brooklands, England, April 6 (7)— Sir Malcolm Campbell, world’s automobile speed champion, had what he described himself as the narrowest “shave” of his life today in a race at While his car was doing well over 100 miles an hour on the first lap of the opening race of the day, a 12-mile handicap, the tie-rod holding the front wheels in position snapped. The wheels locked and the car zigzagged madly from a track slippery from recent rains. With death threatening Campbell and the spectators who lined the rail on either side, the pilot managed somehow to get the car under control after the spokes had ripped out of one of the wheels. “I was braking. The age of the car was against me,” Campbell said, “and then the front wheels locked. I was doing well over 100 miles an hour and I don't know how I held the car on the track. Somehow I managed to pull her in. I suppose my luck holds.” He describ

Cleveland — (>) — British and American buddies in war-time flying corps who have gone on to peace-time accomplishments, descended on Cleveland Tuesday to watch one of the greatest of them all, “Daring Jimmy” Doolittle, receive the Harmon trophy of the Lique Internationale des Aviateurs. Doolittle, the “flying hellion,” who holds a major’s commission in the army reserve, won the award, one of the greatest in aviation, as the first pilot to take off, fly and land blindly. He did it at Mitchell Field three years ago in a plane whose cockpit was covered with canvas so he could not see outside. He flew by radio beacons and landed by special instruments.

(Associated Press) New York, April 7.—The greatest American novels, John Galsworthy, English novelist, said last night, are: “Tom Sawyer” and “Huckleberry Finn,” by Mark Twain. “The Scarlet Letter,” by Nathaniel Hawthorne, “McTeague,” by Frank Norris.

1931-07-29.text: LONDON, July 30.—(#)—An official statement made public today said David Lloyd George “passed a restful night and his strength is well maintained. His condition so far continues to be satisfactory.” The liberal party chief and wartime prime minister was operated on yesterday for a kidney ailment. Since the days when the nation watched anxiously for news from the bedside of King George, no sickroom has been the focus of so much interest and sympathy as Lloyd George's. Every newspaper today featured detailed stories setting forth the circumstances of the operation, and the former prime minister’s house in Addison Road, West London, was bombarded with inquiries and messages of sympathy.

By the Associated Press, Two transatlantic planes—those of Boardman-Polando and of Herndon-Pangborn—had been out of New York 83 hours at 2 o’clock (eastern standard time) this afternoon, Absence of any word of their progress was beginning to cause some uneasiness among airmen. Neither plane, however, was as yet in danger of being forced down by lack of fuel. Seeking Distance Record. Herndon and Pangborn’s red monoplane carried 850 gallons of gasoline; enough to carry them 5,500 miles without halt. At an average speed of 100 miles an hour, they could travel another twenty-two hours without landing. The plane, however, was capable of somewhat greater speed, which would cut down the time in the air by a few hours. The Boardman-Polando plane had 718 gallons of gasoline, sufficient to carry them, they believed, 7,000 miles. At 100 miles an hour—their average speed—this would enable them to st
Sverdlovsk, Russia, July 30. (P)— Amy Johnson, British flier on her way from England to Tokyo, landed here from Kazan today.

LONDON (Wp) — David Lloyd George, 68-year-old liberal leader and war-time premier, critically ill, underwent a severe operation at his Addison Road town residence Wednesday. Lord Dawson of Penn, physician to King George, conducted the operation for kidney trouble at 9:45 a.m. Members of the Lloyd George household said at 3:30 p.m. that the patient’s condition up to that time had been satisfactory. Three nurses were in attendance during the operation on the popular shaggy-haired liberal party leader. An ambulance was held waiting outside the house, ready to rush Lloyd George to a hospital if necessary. Oxygen cylinders arrived shortly before the operation.

LONDON.—Seventeen years ago Wednesday—July 29, 1914—the first shot in the greatest war the world has yet known was fired. In the 13 years since it ended in 1918, the powers have sought to gain peace permanently through such efforts as the League of Nations and conferences on arms limitations. Efforts at present are aimed at a world arms limitation agreement, to be sought at the arms parley in Geneva next February.

London, July 28.—(A. P.)—Germany is beginning to realize that her economic problem is one which demands self-help, Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson said today upon his return from a two-day visit to Berlin, and the country has taken the first steps toward recovery. “The people I saw in the streets and parks,” he said, “were not on the brink of revolution. They looked their chancellor in the eye, and although many recognized us as we mingled with the crowds, there was not a single hostile demonstration.” He talked with Chancellor Bruening, President von Hindenburg and other German officials about the country’s economic and other problems, he said, and he believes the American viewpoint is better understood now than it was before. In very frank discussions he told them they could not re-establish confidence in Germany so long as complaints about hardships continue, and he was informed a

LONDON, July 28 (UP)—‘Some anxiety’ was expressed by his physicians today over the condition of David Lloyd George, liberal leader, ill at his home on Addison Road with a kidney disorder. An official bulletin issued today said: “Mr. Lloyd George passed a somewhat disturbed night, although his general condition is satisfactory. The haematoma is diminishing, but until it subsides, it will be the cause of some anxiety.”

London, July 29.—Two more American planes were believed to have flown across the Atlantic today. The planes, one flown by Hugh Herndon Jr. and Clyde Pangborn, and the other by Russell Boardman and John Poland, had not been sighted, but reports from Valentia Island, on the southwest coast of Ireland, indicated that one or both of them had been heard flying over there. Both planes left New York at dawn yesterday and were due over Ireland at about the time the unidentified planes were heard. Herndon and Pangborn were headed direct for Moscow on an attempt around the world, and the other fliers were headed for Istanbul, Turkey, seeking the world straight line, long distance record. The first plane heard was reported in a private dispatch to London to have passed over Valentia at 1:15 P.M. A United Press dispatch later said a plane had been heard over Knightstown, Valentia Island, at 3:15 P.M

1931-04-16.text: Paris. April 16.—(A. P.)—Spain’s king and queen, driven from their throne at Madrid in a movement which has culminated in the establishment of a Spanish republic, today found asylum in France. Sad faced and tearful, Queen Victoria, who left an English home to become the bride of King Alfonso, reached Paris with five of their children this forenoon. She retired to a hotel apartment where she was said later to be in a state of virtual prostration as a consequence of the strain of the past four days. She shut herself up in her bedroom and would see no one upon her doctors’ advice that she must have absolute rest and quiet until tonight, when Alfonso is expected here from Marseilles where he landed from the cruiser Principe Alfonso at dawn today. With Alfonso’s arrival, a few minutes before midnight, the entire Spanish royal family will be gathered in Paris with the exception of the third so

LONDON —(#)— Government majority on tonight’s division was believed assured by a vote taken by the Liberals this afternoon. Twenty-eight favored supporting the government, seven were in favor of voting for the conservative motion of censure tonight and eight were in favor of abstaining. As the Laborites hold a normal majority over the Conservatives, the margin of 21 votes by the Liberals appeared certain to give the MacDonald ministry victory. Former Prime Minister Baldwin, Conservative leader, today launched a heavy attack on the labor government, moving a vote of censure over the unemployment problem on which the fate of the MacDonald ministry may depend.

LONDON, April 16.——The Labor government of J. Ramsey MacDonald reached what may be the most critical period of its existence today when Stanley Baldwin, Conservative leader, moved a vote of censure in the House of Commons. The motion accuses the government of failing to carry out its pledge to relieve unemployment. If it is passed, the government will resign. The Liberals will decide MacDonald's fate, and can overthrow the government by voting with the Conservatives. The Liberal attitude was not certain, however, and much may depend on the debate which will precede the vote at about 11 p.m. It was generally believed the Liberals will grant Labor a further period of grace, and continue the government in power at least until after Chancellor Philip Snowden introduces his budget on April 27.

MIAMI BEACH, Fla., April 16.—(4’)}—Gar Wood raced his Miss America IX at 103.249 miles an hour one way over the Indian Creek course here today and came within .25 of a mile an hour of equaling the world’s speed boat record of 103.49 miles an hour held by Kaye Don of England. Wood's maximum speed thus far in today's trials was made in his fifth run over the measured mile. On the previous run he went 102.892 miles an hour. Prior to that he had made one run at 102.534 miles an hour. After the fifth trial, he halted temporarily and brought his boat to its dock to inspect the motors.

LONDON, April 16.—Former Prime Minister Baldwin, conservative leader, today opened a heavy attack on the labor government, moving a vote of censure over the unemployment problem on which the fate of the MacDonald ministry may depend. The House of Commons was packed and excited as it assembled to (Continued on page four.)

London, April 15, (4)—There was intense speculation tonight in England regarding the whereabouts of Alfonso XIII, for the cruiser carrying him into exile had not put in at Gibraltar as had been generally expected here. This evening there were apparently well-grounded reports she was heading for Marseilles, and there were rumors also the king might have transferred at sea to another vessel as King Manuel of Portugal did after his abdication. It was noted in this connection that the British cruiser Curley steamed out of Gibraltar this morning, officially for routine exercise. A great many Englishmen were wondering if Alfonso might be on the Curley tonight. If he comes here the Spanish colony in London will welcome him enthusiastically.

WENDAYE, France, April 5 — Victoria Eugenie, a sad-faced English woman who until Tuesday was queen of Spain, reached here Wednesday night with her five children, changed trains and headed north through France to exile. Her train came in just as another arrival from Paris carrying Spanish exiles to Madrid, but the attention of the crowd at the station was focused upon the royal emigres as they left their Pullman car, crossed the platform and entered a French train. “Long live our queen! Long live the monarchy! Long live Spain!” the crowd cried, pressing as close as the police would permit to the royal train.

BOMBAY, India, April 16—(UP)—The special train of the retiring Lord Irwin was reported to have been stoned last night by extremists. The railroad line was heavily guarded to ensure the train's safety. Mahatma Gandhi, nationalist leader, will depart for England probably Saturday. This is Lord Irwin's fiftieth birthday.

1931-07-12.text: 6 Vow ae mo BS SS Sees London, July 11--While Prime Minister MacDonald sat on the platform at the peace demonstration in Albert Hall today, a woman in the audience threw a tear gas bomb at him. She was quickly evicted. The meeting was interrupted only a few moments.

BERLIN, (U.P)—A tacit and unofficial threat that pressure for French and British demands upon Germany would result not only in retirement of the Bruening cabinet, but resignation of President Von Hindenburg if any government acceded to the demands, was believed today to assure at least a temporary shelving of the proposals. The demands in question were for German suspension of building work on the second “vest pocket battleship,” together with relinquishment of the Austro-German customs union program. The question of ship construction had come particularly to the fore in connection with Dr. Hans Luther’s hurried visit to London and Paris in search of Reichsbank credits. It was learned that France had also asked the German government (Continued on page 5)

CHICAGO, July 11, U.P)—Twelve-year-old Hartley De Gerald, a seventh grade pupil, departed alone today on a 7,000 miles exploration trip in the Arctic. “I've been on several such trips since I was six years old,” Hartley said. “Last summer I went to British Guiana all by myself.” Hartley took a motion picture camera and a notebook as equipment on the Arctic trip. His immediate objective was the mouth of the Mackenzie River.

LONDON, July 11. (UP)—The Sunday Express will say tomorrow that it understands the federal reserve bank of New York has cabled to the reichsbank, expressing readiness to grant a $200,000,000 to $300,000,000 six months credit in conjunction with an international syndicate.

BERLIN, JULY 11. (AP).--Dr. Hans Luther, president of the Reichsbank, returned by plane from Paris today without having obtained French assistance and with no hope of obtaining it under conditions acceptable to the German government. He had sought French aid in extending credit to the Reichsbank. The bank head went into conference with Chancellor Bruening immediately after his arrival at Tempelhof airdrome and thereafter the cabinet was called into session to consider the drastic measures of departing from the gold standard and putting all German exports under government monopoly. These developments came on the heels of the news that the Reichsbank run on foreign currencies today reached the record breaking total of 100,000,000 marks (about $25,000,000) during the brief Saturday.

LE BOURGET, France, July 12, (AP), (Sunday).—Joseph Lebrix and Marcel Doret hopped off from Le Bourget airdrome at 4:46 a. m., Sunday on their non-stop flight to Tokyo, Japan. The get-away was without incident. The motor of the “Hyphen” was started at 4:40 a. m., and after a short warming up the plane started down the runway, lifting slowly after a long run, under its load of fuel. Friends and aviation fans began to arrive at the airdrome by 8 a. m., and the crowd surrounded Mechanic Menin, who kept watch over the plane through the night while Lebrix and Doret slept. The fliers were up shortly after 3 o'clock, however, and gave the plane their last inspection as the mist disappeared and the eastern sky began to grow light.

By The Associated Press. July 11.—Chancellor Bruening and his cabinet tonight to discuss what were called “spartan moves” to forestall a financial crash in Germany. The cabinet session began after the arrival of Reichbank President Hans Luther by airplane from Paris. President Luther came home without having obtained French assistance for a German loan and with no hope of obtaining it without what were considered “impossible” political concessions. Among the moves considered tonight by the cabinet was the appointment of a special “commissar of revisen” with authority to seize foreign currencies and other media of payment, including precious metals, in “the interest of national safety.” The most pressing problem before the government, however, was what to do Monday to safeguard the reichsbank. Cabinet members feared the public reaction to today’s phenomenal outflow of devisen, which amoun

(COPENHAGEN. —()—Danish officials Saturday condemned the occupation of eastern Greenland by Norway as a violation of the treaty of 1924 and as disregard for the LN Premie of the two nations. Premier Stuning said: “The Norwegian action is a direct encroachment, I am calling together the privy council today and presumably Greenland will go straight to The Hague. Whether it is necessary for Denmark to take other steps will be considered.” Foreign Minister Nunch said “Denmark by friendly negotiation attempted to avoid a disagreement, but we have to stand on our rights and it is unavoidable to make an immediate complaint to The Hague of this violation of justice.” Berlingske Tidende learned in an interview with Foreign Minister Braadland of Norway that the territory included in the official occupation announcement was smaller than that occupied by the Norwegian Hunter Devold and his college f

1931-01-05.text: London, Jan. 4,--(fP)—The princess royal, eldest sister of King George, died this afternoon at the age of 63. Though she was known to have been an invalid many years, the first intimation to reach the public that her condition had become critical was in the form of a bulletin issued early today from her residence in Portman Square, saying she was showing signs of increasing weakness. Though Princess Louise Victoria Alexandra Dagmar—to give her her full name—was of such a retiring disposition she sometimes was called ‘Her Royal Shyness’ she was greatly loved by all who got to know her. She was the most democratic of royal ladies and on many occasions took rides in buses, the other occupants of which were ignorant (Continued on Page 2?)

LONDON, Jan. 5 (P)—All Britain today mourned one of the most democratic of its royal family, Louise, Princess Royal, nicknamed “Her Royal Shyness,” who died in her sleep yesterday of heart disease. King George, at Sandringham, was notified of her death, the Lord Chamberlain immediately ordering a period of four weeks full mourning for the British court and two additional weeks of half mourning. The Princess Royal, who was the eldest sister of the king, was 63 years old, a year and eight months younger than her imperial brother. Her death was not unexpected. She had had recurrent attacks of the heart trouble, and in 1925 she suffered from a serious gastric hemorrhage, although until recently she had been in somewhat better health. Her physicians at midnight Saturday announced an increased weakness in her condition. Although shy and resentful of the ostentation which accompanies the royal

Warsaw, Poland, Jan. 5—Despite a mishap 60 miles north of here when she smashed the undercarriage of her plane in making a forced landing late yesterday, Miss Amy Johnson, British woman aviator, was understood today to intend continuing her much opposed flight to Peiping, China. Leaving Berlin shortly before noon, the pretty 23 year old girl was driven by the wind to the north of her objective, Warsaw, when she turned about she ran into a heavy fog bank and finally made a forced landing at the village of Amelin, near Krasnosielk. She was not injured. While the plane is being repaired she accepted the hospitality of the Catholic priest at Krasnosielk, who invited her to spend the night at his house. Her failure to arrive in a reasonable length of time had excited considerable fear for her safety here and word had been broadcast for all policemen throughout Poland to be on the lookout.

Warsaw. Jan. 4, (P).—Amy Johnson, the 23-year-old flier who left England New Year's Day on a project flight to Peiping, was driven by fog to a forced landing late today at the village of Amelin, near Krasnosielk, about 60 miles north of here. She was uninjured but the undercarriage of her machine was smashed in the rough landing. Miss Johnson, who last summer flew from England to Australia in 19 days, left Berlin for Warsaw at 10:27 a.m. today in the face of unfavorable weather. Atmospheric conditions were so bad she was driven northward from the German capital and missed Warsaw entirely. Then, before she could get back on her course, a heavy wave of fog engulfed her and she was forced to come down.

LONDON (UP)—The royal courts of Britain and Norway mourned Monday the death of the Princess Royal, the sister of King George of England and Queen Maud of Norway, who died in her sleep here Sunday. The Princess Royal, who would have been 64 years old next month, had been in failing health for several years. Signs of increasing weakness from heart trouble brought her daughters, Princess Arthur of Connaught and Lady Maud Carnegie to her bedside. King George ordered six weeks mourning at the British court after his sister's death. A similar period of mourning was ordered at the Norwegian court. The title of Princess Royal is not hereditary and can only be conferred by the king. It was not believed in court circles that it would be conferred upon anyone for a considerable period of time. Princess Mary, Countess of Harewood, is the eldest daughter of King George V and is expected to succeed to

MADRID. Jan. 4 (By Telephone to London).—Six persons were injured slightly today as mounted police charged to break up a demonstration by 250 persons in Puerta del Sol, the principal square of Madrid. The manifestation, in which mainly railway workers and students participated, was the first such in the Spanish capital since martial law was proclaimed after two attempts at military revolt last month. The trouble began when a group of discontented railway men attempted to visit political prisoners and were refused admittance to the jail because the law limits such a visiting party to eight persons. Later in the afternoon the same group, augmented by other workers and students, attempted to parade through Puerta del Sol, shouting protests against the government. Mounted police scattered them with sabres, but the incident caused intense excitement in Madrid.

PLYMOUTH, Eng. Jan. 5-17, two members of the crew of Lucia, submarine depot were “lodged in naval barracks” today after what is believed to have been a demonstration in first curtailed Christmas. An investigation by the authorities is under way, the 42 crew members have been replaced so that the Inez may join the Atlantic fleet maneuvers. Officers of the ship and of the Devonport Naval Station would make no comment regarding the affair other than that "it was being investigated and that it was not a mutiny."

(By The Associated Press) London, Jan. 5.—South Wales coal miners today asked the MacDonald government to step in as arbitrator in the labor dispute which tied up the South Wales mines and threw 140,000 men out of work. Ramsay MacDonald was expected to take part in the conference before it ended. The miners want the government to induce the mine owners to accept the recommendation of the National Industrial Board of Adjustment of the 45-hour week without reduction in wages. The owners were invited to present their side of the case tomorrow. The miners will remain here to meet the owners if a joint conference seems warranted.

1931-08-17.text: To the Editor of The Eagle: SANTA MONICA, Cal., Aug. 15.—Say, you talk about a people and place being appreciative of what was done for them when they were in trouble, remember England, Ark., that had all the trouble during the drought last Fall? Well, there is a coal mining section of Oklahoma (same as the coal mines everywhere); they were mighty hard up. Well, this England, Ark., just loaded up 13 heaping truckloads of food and sent them to Henryetta, Okla. PRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Ger., Aug. 17 (—The Graf Zeppelin will leave tomorrow morning for Hanworth field, London, with 21 passengers and if all goes well will make the first peacetime landing of a German dirigible on English soil at sundown. After debarking some of its passengers and taking on others, the big airship will nose upwards for a 24-hour cruise over Great Britain. She will land again in London Wednesday evening, tie up overnight and begin the homeward flight Thursday morning. Dr. Hugo Eckener, veteran commander, will be at the press. The dirigible returned from Essen this morning with 24 passengers after a weekend cruise and took off two hours later for a flight over Lake Constance with 39 passengers.

BOMBAY, Mata, Aug. 17. UPK - Redoubled efforts were being made today by unbiased intermediaries to persuade Mahatma Gandhi to follow the first contingent of delegates to London for the second round table conference on Indian affairs. The prospect of his ultimate departure became distinctly brighter when it was learned he was willing to withdraw his demand for the appointment either of an arbitration board or of a high court judge to investigate alleged breaches in the Delhi pact provided the government designates a single trustworthy civilian or government official to bear his complaints. This fact has been communicated to Viceroy Willingdon at Simla and the cabinet in London.

POMBAY, INDIA, Aug. 17—(UP)—Serious threat of a revival of the civil disobedience campaign against British rule in India was feared imminent today. Leaders in the all-India Congress, Nationalist body, were reported prepared to proceed with a renewal of the campaign which a year ago disrupted trade and caused disturbances throughout the country. The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, who previously said he did not plan to renew the campaign he led a year ago, was quoted as calling on Indian leaders to be prepared “for any eventuality.” “Don’t expect anything from London,” Gandhi said in a speech Saturday at Almedabad. “If, however, it is to be peace, do not disturb our calm; if war, the people will not be slow to respond.” The reference to London apparently indicated Gandhi had little faith in the outcome of the second India round table conference scheduled to open there Sept. 15. He cancelled his pla

AHMEDABAD, India, Aug. 16—Mahatma Gandhi returned to his ashram today declaring that his “inner voice” told him he should not go to London for the second round table conference on Indian self-government. He insisted that India, not England, should determine its destiny.

TOKIO, Japan, Aug. 15. WUP— Two American aviators, Clyde E. Pangborn and Hugh H. Herndon, Jr., were fined 2,050 yen today for taking pictures as they flew over the Kahodate secret fortifications while en route to Tokio from Siberia on their trip around the world. In American money, the fine amounted to about $1,000. Japanese officials who imposed the fine had indicated earlier they expected their action in this case to establish a precedent for American-Japanese relations. Besides fining the American fliers, the officials ordered confiscation of a camera which Pangborn and Herndon used for taking pictures during their world encircling flight. Films and a map also were ordered taken over by the government. Settlement of the case, which assumed international importance, cleared the way for Pangborn and Herndon to go ahead with plans for a flight from Tokio to America as a continuation of t

PARIS (UP)—France never will relinquish her claim to reparations from Germany, Pierre-Etienne Flandin, minister of finance, declared Monday. Flandin, in an interview, said that nations such as the United States were entitled to dispose of their reparations as they wished, but that France intended to insist on Germany’s making the scheduled payments. Questioned on Germany's capacity to pay, he said that was a question for the Young Plan experts. “Besides, if certain incapacities arise,” he said, “they need not be permanent. Circumstances change rapidly. Remember France's financial crisis in 1926 and our rehabilitation since.”

Vienna, Aug. 16.—(/P)—— Twelve persons were killed, 11 seriously injured and 30 slightly hurt as an express train from Rome was in collision today with a freight train near Leoben, Syria. The cause of the accident was not determined.

1931-08-28.text: LONDON, Aug. 28 (AP)--Ramsay MacDonald, three times prime minister of Great Britain, today was ousted as leader of the labor party and Arthur Henderson was elected his successor. Henderson now will lead the opposition against the man whom he served as foreign secretary in the recent labor government. Only six of the 280 members of the labor parliamentary party voted to retain MacDonald at today's meeting.

New York, Aug. 28.—(P)—Negotiations for a Franco-American credit to Great Britain were described Friday as having made substantial progress. Estimates of the amount by financial writers ranged from $200,000,000 to a possible maximum of $500,000,000. Information came from J. P. Morgan and Company that discussions had been held both here and in Paris, and that French and American banking interests would participate equally in a credit to the new national emergency government. Presumptions of experts were that the credit would be used by the Bank of England to protect sterling exchange if necessary, but the possibility was recognized that in view of recent improvement in sterling the British government might decide it needed no credit. The credit would be for one year. British treasury bills in proportion to amounts borrowed would be issued to bankers participating in the credit. These bill

LONDON, Aug. 28. — (UP) — Great Britain reached the turning point of her modern political history today, with a vast shift in political leadership imminent. All parties united in the effort to solve the grave financial crisis, with the understanding that after it has been settled, a general election will be held and the country turned over to new leadership. The parliamentary Labor party elected Arthur Henderson, MacDonald's rival, leader of the party today in succession to MacDonald. There were only six dissenting votes. John R. Clynes was elected deputy leader. A resolution was adopted declaring the Labor party the official opposition to the national government. Lord Banquey was the only member of the new government attending. He was given respectful attention when he pleaded for support of the government. Malcolm MacDonald, the premier’s son, attended. The Rev. James Barr presided. Th

NEW YORK CITY, Aug. 27—A private banking credit believed to be the largest in financial history is being marshalled in New York and Paris, Wall Street learned today, as an invincible bulwark for the British pound sterling. Both New York City and Paris bankers, it was said in highest Wall Street banking circles, proposed to make the credit so large there can be no further question as to the stability of the pound, which is so widely used as the common medium of international exchange. While bankers were not prepared as yet to reveal the exact size of the loan, it is believed it will be between $300,000,000 and $500,000,000 provided in equal portions by New York City and Paris bankers. It is known each portion is expected to be larger than the $100,000,000 credit granted to the British government in 1925 by a syndicate headed by J. P. Morgan and Company. It was informally stated at the Mor

LONDON, Aug. 27—) Ramsay MacDonald’s new national government was repudiated this afternoon by the whole British organized labor movement, but continued to grapple with the national financial crisis throughout a crowded day. The Prime Minister began the day by having breakfast with Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson. The breakfast was interpreted in government circles as a gesture of Anglo-American friendship during the present British emergency. No good will was forthcoming for the MacDonald ministry from labor ranks, however. The gathering clouds of opposition broke late in the day in a bitter manifesto denouncing the national government, in the strongest terms and including the charge that private banking interests precipitated Britain's crisis and caused the change in government. The manifesto, which is an open declaration of war on the national government’s economy program that is a

NEW YORK, Aug. 28.—(UP)—Informal British government inquiries were met by assurances today that private American bankers were ready to participate in Franco-American credit of between $250,000,000 and $500,000,000, the largest negotiated privately in this country. Wall Street emphasized that no credit had been arranged, and that with recent improvement of sterling exchange, Britain may decide credit is not needed. Bankers were careful to reiterate that they had made no suggestions to the British government as to how to meet its financial emergency. The laborite Daily Herald of London had charged that Wall Street had issued a “virtual ultimatum” demanding a 10 per cent reduction in the British dole, which caused the fall of the late labor government. This demand, it said, was to force improvement in the government's financial condition, thus making more secure any loan advanced. The Heral

PLYMOUTH, Eng., (UP)—The submarine Nautilus, commanded by Sir Hubert Wilkins, left today for Bergen, Norway, on its daring undersea cruise to the Arctic. The submarine has been in Plymouth undergoing repairs following its breakdown in mid-Atlantic recently. It had engine trouble and was towed to Plymouth by the U. S. S. Wyoming. Wilkins refused to abandon the dangerous voyage under the ice toward the North Pole, however, so repairs were hurried to permit early departure. The work took a little over a month. The Nautilus was especially fitted for its cruise under the ice in the Arctic before leaving the United States. Wilkins was confident the exploration of the polar regions under the sea—in the manner described by Jules Verne long before the submarine was invented—would prove a success and that valuable contributions to science and the knowledge of the "top of the world" would result.

| LONDON--.P)— Chancellor of the Exchequer Philip Snowden served notice today of his impending retirement from British public life. | The chancellor wrote the president of the labor party in Colney Valley Division, his constituency, that he would not be a candidate for reelection to parliament at the next general elections. It was learned simultaneously that Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald was awaiting the action of his constituents at Seaham before deciding on his future plans, but that in any event he would continue to give all his efforts to solving the present national situation. | Reports were current today that Snowden already had resigned but they were denied to the United Press by the chancellor’s secretary. The report was branded “A complete canard”. | Snowden issued a statement saying that he would see the present difficulties through before he retired from office. ‘The chancel

1931-08-05.text: Heinrich Bruening, continuing along the course suggested by American Ambassador Frederick M. Sackett, leaves tonight for Rome with his foreign minister to visit Premier Mussolini as well as Pope Pius XI. Following in the wake of the English, French and German visits, the Rome conference will be one of a remarkable series of meetings among the leading statesmen of Europe which began June 4 with the journey of German officials to London. Herr Bruening hopes to complete the good work by having Premier Laval and Foreign Minister Briand in Berlin late this month and to persuade Mussolini and Foreign Minister Grandi to repay the German visit. Berlin, Aug. 5.—(#)—Chancellor

Aklavik, N. W. T. (via Radio to Edmonton, Alta.) Aug. 5.—(AP)—Charles A. Lindbergh, flying across the wilderness of northern Canada with his heiress wife, landed in the Mackenzie River at Aklavik today, 11 hours and 35 minutes after he had taken off from Baker Lake, 1,115 miles to the east. Averaging better than 100 miles an hour on this most dangerous hop so far of his aerial vacation, Lindbergh, with Mrs. Lindbergh manning the radio, circled the Arctic outpost twice and set his pontoon-equipped Lockheed plane on the river in a perfect Lindbergh landing to the chorus of howling Eskimo dogs and cheers of the entire population of this section. Royal Canadian Mounted Police, in their red jackets and sombreros, rowed out to the Lindbergh plane and helped the fliers bring in the low-winged monoplane to the bank where it was moored safely. The Lindberghs, both smiling at the array of Indians,

BERLIN, Aug. 5.—Reopening today of all German private banks for all normal business, with 2600 municipal and other public savings banks expected to resume full payments Monday, revealed more public confidence in the banks than banking authorities themselves had felt. The opening was almost sensationally tranquil, in contrast to the renewal of panic which had been feared by some bankers. Several hundred policemen stationed in the vicinity of the Berlin banks were idle, with no crowds or disorders to control.

Berlin. Aug. 5.—(#)—Germany's banks, closed for three weeks as an emergency measure during the most acute period of financial uncertainty, reopened for regular business today, and nowhere did there appear the excited crowds which some had feared would be at the paying-teller's windows. The banks were well prepared for any eventuality, but the customers drew far less than had been anticipated and in many cases depositors who had previously notified the banks that they intended to draw large sums cancelled their orders. Some banks which had laid in extra supplies of currency found the demand little above normal and returned their surplus to the Reichsbank. The general experience was that those who had rushed to the banks in panic just before they were closed by President Von Hindenburg’s decree were coming back to return the money they had withdrawn. AKLAVIK, North West Territory, Aug. 5.—(U.P.)—Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and Mrs. Lindbergh soared into Aklavik at 6:05 a. m., Eastern Standard Time, today after completing a daring 1,115-mile non-stop flight across the bad lands of Northern Canada from Baker Lake: Starting from Baker Lake at 6:30 p. m., Eastern Standard Time, yesterday the Lindberghs disregarded advice of northern pilots to follow a semi-circular route to the south, struck out boldly across the barren wastes and followed the most direct line to their destination. The arrival at Aklavik was 11 hours and 30 minutes from the time of the take off. They averaged more than 100 miles per hour for the flight, one of the most dangerous of their 7,000 mile vacation jaunt to the Orient. Both the famous flying colonel and his wife were smiling as they came to a graceful landing after soaring in from across the barren, lake dotted wa

Moscow, Aug. 5.—(P)—Held at Khabarovsk by twenty-four hours of bad weather, the round-the-world fliers, Hugh Herndon, Jr., and Clyde Pangborn were reported by the Tass News Agency today as having definitely abandoned their attempt to surpass the Post-Gatty record. At the same time, it was reported they decided to change their route by taking off for Tokyo tomorrow instead of continuing the course followed by Post and Gatty across the Bering Sea to Nome, Alaska. They plan to remain in Tokyo seven days. Whether they will adhere to their original plan of flying the Pacific or return to New York by some other route and method of travel was not indicated in advices received here. Pangborn was said to be slightly ill.

TOKYO, August 4—(*)—The American aviators Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon apparently have lost their race around the world to lower the record of eight days, 15 hours and 51 minutes set a month ago by Wiley Post and Harold Gatty, fellow countrymen. Whether Pangborn and Herndon were flying over the 2,400 miles dangerous overseas course to Nome, Alaska, or were held at Khabarovsk, Eastern Siberia, by bad weather was uncertain as the hours dragged by and communication with Khabarovsk failed. But after flying 9,250 miles from New York in an attempt to lower the record, the aviators at 9 p.m. (7 a.m., E.S.T.) were 29 hours and 10 minutes behind Post and Gatty’s departure time from Khabarovsk. With a slower plane than their rivals, the chances of Pangborn and Herndon to beat the record were considered negligible. The fliers, however, had expressed determination to continue their air voyage to

BERGEN, Norway, Aug. 5. (AP) — Sir Hubert Wilkins’ polar submarine Nautilus left Bergen this evening. Sir Hubert hopes to take the Nautilus to the North Pole under the ice. She crossed the Atlantic under her own power except for a stretch over which she was towed by an American battleship when her engines failed. Repairs were made in Ireland and she reached Bergen last week. If she goes on schedule she will reach the ice barrier in ten days, including stops at Tromsø and at King’s Bay for fuel.

1931-04-29.text: PARIS, APR. 29. (AP)—Mrs. Whitelaw Reid, of New York, widow of the former ambassador to England, died today at Cape Serrat at the home of her daughter, Lady Ward. Mrs. Reid, who arrived in France only last week, contracted a chill during her voyage across the Atlantic. She was ill when she reached Paris and had grown steadily worse since.

REYKJAVIK, ICELAND, Apr. 29. —(P)—A wireless message received at Reykjavik, Iceland, today purporting to be from Augustine Courtauld, British scientist who is lost in northern Greenland, stated: “Absolutely without provisions.” An airplane leaving Iceland today with the Iceland inspection ship Odin, will fly from the edge of the ice barrier to Tasioak and to Angmagsalik, searching for Courtauld. If the plane can find him it will drop provisions on the ice for his use. He is believed to be somewhere in the vicinity of the station at which he was left to spend the winter and obtain meteorological data for use of the British Arctic air route expedition. The site of this station has not been located thus far by rescue missions which have gone to Courtauld’s aid.

| WASHINGTON, April 29 (P)— In a radio speech that carried across the Pacific Ocean to Japan, Secretary Stimson today said that largely because of the success of the London Naval Conference of 1930 that ocean “no longer separates but rather unites Japan and the United States.” The secretary of state’s message was part of the celebration of the thirtieth birthday anniversary of Emperor Hirohito. Baron Kijuro Shidehara, foreign minister of the Tokyo government, delivered a reply which the radio brought to the United States. The secretary of state, referring to the tour of the eastern United States by Prince Takamatsu, brother of the emperor, and his princess, said their “spontaneous and enthusiastic welcome was because they represented Japan.”

PERTH, Australia, April 29—(UP)—The British steamer Demosthenes reported by radio today that she was afire and making for the port of Fremantle, below Perth. The fire was in the forward coal bunker and the situation was serious, the message said. The Demosthenes, an 11,228-ton steamer, sailed from Fremantle last Saturday for Liverpool. Her home port is Aberdeen.

LONDON, April 29. (AP) — John Harrity, 55-year-old farmer charged with the murder of Annie Tinney, 36, was lodged in a prison cell today to await trial after a bitter but futile fight to escape capture. Harrity, who is a noted sporting shot, embarked with a shotgun yesterday in a rowboat in Lough Swilly, Donegal County, and for six hours held a large force of pursuers at bay until his boat was shot to pieces and sank.

LONDON, April 29.—An urgent call for aid was sent out by wireless from the Arctic wastelands today by Augustine Courtauld, wealthy member of a British Arctic expedition marooned on the Greenland ice cap, according to an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Copenhagen. In a message, picked up at Reykjavik, Iceland, Courtauld reported he was “absolutely without provisions.”

London, April 29.—(U, P.)—Great Britain wants active support of the United States in attempts to solve the impasse between France and Italy in their naval negotiations. Arthur Henderson, foreign secretary, told a questioner in the House of Commons today.

MALMOE, Sweden, April 29— Capt. Albin E. Ahrenberg, noted Swedish flyer, started today for Greenland, on a rescue mission on behalf of a British explorer marooned on the ice cap in the interior of the Arctic island. Augustine Courtauld, son of the British silk millionaire, has been isolated all winter in a meteorological hut on the ice cap, and was feared to be in desperate plight and in danger of starvation. A relief expedition has been unable to find him. Before Ahrenberg departed, friends toasted him in beer and then kicked him which is a Swedish token of good luck. Courtauld is a member of the H. G. Watkins British Arctic air route expedition to Greenland. He was left in his lonely observation post at a considerable distance from the expedition's base, with provisions enough to last the winter. The expedition’s airplanes are out of commission and a dog sled searching party (Turn to P

1931-04-21.text: London, April 21, ()—While kneeling Britons outside prayed for a divine “visitation upon the heads of iniquitous defenders” of the bill legalizing Sunday movies and other amusements, the House of Commons last night passed the measure, 258 to 210, on its second reading. A barrage of prayer was raised by ardent Sabbatarians while debate on the movie bill was in progress. Some of these groups gathered about the statue of Oliver Cromwell, great Puritan leader of the seventeenth century, which stands on the parliamentary precincts. The parties were mixed up in extraordinary manner in the lobbies when the vote was taken on the measure. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and the conservative leader, Stanley Baldwin, for once found themselves in the same lobby waiting for the bill.

PLYMOUTH, England, April 21. — ‘Lawrence of Arabia,’ the most mysterious figure that emerged from the great war, now serving in the royal air force as Aircraftsman T. E. Shaw, lifted today the veil of secrecy which has surrounded his life during the past 10 years. This man who, single-handed, raised the Arabs against the Turks, changed the fate of the allies on the Palestine war front, and for whose body, dead or alive, the Turks offered $50,000 reward, told for the first time why he gave up the position which earned for him the description “uncrowned king of Arabia,” abandoned his rank of colonel in the British army, refused all titles, monetary rewards, decorations and honors, picked a new name and enlisted in the royal air force as a private. As Colonel Lawrence during his war in the desert, he had virtual command of the entire Arab

DOVER, England, April 21—(AP)—Alfonso, exiled monarch of Spain who left his own country in the dead of night to avoid unfavorable attention, arrived in his wife's native land in broad daylight today and attracted no attention at all. His former ambassador at the court of St. James, Merry Del Val, was the only dignitary of importance to greet him as he stepped from the channel boat which carried him from Calais, France. There was a small crowd, but it was composed mostly of reporters and cameramen who were herded here and there with the warning “Keep a respectful distance,” by Scotland Yard detectives. There was no demonstration, as Alfonso strode to the train for the journey to London. He was accompanied by the Duke of Miranda, the Infanta Luisa and Count Quinones de Leon, former Spanish ambassador to France. Alfonso and his party left Paris this morning by automobile and boarded the cro

PARIS, April 21.-(U.P.)-Former King Alfonso of Spain, accompanied by the Duke of Miranda and former Ambassador Jose Maria Quinones de Leon, departed today for London. Although the exiled monarch's fortune is large, it was understood that he had nearly exhausted the funds which he brought to Paris and had asked Quinones de Leon to negotiate a necessary loan. Much of the $20,000 which the former king brought here was exhausted in loans to aristocratic exiles from Spain.

Paris, April 20 (#)—Alfonso of Spain, awaiting in exile for his people to call him home, is to live in the Fontainebleau among the ghosts of the historic past. “His queen will take her children there tomorrow, putting up at the Savoy Hotel for the time being while Alfonso is in London for a few days on business. He will join them there when he returns and later perhaps they will establish a more private residence. Alfonso had chosen to remain in France apparently because he desired to be near at hand in case the elections in Spain next month should go his way. Traveling as the Duke of Toledo, the monarch planned to motor down to Calais tonight to cross the channel to England. Among other things he will arrange to place the Infante Juan in a British naval school.

Albany, N. Y., April 21 — Severe earth tremors which shook nearly all of Eastern New York and parts of New England were believed today to have followed what is known to scientists as the St. Lawrence fault, which extends from Quebec province to the Hudson Valley. Houses were rocked and windows were rattled by two distinct shocks yesterday, which lasted for approximately twenty seconds. No serious damage was reported in any of the affected areas. Dr. Ralph B. Wilson, assistant director of the Dudley Observatory, predicted additional shocks within the next few days. He said that the quakes probably were caused by a slight slipping along the St. Lawrence fault, to which several tremors have been attributed in the past. Madrid — The republican government is moving rapidly to seize for the nation all property of the exiled King Alfonso which can be considered the property of the nation rather than of the man, Alfonso de Bourbon. A special judge has been appointed to investigate reports that valuable jewels and documents relating to the Moroccan wars have disappeared from a showcase at the royal palace which has been sealed by the government. Moscow —(A— Russia's communist socialist government, in the hope of speeding up production, is dropping socialism's principle of equal wages and is instituting piece work, generally associated with capitalistic systems. Under a new wage system to be introduced in factories, plants, collective farms, mines, railroads and the like May 1, the wages of workers will not be based upon the communistic theory of equal division but upon the capitalistic idea of rewarding individual efforts on a basis of skill and ability. The new system will be called "khozrachiot" which means literally "economic accounting," and as interpreted in the government decree means that the affected industries must henceforth take the responsibility of fulfilling contracts and adjudging wages without interference from trade unions. 1931-01-21.text: PARIS—(/)—The French-Italian naval construction truce, agreed upon last year after the two countries failed to adhere to the principal sections of the London naval treaty, was said to have ended. Rome dispatches stated that Italy is prepared from now, independent of its normal construction program, to build gun for gun with France.

MUNICH, Germany, Jan. 21. (AP) Seven of the eight Bavarian constables who were buried in an avalanche near here yesterday were found dead under the snow today. The eighth was still alive but severely injured.

ROME, Jan. 20 (Official sources say that Italy is prepared to build gun-for-gun with France in naval construction this year, since they assert that there appears to be little hope for renewing the construction truce which expired last month. This, it is said, is independent of Italy’s normal program. The suspended 1830 program provides for twenty-nine craft—twenty-two submarines and seven other units—and this will be started with the laying of the keels in a few months. France is said here to have completed her old naval program, and hereafter anything that she builds will be duplicated by Italy. PARIS, Jan. 20 (#)—The naval truce between France and Italy has come definitely to an end. It was learned in official quarters tonight and both countries now are free to engage in whatever warship building they wish. So far as French official circles are aware, the hopes for pourparlers between

MOSCOW, Jan. 20.—The Soviet press today turned shafts of ridicule against the American Congressman Hamilton Fish, Jr., in long editorials denouncing his recent report to the Congress of the United States on his investigation of communist activities in that country. The newspaper Izvestia calls the report a “skyscraper of insolence,” and the newspaper Pravda says of it, “Of all anti-Soviet documents in the recent past, the Fish report is the most impudent, insolent and ridiculous. It is ninety pages of absurdity based on forged documents.”

Bremen, Germany 1° — Max Schmeling, German boxer, sailed aboard the Europa today with his trainer, Max Machon, for New York. Schmeling said that he intended to go in training immediately for a series of exhibition bouts in Baltimore and 48 other American southern and southwestern cities, and Havana. “Whichever way my fight with Stribling turns out,” he said, “I shall come back to Germany even if I have to go out again in September to meet Carnera.” Denver—Regis College, a Jesuit institution, has discarded intercollegiate football. A decision to abandon the game was reached by the athletic board of control last night. Chicago—Art Shires, self-styled passed through on his way to Milwaukee to discuss his 1901 contract with the Brewers of the American Association baseball league. He said he would also sign for a short theatrical engagement.

Unable to agree unanimously on a specific remedy, the Wickersham commission and its eleven members embodied their views in an even dozen conflicting reports. All were laid before Congress today by President Hoover. That of the commission as a whole was a compromise, making no recommendation for repeal or major revision. 1931-03-16.text: NEW LONDON, Conn., March 15. —(P)—A master fleet of rum runners which for several days has been reported hovering outside the 12-mile limit of the New England coast last night attempted to outwit the coast guard. It ended maneuvers minus two vessels, six men and 1,700 sacks of liquor. One of the vessels was captured and the other sank in 120 feet of water. Constantly in motion to avoid the shifting searchlights of the coast guard, the fleet, the largest reported here in many months, sent decoys to lure the guards off the back routes. Unloaded ships dashed back and forth through the patrol boat lines. Where they broke through they were followed by heavily laden liquor vessels. At midnight the fisherman trawl, Notus, with three men and 700 bags of liquor aboard, was cornered and forced to beach on the shores of (Continued on Page 2, Col. 5.)

LONDON, March 15.—(AP)— Victoria station was heavily guarded this evening when King Alfonso of Spain arrived to visit his mother-in-law, Princess Beatrice, who is recovering from a serious illness. The king left Paris at noon, after spending the night there. The credentials of all persons approaching the railroad platform were carefully examined. Those who were not traveling and had no business there were denied admittance to the station. The Duke of York, the Marquise of Carisbrooke, as well as the personnel of the Spanish embassy, welcomed the monarch at the station. The Spanish ambassador had met Alfonso on his arrival at Dover and accompanied him to London. Immediately after his arrival the king, who is staying at the west end hotel, drove to Kensington Palace to see Princess Beatrice, who is the aunt of King George. The princess’ illness followed upon an accident in which she fell a

Heir To Silk Fortune Was One Of Wealthiest Men In Britain. London, March 16—Hugh Morrison, 62, one of the wealthiest men in all Britain, died here yesterday after a long illness. Morrison recently resigned his seat in parliament, which he held for Salisbury, Wiltshire, for thirteen years. He was a Unionist. Morrison's fortune was supposed to be several times the amount left him by his uncle in 1922—about $55,000,000. His own share of the huge family estate built upon the silk trade has been greatly enlarged by the addition of money left by others in the family.

LONDON, Mar. 16 (#)—King Alfonso of Spain had lunch with King George and Queen Mary at Buckingham Palace today after visiting his mother-in-law, the Princess Beatrice, whose illness brought him here, and paying formal calls at the home of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and at the foreign office. The king drove to Kensington Palace immediately on his arrival yesterday to see the Princess Beatrice, aunt of King George, who has been ailing for some weeks. The Spanish king, who came from Madrid by way of Paris, was accompanied in all his movements by a heavy police guard.

London, Mar. 16—(A P)— The majority of the MacDonald government in the House of Commons shrank to ten today when an amendment by the Conservatives to the section of the electoral reform bill dealing with university constituencies was rejected 178 to ... The amendment provided that certain university constituencies should be excluded from the general abolition of university constituencies for which the bill calls. The government was declared by observers to face a possibility of defeat tonight in a final division of the house at the end of debate. The section under argument involves the representation in parliament of certain universities, including Oxford and Cambridge, whose graduates are now permitted to vote and send a member of their own to parliament. The bill calls for abolishing these constituencies. Certain liberals and the full strength of the conservative party are opposed to t

LONDON, March 16,—(UP)— King Alfonso of Spain, who arrived last night apparently in unusually good health and smiling broadly despite the recent threats to his throne, was the object of extraordinary police precautions today. Two inspectors, several sergeants and 30 uniformed police officers assembled in the luggage room and dozens of plain clothes detectives mingled with the crowd at Victoria station upon the arrival of the king, who came here to visit his mother-in-law, Queen Beatrice, who is ill:

Londen, Mar. 16. (AP)—Throughout Europe women are raising their eyes from their hearths to the political arena, some with hope, some with determination and a considerable number with actual ambition. Even Asia has begun to open its political gates to wives and mothers. The house of representatives in Turkey passed a bill granting women equal franchise rights with men in elections for city, town, and village autonomous assemblies. The women of England and Germany have secured a far firmer position in politics than most of their sisters in neighboring lands. Though only in the past few years have they emerged from their harems during their way to parliament. Tokyo, March 16. (4P)—Police credited a dog with having saved the life of a high Soviet official from an assassin here today. The intended victim, Paul Anikeieff, Soviet commercial counsellor here and chief of the trade delegation handling the Japan-Russian fisheries dispute, was wounded dangerously. He probably would have been shot to death, police asserted, had not a dog belonging to a Japanese neighbor interfered. Nobukatsu Sato, 34, later surrendered, declaring he was responsible for the shooting. Anikeieff was leaving his home when the assassin leaped to the running board of his automobile and opened fire with a small automatic pistol. Two bullets struck the Russian before the dog leaped at the assassin. The man swung on the dog, sending two shots into its body, then returned to Anikeieff. The Russian received the last bullet in his chest. Physicians said Anikeieff probably would re
