Look over in England, the Labor Party was in but they had no money. They got out and a different bunch in, New York and Paris banks loaned ’em a half billion dollars. Big money only goes to the party that supports big money. I am entering no crusade to end it. I am just telling you how it is. You go ahead and change it. Yours, WILL ROGERS.

"LONDON: Aug. 79 (4).—Ramsay Macdonald was repudiated in his own constituency Saturday. The Labor party executive in the Seaham Harbor division of Durham passed a resolution demanding that he resign as the representative of the division in parliament. The resolution will be referred to a meeting of delegates at Wheatley Hill September 12, where it probably will be affirmed as a matter of course. Letter Defends Action, The action was taken in the face of a long letter from the prime minister in which he defended his action in heading the new national government and set forth his belief that only by sanctioning a small cut in the dole was he able to insure its continuance at all. "It is the war over again," he wrote, "I know the pressure which will be brought to bear upon me and my friends in Seaham, but I place myself unreservedly in their hands and am willing to do whatever they desire."

London.— (4) —Bolstered by a $400,000,000 credit from bankers of the United States and France, the national government today placed in the hands of committees its parliamentary program for restoring British finances to the right side of the ledger. “One committee was discussing the technical means to be used in balancing the budget and the other was concerned with the procedure to be used in pushing the measures through the House of Commons. Both will report to the cabinet Monday, when Prime Minister MacDonald returns from Scotland. At the same time the government put into effect the first of a number of drastic curtailments in expenditures. The salaries of 300,000 civil service employees were cut to effect an annual saving of $4,000,000. It was evident from yesterday's events that the entire conservative party and most of the liberals would line up in the Commons behind the government a

London, —- (UP) — Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald was asked to resign his membership in the labor party today. The labor party executive committee in the Seaham division at Durham, MacDonald's constituency, adopted a resolution asking the premier to resign from the party. MacDonald wrote his constituency: "I profoundly regret what has happened. If I can only serve you all in the long run I should cheerfully accept any sacrifice in doing it. It is the war over again." The premier apparently was referring to the break in the labor party during the World War, which he opposed. The resolution was interpreted also as a demand that MacDonald resign his seat in the House of Commons. It was anticipated that the premier, however, would delay action until the new national government was formed.

BOMBAY, Aug. 29.—(UP)—Mahatma Gandhi sailed for London and the second round table conference today bearing the blessings of millions of Indians. Unprecedented scenes occurred at the Bombay docks as the diminutive brown leader of the nationalist movement climbed up the gangway of the mail boat Rajputana clad in his customary loin cloth. Those of his followers who could see the little brown man standing on deck, protected by the ship's officers, fell prostrate before him. Hundreds who could not see Gandhi but who were told he had appeared also dropped to the ground. The Mahatma was garlanded with skeins of home spun yarn, symbol of the nationalist determination to free India from foreign made cloth. Gandhi, identified on his passport as a non-practicing barrister, requested accommodations in the lowest class on the ship and would not consider traveling first class. He will be treated as an

London, Aug. 29-7P—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald has been expelled from a Hampstead Labor party "for joining an anti-socialist government formed for the purpose of forcing through parliament anti-working class legislation," it was announced today. Mr. MacDonald has his private residence in Hampstead, a suburb of London, and has been a member of the party there for several years, holding his membership in the Labor party proper through that branch. His expulsion was decreed in a resolution passed by the party last night. Mr. and Mrs. Fred Lappe left Thursday for a visit with relatives at Petersburg and Figin, Neb.

NEW YORK, Aug. 29,—(UP)— Private bankers in America and France have extended to the British government a one year credit of $2,400,000,000 to be used in stabilizing the value of the pound sterling in the foreign exchange markets of the world. The American share of the credit, $200,000,000, was negotiated through J.P. Morgan & Co. and a nationwide group of more than 100 banks. None of it will be offered to the public. The French half, however, will consist of a $100,000,000 banking credit and a $100,000,000 British treasury loan, to be sold to the French public at an interest rate understood to be 4 1/2 percent.

1931-08-04.text: TOKIO, Aug. 4—(UP)—Miss Amy Johnson, British flier who left Manchuli at the Siberia-Manchuria west border today en route from London to Tokio, was forced down at Khailir, 100 miles east of Manchuli on the Chinese Eastern Railway. Any damage suffered was evidently superficial, for she announced she would proceed to Harbin tomorrow. Harbin is the junction point where the southern branch of the T-shaped Chinese Eastern Railway meets the East-and-West Line, in middle Manchuria.

BASEL, Switzerland, Aug. 3—(AP)—Directors of the bank for international settlements today voted to renew a maximum three months the bank's one-fourth share in the $100,000,000 rediscount credit to Germany, which expires at the end of this week. The Bank of France, the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York are equal subscribers to this credit. The directors also formally constituted a committee to inquire into the financial situation of Germany, setting the first meeting for next Saturday afternoon at Basel.

| By The Associated Press. ENGLAND, Ark., Aug. 3.—England, which was seriously affected by last winter’s drought, turned benefactor today. It was organizing a caravan of trucks to take food supplies to the unemployed at Henryetta, Okla., the scene recently of a demonstration not unlike those which took place here last winter. The relief expedition, consisting of six trucks filled by farmers and merchants with vegetables and various food supplies, was a feature of a celebration of the county’s recovery from the 1930 drought. Visitors were invited to come in and inspect the fields of green crops and the pantries that have been filled by bountiful gardens.

LONDON, (UP)—A spare loin cloth and two blankets form the luggage the Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, Indian leader, will bring with him to London early next month, the Daily Express said today. The inspiration for India’s independence movement, coming here for the second round table conference convening Sept. 15, will carry nothing else for his personal comfort, the Express said. The liner on which Gandhi is sailing to London will bring two goats to furnish him with goat milk, a major item in his diet. Gandhi plans an extensive tour of British industrial centers, the Express said. A large number of trade unions have invited Gandhi to visit them and explain his policies and methods.

‘Associated Press) Dublin, Irish Free State, Aug. 4.— Sir Harry Lauder, famed Scottish comedian, was 61 years old today and as energetic and cheerful as ever. He recently returned from a tour of South Athens.

COWES, Isle of Wight, Aug. 4— (AP) —Sir Thomas Lipton’s Shamrock V, unsuccessful challenger last year for the America’s cup, today won the king's cup in the royal yacht squadron’s regatta. No other boat was in sight as the green and white Shamrock came charging across the finish line. It was five minutes before Herbert Andreas Candida was seen coming in second place. The cup race, most important of the British yachting season, was open to boats of 60 feet or over and was a handicap event. Both Shamrock and Candida had a time allowance of five minutes, 52 seconds over the scratch boat Westward, a big schooner. His Majesty’s Britannia originally was entered to compete for second prize only but was withdrawn when the second mate was swept overboard yesterday and drowned.

PARIS, (UP).—Automatic beer delivered on the shilling-in-the-slot system is to be made available to the thirsty in London by a syndicate formed on the Riviera. Beer will be available all hours of the day and night, thus evading the London licensing restrictions. The sponsor of the scheme is a British naval officer. On a visit to Nice, he quenched his thirst at one of the automatic beer pumps there, so he decided similar pumps in the streets of London could make him a fortune.

1931-06-07.text: LONDON, June 7.— (Sunday) — (AP)—England was shaken from one end to the other at 1:30 this morning by an earthquake shock which sent thousands of persons rushing into the streets in alarm. No damage was reported but throughout the early hours of the morning messages poured into London from the Midlands, from South Wales and from the northern counties telling of the quake. Persons on night duty in buildings in the city of London distinctly felt them sway from the shock. The West Bromwich observatory recorded the tremor as of fairly long duration. Windows rattled throughout the city and many persons, rocked in their beds, hastily dressed and began inquiries. A report from Hertfordshire said the tremor woke the inhabitants there and it was accompanied by loud rumbling noise.

BOSTON, June 6.—-(AP)—Sir Hubert Wilkins’ submarine Nautilus, with which he plans to explore the North Pole by the undersea route, was 238 miles east of Cape Cod light at 8 a.m. (B.S.T.) today on her trip to England. From England the craft will go to Switzerland and thence to the polar regions. The Nautilus left Provincetown late Thursday night.

WASHINGTON, June 6. (AP) — Secretary Mellon will sail next week to spend his summer vacation in Europe. He will go first to England where his son Paul graduates from Clare College at Cambridge University. Later he will go to France where he and his son will join his daughter, Mrs. David Bruce, who has a cottage on the Riviera. The secretary expects to be away about six weeks.

CHEQUERS, Eng., June 6.— (AP)—Like four business men discussing the affairs of a great corporation, the head of the British and German governments met here today to talk over Germany's economic plight. - Chancellor Heinrich Bruening sought Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's assistance in sounding out Germany's creditors, including the United States, regarding postponement of some of the heavy reparations payments. Foreign Minister Julius Curtius and Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson talked together of the matters most intimately connected with their offices while Herr Bruening and Mr. MacDonald strolled arm in arm through the garden of the prime minister's estate. London, Manchester, Aberdeen and Cardiff were among the points reporting that the shocks were noted at 1:23 a.m. In the United Press office here, desks and telegraph instruments moved perceptibly. No casualties were reported.

WASHINGTON, June 6.—(U.P) Secretary of Treasury Mellon will sail next week for a protracted vacation in Europe. Mellon, like Secretary of State Stimson, who also is going abroad for the summer, is expected to talk with high foreign government officials. In England, where Mellon will visit first, he will return the visit of Gov. Montagu Norman of the Bank of England, who was here a few weeks ago.
LONDON, June 6 ()—Princess Marie Louise, cousin of King George, was seriously ill today. She was said to have a temperature of 104 after a chill.

1931-11-27.text: NEW YORK, Nov. 27. (AP)— Little Lya De Putti, Hungary's charming contribution to the cinemas of Germany, England and America, died early today. She was 32 years old. A chicken bone that lodged in her throat November 19 was the indirect cause of her death. The immediate cause was pneumonia, complicating a case of blood poisoning that followed the removal of the bone from her throat. She died at 1:05 a.m. after nearly 30 hours of unconsciousness.

BERLIN, Nov. 26 (®)—Police at Darmstadt announced today they had seized documents of a highly treasonable character in the homes of National Socialist leaders in Hesse and tonight the whole country was in a state of political excitement comparable to that in England after publication of the Zinovieff letters in 1927. The National Socialists assert that the documents are forgeries and that they knew nothing at all about them until police announced their discovery. One version was that the documents outlined a plan of campaign to be adopted when the party comes into power. It calls for confiscation of foodstuffs, establishment of public kitchens, confiscation of private property and compulsory labor for all gentile Germans above the age of 16. RIO DE JANEIRO, Nov. 26 (4)—Bert Hinkler, who once held the speed record for a flight from England to Australia, presumably was out over the South Atlantic tonight on his way from Natal to Africa, alone. First word that the flight had started came in an aero postal message from Natal that he had taken off there yesterday for Dakar, Senegal, French West Africa, and had not been heard from since the start. Captain Hinkler made the Australian flight in 15 days three years ago, and the mark stood until Charles Kingsford-Smith covered the distance in 10 days last year. In October the captain flew from New York to Kingston, Jamaica, in 17 hours 45 minutes, a record for that distance, and came on down across the Caribbean to Natal. Should he succeed in reaching Dakar from there he would be the first man to fly across the South Atlantic from west to east. The distance is something more than 1,50

LONDON, Nov. 27 UP—Major General Sir David Bruce, sometimes called the Sherlock Holmes of science, died today while funeral services were being held for his wife, who died on Monday. He was 76. In 1903 he went to Uganda to direct an investigation of sleeping sickness, and five years later went back again to continue the investigation. For three years he directed an investigation of Mediterranean fever, and in 1911 went to Nyassaland to investigate the connection, if any, between diseases of wild animals, domestic animals and humans.

- LONDON, Nov. 26 (4)—Customs duties on agricultural imports are next in line in the new tariff policy launched by the British government this week with the levy of 50 per cent duties on certain classes of manufactured articles. On Monday, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald informed the House of Commons today, a financial resolution will be presented to authorize an agricultural customs levy.

Paris, Nov. 27.—Japanese official quarters here today reported receipt of information from Tientsin that there were “rumors” that American, British and French troops were engaged with the Japanese and Chinese in severe fighting there yesterday. | Dakar, Africa, Nov. 27.—-dLPi—Bert Hinkler completing the first west to east airplane crossing of the South Atlantic, landed at Bathurst, on the coast of British Guiana, this morning. His flight from Natal, Brazil, took 22 hours. Hinkler took off from Bathurst and landed at St. Louis, Senegal, 200 miles northward, today. Hinkler, when he left Natal, intended to land between Dakar and Bissau, in Portuguese Guinea. Winds blew him off his course and forced him to make a difficult landing at Bathurst, on the small island of St. Mary's in the mouth of the Gambia river. Hinkler refueled at Bathurst and started for St. Louis, where there are greater facilities. He intended to start for Port Etienne at dawn.

1931-04-05.text: Bucharest, Romania—(®)— Prime Minister George S. Mironescu resigned this morning with his whole cabinet because of parliamentary difficulties. Nicholas Titulescu, former foreign minister, is expected to be summoned from London to form a new government. * The government of Premier Mironescu took office in October last year. From the outset its fate was considered doubtful. It had hardly been formed and approved by King Carol when its early collapse was predicted. Nicholas Titulescu, who is expected to be called from London to form a new cabinet, is the permanent representative from Romania to the council and assembly of the League of Nations. He was president of the eleventh assembly of the league last year.

New York, April 4. (A?)—Coast guard headquarters today received a message saying the British freighter Symor had been sunk off Nantucket in a collision with the coast guard cutter Legare. The information came from the Legare. The collision, the cutter reported, took place at 8:10 p. m. yesterday. No further details were received, but it was assumed by coast guard officials that the cutter had taken on the crew of the freighter and was making for its base at New London, Conn.

WINDSOR, England, April 6. U.P—A slight renewal of King George's laryngitis complaint caused some concern throughout Britain today, but was described by the King’s physicians as not at all serious. The King was said to be progressing as well as could be expected in view of the old trouble which almost cost his life two years ago. He was attended by Sir Stanley Hewett, his physician, a local physician, Dr. H. L. Martin, and a nurse—all of whom attended him in 1928 when he was seriously ill. King George passed a “fairly comfortable” night, but was not expected to leave his room today due to the weather. His Easter activities were strictly curtailed. He has been able to transact state business, but was forced to absent himself from Divine services yesterday.

|| LONDON, April 4—(UP)—Several thousand Scotsmen have been giving money away for years. But they didn't know it. Many tearful scenes are reported to have occurred when the thrifty hundreds read a newspaper report that they had been paying 32 cents for 26 cents worth of whisky, and Scotch whisky at that. The difficulty arises, according to reports, from violations of the weights and measures act of 1489 which set the imperial measure standard. An average half-gill of whisky in Glasgow costs 32 cents. A “glass” costs the same, but actually contains only 26 cents worth of spirits. The seller is within the law if the buyer calls for a “glass of white” and gets it. The difference was that the Scotsmen didn’t know this. They do now. It is reported the word “glass” may be dropped from their vocabulary.

LONDON, April 4. — (INS)—An erupting volcano on Kuchierabe island, Kagoshima prefecture in southern Japan, today drove hundreds of villagers on its slopes from their homes in terror. Messages from Osaka indicated that the dormant volcano, becoming suddenly active, shot tons of hot ashes and lava into the air. Communication facilities were disrupted almost immediately.

FLORENCE, Italy, April 4—(4)—The “explosion of the sacred cart,” a holy Saturday ceremony which began six centuries ago, was again carried out at noon today in the presence of thousands of Florentines, Americans and British, packed into the square in front of the cathedral. Four white oxen, with gilded horns and hoofs, and with brilliant crimson blankets, drew the cart, which, decorated with flags and flowers, was in reality a moving arsenal of fireworks, rockets, pinwheels and the like. A workman connected to it a wire, the other end of which led to a point just above the high altar of the cathedral. There an artificial pigeon carrying a skyrocket was slid onto the wire. When today’s high mass arrived at the “Gloria” part and the bells rang out, a clergyman lighted the skyrocket. '* Associated Press LISBON, April 4.—A military rebellion was reported in government circles tonight to have broken out at Funchal, on the island of Madeira. The people were said to be supporting the movement which appeared to be of political character. Funchal is the capital and chief port of the Madeira islands, a Portuguese Atlantic group about 525 miles from Lisbon and about 360 miles off.

BY UMS Frew FUNCHAL, Madeira, April 6. — A military movement against the Portuguese government headed by President General Antonio de Fragoso Carmona was in control of Funchal today and in open rebellion against the cabinet at Lisbon. Striking at the dictatorial government which has been faced with latent unrest in various sections of the Portuguese army for months, the military garrison here took over the administration from the high commissioner, Colonel Silva Leal. The new governor also was deposed. The former officials of the government were detained and the garrison leaders announced they would not accept the Portuguese government's orders until a new cabinet is formed to reestablish public liberties. 1931-09-08.text: London——King George's offer to dip into his income for a quarter of a million dollars in order to help tide John Bull over his financial embarrassment made a favorable impression today on members of parliament gathered for the first special session since the war. The willingness of the Prince of Wales to contribute $50,000 income himself to lighten the load of the new national government and that of other members of the royal family to help in accordance with their means were no less well received. The king wrote Prime Minister MacDonald that, in spite of the fact that drastic economies were made after the war, he was of the opinion that “by the exercise of the most rigid economy it should be possible to reduce the civil list by £50,000.” “I am to say that the queen and other members of the royal family who are in receipt of parliamentary grants are all desirous that reductions of these

GENEVA, SWITZERLAND, SEPT. 7. (AP).—Delegates representing Great Britain, France, Japan and Spain today asked the League of Nations assembly, which opened its twelfth session this morning, to invite Mexico to become a member of the league. The assembly will act on the request tomorrow. This formality indicated that Mexico has made known her wish to become a member, but the preliminary negotiations were conducted so quietly that today’s development came as something of a surprise. There must be a special invitation if Mexico is to join, for that country was not included in the original list of nations nominated for membership in 1919. The omission was generally attributed to the fact that at that time President Wilson was not on good terms with the Mexican government.

LONDON, SEPT. 8. (AP).-Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Arthur Henderson, political allies for thirty years, turned on one another in debate today as parliament began its special “economy” session. In the topsy-turvy line-up of the new political organization, Conservatives and Liberals cheered MacDonald and the labor members on whose side he fought for many years jeered and howled as he revealed step by step the course he had followed in trying to stave off financial disaster. With all the vehemence and eloquence he could command the Premier insisted his course was the only one possible, Henderson, attacking the government's method of dealing with the financial situation, asserted formation of the so-called national government was not necessary because the United States and France in their own interests never would have dared to let Great Britain's credit fail.

London, Sept. 7. ()— King George announced tonight in a letter to Prime Minister MacDonald that he wanted a reduction of 50,000 pounds (about $250,000) in the annual income paid by the government to the crown. The Prince of Wales also informed the Prime Minister that he intended to contribute 50,000 pounds to the national funds. The King said all other members of the royal family who receive Parliamentary grants desired cuts, as their contribution to Great Britain in the nation's time of financial emergency. The King has a civil list totaling about $2,350,000 annually. His Majesty has one other source of income, his revenues from the Duchy of Lancaster, which in 1929 were $345,000.

LONDON (UP).-—The House of Commons met in extraordinary session at 2:45 p.m. Tuesday to decide Great Britain’s immediate financial future. Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald, who will ask a vote of confidence to enable his coalition government to proceed with its drastic economy program, arrived accompanied by his son, Malcolm, and his daughters, Ishbel and Sheila. They were loudly cheered by vast throngs on the route from Downing Street to the Houses of Parliament.

——— — Detroit, Sept. 8 (4P)—Miss England II, the world’s fastest hydroplane, lay at the bottom of the Detroit River today and with it were the hopes of Kaye Don, Great Britain’s speed ace, to win the Harmsworth trophy race this year from the veteran Gar Wood. With one heat safely won and needing only another victory to capture the trophy that Wood has held since 1920 when he won it in England, Don was eliminated from further competition in this year’s international race by a double share of ill luck. As Don was swinging wide on the second turn at the lower end of the course on the first lap, his craft struck the wash of Wood's Miss America IX and turned over. Don and his two mechanics, Roy Platford and Dick Garner, were not hurt. Boats Beat Gun, Disqualified. DETROIT, Sept. 7 (#)—The jinx that has hounded every effort of foreign challengers to recapture the Harmsworth speedboat trophy from Gar Wood eliminated Kaye Don of England today. His challenging craft, Miss England II, fastest speedboat in the world, lay at the bottom of the river tonight, having turned over on a curve two miles from the start. Don and his crew escaped unhurt. As if this bad luck were not enough, it was announced almost as the craft foundered that Don had beaten the starting gun by seven seconds and automatically eliminated himself from further competition in this year's event. At the same time it was announced that Gar Wood, driving his Miss America IX, also had beaten the gun to be disqualified. London, Sept. 8.—Rubies, diamonds, platinum and gold, such as the Queen of Sheba is supposed to have worn when she visited King Solomon, have been brought to London by Frank Payter, big-game hunter, from mines which he believes were sources of the queen's wealth. Payter found the gems and treasure in a hidden cavern in unexplored country 320 miles due west of Addis Abeba, Abyssinia. He intends to organize a new expedition within a few months to go back and get what he left behind. “I am sure it is one of the sources from which the Queen of Sheba drew her great wealth,” he said. His story of the discovery was almost as fascinating as the gems themselves, sparkling through their natural roughness. An old Arab, he said, gave an English mining engineer a map in 1930 which the engineer showed to Payter. The two men worked out the directions and discovered the treasure. There has been frequent

1931-06-14.text: New York, June 13.—(—New chies in New York and Long Island sputted detectives anew Saturday to solve the mystery of Starr Faithfull's death. Reports were current that appeals for aid would be sent to England's Scotland Yard. A ragged coat, containing a telegram tucked in one sleeve, was picked from the surf at Long Beach, from miles from the point at which the body of the 25-year-old girl was found last Monday. Police, working on a theory that Starr may have been beaten and drowned by persons who wanted her out of the way, began a check-up to determine if the coat was hers. Meanwhile, they guarded the contents of the telegram closely. Another link in the mystery chain was kept a secret, it was a document which police took Friday night from the home of Stanley Faithfull, a clothing manufacturer and stepfather of Starr. It was rushed to District Attorney Edwards at Riverhead, L.I. by plane

(By the Associated Press.) Germany has declared what amounts to a general moratorium of banking operations, closing all banks except the Reichsbank until Thursday and perhaps longer. It was a precautionary measure, a temporary effort to tide the institutions over until help comes from abroad. The world bank is willing to renew a $100,000,000 credit due on Thursday and it is understood the bank of France and the federal reserve bank of New York which participated in the credit also will grant an extension of their part of the total. The Bank of England has not yet ruled. Reactions Elsewhere- Reactions outside of Germany to the collapse of the Darmstaedter Und National bank has caused the temporary closing of all the banks in Hungary, and suspension of the Mercur bank at Vienna, a subsidiary of the Darmstaedter. At Jassy, Romania, the Dacia bank has closed with a $1,000,000 deficit. Arthur

Paris, June 13. (P)—Paul Doumer was inaugurated president of France today and his first official act was to continue in office the complete cabinet of Premier Pierre Laval. He did this in the face of a strong effort to force him to unload Aristide Briand, the foreign minister. Whispers that Premier Laval would change several ministers in the cabinet after Doumer asked him to remain as premier threatened trouble for the new administration at the outset of its seven-year term. The threat against the government is not yet over, for that chronic enemy of Briand, Louis Marin, informed the premier he had signatures enough to overthrow him when the government presents itself to the chamber of deputies today unless Briand is dropped. Doumer’s ceremony of inauguration, held at the Elysee palace, was over in half an hour. The incoming president rode with Premier Laval from his residence, the littl

SHANGHAI, July 14—Joseph Le Brix and Marcel Doret, who left Le Bourget airdrome, Paris, early Sunday on a projected 6,000-mile non-stop flight to Tokyo, were reported in Irkutsk dispatches today to have been forced down at Nizhne Udinsk, Siberia, 2,400 miles short of their goal. Nizhne Udinsk is 310 miles west of Irkutsk and about 3,600 miles from Paris. Dispatches said one of the fliers received an injured knee and that their plane, the Hyphen, was damaged. Whether the man injured was Le Brix or Doret, or their mechanic, was not stated. The forced landing apparently meant conclusion of the flight, or the fliers were quoted as having asked Russian aviation authorities for aerial transportation back to Moscow. BERLIN, July 14—Prospects of a heavyweight title match in September between Max Schmeling and Primo Carnera went glimmering today as Schmeling’s oculist warned him he must refrain from boxing or training at least two or three months because of eye trouble. Schmeling, who returned yesterday to his home here after whipping Young Stribling in a title defense match in Cleveland July 3, complained of pain in and about his left eye. He said after the match that Stribling had stuck his thumb in the eye in the fight. Schmeling consulted specialists today and was told that he must rest completely for at least two months and probably more. While the champion was aboard ship heading homeward, Joe Jacobs, his manager, agreed in New York to the advice.
ROME. —(JP)— An air joy ride of 20,000 miles over eleven European countries has convinced Captain Frank Hawks, American speed ace, that the United States has much to learn from Europe on flying.

BERLIN, June 13. (P)—The belief prevailed in political circles here tonight that the way has been paved for a victory for Chancellor Bruening and his government next Tuesday. The belief was based on the apparent result of Bruening’s talks with party leaders after his return from Neudeck, where he conferred with President Paul Von Hindenburg, and by the warning given in the Reichsbank decision to raise the discount rate two per cent. Meeting Slated On Tuesday the Reichstag committee of elders will meet to decide whether to yield to the national socialist and communist demands for an immediate convocation of parliament or to support the government's contention that a session of the legislative body would be disastrous at this time. WASHINGTON, July 14 (AP)— Albert B. Fall's jail sentence of a year was changed today to a year and a day to enable him to serve his time in a western prison. The attorney general is expected to designate the prison where the former secretary of the interior will serve. The clerk of the District of Columbia supreme court will then send a warrant of commitment to the United States Marshal in New Mexico or Texas, and he will take Fall to prison. The department of justice has asked the warden of the New Mexican penitentiary if Fall could serve his time there and the warden replied that he could. Frank Hogan, Fall’s attorney, today moved before Justice Bailey in the District of Columbia supreme court, that the sentence of a year in the District of Columbia jail be amended to a year and a day in a penitentiary. Scotland Yard In the face of repeated denials by officials, the Daily Sketch said Scotland Yard had been introduced into the mystery by New York police and that it was conducting a search for certain friends of the girl of both sexes. Two of them already had been interviewed, it was said, and their statements might be sent to America, The investigation was said to be under the direction of Detective Inspector Barker, head of the "narcotic squad," and Divisional Inspector Hester, An unnamed physician was quoted in an interview by the Daily Express as saying that he saved Miss Faithfull’s life on the same visit after she had taken an overdose of a sedative drug. CHICAGO, June 1%. -- (UP) — Philip R. Clarke will be president and Charles G. Dawes, ambassador to England, will be honorary chairman of the $350,000,000 Central Republic Bank and Trust Company, it was announced today as the merger of the Central Trust Company of Illinois and the National Bank of the Republic into the one new institution was completed. Merger of the two Loop banks was announced last Monday at the same time the Foreman banks were taken over by the First National Bank in the biggest financial upheaval in the city's history. Officials of the new banks as well as of other Loop institutions agreed today that all excitement caused by the mergers had passed.

WEIHAIWEI, - June 13 —()— Handicapped by continuing bad weather the O S & Pigeon and other surface vessels today made little progress in the task of salvaging the sunken British submarine Poseidon which was sent to the bottom early this week in collision with a Chinese merchantman. The Pigeon is using her compressed air apparatus to pump water out of the hulk so that she may be raised. Some of them who escaped from a forward compartment by using the Davis "lung" after the submersible had been sunk, today had high praise for one of their non-commissioned officers who claimed the crew and organized their escape, a task which required much skill, knowledge and presence of mind.

PEIPING, June 12 (AP)— Bandits who abducted the Rev. Bert Nelson, American missionary, last October have decided to hold him indefinitely while he teaches them English, a letter from the captive which reached friends here today indicates. His captors are demanding 360,000 feet of telephone wire, a grand piano, a battery of printing presses and a quantity of airplane thermometers as ransom, but these demands are not taken seriously. The missionary’s friends believe they have been put forward only as a pretext for keeping the clergyman in their hands.
Southampton, Eng., June 13—The new liner Empress of Britain has set a new record of four days, 19 hours, 8 minutes, for the crossing from Quebec to Cherbourg, France.

SAN DIEGO, June 13,—(UP)—In broken English and with pantomime that the court sought vainly to restrain, Alexander Pantages denied yesterday that his conduct was improper when he was left alone in a hotel with Lydia Nitto, who claims to be only 17 years old. Pantages denies each allegation that Miss Nitto had made. He claimed he had not sought the girl's company and protested that he urged her to leave him and rejoin others of the party. "She stayed in her chair talking to me,” he testified. “She told me her father was in San Quentin prison and that she was a poor girl down on her luck. The door of the room was open all the time. “Finally I said: ‘Listen, little lady, you better go and join your friends.' She left. Later, Jesse Shreve returned and we checked out and went to another hotel.” Pantages was called in his own defense against charges of contributing to the delinquency of a minor

COVENTRY, Eng., June 15. —{UR—The next war, if it should come, ‘will be the final and absolute end of civilization.” Lady Cynthia Mosley told Boy Scouts and Girl Guides at a meeting last night. Lady Cynthia said a new explosive called by the spectacular name of “the dew of death,” had been invented. It was so powerful, she said, that a spoonful could destroy a city. “This recently invented ‘dew of death’ would kill a million persons if a spoonful were dropped on a city,’ Lady Cynthia told the boys and girls. “A bomb carried in a lady's handbag would be sufficient to raze London.”

(By Associated Press) LONDON, June 13.—Larry Gains, heavyweight champion of Canada, tonight knocked out Phil Scott, English heavyweight, in the second round of a scheduled 15 round bout billed for the “British heavyweight championship.”

1931-07-07.text: (By The Associated Press) Negotiations already have started in Paris for a conference of experts to work out the technical details of applying President Hoover’s moratorium plan, and the British government has renewed its invitation for a conference of the world powers chiefly concerned. In all the capitals of Europe and at Washington the agreement between France and the United States was received with great satisfaction. London is of the opinion that much remains to be done, and Rome has announced that it is ready to participate in any conferences regarding the operation of the plan. The German government in a proclamation has promised that the money released by the moratorium will be used only to assist the country’s economic recovery, warning the German people that they must economize now as never before. LONDON July 7,—A renewed invitation to a conference in London of the powers chiefly concerned in the operation of the Hoover moratorium plan was issued today by Prime Minister MacDonald. Mr. MacDonald did not specify the date of the conference nor its exact composition, but Paris advices late tonight said the British ambassador there had informed the French government the meeting was planned for next week and would be a conference of experts rather than political leaders. Speaking before the House of Commons, the prime minister recalled that the British government last week proposed such a conference to France and the United States "in order to hasten agreement over the Hoover proposal." Both governments, the prime minister said, expressed their willingness to attend such a meeting. If direct negotiations have now resulted in an agreement in principle between the United States and France

Berlin remains in third place; Chicago is fourth and Paris fifth, although the metropolitan population of the French capital is larger than that of Chicago. The five leading cities on the basis of new census figures, are: Greater London 8,202,818 New York City 6,981,915 Chicago 3,376,438 Paris (within walls) 2,871,039 While the cities themselves have added startling growth, the growth of the metropolitan areas is even more significant. For instance, Chicago suburbs are growing at a rate far higher than that of the city proper. PARIS, July 7. (UP)—The “Hoover cocktail” was on sale at Harry's New York bar here today in commemoration of the war debt holiday agreement. The drink, Harry said, is guaranteed to revive anyone after a depressing night. It includes French champagne, Italian vermouth, English gin, German schnapps, and Belgian Genever. The cocktail was said to possess strong merits as a “pick me up.”

LONDON, (P. This still is the largest city in the world, and easily so, Census figures, made public Monday, proved it. In London and the “outer ring,” there are 8,202,818 residents. Greater New York, runner-up in size, has 6,981,917. That puts London 1,220,901 to the good. New York, however, is taking on residents at a faster rate than London. The American metropolis added 1,361,869 during the last ten years. London's increase in that period was 822,619. The census taken April 26 showed the British Isles more populous than ever before. The total is 44,790,485, England and Wales together aggregate 39,947,931 of whom 20,809,087 are females, and 19,138,844 males, a difference of 1,670,243.

SEATTLE, July 7.—(U.P.)—Reginald Robbins announced today that he and H. S. Jones would be unable to leave until tomorrow for Fairbanks, Alaska, on the first leg of their proposed non-stop refueling flight to Tokyo, Japan. Robbins said he had received a message from Telegraph Creek, British Columbia, saying his and Jones’ refueling plane had been forced down there while attempting to reach Fairbanks.

Waupaca, Wis. July 7--(P)--Edward Riske, 48, today was held in jail here without bond for trial at the September sessions of circuit court on charges of murder in connection with the deaths of Louis Hoffman, 32, and Henry Kopitzke, 46, New London laborers, who succumbed to poison at a barn dance June 20. Riske, reputed suitor of Mrs. Hoffman, 35, pleaded not guilty and waived preliminary hearing at arraignment before Justice of the Peace F. A. Archibald. The murder warrant was issued by District Attorney Lloyd Smith at the conclusion of an inquest into the deaths yesterday when testimony revealed a close association between Riske and Mrs. Hoffman. Says Attentions Unwelcome Mrs. Hoffman, widow of Louis, drowned herself in Wolf River near her home Sunday, a few hours after she had been questioned concerning the deaths. London—Keen satisfaction and hope for the future were the dominant reactions today to acceptance of the Hoover moratorium plan by France. Government officials, financial leaders and plain citizens—all of whom have followed the course of the negotiations with unusual interest—expressed relief that the plan had been placed in operation while recognizing that much remains to be done to place Germany on her feet. - The Times echoed the opinion of many that the war debt holiday had averted a serious crisis in Germany which might have spread through all Europe if not the world.

1931-02-03.text: London, Feb. 3—The former Helen Vivien Gould, American heiress who as the youthful bride of the fifth Baron Decies dazzled English society, died here at dawn today of a heart attack which developed from jaundice. She was 39 years old and had been ill three weeks. Death came in a London nursing home. Besides her husband, who has had a famous career in the army, she left three children, a son and two daughters. The granddaughter of Jay Gould, whose railroad manipulations made him a money king of the post-Civil War period, Lady Decies came to be known in England for the spectacles she sometimes presented society, her penchant for the unexpected and as a lavish charming hostess.

CHATHAM, Eng., Feb. 3.—(AP)— Six men were injured, one critically, when an explosion of undetermined origin wrecked the internal combustion engine of the submarine V-1, one of the largest undersea boats in the British navy, today. She had left Sheerness for a trial run after reconditioning and had gone 20 miles on the surface to the Thames estuary when the blast occurred.

Daytona Beach, Fla., Feb. 3. (?)— High wind and poor visibility on the ocean speedway here today prevented Captain Malcolm Campbell, British, from making an official attempt on the world’s land speed record of 231 miles an hour, but in an exhibition run he reported attaining a speed of 260 miles an hour. He made the exhibition run over the nine-mile course at an average speed of 194 miles an hour, and before entering the measured mile, he said he attained the higher speed. His machine slipped out of gear, he said, and he was forced to coast over the mile in neutral. A cold wind blew out of the north all day and whipped white sand from the dunes out over the course. Campbell said he couldn't tell whether he was on his regular course or up near the soft sand close to the dunes. The visibility also was extremely bad and a light drizzle of rain fell at intervals. NEW YORK, Feb. 3 (4).--The severest cold wave of the season swept over New York state and New England last night and made this morning's thermometers read as low as 35 degrees below zero. Many cities experienced the coldest temperatures in the memory of old inhabitants. Pittsfield, Mass. led the plunge with a mark of 35 degrees below zero. Northfield, Vt., reported 22 degrees below. Rochester, N. H., shivered at 23 below and Lowell, Mass., with 18 below, suffered the coldest February 3 since 1885.

Kingston, Jamaica, Feb. 3 (UP)—The Prince of Wales landed from the S.S. Oropesa today amid a great popular demonstration by thousands of persons gathered to welcome the first British heir ever to visit Jamaica. The Prince and his brother, Prince George, landed at 12:15 P.M.

Today at Daytona Beach, Weather Permitting. DAYTONA BEACH, Via, (P) Having attained an unofficial speed of 240 miles an hour today, Captain Malcolm Campbell, veteran British race car driver, announced tonight he would make his official trial for the world’s land speed record tomorrow, beach and weather conditions permitting. In one tremendous burst of speed, he drove his trim Bluebird racing car over the nine-mile stretch of beach at a rate of approximately four miles a minute, and afterwards declared he was "tickled to death" with the machine's performance. As Campbell removed his goggles and climbed out of the huge racing car, a crowd of spectators gathered about him and cheered. Although Campbell's speed today exceeded by approximately nine miles an hour the present world’s official land speed record of 231, it was not officially recognized as it was not officially timed. LONDON, Feb. 3.—Lady Decies, the former Helen Vivien Gould, daughter of the late George Jay Gould of New York, died here today following a brief illness. She had been suffering from heart trouble for the past few weeks but her condition did not arouse any anxiety until yesterday when she was transferred from her home to a London nursing home. Last night it was announced that she was dangerously ill. The end came today when her heart suddenly collapsed. Lady Decies is survived by her husband, the fifth Baron Decies, one son and two daughters. Lord Decies was former press censor for Ireland and aide to the Duke of Connaught. They were married in 1911. Lady Decies was only 38 years old. At the time of her marriage to Lord Decies in New York she was just 19. She was the fourth child of the late George Jay Gould.

ALLAHABAD, India, Feb. 2. After sounding a call to his followers to continue their civil disobedience campaign against Great Britain, Mahatma Gandhi, frail 96-pound nationalist leader, suddenly went into trance-like silence today lasting 24 hours. Not even his favorite spinning wheel, at which he spends so many hours, could draw him from his 24-hour “sacrament.” His friends say it gives him a chance to meditate, (Continued on Page 2, Col. 1.)

MOSCOW, Sept. 1 (#—Amy Johnson, British woman flier, on the way home from Tokyo by plane, landed today at Irkutsk and took off again for Sverdlovsk after half an hour's rest.

LONDON, England, Sept. 8.—(AP) Ramsay MacDonald's new government won its first battle tonight by gaining a vote of confidence from the House of Commons with a majority of 69. The House which convened in special session today, voted 309 to 259 in support of the new MacDonald cabinet made up of members from the Labor, Conservative and Liberal Parties. Voting with the majority were 12 Labor members including Prime Minister MacDonald, Chancellor Snowden, J. H. Thomas and four other ministers. All the Conservatives and Liberals supported the government as did three Independent members. The vote came after an all-day debate which started with an oratorical duel between the Prime Minister and Arthur Henderson, his old Labor colleague and now leader of the opposition. LONDON, Sept. 9. —Attempts to incite riots outside the houses of parliament were curbed by a thousand police early today after Communists and other agitators unsuccessfully harangued a large crowd to demonstrate against the coalition government, which won a vote of confidence last night. Several groups attempted to invade the parliament buildings and were repulsed by police. Several policemen were dragged from their horses. Scuffles were numerous, a score of persons were hurt, and a dozen arrested. The demonstration followed a vote of confidence obtained by the national government headed by Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald by the comfortable majority of 69 votes. The prime minister received a deputation from the unemployed at the House of Commons and listened to their suggestions for meeting the present situation. LONDON, Sept. 9.—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald, speeding the new coalition government's drastic financial reform program, introduced the national economy bill in parliament today. The bill was given its first reading in the House of Commons, and is scheduled to be read the second time at Friday's session. The legislation was designed to provide the government with a quasi-dictatorial emergency measure for rushing through its financial program. It would ‘authorize making orders in council to effect economies in expenditure and improvements of arrangements for meeting such expenditure.’ Meanwhile, the cabinet met for final consideration of the supplementary budget proposals which Philip Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer, is to introduce in Commons tomorrow. It was understood that Snowden would reveal a deficit of 96,000,000 pounds sterling ($465,560,000) in presenting the proposals
| LYMPNE, England, Sept. 9. - Amy Johnson reached here today from Berlin, completing a round trip flight in her own plane to Tokyo.

SEEKS DICTATORIAL POWERS, LONDON, Sept. 9.—(AP)— Minister Ramsay MacDonald, getting down to the business of forcing his economy program through parliament, today presented to the House of Commons a “national economy bill” which would empower the cabinet to govern by orders in council issued by the king without the sanction of parliament. He explained none of its provisions, and the house passed it on formal first reading. The labor party will marshal its strongest opposition: Stanley Baldwin as leader of the government in the house and the prime minister’s righthand man then proposed resolutions that would give the government additional emergency powers, enabling it to monopolize all the rest of the session to the exclusion of members’ bills under the so-called ten minute debate rule. His resolutions also would provide for disposal of the necessary business discussion by midnight in the

WASHINGTON, Sept. 9. — The Nation pauses today to pay honor to Clara Barton — New England philanthropist, school teacher, nurse, and organizer of the American Red Cross. President Hoover led the rest of the country in a speech congratulating the Red Cross on the 50th anniversary of its formation in this country. Born on Christmas Day, 1821, in the little town of Oxford, Mass., Clara Barton began early her work of aiding humanity. In her own home she struggled for two years to aid her brother to restore himself to health. She taught school and various free schools in New Jersey. When the Civil War began, Clara Barton resigned as a clerk in the government and entered the hospital service. She tramped over the battlefields of Antietam, Fredericksburg and Cedar Mountain, feeding the hungry and binding the wounds of the injured. 1931-02-10.text: LONDON, Feb. 10. (AP) — An ominous picture of the next war waged by airplanes equipped with poison gas to wipe out non-combatant populations was drawn today by Arthur Henderson, British foreign secretary. Speaking before 3,000 persons at Queen’s Hall in the first of a series of addresses intended to mold public opinion in preparation for the forthcoming International disarmament conference, the labor minister pleaded for support of his government’s hope of substantial arms reductions.

LONDON, (AP)—The governor of New Zealand today cabled the dominion secretary that known deaths in the earthquake there last week so far number 212 and the injured 954, but the casualty list still is imminent.

LONDON, Feb. 9—()—King George today appointed the Earl of Bessborough, a distinguished Irish peer, to be governor-general of Canada succeeding Lord Willingdon, who has been named vice-roy of India. The announcement caused surprise, for Lord Bessborough's name had not hitherto been mentioned in connection with the post. The date of his departure for Canada was not announced.

AMI Fla. Feb. 9—(AP)—The local radio station here announced tonight that all crew members of the steamship British Chancellor, which went aground off the coast of Colombia at Gallinas Point today, were picked up from small boats by the steamer Tekoa. The message was received here from Santa Marta, Colombia. The crew was reported to have been 125 in number and the Tekoa was said to have arranged to land them at Colon, C. Z.

Plymouth, £n7., Feb. 10. (AP). — “Lawrence of Arabia” that romantic figure who is now known as plain aircraftsman. Show appeared today as one of the heroes of the recent disaster here when nine men were killed in the plunge of a ‘staplane. At the court of inquiry Shaw turned up as one of the principal witnesses and it was revealed that he played a prominent role in the rescue of members of the plane's crew who escaped death in the crash. Because of his military achievement in Arabia Colonel Thomas E. Lawrence might have held a high government position, but in 1927 he suddenly decided to end the brilliant career he had begun and had his name legally changed to Thomas Edward Shaw. He was assigned as an enlisted man to the air service. Today he flitted in and out of the session of inquiry, which was private, with every attempt to escape publicity. Few details of his rescue work leaked from

LONDON, Feb. 9—(AP)—The MacDonald labor government tonight obtained a majority of 45 votes in carrying the agricultural marketing bill on second reading by 258 against 213 votes. The bulk of the liberal party voted with the laborites, assuring their victory in the division. It was the second time within a week that Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald had beaten his conservative opposition with the aid of the liberals.

TOKIO, Feb. 10.—(UP)—Forty-two persons were believed drowned when the Japanese liner Kikusui Maru sank after colliding with the French liner Porthos at 7:40 p.m. yesterday. The collision occurred in Akashi channel near Kobe, during a dense fog and blizzard. The Kikusui Maru sank almost immediately after the crash. Fifty-two were rescued and landed at Tokio. The Kikusui Maru plies between ports of the Inland Sea. The Porthos was leaving Kobe en route to Shanghai when the boats collided. All those reported missing were Japanese. The blizzard held responsible for the wreck is general throughout Japan. Snow storms were exceptionally severe in Tokio.

By ERICK KEYERS (United Press Staff Correspondent) BERLIN, Feb. 10.—The chief opposition parties, led by the 107 Fascist deputies, declared a boycott on the Reichstag today and evacuated the chamber in a body a few minutes prior to the foreign policy declaration of Dr. Julius Curtius. The foreign minister, who had been prepared to meet attacks of the opposition, read his speech indirectly demanding revision of the Versailles Treaty to a chamber dominated by pro-government deputies. Curtius announced Germany has no intention of destroying the Young reparations plan because international law binds her to the plan. “However, we never guaranteed our ability to fulfill the reparations obligations,” he said. “There has been a thorough revolution of world economic relations since the Hague reparations conference but the spirit of international co-operation is scarcely noticeable yet.” The Fasci

1931-06-16.text: LONDON, June 15,—(4)—The labor government was defeated today in a surprise vote on a minor conservative amendment to the land-tax bill, but quickly recovered and re-established its control of the House of Commons by a slim majority of 14. The defeat, administered by a vote of 232 to 208, came when many labor and liberal benches were empty. The government, refusing to look upon the setback as cause for resignation, speedily rallied its forces and, while screaming headlines announced the conservative victory to throngs of home-going Londoners, the counter-blow was delivered. By a vote of 246 to 232, the government forced through closure on debate. The temporary defeat was looked on as if not politically serious, coming as it did on the eve of a vital vote tomorrow on a liberal amendment to the finance bill.

LONDON, June 16.—(#)--The government today provisionally accepted the liberal party’s redrafted amendment to Chancellor Snowden’s proposed penny a pound land tax, averting what had threatened to be a serious crisis. The acceptance is subject to reconsideration of certain details of the amendment. The amendment deals with methods of assessing land under the land tax in connection with provisions of the income tax.

LONDON, June 16 — The crisis that threatened the labor government over its land tax measure was averted today when Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald accepted a liberal amendment to the bill guarding against double taxation on amounts already paid in income taxes. MacDonald told a meeting of the parliamentary labor party that the government accepted the amendment, as redrafted, subject to reconsideration of certain details. The threatened crisis in the House of Commons this evening therefore would pass over, he said. The announcement meant the amendment would go through but would not constitute a government defeat, since the labor party would not be in the position of opposing it.

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil, June 15—(AP)—Two new islands, probably pushed up off the Brazilian coast by volcanic action, are likely to be the prizes of an international race. The islands, near the rocks of St. Peters and St. Paul, were reported Saturday by the master of the British steamer Lelande. The Brazilian government is ordering a cruiser to put out from Rio De Janeiro to plant the Brazilian flag on them. The British have a cruiser at Georgetown, British Guiana, which is slightly farther from the new islands than Rio de Janeiro. It was reported that the French government also might be interested in the islands since they are near the French airmail line between Europe and Brazil.

| COBH, Ireland, June 16—Inhabitants of this port today were eagerly anticipating the arrival of Sir Hubert Wilkins’ polar submarine Nautilus which was being towed here by the American battleship Wyoming. According to latest reports, however, it will take at least a week for the underwater craft to arrive at this port. She was proceeding today in this direction at the rate of about eight knots per hour. The Nautilus broke down in mid-ocean when her starboard engine refused to function. Madrid, June 16~(A.P.)—Cardinal Pedro Segura y Saenz, expelled from Spain, crossed the frontier at San Sebastian today and drove to Hendaye, France, in his own car. His enforced journey across Spain was marked by manifestations against him in San Sebastian and Guadalajara which led authorities to take extraordinary precautions for his safety. A mob collected in the main streets of San Sebastian last night and announced its intention of intercepting the cardinal's car. Authorities telephoned Madrid to delay his arrival until after midnight and placed reinforcements of police and civil guards on patrol to avert possible disorder. A crowd called on the civil governor at Guadalajara and demanded that the cardinal be placed in jail.

CHERBOURG, France, June 16 — Sir Hubert Wilkins intends to repair the engines of the submarine Nautilus and proceed toward the north pole as soon as possible, Lady Wilkins said today. Undaunted by the disaster which halted his reconstructed craft in mid-ocean, Sir Hubert wirelessed his plans to his wife as she passed within 30 miles of him aboard the liner Mauretania from New York to London. Lady Wilkins revealed the interchange when the Mauretania arrived here today. She proceeded to Southampton.

ROME, June 15 (4)—A solution of the controversy between the Catholic church and the Italian state is reported from reliable sources to have been found today in a plan to reopen thousands of Catholic clubs in Italy, after they had been somewhat reorganized and specially governed. It was said the Fascist government, after receiving a note from the pope today, decided to allow the clubs to reopen as religious organizations definitely under control and vouched for by the bishops. This is understood to be satisfactory to both parties. Some of these organizations conducted by Salesians already have been authorized to resume activities. Eight of them were reopened in Turin yesterday and it is understood others throughout Italy are being notified by the police they may function again. This method of adjusting the difficulty had been forecast after Pope Pius instructed his bishops to take charge

Originally Great Britain had wanted the meetings to begin next Monday, but France wanted to delay until after Bastille Day on July 14. LONDON, July 8 (AP)—In line with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald’s invitation for a conference of the powers concerned in the Hoover moratorium, the foreign office was at work today on plans for such a meeting here next week. No definite acceptances have been received, but they are expected before night. The United States, Germany, France, Italy and probably other countries will be represented and it is taken for granted that Colonel Henry L. Stimson, the American secretary of state, who now is in Italy, will come to London if his presence is considered necessary. Great Britain wants the meeting to begin on Monday, but if France wants a delay until after Bastille Day on July 14, that will be agreeable to Downing Street and the conferees might get together on Friday of next week. Details of the conference have not been completed but, it is likely that during the first stages financial exp

LONDON, July 8 —(UP)—The leading powers concerned in the Hoover moratorium have indicated their acceptance of the British government's invitation to a conference here. It was expected a committee of international financial experts would convene next Monday and a committee of statesmen a week later. Between them, they will work out the technical details necessary for putting the Hoover accord, as accepted by Paris, into effect.

FAMILIA, JULY 5 VPI Paves An agreement for economic relief of Germany reached its second stage tonight with the announcement that the committee of treasury experts foreseen by the agreement will meet next week in London. At the same time the part of the United States in sponsoring a moratorium was virtually ended. Secretary of the Treasury Mellon has left for the traditional summer holiday. On the other hand, he rests after the 12 days and nights of arduous negotiations. Refreshed after a night's sleep, Secretary Mellon left by train tonight with his son, Paul, for Cap Ferrat. His son came from London today. The secretary's visit to Cap Ferrat for two months was planned before the reparations moratoria question developed. The quick action in deciding on the experts’ meeting made a good impression here. The French government renounced its wish to have the conference in Paris in deference

LONDON, July 8—(F)—Sir Oswald Mosley, once known as the millionaire Socialist, formally joined the opposition to Prime Minister MacDonald's government today, surrendering his seat on the Labor benches for one on the Conservative back benches. TAKES NEW SEAT As the founder of the “new party” abandoned his seat among the Laborites and walked the few yards across the historic hall to his new place, there were ironic cheers from the labor benches. Lady Cynthia Mosley joined him a few minutes later with several other members of the new party who will vote with him in the critical division on the unemployment insurance bill which comes up for second reading this afternoon. The government's position is somewhat dangerous now, for both Mosley and James Maxton, Labor left winger, have moved rejection of the measure, and some of the insurgent Liberals are sure to vote against it. LONDON, (UP) — An international crusade for relief from the world’s armament burden was believed in the making here today as the second step toward economic recovery. President Hoover’s debts holiday plan, the first step, already was overshadowed by the intimations of early discussions on arms limitation in an effort to see that the world arms conference at Geneva next February is a practical success and achieves something more than promises. U. S. To Lead The United States generally was regarded, here and on the continent, as taking the lead in the move to lay a sound basis of common sense and understanding of mutual problems incident to this greatest of all arm parleys. This leadership, already established in world affairs through President Hoover’s dramatic war debts holiday scheme again was seen evinced in the presence of Col. Henry L. C., July 8 —(UP)— The airplane Fort Worth piloted by Reg Robbins and Harold Jones, passed over The plane passed over the west side of the town, headed North, The plane was not expected before 10 a. m. at the earliest as it passed over Soda Creek shortly after 3 o'clock. The plane evidently was making slightly less than 100 miles an hour.

BERLIN, July 8.—(AP)—A thousand of Germany's strongest banks, industrial firms and shipping concerns, owning properties valued at many billions of dollars, stood ready today to guarantee with all their assets the Reich’s business credit abroad. A drastic decision of the nation’s industrial and financial leaders to undertake a joint guarantee of individual foreign credits was announced by Hans Luther, president of the Reichsbank, at midnight, after it had become apparent during the day that the demand for foreign currencies continued strong, despite the signing of the Hoover plan. Technically, their action was to place at the disposal of the German gold discount bank a collateral guarantee of 506,000,000 marks (about $125,000,000) for which the signers, each of whom has assets of at least 5,000,000 marks, are responsible. 1931-06-08.text: London, June 8—The possibility of a world conference to re-open completely the problem of war reparations loomed today in the weekend conference between the heads of the British and German governments. London newspapers today linked forthcoming visits to Europe of Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson and Andrew W. Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury, with a promise made by the conference to collaborate with other governments. A spokesman for the conversations at Chequers, country home of Prime Minister MacDonald, said that the world field of economic and political troubles was discussed, particularly as affected by the Young Plan and other factors. MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson participated in the conversations for Great Britain; Chancellor Heinrich Bruening and Foreign Minister Julius Curtius for Germany. LONDON, — (4) - The government commission appointed to adjudicate differences between Moslems and Jews over rights to use of the Wailing Wall in Jerusalem for devotional purposes Monday ruled that sole ownership of the wall is vested in the Moslems. At the same time the commission held the Jews should have free access to the wall for purposes of devotion at all times under definite conditions regarding appurtenances of worship. It is stipulated the Jews shall not blow the ram's horn near the wall nor cause any avoidable disturbance to the Moslems and the Moslems, in turn, must not annoy the Jews during their devotions.

By The Associated Press. Chequers, Buckinghamshire, England, June 7.—Promising each other to “deal with the present crisis in close collaboration” Germany’s and England's foreign ministers and premiers today finished their two conferences at the county home of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald here. Every phase of the war's economic situation was discussed thoroughly during the week-end with frankness and openness. After Chancellor Henrich Bruening and Foreign Minister Julius Curtius departed for London a laconic communique was issued to the press. It did not mention the question of reparations, although Herr Bruening is understood to have asked MacDonald's assistance in sounding Germany's creditors, including the United States, regarding postponement of some of the heavy reparations payments. Dr. Curtius was optimistic tonight in discussing the week-end conference with friends after he re

: West Virginia, July 20 — During conversation at Chequers the heads of the British and German governments indicated a disposition to re-open reparations and war debts questions in a way that would present a serious problem for the United States. President Hoover during his weekend at Rapidan Camp was understood to have discussed the situation with Hugh Gibson, ambassador to Belgium and the government’s foremost authority on European post-war relations. Though this government has been rigid in opposing cancellation or downward revision of the Allied war debts, the fall in the general world prices level and possible inability of Germany to continue reparations payments, out of which Allied debt payments to the United States are financed, raised considerations which officials here privately recognize may have to be faced. London. June 7 (*)—Severe earth tremors in England, France, Norway and Belgium early today greatly alarmed inhabitants, but did little material damage and caused no loss of life. At many points persons jumped from beds and rushed to the streets half-clad, and remained outside for Wales, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Wight. Northern France and southern Norway were also affected. J. J. Shaw, seismologist in the West Bromwich observatory, said the shock, which started there at 1:26 a.m., was one of the severest ever recorded in England. The phenomenon was accompanied

London, June 8 (UP)—Fear of a recurrence of severe earthquakes which shook most of the British Isles, part of northern Europe and the Scandinavian peninsula kept inhabitants uneasy today. The quakes were felt throughout England and Scotland, chiefly in Yorkshire and the Midlands where the people, clad in night clothes, rushed from their homes into a heavy rain when the first shock occurred at 1:26 a.m. yesterday. The epicenter of the quakes appeared to have been near Hull, probably in the North Sea off the coast of England. The shocks continued over a period of about 30 minutes, extending from the northern coast of Scotland to the English Channel. Light shocks were felt across the channel in the vicinity of Cherbourg, Dunkirk, Calais and at Heilles near Beauvais, where some damage was reported. BY HERBERT MOORE | (United Press Staff Correspondent). LONDON, June 8—The possibility of a joint representation to the United States concerning the desirability of reducing the financial burdens created by the world war was seen today as one result of the Anglo-German conversations at Chequers over the weekend. An agreement which indirectly would lead toward collaboration of world powers in an effort at war debt reductions was reached at Chequers, the United Press was reliably informed. It was expected the British government would communicate the results of the conversations to Rome, after which the desirability of making a joint representation to Washington would be considered. Wodehouse, the noted English humorist, looked back today over a year's work in motion pictures, just completed and confessed “it dazes me.” “They paid me $2,000 a week — $104,000 — and I cannot see what they engaged me for,” he said, referring to his employment with the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer studio. “They were extremely nice to me, but I feel as if I have cheated them. “You see, I understood I was engaged to write stories for the screen. 1931-07-10.text: London, July 10.—(AP)—The British government is putting the Hoover moratorium into operation immediately by informing the Bank for International Settlements that she will not expect payment of the German annuity due on July 15. This information was contained in a letter sent to the bank by the government today. The government also sent official invitations today to the United States, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium and Japan to attend the conference of Young plan experts which opens here next Friday. ILLINOIS WEATHER, Mostly fair tonight and Saturday;

LONDON, July 10. U.P.—The British government announced that the Hoover plan will become effective today as far as Great Britain is concerned. Great Britain sent a letter to the Bank of International Settlements at Basle announcing that in view of the Hoover plan, it would not expect the reparations installment due from Germany next Wednesday.

By The Associated Press. PARIS, July 10—The council of ministers decided this morning to send five experts to the moratorium conference in London next Friday. Four of them will be treasury officials and the fifth a commercial attache of the foreign office.

| PROVINCETOWN, Mass., July 10 (Two steamers, the freighter Crandon and the passenger liner President Hayes, grounded on Cape Cod shoals today during a dense fog. Both went aground on flood tide and were held fast by the sand as the tide receded. The British freighter Crandon, which came to grief near the tip of the cape, crossed the outer peaked hill bar and her position was difficult. The President Hayes was stranded on Shovelful shoal, near Chatham. She was resting easily on her starboard side and her skipper declined assistance from the coast guard, expressing the conviction that he could get her off under her own power on the evening tide.

Boston, July 10.—The British steamship Crandon went aground this morning on Peaked Hill bar, Cape Cod, in a dense fog. The Coast Guard cutter Mojave on patrol was ordered by radio from Boston to go to the Crandon’s assistance. Eastern division headquarters of the Coast Guard in Boston reported that the British freighter, a craft of 3000 tons, appeared to be hard aground but that additional information could not be obtained at this time. The tide was not quite at flood. The Coast Guard officials said they understood the Crandon was bound from Mexican ports for North Plymouth. The exact position of the Mojave was unreported and consequently it was not known when she would reach the freighter. Coast Guardsmen reported that a “pea soup” fog prevailed along the cape.

EDINBURGH, SCOTLAND, UP. The whimsies of British weather very nearly drenched King George and Queen Mary at their garden party at Holyrood Palace Thursday. Edinburgh dressmakers estimated that members of the best Scots families lost $250,000 in damage to their finery on the occasion. An august gathering of Scottish clansmen and their ladies had assembled for a chat with their majesties when suddenly the rain poured down. There was a general rush to the castle gates and elegantly dressed guests struggled and scrambled to board trams and buses and escape the downpour. The king and queen had just reached the tea marquee when the rain began to fall and they returned to the castle, but the Duke and Duchess of York and the other members of the royal suite were drenched.

BUFFALO, N. Y., July 9—(AP)—A man registered as Randolph Edgar committed suicide by shooting in a Buffalo hotel tonight. He left a note requesting that the Harvard Alumni Association and the Authors' Club of London be notified. "For an obituary see Who's Who," the note ended. Who's Who gives the home address of Randolph Edgar as Boston and lists him as a contributor to the Bellman, Vanity Fair, the Theatre magazine and other periodicals. He was a member of the editorial staff of the Literary Digest in 1910-1912. He was dramatic critic and daily column writer for the St. Paul Pioneer Press in 1924 and publicity man for the Minneapolis Symphony Orchestra in 1925 and 1926. In 1937 he was with the Boston Sunday Advertiser.

WASHINGTON--The big business world long has known that million-dollar deals can be put across best by men who know each other's first names. The State Department has shown faith in the same theory by deciding to send Hugh R. Gibson to the London debt parley next week. Nominally, this forty-seven-year-old diplomat is American Ambassador to Belgium. Actually, he is a Diplomat-at-Large, a trouble shooter. As a pinch-hitter, the State Department sends him wherever extreme tact, and an intimate acquaintance with statesmen are essential. At the London conference—called by the British to work out the technical but politically dynamic details of President Hoover's debt holiday plan—Gibson will be assisted by Frederick Eivesay, assistant economic advisor to the State Department.
