1931-03-13.text: London, March 13,—(A.P.)—The British government is extending an invitation to Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the Indian nationalists, to come to London shortly and participate in further negotiations looking toward granting qualified dominion status to India. Concluding debate on India in the House of Commons last night, J. Ramsey MacDonald, Prime Minister, announced that a second round table conference would be convened in London in the fall, and that prior to that time the federal structure committee of the first conference would meet here. The Prime Minister's announcement was made after the attitude of the opposition parties toward India had been considerably clarified by Stanley Baldwin, Conservative leader, who repledged himself and his workers for striving by every possible means to work out a solution of India’s problems.

POINT BARROW, Mich., March 13.—UP)—Two airplanes bringing a new supply of antitoxin for this diphtheria-stricken village were awaited anxiously today. Joe Crosson and S. E. Robbins, Alaska airmen, left Fairbanks yesterday with the serum. Crosson landed here last Sunday with a quantity of antitoxin, which soon was exhausted. Several new cases have been reported since then, four virulent cases yesterday.

MAESTOG, Wales, March 13 —(— Vernon Hartshorn, lord privy seal since 1930 and formerly president of the South Wales Miners Federation dropped dead at his home here today. The Rt. Hon. Vernon Hartshorn, lord privy seal since 1930, and M. P. from the Ogmore division of Glamorgan-shire since 1918, was fifty-nine years old. He was postmaster-general in 1924, a member of the Indian reforms commission from 1927 to 1930; served on the coal trade organization committee and also on the coal controllers’ advisory committee, and was president of the South Wales Miners’ Federation.

| LONDON, March 13 na — Ramsay MacDonald's government escaped defeat by only five votes in the House of Commons today on a motion to reduce a supplementary estimate of £14,000 (about $70,000) for salaries and expenses of the mines department. Many Laborites voted with the opposition on the motion, which was defeated 173 to 167.

BUENOS AIRES, Arg., March 13. (P)—The Prince of Wales will throw open here tomorrow the greatest British trade show ever held outside the empire, climaxing Great Britain's effort to recapture first place in Argentina’s foreign trade. Twenty million dollars worth of British-made goods have been assembled in Palermo park.

SHANGHAI—(?)—Two hundred persons were believed drowned when the heavily loaded Chinese passenger steamer Pa Chi blew up and sank in the Yangtse Kiang seventy miles from here. Among the 500 passengers aboard the vessel were a hundred Chinese soldiers who were thought to have thrown their cigarette stubs into the cargo, principally cotton. An explosion followed, spreading fire in the hold. Most of those on the boat jumped over the side where a revenue cruiser was able to pick up a few survivors.

By The Associated Press. NICE, France, March 12.—Long hours of merciless questioning today failed to shake the story of Mrs. Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger that when she shot and killed her husband, the Philadelphia theatrical magnate last night, she killed in self-defense. “Do you regret your act?” the police asked her. “If I hadn’t killed him, then he would have killed me,” she said. Friends of Nixon-Nirdlinger and his wife, who was Miss Charlotte Nash of St. Louis, said that he undoubtedly loved his wife very much but was most jealous. Yesterday he engaged detectives to trail her, explaining that he did not intend to use any information he might get against her but simply wanted to know what she was doing. His body is being held at the morgue and while she is being held by police no formal charges have been filed.

NICE, France, March 12--(AP) A story of her husband’s nagging jealousy, which he climaxed with an attempt to strangle her, was told police today by Mrs. Fred G. Nixon-Nirdlinger, who, at midnight, shot and killed the Philadelphia theatrical magnate. Mrs. Nixon-Nirdlinger, who was “Miss St. Louis” and runner-up in the 1923 Atlantic City beauty pageant, was arrested, pending a complete investigation. In substantiation of her plea of self-defense, she exhibited red marks on her throat, which she said were caused by her husband's fingers as he attempted to end a jealous quarrel by choking her to death. The slain theatre man was 54 years old, his wife 26; they were married in 1925, and had two small children. 1931-04-30.text: London, Apr. 30—(AP)—Police of much of the world today made preparations to suppress disorders during widespread observance tomorrow of International Labor Day. In England, May Day celebrations have gone somewhat out of fashion and little beyond soap box oratory and a few small processions was expected in London, but elsewhere in Europe and in Spanish America observance presented a more serious problem. The government has forbidden open air meetings and parades in Paris and vigorous preparations have been made to combat any breach in order. Police of Berlin will be mobilized for the day and a rigid curb placed upon demonstrations. In some of the Balkan countries, celebrations were forbidden, but in others demonstrations under strict supervision were permitted. In Spain, the day was expected to have a dual significance with celebrations smacking of patriotic fervor for the new republic. T

Reykjavik, Iceland, April 30-14) The patrol boat Icelandic Odin headed north this morning with an airplane lashed on her forward deck, and an Icelandic flier aboard, bound for Greenland to look for Augustine Courtlaud, the young British explorer. She is due to reach the ice barrier about sixty miles from Angmagsalik on Friday morning if the good weather holds. Just before she sailed word came from Bergen, Norway, that Captain Albin Ahrenberg, Swedish flier who is also joining in the search, had been advised not to take off from there until the weather improved. The temperature was around zero and there was danger of ice forming on the wings of his plane.

BERGEN, Norway. April 30. (UP) A heavy mist prevented Capt. Charles Ahrenberg from resuming his flight today to Greenland, where he seeks to rescue Augustine Courtauld, British explorer marooned on the ice cap. Courtauld, who went to a hut in the interior of Greenland last Summer, was believed in danger of starvation. A previous expedition had failed to locate him. Ahrenberg, who arrived here after a 450-mile flight from Malmoe, Sweden, said he was confident of finding Courtauld, particularly as a search from the air was likely to be more successful than a land search such as the previous expedition.

Malmo, Sweden, April 29.—Two airplanes headed into the north today to look for Augustine Courtauld, lost somewhere on the Greenland icecap and unable to effect a junction with the rest of the British expedition sent out last year to survey an Anglo-Canadian air route. Captain Albin Ahrenberg, Swedish flyer, took off from here, another plane left Iceland aboard the inspection ship Odin to fly from the edge of the ice-barrier to Tasi-oak and to Angmagsalik, looking for Courtauld on the way. Message Received This morning a radio message apparently from Courtauld reported that his food supplies were exhausted, but the authorities were unable to account for the message, since they could not understand how he could have sent it unless he had established contact with another British expedition which so far has not been able to find him.

CAIRO, EGYPT, April 30.—(AP)—Forty-one persons were counted dead today, with scores injured, because a hot box set a train afire. As the Cairo-Alexandria Express rolled along yesterday afternoon, laden with a holiday crowd of pleasure seekers, a hot box developed on one of the third class coaches and set the coach afire. The train’s motion pulled the flames into the trailing coaches. Passengers were panic stricken. Some burned to death. Others, preferring to jump from the speeding train, lost their lives as they hurled themselves from coach windows to the right of way. Frantic efforts were made to signal the engineer, but not until a signalman saw the flames and flagged him down, did he know what had happened. He stopped the train and the flames devoured the remainder of the three cheap coaches, charring the bodies of those inside, and leaving only the undercarriages unconsumed. Railway

1931-02-14.text: London, Feb. 13,—(AP)—Nancy 'Lady Astor laid about with the rapier of her repartee in the House of Commons today, fighting the battle of temperance, but she voted with the majority in defeating a prohibition bill by 137 to 18. The bill was introduced by Edwin Scrymgeour, member for Dundee, who has spent years trying to prohibit alcoholic beverages in the United Kingdom. Lady Astor sent home telling thrusts against the liquor interests, but even so declared her intention of voting against the measure in the belief that temperance and not prohibition is the cure for whatever liquor evils there may be. The Horrible Example Both sides cited the United States, proponents of the repeal as a guiding light, and the others as a horrible example under prohibition. Lady Astor referred to the peerage as the "beerage."

LONDON, Feb. 14 (.-Sir Laming-ton-Worthington Evans, Bart. secretary of state for war in two conservative cabinets, died in his sleep early today. He was 63 years old, Sir Laming-ton had a distinguished political career and was one of the mainstays in the high councils of the conservative party. He had not been well lately, but his death came unexpectedly.

LONDON, Feb. 18—(AP) The House of Commons, by a vote of 137 to 18 today rejected the bill which would have prohibited the use of alcoholic liquors as beverages throughout the United Kingdom. Lady Nancy Astor, Virginia's contribution to the British House of Commons, had members of that August body alternately laughing and gnashing, when she took the floor in debate on the bill. Lady Astor in a slashing and sometimes vitriolic speech, made it clear that she is against liquor, but did not believe in tackling the problem in the way suggested in the bill. The debate arose on the second reading of the measure introduced by Edwin Scrymgeour, prohibition member from Scotland. Lady Astor protested when the conservative, Sir William Wayland, said Americans were drinking more under prohibition than before. She said she could not vote for the bill because if she voted for prohibition she would not b

LONDON, Feb. 14.—Anthony Hall today served notice on King George to get off the throne so that Hall himself could rule Great Britain. Addressing his majesty as Mr. George Frederick Ernest Albert Windsor, Hall who asserts that he is descended from Tudor kings, set forth his claims in a ten-page clumsily-written foolscap letter, ending with the blunt order to the king to abdicate in his favor. He did say, however, that he intended to have no civil war over the succession. Hall outlined his plans for the reconstruction of Great Britain, including the redemption of the national debt of 7,630,000,000 pounds, the expenditure of 5,000,000 pounds in 20 years for the relief of the unemployed, the return to pre-war strength of British beer and the rebuilding of London to accommodate 160,000,000 inhabitants.

(International News Service) BOSTON, Feb. 14—Major General Clarence Ransom Edwards, beloved war-time commander of the 26th (Yankee) division, died today. The gallant leader of the New England troops overseas in the world war lost the most serious battle of his long career in war and peace at Phillips House of Massachusetts General Hospital.

LONDON, Feb. 24. (GINS) - A manifesto "giving notice" to King George of England to vacate his throne and leave the country has been served by Anthony Hall, who claims direct descent from Henry VII, first of the Tudor kings, according to the Daily Herald account today. Hall, in the manifesto published by the Herald, proceeds to prove his right to the throne by a devious route. He gave his age as 51, and as his first policy change in taking over the throne promised to have beer brewed again at full strength. The newspaper quotes Hall further as saying: --- "I claim the crown. I am of the male line directly descended from the last prince to win the crown on the field of battle—Henry Tudor. "My intention is not one of civil war over this matter. You have no connection with the British royal family; you are an outsider, therefore leave the country!"

MADRID, FEB. 14. (AP).—The government of Premier General Damaso Berenguer, successor to the Primo de Rivera dictatorship, fell today, bringing to a head a crisis which appeared to be the most dangerous of any faced by King Alfonso in the course of his long reign. The King, accepting the resignation of General Berenguer and his cabinet, cancelled the parliamentary elections which were scheduled for March 1 and 15 and immediately began conferring with political leaders with a view to formation of a new cabinet. The situation which brought the fall of the cabinet developed only late last night when the Count of Romanones and other important Liberal monarchist leaders withdrew their support of the cabinet elections program.

CALGARY, Alta., Feb. 14.—(AP)—Heedless of their peril if caught in a blizzard, 500 men, many of them poorly equipped, were hurrying into the Livingstone river valley today in quest of gold. A three-ounce piece of quartz brought from the Livingstone valley country by a prospector which showed traces of gold when assayed at Lethbridge, was the lodestone drawing the gold seekers into the valley. Behind the gold seekers moved a mounted patrol of provincial police sent by Commissioner W. G. Bryun to succor any who might suffer from cold and hunger should a storm overtake them. Many in the rush were from the ranks of Calgary's unemployed, novices in prospecting, who set out on foot with little food and scant equipment. A background for the rush is furnished by the legend of the lost Leman mine. The story is that an Idaho prospector named Leman struck it rich in the Livingstone country in 1870,

1931-04-13.text: | Cowes, Eng., April 12.—(AP)— Tugs tonight were endeavoring to refloat the Holland-American liner Statendam, which, with a number of American passengers aboard, went aground last night at a point southwest of Brambles. The 29,511-ton vessel, which was making the first voyage of the year between Rotterdam and New York, had called at Cowes to take on passengers for America. These, numbering 48, were taken from the Southampton dock by a tender. After they were aboard the liner grounded on the mud in making a swinging maneuver before continuing the voyage.

LONDON, April 13.—(INS)—The revolutionary movement in progress against the government of Portugal in the Madeira and Azores Islands was reported today to have spread to the distant Portuguese colony of Angola, West Africa. According to Lisbon dispatches to the Morning Post here, the Angola garrison turned insurrectionist.
MADRID, April 13.—Alcala Zamora, leader of the Spanish Republicans, who gained a smashing victory in yesterday's elections, called on the king today to abdicate.

Tokyo, April 13--(4)--Disabled as the result of a shot fired last November 14 by a young assassin, Yuko Hamaguchi resigned today as premier of Japan and presented the resignations of his entire cabinet. The appointment of Reijiro Wakatsuki, former premier, as successor to Hamaguchi was regarded as a foregone conclusion and it was expected Wakatsuki would retain most of the Hamaguchi cabinet. The Hamaguchi administration which lasted less than two years, weathered many storms growing out of its acceptance of the London naval treaty and the attempt upon the premier’s life was attributed to dissatisfaction among patriotic extremists with Japan's position regarding the arms limitation agreement.

Madrid, April 13.—()—King Alfonso was considering today what action the government should take in the situation gravely threatening the throne, brought about by the republican victory in yesterday's municipal elections. He will decide late this afternoon at a cabinet meeting whether to accept and announce the resignations of three members of his cabinet which were tendered this morning. In the opinion of qualified observers, the king has three possible courses of action. 1. To continue the district and then the parliamentary elections under Premier Juan Bautista Aznar or a new government. This probably would lead to a republic. 2. To establish another military dictatorship. This might mean an immediate strike, revolution and civil war. 3. To abdicate. BERLIN, April 13(4)—An American woman's anecdote at the expense of Joseph Stalin, Russia’s “Man of Steel,” has cost her her right to live in the Soviet Union and her husband his lucrative Soviet employ as an anthracite mining expert. Mrs. Eve Gareete Grady, an American magazine writer, arriving here from the U. S. S. R., said that a foreign office official had served her with expulsion papers, explaining that while her recent article, “See Russia and Die Laughing” was not offensive, the government could not allow the story about Stalin to go unnoticed. At the same time her husband, William H. Grady, a consulting engineer of New York, was expelled with instructions to keep his wife out of Russia. Madrid, April 12 (4).—Republicans in at least two thirds of the big cities in Spain today rolled up sweeping majorities in the first municipal elections Spain has had in eight years, and government leaders, confounded by the unexpected defeat gathered tonight to see what was to be done about it. Tomorrow there is to be an emergency meeting of the cabinet and resignation of the entire ministry seemed an imminent possibility. It was possible also that King Alfonso might establish a military dictatorship to check any tendency toward revolution which might be inspired by the Republican victory at the polls. The Count of Romanones, foreign minister in the cabinet of Premier Aznar and the richest man in Spain, described the situation as serious. LISBON, Portugal, April 12.—(AP)—Lisbon was quiet today as the government gave its undivided attention to suppressing the rebellions at Funchal, Madeira, and on the islands of Terceira and San Miguel in the Azores. An expeditionary force is gathering at Porto Santo island, 40 miles from Madeira. This soon will be augmented by the cruiser Vasco da Gama, which sailed with additional troops from Lisbon today. President Carmona visited the ship before her departure. Three fishing trawlers have been requisitioned and heavily armed before being added to the fleet. Meanwhile, efforts are being made to enforce rigorously the government’s blockade on the island. The British steamer Avoceta today unloaded a cargo destined for Madeira at Lisbon. 1931-09-01.text: Douglas, Isle Of Man, Aug. 31 (#) —Sir Hall Caine, noted British Novelist, died at 10:50 o'clock tonight at Greeba Castle, his home here, where he had been seriously ill for some time. He was 78 years old. His wife, Lady Caine, and his two sons, Ralph Hall Caine and De'y suse Hall Caine, were at his bedside. More than twenty years ago, Hall Caine, whose early writings were laughed at and derided, was declared by the manager of the Lyceum theatre, London, to be the wealthiest novelist in the world. The theatrical royalties from America and England up to that time amounted to $450,000 and it was said that the sales of his novels produced an even larger income. He produced novels and plays, many of the latter dramatized versions of his books, for nearly fifty years. One of his earlier successes was "The Deemster," and one of his most widely known later books was "The Woman Thou Gavest Me."

LONDON, Sept. 1 (4)—Ramsay MacDonald and “Jim” Thomas have been hounded from the labor organizations to which they have devoted most of their lives but few observers believed either of them will be driven from British public life. There are too many big jobs to be gone after the present financial crisis is solved, it is felt, for them to disappear completely. MacDonald may finally complete his biography of John Knox, something he has been trying to do for years, or return as the dominions secretary to his fireside and pipe. The Indian round table is one which will require great statesmanship to handle. The League of Nations is another international agency that needs able men. MacDonald's skill in diplomacy is recognized by all classes and with his friendship among Americans and knowledge of the United States it is believed he would make an ideal ambassador to that country. Hajputana, En Route to London, Sept. 1.-(4') Mahatma Gandhi, on the way from Bombay to attend the Indian round table conference at London, has added a homespun blanket to the meager costume he usually wears. The loin cloth which ordinarily is his only garment was inadequate protection against the chill winds of the sea, and it appeared likely he would wear the blanket also at London. Miss Slade Also Poor Sailor The Mahatma is not a very good sailor and Miss Madeleine Slade, his English disciple, is the worst sailor in the party even if she is an admiral's daughter. Davidas Gandhi, the Mahatma’s son, has taken over most of her duties.

LONDON, Aug. 31.—Labor continued its warfare against the new national government today with an attack on J. H. (Jim) Thomas, dominions secretary in the cabinet and one of the most picturesque figures in British politics. The National Union of Railwaymen, of which he has been an official for 35 years, demanded that he resign from the three-party government headed by Ramsay MacDonald and he responded by quitting as leader of the union. Mr. Thomas left the union meeting at which this action was taken with tears in his eyes. “This is a terrible moment for me after almost a life's work as leader of the National Railwaymen,” he said. While labor reprisals against the national government continued, the new cabinet pressed ahead with its work of slicing $600,000,000 from the budget. LONDON, Sept. 1.—(4)—Mrs. T. P. O'Connor, widow of “Tay Pay” O'Connor, noted Irish leader, died today of pneumonia after a short illness. Her son, Francis Howard, was at the bedside. She was born in Austin, Texas, the daughter of Supreme Court Judge George W. Paschall and first married F. G. Howard of Washington, D. C. She married O'Connor in 1885. She was the author of several books and plays and president of the London Society of Women Journalists. Her husband died in November, 1929, after a long career of journalism and politics in behalf of Irish freedom.

London, Sept. 1 (UP)—Sir Thomas Lipton will not challenge for America's cup this year it was announced today in his behalf. His secretary said he had decided definitely against challenging because of the heavy depression and unemployment in Great Britain and the United States but a challenge will be issued when times are better, it was said.

Paris, Aug. 31.—(A.P.)—A proposal that the nations of the world place their armed forces under the control of the League of Nations and a prediction that France would lead the way at the 1932 disarmament conference was made today by Joseph Paul-Boncour, chairman of the foreign affairs committee of the chamber of deputies, in a statement to the Associated Press. Inasmuch as M. Paul-Boncour is acknowledged as France's greatest authority on disarmament and is certain to be one of France's chief delegates to the disarmament conference in Geneva next February, his statement was considered to be of such far-reaching importance that it will give an entirely new angle to the struggle for the reduction and limitation of armaments. (By Miles W. Vaughn, United Press staff correspondent.) TOKIO, Aug. 14.—(UP)—The procurator recommended today that a fine be imposed upon Clyde E. Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, Jr., American aviators accused of having photographed Japanese fortifications from the air. The recommendation was believed to have lessened the possibility the fliers might be imprisoned. A verdict in the case will be handed down by the court tomorrow. The procurator said he had decided to proceed with their prosecution because his inquiry definitely showed they took pictures of Japanese forts in the vicinity of Hakodate, on the island of Hokkaido, to the north. The trans-Atlantic fliers were charged with taking the photographs while flying to Japan from Khabarovsk, Siberia, where they abandoned their attempt to set a world flight record recently. VILLEFRANCE, France, Aug. 14 UP—Andrew W. Mellon, American secretary of the treasury, sailed for New York today on the steamship Conte Blancamano.

Tokyo, Aug. 15 (Saturday). — The Renzo News Agency said today it learned the District Court will fine Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, Jr., American fliers, 2,000 yen ($1,000) each for violation of Japan's aviation laws and 59 yen ($25) each for violation of the fortified zone laws. Authorities claimed the Americans flew here from Khararovsk, Siberia, without first obtaining a landing permit, that they flew over fortified areas and took photographs of the fortifications, each of which is prohibited by Japanese law. The news agency quoted official sources as saying the plane will not be confiscated in view of Herndon’s testimony that his mother and sister had an interest in the machine.

TOKYO, Aug. 15. (AP)—A flight from Khabarovsk, Siberia, to Tokyo, during which they passed over Japanese fortified areas and took pictures which authorities claimed included those of fortifications, cost Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, Jr., American fliers, fines of $1,025 each in district court here today. Both fliers were in court as the decision was read, specifying that $1,000 of the fine was assessed because they had violated Japanese civil aviation laws and the remainder for flying over fortified areas. Pangborn and Herndon flew here to attempt a non-stop flight from Japan to Seattle for a $25,000 prize offered by the Tokyo newspaper Asahi after difficulties had so delayed them in their projected round-the-world speed flight that it would have been impossible to break the record set recently by Wiley Post and Harold Gatty. 1931-06-19.text: WASHINGTON, June 19. (AP)— Justice Frederick L. Siddons of the District of Columbia Supreme Court died suddenly today from heart disease. He was 66 years old and a native of London. Justice Siddons presided at the trial of Harry F. Sinclair on jury-shadowing charges in the celebrated Senate contempt case and sentenced the wealthy oil man to jail.

By the Associated Press The nation sweltered today from one coast to the other, Los Angeles sweltered in the nineties; and New England, too. Great sections of the middle west simmered under the persistent sun. Arizona, California and Nevada all reported deaths due to the heat, the total being 63, Salina, Kan., had thermometer readings of 110 degrees. The Dakotas, Nebraska and Oklahoma also mopped brows excessively warm. Winnipeg, Manitoba, reported that July's second heat wave was drifting slowly away from the Canadian prairies, leaving 19 dead. Damage to crops was estimated from 50 percent to total loss in some places, In New York City, after a night of discomfort, during which one death occurred, the temperature hit 92 at 1 o'clock this afternoon, with humidity fluctuating crazily. HATFIELD, Eng., June 15—(AP)—Miss Cicely O’Brien, noted British aviator, and a woman passenger were killed last night when their airplane crashed and burned near the De Haviland flying school. Miss O'Brien and a woman whose name was given as Mrs. Gordon Gallien took off from the flying school after re-fueling and reached an altitude of about 100 feet when the plane nose dived. By the time attendants had reached the scene the ship was a mass of flames and the bodies were charred beyond recognition.

CORK, Ireland, June 19—(AP) Shipping agents here have been informed that Sir Hubert Wilkins’ submarine Nautilus probably will reach Cork under her power late Sunday night or early Monday morning. The weather in the vicinity of Cork today was good.

London, June 19.—The London said Friday that Secretary of the Treasury Andrew W. Mellon was visiting England “in response to a private invitation from the British government to discuss the revision of war debts.” “Mellon is only prepared to discuss the revision on the understanding that Great Britain joins in an international boycott of Russia,” the paper said, “and takes practical steps to reduce British expenditure for armaments.” The Daily Mail said in reference to Mr. Mellon's conferences with Prime Minister MacDonald and Montagu Norman, chairman of the Bank of England, that “something of the fate of nations hung on their words.” Prime Minister Ramsey MacDonald denied the truth of the report.

NEW YORK, June 19 (4)—Grand jury proceedings in the investigation of the death of Starr Faithfull were postponed today until Tuesday pending the arrival of Dr. G. Jameson Carr, Cunard line ship's surgeon, who is en route from England with letters he received from the girl, written shortly before she disappeared. District Attorney Elvin N. Edwards said today that developments in the investigation would be rapid from now on. "If nothing goes wrong," he said, "we should very soon be able to trace her, hour by hour, during those two dark days that preceded her death." Mr. Edwards still holds to his theory that the bizarre young beauty was murdered. Inspector Harold King, chief of Nassau detectives, is giving attention to the possibility that the girl fell or jumped from the Mauretania. Police were still checking the unexplained absence from the city of Sylvia Tucker Faithfull during the week

London, June 18.—(AP)— Andrew Mellon, secretary of the United States treasury, lent an ear to leaders of British political and financial life today, spending an hour with Prime Minister MacDonald, Foreign Secretary Henderson and Montague Norman, governor of the Bank of England. Although it was officially insisted that Mr. Mellon’s visit was nothing more than a pleasure trip, during which he hoped to visit his son at Cambridge, tonight there was an increasing tendency to connect his presence with the momentous question of reparations and war debts. Coincidentally with the appearance of the secretary of the treasury in the house of commons for the second time in two days, it was announced that Mr. MacDonald and Mr. Henderson would go to Berlin July 17 to accept an invitation received from Chancellor Bruening and Julius Curtius, German foreign minister. The whole thing was done by releasing gas until the big ship floated down smoothly on the rubber covered bumpers of her gondolas. The operation was not so simple as it sounds, however. 1931-03-03.text: BEVERLY HILLS, March 3.—[To the Editor of The Register:] Well, let’s see what happened over what the English taught us to call the week-end. We copped all their expressions, week-end, fortnight, plus fours. We are now adopting the street buses that have been our source of amusement over there. We will cop their monocle yet if they don’t watch us. Bernard Shaw had us right in the papers yesterday morning: “We do things well when somebody shows us how.” But with all our monkey traits we are kicking along pretty good. Our Congress is going to adjourn this week, then watch things hum if we can only prevent another drought and disarmament conference. Yours, WILL ROGERS.

PARIS, March 2 UP—With a tripartite naval agreement reached among France, Great Britain and Italy, and approved today by the French cabinet, the next development tonight appeared to be that another five-power parley now may be necessary. Although it is admitted that the modifications to existing naval treaties caused by yesterday’s three-power accord do not affect directly the vital interests of the United States and Japan—other powers which attended the London naval conference last spring—the Associated Press was informed tonight of the likelihood of the five power meeting. This was laid to the supposition it may be difficult to incorporate the modifications without a formal meeting of all the powers which signed the Washington treaty of 1920. Nevertheless, all circles are confident the United States and Japan will accept the new accord.

In the first mass trial staged by communists in America, Yokinen, who speaks and understands but little English, was convicted yesterday by a jury in spite of an impassioned plea by his negro counsel. PARIS, March 3 (4)—No country emerged victor in the naval accord arrived at over the week-end by France, Great Britain and Italy, Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, told the chamber of deputies today. “Every country made the necessary sacrifices,” he declared. “That is the best praise I can give it.” The details of the agreement have not yet been published, pending their study by the Washington and Tokyo governments. “It is a satisfactory accord,” Mr. Briand said, “and when you know all of its details you will be convinced that it is satisfactory.”

New Delhi, March 3 (4)—Mahatma Gandhi and Sir George Schuster, Indian finance minister, conferring today at the Vice-Regal Palace, reached an agreement on the salt question, one of the outstanding problems in the way of abandonment of the civil disobedience campaign. Almost exactly a year ago the Indian Nationalists, led by Gandhi, initiated a campaign of violation of the salt laws, which provide for a British monopoly. Throughout current negotiations for calling off the civil campaign, Gandhi has contended that the Indian people be empowered to make their own salt. It was understood the agreement provides that people living on the seacoast will be allowed to manufacture and sell salt, which will be regarded as nature's gift to them.

MELBOURNE, Australia, Mar. 8 (AP) — Millions of mice suddenly have invaded the Nullarbor plains along the trans-Australian railway. The station master at Loongana today reported that miles of the country served by the railway were infested with the rodents. While he was attending a passenger train thousands entered his office and soon began eating a roll of pound notes. He said that every house in the district had been invaded by the pests which were attacking even the furniture and the bedding.

1931-12-09.text: LONDON, Dec. 5.—(AP)—Prime Minister MacDonald told the House of Commons today that his government feels an international conference to deal with the world economic situation should be held immediately after the financial experts now meeting at Basel have made their report.

Washington, Dec. 9.—U.P)—Taxes which Americans will pay if the new tax plan is adopted, still will fall short of those paid by their British brothers. | PARIS, Dec. 10.—()—Japan and China today accepted the League of Nations resolution on the dispute in Manchuria. Both acceptances were with reservations. ‘Kenkichi Hoshizawa reserved the Japanese right to take measures against bandits in Manchuria, Dr. Alfred Sze stipulated that China reserved “any and all rights, remedies and juridical positions” to which it is entitled under the league covenant and under treaties to which it is a party. With the acceptance, endorsement of the resolution became unanimous. It also has been approved by United States Ambassador Dawes. This arrangement calls for cessation of hostilities in Manchuria, withdrawal of Japanese troops as quickly as possible and creation of a neutral commission of inquiry to study the whole Sino-Japanese trouble.

BERLIN, Dec. 9. —(AP)— The democratic sword of threatened martial law hung over the heads of Adolf Hitler and other opposition forces of Germany. Dr. Heleneleh Bruening, scholar and chancellor, delivered a warning in a radio address last night which followed the signing by President Hindenburg of the new drastic emergency decree which slashed wages, prices, and rents in the nation. This morning the communist newspaper “Rote Fahne” took up the chancellor's challenge and branded him a “dictator” and appealed to the masses to call a general strike Dec. 15 in protest against the “dictatorship wage cuts.

TOKIO—After drinking at least two barrels of tea and wanting to be fair here is about how Manchuria looks to me. China owns the lot, Japan owns the house that’s on it. Now who should have the policemen? China is trying to save its country, Japan is trying to save its investments. The League of Nations is trying to save its face. Now somebody has got to lose. Yours, WILL ROGERS

SHANGHAI, Dec. 8 (UP)—Thousands of Chinese students deserted their studies throughout China today to participate in demonstrations against officials whom they charged with failing to oppose aggression by the Japanese in Manchuria. They also demonstrated for furtherance of the Chinese boycott against Japanese goods. At least 5,000 students went on a strike here demanding a more firm attitude against Japan and 25,000 more were said to be considering joining the movement. At Nanking student agitators were estimated to number 10,000 to 15,000, with the lists steadily growing in spite of the government's efforts to return them to their home cities.

BERLIN, Dec. 8 ()—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening answered the challenge of Adolf Hitler and his fascists Tuesday night by warning the nation in a radio address that President Paul Von Hindenburg will invoke martial law if necessary to save the constitution. “There is no other authority in this country save that prescribed by the constitution,” the chancellor said in a voice ringing with emotion. He went to the country over the air after a new and drastic emergency decree, slashing prices, wages and rents had been signed and made into law by President Von Hindenburg. The decree, a 46-page document, the longest ever issued by the government, was designed to provide the final windup for what Dr. Bruening called the “deflation period imposed upon Germany.” The radical character of the measure was indicated by its reduction of wage scales to the level of January 1, 1927.

OSAKA, Dec. 9—Flying from Japan to Manchuria. Every man, woman and Democrat in the world have seen pictures of Japan's famous peak, with the snow on the top of Mount Fujiyama, but think of flying around it. We come by it this afternoon, and what a beautiful country this is to fly over. I didn’t know Japan was so mountainous. Had old Gibbons rubbering for a landing field, but there wasn't any. This is just one of the villages of Japan. It only has two million. The papers here tonight predict a fight at Chinchow. Yours.

1931-11-05.text: | LONDON, Nov. 5.—Mahatma Gandhi, adhering to his intentions, appeared before George V, emperor of India, today at Buckingham Palace clad only in a loin cloth and with his head bare. Ascending the crimson carpeted staircase to the royal picture gallery, he bowed before King George and Queen Mary with his hands palm to palm, in the manner of a Hindu priest pronouncing a benediction. It was pronounced the most extraordinary scene ever witnessed within the palace walls. While the king smiled benignly on his visitor it was noticed that others surveyed his bare legs and shaven head with a critical eye. The king exchanged greetings with other guests, numbering about 600, and included many robed maharajas, and summoned the Mahatma for a private talk in the royal study.

LONDON, Nov. 4—(?)— David Lloyd George, outstanding member of the Liberal party for more than 25 years, resigned his chairmanship today and announced he would not accept any other party office. He set forth his decision in a letter to Sir Herbert Samuel which was made public just before a meeting of the Liberal parliamentary party at which Sir Herbert was elected to succeed the dynamic Welshman. The Lloyd George letter and the election of Sir Herbert reflected the separation of the historic Liberal party into three factions, two of which are reckoned among the supporters of the Ramsay MacDonald national government.

CAPE TOWN, South Africa, (U.P.) Miss Peggy Salaman, London debutante, arrived Thursday after a record-breaking flight from England. Miss Salaman, who left Lympne airdrome, near London, at 11 p.m. last Friday, arrived at 7:30 a.m., breaking the record of six days, 18 hours, set by the late Captain Glen-Kidston, by approximately 35 hours. Miss Salaman, the 19-year-old daughter of Mrs. Elkin Salaman, who was born in Albany, N.Y., required approximately five days, six and one-half hours for the flight of about 6,159 miles.

(United Press Staff Correspondent.) London. —(UP)— The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, leader of India’s millions in their passive fight against Great Britain for independence, was received by the king and queen at a Buckingham Palace tea party today. He was bare-legged and wore his native costume, including a loin cloth. The party was a reception to the delegates to the Indian round table conference, now going on in London, and about 400 guests attended. Gandhi mingled with guests who wore the conventional formal morning garb, and Indian potentates in turbans and western clothes. Gandhi, sitting between his secretary, Mahadeo Desai, and Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, one of his ardent supporters, entered the gates of Buckingham Palace in the back seat of a small salon car. He was bare-headed and wore the same sandals he had on when he started his famous “salt march” of disobedience 18 months ago, for which

It was in the form of a resolution adopted by a joint committee of the Federation of British Industries and the Empire Economic Union. Today’s Daily Mail said that J. A. Thomas will remain in the cabinet as secretary for dominions, and that he will go to Canada very soon and from there to Australia and New Zealand to prepare the ground for imperial trade agreements. The committee adopted the resolution at the conclusion of an exhaustive study of the currency and financial policy. : By United Press LONDON, Nov. 5. - The reorganised cabinet formed by Premier Ramsay MacDonald was announced tonight. Neville Chamberlain was selected as chancellor of the exchequer. Philip Snowden, retiring chancellor of the exchequer, was made lord privy seal, foreshadowing his elevation to the peerage. Stanley Baldwin, leader of the Conservative Party, was made lord president of the council. Sir John Simon, Liberal, was made foreign secretary. Sir Walter Runciman, Liberal, becomes president of the board of trade. Sir Herbert Samuel, successor to David Lloyd George as leader of the Parliamentary Liberal Party, was given the important post of home secretary. Sir Samuel Hoare, Conservative, remains as secretary of state for India and J. H. Thomas, National Labourite, as dominions’ secretary. Sir Philip Cunliffe-Lister was made colonial secretary. Lord Hailsham war secretary, and Lord Lon

LONDON, Nov. 5.—(4)—Despite the huge majority of the Conservatives, Ramsay MacDonald was made premier of the new cabinet, continuing the national coalition agreement. Stanley Baldwin is lord president of the council. Sir John Simon, famous lawyer and leader of one faction of the Liberals quitting Lloyd George, is foreign secretary.

Mexico City,-Miss Lorna Hogg, daughter of the British consul at Vera Cruz and Alexander S. Taylor, formerly of Glasgow, Scotland, were found shot to death in an apartment house here. Police had established no official version of the deaths but expressed the belief Taylor killed Miss Hogg and then shot himself.

1931-07-15.text: BERLIN, July 18.—(UP)—Government officials said today that Germany regards the Hoover plan as in force and is abstaining from all reparations payments, Germany, an official said, made one month's unconditional payment of 51,000,000 marks due today. German officials said Britain and Italy recently had declared their renunciation of the unconditional payments, while France yesterday informed Ambassador Walter E. Edge that Paris did not expect Germany to pay. Belgium has been silent on the subject. The question of continuance of deliveries in kind and delivery of German railway bonds to the International bank on condition that an equivalent sum be given Germany immediately as a loan, will be left to the experts’ conference starting in London Friday, German officials said. By The Associated Press London, July 14.--The effects of the German crisis were apparent today throughout Europe. The situation at a glance: In London--British banks refused German currency. The stock exchange closed weak. Stockholm--Banks and hotels refused to accept German currency and it was feared that thousands of tourists would be stranded without funds as the banks would not cash German checks. Vienna -- The Mercur Bank, which was controlled by the suspended Darmstaedter Und National Bank of Berlin, closed its doors. The Bourse suspended trading in Hungarian stocks for three days. Budapest—All Hungarian banks were closed suddenly, after a ministerial conference, for three days. Brussels—Reports from the borders of Belgium and Luxembourg told of thousands of Germans who were crossing over with their cash. Luxembourg suspended its marks exchange. Paris, July 15.-(P)--Premier Laval today announced that a conference would take place at eleven o'clock tomorrow morning at the ministry of the interior, the conferees including Secretary of State Stimson, Foreign Secretary Anderson of Great Britain, the premier, Foreign Minister Briand and Finance Minister Flanin. This “conference of six” also will include the American ambassador, Walter F. Edge.

Washington, July 15—The American government has been advised officially that the bank for International settlements, under the Hoover plan, has received notices from Great Britain, France and Italy that they do not expect July 15 reparations payments which otherwise would be due. Some of the unconditional payments, it was said at the White House, will be made to the International Bank by Germany, but they will be loaned back to Germany immediately. Great Britain officially advised the bank some days ago that she would not expect today’s payments but France and Italy had not heretofore announced their intentions. The advices were received by the White House through the usual diplomatic channels.

Newport News, Va., July 15—()—Paul Revere, a resident here would like to take some smart alecks for a ride. He sees no reason why practical jokers should call him on the phone at midnight to tell him the British are coming.

PARIS, July 14—Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson arrived from London this evening for a two-day stay in Paris before going to Berlin to return the visit to London of Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius in June. Mr. Henderson has made no effort to hide the fact that his visit to Paris before going to Berlin has the political purpose of reconciling the French and German views in regard to carrying out the Hoover war debt plan and to the extension of further financial aid to Germany. Tomorrow he will be given a luncheon at the French foreign office by Aristide Briand, foreign minister. (Continued on Page Two) wen Brite

| Berlin, Germany—The German cabinet adjourned shortly before midnight without promulgating any of the emergency financial decrees it had planned to meet the country's financial exigencies. It promised action today. Arthur Henderson, British foreign secretary, arrived at Paris and made no effort to deny that his visit was intended to help in reconciling French and German views on the Hoover war debt plan. The effect of the German situation was felt throughout most of the other countries of Europe, where some banks closed and most others refused to accept German currency. All banks in Hungary were ordered closed for three days. The United States Federal Reserve bank at New York announced its willingness to participate in the renewal of the $100,000,000 credit to the Reichbank.

President Von Hindenburg is back in Berlin to take a hand in straightening out the nation's financial tangle and the cabinet, by emergency maneuvers, is believed to have turned loose enough cash so that the banks may be opened to meet the mid-month payroll. Secretary Henry L. Stimson and Arthur Henderson, the British foreign secretary, are in Paris, presumably discussing Germany's situation, among other things, with the French government. London, watching developments with anxiety, is preparing for the meeting of Young Plan experts on Friday at which that plan will be dovetailed with the Hoover moratorium scheme. The Reichsbank raised its discount rate from 7 per cent to 10 per cent.

1931-07-06.text: London, July 6--4%——-London - still is the world’s largest city by a margin of more than a million inhabitants over New York. Metropolitan London, containing the “outer ring,” which corresponds to that known as greater New York, has a population of 6,202,818, preliminary summaries of the census taken April 26 indicate. The population of greater New York in the last United States census was 6,981,917, or 1,200,901 less than its British rival.

RENO, Nev., July 62-The career of Dr. Thomas “English Tommy” Gilchrist, a wiry little family physician who became a power in eastern gambling circles and a partner of Arnold Rothstein, was ended here today in death. He was 51 years old. A sudden attack of pneumonia which ran its course in less than a week caused his death last night. The illness struck while he was in the middle of an article on “the big circus” of Reno, where he came for his wife’s health. “English Tommy” rose to his greatest powers in Philadelphia and New York, but his start as a gambler was made in the colorful little desert town of Tombstone, Ariz. Gambling was almost second nature in the silver boom town and Dr. Gilchrist was fascinated by it. Haunting the gambling halls, the medico-gamester devised his now famous percentage system for craps and roulette. Later he went east, and in Philadelphia began a double life.

Today's discussions, it is understood, were confined to ways and means of giving effect to the conference resolution of May 22, creating the continuing committee, the purpose of which would be: Establishment of a clearing house of information. Howard Ferguson, Canadian high commissioner to Great Britain, who had been chairman of the larger conference. ROME, July 6 (U.P)—Strained relations between the Holy See and the government of Fascist Italy were dangerously near the breaking point again today as a result of the Papal encyclical issued secretly abroad over the week-end. The encyclical—given out in Paris last Friday night before publication in Vatican City the next day—was a direct attack on the Fascist party for alleged attempts to tear the youth of Italy from the Roman Catholic Church. Amazement and irritation were expressed openly by Fascist government authorities led by Premier Benito Mussolini. The effect of the document, sent outside the realm of Fascism to insure its publication abroad without change, was electric, and a stiffening of the government’s attitude in the prolonged dispute between church and state was at once noticeable. PARIS, July 6. (AP)--Secretary Andrew W. Mellon today gave the French negotiators a new memorandum summing up the entire American position regarding President Hoover's moratorium proposals. The document was regarded as so important that Premier Laval requested time to consult his entire cabinet, promising to give Mr. Mellon his answer later.

Tokyo, July 6—(2)—The most serious inter-racial clash in Korea in recent years left 37 persons dead today and police were protecting Chinese colonies in two cities against further possible violence. The deaths occurred at Pingyang yesterday when a mob of Koreans swept through a Chinese colony and attacked the residents with bamboo sticks. Hundreds were injured and scores of residences were destroyed. The rioters numbered 6,000 to 8,000. Among the injured were two policemen who had attempted to protect the Chinese. More than 100 persons were arrested and the Chinese were rounded up and taken to police headquarters for their own protection. At Chemulpo, near Seoul, rioters attacked the police stations. A mob of 2,000 Koreans coursed through the streets, attacking Chinese homes and business places. Reserves had to be called to subdue the rioters. The trouble started July 1 when 500 Chinese

PARIS, July 6—(?)— Alexander Berkman, deported from the United States with Emma Goldman in 1919 for radical activities, faces expulsion from France after three months. The government has issued an order for his deportation but has granted him a suspension in order to investigate his conduct more thoroughly. He has been living in Montparnasse for some time while his former associate has been staying on the French Riviera. He denied he had been dabbling in political affairs and insisted he had no reason to order him from the country.

1931-01-04.text: (By the Associated Press). ENGLAND, Ark., Jan. 3—Farmers estimated to number 500 or more stormed the business section of England today, demanding food and threatening to forcibly take it from merchants before a hurried call to the Red Cross produced authorization of food distribution. More than 250 were provided with food, but sixty-six stood in line tonight. George E. Morris, attorney, spoke to the farmers, practically all of whom were white men, but his speech was interrupted time and again by those in the crowd, from which shouts of “we want food” and “give us food for our starving families” were heard. Merchants whose stores swarmed with the hungry men called a hurried conference and then obtained from the Red Cross headquarters in Little Rock authorization to give the men food. Allowances Made. LONDON, Jan 4 (Sunday) — Princess Louise, oldest sister of King George and British Princess Royal, was stated in an official bulletin early today to be showing increased weakness. Although she has been seriously ill for some months, this is the first recent indication of a recurrence of the heart trouble from which she has suffered for some time. While the physicians gave no further information about the princess's condition, issuance of a bulletin at the unusual hour—12:45 a.m.—was accepted generally as ominous. Princess Louise will be 64 years old February 20. She is slightly more than two years older than her brother, King George. Her husband, the late Duke of Fyfe, died in 1912, leaving her with two daughters, both of whom are married.

OKLAHOMA CITY, Jan. 3—7}-~ An English sparrow perched on a wire short-circuited a 33,000-volt line here today and cut off electric power to Norman and Moore for several minutes. Interurban service also was halted. Featherless, the sparrow, nevertheless, was chirping happily when located.

Interstate Commerce Commission was notified formally today of the desire of eastern railroad executives to consolidate all eastern lines except those in New England into four major systems, but it gave no indication of its attitude. The commission acknowledged receipt of a communication informing it that an agreement had been reached among the roads. The commission said it assumed that the plan was forwarded by the executives for its information only, pending further steps. The acknowledgments went to Presidents W. W. Atterbury of the Pennsylvania Railroad, Daniel Willard of the Baltimore and Ohio, P. E. Crowley of the New York Central and J. J. Bernet of the Chesapeake and Ohio, who worked out the proposed four-system plan.

(By ‘The Associated Press) London, Jan. 3—Industrial troubles in two major industries make this a gloomy week end for Britain. Today a miners’ conference broke down at Cardiff and in Lancashire it appeared that nothing could stop a threatened strike of 200,000 men in the cotton industry. The miners had hoped for some sort of compromise with the owners, but this afternoon their spokesman said they would have to turn to the government. They were going to try for a conference with Ramsay MacDonald on Monday, It looked as though they would suggest once more that the government take over the pits and run the industry at least temporarily, assuring employment to miners who would face great necessity in a strike. Creasy, the English historian, years ago wrote his “Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World.” The sixteenth — the first battle of the Marne — was won by General Joseph Jacques Cesaire Joffre, commander of the French armies in the west during the first year of the great war. Ending a series of disheartening retreats, after four days and nights of incessant fight, he stopped 2,500,000 Germans and drove them back when they were within 30 miles of Paris. After the battle of the Marne, the Germans in the west took to the trenches and dug themselves in and then began four years of a new type of warfare in which every death-dealing device and artifice of human ingenuity was employed. PARIS, Jan. 3 (AP)—Death came today to Marshal Joffre, last of the chief French military leaders of the great war, after a fortnight’s illness in which it was necessary to amputate his left leg. The Marshal would have been 79 years old tomorrow. The end was peaceful. Three members of his family, Mme. Joffre, his son-in-law, M. Lafile, and his brother, Ferdinand, General Issaly, his chief of staff, Colonel Desmazes of his staff, his doctors and a few others were present. He died without coming out from the coma which closed over him at noon Thursday, his life gradually ebbing since. The announcement was made at 8:30 a.m. A member of his military household, Captain Saint Cernin, pale with emotion, emerged from the hospital and in a husky voice telling newspapermen: “The Marshal is dead, gentlemen.” He displayed a bulletin signed by the physicians, Professor Leriche and Drs. Boulin and Font

The world, no less than France itself, tonight mourned the passing of Marshal Joseph Jacques Joffre, saviour of Paris in 1914, who died at 8:23 a.m., after a long and grim struggle with arteritis. His country, plunged in grief, was to honor by a great national funeral the memory of one of the most illustrious soldiers of her history. Death Comes Calmly Marshal Joffre—the “Papa” Joffre of the French Poilu and of all his countrymen, passed away peacefully.

1931-03-27.text: Dublin, Irish Free State, March 27.—(#)—The Saorstat today mourned Timothy Michael Healy, Irish parliamentarian extraordinary and its first Governor General, who died in the night after a three weeks illness. He was 75 years old. The end had been foreseen for several days, although he was ill with what was thought to be only a bad cold for some time before the seriousness of his malady, a bronchial affection, was appreciated. He took a turn for the worse yesterday morning and his son was summoned to his bedside. Death came at 7:50 P. M. As a member of parliament for what is now the Saorstat, Healy founded a tradition of his own, the “Irish Nights” in which he would sit back with his silk hat tipped over his nose, pretending not to listen to debate. Suddenly he would arise, obtain the floor and make a speech of vitriol coated with honeyed Irish words. He withdrew from the House of Commons

Woods, 32, Buffalo, New York, won approximately $886,360 in the Irish hospital sweepstakes at today’s grand national at Aintree with his ticket on Greeaac, which placed second. His ticket had cost him about $2.50. The other two big prizes in the sweepstakes went to Emilio Scala, London cafe owner, who had the ticket on the winning horse, “Grakle,” and to George Dyamond of Cape Town, South Africa, who won third place with his ticket on Annandale. Scala must divide his prize of more than one and three-quarters millions, however, as he sold part of his ticket before the race. Dublin, Irish Free State, March 26 (P).—Timothy Michael Healy, over whose bittersweet sallies in the House of Commons old timers still chuckle, died today at the age of 75. He was the first governor of the Irish Free State, but he will be remembered longer as one of the most brilliant Parliamentary speakers who ever galvanized the House of Commons into action. In the old days before the Free State got a Parliament of its own he used to sit in his corner of the House his silk hat tipped down over his nose, pretending not to listen. Then he would get up on his feet and begin one of those characteristic speeches in which the vitriol of his sarcasm was overlaid with the honey of his Irish humor.

London, Mar. 25 — After listening to David Lloyd George urge “a policy of cooperation, not frustration,” the Liberal candidates’ association deferred the vote today on the question of general support of the MacDonald government. Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, asked today that the debate on the vote of censure be deferred until after the Easter holidays and the proposal was agreed to by Prime Minister MacDonald. Parliament reassembles after Easter on April 14, but the date for the debate has not yet been fixed. Premier MacDonald already has indicated that, if defeated on this vote the government probably will resign or recommend a general election.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Mar. 26—Timothy Healy, veteran Irish statesman and first governor of the Irish Free State, died here at 7:50 p. m. this evening. “Tim” Healy, as he was known not only in Ireland but throughout the world, was 76 years old. He had been ill for some time but throughout his sickness his doctors were reticent about reporting his progress. It was believed at first that he was suffering from a very bad cold.

LONDON, March 27.—It’s a hundred to five that your next child won’t be a twin and you can take out an insurance policy against it being a twin with a premium of five per cent. Douglas Cox, London insurance broker, is an authority on insurance against twins. He takes the view that his policy is one of the most logical, from an insurance man’s point of view. For five pounds premium, paid six months prior to the expectant birth, a policy is issuable paying 109 pounds in the event twins are born. Both children must live 24 hours under the provision of the policy. Some premiums depending upon the frequency of twins in the ancestors of the prospective parents, might be three pounds.

LOS ANGELES, Mar. 27.—A six-foot boy who weighs 235 pounds wears No. 13 shoes and uses the English language like a ‘college professor,’ today awaited a court decision which will determine if medical science shall be applied to halt his phenomenal growth. At 14 years of age, Adolphe E. Roome Jr. is larger than most men. His father, Dr. Adolphe E. Roome Sr., believes he should receive injections to halt the activity of his pituitary glands. The mother opposed her divorced husband's efforts to secure a court decision compelling her to agree to the treatment. After two days of testimony, the case was taken under advisement by Superior Judge Lester W. Roth. Adolphe Jr., a handsome, black-haired boy who towered over every other person in the courtroom, sided with his mother. He said he feared that the injections would affect him mentally. In a letter to the Seaham labor party, which had demanded his resignation, Mr. MacDonald said: “Any action I may take in response to any resolution passed will be only after I have finished the duty which I am now undertaking and not before. “I regret very much that without knowing any of the facts Seaham Harbor’s deputies have passed the resolution which you have communicated. LONDON, Sept. 2. At the end of an all day meeting of the new cabinet this afternoon it was announced a special session of parliament had been summoned for Sept. 8. The cabinet sat for nearly five hours and completed its financial plan for meeting the budget emergency. It was understood the ministers agreed that Prime Minister Macdonald should immediately demand a vote of confidence when the House of Commons convenes.

LONDON, Sept. 2—(4%—The tide of opposition against Prime Minister Macdonald and his parliamentary economy program was believed by some newspapers today to be turning in his favor. They noted increasing signs that many who followed the premier with devotion in years past are experiencing heartburnings over the split in the labor party and what has been described as the dictation of trade unionism to socialism. Mr. Macdonald receives daily letters of sympathy and encouragement from many parts of the country and some of them are from laborites who indicate that, while they favor his action to balance the budget, they are compelled as trade unionists to follow the directions of their organizations. Macdonald informed his Seaham constituents today that he proposes to retain his parliamentary seat for that constituency at least until he has concluded his task of setting British finances to rig

Krasnojarsk, Siberia, Sept. 2 (UP) — Miss Amy Johnson, British girl flier, arrived here at 8:10 a.m. today on her return flight to England from Japan. She continued the journey after 20 minutes for rest and refueling her plane.

By the Associated Press. London, Sept. 1.—Stanley Baldwin, leader of the conservative party and president of the council in the new three-party government, today appealed to every conservative member of parliament to support the emergency cabinet's financial legislation. “The forthcoming session is to be one of the most critical in our history,” Mr. Baldwin said in a letter sent to all of his parliamentary followers. “I beg you at whatever personal sacrifice to be present on the appointed day and to give your consistent support to the government to enable them to pass the necessary financial legislation.”

TOKYO, Japan, Sept. 2 (U.P)--An airplane race across the Pacific Ocean with a $25,000 prize to the winner was forecast today when government customs officials released the airplane of Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, Jr., from custody. Pangborn and Herndon, who recently flew from New York to Tokyo through Russia, immediately announced plans to leave for Sabishiro Beach, 50 miles from here, and prepare to start across the Pacific. Don Moyle, known as the “Jail or glory” flier, is planning to take off this week on an attempted flight to Seattle. It was considered likely the two flights would be started about the same time.

GENEVA, Sept. 2 (UP)—The French government has made an informal request to the League of Nations secretariat to postpone the world disarmament conference scheduled for February, 1932, the United Press learned today. The request was made Tuesday. Due to its informal nature it was regarded as a “feeler” and was not expected to be discussed publicly in its present form. News of the French request was obtained from reliable sources which vouchsafed its accuracy. The proposal by France indefinitely to postpone the arms parley was motivated by the general elections in France in May of next year, the United States presidential elections and the possibility of elections in Great Britain. Strong opposition to the proposal, however, was expected in the United States, Germany, Soviet Russia and Hungary. These nations favor the original date next February.

BARCELONA, Spain, Sept. 2 WP — (Convicts revolted in 2 prisons here Wednesday, setting it afire, and then turned to fighting the guards. A number of shots were fired. The revolt followed a hunger strike which has been in progress for some time. The prison was in flames and several fire companies were called out in an effort to halt the blaze.

Sir Edward Elgar, “master of the king’s musick,” who has just turned 74 himself, is one of the new barons. He is the composer of “Pomp and Circumstance” and other oratorios. He was made a knight of the British empire in 1904 and decorated with the order of merit in 1911. The other baronetcies, Sir Thomas Jaffrey, consulting actuary of the Aberdeen Savings Bank; Philip Henry Devitt, founder of the Nautical College at Pangbourne, and Sir Herbert Gibson, an organizer of the empire trade exposition in Buenos Aires. LONDON, June 3. — King George V celebrated his 66th birthday today, recovered in health and vigorous enough to resume horseback riding. He had a more strenuous birthday program than usual, including a visit to Epsom Downs to witness the annual running of the derby. A family party at Buckingham Palace was arranged for this evening. A surprise was caused by the king’s birthday honor list, which failed to create new Labor party peers to bolster Premier James Ramsay MacDonald's government in the House of Lords. The list created no new peers and only four new baronets and 25 knights.

London, June 3 (AP)—Englishmen sitting in their own homes saw the derby by television today from the parade of the horses at the start to the flash past the finish line. The “telecast” was by the Baird television company in cooperation with the British Broadcasting Company.

COUNTRIES OF Europe, especially England, are wondering how they can avoid competition and dumping of cheap Russian goods, and, at the same time, eagerly accept money that Russia spends in purchase of machinery and raw materials. This country, a little more virtuous, or, perhaps, more foolish than the others, has cut down Russian purchases in this country by more than half within a year. That may be high morality, but it is poor business. IT WILL TAKE more than words, or dislike of Bolshevist theories, to conquer Russia's industrial campaign, backed by able producers and good salesmen. For instance, when United States soldiers look closely at the little box of matches supplied by the government they will see written in small type: 'Made In Russia.' (BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS; Carnoustie, Scotland, June 3.-- Johnny Farrell, smiling young Irishman from Mamaroneck, N. Y. today shared the lead in the first round of the British open golf championship with Henry Cotton, British pro, both carding 72. Playing through a strong wind Farrell went out in a par-cracking 33, and staggered home in 29, a garrison finish on the last three holes giving him his score. Tommy Armour, former American open champion, came home with a 73. Gene Sarazen, former United States Open champion, had a 74. MacDonald Smith, who led the qualifying field of 109, with 141, lapsed just often enough today to pull him down to a 75.

1931-01-03.text: LONDON, Jan. 2—(4)—General astonishment has been aroused in Great Britain by the departure of Miss Amy Johnson, 23-year-old aviator, on a long lone flight across snow-covered northern Eurasia to Peiping, China. Leaving Hendon airdrome yesterday forenoon, she stopped at Lympne momentarily and proceeded to Liege, Belgium, for the night. She expects to continue to Berlin, then to Moscow, where, equipping her plane with skis, she will fly across barren Byark and to Peiping. In addition to general fear for her safety in view of the extreme hazards of such a journey, her friends were represented today as feeling considerable anxiety on account of her health. The Daily Express said she was in ill health and had become a neurotic from the strain of her flight to Australia. (By the Associated Press) Tharawaddy, India, Jan. 2.—That fantastic figure of actual or assumed princely rank who dreamed a mad dream of creating an empire of his own in the fever-ridden jungles of Burma remains a man of mystery in death as he was in life. British soldiers crawling through the tropical growth which lies like a spider's web about the palace of the man who would be king came upon a detachment of rebels which they routed in a sharp engagement, killing 30 of the enemy. But when they burst into the stronghold they found the master mind of the past month's reign of terror dead. The soldiers were sure this was the mysterious leader of the recent raids on jungle villages in which many peaceful natives and several white men had perished. This man wore rich raiment bearing various symbols of high rank, and on his fair head was wound a royal turban. It was not the might of the Brit

| COLOGNE, Germany, Jan. 3. (P)— Miss Amy Johnson, British girl aviator, who took off from here for Berlin at 11:05 a. m. today on the next stage of her flight from England to Peiping, China. Her route lies over Russia, Siberia and Mongolia and is particularly hazardous at this time of the year.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 3—The British gunboat Mantis, on patrol duty in the Yangtze Kiang, was attacked today by 800 insurgent troops who opened a heavy fire upon her. The Mantis replied with great effect, inflicting many casualties. There were no casualties aboard the Mantis.

BERLIN, Jan. 3 (AP)—Miss Amy Johnson, British woman flier, landed at Tempelhof airdrome near here at 5:34 p. m., today after a flight from Cologne. She is attempting to fly from England to Peiping, China. Miss Johnson drifted clear off her course northward to Leubz, near Parchim, in Mecklenburgh-Schwerin, where she was compelled to make a forced landing. After ascertaining her whereabouts she again took off and reached Berlin without incident.

(7) — In little chapels scattered through the grimy valleys of South Wales, men and women spent today praying that some way may be found to end the dispute between masters and men which sent 140,000 coal miners into idleness yesterday. They pinned their hopes on a meeting tomorrow of the coal conciliation board from which might come a compromise ending the strike, few days more of which would bring misery and want to tens of thousands. Manchester, Eng., Jan. 2.—A great stoppage of work in the Lancashire cotton industry, affecting 200,000 men, tonight threatened to add to the gloom into which the new year has already been plunged by the coal dispute in South Wales. At a special meeting between members of the Cotton Spinners and Manufacturers Association and the Weavers’ Amalgamation, hurriedly summoned tonight, negotiations between the employers’ and weavers’ representatives broke down on the question of “more looms per weaver” demanded by the employers. Since leaders of the workers already have declared they will call out employees from any mill where this system is worked on Monday, the outlook was considered black tonight.

1931-01-12.text: LONDON Eng., Jan. 12 (UP)— The well from which King Richard III had his last drink before he was slain at Bosworth, has been located behind a cottage here. Title deeds of the two old cottages contained this inscription: “With water drawn from this well Richard the Third, King of England, assuaged his thirst when fighting in the most desperate and hostile manner with Henry, Duke of Richmond, and about to lose before night his life, together with his sceptre, August 22, A.D. 1485.

HORTA, Azores (UP)—A strong “northeaster” bringing stormy weather and vicious winds whipped over the Azores Monday while an apparently hopeless watch was kept for a man and a woman who had challenged the Atlantic on a flight of 2,000 miles from Bermuda to the Azores. Anxiety that had mounted during the hours in which Mrs. Beryl Hart and Lieut. William S. MacLaren were not heard from in their white seaplane Tradewind turned to a faint hope that they might have missed their mark, a small group of islands in the ocean and continued to the safety of the European coast. But no word of their progress reached Paris, their ultimate destination, and ships east of the Azores had not reported sighting their plane. The Tradewind left Hamilton, Bermuda, at 11:15 a.m., Saturday. The fliers were 24 hours overdue here at 7 a.m. Monday. Unless they landed at sea and were picked up by a ship without wirel

Shanghai, Jan. 10.—(P)—Hundreds of persons died in a snow and dust storm which subsided tonight after raging two days southward from Mongolia’s deserts to the Yangtse valley. The storm laid an icy siege over all north China; hundreds of thousands were suffering acutely in temperatures averaging 15 degrees below zero. Large numbers continued to freeze to death among the poverty stricken populace.

Shanghai—(—Winter, in this part of the world the harbinger of death and intense suffering, Monday gripped virtually all of North China, Manchuria, Siberia, Korea and Japan. It paralyzed communications, crippled railroads and took an undetermined toll of human life and property. China, from the Yangtse river northward, lay under a mantle of ice and snow, while frigid blasts from the north added to the depth of the white blanket with a mixture of snow and sand from the barren steppes of Mongolia. It was feared thousands had perished from the intense cold in northern China alone, dispatches describing the finding of scores of frozen bodies in the streets of large cities. The fate of western China, much of which was isolated owing to disrupted communications, was uncertain. PHANGHAL, Jan. 11 — Sub-zero weather, spreading death and destruction, gripped virtually all of China north of the Yangtse river today. A vast blanket of snow and ice reached from the sea westward as far as Kansu province and from the Yangtse northward into the barren wastes of Mongolia, when the blizzard came. Fragmentary reports of the storm, which raged fiercely for three days, trickled in over crippled communications. No estimate of the dead was available, but it was feared the toll would run into the thousands. The local weather office described the blizzard as the most severe of many years. Bodies in Streets. Scores of frozen bodies were picked up in the streets of Peiping and Tientsin, Chihli province. Early this morning, not a word had been heard nor a sign seen of Mrs. Beryl Hart, flying widow, and Lieut. William S. Rockets flashed through the dark and stormy sky in attempts to pierce a heavy cloud-bank which hemmed in this island city. (By The Associated Press) Tokyo, Jan. 12.—Five persons were killed and 70 or 80 injured as part of a passenger train jumped the track and fell into a river while crossing a bridge near Kochi at 4 o’clock this morning.

BOMBAY, India, Jan. 12.—Serious disorders broke out again today for the first time in recent weeks of the civil disobedience movement. Police clashed repeatedly with independence volunteers and members of the Congress who attempted to enforce a hartal or strike in protest against the execution of four men charged with the murder of a policeman at Sholapur. About 150 persons were injured, at least 25 of them seriously.

It lacked one hour of 12 o'clock last night when he was hustled out the back gate of the penitentiary and placed in a motor car which sped through the darkness of the Poona hills and deposited him on a Bombay train at a point ten miles distant. But before he left, the bent little nationalist leader startled officials with these words: “I expect to be back here within two months. I am not at all happy at the thought of entering again the whirlpool of life in the outside world, with its overwhelming suffering, sorrow and sordidness.
