LONDON, Jan. 26.—(P)—Premier Ramsay MacDonald warned the House of Commons today that unless Great Britain is willing to continue peaceful negotiations for the settlement of the Indian problem, British soldiers must be prepared to subdue by force not only the Indian masses but also the spirit of the times. Mr. MacDonald said that by a policy of repression Great Britain would obtain neither credit nor success. A great proportion of the masses, he said, were women and children, and the task would develop into one of repression of the entire Indian population. “If we are prepared,” he said, “to stage for the whole world the failure of our political genius and at the same time provide a spectacle which will bring our name and fame very low indeed, then refuse to allow us to go on. “But if, on the other hand, you want to bind India to you by bonds of confidence and make her happy within your e

LONDON, Jan. 27 (#)—Developments in parliament today were believed generally to point to a government victory when the ministry’s trades dispute bill comes up for its second reading tomorrow. So strong has opposition to the measure grown that the prospective division has been regarded with the utmost apprehension by the government. The chief Liberal whip told a party meeting last night that the majority of the Liberals had agreed to abide by the official Liberal decision to abstain from voting and that fewer than twelve Liberals would vote against the government. A motion of censure of the government offered by the orthodox Liberal following criticizes the government on its unemployment record. The motion of censure forestalls a Conservative motion which has been in the offing for weeks. It is generally believed that David Lloyd George, the Liberal leader, has neither wish nor hope for h

Bombay, India, Jan. 27.— Mahatma Gandhi, released last night from the British prison, urged the authorities to liberate thousands of Nationalists still in jail, emphasizing the necessity for a general political amnesty if peace is to be restored in India. Tumultuous multitudes surrounded Gandhi upon his arrival here. They gave him one of the greatest ovations of his strange career. The women garlanded him with flowers and entwined his neck with thousands of yards of material which resembles American ticker tape. Outside the house in which he will stay crowds prostrated themselves before the mystical leader in adoration and worshipped him as if he were a god.

The Nationalist boycott of foreign cloth, the party’s refusal to pay taxes and its picketing of liquor, drug and cloth shops will go on. The Mahatma, idol of millions, issued this first concrete statement of the policy of his party as he sat Hindu fashion on a stone floor here, surrounded by newspaper men. It was the first statement of the kind since his release from the prison at Poona last night. Gandhi, leader of the Indian Nationalists, served notice on Great Britain today that his efforts in behalf of Indian independence cannot cease. THE HAGUE, Jan. 27 (UP) — Memorial services were held here today for Mme. Anna Pavlova, the Russian ballerina, who died here last week. The body will be sent to London tonight where it will lie in state before cremation.

Washington, Jan. 27.—(4)—The British government has made formal representations to the state department regarding “unsatisfactory conditions” under which British subjects are being held at some centers and particularly at Seattle, Wash., for deportation. The state department, in a reply to the note presented December 18 by Ambassador Lindsay, stated the labor department expected the new building at Seattle to be ready for occupancy in August. The state department communicated the British representations to the labor department, which answered the unsatisfactory conditions due to the lack of space at Seattle had been known to the department for some time.

1931-08-13.text: Bombay, India, Aug. 13—(/)—The Indian National Congress today decided definitely not to participate in the second round table conference on Indian affairs at London this fall. Mahatma Gandhi's son, Devdas Gandhi, said as he left the meeting of the Congress working committee: “There is absolutely no chance that my father will go to London.”

LONDON, (UP).— The gravity of the financial and political situation in Great Britain was emphasized Thursday by the dramatic and sudden arrival of Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, in London. Baldwin arrived from Aix-Les-Bains, almost without baggage, to be present in case of an appeal from Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald for the co-operation of the opposition parties in the labor government's urgent efforts to meet the nation’s pressing financial problems. Meanwhile, the labor cabinet's economy committee resumed its special sessions at No. 10 Downing Street at 11 a.m., for a further searching study of the economic situation. It adjourned 90 minutes later. Neville Chamberlain, chairman of the conservative party, arrived after an all-night ride from Scotland, and Sir Herbert Samuel, prominent liberal party leader, reached London from Sheringham, in Norfolkshire. YORKTOWN, Va, Aug. 1—(r) Cornwallis again will surrender at Yorktown in October. After weeks of controversy over whether the capitulation of the British Revolutionary War commander should be depicted this Fall at the 150th anniversary celebration, the United States Yorktown Sesquicentennial Commission announced last night the surrender scene would be re-enacted. A variety of reasons were given for the proposed deletion. Among them were that the scene might be offensive to British visitors, that difficulties would be encountered in training a large body of troops in 18th Century tactics and that it was against the tradition of the army to re-enact the surrender of a foreign foe.

BOMBAY, (UP).—The Mahatma Gandhi probably will not go to London for the much-heralded second round table conference. This decision has been reached, it was learned Thursday, because the executive of the all-India congress regards as unsatisfactory the reply by the Viceroy, the Earl of Willingdon, to representations by the Indians regarding alleged British infringements of the pact signed by Gandhi and the former Viceroy, Lord Irwin. There have been recent rumors that dissension might halt the Gandhi trip to London, but reports were not taken seriously until today when Gandhi indicated he will stand as firmly on principle in this matter as in others of the past.

LONDON, Aug. 14.—Twenty-six persons were killed and sixty-two injured when a powder magazine exploded at Macao, a Portuguese colony in China, today, according to dispatches received in London. The dead included five children and damage was estimated at a million dollars. The explosion was due to the spontaneous combustion of ten tons of powder.

LONDON, Aug. 15—The three major British political parties were prepared today to cooperate in seeking means to solve the nation's grave financial problems. Following a hurried conference with the conservative leaders Stanley Baldwin and Neville Chamberlain, Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald invited the Herbert Samuel, liberal leader, to a three-party conference on governmental economy scheduled for early next week. Baldwin rushed back from France and Chamberlain made an overnight trip from Scotland to meet the prime minister and chancellor of the exchequer Philip Snowden at 10 Downing Street today. HONG KONG, China, Aug. 13—Twenty-six persons were killed and 62 injured in the explosion early today at Macao, Portuguese concession seaport 35 miles southwest of here, it was found after investigation. By The Associates Firm. LONDON, Aug. 13.—Despite the decision of the Indian national congress not to participate in the all-India round table conference, that conference will be held beginning Sept. 6 as planned, it was stated today in authoritative circles.

1931-05-02.text: REYKJAVIK, Iceland, May 2, —Search for Augustine Courtauld, British explorer who is marooned on the Greenland ice cap, moved toward its goal today by land, by sea, and by air. Captain Albin Ahrenberg, Swedish flier, landed here last night after a flight from Bergen, Norway, via the Faroe Islands. He hopes to resume his flight today. The patrol boat Odin reached the ice barrier of Greenland some time earlier and unloaded an airplane for Siguard Jonssen to take off. The crew refitted the machine with skis. Weather and sea conditions were favorable for a flight. Two groups of dog teams, driven by friends of the scientist, were believed to be mushing across the frozen wastes toward the tiny meteorological station in which he volunteered to spend the winter. LONDON — (U.P) The annual threat of world-wide violence in international labor's celebration of May Day was safely passed today except in Portugal, where disturbances assumed a serious character. A United Press survey showed demonstrations - some peaceful and some violent - on every continent, with Moscow's great parade and demonstration at Red Square setting a pace far in advance of any other country. Except in the new republic of Spain, where an imposing but quiet demonstration occurred in Madrid and a gun fight killed one and wounded a dozen in Barcelona, the manifestations were closely restricted and lacked enthusiasm. Three persons were killed in Cuba demonstrations. Two were killed in Lisbon and a dozen others injured in an outbreak which was considered political in character due to recent revolutionary moves in Portugal. BUCHAREST, Rumania, May 1. (AP) — Two devoted women tonight risked their lives by remaining at the bedside of nine-year-old Crown Prince Michael, gravely ill with diphtheria. One is his mother, Queen Helen, estranged wife of King Carol. The other is an English governess. Both watchers were given anti-toxin injections today. As a result, the queen had a slight fever tonight, but she made light of the indisposition. The condition of the prince meanwhile had improved, and royal physicians expressed conviction that he would live, although the crisis has not yet been passed. There seemed a possibility the child’s sickness might, to some extent, bring his parents together. Yesterday King Carol saw Helen briefly in an antechamber of the sick room in her quarters of the Sinaia palace. It was learned that two groups of dog-teams left Angmagsalik this afternoon, manned by friends of the missing scientist. Meantime, Captain Albin Ahrenberg, a pilot, landed here at 10:05 tonight from Bergen, Norway, by way of the Faeroe Islands. He hopes to proceed early tomorrow. Serious motor trouble developed, the message said, and the expedition would have to be abandoned. Failure of the Odinn’s efforts had no effect on other expeditions setting out to find Courtauld. Captain Albin Ahrenberg, the Swedish aviator, took off for Angmagsalik this afternoon. He landed here last night from Bergen, Norway. The Odinn got as far as the ice barrier, the plane was unloaded, and prepared for a take-off when the trouble developed. Examination showed that it was so serious that the plane will have to be brought back here for repairs.

LONDON, May 1 (®)—The tripartite naval accord, heralded some weeks ago as a triumph settling European naval problems, apparently has simmered down to an Anglo-Italian agreement with France on the sidelines. Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson has not despaired of better success, but formal drafting of the triangular treaty is definitely suspended. Little can be done until the foreign ministers of the three nations meet formally at Geneva this month in connection with the council of the league of nations. The British efforts are at present directed toward preventing a situation which might prejudice the success of the world disarmament conference in 1932.

BATAVIA, Java, April 20 (ADP) Wing Commander Charles Kingsford Smith, flying the Australia to England airmail in his plane the Southern Cross arrived here at 2:16 p.m., from Sourabaya, where soldiers yesterday helped to extricate the machine when it stuck in the mud as he was taking off.

Las Palmas, Canary Islands, May 2—(AP)—Commander Friedrich Christiansen of the German seaplane DO-X sent word today from Rio de Oro that he planned to take off tomorrow morning for Bolama, Portuguese West Africa, on the next stage of his flight to South America. The plane left here yesterday morning and covered the 200 odd miles to Rio de Oro on the African west coast without incident. The distance from there to Bolama is about 950 miles. Named Oklahoma Delegate Oklahoma City, May 2. (AP)—H. M. Arnold, Buffalo, was appointed today by Governor Murray as his representative to a conference of states called by Governor Woodring of Kansas at Wichita, May 17. Governor Murray will not be able to attend.

1931-10-29.text: | London, Oct. 29 (AP)--The British national government was back at work today under the direction of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, cautioning humility over the results of the election and addressing itself to the sober task of executing the “doctor’s mandate” it asked and received from the people. Backed by an unprecedented majority of more than 500 of the 615 seats of the House of Commons, the Prime Minister began today a series of conferences with King George and with his cabinet to lay the groundwork for the rehabilitation program which is to be presented to Parliament early next month. The British Press, adding its voice to that of Mr. MacDonald and Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, cautioned the country to remember the victory was a triumph of the national government and not of any party, in spite of the fact that the conservatives will occupy nearly five-sixths of the seats

London, Oct. 29—Swept into power with a mammoth majority of more than 550 of the 615 seats in the House of Commons, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's National Government will be able to dominate Parliament as no other administration in the history of Democratic Britain. No British Prime Minister was ever confronted with more serious problems at home and abroad than those before Mr. MacDonald. None was ever so potentially empowered to deal with them as the tired, disheveled Scotsman who flew from Seaham Harbor to London yesterday to save precious time in getting to work. Returns to Downing Street with a bunch of white heather in his hand—the same sort of lucky token he has used since the emergency government was formed—he entered the big door of No. 10 Downing Street yesterday afternoon to begin another chapter of his remarkable political life. The Prime Minister’s first task will be the

By The Associated Press. LONDON, Oct. 28.—A Reuters Agency dispatch from Tokyo today said that Japan has accepted the ‘League of Nations’ plan for a year’s holiday on armaments on condition it does not affect plans already authorized and that neighboring states, especially non-members of the league, also agree.

LONDON, Oct. 29 (4j)—An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Dar-Es-Salaam, Tanganyika, East Africa, today said an American tourist named Heron was clawed to death by a lion which he was in the act of shooting while two American companions prepared to photograph the feat. The first names of the men were not learned. The last names of Heron's two companions were Peret and Homer, the dispatch said. The tragedy happened on the Serengeti Plains. Peret and Homer had their camera trained on Heron and he was about to shoot when the lion charged. Heron was badly clawed and was rushed to a hospital, but he died later.

| London, Oct. 28 —(4)—Fourteen women, led by Nancy, Lady Astor, contribution of First Families of Virginia to British politics, will grace the green leather-backed chairs of the House of Commons when the new house is convoked next month. Thirteen of the 14 have staunch conservation convictions. One, the incalculable Miss Megan Lloyd George, whose election platform was Ruth’s “Whither Thou goest, I will go”—she applied it to her father—is a liberal. Not one of the 38 woman candidates of the labor party was elected although there were 10 women laborites in the last parliament. Four Are Veterans Only four of the 14 victors have sat in the House of Commons before—Lady Astor, Lady Iveagh, the Duchess of Atholl and Miss Lloyd George. Among those who will be missing when parliament convenes will be 26-year-old Jenny Lee, Scottish miner's daughter, whose pretty features, black eyes, black bobbe

LONDON, Oct. 29. (4%-—Premier Ramsay MacDonald held the first meeting of the nationalist cabinet since before the election to lay plans for the groundwork in a rehabilitation program to be offered the House of Commons next month. Chief problems are stabilization of the pound, review of war debts and correction of an adverse trade balance. It was expected the conservatives, holding nearly five-sixths of the seats, would demand a strong protective tariff. The press cautioned the country that the victory was one of the nationalist government and not of a single party. MacDonald and Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, made similar statements.

BUENOS AIRES. Oct. 29—A sharp rise in the prices of wheat and corn today was attributed to heavy buying in London on the theory that a tariff is imminent in Great Britain and that grain was being rushed to British elevators before the new government could take any tariff action. The spot value of wheat rose to approximately 48 1-2 cents a bushel.

Aberdeen, Wash., Oct. 29 (P)— Will F.B. Herren, Aberdeen contractor and big game hunter, died Monday in Nairobi, British East Africa, from injuries suffered October 21, when mauled by a lion, said a cable received today from Gus Peret, of Yoncalla, Ore., one of Herren's companions on an African big game photographing expedition. The lion charged while the party was taking motion pictures on the plains of Tanganyika. The beast felled Herren and was clawing and chewing him when a bullet from Peret’s rifle ended his life.

1931-10-28.text: LONDON, Oct. 28 —(/P)—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald, swept into parliament by the landslide which gave the national government more than 500 seats in the new House of Commons, won by nearly 6,000 votes in the Seaham Harbor constituency where the official Labor Party repudiated him a month ago. Running as the national Labor candidate, he defeated the regular Labor Party’s nominee and snowed under a communist opponent. His victory left Arthur Henderson, who succeeded him as the Labor chief, the only party head not sent back to the House of Commons. Stanley Baldwin was returned unopposed; David Lloyd George won, though his old-line liberals in the House will number fewer than half a dozen; Sir John Simon, chief of the liberals who broke away from Lloyd George, won by a substantial majority. The Conservatives, with 567 returns available, had 447 of the 615 seats in the House, breaking a

LONDON, Oct. 28 (Wednesday) — Amazing turnovers in former labor pluralities indicated this morning on the basis of almost one-half of the returns from Britain’s general election that the supporters of Ramsay MacDonald's national government would win hands down. With 282 constituencies heard from, the government had a total of 255 seats in the House of Commons against 95 for the opposition and two independents. The membership of the House is 615. Henderson Defeated The government forces swept out of office labor's most important leaders, chief among them being Arthur Henderson, foreign secretary of the MacDonald cabinet, who broke with his life-long friend and refused to follow him into the national ministry. J. H. Thomas, dominions secretary who stuck by Mr. MacDonald, showed the other side of the picture by again winning his seat in the House. So great was the strength of the

LONDON. (UP) — Great Britain has repudiated the Socialist-Labor party in one of the most decided revulsions of national sentiment in its history. Returns from yesterday’s general election gave the national coalition government and the Conservative party an overwhelming vote of confidence to proceed with its program for National rehabilitation. Labor was defeated, shattered and humiliated in the landslide. Its chief, Arthur Henderson, and all but two or three of its leaders lost their seats in parliament. The conservatives, the National government Liberals who turned from David Lloyd George, and the few Labor followers of Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald swept constituency after constituency, taking from Labor the seats it had won in the 1929 election. The national government attained its actual majority of 308 early in the afternoon. With 282 returns yet to come, the government had 308

London, Oct. 28—(4)—"The country has been frightened out of its wits and has run away," George Bernard Shaw observed this morning, "straight into the very danger it was trying to avoid." "It wasn't an election—it was a Stampede," the noted playwright said. "The returns show it. I have no hope for the rest of the country. There isn’t going to be any opposition. Of course it won't make much difference because the real government is underground." The government, he said, is going to be one of financial interests and the press. "The danger," he said, "lies in the political ignorance of these financial interests. They are clever in high finance, but hopeless duffers when it comes to genuine public finance. These financial interests are very much at the mercy of circumstance and one does not know exactly how the circumstance will go."

SEAHAM HARBOR, Durham, England, Oct. 28. (AP)—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald was reelected to the House of Commons from this constituency. He was in a three-cornered fight, running against William Coxon, a school teacher, the regular labor candidate, and George Lumley, a communist. The Prime Minister’s majority was 5,951.

London, Oct. 28—(4)—Ramsay MacDonald's government today rode the crest of one of the most surging electoral tides of British political history, a sweep of votes that seemed to have flattened the labor party and all but obliterated David Lloyd George's liberals. Confident predictions were made that when the results are all known the MacDonald ministry would have a majority of 400 in the new Parliament which meets next December—the answer of Britain's 20,000,000 voters to the Prime Minister’s appeal for a “doctor's mandate” to cure the country's financial ills. Returns from 312 of the 615 British Parliamentary districts shortly after noon left the standing of the parties as follows: Conservatives 245; National Labor 7; Liberals 87; Opposition Labor 27; Communists 6; Independents 1. This gave the national government a potential total of 289; opposition 23; doubtful 1. A total of 302 seats r

28,— (IPI © postalist prime-minister, “led” the conservatives and their Allies to a smashing victory in yesterday's general election. His former Labor party was crushingly defeated in the coalition government's appeal to the country for a “Doctor's Mandate” to solve the economic crisis. Labor, which on dissolution of parliament was the largest party with 280 seats, emerged from the people's verdict with less than 50 seats, returns today showed. The national government probably had more than 550 and the conservative party alone close to 500. It was an astounding victory for MacDonald, the war-time pacifist and outcast, who led the labor party to the rule of the country and then deserted it for what he deemed the country’s good. Fighting MacDonald and the conservatives, the party was almost destroyed. Its leader Arthur Henderson, and nearly every one of its prominent members, failed of re-

LONDON, Oct. 28.—(#)—Leading figures in the British general election fared as follows: Elected: Ramsay MacDonald, national labor. Stanley Baldwin, conservative. David Lloyd George, liberal. Sir John Simon, national liberal. J. H. Thomas, national labor. George Lansbury, labor. Malcolm MacDonald, national labor. Lord Burgley, conservative. Herbert Samuel, national liberal. Sir Samuel Hoare, conservative. Sir Austen Chamberlain, conservative. Neville Chamberlain, conservative. Sir Philip Cunnliffe-Lister, conservative. Winston Churchill, conservative. Defeated: Arthur Henderson, labor. Tom Shaw, labor. J. R. Clynes, labor. A. V. Alexander, labor. Arthur Hayday, labor. Arthur Henderson, jr., labor. Sir Ben Turner, labor. Oliver Baldwin, labor. S. Saklatvala, communist. Edwin Scrymgeour, prohibitionist. Edgar Wallace, liberal. Philip Guedalla, liberal. Sir Oswald Mosley, independent. Ben Til

1931-02-28.text: ROME, Feb. 28 (A. P.)—Great Britain and Italy today reached an accord in principle for the settlement of all naval problems left pending by the London conference of last year. The accord will be submitted to the French foreign minister, Aristide Briand, in Paris tomorrow, and if he accepts it a five-

LE BOURGET, France, Jan. 16. (AP) The Prince of Wales and his brother, Prince George, landed here this afternoon after a flight from the Hendon airport, England, on the first stage of their 18,000-mile journey to South America. The little moth plane came down to a perfect landing in rather poor flying weather with low visibility, threatening clouds and some fog. The trip from London had taken two hours and eighteen minutes.

ROME, Feb. 28.—British and Italian officials conferring here on Franco-Italian naval problems reached an agreement in principle on questions left outstanding at the London Naval Conference, it was announced officially today. British Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson and First Lord of the Admiralty A. V. Alexander will proceed to Paris this afternoon to submit the agreement to the French government. The agreement then will be submitted to the governments of the United States, Great Britain, Japan, and the British Dominions represented at the London Naval Conference.

| Paris, Feb. 28 (UP) — A new scheme of naval limitations whereby world powers will be asked to limit their construction to 25,000 ton warships will be proposed by France, Britain and Italy, the United Press learned at the foreign offices today. The limitations scheme confirmation was coincident with the announcement that Italy had agreed in principle to the Franco-British proposal entailing adhesion to the London naval treaty and giving up the claim for naval parity with France. British Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson, Foreign Minister Aristide Briand, and other officials, will confer here when the British delegates return from Rome. They are expected to decide whether the new scheme of limitations will be submitted to the United States and Japan immediately or held until the League of Nations world disarmament conference meets at Geneva. An enormous saving is expected to result from

ROME, Feb. 28 (P).—The Italian government this morning accepted proposals advanced by Great Britain which will permit its full adhesion to the London naval treaty. The proposals previously had been accepted by the French government. Adhesion of the two governments to the London treaty, reached at the conclusion of the naval conference almost a year ago, will make that pact a five-power instrument instead of a three-power treaty as it is now. Negotiations which brought the Italian acceptance were carried on by Arthur Henderson, foreign secretary, and A. V. Alexander, first Lord of the Admiralty for Great Britain, and Dino Gianni, foreign minister, and Rear Admiral Siriana for Italy. Premier Mussolini himself carried on part of the conversations for Italy. Parity Postponed. The proposal advanced by Great Britain, some reports said, specify (Continued on Page 12)

LONDON (UP)—Staid and dignified London “went Hollywood” Friday night when Charles Spencer Chaplin appeared in person at the premiere of his latest film, “City Lights.” The only thing missing from the brilliant first night was the Hollywood weather. London retained all of its typical winter rains for the opening. But there were immense crowds, titled persons, celebrities, flood lights, limousines, and full dress as members of all classes of the city gathered inside and outside the Dominion Theatre. George Bernard Shaw, Lady Astor, many peers and peeresses and British notables by the score gave Chaplin’s picture an enthusiastic welcome. The greatest ovation of the evening, however, was accorded the comedian himself when he appeared on the stage for a curtain speech after the presentation of the film. As he moved toward the wings, the comedian suddenly went into his famous Chaplin walk. The

ENGLAND, Ark., Feb. 28 (4”) — The huge copper kettle from a still that bootleggers contributed to drought relief here has been stolen. When Will Rogers visited England a short time ago he was especially interested to find the kettle in use for soup-making in the High school, and remarked that it ‘must have been the bootleggers’ contribution.” It was, although not voluntary—officers having seized it in a raid—and now the authorities say they suspect it was pilfered to brew something stronger than soup. The school is seeking another cauldron to prepare food for its pupils.

LONDON, Feb. 27.—After thirty years, Miss Emily Payne of Temple, Texas, has traced three brothers now living in England. For three decades she had sought Joseph, Sydney, and George Payne, succeeding at last through the joint efforts of the American and British post office service.

1931-01-17.text: ENGLAND, Ark. (UP)— The news that citizens of Morrill, Neb., were sending them a carload of potatoes and 20 sacks of beans caused a ripple of joy Saturday among England farmers who only two weeks ago threatened to raid the town to get food for their starving wives and children. It was only a ripple, however, and there were no shouts like those that rang through the business district when the farmers threatened the merchants. Mayor W. O. Williams explained that the heart had gone out of the men and that potatoes and beans, not just the news they were enroute, were needed. Williams, a quiet, middle-aged man, has “almost broken” during the last month, his neighbors say, because of the suffering he has been called upon to deal with daily.

LONDON, Jan. 17 (AP) — A violent storm which raged over England during the night abated today. The gale ripped open the roof of the Claydonotyne chemical factory spilling 100 tons of sulfuric acid. Employees hurriedly neutralized the acid, preventing what would undoubtedly have been serious consequences as it spread through the neighborhood. Three persons were killed by falling chimneys and signs. Many signs were torn from their hangings but absence of pedestrians at the early hour kept the casualty list down.

Paris, Jan. 16, (JP) - Two traveling salesmen from London spent this evening in comparative quiet at their hotel here, but they were the object of considerably more attention than is usually accorded a commercial traveler. They were the Prince of Wales and his brother, Prince George, but they were strictly incognito and there was none of the pomp which visiting royalty is usually pestered. The two young men, on their way to South America where the Prince of Wales is to open the British Trade Exposition next March, crossed the channel in the prince’s airplane, reaching Le Bourget field after two hours flying over threatening clouds and through fog. The Prince of Wales was a little deaf from the roar of the motors after they landed, but he recovered quickly. To Take Liner Tomorrow the brothers will get up early to catch a train for Santander, Spain, where they will board the liner Oropesa

LONDON, Jan. 17.—(OP)—Three persons were reported killed by falling chimneys and signs during a violent gale which swept over England. At Liverpool the Canadian liner Duchess of York, due to sail at 4:50 p.m. was pinned to her dock by the force of the wind, notwithstanding the efforts of tugs to get her into midstream.

London, Jan. 17.--(#)—The Daily Express says that, as a consequence of recent gunnery developments, naval experts now believe British ships to be immune from aircraft attacks at sea. This, it was claimed, is due to the mounting of eight inch guns in the latest battle cruisers in such a way that they can be raised and fired effectively at an elevation of from 75 to 80 degrees. At that elevation they could have an effective range of 27,000 feet, which is higher than any bombing airplane could fly. The guns could fire a curtain of shrapnel which it would be impossible for any airplane to penetrate. Low-flying ships would be guarded against by means of various types of guns which would put a wall of bursting shells around any ship.

By The Associated Press. Cardiff, Wales, Jan. 16.—All this day well into the night the coal miners of South Wales, who have been out of work for two weeks, trudged to their meeting halls and voted to accept terms reached by their representatives with the coal mine owners on the basis that work would be resumed Monday. After they had voted and as they trudged back home through grimy, muddy streets they sang the rhythmic songs of Wales, for from those homes and the women and children in them had been driven the grim specter of starvation.

GENEVA, Jan. 17—(UP)—A sub-committee of eight, appointed to determine whether to invite Russia and Turkey to participate in Aristide Briand’s proposed European Federation, today recommended an immediate invitation be sent to them. Dino Grandi, Italian foreign minister, thereupon immediately proposed that sessions of the organization meetings be suspended until the arrival of the Russian and Turkish delegates.

Geneva, Jan. 16,—--(4?)-—-Twenty-six European foreign ministers met here today to talk about Aristide Briand’s project for a federation of European states, but a hitch developed at the very outset when the German and Italian representatives proposed that Turkey and Soviet Russia be invited to participate. Neither of these two countries is a member of the League of Nations, but Dino Grandi, Italy's bearded young foreign minister, asserted that any federation excluding them would merely divide Europe into two camps.

1931-02-07.text: TOKYO, Feb. 6—(AP)—Bitterness over the London Naval treaty caused a free-for-all fight today in an ante room of the Diet, and a dozen persons, two of them members of the Diet, were injured. — The fight started when a member of the opposition party wielded a dagger during hot debate of Foreign Minister Shidehara’s explanation in the Diet that Emperor Hirohito, by approving the treaty, had proved it did not endanger the security of Japan. The explanation was regarded by government opponents as an effort to blame the emperor for any defeat in the treaty. Fifty men milled about the ante room wielding clubs and hurling anything they could get their hands on. Several were cut about heads and hands. Others were bruised and were cut by crashing glass. Baron Shidehara, acting head of the government since Premier Hamaguchi was shot and severely wounded in November by a fanatical patriot, was in an

Oxford, England, Feb. 6 (P)—A city so ancient that its ruins show watermarks reputedly left by the Biblical flood has been discovered a few miles east of Babylon by the Oxford University Field Museum expedition in Mesopotamia. On top of it is the first well-preserved palace of the Sassanian dynasty of Persian kings ever found. And the discovery of the palace was largely accidental, Prof. Stephen Langdon, the American-born director of the expedition, explained it to the Associated Press today. The field director, he said, waiting to begin excavations on the main hill over the site of the ancient city, set his Arab workmen to leveling the mounds of earth nearby. They had not been at work for a week before one wall and two gateways of the Royal Persian Palace had been laid bare. Prof. Langdon estimates its date at about 360 A.D. Below it, in layers representing the various stages of civiliz

DAYTONA BEACH, Fla., Feb. 7.—Having hung up two new speed records in two days, Captain Malcolm Campbell, intrepid British race car driver, today began making preparations for his return trip to England. He plans to leave about the middle of next week, stopping off for a day in Washington before proceeding to New York, where he will board a liner for Southampton. Although not satisfied with his world’s land speed record of 245.733 miles an hour, established here Thursday in his giant Bluebird racing car, Campbell said he would not make any more straight-away trials until someone bettered his mark. As a climax to his racing in this country, Campbell went out yesterday in a tiny four-cylinder machine and established a new record of 94.031 miles an hour for automobiles with a piston displacement of less than 45 cubic inches. The previous record was 87.76 established in France several years a

Birmingham, England, Feb 6. (P)—A letter recently arrived at the home of Tom Winshull, jr. It stated that the writer, who signed herself “Lilly,” regretted her hasty refusal on the previous evening and indicated that if Mr. Winshull would call that started a little research. He learned the letter was mailed in 1908 and was meant for his father, who died several years ago. “Lilly” also was dead, he learned. She never married.

(International News Service) LONDON, Feb. 7 - According to figures 160 bodies have been recovered from the ruins of the cities of Napier and Hastings, New Zealand, said an exchange telegraph company dispatch from Wellington today. Sixteen hundred persons injured in Tuesday's earthquake were treated in emergency hospitals erected in the two cities. Twelve thousand of Napier's 20,000 inhabitants, including most of the women and children, have been evacuated from Napier.

LONDON, Feb. 6 (4)—Sometimes Sinclair Lewis wonders whether he wasn't better off back in Sauk Center, Minnesota, before all this Nobel Prize business began. “It's no bed of roses,” he said today, “I'm still getting letters, and they all want money. I tell them I'm poor, too, but it doesn’t do any good. “There was a Gypsy sent me a letter in Berlin asking me to pay off the mortgage on his old homestead and when I said I couldn't do it he sent me five postal cards calling me some names I never heard of and saying he was praying every day at his mother’s grave that something terrible should happen to me and my wife.”

By the Associated Press. | Rome, Italy, Feb. 6.—Michele Schirru, a naturalized American citizen born in Sardinia, must face trial before a special tribunal on a charge of planning to assassinate Premier Mussolini with a bomb. Under the law he may be executed. Today the police gave out the gist of a confession they said he had made yesterday in the hospital where he was taken after an unsuccessful attempt at suicide at the end of a battle in a police station. In the scuffle he wounded three policemen. The alleged confession admitted a plan for the assassination. Schirru said he had been an anarchist for years and had been plotting against Mussolini since last summer.
BERLIN, Feb 7 (UP).—The Reichstag rejected motions of no-confidence against the Bruening government, introduced by fascists and communists, by a vote of 293 to 221 today.

1931-01-09.text: LONDON, Jan. 9.—Airplanes dropped food, clothing, and fuel to 16 fishermen stranded in a small boat on an ice floe eight miles off Styrsudd lighthouse today while an ice breaker was en route to their rescue, a dispatch to the Exchange Telegraph Company from Helsingfors said. Seven fishermen and two women, adrift in the Baltic for 36 hours, had reached land after forcing their boat through thin ice. The fishermen were lost among drifting ice when they went to sea in an effort to save their nets, cut loose by a storm. Airplanes were sent from Helsingfors to look for them.

United Press Staff Correspondent. London, Jan. 9.— (UP) —George Bernard Shaw, materialistic and stalwart westerner, and Sir Rabindranath Tagore, dreamy and timid poet of the East, met in cosmopolitan London and agreed that politicians constitute a menace of some sort or other. Tagore, addressing the All Peoples Association, deplored the fact that nations are represented by politicians. "It is almost as bad as allowing a band of robbers to organize the police," the Indian said. Shaw greeted Tagore at a reception after his speech. "I have always been telling my people not to listen to politicians," he said, "I have tried to do this in my own writings, but you know what uphill work it is to try to convince people against their own will." The Irishman and the Indian then posed for their photographs. Shaw was the distinct loser so far as facial decoration was concerned, Sir Rabindranath’s flo

London, Jan. 9. (AP).—Captain Malcolm Campbell, British racing driver, will sail for America next Wednesday on the Homeric with a new “Bluebird,” said to be his most powerful racing machine. He will take the automobile to Daytona Beach where he will seek a speed above 231 miles an hour, the world’s record. His weird car has the center of balance off the center to the right. It was exhibited here this week beside a fleet of motors picked by the Prince of Wales for his South American trip.
On SUING Arbitration A abls. CARDIFF, Wales, Jan. 9. (F)— Negotiations looking to the settlement of the great South Wales coal strike collapsed this afternoon.

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS. Glasgow, Scotland, Jan. 8 — Sir Thomas Lipton today gave the city of Glasgow $50,000 for distribution among the poor mothers and children in his native city. He made the gift, he said, in memory of his mother, "the guiding star of my life," and in appreciation of the "many kindnesses" he had received from the city.

(By The Associated Press) | Rome, Jan. 8—The full power and authority of the Roman Catholic church were invoked by Pope Pius RI today to uphold the sanctity of Christian marriage and to stamp out the practices of birth control, “companionate” marriage and divorce. In the most sweeping exposition of the church's views on matrimony in many years he condemned the use of contraception, abortion, sterilization or any other means to prevent the fruitfulness of wedlock. His pronouncement came in the form of a long encyclical, the first of its kind in 50 years of ecclesiastical history. In it he enjoined his bishops to propagate the church's view that marriage is indissoluble except by death, and that the family, within the meaning of this sacrament, “is more sacred than the state.” Shameful, Vicious Deed Birth control is a deed “shameful and intrinsically vicious” and a “horrible crime,” the po

MADRID, Jan. 9—The Spanish Army Air Service was disbanded and plans for its reorganization were outlined in a decree published today. Officers and men of the service were given 15 days in which to apply for membership in the new air corps, or to return to the branches of the army with which they served originally. The decree had been expected in view of the attempted revolt at Cuatro Vientos Airdrome recently, led by Ramon France.
(By United Press.) BERLIN, Jan. 9.—Sixty persons were injured, many of them seriously, in a collision between a passenger train and a freight train near Vilnius Friday.

1931-08-06.text: Tokio, Japan, Aug. 6—(U.R)—Miss Amy Johnson, British flier, ended her long London-to-Tokio flight today. She brought her tiny Puss Moth light plane to earth at 5:17 p.m. (2:17 a.m. C.S.T.), after a swift flight during the day from Seoul, Korea.

London, Aug. 6.—(UP)—J. A. Mollison, youthful Scottish flier, landed today at Pevensey Bay from Le Bourget airdrome at 2:30 p.m., breaking the Australia-to-England flight record by more than a day. The previous record, held by C. W. A. Scott, was 10 days, 23 hours. Mollison intended to proceed to Lympne as soon as possible, and to go from there to Croydon,

Tokyo, Japan, Aug. 6. (4?)—Amy Johnson, British woman flier, landed at Tachikawa airdrome at 5:17 p.m. (2:17 a.m. Creston time) today at the conclusion of a flight by easy stages from England. She was accompanied by C. S. Humphries. The British aviatrix, the first woman to fly from London to Tokyo via Siberia, completed the flight in 10 and one-half days and beat by a few hours the 11 day light plane record between the two cities, made by Seiji Yoshihara, Japanese aviator. Miss Johnson's last hop was made from Seoul, Korea. A few minutes after her arrival, the American fliers, Hugh Herndon, Jr., and Clyde Pangborn, congratulated her at the airfield.

LONDON, Aug. 5.—(AP)—An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Copenhagen tonight said radio messages had been received from Angmagsalik, Greenland, saying Parker Cramer, American aviator, landed there at 1:45 p.m. today after a flight from Canada and it was understood he would continue to Copenhagen. The report was said to be something of a mystery in Copenhagen and nothing farther was known about the flight. (Parker Cramer, who with Bert Hassel, attempted a flight in 1928 from Rockford, O., to Stockholm, formerly lived in Clarion.
TOKYO, Japan, Aug. 6—(Thursday)—(P)—Amy Johnson, British aviatrix who is flying from London to Tokyo, left Seoul, Korea, at 7:30 A. M. today for Hiroshima, Japan, according to reports received here.

NEW YORK, Aug 6. (4)—Prince Jean de Liechtenstein and his bride the former Aleene McFarland of Weatherford, Tex., arrived today from London where they were married one day before sailing for the United States. After a stopover of several days in New York, the couple will proceed to the small Texas town where the princess’ father, the late Charles MacFarland, accumulated a fortune in cattle and oil investments.

— LONDON, Aug. 5 (/P)—The Marquis of Reading, once ambassador to the United States and later viceroy to India, will be married tomorrow to the young woman who aided him in his rise to be one of Great Britain's foremost statesmen. His engagement to Miss Stella Charnaud, daughter of the late Charles Charnaud, who represented Great Britain on the international public debt mission to Turkey, was announced today. He is 70 years of age and she 37. Miss Charnaud was a member of the vice-regal staff when Lord Reading was in India from 1921 to 1926 and returned with him to England in a similar capacity when he was succeeded by Lord Irwin. She became his chief assistant in all political matters and played an active role in his work in behalf of India at the first round table conference. The marquis' first wife, the former Alice Edith Cohen, died here in March, 1930.

(By Associated Press) - LONDON, Aug. 5—The Marquis of Reading, former viceroy of India and for twenty years an eminent figure in British politics, and Miss Stella Charnaud, known as “the most remarkable woman in London,” will be married tomorrow. The announcement of the engagement was made today when they called at the prince’s row registry office to arrange for the civil ceremony. Lord Reading is 70 years old, and Miss Charnaud, who has served as his secretary for several years, is 37. Spurned Big U. S. Offer “I am still going to be the perfect private secretary,” she said today as she left the registry office. Her perfection in that capacity has been commented on for years. An American businessman recently offered her $25,000 a year if she would join his organization. In addition, she has a reputation as a beauty, a musician, and a linguist. “Ran Away as Cabin Boy The rise of Lord Read

1931-12-28.text: Bombay, India, Dec. 28.—Mahatma Gandhi declared today that he would not flinch in sacrificing the lives of a million people to purchase the liberty of India. The Mahatma made this statement to 50,000 nationalists gathered in an open field to hear his first speech since his return from the London round table conference. “If the fight is inevitable, I will expect every son and daughter of Mother India to contribute his mite,” the Mahatma said. “However, I will not abandon attempts to save the nation from a fiery ordeal. If, on the other hand, there is no single ray of hope I shall not hesitate to call upon you to bear any amount of suffering.”

Bombay, Dec. 28. (/P)—Blood ran as Mahatma Gandhi arrived home in India today after his four months’ absence at the round table conference in London. Twelve persons were injured in a clash which took place at the pier where a huge crowd awaited his landing from the S.S. Pilsna. About 1,000 “untouchables,” carrying black flags had gathered for an anti-Gandhi demonstration and they tried to rush the pier. Delegations of the national congress caught the rush of the mob. Police, with the assistance of the congress adherents, finally dispersed the crowd. Riots In Other Parts, — The mahatma also heard news of the serious riots in other parts of (Continued on page 2.)

BOMBAY, India, Dec. 28.—(UP)— Mahatma Gandhi “came home” today to an India aroused by serious rioting and fighting, with “a declaration of war” against Britain, and a boycott of British goods. Deaths in rioting in Peshawar, where troops and police given special powers by the viceroy have rounded up for deportation leaders of the “red shirt” movement, totaled eleven. Bombay had taken on the aspect of the city during the civil disobedience campaign. There were reports of increasing violence, terrorism, and a demand for hostilities against Britain as the smiling Gandhi came ashore from the liner Pilsna greeted by cheering of thousands. The welcome given the hero of India’s masses was even greater than the homage paid him when he departed for the London round table conference. Police and officers of the steamship line had difficulty in controlling the half million who jammed the docks and sp

LONDON, Dec. 28 (AP).—A meeting between Prime Minister MacDonald and Premier Laval of France, similar to that between Laval and President Hoover, seemed possible today as a result of a letter from the prime minister to the premier in connection with the reparations issue. It was a private letter. Although it did not explicitly suggest a meeting, it was phrased in such a manner that a meeting easily might result if both parties desired it. Laval has not yet replied, so far as could be learned. It was understood MacDonald did not confine himself to the reparations problem as such but also touched upon broader phases of the economic situation. Meantime, it appeared that the tentative date for the international reparations conference had been advanced to January 15 from January 18 and that The Hague is still the most likely place for the meeting.

Varis—Reports that Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald had invited Premier Laval to London for a conference regarding reparations brought a guarded denial from the premier today. ‘Contrary to a story published today,' the premier's statement said, 'no invitation has been addressed to M. Laval to go to London for a conference with Mr. MacDonald. The English and French experts are now discussing the subject of reparations and a meeting between the two government heads would not be opportune until the experts have completed their work.' There is great interest here in the possibility of an attempt to achieve an agreement on reparations between France and England before the international debts conference scheduled for some time next month, and it is believed that there is a strong likelihood of such an agreement as a result of the visit of Sir Frederick Ross, British financial expert, and his di

| Paris, Dec. 27 ()--Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain has invited Premier Pierre Laval to a personal conference to co-ordinate the French and British policies on reparations before the International Reparations Conference, it was semi-officially announced today. The personal conversations between the heads of the British and French Governments would be held soon, if Premier Laval accepted the Prime Minister's invitation, the announcement indicated. The general conference of nations on the reparations problem is tentatively set for January 18 at The Hague.

LOSSIEMOUTH, Scotland, Lev. 28 (P) - Prime Minister Macdonald, issuing one of his most outspoken statements, described the situation in India tonight as “most deplorable” and denounced Indian agitators in vigorous terms. Recent disorders in the northwest frontier province and in Bengal, he said, did not represent a “baffled and oppressed India struggling to be free” but a “mischievous movement trampling in its own self-will upon Indian progress. “An enlightened India would not only give them no countenance, but would turn and rend them. The people in the agencies in this country who have been working many years for the enfranchisement of India must share in the government's regret at the recent happenings,”

Peiping, China, Dec. 24.—Get a lot of British news over here in the papers. She may be off the gold standard but she has got a navy that will make the other nations think a long time before they start throwing rocks at her. When a British warship steams into these ports she anchors just close enough in to give the local congress and senate a real view of what a dreadnought is. When you see those guns pointing at you, you don't ask whether they are on a gold, silver, waste paper or zinc basis. With that navy Nicaragua could go on a banana basis and still be cock of the walk. Merry Christmas.

1931-10-16.text: (By Associated Press) YORKTOWN, Va., Oct. 16—The nation’s four day observance of the battle which made its existence possible opened here today with dedication of a monument to the defeated British commander, Lord Cornwallis, and the reception of Marshal Henri Petain of France, as high water marks in a day of historical events and pageantry. Sun Dissipates Crowds The threatened skies that hovered overhead when the English earl who now bears the title of Lord Cornwallis voiced his belief that the memorial to his distinguished ancestor further cemented the bond of friendship between the English speaking people, rolled back and gave way to a bright October sun at high noon. And as the bright sun appeared, a salute of 17 guns announced the approach of the noted French leader sent by his nation to represent its people in the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the battle of Yorktown where

YORKTOWN, Va., Oct. 16—(AP)—Lord Cornwallis, descendant of the English Earl who surrendered at the Battle of Yorktown, today responded to Virginia’s dedication of a memorial to his ancestor, with the statement that “War is behind, peace is in front, we hope, for evermore.” “Friends have sent me press clippings intimating that I might find some delicacy in appearing here today,” Lord Cornwallis said. “I assure you that such delicacy never crossed my mind. “Forty-eight hours after Yorktown General Washington entertained Lord Cornwallis and from that moment all animosity was forgotten. I feel that it would be agreeable to him as it is delightful to me that a member of the family can be here today.” Dedication of the bust of Lord Cornwallis at York Hall, home of Thomas Nelson, war governor of Virginia and Cornwallis’ headquarters at Yorktown, officially opened the four-day celebration of the

Dublin, Oct. 16—(2)—G. Boland deputy from Roscommon, told fellow members of the Dail Eireann that he had been to Russia to seek Soviet aid against the arch enemy England. "But they were too busy with their own troubles to bother with me," he added.

YORKTOWN, Va., Oct. 16. (U.P)— Guns of the American Scouting Fleet boomed forth in the York River today near the spot where 150 years ago Lord Cornwallis, British General, surrendered to George Washington and the American colonists won their independence. France, the nation that fought side by side with the Colonists, was represented today by Marshal Henri Petain, “savior of Verdun.” With Petain was the American General, John J. Pershing, who almost 140 years later helped repay America’s debt and save France. The four day sesquicentennial celebration observing the 150th anniversary of the Battle of Yorktown opened today when the scouting fleet fired its salute at eight o'clock. Lord Cornwallis, British nobleman and direct descendant of the Cornwallis who surrendered to Washington, arrived at six o'clock this morning. He unveiled a tablet erected by Virginia to the mother country. Descend

By The Associated Press | Berlin, Oct. 16—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening’s cabinet was sustained this evening on a vote of confidence in the Reichstag. The vote was 294 to 270. Thus the Chancellor turned back again the threat of Adolf Hitler’s national socialists who combined this time the Nationalist party headed by Alfred Hugenberg. These two, who have been the government's most bitter enemies since it took office, combined forces after the recent overturn in the Bruening cabinet and recently at a joint meeting in Harzburg served notice of their intention to turn the Chancellor out of office if they could.

| Harve, France, Oct. 16—UP—Premier Pierre Laval, accompanied by a staff of financial experts, sailed aboard the liner Ile De France this afternoon for the United States where he will discuss important world problems with President Hoover.

GENEVA, Oct. 16— (AP) — The council of the League of Nations formally ratified over the objections of the Japanese delegate today its invitation for the United States to engage in arbitration of the Sino-Japanese conflict. Chairman Aristide Briand, in summarizing the council's decision, said that the objections of a constitutional and juridical nature raised by Kenkichi Yoshizawa, Japanese delegate, remained in reserve. The council again overruled by a vote of 15 to one the Japanese delegate’s objection and declared that the question was purely one of procedure, requiring only a majority vote. It was made clear that the American representative would not have a vote on the merits of China's appeal. Japan Votes “No”, Supporting the invitation were the delegates of France, Great Britain, Italy, Germany, Poland, Spain, Norway, China, Peru, Ireland, Yugoslavia, Guatemala and Panama. Only Japa

VANCOUVER, B. C—()—The American Federation of Labor has handed an officially approved unemployment relief program to America and ended its 51st annual convention here. In a seven-point program to deal with the business depression, the convention Thursday reaffirmed its stand for modification of the Volstead Act to permit the sale of 2.75 per cent beer. Resolutions advocating repeal of the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act were side-tracked. William Green, re-elected president of the federation by acclamation, stated that the program would provide for "every hungry man, woman and child in the country" if the nation fails to reduce unemployment in other ways. Here are the chief points in labor's program. 1.—Maintenance of the United States wage standard to keep up 2.—Prohibition of child labor. 3.—National planning to balance production and consumption. 4.—Employers to take on more

1931-10-08.text: - LONDON, Oct. 8 (4) — Mahatma Gandhi announced today at the meeting of the Indian minorities committee, presided over by Prime Minister MacDonald, that he had failed completely to settle the Hindu-Moslem communal problem. He qualified his statement, however, by saying that this does not mean that he has abandoned hope of ever arriving at a solution to this issue.

| LONDON, Oct. 8 (—British workers who actually work and those who don’t will go home to | their “high tea” tomorrow night with even fewer pence in their pockets than on their last pay day. For Friday is both the British | pay day and dole distribution day and this week the new dole rates lees in effect. Three pence, or six cents more, will be deducted from the wages of some nine million workers to | help pay for the dole. Even more will be missing from the weekly benefits handed over the counter to the unemployed. | The housemaid and the farm hand will be unaffected. But the waitress and the mill hand will feel ‘the latest pinch in the government’s economy campaign. |. London, Oct. 8.—(#)—Mahatma Gandhi is willing to go to the United States at the conclusion of the round table conference if his American friends can convince John Haynes Holmes, New York pastor, that the Mahatma would not be made a laughing-stock. Pressed to make the trip by a number of American visitors, Gandhi said today: “Holmes, in whose opinion I place the greatest reliance, tells me my visit would be misunderstood, that I would be exploited, ridiculed and misinterpreted. On the other hand, I’ve had several invitations signed by leading Americans. “If these latter can convince Holmes I ought to go to America I shall be glad to reconsider my decision. I have a great affection for the American people and feel sure that I have a great many friends across the Atlantic, and I don’t want to sacrifice that friendship.” “Einstein, after visiting America, said it was the greatest mistake of

Glasgow, Scotland, Oct. 7.—(#)— The money of every land which came to Sir Thomas Lipton in exchange for his tea and other commodities was passed on to the sick and needy today by his will, which was read by the executors a few minutes after his body was lowered into the grave. The bulk of the estate, which is about $4,000,000, goes to hospitals, infirmaries and old men’s and old women’s homes in Glasgow, al- (Continued on Page 7)

Peiping, China, Oct. 28.—(#/)—J. G. Thomson, British manager of Peiping-Mukden railroad, reported today that 12 Japanese airplanes had dropped 36 bombs on the town of Chinchow, 130 miles south of Mukden, inflicting an undetermined number of casualties. He said the bombs were chiefly directed at the university buildings which temporarily house the headquarters of the Manchurian provincial government. One bomb was said to have hit a railroad service car and killed two Chinese servants while another struck a locomotive shed.

- Glasgow, Scotland, Oct. 8—(7)— The poor, the ailing and the aged rejoiced today that Sir Thomas Lipton remembered them in death as well as in life. The bulk of his estate, estimated to exceed a million pounds, will go to hospitals, infirmaries and old people's homes in London, Glasgow and Middlesex. More than $300,000 will go to help working mothers and their children here. The gold loving cup presented by the American people in recognition of his sportsmanship was left to the New York Yacht Club.

LONDON, Oct. 8.—The sixth parliament of the reign of King George V was dissolved Wednesday and Britain swung into an intensive three-weeks campaign for a general election that will be historic. Ramsay MacDonald's national government will be returned to power or wrecked on the broken ranks of conservatives and liberals, over which labor again may march to victory. On the London stock exchange where election bets take the form of business transactions in “majorities,” deals were made Wednesday that the national government will be returned with a majority of 150 in the House of Commons. The total production of electricity by public utility plants in 1929 amounted to 97,283,000,000 kilowatt hours, an increase of nearly 12 percent over the total for 1928.

London, Oct. 8 (UP)—Mahatma Gandhi failed to effect conciliation among representatives of Indian minorities today despite his threat of forcing an all night session of the informal conciliation committee. Gandhi, chairman of the committee, reached St. James’ Palace wearing an extra blanket and informed the committee he would not allow them to leave until they had reached a settlement. A van load of sandwiches and coffee was brought for the delegates. The meeting broke up soon after midnight, without a decision.

1931-08-19.text: LONDON, (P)—A long step toward peace in Europe was believed to have been taken Wednesday with the conclusion of a treaty of non-aggression between France and Soviet Russia. The United Press learned that the pact had been initialed by representatives of France and Russia in Paris, concluding negotiations started in May. The pact binds these nations, two of Europe's most intense political rivals since the World War, to maintain strict neutrality in the event the other is attacked without provocation by a third power or group of powers. Otherwise, it was understood, the agreement closely follows the lines of the German-Soviet union neutrality accord. The conclusion of the treaty was regarded as significant in the relations of France and Russia. It furthermore was believed certain to have a strong influence on other European nations. The Soviet authorities have charged France with participat

LONDON, Aug. 19.—(AP)—Soaring above the rain clouds, the Graf Zeppelin’s first party of British tourists early today saw the sun rise over the Mull of Galloway with the hills of Scotland dimly defined in the distance. After making the first peace-time landing of a German Zeppelin on English soil last night, the dirigible circled southern England. She headed for Ireland by way of the Bristol channel and after passing over Dublin steered for Ulster and Scotland with the breaking of dawn.

London, Aug. 19.—(U.P)—Willette Kershaw, American actress at present starring in London, was found chloroformed in her apartment today. She was unconscious for hours after being found but was expected to recover. Police found that the apartment had been rifled. Miss Kershaw was appearing in "The Well of Loneliness" at the Caumartin theater.

- -HANWORTH, Eng: Aug. 18 (P)—. The German Dirigible Graf Zeppelin darted among angry-looking rain clouds over London late this evening and landed in the dusk with its 28 passengers at Hanworth Airdrome. The Graf is the first Zeppelin to land in England since the World War when some of its elder, but smaller, sister ships were shot down. The Graf was cheered by thousands of citizens who watched its progress over the city. Another large crowd awaited the ship at the airdrome and cheered the commander, Dr. Hugo Eckener. The Graf will return to Germany tomorrow after a cruise around Great Britain, upon which it took off last night.

CALSHOT, England, Aug. 18—(U.P)—Great Britain lost another of her Schneider cup defenders today when Lieut. G. L. Brinton, 26, was drowned in the wreckage of his racing plane after it crashed into the sea. Brinton’s death was the fourth of a famous Schneider cup racing plane pilots in the last few months. He was putting his super-marine S-6 plane over the Swient course at a fast clip in a trial for the forthcoming cup races with Italy and France. The plane dipped to about 30 feet above the water and suddenly dived. It came to the surface with his huge floats uppermost and the tiny, wasp-like body of the plane under water. Speedboats put out from the shore carrying Brinton’s teammates, including flying officer L. S. Snaith, his partner, who dived repeatedly in an effort to recover Brinton’s body.

Caishot, England, Aug. 19—The body of Flight Lieutenant G. L. Brinton, Schneider Cup pilot, who plunged to his death while testing his seaplane yesterday, was found today in the tail-end of the fuselage. It was believed at first that he had been lost at sea, but when his wrecked plane was taken into the hangar and examined thoroughly, his body was found apparently having been forced back by the impact of the crash. Speedboat patrols had searched the waters of the Solent all night in search of Brinton. The tragedy did not affect plans for the meet on September 12 and training went ahead as usual.

TOKYO, Aug. 19 (Wednesday) — Forced down by motor trouble at Avatchu Bay soon after their take-off from Petropavlovsk, Kamchatka, for Nemuro, Japan, Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh took the air again at 10:45 A. M. today, Tokyo Time (7:45 P. M. Tuesday, CST), a message to the communications department here said. The Lindberghs left Petropavlovsk, Kamchatka, at 9:45 A. M. (6:45 P. M. Tuesday, CST), but had flown only a few miles toward their destination when they were forced to descend on Avatchu Bay. The trouble apparently was not of a serious nature, for they were on their way again within an hour. It was learned today that Col. Lindbergh last night wirelessed the American embassy here stating he might not be able to reach Nemuro today and requesting the embassy to ask the Japan aviation bureau for an emergency landing permit somewhere in the Kuriles. The application was granted.

Basel, Switzerland, Aug. 19. (4) A recommendation that the entire structure of inter-governmental war debts and German reparations be revised as the first step toward the return of world prosperity was made today by the Wiggin Bankers’ committee. The committee was set up by the Bank for International Settlements at the behest of the seven-power conference in London to investigate Germany's credit needs. It is headed by Albert H. Wiggin, of New York, chairman of the board of the Chase National Bank, and is composed of the representatives of the ten leading banking nations in the world. Political Differences Criticized Their report criticized political differences existing between Germany and her European neighbors and urged that current disputes be cleared up in order that “good times” might again prevail in all nations. Germany's reparations payments were assailed as an immense obstacle

1931-07-28.text: Berlin, July 28 () — Great Britain is diametrically opposed to the balance of power theory, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald said today, because it is incompatible with disarmament. So long as nations try to maintain national security on a basis of balance of power, they will need big armaments, he told a delegation of German newspaper men. Following a conference with President Von Hindenburg, the Prime Minister said he believed Germany's industrial position was fundamentally sound, and the present conditions were due to a wrong psychology.

LONDON, July 2—Alfonso de Bourbon, former king of Spain and his third son were reunited in exile on the Paddington station platform today. Meanwhile, London seethed with stories, which Alfonso himself denied, that he had abdicated his right to the Spanish throne in favor of the boy. Don Juan, the 18-year-old prince, who has been a cadet at the Dartmouth naval school since the royal family left Spain, came up from Dartmouth this morning to meet his father who arrived yesterday from Fontainebleau. They embraced each other and started off with Lord Londonderry, the former king's intimate friend, who a short time previously had denied a newspaper report of the abdication. As they stepped into their car Alfonso turned to Lord Londonderry and said “there's no truth in it,

BERLIN, July 28. — Germany attacked the task of solving her financial crisis with new heart and new energy today, as a result of Prime Minister MacDonald's declaration that if she did not give way to despair "other nations will help her and not suffer her to go under." The head of the British government made this statement at a dinner in honor of himself and his foreign secretary, Arthur Henderson, who are here on a visit. They have been acclaimed by Berlin crowds with a fervor not exceeded by the receptions in the old days accorded popular members of royalty. Chancellor Bruening’s mouthpiece, the newspaper "Germania," declared the evidence of British readiness to help the distressed Fatherland ranks with President Hoover's plan granting a year's respite from reparations. The keynote of the speeches by MacDonald and Herr Bruening at last night's dinner was the necessity of solidarity and

LONDON, July 28—(AP)— Secretary of State Stimson arrived here today from Berlin, admitted he had had “a fine trip” and wouldn't discuss the details of his conversation with the German ministers and President Paul Von Hindenburg. “I enjoyed seeing Germany very much and I found Holland very interesting,” he said. The Secretary of State drove directly to a hotel where he will remain for a few days before he travels north to Scotland for his vacation. The trip back to London was made by plane, automobile and train.

LONDON, July 28:—(Tuesday)—(AP)—The Daily Express this morning says, under a Madrid date, that former King Alfonso formally abdicated the Spanish throne in favor of his third son, Don Juan de Borbón, at a family council at Fontainebleau last week. The Express attributed the story to a former minister under the Primo de Rivera dictatorship who, it is said, spent a few hours in Madrid on business recently although he was sought by police. Alfonso, it was said, looked much elder than the night three months ago when he said goodbye to his tearful court. All the papers, the story said, had been carefully prepared in advance and there were four abdications, first that of Alfonso himself, then that of his eldest son, the Prince of Asturias, who is a victim of hemophilia, and then that of Don Jaime, the second son, who is deaf and dumb. The fourth and unexpected abdication, it was said, was that

AMSTERDAM, Holland, July 27. (AP)—Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson arrived here by airplane from Berlin tonight on his way to London. He said he was "tired of politics" and, after three or four days in London, intended to "take a good rest."

| Plymouth, England, July 27. — The polar submarine Nautilus moved out of the basin here into the river today preparatory for probably resumption tomorrow of its voyage to the North Pole. Repairs on machinery which broke down during the Atlantic crossing had been underway for more than 4 months in the Devonport dockyard.

LONDON — (4) — Former King Alfonso, of Spain, through a member of his staff, today denied a report in the Daily Express that he had abdicated his right to the Spanish throne in favor of his third son, Don Juan De Bourbon. The boy, who has been a cadet at the naval school at Dartmouth since the Royal family left Spain, came to London this morning, traveling third class with a number of his schoolmates, and was met at Paddington station by his father.

1931-03-24.text: LONDON, Mar, 24—(#)—Continued co-operation between liberals and the labor government, but not an out and out pact for maintenance of the government in power, was reported in political circles today to be the probable outcome of present negotiations between the labor and liberal party leaders. Liberal circles buzzed with activity today as the liberal parliamentary party assembled for a meeting at which policies were to be outlined. Recommendations of the shadow cabinet, containing the leaders of the party, both pro and con Lloyd George, which met last night will be submitted to the parliamentary group meeting. It was understood today that the sense of the shadow cabinet’s deliberations was that the liberals should maintain their party entity although giving the government cooperation on such measures as come within the scope of broad liberal policy. Karachi, India, March 24,-(4)- Famous as a terminal for trans- continental fliers entering and leaving India, Karachi resembled an armed camp today as the result of the triple execution of three Indians in Lahore yesterday. In anticipation of possible trouble from Indian Nationalists British authorities brought military reinforcements from places as remote as Beluchistan. They will remain throughout the period of the Nationalist Congress here. All British forces have orders to hold themselves in readiness in their barracks for any eventuality.

In offering Mr. Brisbane's daily editorials, The Anniston Star does not necessarily concur in his opinions but offers them as the sentiment of the highest paid editorial writer in this country. This artificially produced cancer is, in all respects, similar to the cancer tissue in human beings. The serum, harmless to all tissue except cancer tissue, may destroy cancer in the human body. The announcement is, theoretically, of highest importance, but it may be difficult to apply the serum to cancers far below the surface. We are more fearfully and wonderfully made than we had thought. St. John’s, N. F., March 24.—(A9 The Sealer Sagona, victor over the ice, pierced the darkness of the early hours today and steamed into St. John’s port. She bore survivors of the Viking, some sick, one dead. There were no shouts of greeting, no bustle as the ship berthed. A silent crowd watched, with it the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Stretcher bearers worked swiftly, silently. Loaded ambulances began to depart as soon as the gangplank was down. Eager ears listened for firsthand stories of the Viking’s fate, how she exploded on Sunday night, March 15, eight miles off Shore Island, White Bay. The stories came reluctantly. At 8 o'clock that fateful Sunday the crew of the Viking were below singing hymns. The sealer, making slow progress, hit a pan of heavy ice and lurched. “Hell burst loose!” said one survivor.
