Dudley, Iowa, Aug. 26—(UP)—Choke damp, heavy suffocating gas in the stagnant air of an unventilated mine shaft, today had claimed the lives of two brothers and their 18-year-old nephew whom they sought to rescue. The dead: Glenn Hanson, 33, Harold Hanson, 31, and their nephew, Earnest Redburn, 18. The Hansons were repairing an engine which powered the ventilating system in the mine. Redburn started to descend the 20-foot ladder into the shaft which had been unused for a year. Halfway down he dropped to the bottom and into a pool of water. In the damp, gas-filled air, he was overcome. The two brothers died as they descended, one after the other, in a rescue attempt.

1931-07-31.text: London. July 30 (#).—The Prince of Wales, returning from a game of golf this afternoon, was badly shaken when his car collided with another machine, in which three women occupants suffered minor bruises and one young woman lost several teeth. This evening he inquired at the hospital to learn the condition of the women. They had been allowed to go home.

PUT-IN-BAY, O., July 31.—(P) The famous victory of Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry's American fleet over the British on Lake Erie in the war of 1812, which paved the way for the more than a century of peace between the two countries, was commemorated here today with the dedication of the Perry victory memorial, a granite monument 352 feet high. Although the monument memorialized an event of war, the keynote of the dedication was one of peace. Citizens and officials of both Canada and the United States joined in the ceremony.

BERLIN, July 30.—(#)— Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, Jr., flying around the world in their red monoplane, landed at Tempelhof airdrome this evening at 7:30 p.m. (12:30 p.m. C.S.T.) from Croydon, England. It was getting dark when they brought their plane down and a tremendous crowd was gathered about the Graf Zeppelin which had landed only a short time before, ending her cruise into the arctic. So intent was the crowd watching the Graf that the monoplane was virtually unnoticed. Only one of the correspondents at the field and a single airport policeman recognized it at first and ran out to meet the fliers. CROYDON, Eng., July 30.—(@)— Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon Jr., who landed their transatlantic monoplane in Wales last night and came on here this morning, took off for Moscow, their original objective, at 2:18 p.m. today. (7:18 a.m. C.S.T.) The take off was nearly six hours after t

LONDON, July 31 (P)—The Misses Daphne and Beryl Riggs, actresses, were undergoing hospital treatment today for injuries received when an automobile in which they were riding collided with the car of the Prince of Wales, who escaped unharmed. A third woman who was with them also was injured, but none of them was badly hurt. One of the victims lost several teeth. A large section of the paneling on the prince's car, alongside where he was sitting, was ripped away.

Aviatrix Continues Toward Tokyo. Shanghai, July 31.—(/)—Amy Johnson, British woman flyer, en route from England to Tokyo, took off today from Omsk. She telegraphed here that she expected to reach Krasnojarsk tonight.

London t—The Prince of Wales is recovering today from minor bruises and a severe shaking-up suffered when his motor car collided with another while going at high speed yesterday. The Prince, driving his own powerful "Zeppelin type" machine, deliberately drove through a fence to avoid a more serious accident. He escaped with a bad shaking; three women in the other car were hurt. Only the quick-thinking and courage of the Prince prevented a more serious mishap, it was said. The Prince aided the injured women and arranged for their removal to Windsor hospital where he provided a private ward for them.

BERLIN, July 30. (A) — Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, Jr., Americans who hope to fly around the world in their red monoplane, took off from Tempelhof airdrome here at 10:49 p.m. (4:49 p.m. EST) for Moscow on the third leg of their journey. The fliers, who landed in England yesterday and hopped here from London this morning, expected to get away for Moscow nearly two hours earlier, but they were delayed by battery trouble which put their navigation lights out of commission. Repairs Are Made Mechanics worked steadily at the field during the early hours of the night in an effort to make the necessary repairs. They expected to make the hop to Moscow without

LONDON.—(#)—Both houses of parliament adjourned Friday afternoon until October 20, or until any earlier date decided upon by Lord Chancellor and the speaker of the financial situation be considered in the national interest.

1931-05-26.text: By se AO ote £2 Love Boston, Mass., May 25.—New England thrilled today to the onrush of nearly 700 army airplanes that swept eastward to the sea, from Springfield, Mass., and Hartford, Conn., to repel a mythical invader threatening the coast. One group of 36 raced northward across Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont to come to rest, finally, at the airports at Schenectady and Albany, N. Y., more than 600 others took part in a tremendous demonstration over Boston. The planes later flew back over southern New England to the four airports at Springfield and Hartford, at which they were quartered. In Boston schools were closed and thousands crowded the shores of Dorchester Bay. There, 39 pursuit, attack, and bombing planes roared through the sky in attack demonstration, low-altitude formations, pursuit assaults, bombardment formations, high speed formation flying, and combat acrobatic battles.

BOSTON, May 25—(4)—Nearly 700 army airplanes darkened the skies over New England today and demonstrated to hundreds of thousands of neck-craning citizens the aerial defensive resources of the nation. A parade of more than 500 planes, consisting of all types of fighting craft, converged on metropolitan Boston from Springfield and from Hartford, Conn. For approximately an hour before their arrival, a composite group of 39 planes, ranging from fast pursuit and attack ships to the ponderous bombers, engaged in a tactical demonstration over historic Dorchester Bay. This consisted in high-speed formation flying, bombardments, pursuits, attacks, a “dog fight,” and combat acrobatics. The final curtain fell in the form of a dense and spread smoke screen. Then the demonstration group joined its parading brethren for the return flight to its base in Springfield.

SANDRINGHAM, Eng., May 26.—(UP)—Queen Mary of England celebrated her 64th birthday quietly today, surrounded by members of the British royal family at Sandringham. For the first time in many years, the birthday of the queen was commemorated away from Buckingham Palace. Queen Mary and King George V came down to Sandringham a few days in order to spend the Whitsun-tide holidays at Sandringham House.

Calcutta, India, May 26.—Four British battalions proceeded to Rangoon today and three other battalions were under orders to proceed to Burma. Thus a total of 5600 troops were ready to quell a rebellion reported to have been planned to center in the Lashio district, where villagers have been tattooed with the mystic sign of a hawk. Three rebels were killed and several wounded in the Hanzada district when Sepoys (native troops) fired and repulsed an attack on a new police post.

ROLAND GARROS STADIUM, Auteuil, France, May 28 (P)—George Lott, Jr, aspiring to the French tennis throne vacated by Henri Cochet, today defeated Charles H. Kingsley, of England, in three straight sets to advance to the third round of singles in the French hard court tennis championships. The scores were 6-0, 6-1, 6-4. The American took 11 straight games before the former Cambridge captain, figured to give him a battle, was able to break through. Only two of the 11 games went to deuce. Lott meets I. Von Kramm, young German, in the third round. Betty Nuthall, one of the British favorites to take the women’s title, easily won her match from Mme. Nanetie le Besnerais 6-0, 6-2. Elizabeth Ryan, the former Californian, continued her steady march in the women’s singles, defeating 18-year-old Hedwiga Jedrzejowska in the second round 2-6, 9-7, 6-3.

SANDRINGHAM, Eng., May 26 (P)—Queen Mary was 64 years old today and felicitations poured in on her from a wide circle of relatives, friends and admirers. No public ceremonies were planned but she looked forward with King George to receiving guests at Sandringham palace. The press was particularly laudatory in recording the event. This was the first time in several years that Queen Mary had spent her anniversary day in Sandringham house, her favorite residence and always "home to members of the royal family." It was a private celebration, featured by the receipt of gifts from her children and grandchildren. After reading congratulatory messages from many parts of the world, she took her usual walk with the king through the beautiful gardens and heard the bells of the nearby church ring out the honors of the day. The villagers observed the occasion by flying flags and extending their loyal

Rome, May 26—(UP)—An increased strain was placed on the relations between the Holy See and the fascist regime today by recent clashes which resulted in charges from the Vatican that fascists were guilty of frequent mistreatment of Catholics. Counter-charges were immediately made by the fascists, asserting that parish priests in several instances had openly prayed against fascism. The strain was intensified Sunday when fascists beat the driver of a Vatican City mail truck carrying personal letters of Pope Pius XI to the station in Rome. The driver had failed to halt his truck during a fascist parade. A fascist militia officer struck the driver's assistant. The Osservatore Romano, semi-official organ, has started a column listing purported fascist anti-Catholic manifestations. The paper charged that fascist students burned copies of Saturday’s issue of the Osservatore containing the speech
Madrid, May 26.—Army units and extra forces of civil guards were called out in two widely separated regions today, Andalucía and San Sebastián, to deal with threatened labor disturbances.

1931-10-05.text: | Shanghai, Oct. 5. (UP)—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, undaunted by the spectacular airplane crash that hurled them at 100 miles an hour into the muddy Yangtze river, neared Shanghai today aboard the British airplane carrier Hermes, determined to continue their vacation flight. The Hermes with Lindbergh's undamaged monoplane aboard was due in Shanghai today from Hankow but reported by radio that it would not arrive off Woosung until late tomorrow. It will proceed to Shanghai, 15 miles up the river, early Wednesday. Native workmen at the China National Airways plant awaited the arrival of the fleet black monoplane to start repairs. Examinations of the ship indicated that the wing and fuselage, damaged when it shot into the river during take-off, could be repaired without difficulty.

| London, Oct. 4 (#)—Great Britain's troubles are expected to be carried to the electorate this week, unless some unforeseen development arises. | Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald is expected to announce the dissolution of parliament Tuesday or Wednesday and a general election to take place before the end of this month. The plan, it was understood over the weekend, is for the National government to seek a nationwide vote of confidence and the return of its support to the House of Commons on a platform of broad powers to the prime minister to meet the national emergencies. This “doctor's mandate,” as Mr. MacDonald was said to have termed it, if approved, might shortly bring Great Britain, one of the greatest free trade countries in the world, to the point of an imposition of revenue and protective tariffs against imports. With the dissolution of parliament almost reached, the general polit

LONDON, Oct. 5 (P) — Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald went to Surrey today and talked for two hours with David Lloyd George, leader of the Liberal party, who is recuperating from an illness at his country place in Churt. Mr. MacDonald sought Mr. Lloyd George’s views regarding the general election which almost everyone expects before the end of this month.

LONDON.—(U.P)-Splits in the liberal party and in the Seaham division of the laborites appear today to have given Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald the opportunity to head a coalition ticket as a bona fide laborite candidate. The Seaham division asked MacDonald to resign his parliamentary seat after the formation of the present national government and declined to recommend him after the Prime Minister travelled to Durham Friday and addressed the Seaham delegates. But the Merton miners lodge and the Merton branch of the labor party decided to nominate MacDonald as a labor candidate and asked the Seaham divisional executive to reconsider its position. The decision asking for MacDonald's resignation was carried by only one vote. Action of the Merton miners may prove the decisive factor in enabling MacDonald to avoid becoming a candidate for a conservative division, which he is anxious to avoid

LONDON, Oct. 5. () — The Prince of Wales may adopt a bicycle in addition to his horse for early morning exercise. His cycling activities while on vacation in France kept him so fit that the vehicle is being shipped to England. Princess Elizabeth, his niece, is the only other cycling member of royalty. She has a tricycle.

LONDON, Oct. 5 UP—Premier David Lloyd George, Liberal leader, conferred with MacDonald at the latter's country home, where he is ill on the question of calling a parliamentary election. He did not expect to get his active support for the coalition government but hoped for only moderate opposition. MacDonald, repudiated by the Labor party in his own constituency, has been invited to run for re-election by two small groups of Laborites there and by several other constituencies.

VANCOUVER, F.C. Oct 5 —Pared by the gravest problems in its half century of existence, the American Federation of Labor opened its fifty-first annual convention here today. Four hundred delegates will seek, during the two weeks of the convention, to point the way for both capital and labor out of the slough of industrial depression. Immediate legalization of 2.75 percent beer, opposition to wage cutting, division of available work, stimulation of public projects, and better division of wealth are among the factors labor leaders propose as means of attaining this end. The goal of the federation as outlined by President William Green is to raise the standard of living for 2,900,000 members and to save an estimated 7,000,000 of America’s 29,500,000 workmen from unemployment this winter. “No more important convention of the federation was ever held,” said Green. “On our hands is the job of o

SHANGHAI, Oct. 5.—()—Two Japanese destroyers arrived here today and two others are on their way to reinforce Japan's flotilla on the Yangtse river in the face of Japanese officials’ fears that serious trouble may break out against their nationals in many river ports. The Japanese exodus from various Chinese cities developing since three started openly two weeks ago with the occupation of southern Manchuria by Japanese troops, quickened today. The Japanese legation here announced that its consulate at Chengshow, Honan province, had been closed and all its staff and other Japanese residents there had withdrawn to Hankow. At Chengtu, Szechwan province, authorization was given to close the Japanese consulate and withdraw Japanese nationals if advisable. The exodus from smaller Yangtse area cities continued, all Japanese women and children quitting Chungking, Shasi, Ichang and Changsha. Only

1931-01-13.text: MARYVILLE, Mo., Jan. 13. (AP)— Having methodically and with little excitement lynched a negro accused of attacking a white girl, the community of Maryville waited quietly today to see what, if anything, was to be done about it. Sheriff Harve England, who was injured by a mob that took Raymond Gunn by force, chained him atop the school house where he admitted he had killed Velma Colter, and burned him alive with the building, showed no disposition to arrest any of the ringleaders, although admitting he knew their names. He said, however, that if either a grand jury or Gov. Henry Caulfield asked him the names he would tell them. “I didn’t want to aggravate that mob,” England explained in telling why he had not called upon 60 National Guardsmen to stop the lynching after Gunn was taken away from him. The Guardsmen had been sent to Maryville in anticipation of trouble when Gunn was arraigned

MARYVILLE, Mo. Jan. 13: Sheriff Harve England said today he contemplated no action against leaders of a mob which yesterday seized his prisoner, Raymond Gunn, Negro, and beat him to death on the school house where he was charged with assaulting and abusing the teacher, Miss Velma Colter. D. D. Reeves, circuit judge, said today he had “not made up his mind” whether he would call a grand jury to investigate the incident.
MOSCOW, Jan. 14. — Amy Johnson, British aviatrix, left for Warsaw to fly back to London. She has abandoned her solo flight across Siberia to Peking.

LONDON, Jan. 13. (AP)—A combination of characteristics of the American and British parliamentary system is the plan of the Indian round table conference, which adjourns Monday, for a future government for India. The plan, evolved by the federal committee of the conference after weeks of labor, was presented substantially to the meeting yesterday by Lord Chancellor Sankey. It virtually outlines a dominion status for India, but must be accepted by parliament before it can become effective. There are to be two legislative houses, the upper one of which Lord Sankey called the “Senate.” It is to have probably 100 members, who will hold office for overlapping terms, so that its entire membership never will be new. The lower house, either a house of representatives or chamber, will have 250 members, elected for five years after the manner of members of the British House of Commons at a general

| SZOLNOK, HUNGARY, JAN. 13. (AP).—Crying “God help me,” Frau Marie Kardos was hanged today in the prison courtyard here in atonement to the state for the murder of her husband and 22-year-old son last year. | She was the first woman to be hanged by court sentence in Hungary for many generations. Frau Kardos, who was 46 years old, was one of forty women who appeared in the group poisoning trials of last spring and summer, resulting from the wholesale deaths of husbands and sweethearts, and one of three to receive the death sentence. She lost the jaded ennui which marked her early demeanor in the few days preceding her death. As execution became imminent she was stricken with terror at the prospect of the gallows: She ate heartily in her prison cell last night, a bowl of goulash being allotted her for her last dinner. Then followed a period of prayer with friends and a Protestant clergyma

Horta, Azores, Jan. 12. ()—Hope that the transatlantic “payload” aviators, Mrs. Beryl Hart and Lieutenant William S. MacLaren, were still alive was virtually abandoned tonight. Not a word or a sign of them had been received since they took off from Hamilton, Bermuda, at 11:15 a.m., (e.s.t.) Saturday for Horta on the second lap of their flight in the monoplane Tradewind from New York to Paris. Strong winds and high seas have prevailed since that time and it was feared that had they been forced down their frail machine could have withstood the seas only a few minutes. They had expected to take 21 hours for the flight and were due at 8:15 a.m., (e.s.t.) Sunday morning. Tonight, indicative of the fear that they were lost, gasoline supplies which had been kept on a scow in the harbor in readiness for refueling were withdrawn. There was still a possibility they had been forced to come down nea

Lisbon, Jan. 13.—(4)—A bit of hope for the safety of Lieutenant William S. MacLaren and Mrs. Beryl Hart, missing since they left Bermuda Saturday noon in the seaplane Tradewind for the Azores, was dashed tonight. Portuguese admiralty officials ordered an eager search today when they received reports from New York that the plane was alleged to have fallen into the sea about twenty miles off Mosteiros point of San Miguel island, one of the Azores group. Villagers were said to have seen the plane diving for the water but the San Miguel wireless station, to which the report was attributed, informed the government tonight that the object which fell was only a rocket fired from a British cruiser engaged in gunnery practice near by.

TOKYO, Jan. 18—-(AP)—Reports of the movement of Russian troops toward the western frontier of Manchuria reached official circles here today. The military movement was described as being due to Moscow's belief China may not abide by the Khabarovsk agreement of 1929 giving Russia virtual control of the Chinese Eastern Railway, which connects Vladivostok with the Trans-Siberian Railway by crossing Manchuria. Manchurian troops also were reported concentrating near the Russian frontier. Neither of these reports could be confirmed.

1931-05-04.text: Angnagsalik, Greenland, May 4. —(AP)—Capt. Albin Ahrenberg, Swedish aviator, was within flying distance today of the tiny hut on Greenland’s ice where Augustine Courtauld, British explorer, has been marooned for many months. After one false start, Captain Ahrenberg flew here yesterday from Reykjavik, Iceland, in five hours, completing a dangerous flight across the north Atlantic from Malmoe, Sweden, in four stages. Formation of ice on the wings of his plane prevented him from continuing his journey in search of the isolated Britisher. Captain Ahrenberg’s immediate destination is the main camp of the British Arctic air route expedition, about forty miles inland, and thence to the meteorological station, about 150 miles inland, where Courtauld volunteered to spend the winter gathering data for a proposed air line to Canada. He plans to drop food to the explorer and possibly make a landing

took off at 10:10 am. today (8:10 p.m. Sunday EST) on the first leg of a 6,248 mile flight to San Francisco via the Aleutian islands and British Columbia. Alone and without radio, the “Lindbergh of Japan” as he is often called, started his open seaplane on a good-will trip to America carrying to President Hoover a diadem from the Japanese magazine king, Seiji Noma, the backer of the flight. To Go by Way of Alaska He hoped to complete the first stage of the journey to Numasaki, 368 miles north of Tokyo, before nightfall. The next jump would take him 297 miles further north to the extreme tip of Hokkaido island. Then his itinerary calls for flights over the Kurile islands to Petropavlovsk, Siberia, over the Bering sea to the Aleutians and after several stops, to Seward, Alaska. From there he would fly southward to Seattle, then to San Francisco. He would then go to Washington. The flier sp

Manchester, England, May 3. (®)— The peaceful countryside of East Lancaster was shocked early today by a sharp earth tremor, which was felt over a large area. No casualties were reported but there was some property damage. At Eccles buildings were slightly damaged and a number of chimneys and flower pots were shaken down. A telephone operator at the exchange was hurled from her seat when the building shook. The incident was an unpleasant surprise to Lancashiremen who are not used to such manifestations of nature.

REYKJAVIK, Iceland, May 3.— (AP)—Captain Albin Ahrenberg, Swedish flier who will search for Augustine Courtauld, British scientist missing on Greenland’s ice cap, arrived in Angmagsalik, Greenland, this afternoon after a flight over the Strait of Denmark from Reykjavik. The aviator had intended to continue the flight immediately in search of the missing Englishman, but he was prevented from doing so by formation of ice on the wings of his plane. This compelled him to land at Angmagsalik. Ahrenberg made the flight from the Iceland capital in five hours, landing in Greenland at 3 p. m. During the trip he passed over the Danish cruiser Hvidbjorn, which lies near the Greenland ice barrier. The Icelandic patrol boat Odin, which went to aid in the search for Courtauld also is in the Strait of Denmark on its way back here to repair its damaged airplane. The Swedish flier tried to reach Greenlan

LONDON, May 4. — (NS) — The Norwegian government may take active measures to prevent Captain Sir Hubert Wilkins from making his projected journey to the North Pole in a submarine, it was stated in an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Oslo, today. The message quoted the Oslo newspaper Arbeiderbladet as saying the government considers the expedition as an “unnecessary risk of human life.” If the Wilkins expedition calls at Norway en route to the pole, the dispatch said, the government plans to enforce the regulations enabling it to exercise definite control over all Arctic expeditions starting from that country.

MANCHESTER, Eng., May 4—Its an ill earthquake for golfers that doesn’t make a hole in one. As a sharp earth tremor shook the east Lancaster countryside yesterday, a golfer on the Chorlton links drove to within a few inches of the hole. The earth rolled gently and the ball dropped in. Although seismographs registered only one two-thousandths of an inch, the temblor alarmed thousands in this vicinity. Minor damage was done to smaller buildings but no one was injured.

LONDON, May 4.—Major D. R. Larcombe, secretary of the All-England tennis club today received a letter from Mrs. Helen Wills Moody, of Berkeley, Cal., indicating she may come to England for the Wimbledon tennis championships to defend the title she has held since 1927. Mrs. Moody previously had announced her intention of playing only in tournaments in the United States this year.

LONDON, May 4 (AP)—Dr. Harriett Clisby, who celebrated her 100th birthday last August and was said to be the oldest woman physician in the world, is dead at her home in West Kensington. She studied medicine in Australia.

1931-02-09.text: LONDON, Feb. 9, UPA mother of four children, who was sentenced to hang for having murdered the fourth baby, has given birth to twins in the hospital of Holloway prison. The woman is Mrs. Olive Catherine Wise, who once was married and bore three children legitimately to her husband. They were separated and she bore a fourth child to another man. He deserted her and she attempted desperately to feed the four hungry mouths. She even chopped wood and hawked it through the streets but finally gave up the struggle, placed the baby in an oven and turned on the gas. British law takes no cognizance of exceptional circumstances or temporary insanity in murder cases and she was condemned to hang. A storm of public indignation followed and her sentence was commuted.
By United Press LONDON, Feb. 9—The Earl of Beauchamp was appointed today as governor general of Canada, succeeding Lord Willingdon, who has been named viceroy of India.

London, Feb. 9. (4) — King George today appointed the Earl of Bessborough, a distinguished Irish peer, to be governor-general of Canada succeeding Lord Willingdon, who has been named viceroy of India. Lord Bessborough is the ninth Earl of that name and comes of a distinguished family which gave to Ireland and Great Britain many noted soldiers, parliamentarians and lawyers.

New York, Feb. Y-(Mj)—After crossing three continents in a tiny biplane—the smallest and cheapest flying machine she could buy in England—the honorable Mrs. Victor Bruce is taking home a spoken record of her globe-circling flight. It was in a “honeymoon model” with seats for two, close together—the 29-year-old amateur flier set out on her adventure last September. Married for more than a decade, she decided a 50-gallon tank of gasoline would be of more use to her than a husband in that extra seat. Made Fifty Records “But a woman must talk,” she said, “and since I was not taking my husband along to listen, I placed a recording device at my side.” As she flew over the plains of Hungary, the deserts of Persia, the jungles of India, the pagodas of China, the imperial palace of Japan, the forests of western Canada, the mountains, valleys, deserts and farms between California and New York, Mrs

WASHINGTON, Feb. 2- The Navy Department was advised Monday by the commandant of the Key West, Fla., naval station that the steamship “British Chancery” was reported ashore off Gatienan Point, on the coast of Colombia and in need of assistance.

This placed the spot about 180 miles north by west of Corvo Island, the northernmost and smallest of the Azores group. The wreckage was grey, he said, was approximately three feet wide by seven feet long and looked like part of an airplane wing. “We also saw other wreckage,” he said, “which looked like part of ; ; | | | (Continued On Page Eight)

LONDON, Feb. 9.--(UP)--Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald told the House of Commons today the government was not considering any proposal to summon an international round table conference on the subject of inter-allied debts and war reparations. MacDonald's statement was in reply to a question asked by Commander J. M. Kenworthy, who sought to bring the question of a readjustment of war debts, which recently has aroused wide comment in unofficial circles, to the House of Commons.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 9. (AP).— A radio dispatch to the Navy Department today said the steamship British Chancellor was ashore off the coast of Colombia at Gallinas Point, and asking for immediate assistance. The message came from the commandant of the seventh naval district at Key West, Fla., which advised that the steamship Statendam was 100 miles away. Vessels near were advised to communicate with the Statendam. Navy Department records list the Chancellor as a British oil tanker of 7,000 tons. It is owned by the British Tanker Company and registered at London.

1931-11-01.text: LONDON— Industrial revival in England following temporary suspension of gold standard engages attention of newspapers which find pickup especially noticeable in cotton and textile industries. Iron, steel, coal, pottery up. Bank of England granted three months extension by Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and Bank of France on March part of credit advanced last August to restore confidence in pound sterling. Nearly £15,000,000 in bar gold withdrawn as first step toward repayment of the credit. NEW YORK—Initial dividends declared by eight companies during past week, extras by four. Fourteen favorable changes recorded against only nine the week before. Dividends on more than 600 stock issues payable on Monday as part of more than $1,200,000,000 investment turnover scheduled for month of November. Commercial agencies find signs of improvement not lacking and predominant note in general busi

LONDON, Oct. 31. — Mahatma Gandhi does not intend to dress up to attend a party at Buckingham Palace to which he has been invited. "I will wear my habitual dress of loin cloth, shawl and sandals," he said. "If the king or the government prescribe European dress, I will be obliged to decline the royal invitation."

LONDON, Oct. 23. (AP)—A blind man, leaving the National Institute in Great Portland Street, touched the arm of another man. Thinking he was being offered a helping hand, he took the arm and stepped off the walk to cross the street. After a few steps he was struck by a car. The other man was blind, too.

(By Associated Press) A Japanese announcement said reinforcements have been sent from the South Manchuria Railway gone to Tsitsihar, where the situation is described as “dangerous” because of the Chinese advance. A Hailun Exchange Telegraph message to London from Hailun said 200 bandits attacked the Hureta railway station and killed several railway guards, after which they robbed the place. The League of Nations continued to work on the Japanese delegation to obtain acceptance of the League plan to restore peace. Mavora-Shitgemitsa, Japanese minister to Nanking, said Japan welcomed the Chinese proposal for neutral ground between Chinchow and Mukden: With China announcing acceptance of the League council's proposal, the council sought to overcome Japan's insistence of its right to continue to police the area against bandits. On this point Japan's position is at variance with the League pl

LONDON, Oct. 31.—Eleven members of the royal family of Luang Prabang, part of the French protectorate of Laos in Indo-China, drowned after a royal canoe struck a rock in the Moking river, said dispatches received here today. Just which members of the family drowned was not made known, but it was believed the majority were children.

(By United Press.) TOKIO, Oct. 31.—A movement of Japanese troops northward from Manchuria into Russian territory is impending, according to a Nippon Dempo News agency dispatch received here today from Mukden. The report of the concerted advance followed an exchange of notes between Tokio and Moscow in which the Soviet government claimed it was "strictly neutral in the Manchurian controversy between China and Japan." The dispatch reported three Soviet officials had departed from Harbin, a Russian center in Manchuria, for Moscow on receiving word of the impending Japanese troop movement. White Russians in Manchuli and other points in Manchuria are withdrawing to Harbin, the dispatch said. While Japan apparently was preparing to enforce its "friendly" warning to Russia, it was understood that Chinese military commanders in Heilungkiang province were strengthening their forces with evident i

GENEVA, Switzerland, Oct. 31.—Thirteen nations, including the United States, have signified their willingness to participate in a one-year armament building truce proposed by the council of the League of Nations, and although there was no official statement from the league secretariat today there was a disposition to believe that some sort of truce can be put into effect. The building holiday, the league proposed, would begin tomorrow and continue for 12 months. France accepted conditionally, asserting that it was willing to participate if the nations which border that country also agreed. “So far, in addition to the United States and France, affirmative replies have been received from Japan, Russia, Hungary, Holland, Australia, New Zealand, Czechoslovakia, Egypt, Albania, Latvia and Luxembourg. Great Britain has not replied nor has Switzerland, and there has been no word from Italy or G

TOKYO, Oct. 31. (AP)— That Japan and Russia are seeing eye to eye, for the time being at least, regarding the situation in northern Manchuria was made clear here today in reports received from the conversations in Moscow between Ambassador Hirota and L. M. Karakhan, acting foreign affairs commissar of the Soviet government. The reports indicated Russia was not sending any troops to guard the Chinese eastern railway, Sino-Russian operated line crossing Manchuria, and that Japan was not dispatching any soldiers to that railway region unless there were unexpected developments. Hirota emphasized that if Rus- (Continued on Page 6)

1931-02-27.text: LONDON, Feb. 27. (UP)—The resignation of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's labor government was considered a possibility in some political quarters today after a Liberalist amendment to the trades disputes bill had taken most of the original flavor out of the measure. The bill, intended to legalize general strikes, in its amended form defines as illegal "any strike or walkout the effect of which at any time by reason of its extension or continuation endangers public health and safety by interfering with supplies or distribution of water, fuel, lights, medicine and sanitary service or other necessities of life." Trade unionists were particularly bitter regarding the amendment and said it violated the entire trade disputes bill.

LONDON, Feb. 27 (AP) — Queen Mary has broken her rule about wedding presents. Usually brides in the court receive from the queen a piece of jewelry set with the royal cipher. But to the Hon. Imogene Grenfell, who yesterday married Viscount Gage, a captain of the Coldstream Guards, she gave a beautiful dressing case. The bag was small, in a handbag design, of green crushed Morocco leather. The top is nearly covered by a circular plaque of white jade in a delicate pattern. Bottles and other fittings are done in a soft green enamel to match the leather.

PARIS.—Police Friday seized a high-powered grenade which had been placed in the automobile of Count Manzoni, the Italian ambassador to France. The explosive was discovered by the ambassador's chauffeur before Count Manzoni entered the automobile. A police investigation was started immediately.

MOSCOW, Feb. 27.—The Soviet Union prepared today for the trial of 14 men who had attained high positions in the economic workings of the government, indicted on charges of planning intervention and sabotage. The accused are members of the Menshevik minority. The state alleged that their backing came from France and Germany. The proceedings will start Sunday and were expected to be similar to the recent trial of eight prominent engineers and professors who were sentenced to prison for alleged intervention plots. As in the previous trial, the 14 men involved in the new process confessed and pleaded guilty. Their trial may be even more significant than that of Professor Leonid Ramzin and his comrades, for it will involve the correct application of Marxist doctrines to the problems of Communist government and may be the final round in the battle between Mensheviks (minority) and Bolshevik fa

PARIS, Feb. 27.—(UP)— The 16th anniversary of the death of Edward Mandelstone, of Chicago, first American killed in the World War, was observed today with a ceremony before the monument to Americans who died for France. American and French war veterans, many of them with an arm or leg missing, gathered before the monument and placed a wreath in memory of the first American blood spilt there. The ceremony was organized by Trench and Air, an association of American volunteer combatants in the French army, of which John G. Hopper, of San Francisco and Paris, is president.

| TOKIO, Feb. 27.—(AP)—An “interesting event” of paramount concern to the 90,000,000 subjects of the emperor of Japan is expected within a few days, for the birth of an infant that may become the sovereign of the empire should take place about March 10. The Empress Nagako is about to present her consort, Emperor Hirohito, with a child, and in the imperial palace preparations for the expected arrival have taken precedence over everything else. Even if the little mite of the blood imperial is a girl there will be nation-wide rejoicing for the safety of the empress and her baby, but the celebrations will not be so extensive as if it is a prince to be welcomed. In either case, however, there will be ceremonies to announce the birth in the three shrines of the imperial palace—the Kashikodokoro, or Holy of Holies, where the imperial mirror of the sun goddess is enshrined; the Korei-Den, dedica

MOSCOW, Feb. 27.—Fourteen prominent Russians will go to trial tomorrow for treason here March 1, charged with counter-revolutionary activities. The defendants, who are described in the indictments as friends of the recently condemned group of engineers led by Professor Leonid Ramsin, are headed by the widely known agronomist, Professor Groman. They are all members of the Menshevik (minority as opposed to Bolshevik, majority) faction of the Communist party.

Naples, Italy, Feb. 26.—(AP)—Cyclonic storms, which have battered southern Italy for almost a week, had abated tonight, leaving in their wake about 27 persons drowned and several million dollars damage. The storm which reached its most northern point here, wrought its worst damage on small vessels, sea-ports and country districts. The southern provinces were hardest hit in recent years. As reports trickled in from outlying towns the death toll climbed steadily.

1931-04-02.text: Malaga, Spain, April 2 — The French consul here reported today that thirty persons had been killed and five seriously injured when the French liner Florida collided with the British aircraft carrier Glorious during a fog in the Mediterranean yesterday. The dead and injured are all steerage passengers, Italian, Spanish, French, or Greek returning to Europe from the Argentine. Passengers of the first and second classes escaped unhurt... The Florida, badly damaged in the bow, was brought to Malaga this morning accompanied by a British gunboat and five British destroyers. Both the Florida and the Glorious are now at Malaga, the Glorious bringing with her all first and second class passengers and injured steerage passengers of the Florida. The dead and injured of the Florida will be transferred to the Glorious and then put ashore.

LONDON, (UP)—Twenty-three passengers aboard the French liner Florida, which collided with the aircraft carrier Glorious off Gibraltar yesterday, are missing and believed dead, the foreign office announced today. One passenger was known dead, the announcement said, and 15 were injured, two seriously.

London, April 2 (UP)—Lady Jean Doyle, widow of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, told the United Press today that she had received a written message from her husband who died July 7 last. She said it was “the first time a message has been received from my husband in his own handwriting since his death.” Lady Doyle said the handwriting in the message from the famous spiritualist and creator of Sherlock Holmes was “100 per cent evidence of his psychic powers.” “My son and I were sitting with a famous photographic medium before us hoping that my husband would be able to show himself or the plate by us,” Lady Doyle told the United Press. “No hand but my own touched the plate from beginning to end including the development of the negative. “We developed the negative ourselves. In addition to my husband’s face which was shown on the plate as it appeared over the shoulder of my son, there was, to our ama

PARANA DE LOS PALMA Argentina, April 2—(P)—A new world's speed boat record was claimed for Kaye Don, English speed driver, this afternoon. His speed, pending compilation of official figures, was calculated at 103.7 land miles an hour. Don drove his boat, Miss England I. The former world’s motorboat record, established March 26, 1931, is 102 miles an hour and is held by Gar Wood, American.

London, April 1. (AP)—Several of the crew of the French liner Florida were killed today when that vessel collided with the British aircraft carrier Glorious, sixty miles east of Gibraltar. An announcement by the British admiralty said the bodies had been left in the Florida, which was taken in tow by the Glorious. Others in the crew were seriously injured. All were transferred with the passengers to the man-of-war. So far as could be ascertained tonight none of the passengers were killed or injured. The commander-in-chief of the British Mediterranean fleet was proceeding to H.M.S. Queen Elizabeth to join the Florida off Malaga at daylight.

Malaga, Spain, (UP) — Thirty steerage passengers were killed in the collision between the French liner Florida and the British aircraft carrier Glorious, the captain of the Florida announced today. The captain gave the list of missing persons as 17 Italians, four Poles, three Yugoslavs, five Syrians and Turks, and one Spaniard. One injured passenger died after being taken aboard the Glorious. Seven bodies had been recovered from the wrecked steerage quarters of the Florida. The passengers were killed when the force of the collision threw quantities of cargo upon them. Six injured persons were placed in a hospital here. Estimates of the total number of injured ranged between 20 and 30.

NEW YORK, April 2. (4)—Raymond Staines, 15 months old son of a British consular worker at Tampico, Mexico, was accidentally strangled by the neck cord of a sleeping bag in the Hotel Pennsylvania last night while his parents attended a theater. The child was found by a floor maid, who had been asked to look in at intervals, just before the parents returned.

(International News Service) LONDON, April 1.—In a report to the British Admiralty, the commandant of the British carrier Glorious stated that twenty-three emigrant passengers of the French liner Florida were found to be missing following a collision between the two vessels. The report stated they were probably killed when the two ships crashed in a dense fog sixty miles east of Gibraltar. Most of the French liner’s passengers were Italians and Syrians. Seventeen planes from the Glorious’ complement were in the air at the time of the collision. Four passengers from the Florida who were thrown into the water by the impact were rescued and taken to Malaga by the airmen. The Florida was beached at the first opportunity, but the Glorious was found seaworthy and proceeded to Gibraltar. The foreign office announced that one of the Florida’s passengers was known to be dead and two seriously and

1931-07-05.text: The nation’s 155th birthday party yesterday took a toll of human lives that had approached the 175 mark late last night. Unlike former years, fireworks accounted for only two deaths—one in the southwest and the other in New England. Automobile accidents and drownings each had accounted for more than 50 lives, or approximately two-thirds of the total. Twelve were drowned in Los Angeles. Scores of injuries, many serious, also were reported from traffic accidents due to the crowded conditions of highways. Fireworks, although not causing as many deaths as in previous years, accounted for scores of injuries. Wisconsin alone reported 42 such casualties. Airplane wrecks were responsible for six deaths and one man was killed in an automobile race in Colorado. The rear guard of the heat wave sweeping eastward took four more lives in Pennsylvania and one in Ohio as its death toll neared 1,300. The

NEWPORT, R. I., July 4.—(U.P)—Ten bounding little craft, the smallest only 34 feet long, left here at 1 p.m. today on a transatlantic race to Plymouth, England. The yachts, all sturdy little sailboats, eight American-owned and two representing England, are the smallest ever engaged in the perilous race across the stormy northern route. Word from L. Schlimbach, owner and skipper of the hoped-for German entry, "Storekeeper," said he was unable to enter the race. After covering 1,200 miles in an effort to get here on time, the German captain put in at Vigo, Spain, due to heavy seas. Not a pet was to be found on any of the entries. On George E. Roosevelt's schooner "Roosevelt" there is a crate of roosters but they won't even have time to develop sea legs before they are put into the broiler. Popularity of the small-sized cruising yacht, with strong hull, moderate amount of sail, and a motor

BEVINBURGH, Scotland, July 4 (4)—King George and Queen Mary arrived here tonight and drove the two miles to Holyrood Palace where tomorrow they will celebrate their thirty-eighth wedding anniversary. It was their first joint visit in four years. Queen Mary's breakfast table tomorrow will be adorned with a tiny box containing a pearl pendant, the king’s anniversary gift. The royal romance reads like a fairy tale. The king first met and wooed the queen while both were still virtually children. But the king’s brother, the Duke of Clarence proposed first, and was accepted. Six weeks before the marriage was to have taken place, however, the Duke of Clarence died of pneumonia and 16 months later Prince George and Princess Mary of Teck were married.

(By The Associated Press) Paris, July 4—French and American statesmen early this morning reached the basis of a complete agreement for the application of the Hoover plan for economic relief to Germany. After a series of negotiations which had been always laborious, and sometimes delicate and even critical, the statesmen reached their accord after midnight. The draft of the text, which was to be telegraphed to Washington immediately, is subject to the approval of President Hoover and his governmental colleagues. If the President finds that it conforms to the principles of his plan, a final decision is expected on Monday and the agreement will be put into final form at another conference of the French and American statesmen which probably will also be held Monday. It will then be initialed by the negotiators. The Havas News Agency said that the Franco-American agreement fixed 12 years as t

Rome, July 4—(/#)——Possibility of the withdrawal of the papal nuncio at Rome was a subject of discussion by diplomatic observers tonight as a result of the widening of the breach between the church and state by the encyclical of Pope Pius XI on Fascism. Nothing approaching a diplomatic rupture was foreseen, but observers believed the Vatican might withdraw its nuncio as a gesture of indignation to emphasize the pope's reiterated disapproval of Premier Mussolini’s action against the Catholic clubs. Il Duce Silent. The government remained officially silent tonight. The last Italian note to the Vatican protested against what it called the pontiff’s ‘“‘trying his case’’ before world public opinion. Regarding the pontiff’s contention that the education of youth belongs to the church, the Fascist creed is so squarely opposed to this that neither the government nor the Vatican authorities could

(Copyright, 1931, by the Associated Press) PARIS, July 4. (Saturday) (@)— Satisfactory progress was achieved Friday night at a meeting by the French and American representatives discussing President Hoover's moratorium proposal, the American embassy informed the Associated Press early today. No complete accord was reached, as was indicated by an official statement issued at the end of the meeting, but the statement describes the points which remain unsettled as minor points. Two Points Remain Of four points outstanding, it was learned this morning on reliable authority two have now been eliminated and two remain to be settled. These two unsettled points, one of which is believed to concern the question of the guarantee fund to be deposited by France with the bank for international settlements in the event of a German moratorium under the Young plan, will be discussed by the French cabine

Turin, Italy, July 4—(#)—The Duke of Aosta died at 1:30 o'clock this afternoon. The duke, cousin to the king of Italy, several times during his lifetime was mentioned as a candidate for the Italian throne. He also might have been king of Greece, but political fortunes were against him. During the war he won fame as a soldier but sacrificed his health. Bronchial and lung affections endangered his life several times. A weak heart complicated his illnesses and during recent years he lived in retirement. The duke was 62 years old. His chronic illness became critical a week ago and the King of Italy visited his bedside.

(By The Associated Press) Paris, July 4.—General Pershing and President Hoover shared individual honors today in Paris’ celebration of the Fourth of July. The general was told by Francois Latour, president of the municipal council, that a Parisian street will be named for him. Mr. Hoover was extolled as the pre-war revictualler of the allies by Edouard Renard, prefect of the department of the Seine. Both tributes were rendered during the course of an elaborate reception at Paris City Hall at which representatives of 22 American republics marked the closing of the “Week of American Nations” sponsored by the France-America committee. General Pershing in his reply to M. Latour said he greatly appreciated the honor which the municipal council was about to confer on him but “I accept it not for myself personally but for the 2,000,000 Americans who crossed the seas to aid France and maintain t

1931-01-24.text: To the Editor of The Eagle: PINE BLUFF, Ark., Jan. 26 Just came from England, Ark., town you read about, where the people wanted food. It seemed mighty peaceful and happy now. Went to the school there where the children were being fed at lunchtime all they wanted of fine vegetable soup, cooked in a big vat, that had been a whiskey still, presented to the cause by some eccentric moonshiner. This is the very heart of the most needy section of America, and yet it’s the most fertile land you ever saw. But the country people absolutely lack nothing. The Red Cross, as usual, are doing great work. In just these two counties I visited, they are feeding 8,000 families, with an average of six to the family! You don't know what hard times are till you go into some of these houses. Weather is with 'em pretty good but if it weren't for the...

LONDON, Jan 24 (P)—A gale of fifty miles an hour velocity swept Western Europe and the British Isles during the night. There was an accompanying deluge of rain and thunder and lightning. High seas led to some anxiety for shipping. A Portuguese trawler was sunk in the mouth of the Tagus and two of its crew were drowned. The liner Vardulia, en route from St. John to London, damaged a rudder in the Bay of Biscay and broadcast a distress signal which brought the Dutch tug, Witte Zee, to her assistance. Two other tugs already had gone to her help so the Witte Zee returned. The Vardulia radioed her position to Lloyds as somewhat south of her course, indicating possibly she was being driven by the storm. She was not considered in any danger. No anxiety was felt for the British cruiser Canterbury en route from the Mediterranean although she was many hours overdue at Plymouth.

HONGKONG, Jan. 24 (#)—The American liner President Hayes, while proceeding on its round the world voyage yesterday outside of Amoy, China, ran into the British steamer Kumsang, bound from Calcutta for Osaka. Both liners were damaged. The Kumsang put into Amoy. Damage was said to be above water line. The President Hayes has reached Hongkong and the damage will be surveyed. The President Hayes is a Dollar Steamship line boat of 6,195 tons register. She left San Francisco Dec. 26 and Honolulu Jan. 2 proceeding to Japan. The Kumsang belongs to the Indo-China Steam Navigation company and is of 3,341 tons net register.

BY ALPEN ALAN, PER. 29° "A R FUR tentative plan for consolidation and acquisition by eastern trunk lines of the principal New England railroads has been evolved by the presidents of the four major eastern roads, it was learned here today. - The plan calls for the following allocations: : The Boston and Maine to the Nickel Plate (Van Swearingens); The Boston and Albany to B... New York Central, and the New York, New Haven and Hartford to the Pennsylvania and Baltimore and Ohio, jointly. The proposal will be submitted to the interstate commerce commission as soon as it has disposed of the eastern executives' plan for consolidation of 54 eastern roads into four railway officials here.

MANCHESTER, Eng. Jan, 24.— (UP)—A prolonged mill stoppage was foreseen in Lancashire today when the weavers voted against resuming negotiations for settlement of the present conflict which has put some 250,000 men out of work and threatens to make as many more idle. The vote was 90,770 to 44,990 against resuming negotiations. The cotton trouble grew out of efforts of employers to put the "more looms per weaver" system into effect. The workers objected.

NEW DELHI, India, Jan. 23.—(”) Before another 24 hours have passed, Mahatma Gandhi, imprisoned leader of the Indian nationalists, probably will be a free man, it was predicted here today. The end of his eight months’ imprisonment appeared to be delayed only by a decision as to what other leaders of the congress party should be given their freedom with him. The viceroy and his council were discussing this matter today but it was believed they already had decided to restore Gandhi's freedom. His liberation and that of his associates is bound up with the issue of general amnesty for all India’s 60,000 or more political prisoners. At the close of the round table conference in London, Ramsay MacDonald said amnesty would be granted if order could be restored in India.

MOSCOW (UP)—A statement issued Saturday under the signature of Josef V.Y. Stalin announced the beginning of “a decisive final drive” to eradicate the kulaks of Russia as a class. The drive against the kulaks (a term chiefly applied to rich peasants) will be carried out with the intention of eliminating the class within the present year. It was interpreted as meaning a new offensive in behalf of the collectiveization campaign which probably would exceed the intensive drive of 1939.

GENEVA, Jan. 4—(#)—The council of the League of Nations today formally invited the governments of the world to assemble for a general disarmament conference Feb. 2, 1932. The date was designated at the first Tuesday after the session of the council in January 1932, which will begin Jan. 25 and last about a week. Geneva was designated conditionally as the place for the conference.

1931-01-14.text: Horta, Island of Fayal, Azores Jan. 14. (4)—A British cruiser engaged in gunnery practice off Sao Miguel island, Azores, Sunday night, unwittingly gave rise to a false hope of a clue to the disappearance of the airplane Tradewind on its flight from Hamilton, Bermuda, Saturday. The cruiser sent up several rockets. One of these which disappeared into the ocean about 20 miles off Mosteiros point, Sao Miguel, was mistaken by some for the Tradewind falling into the sea, and a radio station there is said to have broadcast an appeal to ships to (Continued on Page 5)

PONTA DELGADA, San Miguel Island, the Azores, Jan. 14—(UP)—Reports that distress signals had been seen from the missing seaplane Tradewind were traced today to fishermen who mistook star shells fired by two British cruisers for flares dropped by aviators. No news of the Tradewind has reached the Azores. The cruisers fired star shells off San Miguel Monday night. Native fishermen saw the lights breaking over the sea and confused them with S. O. S. signals from an airplane when they learned later that Mrs. Beryl Hart and Lieut. William S. MacLaren were missing in the Tradewind on a flight from Bermuda to the Azores.

LONDON, Jan. 14 (AP)—British radio systems today paged Sir Francis Barrow, English baronet who mysteriously disappeared 18 years ago and has not since made his whereabouts known. A broadcast carried the urgent appeal of friends to come home immediately since his eldest son, Wilfred John Wilson Croker, heir to his title, is seriously ill. The broadcast was the first revelation to the general public that the baronet, who is the fourth of his line, was missing. Lady Barrow, his wife, and other members of the family declined to discuss the disappearance or other circumstances of the case. If still alive Sir Francis would be 68 years old.

LONDON (iUP).—Capt. Malcolm Campbell sails for the United States Wednesday, confident that the New Blue Bird speed automobile he will take to Daytona Beach will set a new world record of around 250 miles an hour. The New Blue Bird, which was shrouded with much secrecy during its construction, was described as more than half again as powerful as the famous Golden Arrow in which the late Sir Henry Segrave attained a speed of 231.447 miles an hour to set the present mark at Daytona in 1929. One of Campbell's chief aides during the trials which he will make in Florida probably will be R. J. Leech, who was on the giant British dirigible R-101 when it crashed in France three months ago. Leech was one of the few survivors of the disaster. He was invited by Campbell to assist in the noted driver’s attack on the speed record.

SZOLNOK, Hungary, Jan. 13—(AP)—Marie Kardos, the first woman to be hanged in Hungary in many years, went to the gallows today for the murder of her husband and her 22-year-old son last year. Seventy persons watched the execution which took place early in the morning. The woman had lost all the composure which had remained with her during the period of her imprisonment, and she was on the verge of collapse when she was led from the cell to the scaffold. Frau Kardos was one of forty women who were tried together last spring and summer after their husbands and other relatives had died mysteriously of poison. Most of the crimes were traced to an old woman called "Aunt Susie" who, it was established, incited most of the murders and in most of the cases administered the poison for a fee. She was said to have made a small fortune this way, after she had been convicted of murder she took her own

Lisbon, Jan. 14, WUP—The Dornier flying boat DO-X will proceed to Rio de Janeiro between January 25 and 31, Capt. Christiansen, commander, said today. The ship will fly south via Madeira, the Canary Islands, Fernando Noronha Island, Natal, and Dakar, Capt. Christiansen said. The flight was postponed several weeks ago when fire damaged one of the ship’s wings in Lisbon harbor. Lieut. H.C. Schildhauer, American flier and co-pilot of the DO-X, is en route from the United States to rejoin the ship here.

PONTA DELGADA, AZORES, Jan. 14—The steamer Norfolk, which for two days has been searching the seas about the Azores islands for the missing monoplane Tradewind, and the Swedish steamer Nuolja, which also has been looking for the missing plane, reported today their search had been fruitless.

Ry International News Service, LISBON, Portugal. Jan. 14—The Portuguese destroyer Ibo, ordered to search the vicinity of Sao Miguel island on reports here that an "object" thought to have been the New York-to-Paris monoplane Tradewind had been seen falling into the sea Sunday morning, was recalled today when the rumors could not be substantiated. The naval authorities dispatched the destroyer in the hope of finding the aviators, Mrs. Beryl Hart and William MacLaren, alive somewhere in the designated vicinity. Later advices from authentic sources on San Miguel island said there was no foundation for the rumor, following an extensive search in the parts where the "object" was reported to have fallen.

1931-07-09.text: BERLIN, July 9 ()—Hans Luther, president of the Reichsbank, left for London today to discuss a large loan for Germany. He will discuss with the heads of British banks, particularly with the Bank of England, a large loan which Germany must have promptly, and he has to convince British financiers that the action of German industries in guaranteeing the Gold Discount bank up to $125,000,000 entitles Germany to confidence abroad. He hopes that the long term credit Germany requires can be obtained in London and it is understood he will propose a loan of $250,000,000, a sum regarded as necessary at this time to German economic life. Plans were being made for the experts committee on the Hoover moratorium plan to meet at London next Friday, on the same day that Prime Minister MacDonald and Foreign Minister Arthur Henderson of Great Britain will leave for Berlin to return the visit of the German chancellor and foreign minister. It was announced at Washington that the United States would send an observer to the London experts’ meeting and the announcement was also made that the American government would accept an invitation received today to participate in the general disarmament conference at Geneva next February. Secretary of State Stimson arrived at Rome last night almost simultaneously with a proposal from the French government to the Italian government suggesting a renewal of Franco-Italian naval limitations discussions. In most of the capitals of Europe and in other countries of the world the Franco-American agreement was hailed with satisfaction and enthusiasm. European stock markets generally reacted favorably to the announcement of the accord, although the New York stock market broke sharply during the day, recording net losses of from $2 to nearly $10 a share. Secretary Mellon left Paris for the Riviera and the impression prevailed that the part of the United States in sponsoring the moratorium was virtually ended. Although the United States is not a signer of the Young plan, she will be represented by an “observer.” Experts to Gather Preliminary negotiations will be conducted by financial experts only, but it was regarded as highly probable tonight that these technical discussions would be followed by a meeting of statesmen of major calibre. The nature and scope of such a meeting, assuming that it occurs at all, would naturally depend on the course taken at the experts conference. LONDON, July 9 (AP)— Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald was slightly ill today with what was variously termed an “internal chill” and an attack of “nervous indigestion.” The strain of work in connection with difficulties in parliament and the reparations situation was believed to be responsible for his indisposition. He surrendered his place in the House of Commons to Chancellor Philip Snowden last night and went home to rest. Consultation with his physician Sir Thomas Horder failed to bring a statement but it is understood that the diagnosis was not alarming and that cessation from work for the next ten days was the doctor's prescription. Mr. MacDonald may go to his country home at Chequers for a rest but plans to attend a peace demonstration at Albert Hall, Saturday. With Stanley Baldwin, David Lloyd George and representatives from other walks of life he will issue a united call for reduc

Mississauga Country Club, Toronto, July 9.--(GP)--Tommy Armour, British Open champion and current defender of the Canadian Open crown, blazed his way around Mississauga today in a par-shattering 68—four strokes under perfect figures to take an early lead in the first round of the Canadian Open golf championship. Horton Smith, the Missourian, came in with a 72 to take his place among the leaders. He had a 35 going out, one under par, but required one over perfect figures to come home in 37. MacDonald Smith, Canadian champion in 1926, and Abe Mitchell and Willie Davis, of the British Ryder Cup team, withdrew from the tournament this morning. Wiffy Cox, American Ryder Cup player from Brooklyn, came in with a 68 in mid-afternoon to tie Armour for the lead. Gene Sarazen of Great Neck, L. WASHINGTON, July 9 -- Acting Secretary of State Castle Thursday announced the appointment of Hugh Gibson, American ambassador to Belgium, as the United States representative at the London meeting of fiscal experts to discuss means of putting the Hoover debt postponement plan into effect. Gibson will be assisted by Frederick C. Livesay, assistant economic adviser of the State Department as a technical expert. Livesay is considered an authority on international finance and on such financial conventions as the Young plan. Castle explained the two might be considered as the United States "representatives" at the debt parley. He declined to call them "unofficial observers." Gibson and Livesay will have no votes, but will be present at all meetings of the committee. Their presence there will be considered a safeguard against departure from the spirit of the Hoover plan, which provided unqualif

LONDON, ‘UP)--Out of 66 nations invited by the United States to adhere to the Kellogg treaty for the renunciation of War, only six have failed so far to sign, Arthur Henderson, foreign secretary, told a questioner in the house of commons Wednesday. The six who have not acted are Latin-American states—Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Ecuador, San Salvador and Uruguay.

1931-01-07.text: | London, Jan. 7.--(AP)--Britons, accustomed to iron-handed discipline aboard the ships of His Majesty’s navy, were astonished today at reports of widely extended insubordination at the naval yard at Devonport. Sailing orders of the submarine depot ship Lucia were countermanded. Thirty of her crew were arrested Sunday after a demonstration in protest at curtailment of Christmas leaves. | The Plymouth correspondent of the Daily Mail asserted in a dispatch to his paper that such startling revelations had come from investigation of the Lucia incident that movements of several other ships on spring maneuvers had been canceled. The ships held at Devonport navy yard, the dispatch said, included the cruiser Norfolk, whose captain, C. B. VRCrOUrR, NOTIAEMOCRIANG, Si h- —(P)—Her head bashed in and her body virtually roasted, pretty Evelyn Foster, 28, was found semi-conscious beside the smoking ruins of her automobile on the frost-bound moors near here last night. In a moment of lucidity before she died today she told her father that a stranger had accosted her Tuesday night, asking her for a lift to Newcastle, saying that he had come from Scotland. About 14 miles from Newcastle the stranger ordered the girl to halt the car. He then clubbed her over the head, tossing her on the back seat and setting fire to the automobile which he shoved over a cliff. Miss Foster told her father that she fought off unconsciousness while the car bounced down the valley, flaming furiously. LONDON.—The German steamer Carl sank after a collision with the Swedish steamer Themis in Swinemunde harbor today, Lloyd’s at Stettin reported. Casualties were unknown.

PARIS (A.P.)—France mourned her “savior,” Marshal Joseph Joffre, with all the splendor due one of the generation's outstanding heroes as the old soldier's funeral procession passed through the streets of Paris from Notre Dame cathedral to the Invalides Wednesday. Joffre's body was placed in a circular sacristy inside a square tent, draped with black and violet, at the Invalides. Battle flags were arranged in the formation of mounting guard. A Napoleonic bronze stood in each of the four corners around the marshal's resting place. Princes, generals and statesmen whose names are famous throughout the world marched in the procession with maimed privates who served in the trenches. The marshal’s body was carried on a gun carriage while ex-soldiers and men and women who lost relatives in the World War knelt in pious tribute. A million persons lined the route followed by the cortege in a journe

(By The Associated Press) Paris, Jan. 7—France paid homage to the still form of Marshal Joffre as it lay banked by flowers on a catafalque in the chapel of the Ecole Militaire. Last night in a plain oak coffin which will never be opened again, the Marshal's body lay in the cathedral of Notre Dame. On the coffin was the simple inscription, “Joseph Joffre, Marshal of France, 1852-1931.” This morning at 9 o'clock after funeral services in the cathedral, an impressive cortege escorted the body to the Invalides, where it will repose in a vault for several months before being buried in its final resting place at Louveciennes. Thousands still stood outside (Continued on page three)

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Jan. 7. —(AP)—The romance, intrigue and tragedy which tangled the life skein of Mary, Queen of Scots, was recalled today as Danish police sought to unravel the mystery surrounding the rifling of the sarcophagus of the Earl of Bothwell, Mary’s third husband. Whether a desire for jewels once belonging to Mary and said to have been buried with Bothwell, or a feeling of revenge maintained through four centuries by descendants of those he wronged motivated the violation police would not say, pending investigation of the strange incident. Police yesterday found the sarcophagus, containing the remains of the earl, who was the fourth in his line and who died insane in a castle in Zealand on April 14, 1578, broken open and its contents disarranged. There was no evidence that any jewels were found. The life of the Earl of Bothwell was hardly less tempestuous than that of Mary,

I. N. S. Staff Correspondent PARIS, Jan. 7.—In majestic manner enriched by the presence of representatives from Governments in many parts of the world, France said farewell today to Marshal Joseph Jacques Cesaire Joffre, the cooper’s son from the hillsides of the Pyrenees who became the hero of the Marne and the nation’s idol. As a last token of appreciation for a life of unstinted devotion and service to his country, France bestowed upon him the highest final honor it can offer—a national funeral. The church bells of Paris tolled forth the opening memorial service at the Cathedral of Notre Dame at 9 a.m. (4 a.m. Eastern Standard Time). A hush settled over the city in the morning, and solid banks of humanity waited in silence along the route to Les Invalides, where the body will rest in a special vault until removed to Louveciennes, home of the Joffre family. 1931-12-06.text: PARIS, Wt. o.—Wearing a new shawl and loin cloth, Mahatma Gandhi, on his way home to India after the round table conference in London, arrived here this afternoon and was cheered by a large crowd at the railway station. With the Mahatma was Madoline Slade, his disciple, whose weaving ability was responsible for his new clothing. A group of Indian students met Gandhi and he informed them he was taking home the hope that all India’s creeds and classes might be united. Characterizing the round table conference as a complete failure, Gandhi declared he had nonetheless become acquainted with British officials, and he hoped his knowledge of them would assist in his battle for Indian independence. The Mahatma crossed the Channel third class in the steamer Maid of Kent.

By The Associated Press Springfield, Ill., Dec. 5.—Death today quieted the Leonine road and stopped the virile pen of one of the unique modern poets of the English world. Vachel Lindsay is dead at the age of 52 years. He died here in the city of his birth at 1 o'clock this morning from a clogging of the coronary artery. Tonight his body lay in the Lindsay homestead where he wrote the poetry that made him famous and where, in expressing his “gospel of beauty,” he wrote of Springfield remade in “The Golden Book of Springfield.” Minstrel, troubadour, tramp exponent of the art of the motion picture, art critic, journalist, Y.W.C.A., and anti-saloon lecturer, his interests were varied and contacts world-wide. The loss literature sustained by his death was expressed by inpouring telegraphic tributes and regrets. Time alone will determine the permanence of his place in literature but no book of

Tokyo, Nov. 6. (4?) — Japanese troops crushed a Chinese army in a three-day battle in Manchuria, and sent them flying back northward in disorderly retreat, said dispatches from Mukden today to the Rengo news agency. The Japanese lost 130 killed in the Nonni river bridgehead area in north-central Manchuria. The battle ended at 10:30 o'clock tonight when reinforced Japanese launched an offensive which dislodged the Heilingkiang province army. Dr. Alfred Sze, Chinese delegate, in two notes to the League of Nations blamed the fighting on the Japanese whom he said had been “actively provoking” clashes about the Nonni river bridge for the past few days. At least 120 Chinese soldiers were killed according to his figures. The Japanese version of the battle is contained in a dispatch to the London Daily Mail, accusing General Mah of making the first attack after hoisting a white flag of truce. So

By The Associated Press Paris, Dec. 5.—China will not evacuate Chinchow, but will “fight and die there if necessary,” Dr. Alfred Sze, Chinese delegate to the council of the League of Nations, told council leaders today. After he had made this statement Dr. Sze conferred with Ambassador Charles G. Dawes for the purpose of determining the attitude the United States government would take if Japan occupied Chinchow. What Mr. Dawes told him was not made public. Meanwhile Nobumi Ito, legal expert of Japan’s league delegation, informed the council's drafting committee that Tokyo was unalterably opposed to intervention by a third party, either through a commission of inquiry or through neutral observers, in the Manchurian conflict. The upshot of these interchanges was that the deadlock over the far eastern quarrel seemed tighter than ever. Dr. Sze, it was understood, received no hope from member

LOKRYO, Dec. 6—(Sunday)—(P)—A Rengo dispatch from Mukden, today said there was an unconfirmed report from a Chinese source at Peiping that General Honjo, Japanese commander in Manchuria, had served final notice on Chang Hsueh-Liang to withdraw his Chinese troops west of Chinchow immediately. There was no confirmation of such an ultimatum at Japanese war office. The Mukden dispatch said the deposed governor of Manchuria had been warned to withdraw his troops on the ground that massing of Chinese east of Chinchow signified an aggressive attitude against the Japanese. The dispatch appeared to have been censored and several sentences deleted, which was taken here as an indication that it had been referred to military headquarters for approval before it was forwarded to Tokyo.

W. Anais. WIN, INOV, 0., (aa p-— A renewed American protest against armed hostilities in war-clouded Manchuria lies before the Japanese government. Its contents carefully guarded, the note was presented yesterday to Baron Shidehara, the Japanese foreign minister, by Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes. As have been other representations of this government to prevent open war between China and Japan, the communication maintained this country’s attitude of strict neutrality. In Tokyo the government considered it a ‘friendly representation.’

Man, Burns When Plane Dives at Detroit Airport. DETROIT, Dec. 5 (F)—With the record he has persistently sought during the last month almost within his grasp, Lowell R. R. Bayles, Springfield, Mass., flier, crashed to his death at the Wayne County airport this afternoon while traveling at an estimated speed of 300 miles an hour. Bayles was only 75 feet above ground, streaking over the 1.8 mile course "like a yellow flash" as one observer described it, when the plane started to spin, dived in a short arc and struck the ground, landing on its back. The motor broke loose from the plane and rolled 500 feet across railway tracks to crash into a fence. The plane burst into flames as it struck. Bayles’ body, wrapped in his overcoat, was found several feet from the wreckage, a column of smoke rising from his clothing. He apparently had been killed instantly. Three Theories Held.
