PARIS, July 20. (AP)—The heads of the French and German governments, dedicated to laying the groundwork for effective collaboration both politically and economically as the results of two days of tense negotiations, now take part in a seven power conference in London which will attempt to put that policy in operation and to rescue Germany from ‘her financial crisis. Although the Paris conversations of Premier Laval and Foreign Minister Briand, for France, and Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius, for Germany, did not yield all they had hoped, they spoke confidently of the outcome of the London meeting. The new spirit in Franco-German relations was set forth in a communique issued when the negotiators concluded their work in Paris. “From now on representatives of both governments insist upon emphasizing their firm intention of creating by common effort as much as possible the

Washington, July 19.—()—An optimistic view that the London conference of ministers would succeed in solving the stringent emergency financial situation in Germany was telephoned to Washington today by Secretary Stimson in Paris. Acting Secretary Castle of the state department talked by telephone with Secretary Stimson and immediately telephoned the secretary’s view to President Hoover at his Rapidan camp. Coming on the eve of the London meeting, and practically after the United States and Great Britain had rejected France's proposals in connection with the proposed $500,000,000 loan to Germany, the favorable turn in events cheered Washington officials. With rejection of the French loan plan, which included financial and political demands, the United States and Great Britain would not participate in, attention tonight was centered on prospects of a compromise at the London sessions.

LONDON, July 20 () — Queen Helen of Rumania, who arrived here yesterday and was ignored by the Rumanian legation, rested today in a quiet west end hotel. The legation professed official ignorance of her arrival, an attache explaining, “all we know is what we read in the papers.” The queen gave out—through her principal lady-in-waiting—a statement to the effect that she was in England “for a holiday, to pay a visit to my family and to take a cure.” “This journey,” the statement said, “has been taken in mutual understanding with the king, and I will be returning to Rumania at the end of October to be back for my son's birthday.” When Helen left Bucharest it was reported that she was going into virtual exile at the order of King Carol. Her visit to her family started as soon as her train pulled in. Her brother, former King George of Greece, and her mother, the former dowager queen of Greece

PARIS, July 20. — (UP) — Cabinet ministers of four powers — France, Germany, Italy and Belgium — left for London today, to continue the conversations looking to a settlement of Europe's economic problems growing out of the German financial crisis. Premier Pierre Laval, against the advice of many of his supporters, headed the French delegation to these historic parleys. He appeared happy, almost gay, as the statesmen left Paris in a group at 10 a.m., while the Germans were reserved, if not glum. An extra force of some 500 police held a respectfully silent crowd of 10,000 persons quiet in the vicinity of the station. “I am an optimist by nature,” Premier Laval replied to a query from the United Press correspondent on how he felt about the success of the seven-power parley. Chancellor Heinrich Bruening of Germany was less responsive, and refused to commit himself. “I cannot say,” Bruening s

1931-03-30.text: London. March 27. (#)—Enoch Arnold Bennett, one of the greatest literary figures of this century, died here tonight at the age of 63. Stricken with influenza seven weeks ago, the famous novelist and playwright was recovering when he contracted typhoid fever. After hours of unconsciousness he passed away peacefully. Bennett's plays. Of thousands throughout the English-speaking world were familiar with his works. His earlier novels of the drabness of "The Five Towns," England's pottery district—particularly "The Old Wives' Tale"—were rated as classics even in the author's lifetime. In less serious works he acted as guide to what is best in literature, travel and recreation, having always been a keen observer of human life. His manifold interests were shown in all of his writings. Though personally of a deeply reserved nature, he could chat with the common man on paper as few authors of his

By International News Service, | LONDON, March 30—Because he feared that his thirty-year-old automobile might fall into unkindly hands, Dr. Francis Pearse today decided to bury it with all honors in a plot of ground near a cemetery. Up until three years ago he drove the car regularly.

Detroit—(U?)—Capt. Arthur Walpole Rowland, 104-year-old soldier of fortune, is at the end of his long adventurous trail, dead in the Bertha M. Fisher Home for the Aged. The trail started in an Indian Hill post in 1827, where his father was a British officer. It led through the charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava in 1854, through the Indian mutiny, through Garibaldi’s fight for freedom, through the Union side of the Civil War, with Maximilian’s Lancers in Mexico, and through the Spanish-American War. He will be given a military funeral under the joint auspices of Veterans of Foreign Wars and the Canadian Legion.

NICE, France, March 30.—(AP)—Her nerve bolstered by brandy, Mrs. David Townsend, former Broadway “Follies” girl, drove her car off a 200-foot precipice near here and found in death the rest that life denied her. While she drank she scribbled a note to her husband, reputedly wealthy Wall Street broker, which read: “Please take care of my mother. Pay 4,000 francs to Wally.” Another paragraph which referred to the possibility of her going back to the stage was undecipherable. When she did not appear at a party Saturday evening which she had planned, friends sought her, but their search was unavailing until Sunday morning when police saw her car crushed on the rocks below one of the sharpest precipices on the Riviera. Her husband, identifying the body, was prostrated. He could think of no reason, he said, why she should have ended her life, other than that she had suffered a sudden neurasthe

Shanghai, China, March 30— 2p--- Word has been received here by the St. Columban’s mission of the death Mar. 5, of Father Superior Tierney of the Kiencheng mission while a captive of Chinese communities. While details of his death were not learned, the bandits frequently had said they would kill him if ransom of $40,000 were not immediately forthcoming. In a letter which he contrived to smuggle through his captors some weeks ago he wrote he was failing and that he was quite resigned to die. Father Tierney, superior of St. Columban’s mission at Kiencheng, a small interior city located southeast of Nanchang in the south China province of Kiangsi, was captured last November 17.

Turin, Italy, March 30—(A.P)— Reports were current here today that a bomb had exploded in the Piazzetta Pasello near the royal palace where the Crown Prince Humbert and his bride Marie Jose, princess of the Belgians, live. Officials denied any knowledge of such an affair. The infernal machine was said to have been in a box of explosives, close to the wing of the building occupied by the royal apartment, the royal armory and the prefecture seat of the provincial government.

BERLIN, March 30—(UP)—The communist members of the Reichstag petitioned Speaker Paul Loebe today to reconvene parliament immediately for the purpose of rescinding the dictatorial decree issued by President Paul Von Hindenburg and Chancellor Heinrich Bruening for suppression of political violence in Germany. The fascists and nationalists likewise have expressed their desire for reconvocation of the Reichstag in an effort to force withdrawal of the decree, which enforces drastic penalties and regulations to prevent disturbance.

PARIS, March 29 — Aristide Briand’s senate speech yesterday in which he declared he would continue to the bitter end protesting against the proposed Austro-German customs accord was interpreted today by the semiofficial newspaper Le Temps, as a warning to Berlin and Vienna. “It must be understood,” the newspaper said, “that the entire French nation supports the government in any diplomatic action calculated to thwart this customs union - which would compromise Austrian independence and create a dangerous situation in central Europe.”

1931-08-20.text: BOMBAY, India, Aug. 20. UM— All hope that Mahatma Gandhi might help England frame a new constitution for India appeared to have vanished today with a blunt statement by Gandhi at Ahmedabad that he is unrepentant for publishing his indictment against the government. Similarly, Viceroy Willingdon suddenly stiffened his attitude at Calcutta and decided to abandon his fortnight tour of India and return to Simla to deal with Gandhi's challenge. He was represented as feeling that Gandhi's presence at the second round table conference is impossible in view of his broadside charging breaches in the Delhi pact. Thus India seems once more to be on the verge of a calamitous civil disobedience campaign, for Gandhi already has declared he will not accept the conference's decisions as binding upon the nationalists and will renew his fight against the government if it fails to grant his demands for sel

LONDON, Aug. 26. — The labor government's efforts to solve Great Britain's financial problems and balance the budget came close to failure today. It was feared unless a satisfactory plan could be worked out, a government crisis would arise. Philip Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer, and financial genius of the Socialists, was considering resigning if the government abandons Britain's traditional policy of free trade.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Aug. 20 (A —Flying over Belgium for the first time, the Graf Zeppelin came home from England in a pouring rain today to complete a cruise which marked the initial landing of a German airship on British soil since the war.

New York. —(UP)—Stories told by two actresses questioned in the mysterious disappearance of a millionaire Japanese silk importer while on a whoopie cruise to Halifax have interested representatives of three governments. The United States, Japan and Great Britain are involved. Mary Reisner, revealed during a five-hour questioning late yesterday as Mary Dale, once of George White’s "Flying High," told of Hisashi Fujimura’s “fear of a man aboard the Belgenland.” The actress had accompanied the merchant as governess of his seven-year-old daughter, also aboard. At least, she had been identified previously as a governess, but in a statement accredited to her by U. S. Attorney J. Edward Lumbard, she said: Not a Governess “I was not employed as a governess. He and his daughter had one room, I was in the adjoining room. We quarreled the night he disappeared because he didn’t want me to go to Miss

LONDON, Aug. 20 (UP).—A project to raise a revenue tariff wall around Great Britain—a revolutionary scheme born in the empire’s hour of financial crisis—was given serious consideration Thursday. The empire was built on a free trade foundation. The labor government was understood to have included a 10 per cent tariff for revenue only in its tentative program for relieving the present emergency and balancing the budget which faces an estimated deficit of $600,000,000. The cabinet, in lengthy session, completed a set of figures for balancing the budget—its primary task at the moment—but held over its decision of the vital tariff project until another urgent session scheduled to convene Thursday. A conference between Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald and Philip Snowden, chancellor of the exchequer, for the labor government, and representatives of the opposition (conservative and liberal) parties,

LONDON, Aug. 19-~/Pi--The cabinet adjourned at 19:25 p. m. after a day and night of discussion of the “big five” sub-committee proposals for slicing a deficit of more than $500,000,000 from the budget. No statement was issued but it was understood a general agreement had been reached on a budget balance. No decision was reached on the revenue tariff, however, it was said. The prime minister and his colleagues spent a considerable part of their nine hours of discussions today reviewing the ground covered by the economy report of Sir George May, which recommended budget cuts totaling more than £96,000,000 by cutting the salaries of police, teachers and other public service staffs and also by downward revision of the “dole.”

London, Aug. 20—(P)—After a “rubber neck” tour yesterday over England with a load of sight-seeing passengers, the Graf Zeppelin last night started on her return trip to Friedrichshafen, Germany. The dirigible landed at Hanworth aerodrome after the tour, staying for less than half an hour. She discharged some passengers, took on mail and took to the air again at 7:34 p.m. Flying back over London, she paused over the mansion house, dipped three times in a farewell salute, then pointed her nose toward Germany.

NEW YORK, Aug. 20.--Trudy Ederle is thinking of putting the reverse English on the channel. She says if her plans materialize she will attempt to swim from England to France next year. In 1926 she swam from Cape Gris Nez, France, to Kingsdown, England, in 14 hours, 30 minutes. It is as easy one way as the other, she thinks.

1931-01-18.text: MANCHESTER, England, Jan. 17 (P)—Lancashire cotton mills were closed today against 250,000 weavers, whose representatives have refused to accept a “more looms per weaver” system inaugurated by the mill owners. The lockout brought England face to face with an even more serious labor crisis than represented by the South Wales coal mine strike on the same day that the Wales coal strike officially ends, allowing 150,000 miners there to go back to work. In addition to the weavers, 250,000 spinners and members of the various finishing trades also will be laid off shortly, since without the weavers there will be no work for them to do. This will bring the number affected by the Lancashire lockout to about half a million.

MANCHESTER, Eng. Jan. 17— Lancashire cotton spinning mill owners made good their threat of a lockout today when 700,000 looms stopped operating promptly at noon, putting 200,000 operatives out of work. The mill owners had threatened last night to put the lockout into effect today if the workers did not meet certain of the operators’ demands. The chief one of which was operation of eight looms by each individual. Workers refused. No further negotiations were arranged.

LONDON, Jan. 17—Dispatches to the Evening News from Calcutta today said four persons had been killed and twenty others injured in rioting at Jhalda in the Bihar province of Bengal. The reports said police used guns to defend themselves against a mob which refused to disperse.

Paris, Jan. 17.—(UP)—The Prince of Wales and Prince George left tonight for Santander, where they will board the S.S. Oropesa en route to Central and South America. The two princes, who arrived here yesterday from London by airplane, abandoned air travel until they reach South America. They left Paris at 8:40 p.m. on an overnight train bound for the famous Spanish coastal resort where King Alfonso has his summer residence. From Santander, the Oropesa will go to Vigo and, after leaving the European coast, strike out across the Atlantic for Bermuda, where it is scheduled to arrive January 27. The two princes will spend only about ten hours in Bermuda.

Cardiff, Wales, Jan. 17.—(AP)—By a vote of 169 to 72 the Wales miners’ union tonight voted to accept the terms of a provisional settlement reached with the mine owners last Thursday and to go back to work on Monday. This ends the strike which began on January 1 and affected 150,000 men.

Budapest, Hungary, Jan. 17,—(P) —General Alexander Kirchner, 68, Hungarian military expert at the Versailles peace conference, last night watched his daughter die of diphtheria. A minute later he dropped dead across her bed, a victim of heart disease.

| WARSAW, POLAND, JAN. 17. (AP).—Orders to hunt down and destroy every American apple in Poland went out to all cities and larger towns of Poland today. | The health authorities some time ago prohibited the sale of apples from America alleging they had been sprayed with arsenic but despite the prohibition there was evidence that the American apples still continued to penetrate the market, hence the extermination order.

AMSTERDAM, Holland—A destructive storm ravaged Holland Saturday. Telegraph and telephone lines were badly damaged. Shipping and other traffic was disrupted and several floods were reported in various sections of the country.

1931-08-24.text: Ramsay MacDonald's labor government resigned Monday in the face of the national financial crisis and Mr. MacDonald was asked by the king to form a temporary national non-party government whose first duty will be to balance the budget. It will include conservatives and liberals. Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, and liberals who have taken over active management of their party during the illness of David Lloyd George agreed at Buckingham Palace in the presence of the king to participate in a cabinet in which Mr. Baldwin will serve under Mr. MacDonald. This arrangement has its precedent in the coalition government of 1916, formed to create national unity in waging the war. The new cabinet also has a war of sorts on its hands. Its campaign will be to restore Great Britain's threatened credit in the world of international finance. Balancing the budget will be the one task of the national

LONDON, (UP) — Great Britain’s second labor government, beset by financial difficulties, came to a formal end today when Premier J. Ramsay Macdonald called on the King and presented the resignation of the Labor cabinet. It was officially announced that Macdonald was forming a national coalition government. The official announcement said the King had accepted the resignation and commissioned Macdonald to form a national government. Macdonald accepted. A semi-official statement said Macdonald had called at the palace to present the cabinet’s formal resignation and submit a new cabinet. Macdonald left the palace at 4:35 P. M.

LONDON, Aug. 10 (Monday)—A national government in which all three of the principal British parties will be represented seems a possible outcome of the British political crisis after a feverish day of conferences, alarms and semi-sensations yesterday. The MacDonald government has not resigned, but it was believed early this morning in the best informed circles that its resignation is in contemplation. Lobby correspondents in close touch with today's developments say the formation of a national government was discussed by leaders of the parties after the cabinet meeting broke up at 10 Downing Street late last night. Expected To Resign In these same circles it was asserted that the government's resignation probably would occur today. It was emphasized, however, there was no official confirmation of this, or of any other similar report at present. A report that the government was about to re

WASHINGTON (UP).—The federal reserve board is prepared to extend further credits to Great Britain if needed to tide over the present financial emergency reported from London, it was learned Monday. Eugene Meyer, governor of the federal reserve board, was in New York Monday. He was understood to be discussing the situation with George L. Harrison, governor of the New York federal reserve bank, which handled the previous credit of $125,000,000.

London, Aug. 24 (#) — An exchange telegraph dispatch from Riga today said Lithuania and the Vatican had broken off diplomatic relations as a result of the dispute concerning Monsignor Ricardo Bartolomi, the papal nuncio. Last June Monsignor Bartolomi was asked to leave Lithuania because he was charged with collaborating with the political opposition in that country. He went to Germany.

Osaka, Japan, Aug. 24.—(U.P)—Miss Amy Johnson, England's girl flier, landed here at 3:45 p. m. today when storms blocked her path on a return flight to England. Miss Johnson left Tokio at 4:45 a. m., accompanied by a mechanic. She passed Hiroshima, but returned here to spend the night due to storms over Warea.

TOKIO, AUG. 24. (AP).—High government officials apparently did not take seriously the report today that the suspicions of certain authorities had been aroused by the landing of Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh on water in prohibited zones in the Kurile Islands. The high authorities pointed out that the matter quite naturally might have been discussed in some circles, but nothing more. Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh finally reached Nemuro today after having spent five days and made four forced landings in negotiating the 897 miles from Petropavlovsk, Kamchatka, via the foggy Kurile Islands route.

TOKIO, Aug. 24. (U.P)—The Nemuro correspondent of Nippon Dempo News Agency reported today that Col. Charles A. Lindbergh had denied he intends to continue around the world after reaching Tokio. The aviator indicated, however, that he would go to China and might fly to the Philippine Islands. NEMURO, Japan, Aug. 24 (U.P)—Shouting residents of Nemuro today took Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh to their hearts in giving the fliers their first scheduled welcome to the country which thus far has been to them a land of fog instead of orange blossoms. From the moment the Lockheed monoplane landed near Nemuro wharf until the aviator and his wife were tucked under the specially made quilts at Nibici Inn, their appearance was the signal for prolonged and vigorous cheering. This little seaport on the Eastern shore of Hokkaido Island had never seen a celebration like it. All day farmers and fisher

1931-05-29.text: LONDON, May 28.--()—One man was drowned and three persons were struck by lightning in a terrific electrical storm which swept Southern England and Wales last night and struck the London area heavily this morning. — In South Wales bridges were swept away, roads, fields and homes were flooded and there were several landslides, one of which wrecked a colliery train, injuring several miners. Old residents of Cardiff said it was the worst storm in their memory. The streets were flooded and homes and business places were under several feet of water.

LONDON, May 28.—(4)—Queen Helen of Rumania is represented as being reconciled to the fact she soon must leave her adopted country and her 9-year-old son, Crown Prince Michael. She is quoted by an Englishwoman friend here as having said recently in Bucharest that she probably would go into voluntary exile as soon as the new Rumanian parliament is convened. She said she would live either in France or Italy. "No choice is left me," she said, "as between humiliation and departure. I have chosen the latter—that is to say, I have resigned myself to what had to come sooner or later. I could do nothing. "My life has been a sad one for years and now I am going out into the dark. There is no key to my fortune. I have lived in enforced retirement for a full year now and I shall live the life of a recluse henceforward. "My dear boy Michael was unconsolable when I told him what my life was to be. I n

LONDON, May 28. (AP)— Mrs. Mary Hughes, who is said to be the Mary who owned the famous lamb, celebrated her 90th birthday at her farm home at Llangollen, North Wales, today. She received congratulations from children in all parts of the world. “Mary,” who is blind, and suffers from chronic rheumatism, delights to relate how years ago her little lamb was turned out of school. The lamb had followed her from her father’s farm two miles away. The rhyme was written by Miss Sarah Buell, who was staying at the farm at the time.

LONDON, May (AP)—For the first time since his grave illness of two years ago King George went horseback riding today in the famous "Rotten Row" of Hyde Park. He was accompanied only by Colonel Erskine, his equerry. On Saturday, June 6, the King will attend in person the trooping of the colors in belated celebration of his birthday which falls this year on Derby Day, June 8. At that ceremony he will be in the saddle for a considerable time.

New York, May 28. ()—Pre-summer weather in all its mid-season ardor slipped into the East today, sending temperatures soaring to record altitudes in many cities. The heat wave was especially severe in New York City and State and throughout the greater part of New England. In New York the heat caused one death and several prostrations. The temperature reached 85 degrees. Rochester, N.Y. reported a high mark of 89. At Boston it was 92, an all-time record for May 28.

ROME, May 29 ()—Convicted of plotting the assassination of Premier Benito Mussolini, Michele Schirru, an American by naturalization, was executed at dawn today by a firing squad. He was led into the interior court of Fort Braschi and seated astride a chair with his back to the marksmen. A battalion of blackshirt militiamen formed three sides of a hollow square around him and directed a volley of shots into his spine. Schirru, 32 years old and once a resident of New York, was the first American to taste Fascist justice for such an offense and the seventh person to be executed under the defense of the state law, designed to punish attempts to overthrow the regime or to plot against the premier. Italy has not had capital punishment for 68 years until the first of these executions in 1928.

ROME, May 28.—()—Destruction of a portrait of Pope Pius XI by fascist students during an attack on a Catholic publishing house cast new fuel today on the smoldering resentment of the Vatican toward the Italian government. The young blackshirts stormed the headquarters of Civilta Cattolica last night, stoning the windows and committing other depredations. They tore an oil painting of the pontiff from the wall, carried it into the streets and trampled on it, crying meanwhile: "Here is a traitor to his country." Heaving copies of the book "Il Papa" (The Pope) out of the windows, they took them to the Piazza Colonna, near the foreign office, and consigned them to a bonfire, together with copies of "Osservatore Romano," the paper which has been publishing accounts of purported indignities. The march on the publishing house was without interference by the police. Later, authorities dispersed t

OBER-GURGL, AUSTRIAN TYROL, (May 22.)—Recovered from their perilous thrust into the upper reaches of the sky, Dr. August Piccard began compiling his scientific data today while Charles Kipfer, his assistant, started his three hour climb to recover their balloon from the glacier on which it came to rest. Dr. Piccard said in conversation with newspapermen that the stratosphere, which he claimed to have penetrated in an ascent of more than 50,000 feet, was the only practicable element for long distance aviation. "This can be done, however," he said, "only if the cabins are as airtight as our gondola was." Dr. Piccard said that he and Kipfer had attained the objective of their ascent—a study of cosmic rays—and in addition had established a world’s altitude record—9,936 miles or more than 50,000 feet. Moon Is Brighter He obtained a measurement of the conductivity of gases generated by cosmic

1931-08-09.text: London, Aug. 8—(P)—An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Copenhagen today said Parker D. Cramer, who reached the Faroe islands last night on a flight from the United States, took off at noon for Bergen, Norway, whence he will proceed to Copenhagen tomorrow. He came down in the ocean between Thorshaven and Reykjavik in the night and there were reports that he had been forced down by engine trouble, but the flier said this morning he had not been obliged to land but had done so partly to test the seaworthiness of his ship. The plane is in good condition.

ROME, Aug. 8—/P)— Premier Mussolini today accepted Chancellor Bruening’s invitation to go to Berlin for a return visit with German officials at a date yet to be determined. It will be the premier's first formal visit outside Italy since he went to London in 1922 shortly after he became head of the Italian state. He himself will fix the date for the trip to Berlin. Announcement of his plans came after he and Dino Grandi, the Italian foreign minister, had conferred for an hour at the German embassy with Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius. At the same time the conferences issued a joint statement of the results of the meetings today and yesterday, "Various exchanges of views have taken place, accompanied by a sense of reciprocal friendly comprehension, and deep cordiality,” the statement said, “the general European situation has been extensively examined and the necessity for

Hankow, China, Aug. 9.—(Sunday)—(AP)—Four hundred patients and attendants perished today when a wing of the Hankow Union Mission Hospital collapsed as the result of floods. The hospital is maintained in a native section of Hankow by the London Missionary Society and the Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society, both British organizations. Thousands Drowned The “corpse recovery society,” which has been gathering bodies of the flood victims during the last several days, estimated yesterday that at least 8,000 persons have drowned in the Hankow district. The Yangtse River continued to rise today, threatening further damage to the Wuhan area, com- (Continued on Page 10)

Croydon, Eng., Aug. 8. — The 2200 horsepower airliner, Hannibal, one of the world’s largest and most luxurious, crashed near Tonbridge today carrying 18 passengers en route to Paris. None was seriously injured. The crash was the result of simultaneous failure of two of the four engines. The wing and the undercarriage were smashed. The liner has been hailed as one of the costliest and largest in regular transport service. Its estimated cost was $175,000, and its weight is 13 tons. The Imperial Airways issued a communique on the crash of the airliner Hannibal, asserting none of the passengers was injured. The statement said all passengers would proceed by automobile to Lympne airport, where another plane would take them to Paris. The police at Tonbridge reported that the Hannibal had made a “forced landing” at Tudely, near Tonbridge, Eng. Their report said none was injured, and that the ma

NEWS FROM SPAIN takes you back to Henry the Eighth of England and his many wives. Rome refused him a divorce that he particularly wanted and Henry seized the great wealth of the church and the religious orders in England, starting a new church, the Episcopalian, and persuaded Charles the Fifth to protect Luther, to spite the Pope. SPAIN’S CONSTITUTIONAL committee asked parliament to expel all members of religious orders from Spain and seize their wealth. Increasing through the centuries, the estate, the property could not be taken out of Spain. THIS NEWS, combined with recent events in Mexico and Italy may cause the church to consider as its principal investment property other than real estate. Freedom from taxation and assessments makes land an ideal investment for all religions, but only in countries where property rights are respected. Spain's constitutional committee wishes a constit

WICK, SCOTLAND, Aug. 8—(INS)—The first transatlantic flyer to be forced down at sea and then rescued to continue his journey, Parker Cramer, landed safely at an undesignated point in the Faroe Islands at 11.20 p.m., last night (9.30 p.m. e.d.t.), according to a message picked up today by the wireless station here. The message came from Thorshavn, on the Faroe Island of Strono, and it was considered probable that the plane had landed at that town, the most important in the Islands. Flying on a secret journey from Detroit to Copenhagen via the Danish Islands of the North Atlantic, Cramer, with Oliver Pacquette, radio operator, left Deykjavik, Iceland, for the Faroes, a distance over the water of about 500 miles, at 2.11 p.m., yesterday. He had flown to the Iceland capital across the Denmark straits from Angmagsalik, Greenland, the night before, in a monoplane using crude oil for fuel inste

WASHINGTON, Aug. 8—(U.R)—Officials here who had become somewhat concerned over the fall in the British pound sterling have been reassured by confidential advice and inquiry into the situation. One official said today that whatever the temporary difficulties may be accompanying the drain of gold from the Bank of England, in the long run Great Britain is on a sound footing. She holds some $20,000,000,000 in foreign securities, American investments abroad are about $14,000,000,000. At the moment Britain may have a shortage of gold, but Britain is regarded as being in no more trouble fundamentally than a man who owns a large estate but happens not to have a large supply of cash on hand. Charles G. Dawes, American ambassador at London and a banker, reported the decline in the British pound was caused by a short flurry and was not regarded as serious by informed persons. Probable factors are h

Berlin, Aug. 8—UP.—The German government has offered to buy 500,000 tons of United States wheat for delivery in the spring of 1982. The United Press learned today that such an offer was handed yesterday to Frederic M. Sackett, American ambassador, to be forwarded to Washington. The offer envisaged purchases of three grades of hard wheat on a basis of a three-year credit bearing interest at 4% per cent. The German offer originally suggested a fluctuating price scale, it was learned. Subsequently it included terms fixed in advance, but price was understood to be still a matter of difficulty. The Federal Farm Board's rejection of the German cotton purchase offer was communicated to the German government today, and the government had the message under examination. Washington’s alternative scheme as embodied in the communication would enable the Germans to buy direct from United States cotton

1931-12-18.text: (Associated Press Staff Writer) London, Dec. 18.—(4)—The world is standing on the threshold of the greatest prosperity it ever has experienced—if only the necessary steps are taken—Sir George Parish, noted British economist and member of the British official mission to the United States in 1914, said today in an exclusive interview with the Associated Press. Three of the chief recommendations made by the noted economist are: 1. Federal and state temporary bank guaranty acts. 2. An international conference at which every nation would be ready to make contributions to world recovery. 3. Revision of reparations payments to insure eventual repayment of Germany’s commercial debt which he estimates at $2,250,000,000. It is possible, he said, to revive trade immediately to a marked degree and to banish the fear complex now besetting the nations. Sir George recently affirmed his belief that a wo

LONDON, Dec. 17—(AP)—A wrestling match between a tiger and his trainer in an airplane flying over the English Channel from France was reported by the newspaper Star today. The tiger was said to have broken out of a large wooden cage and started grappling with his caretaker—his customary circus act. Fearing the location was hardly suitable for such an act, the trainer dashed into the cage with the beast clinging to him and closed the door. They made the rest of the journey apparently in perfect harmony. The pilot and his mechanic were ignorant of the events occurring in the cabin behind them.

STEAMSHIP PILSNA, Dec. 17 (AP)—Mahatma Gandhi homeward bound to India from his three months’ stay in England at the second round table conference, pitched a tent on the deck today to live in during the remainder of the journey. The Mahatma found the chill Mediterranean winds too severe for him and his loin cloth at night. His odd habitation is stretched across wooden planks which cover the freight hatchway in the stern and it has become an object of great curiosity for the other passengers. The faithful Mira Behn, his patient disciple, watches over him while he sleeps, like a solicitous mother caring for a child. A half dozen other disciples sleep in rows nearby on bare boards. Pitying the holy man’s plight, the genial Italian captain of the steamer offered Gandhi a comfortable cabin but the Mahatma declined to abandon his present abode.

TOKIO, (UP).—A war office statement Friday that Japanese troops in Manchuria ‘were compelled to undertake an extensive punitive expedition’ against Chinese troops and ‘bandits’ was regarded as a possible preliminary to an advance on Chinchow. The statement said the expedition would be undertaken west of the Liao River in the Chinchow area. The Tientsin correspondent of the Japanese news agency Nippon Dempo reported that Marshal Chang Hsueh-Liang expressed belief that a Japanese attack on Chinchow was impending. He ordered Gen. Jung Chen, commanding the 25,000 troops in the Chinchow area, to resist ‘to the bitter end,’ the report said.

| TOKYO, Dec. 18.—()—Plans for a new and extensive military campaign against alleged bandits in Manchuria were announced by a spokesman for the war office today as reports were received of fighting in which one Japanese and 14 Chinese were killed, and several wounded. A dispatch to the Rengo News Agency from Tientsin, China, said the Chinchow situation has become so acute that the Japanese residents of Shanhaikwan decided to evacuate the city and retire to Tientsin. The new military campaign, the war office spokesman said, will be a drive against bandits in the area of the South Manchurian railway, particularly the region west of the Liao river. This is the territory just north of Chinchow in which the Japanese drive against that place was halted last month. At the time the announcement was made, the reports of fighting were received and also reports that bandits are unusually active aro

BASEL, SWITZERLAND, Dec. 18—(AP)—The Young plan committee of experts decided today by unanimous vote that the German railways will be unable to meet their non-postponable reparations payments next year. The experts committee accepted a sub-committee’s report which contained the statement that it will be impossible for the railways to balance their budget in 1932, even though the unconditional payments, which the Young plan places upon them, should be turned back to them now in the Hoover plan. This disclosure was accepted as the first official indication that the experts’ final report would contain a recommendation for a moratorium on conditional payments rather than for cancellation. “As soon as Germany gets back to normal,” the sub-committee report said, “the railways may be expected to attain net earnings comparable to those of the railways in other countries.”

BASEL, Switzerland, Dec. 17. - Members of the Young Plan committee examining Germany's capacity to pay reparations are holding up their recommendations as to the time and place for an international conference on this matter until after the American Congress has acted on the Hoover moratorium. The interested powers, it was said, are unwilling to make any definite plans in this respect until the outcome in Washington is known. It is expected that the conference, which will approve or reject the Young Plan committee's report, will be held in the middle of January, probably at Geneva or Brussels. Preliminary conversations are going on between the European capitals in order to get the reparations business out of the way before the disarmament conference starts Feb. 2. The statisticians’ sub-committee of the commission reported today, it was understood, that the Reich's foreign trade balance s

' Ariccia, Italy, Dec. 18.—One of the most vivid careers in the Roman Catholic church came to an end today with the death of former Cardinal Louis Billot, 86, who several years ago was the center of a bitter fight between the Holy See and the Action Francaise movement. He was the first cardinal to resign in many generations. After he had put away his red hat, he became a simple priest, but his name was stricken from the pontifical annual. He died in his humble cell at a Jesuit monastery here. Pope Pius X made him a cardinal in 1911 and it was he who crowned the present pope.

1931-02-12.text: WASHINGTON, Feb. 12. UP-- Official advices to the state department today from American diplomatic representatives in Europe said British efforts to facilitate a Franco-Italian naval accord were continuing. Press dispatches telling of a collapse of the British efforts were described by Secretary Stimson as contrary to official messages to him. The United States and Japan still are interested in discovering a basis for a Franco-Italian accord and have not ceased attempts in that direction.

London, Feb. 12. (47)—One of the most violent of gales of the winter blew over England and adjacent seas during the night. The wind reached a velocity of 50 and 60 miles frequently and occasionally blew more than 70 miles an hour. The channel was lashed into furious waves which seamen estimated to be 30 feet high. Channel steamers suffered some damage and many arrived at ports hours late. The Bemridge lifeboat searched for six hours last evening for a small unidentified vessel seen earlier drifting in the channel. It returned unsuccessful and it was feared that the small vessel was lost. Many trees were uprooted and chimneys and roofs damaged.

LONDON, Feb. 10—Shipping badly buffeted by a fierce gale which rose suddenly yesterday and continued to blow all day today with little diminished force. One steamer was reported in distress tonight. She was the British freighter Built Way, of 2,917 tons, which left Las Palmas, Canary Islands, Feb. 1 for Limerick, Ireland. Her steering gear was carried away and she was drifting helplessly in the vicinity of Southwest Ireland. Two tugs left Cobh (Queenstown) to assist her. High seas raged in the channel and drove all sorts of craft to shelter in various ports, a large number taking refuge in Plymouth Sound while a score of Welsh trawlers, fishing in Irish waters, sheltered in Battery Bay. A number of vessels reported more or less damage.

LONDON, Feb. 12 (AP) — A large question mark was written across Britain's immediate economic future today as businessmen and politicians alike asked what Philip Snowden referred to in the Commons yesterday when he spoke of impending ‘drastic and disagreeable measures’ to maintain the budget. Prime Minister MacDonald, triumphant by a 75-vote majority in repulsing a conservative motion of censure on a count of extravagance, turned to face grave differences in his own party growing out of the chancellor’s speech. The comment was heard in the lobbies that he had won ‘worse than a pyrrhic victory.’ Increased death duties, an increased supertax, delayed application of some measures involving large expenditures which have passed the House but have not yet been finally enacted, and reduction of interest on government loans were some of the measures which popular speculation credited Snowden with
LONDON, Feb. 12, (1A radio message received here today said that Sir Charles Parsons, inventor of the turbine steam engine, died last night while on a trip to the West Indies. He was 76 years old.

LONDON, Feb. 12.—A prolonged and severe earthquake shock was felt at Napier and Hastings, New Zealand, today, it was stated in an Exchange telegraph dispatch from Wellington.— These two cities were virtually wiped out by a series of earth temblors last week which took a toll of hundreds of dead and injured. Floods are menacing as a result of a heavy rainfall, the dispatch added.

LIMA, Peru, Feb. 11.--Lima, named the “City of Kings” by the Conqueror Pizarro, greeted the heir to the British throne today with gay merrymaking, a display of flags and a cheering populace. The Prince of Wales and his brother, Prince George, bowed their acknowledgments to shouts of “long live the princes” and “long live England” as they arrived by automobile from Callao on their goodwill tour of South America. Later the royal travelers were received by Provisional President Luis M. Sanchez Cerro with ambassadorial honors at the presidential palace and received from him the crosses of the Order of the Sun, created by the Peruvian liberator, Jose San Martin. It was understood tonight that the princes would remain in Lima until Sunday. They will continue their journey to South Peru by airplane.

Glasgow, Feb. 11.—(#)—Testimony that a sister of Mrs. Anna Berrigan Arnot died in the hospital for the insane at Fergus Falls, Minn., in 1927, was given here Wednesday by Mrs. John Foley, of Johnstown, N. D., a cousin of Mrs. Arnot... The sanity of Mrs. Arnot is being determined before a jury in district court in an effort to decide whether she is to face trial on a murder charge growing out of the death of her husband, J. E. Arnot, former Glasgow banker, from what the state contends was poisoning. The defense offered in evidence certified copies of the commitment of Margaret Levitre, sister of Mrs. Arnot, to the Fergus Falls institution and of the petition for inquiry into her sanity in Clay County, Minnesota. There also was submitted a certified copy of the findings of the examining physician, G. J. Vigeland. It stated the patient was violently insane and showed a disposition to injure

1931-11-15.text: NEW YORK, Nov. 14.—A rescue at sea led to the seizure today of the American freighter Arlyn on a charge of her officers and crew violated federal laws by landing 4,000 cases of liquor and 14 sailors in New York, after taking them off a water-logged British rum boat. The $1,000,000 freighter, the Arlyn, was enroute from New York to Florida last February when she picked up a distress signal off Cape Hatteras. She went to the rescue and found a disabled rum runner flying a British flag. Federal officials charge she took aboard the crew, stood by until the weather abated, and then transferred the rum boat's $500,000 cargo of liquor to the hold of the Arlyn. Because the Arlyn was in the coastal service, she was not required to stop at quarantine when she reached New York, but went directly to her pier near 36th street. There, authorities charge, she put the British sailors ashore in violation

London—(P)—If England does not grant complete self-government, India will be “plunged into turmoil and suffering” again, Mahatma Gandhi said today. He made this statement to Lord Irwin, the former viceroy, who is said to have more influence with Mr. Gandhi than any other Englishman. Lord Irwin was making a final effort to win the mahatma over before the round table conference ends next week. Mr. Gandhi has said several times, and he said it again today, that he has no hope that the conference will grant any of the Indian nationalist demands, and that if he goes home empty-handed the civil disobedience campaign in India will start again.

India, November 7, 1931, LONDON, Nov. 14—(U.P.)—The Mahatma Gandhi, Indian Nationalist leader, will return to India, via Geneva and Genoa, on Nov. 21. Gandhi decided to leave England as a result of the virtual failure of the Round Table Conference for a new India constitution. Failure became apparent when the minorities committee yesterday was unable to approach an agreement on the question of Hindu-Muslim representation in the new government.

ROME, Nov. 14—The first thing Signora Donna Anseanente Grandi intends to do when she and Foreign Minister Dino Grandi arrive in Washington Monday is reach for a telephone. In her richly Latin-accented English she will ask the operator: “Can you connect me with Franco Grandi at 9 Trale?” And within a few moments the two happiest children in Italy will be Franco Grandi, 6, and his little sister, Simonetta, 4. Their mother promised to call them right after reaching America as they will be waiting for their governess to tell them her voice is on the other end of the wire. They are eagerly looking forward to the call, but not more than Signora Grandi who has been sending radiograms with them daily. Due to the difference in time, it will be after midnight in the Grandi home in Frascati when the Italian foreign minister and his wife arrive in Washington, Monday, although the couple most probabl

(Copyright 1931, by United Press) DUBLIN, Nov. 14.—(UP)—The government of President William T. Cosgrave is facing a thorough test of its drastic machinery for maintenance of peace in the Irish Free State. Political terrorism, which the president contended was a threat to the established order, prompted the government to bring a long period of internal strife to a head by establishing a quasi-military system to stamp out revolutionary violence. The military tribunals will begin trials of accused terrorists next week, when the efficiency of the system and the public reaction may be definitely determined. There have been many acts of violence, including murders and shootings, throughout Ireland in the last few months. Terrorists have intimidated witnesses. Public officials have found it difficult or impossible to prosecute, because of the political nature of the crimes. Republican extremist

PARIS, Nov. 14.—Two veterans of international diplomacy, Charles Gates Dawes and Aristide Briand, put their heads together in an office at the Quai D’Orsay today in an effort to work out a solution of the Manchurian crisis. The American ambassador to Britain visited France's foreign minister shortly before noon, and then repaired to the United States embassy to cable Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson a complete report of the conversation. With reports persisting that Dawes had worked out a plan of compromise before he left London to be here during the forthcoming League of Nations council meeting, it was assumed his cable informed Secretary Stimson just how Briand felt about the proposal he had to offer.

The $1,000,000 American steamship Arlyn of the Bull-Insular Line was detained at the Long Island City pier tonight on a charge of landing a $400,000 cargo of liquor. White detectives questioned the sailors about a story that the Arlyn picked up and the crew of a foundering British rum runner last February and brought them safely into port. The government agents prepared papers in a forfeiture proceeding to be started in Federal Court. Anonymous letters received in connection with the seizure of the heretofore respectable merchant steamship stated that the writers said they were members of the crew. Dissatisfied at receiving only $20 each for their share in the alleged deal, the writers told how the Arlyn, while bound north last February from a Florida port, ran across a sinking British rum runner off Cape Hatteras. Tokyo, Nov. 14.—(AP)—A fresh brigade of Japanese troops left for Manchuria today, cheered by the Japanese people, and the war office announced General Shigeru Honjo, Manchurian commander, has been instructed to demand the evacuation of the Nonni river area by General Mah Chan-Shan not later than Nov. 25. The alternative, the onrushing general is to be informed, will be “effective steps” by Japan. The conditions of evacuation to be laid down for General Mah include withdrawal himself to Tsitsihar and return of Chinese forces now concentrated at Tsitsihar and Anganchi to their original posts. General Mah was also forbidden to come south of the Chinese Eastern railway and it was specified the Paonan-Anganchi railway is to be administered by a board of administration under a Japanese adviser. In return, the instructions said, the Japanese troops will be withdrawn from the Nonni river area as

1931-08-10.text: POINT BARROW, Aug. 10. — Simple life of an isolated Arctic settlement held Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh here Sunday as they awaited better weather for the continuation of their vacation flight to the Orient. A heavy rain and falling barometer at Nome, their next stop 592 miles southwest of here, delayed their takeoff. The Lindberghs brought their plane down here Saturday at 4 a.m. (central standard time) after a 536-mile flight from Aklavik, Northwest Territory. The white residents of Point Barrow, who have had no mail for four months and are literally starved for news from the outside, are getting an “earful,” and the Lindberghs are seeing much of the life of this settlement. Everywhere the Lindberghs were taken they expressed interest and everywhere they were plied with questions by their eager hosts.

Bombay, Aug. 9. — Mahatma Gandhi today drew tears from the eyes of his large audience of Indian people as he delivered a speech concerning his indecision about going to London for the round-table conference. At one point the Mahatma himself broke down, saying his heart was too full of anguish to proceed. His first decision not to participate in the second conference unless the commercial problem in India was settled was unkindly interpreted, he said, by the American and British press "as a means for backing out of the Delhi pact." "By the terms of that pact," Gandhi said, "I gave my solemn word I would go to London, but it is necessary there should be a certain atmosphere for my going. First of all, I must be assured that the Indian peasants will not suffer in my absence at the hands of the government. Secondly, I want to feel certain that the government will carry out all the terms of t

LONDON, Aug. 10. (UP) — Wild scenes were witnessed in Liverpool and Manchester cotton exchanges Monday following publication of Saturday's United States cotton crop estimate of 15,846,000 bales. Tensely anxious traders rushed about gesticulating madly while prices sagged throughout the morning. By noon they had touched the lowest bottom reached in 30 years. The visitors’ gallery was crowded with spectators gazing oddly upon the frantic scenes being portrayed below.

| - Restated Press TOULON, France, Aug. 10—Fifty vessels were wrecked in a tornado which swept the sea near here today. Six bodies already have been washed ashore, and it was believed the death toll would reach 20. The cyclone swept up mountainous seas which pounded against the shore so hard as to wreck houses along the sea front. Throughout the night lifeboats went out to search for missing vessels. The wind lifted roofs off houses well inland. It was feared that inland as well as ship damage might prove extensive.

OSLO, Norway, Aug. 10 (UP)— Capt. Riiser Larsen, famous Norwegian aviator and explorer and chief of the air force at Bergen, was ready today to begin a search for Parker D. Cramer, missing American aviator, when weather conditions permitted. It was believed here that Cramer, long overdue at Copenhagen on the last lap of a trans-Atlantic flight, was drifting toward Denmark.

Berlin, Aug. 10.—Stern measures were taken today to suppress communists and to apprehend those responsible for rioting Sunday night. A reward of $20,000 marks ($4700) was offered by police for information leading to conviction of the slayers of two police captains. Meetings in Buelow square, scene of the outbreak, which followed defeat of extremists in Sunday's Prussian plebiscite, were forbidden for an indefinite period. The Rote Fahne, communist newspaper, was suppressed for two weeks. Police occupation of Liebknechthaus, communist headquarters in Berlin, was ordered for a period of 10 days. Reports from the provinces today said that casualties in Sunday’s referendum voting in Prussia were one dead and 43 injured.

COPENHAGEN, Aug. 9. — Parker D. Cramer, American aviator, who was expected to land here at least by 6 p.m., today was still unheard from at 7:30 p.m., and it was believed he may have been forced down somewhere between here and the Shetland Islands, where he hopped off today. Several Danish radio stations for some time had been calling him without success. A tremendous crowd was gathered at the airdome here to welcome him, among them, the American charge d'affaires, North Winship. The chairman of the Danish aeronautical society was on hand to present Cramer with the society's gold medal. Cramer left the Shetland Islands at 10:40 a.m. Before it became known that he had hopped off and was planning to reach Copenhagen, it was believed here it would be impossible for him to do so today. Even if he encountered no mechanical difficulties. (Continued on Page 2, Col. 1.)

BERLIN — (4) — Police clapped a padlock today on the headquarters of Communism in Germany, posting a heavy guard at Karl Liebknecht Haus on Buelow Platz where at least three were killed in last night’s rioting. The headquarters building will be padlocked until Aug. 20, and the Communist newspaper, Rote Fahne, has been suspended for two weeks. An emergency decree authorized by President Von Hindenburg bans all open air meetings in the vicinity under penalty of three months imprisonment.

1931-11-20.text: Tokyo, Nov. 20.—(A.P.)--The government announced today that a group made up of the American, French, British and Polish military attaches would start today for Manchuria; as official guests, to investigate actual conditions there... °° ~ Official circles flatly denied that Japan had made acceptance of its five-point demand on China a necessary condition for its approval of a Manchurian investigation by an official commission of the League of Nations. It was emphasized, however, that Japan considers this as a considerable concession on her part and it was intimated that the original intention was to compromise on a two-fold suggestion—that the League should send a commission but insist, at the same time, on China's opening direct negotiations with Japan. Japan agreed to drop the second point, it was said, when it became clear that China would not accept it, Announcement that the military

LONDON, Nov. 20 (UP) — The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, Indian Nationalist leader, declared today that resumption of the civil disobedience campaign against British rule in India "seems to be inevitable." "There is not much hope for success of the round table conference," Gandhi told the United Press while the British cabinet was meeting today to decide Indian policy in regard to termination of the conference for new constitution. "The eventual resumption of civil disobedience seems to be inevitable. It all boils down to the attitude of the government.

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, Nov. 20— (Friday). —A Reuters dispatch from Mukden said Japanese airplanes bombed and annihilated 3,000 Chinese troops of General Mah Chan-Shan at Hailun, Manchuria this morning.

LONDON, Nov. 15—A Tokyo dispatch to the London Daily Mail today said there were indications the Japanese army in Manchuria was preparing to attack Chinchow, last strategic point in Manchuria held by the Chinese. (Copyright, 1931, Associated Press) HARBIN, Manchuria, Nov. 19.—Chinese authorities have said tonight Gen. PARIS, Nov. 4.—(A.P.)—Both Japan and China agreed in principle tonight to a proposal for an armistice in Manchurian military activities. The cessation of hostilities would be based on the creation of an international commission to investigate the whole Manchurian situation. Representatives of China and Japan and all the other members of the council adopted this proposal, which is largely a Japanese suggestion. After its adoption the council was informed that the Chinese were ready to accept it in principle.

The government in a memorandum to the World Bank made public today applied for the convocation of a special advisory committee to examine her ability to pay reparations as provided in the “new plan of Hague agreements of January 20, 1939.” This is the Young plan. The memorandum said: “As the present circumstances require that measures be taken with the greatest urgency, the German government proposes that a special advisory council should meet without delay and that it should carry out its task as quickly as possible so that a conference of those governments which are concerned with decisions to be reached may take place in the very near future.” Reviewing developments since last June when Germany decided it would be unable to continue payment of annuities, the memorandum recalled that this conclusion was followed by the “far-seeing initiative of President Hoover in his proposal for a ye

By RICHARD D. McMILLAN (United Press Staff Correspondent) PARIS, Nov. 20 (U.P.)—The United States "must preserve its full freedom of judgment" as to its courses in international action to restore peace in Manchuria, United States Ambassador Charles G. Dawes announced today after a conference with Aristide Briand, president of the League of Nations Council. Dawes’ statement indicated the council, facing a vital test of its prestige in peace efforts in the Far East, was preparing to take up suggestions for drastic action to end the Manchurian warfare. More Grave Every Hour, Dawes' statement said definitely the United States could not sit in at the council table in discussions "bearing upon application of the League covenant machinery" for enforcement of peace. A reliable source said Dawes told Briand, "Washington regards the situation as more grave every hour." He was emphatic in insisting
By The Associated Press. MADRID, Nov. 20—(Friday)— Former King Alfonso of Spain was outlawed by the Spanish national assembly early today. The vote was by acclamation.

1931-08-26.text: HOLLYWOOD, Calif., Aug. 25— Did you ever see as many things happen to a country in one year? One disappointment after another. Had Al Capone headed for the jail and then he notified us that he didn’t care to attend this semester. Ramsay MacDonald was our only friend in England. Now he is “on the dole.” When Uncle Andy Mellon, the missing link between finance and government, pulled up one billion lame, our financial “giants” had failed to giant. We knew our laws had crumbled. We knew the weather was against us. But to have Lindy keep a reception committee waiting one month, that was our last straw. Yours, WILL ROGERS

LONDON, Aug. 26 (‘UP)--Britain’s new government of sacrifice, headed by Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald, received the seals of office from King George at Buckingham Palace at 11 A. M. today, as the Labor party prepared to fight the proposed dole out. The new cabinet took the call at a meeting of the Privy Council after members of the late Laborite government had handed over the seals of office to the king. The cabinet was to meet immediately to begin the task of effecting economies in government expenditures sufficient to balance the budget and restore foreign confidence in the pound sterling. MacDonald “Disowned” Members of the late Labor cabinet who refused to sanction a reduction of unemployment benefits prepared strenuous opposition to the new regime. MacDonald was disowned in a Labor party statement and his right to represent the party in the new cabinet was challenged. MacDonald addres

London, Aug. 26.—(A.P.)—Ramsay MacDonald became, in a manner of speaking, a British dictator today as he presided over the first cabinet meeting of the non-partisan government which is preparing to cut $600,000,000 from the budget expenditures. Charged by the king with forming the emergency government, the prime minister holds his post of power as an individual but not as representative of organized labor which is now marshalling solid opposition to its former leader. The program which he laid out today was not much different from that which he and Chancellor Philip Snowden tried to force through with the labor government. The platform of the new ministry is virtually the same as that on which the labor government split and fell. It is proposed that the greater part of the money needed to balance the budget be made available by reducing expenses instead of by increasing taxes. Probably t

London, Aug. 25. (4)—J. Ramsay MacDonald, twice socialist prime minister of Great Britain, took up the reins of non-partisan government today with the realization that either he had committed political suicide or that history would number him among the empire’s great statesmen. In some circles it was said that by going into the wilderness with a handful of followers in a desperate effort to set the nation’s financial house in order he had incurred the bitter animosity of the immensely powerful trades union congress and probably won the hostility of a considerable section of the labor party. Slash Dole. It was freely commented by these observers that whatever else might happen Mr. MacDonald never again would be the head of a labor government or even an outstanding figure among labor politicians. London, Aug. 26.——(AP)— Prime Minister Ramsay McDonald’s new national government at its first cabinet session today reached a complete agreement on methods of dealing with the nation’s financial crisis. Mr. McDonald, Stanley Baldwin, the conservative leader, and Sir Herbert Samuel, representing the liberals, pledged themselves to complete their task swiftly and effectively.

HARLAN, Ky., Aug. 25.—(P)—Thirty-six more indictments were returned in the Harlan coal field cases here today including one charging criminal syndicalism against Mrs. Jessie London Wakefield, former University of Washington co-ed. Other indictments included one against Ralph Steel, charged with criminal syndicalism; one each against Woody Emery and Hager Layne, charged with slaying Jesse Pace, a deputy sheriff last April, and three against Lloyd Gilbert in connection with the Evarts clash May 5, in which four men were killed. The other indictments charged robbery of stores at Evarts.

London, Aug. 25 (#)—Great Britain’s new “government of individuals” took over power tonight and plunged into the task of pulling the nation through its financial crisis. The new cabinet, composed of only ten members, was presented by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald to King George this afternoon and received the approval of the throne. Tomorrow the members of Mr. MacDonald’s old Labor government will hand in their seals of office and the new government, headed by Mr. MacDonald and participated in by Laborites, Liberals and Conservatives will hold its first meeting. After he had been present at the death of his second labor ministry, Mr. MacDonald, speaking from his official residence at 10 Downing Street, tonight told the nation over the radio why it was impossible for him any longer to carry on with the Labor ministers who have been his colleagues for two years. LONDON, Aug. 25—Great Britain's new national government went into action tonight with the announcement of the appointment of a cabinet of only ten members, the smallest since the war when at one time there were five. The new administration, which is expected to lead the nation out of economic and financial doldrums, is noteworthy in that all except one of the so-called “spending departments” have been excluded from the cabinet. Among those thus passed over are labor, education, agriculture, air, war and navy. 1931-05-19.text: LONDON, May 18.—(4)—Howard Ferguson, Canadian high commissioner, convened the world wheat conference here today, outlining in his inaugural speech broad methods of alleviating the world surplus. Delegates of 11 wheat exporting countries were attending. At the outset Mr. Ferguson termed disposal of surplus wheat stock a matter of outstanding importance to the world, explaining that the wheat growing industry contained two essential problems, that the wheat reaches the customers when required and that the producer gets a reasonable price for his product. “Low prices,” he said, “have a tendency to correct themselves — acreage shrinks and business decline shortens supplies and raises prices. “The result is dearer bread. Our efforts must be directed to help the farmers get a fair wage and maintain their families without overcharging their fellow workers who must buy bread. Ferguson said that

CHICAGO, May 18 (AP)—Reports were current today that John Factor, known as "Jake the Barber," alleged swindler of English stock investors, was sought by lawless as well as by the law. The Chicago Daily Tribune said a price had been set on Factor’s head by Jack (Legs) Diamond, New York gangster, and quoted federal agents as fearing he might be slain before he could be arrested for extradition to England, where he is accused of defrauding investors of several millions of dollars. "Jake the Barber," reputed to have made big money illegally since he closed up his cut rate shop on Halsted street, was at odds with Diamond, the Tribune said, because of his failure to split the profits of a stock selling scheme after Diamond had "grubstaked" him on a trip to England. The story was that Factor accepted Diamond's aid at a time when the former barber was in trouble over Florida land deals. It was r

London -- Expert views of the world wheat crisis today were emptied into the mill of the International conference after an address by Samuel R. McKelvie, head of the United States delegation, at its first open meeting today. The conference went into committee session to analyze the various plans for relief before submitting reports to the full conference. In rapid succession the United States, Poland, Australia and the Danubian exporters filed their views. Little detail was available. Russia and Canada have not yet placed themselves on record and observers are saying that Russia intends to hold back until she sees what the other powers propose. London, May 19.—(#)—King George and Queen Mary, assisted by the Prince of Wales, will receive in historic Buckingham Palace tonight, among others debutantes and the wife of an American minister in the first of the social season’s four court presentations. The last curtsy was practiced today and the last ruffle patted in place in preparation for the crowning event in the social lives of the elect. They will wear gossamer gowns of tulle, chiffon and lace, the majority of them white but some in pale shades of color. Pearls will be the most favored adornment and feather fans will be preferred to bouquets. [Associated Press Leased Wire] WESTWARD HO DEVON, England, May 19.—George Voigt of New York continued his march through the British amateur golf championship today winning his third round match from J. R. Abercrombie of Liverpool two and one.

by the Associated Press. - GENEVA, Switzerland, May 19.— Denouncing the high tariff system as the biggest contributor to the world’s economic crisis, Arthur Henderson, British foreign secretary today called upon the Pan-European commission to adopt some common plan to save Europe from economic disaster. As the commission resumed its sessions persons usually well-informed said it was virtually certain that Henderson would be chosen as president of the general disarmament conference to be held in 1932. “We are faced with a great international dispute,” Henderson said, referring to the proposed Austro-German customs accord. “It is the first dispute of the great powers before the League of Nations.” He proposed creation of a sub-committee to weigh all the projects suggested for general economic relief and to bring in a common plan in which all the nations might engage.

NEW ORLEANS, La., May 18.—(U.P.)—Edgar Bouligny, hero of the Foreign Legion and the first American wounded in the World War, was killed at his home here today by his French wife. She told officers in broken English that Bouligny had whipped and slapped her.

By The Associated Press. LONDON, May 18.—Samuel R. McKelvie, former governor of Nebraska, and head of the United States delegation to the world wheat conference which opened today, outlined his country’s program this afternoon at a conference with newspaper men. By July 1, he said, the United States will be faced with a carry over of roughly 275,000,000 bushels of wheat in the face of the new crop, as compared with an ordinary annual carry over of from 100,000,000 to 125,000,000. “Consequently,” he said, “we have come here prepared to cooperate. But we do not propose to join nor will we agree to join any international pool. “Furthermore,” he paused so that his hearers could get the full meaning of his words, “we do not propose to dump one bushel of the farm board’s holdings.”

1931-06-11.text: (By The Associated Press) Weiheiwei, China, June 11—A thrilling battle for the lives of eight men trapped in the steel hull of the British submarine Poseidon was waged on the waters of the North Yellow Sea. Victory was in doubt last night, but there still was strong hope among the officers of British ships assembled at the scene of the disaster that, with the aid of a Japanese salvage tug, they might raise the stricken vessel before the foul air of its interior overcomes the imprisoned men. The Poseidon’s parent ship, the Medway, succeeded in establishing communication with the eight men who were trapped in a rear compartment when the submarine went to the bottom in twenty fathoms after a collision Tuesday. The prisoners reported themselves uninjured, but the length of time they would be able to survive with their limited supply of oxygen was necessarily fast diminishing. So far as the M

NEW YORK, June 11 (P)—Aid of Scotland Yard, London’s great detective organization, was sought today in an effort to unravel one of the most complex mysteries this city has followed in years—the death of 25-year-old Starr Faithfull. Cultured, beautiful and with a host of friends among the best people of New York and Boston, this daughter of a well-to-do family living in an aristocratic corner of Greenwich Village has left in the wake of the tragedy a life record both fascinating and sordid, and one which presents a horde of theories confusing to investigators. A diary, kept since the young woman’s school days, appeared likely to yield fresh clues in the strange case which has grown out of the discovery of Miss Faithfull’s body on the shore of Long Beach. ‘Tomorrow, when he will have his case ready for the grand jury, Elvin N Edwards, Nassau County prosecutor, expects to obtain murder indi

London, June 10.--Developments relative to the suggestions for a new world conference on the revision of German reparations payments indicated tonight that it was not likely such a conference would be called soon. French political circles continued to oppose the proposal and predicted that any amendment to the Fora plan would cause a new round of naval construction competition among the principal European powers. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald told a conservative member in the House of Commons that such a conference "would serve no useful purpose." American Ambassador Frederick M. Sackett was reported to have informed Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius of Germany that a new reparations conference would be very unpopular with the people of the United States at present. Meanwhile, Chancellor Bruening returned to Berlin and was reported to be facing the most difficult task of

TSINGTAO, CHINA, JUNE 11. (AP).—Efforts to save the eighteen men trapped in the sunken British submarine Poseidon, which went down off Weihaiwei, China, Tuesday after a collision with another ship, were spurred tonight after naval officials here said they believed the men were still alive and that their rescue depended solely upon speedy action. Experts said the American salvage ship Pigeon, which is proceeding to the scene of the disaster, might render valuable assistance in saving the trapped men because of the modern compressed air equipment it carries for such work.

LONDON, June 11, —(UP)— The admiralty announced today that the British commander-in-naval forces in China had stated there was no truth in a report that any men entombed in the sunken submarine Poseidon were alive. The aircraft carrier Hermes reported it received no reply to external tappings on the hull of the Poseidon.

Berlin, June 11 (UP)—A three-cornered conference on war debts and reparations among the United States, Great Britain and Germany during the forthcoming visit of Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson was anticipated in government quarters today. Arthur Henderson, British foreign secretary, will arrive in Berlin about the same time that Colonel Stimson reaches the German capital, it was learned. The presence here of both Mr. Henderson and Mr. Stimson at the same time, it was indicated, almost inevitably will lead to a consultation among these statesmen and the government leaders concerning reparations and war debts. The German officials hope that the presence of Mr. Henderson will help to impress upon Colonel Stimson the urgency of decisive action. New York, June 10 ()--Andrew W. Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury, sailed today on the Mauretania for England, where he will attend the post graduation of his son, Paul, at Clare College, Cambridge. Told there is belief in England that he is going there to discuss war debts and reparations, Mr. Mellon's only reply was: “Sorry if they think so. I am not.”
