1931-06-04.text: LONDON (UP).—An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Amman, Syria, today said Hussein, exiled king of Hedjaz, Arabia, died at dawn. King Hussein, at one time one of the most powerful potentates in the Near East, had long been ill. He will be buried at Jerusalem, according to present plans.

PORTO PRAIA, CAPE VERDE ISLANDS, June 4— (UP)—The German sea-plane Dornier Do-X resumed its long-interrupted flight to South America today several hours after her flight was making good progress. The British steamer Teresa reported sighting the Do-X at 3:55 p.m. in latitude 10 north, 22 west, apparently going at good speed and with all well aboard. Previous great excitement had been caused here by false radio reports that the Do-X had fallen into the sea 64 miles from the islands. A tug was sent to the rescue, but the reports subsequently were corrected by the radio stations, which appeared to have received garbled messages from ships, one announcement even saying that the Do-X herself had radioed that she is falling. All subsequent information indicated that the reports were without foundation. Latest reports said the Do-X was making 125 miles an hour. The position given by the Teresa i

CARNOUSTIE, SCOTLAND, June 4.—(P)—An Anglo-Argentine entente of Jose Jurado and Henry Cotton led the field at the end of the second round of play in the British Open golf championship with 36 hole scores of 147. In third place was the Scottish-American, Tommy Armour, with 148, and Johnny Farrell, the smiling Irishman from Quaker Ridge, was fourth with 149. Grouped within five strokes of the leaders were four other Americans, Joe Kirkwood and Gene Sarazen at 150, Willie Hunter at 151 and MacDonald Smith 152. At 150, also was W. T. Twine, the young Kent professional who shared the lead yesterday with Cotton and Farrell. At 151 were Marco Churio, another Argentine, Arthur Havers, open champion, 1923, and Abe Mitchell, the British veteran. Percy Alliss of Germany was tied with Mac Smith at 152, Horton Smith trailed the other Americans with 156 while Joe Turnesa and Tony Manero were eliminate

LONDON, June 3 (7i)—King George V, in celebrating his 66th birthday today, postponed the customary pomp and ceremony of the anniversary in order to go to Epsom Downs to witness the greatest classic of horse racing, the derby. With Queen Mary, he motored to the race track before noon. There he met the Prince of Wales and the Duke of York for luncheon. Cheered by the thousands at the track, the king and his party entered a special box, from where they saw Cameronian's thrilling finish to win the historic race. Later the monarch returned to Buckingham Palace, where he dined quietly with the queen this evening.

Carnoustie, Scotland, June 4—Jose Jurado, little Argentine flash, equalled the course record with a 71 in the second round of the British Open golf championship today to take a lead at the halfway mark with 147. Playing brilliant golf all the way, Jurado covered the first nine holes in 34 and then came home in 37 to equal the record set up in the qualifying round on Tuesday by MacDonald Smith and equalled later in the same day by the British star, Archie Compston. Just in back of Jurado was Tommy Armour, Detroit, former American Open champion, who shot a 75 today for a 30-hole total of 148. Armour played steady golf on the outgoing nine which he covered in par figures but ran into trouble on the first three holes of the second nine and took 39. Golf Is Spectacular Armour’s golf was spectacular—very good in spots and very bad in others. In a stretch of six holes through the middle of his

LONDON, June 4.—(UP)—Over-enthusiasm led Joseph Kennedy, a member of the crew of the steamer American Banker, to announce he had drawn a ticket on Cameronian in the Irish sweepstakes on the derby, officials of the United States lines said today. It was explained that Kennedy was over-eager to celebrate when he read of the drawing of a ticket by a Boston man with a name and address similar to his.

Rome, June 3.—(AP)—Premier Mussolini today declared war on anti-Fascism in Italy, “under whatever banner,” and according to news from the Vatican at least one of the Catholic Action society leaders was under arrest. The one Catholic Action leader who was named by the Vatican as having been arrested was an attorney named Corsanego. It was said he probably would soon be on his way to political exile on the Island of: Tanar?: Other reports said a dozen of the Catholic Action leaders had been arrested in various cities. It was said that they were all men who had opposed Fascism previously. Meaning Clear Premier Mussolini’s “declaration of war” against anti-Fascists was made at a special meeting of a small body of Fascist leaders which formed the directorate of the party. The premier presided at the meeting and it was said he definitely mentioned the Catholic Action society. Orders were issue

Rome, June 4.—The government stood today on a blunt declaration that the Fascist party would refuse to tolerate anti-Fascist activities "under any flag," in the controversy with the Holy See. The directorate of the Fascist party, headed by Premier Benito Mussolini, issued a communique reiterating that certain sections of the Azione Cattolica, Catholic laymen's organization, were either openly or secretly hostile to Fascism. "The directorate is determined it will not tolerate anti-Fascism," the communique said, "nor shall such activities find refuge or protest under any flags, old or new." The reference to flags was interpreted to mean the papal emblem, now since the sovereignty of the pope has been recognized again in the Lateran treaty signed early in 1929. A frankly conciliatory statement was issued by the Vatican, although it was said that police measures, including many arrests, had

1931-05-14.text: To the Editor of THE EAGLE:— BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., May 13. Here’s about all I can find in newsprint today. Spain is in a mess. Now we know they are becoming a regular republic. Hawkes got in his plane in Europe yesterday, so naturally he broke a record. Prince of Wales lays England's depression to not advertising enough. We lay ours to over-advertising. We were such good salesmen we sold to each other and went broke. Secretary of the Navy Adams is out here on the ocean watching manoeuvres. He is the only secretary our navy has had that could stay on deck long enough to see anything. Yours, AD lea Ww. ui Rogers.

London, May 12 Thomas Lipton, noted British tea merchant and sportsman, today was elected to membership in the Royal Yacht Squadron, the most coveted honor in British yachting circles. The membership was conferred in recognition of Sir Thomas’ contribution to British sport by his repeated efforts to wrest the America’s Cup from the United States.

CAIRO, Egypt, May 16. (AP)— Ten men were reported killed and 86 injured today when striking railway shop workmen fought with police in the streets. Two of the injured were British engineers. Unofficial estimates placed the number of dead at more than a score but there was no opportunity to check these figures for the riots spread from the railway shops to other sections of the city and the government was considering calling out the troops.

By The Associated Press. LONDON, May 14.—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald told the House of Commons today in an announcement of government airship policy, that Great Britain would not build any new airships for the present but would retain the R-100 without alterations as an “experimental airship.” Since the wreck of the R-101 there has been keen interest in the government’s future course regarding airships. Mr. MacDonald said today that the British airship is a modern craft not yet proven either a failure nor a complete success.

SOUTHPORT, England, May 14 (®) - Horton Smith, from Missouri, and Mario Curio, from Argentina, today tied for the first place with only a few more to finish in the second round of the $7500 Southport professional golf tournament with 26 hole totals of 148. They were one stroke ahead of Henry Cotton, young British professional who led yesterday's first round with a 70 but could do no better than a 77 today. Smith had a stroke advantage on Curio yesterday but he took a 75 today to the South American's fine 74. Curio has been one of the sensations of the tournament with his steady play. He qualified at 150, well up with the leaders. Joe Turnesa, the fourth and last American to finish, turned in a poor 79 today to give him a second round total of 158.

Hongkong, May 14—CP}—Gunboats loyal to the Canton government today engaged in an artillery duel with rebellious forces attempting to take the southern capital’s forts. British river and coastal steamers were advised to halt all sailings between Canton and Hongkong. Only scanty particulars were available from Canton.

SIMLA, India, May 14.—(7)— The second round table conference in London, which is expected to determine India’s status within the British Empire, will be held the first week in November and the presence of Mahatma Gandhi is definitely assured, it was learned here today. Lord Willingdon is holding discussions today with the round table delegates and is reviewing with them developments since the first round table conference adjourned as well as the program for the second conclave.
VISCOUNT RAY MEET VVVey LONDON, May 14 (#) — The Bank of England reduced its discount rate today from three per cent to two and one half per cent.

1931-02-04.text: PLYMOUTH, ENGLAND, Feb 4 (UP)—A royal air force plane was wrecked in Plymouth Saturday and eight of the 12 men aboard were drowned. Another man critically injured in the crash, died later, making a death toll of nine. Three men were in a hospital critically injured. The plane crashed when the pilot, apparently confused by bright sunlight on the water, misjudged the landing surface. An explosion wrecked the craft, which sank and trapped the men in the submerged cabin from which only four were able to escape. One of the survivors was an officer. The demolished plane was a R. A. F. Blackburn-Irish flying boat, a tri-motored craft which carried a complement of 12 including four officers, led by wing commander C. G. Tucker. Tucker was killed. Returning From Practice The plane was returning from aerial firing practice just before noon. It glided gracefully toward the water, eye witnesses said,

Plymouth, Eng., Feb. 4.—(AP)— Nine men in the crew of a Royal Air Force seaplane were feared lost today when the ship went into a dive while maneuvering over Plymouth Sound, struck the water with great force and was wrecked by an explosion. As she struck, she heeled over on one side and sank immediately. When rescuers went out in small boats, they picked up two officers and one of the crew, all injured. Commander Tucker, Flying Officer Wood and several enlisted men were missing. Divers recovered one of the bodies this afternoon. The cause of the accident was not immediately determined.

DAYTONA BEACH, Fla.—(4)—A strong wind Wednesday prevented Captain Malcolm Campbell, British race car driver, from attempting to better the world’s automobile record of 231 miles an hour on the ocean speedway.

Allahabad, India, Feb. 4.--The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, leader of the civil disobedience movement against British rule, today asked the viceroy, Lord Irwin, to make “a peace gesture” toward settlement of the independence controversy. Gandhi, in a letter to the viceroy, urged an official inquiry into six test cases of charges of police excesses against the independence volunteers. He said he would interpret the consent of the viceroy to the inquiry into a genuine instance of “excess” as a peace gesture. Gandhi said he would then attempt to persuade the leaders of the nationalist congress to realize the advantage of the offer of Prime Minister MacDonald toward a federal government for India.

Kingston, Jamaica, Feb. 3. (*)— Greeted by an ovation from 50,000 who crowded the docks, the Prince of Wales and his brother, Prince George, stopped over here today on their voyage to South America. Despite the busy day which awaited him on this island, the heir to the British throne found time this afternoon to open a new golf course at Constant Spring, six miles from here, and to attend a polo match. Tonight the royal guests were guests of honor at a dinner given by Governor Sir R. E. Stubbs and Lady Stubbs at Government House. There they met the high dignitaries of the island. Panama is their next stop.

- DAYTONA BEACH, Fla., Feb. 4 (AP)—Weather conditions today held in the balance plans of Captain Malcolm Campbell, British race car driver, to make an official attack upon the world’s automobile speed record of 281 miles an hour. The 46-year-old veteran of the roaring road hoped conditions which yesterday made an official trial impossible, would permit a record attempt at low tide, today. Campbell’s anxiety over the condition of his motor, at first believed damaged when the car slipped out of gear while traveling at a speed he estimated at 265 miles an hour yesterday, was allayed after mechanics made a thorough inspection.

(International News Service) BOMBAY, Feb. 4. — Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the campaign of civil disobedience against British rule in India, today made a definite offer to seek peace with the British Government. India's Holy Man wrote a letter to Lord Irwin, the viceroy, urging him to institute an inquiry into six specific instances of alleged police excesses against Indian nationalists since the start of the civil disobedience campaign. Gandhi asserted in his letter that he would interpret the viceroy’s favorable reply to his request as a genuine gesture of peace, and in that case he would exert all his influence to persuade the all-India Congress, representing the Nationalists, to accept the offer of the British Government of eventual qualified dominion status for India. The annual meeting of the all-India Congress has been fixed provisionally for April 6. The viceroy's reply is awaited

London, Feb. 3.-- (AP) -- The MacDonald labor government won an easy victory in the House of Commons tonight, carrying the electoral reform bill on second reading by a majority of 65 votes. Most of the liberals in the House of Commons voted with the laborites and thus upset the conservative attack.

1931-10-24.text: London, Oct. election campaign Great is His witnessed in years rounded the turn today with eyes right, and a shiver of fear lest the ghost of the notorious "Zinoviev letter" again walk on the eve of the voting. Arnold, labor peer, warned the electorate there would be "an attempt to scare the people" with something like the famous purported Russian document which appeared at the last minute in the 1924 campaign and to which the labor party attributed its defeat. There also were whisperings that the labor party had up its sleeve a disclosure of "secret financial correspondence" which would be aimed at blasting the prospects of the national government and its followers. In the meantime, both sides claimed victory today, with the voting only three days away. The supporters of Prime Minister MacDonald assured the country that he would be given the "doctor's mandate" he asks, by a huge majorit

NEW YORK, Oct. 25.—'Whoopee cruises' of British liners from American ports, one of which furnished the background for a story of a hat room fight, have prompted a group of old seafaring men to demand an investigation by the Treasury Department. Their charge that the ships are violating the coastwise laws and prohibition laws was turned over to the customs bureau at Washington today as the New York Sun described a fight between detectives and gamblers on the last cruise of the White Star liner Majestic. The Majestic arrived at her dock here last night after a 100-mile, 24-hour cruise from New York to 'nowhere' and back with 476 passengers. A representative of the line said there had been a disturbance near dawn Thursday outside the 12-mile limit, while the ship’s bar was open. However, most of the passengers were in bed, he said. He refused to comment on the Sun's story that one participa

London, Oct. 23. (P)—The island of Cyprus’ revolutionary movement toward unification with Greece was understood tonight to have subsided in the face of the arrival of British troops by air and by sea. Governor Ronald Storrs attributed the uprising to “certain political leaders who have been endeavoring to break down the government's efforts for understanding and cooperation among the people.” Cooperating with Cyprian authorities, the troops were deployed in vigilant patrols through principal cities and the effect of their presence was to ease the tension and discourage rebellious elements from resuming rioting. Mobs which had burned the governor’s home at Nicosia and held full sway in the streets for several days assembled again last night but were dispersed when police threatened to fire on them from behind barbed wire. It was estimated that only one Cypriote had died from the disturban

Nicosia, Island of Cyprus, Oct. 24.—British marines put ashore from warships which arrived yesterday have arrested half a dozen leaders of the disturbances which occurred here early this week. The prisoners, including the Greek Orthodox bishop of Lanarka, were taken aboard one of the British vessels and will be removed to a foreign port. The situation is quiet and a censorship has been established by the island.

SYDNEY, Australia, Oct. 24 (®)—Consternation was created in divorce court here when it was found the plaintiff was calmly sitting in the jury box. By an accident he had been summoned as a juror and was waiting to try, as it happened, his own case, in which he claimed $20,000 from his uncle on a charge of alienating his wife's affections. It was the uncle who drew the attention of the judge to the presence of his nephew on the jury. A new panel was drawn.

Geneva, Oct. 25 (4).--The League of Nations’ labors to re-establish peace in Manchuria were blocked again tonight when the Japanese representative, acting on fresh instructions from Tokyo, reiterated at a public session of the League Council his government's refusal to withdraw its troops by November 16. Kenkichi Yoshizawa, the Japanese spokesman, voiced this refusal after Dr. Alfred Sze for China had accepted with reservations the Council’s plan for peace, including the time limit on evacuation. This interchange clearly defined the deadlock between Japan and the other members of the Council and aroused anxious speculation about what will happen tomorrow when the problem is to be debated again. M. Yoshizawa assured the Council that his government was determined to get its soldiers back within legal territorial limits as quickly as possible without endangering the lives and property of Ja

GENEVA, Oct. 24—(UP)—Japan rejected the League of Nations formula for settlement of the Manchurian dispute with China today. Kenkichi Yoshizawa, Japanese delegate, told the League Council that his government was unable to accept the council’s draft resolution. The League council adjourned until 4 p.m., without voting on either the council’s resolutions or the Japanese counter-proposals. The resolution was made public yesterday. It recommended that China and Japan appoint representatives to arrange details of evacuation of Japanese troops to within the treaty zone in Manchuria and that they begin direct negotiations as soon as evacuation was completed. It also suggested the creation of a permanent Sino-Japanese conciliatory committee... Lack of explanation of the “fundamental principles” on which Japan demanded direct negotiations ruined chances of a settlement at the morning session of t

GENEVA, Oct. 4.—(AP)—On the point of overriding Japanese opposition and fixing November 16, as the time limit for complete evacuation of Japanese troops from Manchuria, the League of Nations council adjourned a morning session today until late in the afternoon, in the hope that some way might be found to remove the opposition. With Viscount Cecil, British representative, and Salvador De Madariaga of Spain leading a drive against the objections of Kenkichi Yoshizawa, Japanese delegate, the lineup was clearly drawn 13 to 1 in favor of the council's proposal. M. Briand joined the British and Spanish delegates in evincing anxiety with regard to the "mysterious fundamental points" which Japan insisted should be settled in advance by direct negotiations between the two parties. Concern was expressed lest Japan, under cover of an "unexplained phrase," intended to force China to acknowledge the

1931-11-07.text: LONDON, Nov. 5.—(#)— Prime Minister Ramsey MacDonald remains head of the British government in the new cabinet, with Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council and Neville Chamberlain as chancellor of the exchequer, succeeding Philip Snowden. The cabinet list was announced at No. 10 Downing Street this evening. Sir John Simon, one of the country's greatest lawyers and leader of one wing of the Liberal party which broke away from David Lloyd George, is foreign secretary.

(By The Associated Press) London, Nov. 7—Joseph Martin of Los Angeles said today that he had delivered an invitation to the Prince of Wales to attend the 58th annual Shriners’ convention at San Francisco next July.

GENEVA, Nov. 6 (A.P.)—A concerted withdrawal of diplomatic representatives from Tokyo as the next move in the Sino-Japanese conflict was considered by League of Nations leaders tonight in planning for the next meeting of the council in Paris November 16. When the council reassembles a three-fold program will be considered, according to league authorities. First, effort will be made to induce Japan to adopt a conciliatory approach. (Continued on Page 11, Col. 5)

Geneva, Nov. 7.—Aristide Briand, president of the League of Nations council, sent another strongly-worded note to Japan and China today insisting that they cease military activities in Manchuria, It was the third note sent to the two nations by the League during the present conflict in the far east.

Rome, Nov. 6.—(#)— Fortified by Premier Mussolini, Foreign Minister Dino Grandi sails for the United States tomorrow to present to President Hoover a ‘“neutral’’ viewpoint on what ails the world’s economic and political machinery. He had a long talk with Il Duce and therefore goes as the premier’s personal representative, empowered to speak in the latter’s name. Both statesmen are said to feel that Italy is in a more detached position than any other European nation and alone among them is able to move quickly in any direction that the premier approves.

TOKYO, Nov. 6—(”)—The three-day battle of Nonni River ended today with the Japanese army in control of that part of northwestern Manchuria and the Chinese Heilungkiang provincial army in wild flight. Japanese losses included 130 killed. No estimate of Chinese casualties was available here, but press dispatches said they were apparently large. The battle was concluded by the arrival of Japanese reinforcements which swept the Chinese out of their hillside position around the town of Tahsing, six miles north of the bridge, and sent them northward in disorderly retreat. Japanese bombing planes so hastened their panic-filled flight that the Chinese rear guard passed a village three miles north of Tahsing an hour after the battle. The fighting developed from Japanese efforts to place a military guard in the Nonni region as protection for a Japanese crew, assigned to repair a railroad bridge ac

GENEVA. (UP). The Soviet Union denied the right of the League of Nations to publish statistics on Russian armaments. Maxim Litvinoff, Soviet foreign commissar, sent a note to Sir Eric Drummond, secretary general of the League, saying the Soviet would not consent to publication of arms records which they had asked be submitted in preparation for the 1932 world disarmament conference.

Moscow, Nov. 6 (P)—The “workers and oppressed people of all the capitalistic world” were urged today by the Communist International to lend active support to the “Chinese proletariat” in their conflict with Japan over Manchuria. The executive committee of the International, which represents the Communist parties in every nation and is not allied with the Soviet government, issued the appeal on the eve of the fourteenth anniversary of the October Revolution. “This war against the working masses of China,” the statement read, “is a war against us and a step toward war against the Soviet republic. Organize mass revolutionary barriers against that war for a united, independent Soviet China. “The leaders of all capitalistic countries are wandering about in search of an outlet, afraid of complete bankruptcy before the mounting proletarian revolution. The class fight is becoming more acute. The

1931-05-31.text: London, May 30 (4P)—The very Rev. William Ralph Inge, “Gloomy Dean” of St. Paul’s Cathedral, hopes that in a thousand years England will be a land in which there are neither rumors of war nor politics nor disease nor crime nor many clothes. In fact, he told the Royal Institution last night, “if we want it, there will in 3,000 A.D. be a population of only 20,000,000 living mostly in towns and villages, physical perfection will be the hallmark of social prestige, national taxation will be almost nil, hours of labor will be at a minimum, radio will be the principal method of education—but the common cold still will be a menace. This vision of a utopia was introduced into a scientific lecture, he said, “chiefly in self-protection, because there is a legend, quite without foundation, that I am fond of finding fault with society as it is without having anything better to suggest in place of it

BELVIDERE, Kent, England—(?)—Scotland Yard “Big Five” last night were pooling their efforts to find Charles Frederick Lewis, 60-year-old school master. They wanted to question him regarding the finding of the bodies of his wife and step-daughter beneath fresh concrete in a fish pond in the back yard of his home Friday night. The mystery of the disappearance of Lewis and the finding of the bodies promised to be one of the most sensational with which Scotland Yard has grappled in many years. Lewis is a prominent educator, tall and distinguished, one of the assistant directors of education for the county of Kent, choir master at the local church and an active participant in civic affairs of the district. Mrs. Lewis was 50 and her daughter (continued on page 3)

OXFORD, Eng. May 23.—Prof. Albert Einstein, who developed the ‘theory of relativity, today was praised as “a brilliant ornament of our century” when Oxford University conferred the degree of doctor of science on him. Wearing the scarlet degree robe which marked him as the holder of this honor, the noted mathematician went from the meeting to a lecture room where he completed his series of Rhodes lectures.

LONDON, May 30 (4)—"One reason why the officers and men followed Joan of Arc so blindly," George Bernard Shaw declared in a radio address tonight, commemorating the memory of the Maid of Orleans, "is that she lacked sex appeal." "I'm sorry to disappoint those who thought she was beautiful," Shaw said, "but it is an established fact that her followers believed her to be divine because she lacked that quality so well-known in Hollywood—sex appeal." The burning of Joan was useless and cruel, he said, and the question had arisen whether or not she was a "dangerous woman." Booked to speak 20 minutes, Shaw talked an hour and then concluded with: "That's just like me, isn’t it?"

Havre, France, May 30.—-()— Texas Guinan and her “gang” of girls and musicians will be sent back to America on the steamer Paris, sailing next Wednesday, a spokesman for the French immigration bureau said tonight. Their return will be by order of the French government and they will not be permitted officially to enter France. No Permit A member of the immigration bureau here said the decision was made on the ground that Tex has “no working permit or contract.” The bureau member said: “We have been criticised because others slipped through the ports without contracts and we refuse to let Miss Guinan do it. It is sometimes possible to let in one artist to compete with French amusement talent, but she is trying to bring in a whole troupe.” Too Gay The immigration bureau has heard about parties conducted by Tex and her “gang” on board the steamer Paris. “The second-class passengers told us a

ROME, May 30.—(4)—Premier Mussolini tonight extended his order disbanding the Catholic Action society to all of Italy, and Pope Pius XI, after a conference, placed the organization directly in charge of the bishops of the Catholic dioceses throughout the nation. The membership of the society, including its six branches, totals 500,000 men, women, boys, and girls. ROME, May 30.—(4)—Relations between the church and state, strained by anti-Catholic disorders of the past few days, became even more critical today when the police closed all the Catholic clubs in Rome and Pope Pius cancelled the Eucharistic Congress that was to have been held next week. The government also closed three playgrounds financed by the American Knights of Columbus and the pontiff revoked the appointment of a papal legate to the centenary celebrations of St. Anthony of Padua. Participates in Politics, The government’s

Paris—(P)—From the imposing cemetery of Romagne-Sous-Montfaucon, where sleep nearly 15,000 former wearers of the olive drab and forest green, to the humble and isolated tombs of the blue-denimed stevedores near Bordeaux and Marseilles, the graves of the war dead of the American Expeditionary Force throughout France today were decked with flowers and flags. At the same time the last resting places of four veterans of the Civil War, “Uncle Abe's” bluejackets of U.S.S. Kearsarge, killed in action off the French coast in June, 1864, after a memorable contest with the Confederate raider Alabama, were similarly decorated near Cher- «Continued on Page 6)

Ober Gurg, Austria, May 30. (AP) - Without speeches or ceremony the mountaineers who live in this newly famous corner of the world today "dedicated" a monument to mark the spot where Professor August Piccard ended the highest flight man has ever made. Seven-Foot Sphere It is the seven-foot aluminum sphere in which the Swiss scientist and Charles Kipfer, his aide, rose ten miles into the stratosphere. Perhaps no one would have had the happy thought of leaving the big red and white ball as a memorial on the sweeping Gurgi glacier had it not become obvious that its removal would be impossible without breaking it up into pieces or rolling it down the mountainside where it probably would be smashed on the rocks. May Be Buried Forever Under Snow In Fall Consequently for the rest of the summer Alpine tourists will be able to look it over at close hand if they can reach the spot where it came do

1931-01-25.text: London, Jan. 26...P)—Dame Nellie Melba, famous singer, is seriously ill at Sydney, an Exchange Telegraph dispatch said today. Dame Melba was too ill to go ashore when her ship reached Australia some weeks ago. She was said later to have been suffering from prickly heat, contracted during a voyage through the tropics.

PARIS, Jan. 24—Pierre Laval, youthful Independent-Socialist senator, and one of the leaders of the Left Center Moderates, tonight took up the task of forming a cabinet to succeed that headed by Senator Theodore Steeg, overthrown in the chamber of deputies on Thursday. He accepted the task at the hands of President Doumergue after Aristide Briand, veteran of many ministries, had declined the premiership for a fourth time in a year and a half. In two long conversations with President Doumergue by telephone from Geneva where he was attending the sessions of the council of the league of nations, M. Briand said he preferred to retain the post of foreign minister and the premiership should go to a younger man. Senator Laval attempted to form a government after the defeat of the Tardieu cabinet in December last year, but was prevented by what seemed an irreconcilable battle between the Right an

Geneva, Jan. 24. —-(#)—- The council of the League of Nations topped off a week of laborious sessions tonight by composing the inflammatory German-Polish minority question with a settlement hailed in Geneva as one of the most important decisions of the League in recent years. In effect the council unanimously condemned the activities of certain patriotic organizations in Poland which were charged with violent acts against the German minority and summoned the Polish government to break off all connections with these bodies. Must Report: Further, the Warsaw government was asked to report to the council before its session next May what measures had been taken to execute the league’s mandate.

Philadelphia, Jan. 24. (P)—The Mayflower, famous presidential yacht of other days, lay a blackened and blistered wreck tonight at her pier at the Philadelphia navy yard. She was burned almost to the water line and listing badly, her stern near bottom. Naval men, when they saw her plight shook their heads, her days as a sailing ship, they said, were over. Fire from an undetermined cause burst from the Mayflower shortly before 10 o'clock, an explosion tearing hatches away and sending out clouds of smoke and flame. All the fire fighting apparatus in the navy yard was sent to the scene, and virtually every marine and sailor in the yards fought the fire with hose lines and extinguishers. The Mayflower, decommissioned more than a year ago, has been tied up at the navy yard undergoing reconditioning and repair.

HELENWOOD, Tenn., Jan. 24.—(7)—The Suwanee river special of the Southern railway was derailed near here at 12:35 p.m. today and late this afternoon five bodies had been taken from the wreckage. The names of four of the dead were given at Somerset, Ky., division headquarters of the road, as Harry Lindole, 50, engineer, Somerset; Charles Sexton, 40, fireman, Somerset; Mrs. Charles D. Rinehart, Pasadena, Calif.; and Mrs. Logan Cowgill, Indianapolis, Ind., and Tampa, Fla. The fifth was an unidentified woman passenger. Six other persons reported seriously injured and 15 others slightly hurt.

Chicago, Jan. 24.—(AP)—Mrs. Myrtle Tanner Blacklidge resigned as collector of internal revenue for northern Illinois. It was the culmination of the $50,000 faro swindle of Springfield, Ill., into which, she said, she was innocently drawn. In sending her curt relinquishment to Washington she brought to a close the federal investigation into the charges made by Edward R. Litsinger, member of the Cook county board of review, that she was a party to a plot by which he was mulcted out of $50,000 which he had lent her. If prosecution is to be made as a result of Litsinger’s accusations, it must come from city and county authorities. Denies Guilt Claiming innocence of any wrongdoing, disclaiming any part in the swindle, and turning bitterly on Litsinger, Mrs. Blacklidge gave out a statement from a downtown hospital. She had been in hiding since Thursday and under the care of a physician. Dresse

JEFFERSON CITY, Mo., Jan. 24. (Officials and guards of the Missouri penitentiary tonight quelled a disorder in 'Y' hall, the 'hard-boiled prison' inside the penitentiary, within a short time after the trouble broke out. The trouble started about 8:39 p.m.; a few hours before the annual governors military ball was to begin at the state capitol, and at 7:46 p.m. penitentiary officials announced the outbreak was quelled, with no one injured. The rioting convicts in the cell building, in which 478 of the worst inmates are quartered, overpowered three guards, Frank Weimeyer, O. F. Dougles, and another guard named Bailey, and took their pistols. With these they fired from windows at guard towers on a wall nearby. No details were given with the announcement the trouble was ended, except that four convicts, apparently the ringleaders, had been captured and had surrendered the guards’ pistols. Th

| Washington, Jan. 24.—(#) While the house leisurely approached the relief fund loaded upon a supply bill by the senate, the Red Cross drove ahead today toward its $10,000,000 goal. Chairman Cramton of the appropriations subcommittee which will conduct house hearings on the $25,000,000 proposal, conferred at the White House with President Hoover, and said later that the hearings would be conducted as expeditiously as possible. He added that ‘the very existence’ of the Red Cross was bound up in the matter. Would Remain Private The Red Cross has insisted that it should be allowed to take care of the needy in the regular manner, through private subscriptions. A demand came from the democratic side of the house today for public hearings on the measure. Representative Byrns of Tennessee, (Continued on Page 6)

1931-11-09.text: London, Nov. 9.—(A.P.)—Mahatma Gandhi told the Associated Press tonight that the Indian round table conference was doomed to failure, and that he would sail for Bombay Nov. 29. “Only a miracle, which I do not expect to happen, can save the conference from failure,” he said, “and therefore I have decided to abandon the European tour I intended to make, and will sail for Bombay from Genoa on the 29th.”

Bombay, India, Nov. 8.—(#) — Asserting the British government had failed to grant its demands for independence, the Indian National Congress today cabled Mahatma Gandhi in London that his further attendance at the round-table conference was unnecessary and urged him to return to India at once. While leaving the final decision to Gandhi, the Congress’ working committee adopted a resolution saying, "The people of India should not allow themselves to be deflected from the right path, but should organize themselves and prepare for united effective action." Recent attempts by radicals on the lives of British officials were condemned.

| Port Darwin, Australia, Nov. 9 | (AP)—Flying one of the smallest airplanes in the world, wearing carpet slippers for comfort and carrying a tomahawk for a weapon, C. A. Butler, English aviator, landed at 4:25 p.m. today. Butler clipped 1 hour and 42 minutes off the previous England to Australia record made by C. W. A. Scott who covered the 13,187 miles in 9 days, 4 hours and 11 minutes.

London, Nov. 9, (UP) —The London Stock Exchange next Monday will resume margin trading which has been banned since the market reopened after closing for a few days following suspension of the gold standard. The announcement, made today, was taken to mean that conditions have improved to the extent where restrictions on credit operations no longer will be necessary. Following suspension of the gold standard, September 21, the London Stock Exchange was closed for several days. When it reopened all business was done for cash, thus eliminating the margin dealings. Lifting of the restrictions will help restore confidence in the market and business, according to observers.

PORT DARWIN, Australia, Nov. 9—Charles Butler, a Briton, flying a Comper-Swift airplane, said to be the smallest in the world, set a new record today for flight from England to Australia. Butler left Lympne Airdrome, England, at 5:16 a.m., October 31, and arrived here at 4:23 a.m., today, beating the previous record held by C. W. A. Scott by about an hour. Butler’s time was 9 days, one hour, 32 minutes. Butler wore carpet slippers throughout the flight and his meager equipment included a tomahawk for use in case he was forced down and attacked by tribesmen. Butler estimated that the entire flight cost about $170 because of the low oil and gasoline consumption of his plane.

LONDON, Nov. 8—(4)—On receipt of a cablegram from the Indian National Congress, a number of Indian delegates to the round table conference today went to Oxford where Mahatma Gandhi was speaking to confer with him on his plans for the future. Gandhi has said repeatedly he was wasting his time in London because the conference was making no progress, but he was promised Prime Minister MacDonald to remain until its conclusion, expected about November 23. Asked in Oxford whether he would renew the civil disobedience campaign, he replied: “If England shows no change of heart toward India, then a fiery ordeal and more suffering lie ahead of us.”

SORIO, Nov. 9 (Reports that the Chinese general Mah Chan-Shan, head of the Heilongjiang army, had declared war against Japan and actually opened hostilities by bombarding the Japanese position at Tahsing, Manchuria, where he was defeated in sharp fighting last week, stirred the government to action today. The bombardment, begun by the Chinese this morning, could be heard for miles in the region of the bridge, reports said. Gen. Mah's troops, which according to estimates here number somewhere between 8000 and 13,000, were said to be using field artillery and machine guns. The Japanese forces at last reports were only a little in excess of 1000. In the face of reports indicating Chinese troops were concentrating south of Aanganchi, near last week's battleground, Japan decided to move more troops to that area. In the diplomatic phase of the controversy she prepared a sharp answer to the lat

Nice, France, — The Nizam of Hyderabad, reputed to be the richest man in the world, today gave $200,000 in cash and a million dollars worth of jewels to Prince Abdul Medjid Effendi, former Caliph at Istanbul and supreme spiritual ruler of 300,000,000 Mohammedans, in return for the marriage of the former Caliph’s daughter and niece to the Nizam’s two sons. At the same time the ruler of Hyderabad, whose wealth is estimated at more than two billion dollars, increased the former Caliph's living allowance to $2,000 a month. Ever since Medjid was exiled from Turkey by Mustapha Kemal, seven years ago, the Nizam has been paying $1,500 a month to the wearer of Mohammed's temple. A double wedding uniting Prince Azam Jah, heir to the Hyderabad throne, with the 18 year old Princess Durai Shehvar, only daughter of the former Sultan, and the Nizam’s younger son with Princess Nilufar, 16 year old niece

1931-12-03.text: LONDON, Dec. 4 UP —The chill from which the Prince of Wales is suffering is taking a normal course, it was officially stated today. The prince has no temperature and passed a comfortable night.

LONDON, Dec. 2—(AP)—Mahatma Gandhi, exhausted by his labors with the Indian round table conference, was sent to bed tonight with a feverish cold. Ever since he came to London several weeks ago for the round table meeting, the Mahatma has insisted upon wearing his scanty native costume despite the rigorous British climate. Before he would go to bed tonight, however, he insisted upon observing his usual period of evening prayer. The Mahatma, whose diet is almost as scanty as his costume, is 63 years old.

LONDON, Dec. 1 (4) — Charlie Chaplin played a courtroom role today, and didn’t like it very well. The comedian, looking the part of complete gravity, gave a performance that failed to impress the judge; in fact, he was pretty free with his criticism. The upshot of the proceedings was that Chaplin paid 100 pounds and costs to Miss May Shepherd in connection with his visit to England. He dropped his defense of the suit, he explained, because the names of prominent persons had been brought into it. Yesterday Miss Shepherd’s testimony that Chaplin ducked out of a dinner engagement with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and had to write his letter of apology provoked the judge to remark, “this is going to do us a lot of good in foreign countries. Fancy how foreigners will laugh at us, and quite rightly too.” When court opened this morning Chaplin, who wasn’t present yesterday, showed up with hi

London, Dec. 3—(P)—A general tariff against foreign wheat of about 9 cents a bushel, at the present rate of British exchange, the Daily Express said today, has been proposed by British millers. The millers also proposed, the Express said, that a similar duty be imposed on unsold foreign wheat stored in Great Britain, particularly thousands of tons of Soviet grain lying in port elevators. The suggestions were made to Sir John Simon, minister of agriculture, who is working over the task of applying to the products of British farmers the effects of the new tariff policy recently announced by the National Government as a protection against so-called “dumping” of foreign-made goods in Great Britain.

| LONDON, Dec. 3 (UP)—Mahatma Gandhi suffered with a cold and a temperature slightly above normal today, due to the excessive strain during the final sessions of the round table conference and the recent bad weather. Gandhi had a temperature of 99 degrees last night. He was not confined to his bed today, however, and did not cancel any engagements. He did not consult a physician and members of his staff said there was no cause for alarm.

LONDON, Dec. 3, (#)—Mahatma Gandhi, who was put to bed last night with chills and fever, was well enough today to take his usual morning walk through London's East End. Tomorrow he is to plant a tree in front of Kingsley Hall, the settlement house where he has been living during the Indian round table conference. Before he leaves on Saturday he will talk with Prime Minister MacDonald and other government officials actively concerned in the Indian discussions. Whether or when he will renew his civil disobedience campaign for peace will not be decided definitely until he returns to Bombay on Dec. 28 and a full report to Congress.

- LONDON, (UP)—A worldwide anti-religious movement, gaining impetus from Russia, now embraces nearly 10,000 organized members, Joseph Lewis, American Atheist leader, declared today. Lewis, president of the Freethinkers of America, has just completed a three-reper tour of the area to urge non-religions to unite here. "The spread of education among seen its workings not only in Russia but in Spain and many other countries. Germany has a stronger anti-religious movement aside from Soviet thought," Lewis said.

LONDON, Dec. 2—(AP)—The Indian round table conference is over, but Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald told the House of Commons today the work of hammering out an Indian constitution will go right ahead. There is a prospect, he said, the minorities whose disagreement over the communal problem seriously hampered the work of the conference would settle their differences, and in any case those differences do not provide an excuse for the government to relax its efforts. “We could never be forgiven,” said MacDonald, “if we said we could do nothing at all until the communal question is settled. We would be denounced from every platform in India.” The next step, the Prime Minister explained, will be to send out committees to India early next year to study there the problems raised as the round table conference.

1931-10-26.text: (By the Associated Press) London, Oct. 26—Newspapers supporting the national government predicted today that it would win a majority of 150 to 200 seats in parliament at the election tomorrow as the answer to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's appeal for a ‘doctor’s mandate’ to rule the country. At the same time Arthur Henderson, leader of the opposition, declared there has been a strong leaning toward the Labor party during the last few days and that it was difficult to forecast results. Henderson, veteran Labor leader who was secretary of state for foreign affairs in the Labor cabinet up to its fall, was taken ill last night at Burnley with a chill and was ordered to bed by his physician. David Lloyd George, leader of the Liberals, himself convalescing from a recent illness, called upon his followers to vote for free trade candidates, preferably for Liberals, but for Labor candidates ra

London, Oct. 25.—(P)—Last appeals were addressed by British political leaders to the electorate tonight before the nation goes to the polls Tuesday either to continue the MacDonald coalition—the so-called national government—in power or thrust it out and put another in its stead. “Labor’s return would be an irreparable disaster,” said Philip Snowden, chancellor of the exchequer, in a statement which emphasized the topsy-turvy nature of the campaign in which former labor leaders have been fighting their own party. “The fate of the country is in the hands of the liberals,” said David Lloyd George, repeating his adjuration that the liberals vote ‘for free trade candidates for the house of commons, preferably liberals, but labor nominees, rather than tories. Plans Fighting Finish Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald rested today in Easington in his own constituency. Tomorrow he will make a person

London, Oct. 24. —— (#) -—— The campaign for the general election Tuesday swept into its final phase today both the government and the opposition, warned by covert and open charges, prepared for last minute trouble. Labor circles were suspicious that an attempt would be made to ‘scare’ the voters with something akin to the famous ‘Zinovieff letter’ of the 1924 campaign—the document which purported to show unanimity between the labor government and Communist Russia. To Drag Bankers In Labor, too, was suspected of having ready last-minute ammunition in the form of ‘secret financial correspondence’—apparently dealing with the labor charge, made unceasingly during the campaign, that in forming the national government, Ramsay MacDonald succumbed to the threat of international bankers, particularly Americans, who demanded that the dole be cut 10 per cent.

- London, O.—Mayor Harry Van Cleve, of London, Saturday threatened to evoke the old curfew law in London immediately unless pre-Hallowe’en celebrators halted their depredations. The mayor said the police headquarters was swamped during the past five days with reports of property destroyed and stolen by the celebrators.

TOKIO, Oct. 26. — Japan stood firm today on her refusal to set a definite date for withdrawal of her troops from Manchuria. A restatement of the Japanese policy after refusing a League of Nations demand for withdrawal of troops by Nov. 16, was framed by the cabinet. There was no change in the government policy, and emphasis was placed on “scrupulous respect for Japan's rights and interests in Manchuria acquired by treaty.” There was no indication that Japan would withdraw from the league at present. No change was expected in her position. Japan's vote against the league council’s formula for settlement of the Manchurian dispute with China made the council resolution ineffective, as it required a unanimous vote. The Japanese Press felt that Kenkichi Yoshizawa, head of the delegation at Geneva, failed completely because he did not state Foreign Minister Baron Shidehara’s five points for a

NAPLES, Italy, Oct. Premier Mussolini told the Italian people today that the world ‘must disarm, nations must be “just” and “the tragic bookkeeping” of debts and reparations must end if the world is to recover from its economic plight. He spoke directly to half a million persons gathered in the great 20-acre Plazza dei Plebiscito here and to another half million in adjoining streets and nearby squares who were served by amplifiers. At the government palace he addressed the solid mass of Fascist “black-shirts,” militiamen and colorfully garbed Neapolitans whose ranks reached out as far as the eye could see. “Something is jammed, perhaps broken” in world economics, Il Duce said, and he asked how there could be European reconstruction unless there was a modification of “some clauses of some peace treaties which have pushed whole peoples to the brink of material disaster and moral desperatio

Premier Benito Mussolini, who rose to power leading the Fascist army's march on Rome nine years ago, has joined the ranks of world leaders clamoring for revision of world war peace treaties and reparations. Addressing the largest audience he had ever faced, Mussolini told 300,000 Italians here such action was to lead the world from the darkness into which it was plunged by the world war. His audience packed the immense Piazze Plebiscito and overflowed into the streets. The premier’s remarks were addressed to all Italians and to the balance sheet built on the blood of 10,000,000 youths, we see a light of day. On the other hand, there are those miserably condemned to be disarmed? WASHINGTON, Oct. 26 (UP) Prospect of further relief for war debts and reparations opened up today as a result of the visit of Premier Laval just ended. It is a move aimed at the heart of the world-wide depression.

HELSINGFORS, Finland, Oct. 25. The Finnish radio station at Viipuri reported today the entire crew of an unidentified Russian submarine which was reported in collision yesterday with a German freighter in the Gulf of Finland had been rescued. The station made repeated, but futile, efforts to re-establish communication with the freighter, Gratia. It was understood, however, that the Gratia was at Kronstadt, with its bow dented and the forepart of the ship filled with water.

1931-12-07.text: BATON ROUGE, La., Dec. 7.—(P)—An appeal for full American naval strength under the terms of the London treaty and an increase in the standing army as means toward unemployment relief has been voiced by Henry L. Stevens, Jr., of North Carolina, national commander of the American Legion. Speaking at a conference of Louisiana Legion officials here yesterday, he said: “The regular army is down to a point where they are simply a bunch of technicians, army college professors, who, in the case of emergency, would become the instructors and perhaps the higher officers and commanders of any army that would be formed when such an emergency arrives. He criticized sharply what he termed “false economy in the matter of our national defense.”

United Press Staff Correspondence TOKIO, Dec. 7.—Japan instructed the Japanese delegate to the League of Nations Council meeting at Paris today to accept the League’s resolution for settlement of the Manchurian dispute, reserving freedom of action for the Japanese army. Acceptance also applied to Aristide Briand’s presidential declaration regarding the right of the army to suppress bandits, with the same provision for a reservation. It was stated that this provision would satisfy Japan if China would merely make a similar reservation. It was doubted in many quarters, however, if China would accept such a plan. It was believed the Council’s final action then would be the appointment of a commission of inquiry under Article V of the League Covenant, without Japanese or Chinese consent.

TOKYO, Dec. 7.—The Japanese government, it was said authoritatively today, is prepared to accept a suggestion by the League of Nations council that Japan make a separate reservation regarding the right to suppress banditry in the proposed Chinchow neutral zone, which the league would establish in Manchuria. This, however, would be on the understanding that no counter-reservation nullifying that made by Japan is permitted. The government also has decided, it was said, to agree to the formula proposed by its league representative, Nobumi Ito, regarding the scope of the proposed neutral commission of inquiry into Manchuria, and instructions to this effect probably will be sent to M. Ito tonight. Reports from Mukden, Manchuria, that about 300 Chinese were killed when Japanese airplanes bombed Kungtapiu to the southwest, were confirmed in a dispatch to the Rengo (Japanese) news agency today,

- ROME, Dec. 7 (CP) — Giovanni Giuriati resigned today as secretary of the Fascist party and was succeeded by his assistant, Achille Starace. His successor was leader of the Venice and Trento sections of the Fascist march on Rome in 1922. He has been vice secretary of the party since 1921.

TOKYO, Dec. 6 (2) — A Sino-Japanese clash on a much larger scale than in the past appeared inevitable to informed circles today unless Marshal Chang Hsueh-Liang disregards the Chinese government’s rejection of the neutral zone proposal and withdraws his troops from Manchuria. The Japanese army is determined that all semblance of Marshal Chang’s authority in the Chinchow area must be eradicated and is supported on this point by the civil departments of the government. Warning Issued. Press dispatches from Mukden reported that General Honjo had issued a final warning to Marshal Chang to evacuate his forces behind the great wall. The fact that these messages passed the Japanese censor

TOKIO Dec 7—The Japanese general staff meeting in secret today outlined details of the plan for the capture of Chinchow, Manchuria. The staff met at the war office immediately after the return to Tokio of General Harushigo Vinomya, assistant chief of the staff. The plans were kept secret, but the dispatch of the Agothe division to Manchuria was decided upon as a necessary measure to carry out the campaign. Meanwhile, at Peking, the Chinese minister to Tokio telegraphed to Marshal Chang Hsueh-Liang an unconfirmed report that General Honjo, the Japanese military commander in Manchuria, had issued an ultimatum demanding immediate retirement of Chinese forces south of the Great Wall. The text of the ultimatum was published in the Japanese press and included a demand by Honjo that the civilian officials attached to Marshal Chang's provincial government at Chinchow also withdraw. The Japanese

(Sey SRE ROMA Pes) A contract bridge match which has attracted the attention of millions will open tonight in New York, Here is what it is all about Ely Culbertson, Russian emigre of American descent, who has gained wealth and a great following with a system of bidding in the game of contract, will play with Mrs. Josephine Murphy Culbertson, to whom he gives much of the credit for his success. Their rivals will be Sidney S. Lenz, landowner, author, amateur magician and “big shot” of the so-called “official” system, recognized by Culbertson as a player without a superior, and Oswald Jacoby, actuary, amateur contract expert and former football player, the youngest of the four. Conditions. 150 rubbers to start at 8 o'clock Monday night and to be completed by Jan. 15. Last rubber of a session must begin before 12:30 a.m. Play: Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday nights unless further sess

1931-01-06.text: By The Associated Press. England, Ark., Jan. 5.—Red Cross relief headquarters was moved to more commodious quarters late today to handle the crowds which came seeking food. At one time during the afternoon more than 200 persons, mostly negroes, grouped about the station waiting their turn to fill out requisitions.

Plymouth, England, Jan. 5—(/P)— Thirty seamen of H. M. S. Lucia, submarine depot ship, were under arrest today, facing possible court martial for refusing to work when their week-end shore leave was cancelled. An official inquiry went forward into the affair, which was termed by Admiral Sir Hubert Bland, commander-in-chief of the Davenport area, as “not a mutiny.” The men were held in barracks ashore. All communication between the Lucia and the shore was cut.

Surat, British India—/—Lamd as Gandhi, son of Mahatma Gandhi, Tuesday was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment at hard labor. He was arrested last month for delivering a speech on civil disobedience.

DUNGENESS, England, Jan. 6. The British steamer Nurtereton, a 6,500-ton ship, crashed ashore today in a dense fog off the coast here and broke its back. Lifeboats from the coast guard stood by to take off the crew of fifty men. The ship is believed to be a total loss.

Almost every day is inaugural day somewhere in the United States during the first weeks of the New Year as governors in 33 states take the oath of office as designated by their constitutions. The advent of new administrations in many states recalls the Democratic victories of the election in November with many Democrats replacing Republicans in state executive offices. Two names long prominent in American politics are listed in the roster of new governors. Philip Fox LaFollette was inaugurated in Wisconsin yesterday. Governor LaFollette is the second son of the late Senator Robert M. LaFollette and a brother of “Young Bob,” who now occupies his father's seat in the Senate. Like the other LaFolletes, he is a Progressive. He succeeds Walter J. Kohler, Conservative Republican. Charles W. Bryan, brother of the late William Jennings Bryan, will be inducted into office as governor of Nebraska

PARIS, Jan. 3. — (4) — Marshal Joseph Jacques Joffre, the “Defender of Paris,” as he will go down in history, lay in state today to receive an homage from the people of France that has rarely, perhaps never, been surpassed in his country’s annals. The crowd began to take form at dawn and slowly, as the day advanced, it grew until just before nightfall it became a vast multitude which at one moment got out of bounds and women were knocked and trampled upon before order was restored. At first a single line, the stream of those who filed through the portals of France's famous military school to pause for a moment beside the body of the old warrior, grew so deep and stretched from the entrance of the school nearly a quarter of a mile away across the Champ de Mars. There were many thousands of them and one of the most touching tributes was that of the hundreds of children who joined in the so

Berlin, Jan. 6—The Dornier works announced today that the big seaplane Do-X is scheduled to start her transatlantic flight to America on Jan. 20. The crew left for Lisbon, Portugal, to take over the plane last year.

PARIS—Foreign troops and distinguished visitors arrived today to participate in the state funeral services tomorrow for Marshal Joffre. A long line of Joffre’s countrymen meanwhile formed outside the Chapel of Saint Louis, several hours before the doors opened, and 20,600 walked past the camp cot where he lay during the morning. A detachment of The Glorious Contemptibles, survivors of the British Expeditionary Force that fought with Joffre at the Marne in 1914, were received enthusiastically by Parisians. Notre Dame Cathedral, where Joffre’s body will be taken tonight, was draped in black today. Post No. 2 of the American Legion in Paris will not participate in the funeral, it was announced today. It was recalled there was some adverse criticism to the Legion’s representation at the funeral of Marshal Ferdinand Foch.

1931-01-10.text: HAVANA, Jan. 10.—(AP)—Only three Havana newspapers appeared on the streets today—The Heraldo De Cuba, government organ, and the English language papers, the Havana Post and Havana Telegram. All other papers, among them El Mundo, El Pais, Diario De La Marina, Informacion, and the Havana American were suspended yesterday by President Machado in a decree charging “exaggerated and distorted” accounts of recent disorders. In addition to the papers suspended the periodicals Karikato, Carteles, La Semana and Bohemia, were made to cease publication. The Havana American was the only English paper suspended. Its editorials recently have criticized the president and yesterday recommended his resignation. El Mundo, El Pais and Diario De La Marina are among the four or five most important papers in the republic. Informacion is an afternoon paper, appearing for the first time Thursday, published by Di

BURNLEY, Eng. Jan, 10.—(P)— Twenty-five thousand weavers in the cotton textile industry were locked out this morning by ninety per cent of the mill owners, carrying out the owners’ threat that the mills would be closed unless 5,000 men who struck earlier in the week returned to their jobs by today. It seems a bit unlikely that any of the mills would reopen. The textile dispute arose from the weavers’ refusal to accept the mill owners’ demand that each man now operating four looms take over eight. There were fears that the difficulties with the weavers would spread throughout the industry, affecting about 250,000 weavers and as many spinners.

London, Jan. 9. (P)—Today’s developments in the labor disputes of two great British industries, coal and cotton, developed the gloomy probability of extended unemployment for about 650,000 workers, with resultant hardship for three or four times that number of their dependents. Hope for a settlement of the South Wales coal stoppage affecting 140,000 men, died when a “peace” meeting at Cardiff, Wales, broke up over interpretations of a single phrase. The mines will remain closed at least until next week. In the cotton dispute over the owners’ announced intention of introducing more looms per weaver, the central committee of the Cotton Spinners and Manufacturers associations at Manchester recommended that association members close their mills on January 17 if the dispute remains unsettled on that date. This action would throw about 250,000 weavers out of work, and also would suspend automa

[INTERNATIONAL NEWS SERVICE] LONDON, Jan. 10.—Three bodies have been recovered and many other persons were feared dead after a landslide at Lecco, Italy, according to reports today from Milan to the London News-Chronicle. Part of the town was demolished by the tons of earth and rocks that tumbled down, it was stated.

NEW YORK, Jan. (AP) Rags, a shaggy, taffy-colored mongrel terrier whose picture—autographed with his paw mark—hangs in the British Museum among portraits of the great heroes of the World War, got another medal today. It was presented by the American Anti-Vivisection Society, amid speeches and lots of applause. All the fuss incident to its bestowal bored him not a little, but he was a gentleman. Gravely courteous, he permitted small boys and girls to crowd round him and pat him, and with tongue rolling out and a gently humorous expression he watched grown-ups crowd exalted and very sentimental. He was a bad dog: “only” twice. When they lifted him up on a table he squirmed a bit, and he almost collapsed from fright when they tried to take his picture by flashlight. Rags’ career with the American Army began in Paris in 1916. Private Donovan, signal corps, first division, picked him up one b

- Windsor, England, Jan. 10, WA— Funeral services for Lavise, the princess royal and sister of King George V., were held in the newly restored St. George’s chapel at Windsor Castle today. King George and Queen Mary, the Prince of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of York, other members of the royal family and several members of the government and diplomats attended. The coffin was placed in the royal tomb house holding the remains of King Edward and Queen Alexandra.
MOSCOW, Jan. 10—(7)—Amy Johnson, the British aviatrix, arrived here today by train from Warsaw and announced that she had given up her plans to fly to Peiping across Siberia, at least until!

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Jan. 10 (AP)—One man was killed, one was missing and another seriously injured today in a violent explosion which wrecked a tank of the Municipal Gas Works. Several other persons were less seriously hurt.

1931-05-08.text: ANGMAKSALIK, Greenland, May 8. (AP) — A dog sledge trailed by four men, winding through the icy crags of Greenland today took Augustine Courtauld, youthful British scientist, back to safety and human society after a winter spent alone on the Greenland ice cap. Of the three men with Courtauld the leader is H. G. Watkins, chief of the British Arctic air route expedition which last fall left him in an igloo on the ice cap with the promise to return in March to relieve him after a winter spent in observation of meteorological conditions. Watkins, who searched in vain in March and April for the igloo which was Courtauld’s winter home, yesterday morning—two months late—kept his promise, found Courtauld, in whom hope of rescue must have begun to fade, and started back with him over 105 miles to the expedition's base, at Seremelik Fjord, 35 miles inland. Watkins’ success was attained as six expe

London, May 7. (INS)—Flight Lieutenant H. R. D. Waghorn, who won the last Schneider cup race for Britain in 1929, died to-day in the Cambridge Military Hospital from injuries in a parachute jump from a disabled plane on Tuesday. Waghorn and his civilian assistant, E. R. D. Alexander, were injured when a new machine they were testing near Farnborough went into a spin. When they saw they could not right the plane, both men jumped from a height of 200 feet. Alexander was only slightly hurt when he alighted on the glass roof of a factory, but Waghorn fell heavily to the ground, sustaining a broken thigh, a compound fracture of one ankle and serious head injuries. An emergency operation was performed early yesterday in an unsuccessful attempt to save his life. A preliminary investigation revealed Waghorn's parachute had failed to open completely in time to give him buoyancy before he reached

Dr. W. H. Coates, British delegate, said Europe would “shut out” products of United States efficiency “if you will not take the products of our efficiency, whatever be their form, or whatever their nationality.” International debts, he added, could be paid only by the transfer of physical goods or services. Since high tariffs exclude goods “they prevent payment of international debts of all kinds,” he held. ‘It is no answer to say there is no tariff on raw materials, if the debtor has few or no raw materials to sell,” he said. “The war international debts are owed by industrial nations.
