London, Jan. 29.—(4?)—Princess Beatrice, daughter of one queen and mother of another, lay gravely ill at Kensington palace tonight but her aged face was lighted with a smile of happiness. For her daughter, Queen Victoria of Spain, arrived today to tend her. A slight improvement in the princess’ condition was noted in a bulletin issued tonight.

Washington, Jan. 30. — (4) — Prime Minister R. B. Bennett of Canada arrived in the capital at 12:55 p.m. today aboard a private car. He was met by British Ambassador Lindsay, high state department officials and members of the staffs of the British embassy and Canadian legation. Hume Wrong, Canadian charge d'affaires, joined the premier at Baltimore. Mr. Bennett, who was accompanied from Ottawa by Hanford MacNider, American minister to Canada, will confer with President Hoover and Secretary Stimson during his brief visit.

London, Jan. 30—(INS)—Many prominent persons, including several members of European royal families, are stricken today with grippe, influenza and allied ailments. The epidemic is sweeping all Europe. The list of sufferers includes the following: London: Princess Beatrice, aunt of King George and mother of the Queen of Spain, suffering from acute bronchitis, whose condition is considered serious. The Marquess of Reading, former Viceroy of India and wartime ambassador to the United States, confined to his house with an attack of influenza. Evelyn Laye, British musical comedy and talkie star, suffering from bronchitis. Madrid: Princess Isabella, aunt of King Alfonso, recovering from an attack of grippe. Sofia: Queen Joanna, formerly Princess Yolanda of Italy, suffering from influenza. Her condition is considered serious but not grave. Prince Cyril, brother of King Boris, recovering from an

1931-07-14.text: Washington, July 14.—As a step toward building up to London treaty strength, the navy is about to begin the job of replacing some of its destroyers built in the days of the dreaded U-boat activities. The eleven on which the department plans to advertise for construction bids tomorrow will be a move in this direction. Secretary Adams indicated he may ask the new Congress to provide money for more of this type. In this small but important type of fighting ship, the United States at present is over the 150,000 tonnage specified by the London treaty for December 31, 1936. Scrapping on account of age, however, will pull the total well below by that date and necessitate replacements. At present the navy has 219 destroyers, most of which are under 1200 tons as compared with 1,500 tons for the 11 which are to be built. No vessel of this class has been laid down since the war and Secretary Adams

TORONTO, July 14.—(@)— Percy Alliss, British born professional of a Berlin club, was one stroke ahead of Walter Hagen, of Detroit, at the end of the first 18 holes of their 36-hole playoff today for the Canadian open golf championship. He had a 73 to Hagen's 74.

The “Justice for Hungary” monoplane on a one-stop flight to Budapest awaited favorable weather at Harbor Grace, N. F., Tuesday for the long hop, after two other planes on long flights had been forced down. Seth Yerrington and Edward Maloney on a non-stop flight to Mexico City had crashed about 200 miles from Brownsville, Tex. Laura Ingalls, en route from Burbank, Calif., to New York for a solo flight to Paris, is expected to reach New York from St. Louis Tuesday. Reggie L. Robbins and Harold S. Jones, who had planned a non-stop refueling flight from Seattle to Tokio, returned to Seattle last night.

(Associated Press Financial Editor) NEW YORK, July 13—The world’s major financial markets active today—New York, London and Amsterdam—calmly awaited developments in the German financial crisis after some excited selling in the early trading. . . The three major security markets in which there was trading registered substantial recoveries after the early setback. The Berlin market was closed as an emergency measure, and Paris was closed in advance of the Bastille Day holiday tomorrow. In the Amsterdam market, quotations of German issues, other than the Dawes and Young plan bond issues, were prohibited. Frederic M. Sackett, United States ambassador to Germany, notified President Hoover of the acuteness of the German situation. He urged that all possible help be extended to the Berlin government. LONDON, July 14 (47), — Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson left for Paris this morning to talk with French officials regarding the German financial crisis before meeting Prime Minister MacDonald in Berlin for a fine Anglo-German parley on Friday. While Mr. Henderson's trip had been scheduled ever since Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius came to England last month, it took on special significance in view of Germany's travail and the probable necessity for collaboration among European nations to save her from collapse. “Referring to his own and Mr. MacDonald's situation, he said: “We are going under exceptional circumstances. We realize it. But the decision of the World Bank yesterday must have eased the situation. At any rate, I hope it has eased the situation. “Our whole object, both of the prime minister and myself, in paying a return visit to Berlin is to do everything we

MOSCOW, JULY 14. (AP).—Joseph Lebrix and the two French fliers who started with him from Paris on a non-stop flight to Tokyo are waiting in the middle of Siberia today for another ship to bring them back to Moscow. Their ambitious project ended last night in disaster when something went wrong with their plane, the Hyphen, and the three of them—Lebrix, Parcel Doret and Rene Mesnin, their mechanic—bailed out in parachutes and landed in the rocky foothills of the western Sayan mountains, about half-way between Paris and Tokyo. The place where they landed is so remote from civilization that only the most meager details of the accident have been received. Lebrix asked that another plane be sent out to bring them home but the brief messages which have come from him have not disclosed the identity of the one of the fliers who was said to have sprained an ankle.

(Copyright, 1932, by United Press) MUNICH, Germany, July 14.—Adolph Hitler, fiery fascist leader, declared himself ready today to seize power, by force if necessary, to save Germany from Bolshevism. Hitler told the United Press correspondent in an exclusive interview on the present financial chaos that the people rapidly were becoming 'desperate' and ready for any experiment in an effort to save themselves from ruin. He said Bolshevism and other forms of violence were inevitable unless the tenets of fascism were followed under the guidance of his party. “We are ready to assume governmental power at any time,” Hitler said, “because the national opposition is convinced that it alone is able to halt the extremist development. (Continued on Page Two)

IRKUTSK, Siberia, July 14.—(UP)—The daring trans-continental flight of the French monoplane Hyphen, from Paris, was at an end today, the three fliers having leaped in parachutes to safety when their plane was forced down about 800 miles west of Irkutsk during the night. The fliers, Joseph Le Brix, Marcel Doret and Mechanic Mesmin, were reported safe at Schiborga Station on the trans-Siberian railway. One of the aviators was reported in the leap as the plane shot to earth near Nizhneudinsk, nearly two-thirds of the way to Tokyo, Japan, their non-stop goal. The airplane which they deserted in their forced leaps was not found. Search parties went in quest of the machine. The fliers were expected to proceed to Moscow. They asked to go by airplane, and aviation authorities were understood to be inclined to lend them every facility. The end of the flight came suddenly after hazardous flying ov

1931-12-14.text: NEW YORK.—(UP)—Winston Churchill, noted British statesman, was forced to cancel lecture engagements in New York and Chicago today because of injuries suffered last night when he was struck by a taxicab. Police questioned the driver about the mishap, but when Churchill told them it was unavoidable and that he was crossing the street against traffic lights, the driver was released.

London—The Duke of York, second son of King George, and who might be his successor on the British throne, celebrated his 35th birthday today. The King and Queen gave a family birthday party at Buckingham Palace. Prince George, youngest of the Monarch’s sons, and Queen Maud of Norway, who is King George's sister, were among the guests. The Duke is known to the country at large as a man of determination and keen sense of duty who has always seen to it that nothing stood in the way of his filling his position with efficiency. Industrial welfare, and trade and manufacturing problems have been his special study. His grasp of the technical processes of many industries has been described by experts as amazing, and his contacts with working people in the factories he has visited have invariably been very successful.

London, Dec. 14. -(AP)—London newspapers showed unusual interest today in last week's statement of Secretary Mellon regarding war debt payments to the United States but indicated some doubt about the attitude of the American congress to debt postponement. The secretary's statement led the news in all morning papers today, under headlines and it was an almost general topic of editorial comment! It was greeted enthusiastically in some instances and everywhere with appreciation, although most papers pointed out the last word is with the congress and the latter has shown no sign of endorsing the secretary's views. President Hoover's message, the Times said, "was not an inspiring document and had a disappointing reception." Congress, it said, fails to see a close connection between the economic collapse in the rest of the world and the difficulties in the United States or to realize how impos

LONDON, Dec. 14.—(U.P.) — Reports to the Daily Herald from Doorn, Holland, today said that ex-Kaiser Wilhelm receives a daily report of the activity of Fascists and Communists in Germany. Wilhelm has an annual income estimated at £200,000 from castles, lands, and forests in Germany, which might be jeopardized if Fascists were given power in the fatherland.

By The Associated Press Tokyo, Dec. 14.—The new Japanese government in its first official act suspended the gold standard yesterday effective from midnight last night and reimposed an embargo on the export of gold. Premier Tsuyoshi Inukai and his Seiyukai party cabinet met within a few hours after their installation by Emperor Hirohito to settle a financial policy. Finance Minister Takahashi subsequently issued a statement designed to deal with the critical economic situation which has been facing the country for months. It was short and to the point, declaring that "anyone desiring to export gold specie or gold bullion must obtain permission from the finance minister." Violation would bring a penalty of three months imprisonment, it was announced, or a fine of not more than 100 yen (about $50). TOKIO, Dec. 14 (UP).— The stock exchange was closed today until Thursday after the new government of Premier Tsuyoshi Inukai announced abandonment of the gold standard. Suspension of the gold standard was virtually completed by the cabinet’s decision to suspend conversion of notes for gold. The Yokohama Specie Bank, which ordinarily makes exchange rates, did not quote the yen during today's business. Unofficial rates ranged between 38 and 40 cents with actual settlements on New York at around 40 cents. It was understood the government had decided to let the yen find its own level, which experts predicted would be near today’s settlement figure. A section of the Japanese press believed parliament would be dissolved late in January and a general election would follow. The new government has only 170 seats in the lower chamber of parliament compared with 267 held by the resigned Manseito pa

SHANGHAI, Dec. 14.—At least thirty passengers lost their lives today when the Chinese steamer Tateh caught fire on the Yangtze river and burned to the water's edge. Most of the known dead were victims of the fire but it was feared many others had drowned. There were 250 passengers on board.

MADDALENA, Sardinia, ©? Thirty sailors and marines were thought to have drowned when the Italian tug Teseo sank in a storm off the coast of Sardinia Sunday. More than 100 persons were rescued by the cruiser Trieste after hours of struggling efforts to launch boats and shoot lifelines to the foundering vessel. The Teseo ran into a terrific gale Saturday, after leaving here for Civita Vecchia, 300 miles across the Tyrrhenian Sea, on the Italian mainland. It lost its rudder and its masts were swept away. After twelve hours it was only twenty miles from this coast. The tug sent out several S. O. S. calls and the Italian ministry of marine sent boats to the tug’s rescue from Spezia, Civita Vecchia and Sardinian ports. The Trieste alone was able to ride the turbulent seas to the tug’s position to pick up the sailors who were struggling in the water. An unidentified German ship was the first to

1931-12-24.text: | Tokyo, Dec. 24—(LP)—The United States, British and French governments were understood today to have expressed to the Japanese government what Tokyo considers a “warning” upon the new Japanese military operations in the Chinchow region. The apprehension of the United States government was understood to have been conveyed to Premier Iukai this afternoon by W. Cameron Forbes, American ambassador. At the same time the Rengo News Agency said warning notes were received from Great Britain and France and that the text of these is to be published soon, with the Japanese reply. Ambassador Forbes was understood to have expressed Washington’s apprehension and to have declared a rousing of American public opinion might follow a new Sino-Japanese clash. The Japanese reply to the French and British notes, the Rengo Agency report said, will stress the claim that there is little difference between “re

TOKYO, Dec. 24.—(GP)—A new “hands off” warning was prepared by Premier Inukai today in answer to notes from the United States, France and England which expressed concern over Japanese military operations against Manchurian bandits. It was understood the government was greatly displeased by the attitude of the three powers, and considers their representations are impertinent and unwarranted. The premier was understood to have taken the position that the notes of America, France and England strengthen Chinese resistance and render impossible the restoration of peace and order.

SEATTLE, Dec. 24. (#)—The historic tug Roosevelt with a crew of 10 men and a radio operator whose last plea was “for God’s sake, hurry,” was feared lost in storm-tossed seas off southern Vancouver island. For several hours last night, the British Columbia coast guard cutter Givenchy, the first ship to arrive at the Roosevelt's reported position, patrolled the waters without finding any trace of wreckage. LONDON, Dec. 24—(4)—Ambassador Charles G. Dawes will sail for the United States December 30 on a rush trip to consult with President Hoover and Secretary Stimson before the opening of the world disarmament conference at Geneva, at which he will be head of the United States delegation.

BASEL, Switzerland, Dec. 24, — The Young plan advisory committee Wednesday night called for adjustment of all reparations and other war debts to the troubled situation of the world’s finances. The committee warned that this “must be done immediately if disasters are to be avoided.” All financial experts on the committee agreed unanimously in the report. An official advance summary said Germany “would be justified in declaring that in spite of steps taken to maintain the stability of her currency she will not be able” in the year beginning July 1, 1982, to transfer the conditional part of reparations annuities.” No direct reference was made to unconditional reparations annuities, which the committee had no power to touch. The committee recommended that interested governments get together and work out a practical agreement in line with their recommendations. Delay Comment LONDON, Dec. 24,

BASEL (#) — Any claim of Germany that she is unable to meet her conditional reparation payments, beginning next year, stood defined as “justified” today by the report of the Young plan advisory committee. In its report, made public late Wednesday night following a long inquiry into the reparation and debt questions, the committee of experts called for an adjustment of all reparation and other war debts “to the troubled situation of the world.” This, it said, must be done without delay if new disasters are to be avoided, and it described such action as the “only lasting step capable of re-establishing confidence” and as “the very condition of economic stability.” Germany, the committee decided, is taxed to the utmost and no margin is left for increased taxes. ‘By The Associated Press) TOKYO, Dec. 24.—(Thursday)—Fifty passengers were reported missing this morning after a collision on the inland sea between two coast vessels, the Yaeyama Maru and the Kansai Maru, in which the former sank. The inland sea is between the islands of Hondo and Shikoku.

1931-12-05.text: SANDRINGHAM, Eng., Dec. 5. (AP)—Queen Mary, who has been suffering from a head cold, was reported better today but it was said she will continue to remain indoors today and Sunday. She plans to return to London Monday with King George.

LONDON, Dec 5 —(#)— Mahatma Gandhi, disappointed over the failure of the second round table conference to grant India what he considers “real freedom,” left London to return to India at 6 a.m. today. He took the boat train at Victoria station, on his way to Paris, traveling third class.

Folkestone, Eng., Dec. 5.—(4)—Mahatma Gandhi bade farewell to England Saturday, sailing for Boulogne on his way to Paris. The Mahatma put behind him three months of labor at the round table conference but he left with nothing tangible to offer nationalist India. Although physically exhausted and mentally weary, he refused to call his trip a failure. “England knows me now,” he said. “I am no longer a vague, indefinable figure in a distant land. The thousands of friends I have made here alone repay all my efforts. “Had I not come to the conference, as was my first intention, the government and my critics could have said I deliberately refused to negotiate and threw away my chances of peace. “I return with a clear conscience. I have explored and exhausted every approach to peace.”

London, Dec. 4 (?)—Queen Mary nursed a cold at Sandringham palace today as the Prince of Wales left a sick bed at York House. The queen developed a cold in the head early this week and was ordered to remain in her room until she had completely thrown off its effects. It was emphasized her condition was in no way serious. The prince went to Fort Belvedere, his country home near Windsor, after several days’ treatment for a chill with malarial symptoms.

The League of Nations turned yesterday to the diplomatic representatives of the United States, Great Britain and France in Tokyo for help in clearing up Japan's attitude toward the establishment of a neutral zone in Manchuria. The league council's drafting committee drew up two questions which were dispatched to Tokyo. These questions covered the scope of police operations Japan wishes to carry out against Manchurian bandits, and the location and extent of the proposed neutral zone. It was assumed the American, British and French diplomats at Tokyo would be asked to assist in straightening out these two points. At Mukden Japanese military authorities again declared Chinese were massing in menacing numbers in the Chinchow area. Air observations have shown 35,000 to 40,000 Chinese regulars in the district, it was said at army headquarters. A firm stand against foreign supervision in the pr

Press) Paris, Dec. 4—Groping through a maze of conflicting proposals regarding establishment of a neutral zone in the Chinchow area of Manchuria, the twelve neutral members of the League of Nations council decided tonight to ask the Tokyo representatives of the United States, Great Britain and France to assist in clearing up the Japanese attitude toward this proposal. Officials who attended tonight's long private meeting admitted that the council had gotten nowhere. No new instructions from either were presented today, although they have been awaited for some time. The Chinese are still asking for neutral control and neutral guarantees in the evacuated area before withdrawing their troops. 1 FOLKESTONE, Eng, Dec. 5— Voicing an urgent appeal to Great Britain to revoke the drastic anti-terrorism ordinance put into effect in Bengal, Mahatma M. K. Gandhi left England today on the first stage of his homeward journey to India. The Mahatma termed the ordinance as the “most inhuman piece of legislation in history.” He declared that India was prepared to sacrifice “a few innocent heads” but railed against the “unmanner of a whole people.” Gandhi's departure from England was unostentatious. Accompanied by his secretaries and assistants, he boarded the channel steamer Maid of Kent, witnessed only by newspapermen, the usual quota of cross-channel voyagers, police and detectives. No government officials were on hand to bid him farewell either at London or Folkestone. “I am glad to be going back to India,” Gandhi told International. Continued on Page Three

London, Dec. 5—(#)—Santa Claus will visit Tristan da Cunha, probably the loneliest inhabited island in the world, this Christmas, in the trim grey cruiser, H. M. Carlisle. His cargo will be not so much toys and trinkets for children, as mail, the only letters received in more than a year, and clothes and scores for the 100 or more inhabitants, made possible by the generosity of the comparative few who know of the island colony’s existence. There are more than 100 inhabitants in the little island colony, unless some disaster has taken many of them during the last year. The permanent settlement began in 1817. William Glass, a corporal of Royal Artillery, his wife, two children, and two masons were left behind when the island was abandoned by its British garrison. 1931-09-19.text: DENVER, Sept. 19—(4)—A secret meeting of the House of Bishops held the attention of the general convention of the Protestant Episcopal Church today. The session, called to consider the action of the Lambeth conference in England "on certain subjects" was expected to bring out a discussion of questions regarding birth control, divorce and marriage. The rules of the House of Bishops were waived to permit the attendance of the Rt. Rev. Michael Bolton Furse, Lord Bishop of St. Albans, England, an ardent foe of birth control. Delegates speculated over the possibility of an open controversy between the English church and the Protestant Episcopal Church of the United States on the question of birth control. NEW ORLEANS, La., Sept. 14. —()—New tales of the horror and destruction wrought by the hurricane that swept Belize, British Honduras, 10 days ago were related here today by a little company of the survivors who arrived aboard the steamer Parismina. Among those who told their stories of the stricken region were Mrs. Althea Hargreaves of Chicago, wife of a steamship manager of Belize, and John M. Staub, of New Orleans, two of the more than a score of refugees who left to escape the peril of disease and distress. The Hargreaves and Staub were among a score of persons in the Hotel International during the storm. They told of standing by helplessly and watching the destruction of the city. Most of the persons killed were Negroes, Mrs. Hargreaves said. Her estimate was 3000 dead, but there was no way of telling how many died. @y 280 secreted Press.) New York, Sept. 19—British government bonds and the British pound sterling were subjected to sharp pressure in today's financial markets, and stocks had another sinking spell. The United Kingdom 5% percent issue of 1937 dropped more than $50 per bond of $1,000 par value, touching $960. Last June, these bonds sold as high as $1,087.50, and in the past few days, have sold above $1,050. The British pound sterling dropped to $4.84, for cable transfers, off 1 cent from yesterday's close. Efforts were made to sell sterling short, but banks refused to accept short sales. Some future offerings lower than $4.75 have been reported, but at leading banks these were said to have been of purely speculative origin. Selling of sterling reflected growing uncertainty over Great Britain's ability to maintain the current gold parity of $4.865.

| FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany — (P) — The Graf Zeppelin reported early today that she had passed the Canary Islands and was headed south along the west coast of Africa. She is on a non-stop cruise to Pernambuco, Brazil, with 10 passengers. At 6 A. M., G. M. T. (1 A. M., E. S. T.) Capt. Ernest Lehman gave the airship’s position as about 150 miles due south of the Canaries.

Tokio, Sept. 19—(U, P.) —Fierce fighting between Japanese and Chinese in the Mukden area, with many casualties, was reported to the war office today. Japanese detachments were meeting strong opposition in their attempts to occupy Chinese military posts, the advices said. Reports to Tokio said 10 Japanese had been killed and 40 injured in these efforts to capture the posts. Chinese casualties were reported heavy in an engagement near the north peak of Kirin. Five hundred Japanese were attempting to occupy the peak and reportedly have surrounded it. According to the advices here 10,000 Chinese appear to have recaptured the eastern barracks at Mukden. The Japanese 29th Regiment of 99 men is reattacking the barracks and considerable casualties were reported there. At Changchun there were casualties reported in the occupation of the south peak. TOKYO, Sept. 19. (AP) — After long consideration the Japanese bureau of communications today issued a permit to Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, Jr. American fliers, to take their airplane from here to Samushiro Beach preparatory for a takeoff on an attempted nonstop flight to Seattle. The government had given the case unusual consideration because Pangborn and Herndon had been fined recently for flying over and taking photographs of fortified Japanese territory. Some authorities maintained that since they had violated the law, they should not be permitted to fly again in Japan. The application, which was made by the American embassy in behalf of the fliers, was granted, however, only in a manner that, taken in conjunction with projected legislation to revise the present laws governing foreign aviators, it will not be possible to consider the Pangborn-Herndon case a precedent. A railway cutting incident which allegedly precipitated the initial battle in the Japanese occupation of every strategic point in southern Manchuria. Manchuria’s principal port, Kwangchentee, the northern terminus of the South Manchurian railway and was astride the Peiping-Mukden (Chinese operated) railway at Kow- mouth of the Yalu river and were in control of the Manchurian arsenal at Mukden, the radio, telegraph and telephone stations and the government offices, Japan had disarmed the Chinese garrison at Mukden and had 12,000 troops in that vicinity with two divisions in Korea ready to cross the Manchurian frontier. 1931-06-10.text: WEIHAIWEI, China, June 10. —(P)—Twenty fathoms under the Yellow Sea, eight men in the sunken British submarine “Poseidon” waited helplessly today, while on the surface desperate efforts to rescue them proceeded. The parent ship “Medway” was able to maintain communication with the submersible, while the naval vessels “Hermes” and “Cumberland” worked with a Japanese salvage ship to raise the bulk off the bottom. Naval officers believed they could do that within a few hours. The eight men still living are believed to be the only ones of the 18 missing after the submarine collided with the Chinese steamer “Yuta” 21 miles north of this port, shortly after noon yesterday. The other 10 were believed to have been trapped in one of the compartments from which rescue would be virtually impossible even if they were still alive. Five officers and 39 men were saved, six of them popping up through the

LONDON, June 10,--(/)--Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald told the House of Commons this afternoon that the government has no present intention of making any moves toward an international war debt conference. Asked by a conservative member whether he considered “calling a conference of the powers interested in international settlements with a view to mutual cancellation of obligations on the largest possible scale,” the Prime Minister replied, “The attitude of this country in regard to war debts is well known and action on the lines suggested would not in the present circumstances serve any useful purpose.”

BEVERLY HILLS, June 10.—To the Editor of The Register: Mr. Mellon and Mr. Stimson are going over to London to another conference. We say we are not going to cut down on the debt payments. We could write and tell ’em, but we like to get in wrong personally. We have another delegation at Geneva on dope. We want to limit the output. We don’t manufacture it and the other nations do, so you know where that conference will end. We get nothing at a conference but the trip. It looks like the depression would hurt the conference business, but it don’t. They can always dig up enough to go and get in wrong, Yours, WILL ROGERS.

FANS, June 10.—-(4P)—Queen Helen of Rumania is expected to go into exile as soon as King Carol makes provision for her financial welfare—probably in a few days. Dispatches from Bucharest say that the king has opened negotiations with a London bank to pay her $40,000 annually when she leaves Rumania. She will be entitled to visit her son, Crown Prince Michael, three times a year and the king has promised to notify her if the child becomes ill. The palace at Bucharest and her summer residence on the Black Sea will remain her property for use on these trips. A Rumanian lawyer, just arrived from Bucharest, said that King Carol last week purchased in the name of his mother's secretary a beautiful villa with surrounding park for $66,000. Well-informed circles said it was intended to be the future home of Mme. Maeda Lupeseu, with whom the king roamed throughout Europe during his years of volunt

LONDON, June 9 (P)— Two men are dead and 18 missing as a result of a collision today which sank the Poseidon, one of Great Britain’s largest and finest submarines, near Weihaiwei, on the north shore of the Shantung Peninsula in China. News of the catastrophe was conveyed to England by an admiralty announcement which said that the Poseidon was sunk in a collision with a merchant vessel about 21 miles north of Weihaiwei. Five officers and 26 men of the ship’s crew were saved but two of those who were rescued died later. Eighteen were still missing tonight. Three ships were on the scene of the collision tonight. They are the Aircraft Carrier Hermes and the fast modern cruisers Berwick and Cumberland. Just how the Poseidon sank to her doom, the Laconic Admiralty Communique does not disclose. Even the name of the merchant vessel which collided with her has not been made public. The names of t

WEIHAIWEY, China, June 19— The story of six men who made a remarkable escape from the British submarine Poiseden after it had sunk in the Yellow Sea yesterday was revealed today. Two members of the crew emerged from the submersible two and one-half hours after it had been struck by the Chinese coastal steamer Yuta and four others reached the surface more than three hours afterward, all through the Davis escape apparatus. They were picked up by boats from British warships, attached to the British Far East fleet. The fact that the men were able to get away from the submersible from two to six hours after it had sunk was described as remarkable. The men who reached the surface safely said it was like a nightmare trying to adjust the Davis submarine escape apparatus in the dark, partially water-filled hull. The British Admiralty said 18 men were missing and 31 were saved, two of whom later d

By United Press SHANGHAI, June 10.—Hope for the lives of some or all of the 18 men trapped in the sunken British submarine Poseidon off Wehaiwei was held out in dispatches from there today. The messages were conflicting, however. One said that all the men had been saved; another said the submarine tender Medway had located the submarine, in 120 feet of water, and that eight men were known to be alive in it and could be saved.

- London, June 10. — (Pp) — An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Hongkong today said it had been officially announced the Poseidon, sunken British submarine, had been located off Weihaiwei, northern China. Efforts to raise the submarine were proceeding, the dispatch said. The Poseidon sank after a collision yesterday with the Yuta, a Chinese merchant ship. Reports that the Poseidon was on the surface at the time of the disaster were confirmed, the dispatch said. It was revealed that six of the survivors escaped in two groups by the Davis submarine escape apparatus. The first reached the surface in 1.35 minutes and the second in 1.95 minutes, the report said, and were picked up by warships on the scene. Five officers and 30 men were reported saved, but two died of injuries. Eighteen were reported missing. It was believed the missing men were trapped in a compartment. Unofficially, it was h

1931-05-16.text: ANGMAGSALIK, Greenland, May 14.—(AP)—A story of being buried two months beneath ice and snow in an igloo was told here today by Augustine Courtauld. The British scientist, who was rescued last week by fellow members of the British Arctic air route expedition, had only a chimney way to provide air in his place of refuge on the Greenland ice cap. Courtauld, whom Capt. Albin Ahrenberg, Swedish aviator, brought here with H. G. Watkins, chief of the rescue party, from their inland base, was unrecognizable beneath a long growth of beard, and appeared somewhat the worse for a long enforced diet of seal meat. Party Had Hard Sledding. Watkins said his rescue party had toiled for many weeks over the ice crags toward the locality where at the winter's beginning they had left Courtauld to observe weather conditions. They frequently lost the trail and were delayed for days when the skies clouded up a

MADISON, Wis., May 16. (AP) — Sterling A. Leonard, 43, associate professor of English at the University of Wisconsin, was drowned in Lake Mendota last night and his companion, I. A. Richards, 38, critic, lecturer and professor at Magdalene College of Cambridge University, England, was rescued. Richards, here for a lecture engagement, said their canoe overturned in the waves and they clung to the gunwale for two hours awaiting help. Finally Leonard became exhausted and sank. Richards said he made an unsuccessful attempt to reach him. Richards righted the craft but was unable to get ashore. Don Tracy, a boathouse owner, spotted the drifting canoe and rescued Richards.

Chicago, May 16—(*)—A former tonsorial artist was sought today by American agents and detectives for the British government in connection with an alleged stock swindle in England, which may involve a total close to $5,000,000. John Factor, known as “Jake the Barber,” when he conducted a cut rate barber shop in Halsted street, was the man. The officers were also seeking his companion, Harry Green. The wanted men were accused of fleecing thousands of middle class investors in England with fraudulent stock shares. A third man, alleged to have been involved with them, was reported under arrest in New York. His name was given as Harry Kline. The specific complaints against Factor alleged that he and his associates defrauded the firm of the Broad Street Press, Ltd., of approximately $2,500,000. The American agents reported they had visited Factor’s “Gold Coast” apartment here, but that Factor

GARDONE, Italy, May 16. — A new unofficial speedboat record was believed made today by Kaye Don, British racing driver in the Miss England II. In a trial run last night, he made 170 kilometers an hour, it was said. That is 105.57 miles an hour, bettering his record made in Argentina recently. Don in Miss England II established the official record for speed boats of 103.4 miles an hour over a measured course in the River Paraná, near its confluence with the River Platte, Argentina, on April 2. He broke the former record held by Gar Wood, American, of 102.256 miles an hour. The trial run was made on Lake Di Garda prior to official tests today. Don had said he believed his boat capable of a greater speed than he made in Argentina, and declared he intended to establish a record which would “stand for a long while.”

Sunderland, Eng., May 16. ()— The 286-ton steamship Reclaimer sailed at dawn today on a mission known only to her owners but generally believed to be a treasure hunt. The customary hail from harbor guards of “Where ahoy” brought only the reply “To Sea.” She sailed under sealed orders deliverable to the captain after reaching the North Sea, bearing a picked crew, provisions for five months and four expert divers with modern apparatus. General opinion was that the Reclaimer planned to locate the liner Tubantia which was sunk in the North Sea, presumably by a German submarine unaware that she was carrying $5,000,000 from Rotterdam to Buenos Aires to bolster Germany's credit in South America. Rumor said that the bullion was packed in Dutch cheeses, preparatory to the voyage.

Chicago, (UP)—John Jeactor, who once was “Jake the Barber” in Chicago and then made millions in huge transactions which police of two continents say were fraudulent, was hunted today throughout the west, "Jake the Barber,” an American police character for 15 years, was being sought by London officials on charges of frauds involving millions. Federal and city detectives raided his 14-room apartment in the Gold Coast last night only to learn from his beautiful wife that he had “just left for Las Angeles on business.” Although there were rumors that not long ago Factor won a large sum from the prince of Wales in a gambling game, the federal agents disclosed it was not (Continued on Page 2)

ROME, May 15.—Reconstruction of the entire economic system by “bringing it back to the requirements of social justice so as to insure more equitable distribution of the united proceeds of capital and labor,” is urged in an encyclical letter issued today by Pope Pius XI. Only a resume of the text was made public. It will be broadcast by the pontiff this afternoon and the full text will be given out in ten days. The letter bears the title “Quadragesimo Anno.” (in forty years) and carries still further the encyclical Rerum Novarum issued forty years ago by Pope Leo XIII. The letter is divided into three parts. In the first, the pontiff enumerates the benefits which have resulted from Pope Leo’s encyclical. These, the letter says, consist in giving form and substance to the development of sociology and economics according to the Catholic principle; promoting more solid organization of workin

Representations protesting the past week's destruction of Roman Catholic church property in Spain were under consideration Saturday by the republican government. Perhaps by coincidence there was published also a statement by the minister of justice, Fernando de Los Rios, that the provisional government intended to bring about a separation of church and state, an attachment which has been maintained for centuries. The papal nuncio, Monsignor Federico Tedeschini, conferred for more than an hour Friday with the Provisional president, Don Niceto Alcala Zamora Torres, and while no announcement was made of the nature of their conversation it was understood the nuncio sounded a strong note of protest.

1931-11-25.text: London, Nov. 25, 1940 The Mahatma Gandhi has been threatened with deportation if he foments further disturbances in India. The threat came last night in a demand by Lord Elibank, former under-secretary of state for colonies, speaking in the House of Lords. “Gandhi frequently has told us that he wants us out of India,” Lord Elibank said. “If that is his proposal, let us do unto Gandhi what Gandhi wants done unto us.” Lord Elibank suggested that the leader of the Indian nationalists be sent to some island archipelago, such as the Andaman Islands, if he continues his campaign against British rule in India. Lord Lothian, under-secretary of state for India, told the House of Lords that the government intends resolutely to suppress Indian terrorism, which he said had created a grave situation. “Drastic action must be taken to end the menace.” Lord Brentford, former home secretary, said that si

London, Nov. 24 (P)--The customs sheds of British ports hummed with activity today as officers wrestled with mountains of manufactured goods sent to Great Britain in the past two days to beat the new 50 percent tariff duties which go into effect at midnight. The crucial hour was 4 o'clock as all goods not cleared by the customs at that time will have to pay duty. Inquiries at many ports showed that the number of ships arriving from abroad with imports maintained the high average set since the beginning of the month. The last minute efforts of continental manufacturers to get their goods in before the axe fell were by air rather than by sea. The Croydon airdrome was one of the busiest spots in the country as typewriters, gloves, glassware, cutlery and scores of other articles were unloaded from planes arriving from France, Germany and elsewhere.

London, Nov. 25—The status of Ireland as an independent unit of the British Empire was upheld today following the defeat last night in the House of Commons of an amendment to the bill granting the dominions complete independence from the British Parliament. The vote on the amendment which was defeated 350 to 50, also recorded the first considerable split in the majority of the national government. The bill was then sent to the House of Lords. The amendment sought to add a clause to the bill making an exception in the case of the Irish Free State and specifying that the Irish government should have no authority to repeal the treaty of 1922, under which the Free State was authorized.

London, Nov, 25.—(4)—Information received here today from India said that agitation has begun there for a campaign of violence, following indication that the round table conference here will probably end this week without a settlement satisfactory to the nationalists. The situation in Bengal is said to be especially critical and the Marquis of Lothian, undersecretary of state for India, declared in the house of lords that in some Bengal districts every British officer is doing his duty in “deadly terror of his life.” Coincident with the undersecretary’s warning, fourteen Indian delegates to the conference issued a statement saying that the mere grant of provincial autonomy to India would not be accepted.

PARIS, NOV. 25—(UP)—United States and Japan replied to the League Council’s latest effort to mediate the Manchurian dispute today by standing firm on their demands. A high League official said: “if the Council is unable to achieve further mediation, it most likely will proceed with drastic action.” PARIS, Nov. 25—(UP)—Reports that negotiations for settlement of the Manchurian conflict might be shifted from the League of Nations to signatories of the nine-power Washington pact gained credence here today, though lacking any official confirmation. Ambassador Charles G. Dawes would not discuss rumors that Washington envisages calling a conference of signatories of the nine-power pact, which provides for the consideration of grave crises in China. League personalities, however, told the United Press the council would end willingly the present negotiations by a formal resolution shelving the M

TOKYO, Nov. 25 (/#)--The Japanese government today instructed Kenkichi Yoshizawa, its representative at Meris, to accept the league council's Manchurian peace resolution with the single reservation that the second clause be understood not to preclude “such military measures as may be required for the protection of Japanese lives and property from bandits and other lawless elements.” The situation at Chinchow, which was reported here to be becoming gradually more threatening, prompted the reservation, which was made at the eleventh hour.

Tokio, Nov. 25 — A Japanese change of attitude has removed the threat of a drive on Chinese troops mobilized at Chinchow, it was believed. The government withdrew its objection to non-aggravation provisions of the League of Nations resolution and decided to accept them with reservations. This action was a move toward breaking the deadlock in the league council negotiations at Paris. The provisions to which Japan withdrew her objections provided that neither party take any initiative which might lead to further fighting or loss of life. Japan's revised stand is that she will not initiate military action but retains the right to protect Japanese life and property against bandits and other lawless elements.

| Moscow, Nov. 25. (4)—Charges of a Japanese “white” Russian plot to seize the Soviet-owned Chinese Eastern railway in Manchuria and set up a buffer state in the Far East between Russia and Japan were printed by Moscow newspapers today, credited reports from Peiping. The report said “according to trustworthy information from Osaka, Japan,” an official Japanese military mission has gone from Harbin to Mukden, Manchuria, to make a report to the Japanese command there on an alleged agreement with “white” Russians to seize the railroad, which is owned by Russia, but operated jointly by Russia and China. Japanese Back of Move The Japanese were also reported engaged in “feverish activities” to determine how and to what extent the white Russians might be used in the event of a conflict between the Soviets and Japan. 1931-03-31.text: Karachi, India, March 31.—-(4)-- The working committee, or cabinet, of the All-India National Congress today drew up resolutions indicating the sweeping scope of demands for Indian independence which Mahatma Gandhi will make at the second round table conference to be held soon in London. The resolutions must be passed by the Congress itself, in annual Session here, but since Gandhi's address last night on the truce with Viceroy Lord Irwin and the approval of the truce by the Congress there is no doubt of this issue. The program outlined by the resolutions today enjoining the delegation, which is to be headed by Gandhi to demand not only Indian independence, with Indian control of army, finances, and foreign affairs, but complete Indian commercial and social equality with Britishers. Gandhi, in introducing the resolutions, said that he was aware that the demands embodied in them were revo

New York, Mar. 31.—()—Captain Frank Hawks and the airplane with which he set a transcontinental speed record are en route to Europe. Mrs. Hawks is staying. The flier embarked yesterday on the liner Kurepa. He will go first to London and then tour the continent. The plans to visit the international aircraft show in Stockholm in May. LONDON, March 31.—The disaster to the dirigible R-101, which stunned the world when it came down in flames on a hillside near Beauvais, France, last October, killing 48 men, was attributed today to mechanical causes, and not to human failure. The report of the Simon commission, which made a long study of the disaster, made public this evening, attributed the disaster mainly to ‘a substantial loss of gas in very bumpy weather.’ The report considered it probable that the forepart of the ship's envelope was ripped. “Something of this sort happened on a previous occasion and no amount of care could assure that it would not happen again,” the report said, emphasizing the possibility of mechanical failure in dirigibles as at present constructed. The commission refused to take a position one way or another regarding the effects of the tragedy on the future of lighter than air navigation. The re

New York, March 30. (#)—The acquisition of Pacific and Atlantic, a British corporation, by the Associated Press News Photo Service was announced tonight by Kent Cooper, general manager of the Associated Press. "The taking over by the Associated Press of the activities of Pacific and Atlantic, Ltd., a British corporation, is another step in the expansion of the Associated Press News Photo Service," Mr. Cooper said. "The Pacific and Atlantic, Ltd., has been operated several years by the parent company of the same name in this country and on January 1 consolidated with Acme News Pictures." "The Associated Press thus acquires its own news photo staff in Europe."

The Pas, Man., March 31.—(4)—Master Miller came down here out of the sky Monday, possibly the first child born unexpectedly in an airplane in full flight. The plane which takes its place with elevators, taxicabs, steamboats and trains which have figured in similar emergencies—started here from Mile 214. Mrs. Alex Miller was being rushed to a hospital by Flight Lieutenant A. L. McPhee of the Royal Canadian Air Force. Fifteen minutes after the take-off her son made his appearance in a cabin monoplane at a height of 4,000 feet.

Winnipeg, Man., March 31—(U.P.)— The child born Sunday to Mrs. Alex Miller while she was in an airplane 4,000 feet in the air was given the name today of Lindbergh Wright Cook Miller. The 21-year-old Indian mother and her baby, the first ever born in an airplane over Canada, were reported "doing splendidly". Mrs. Miller was at Mile 214 on Hudson's Bay railway when it was decided to "race the stork" to The Pas. The trip was made in a speedy Fairchild ship of the Royal Canadian Air Force. L. A. Bailey, mechanic, was the only other passenger with Mrs. Miller in the cabin of the plane when the child was born.

. {By Associated Press) The Pas, Manitoba, Mar. 31.—The stork flies high. A cabin airplane, 4,000 feet in the sky was the birthplace of a son born to Mrs. Alex Miller. She was being rushed to a hospital by Flight Lieutenant McPhee of the Royal Canadian Air Force.

PARIS, March 31, (AP) - The government of Pierre Laval was sustained by a vote of 347 to 318 on a motion in the chamber of deputies to refer the pension phase of the budget to a committee for a detailed study, which would require a month. A proposal has been made to put all pensions granted prior to 1914 on the same basis as those granted now. Laval was firm in seeking further study of the measure. He said it would add almost $23,000,000 to the budget.

1931-04-01.text: LONDON, March 31.—Lord Stamfordham, private secretary to King George, died today, aged 81. Secretary to royalty for the last fifty years, Lord Stamfordham started in the Zulu Bush country and rose to a place unique in European court circles. He was possessed of more state secrets than any living man, it was said, acting as England's "Man behind the throne."

Earthquakes and fire in Managua, Nicaragua, took an estimated toll of 1,000 dead and many thousand injured, many of them Americans. The American legation, the British legation and Nicaraguan government buildings were destroyed. Fire razed 20 blocks of the business district, causing an estimated property damage of $30,000,000. United States marines took charge, declaring martial law, carrying the dead and injured out of the wreckage and mending their hurts in the one hospital left standing. The army, the navy and the Red Cross dispatched assistance by land, water and air as soon as the disaster became known. London, March 31, ().—Leaking gas bags and bad weather were held by a court of inquiry to have caused the crash of the giant dirigible on a hillside near Beauvais, France, on the early morning of October 5, with the loss of 48 lives. The conclusions, published today, closely agree with the opinion of Dr. Hugo Eckener, commander of the Graf Zeppelin, who testified at the inquiry.

| OTTAWA, Ont., April 1 (AP)— The historic city hall, built in 1876, was hardly more than a smoldering memory today. Fire swept the structure last night and this morning, caused damage estimated at $200,000 and endangered the lives of firemen who fought many hours to save it. Seven firemen were hurtled from the fourth floor to the basement when a heavy vault crashed through the floors. Four were pulled from the debris almost immediately, the other three several hours later. None was seriously injured.

Parla, March 31 (UP)--The 1931 budget was approved today after an all-night session, during which the chamber gave the government of Premier Pierre Laval a vote of confidence. The budget, which was approved yesterday by the Senate, was voted by the Chamber after the surplus had been reduced to 60,189,000 francs. The budget provides for receipts of 50,771,458,409 francs and expenditures of 50,711,358,800 francs.

Managua, Nicaragua, April 1 (?)—United States marines at one o'clock this afternoon had the fire which followed the earthquake here yesterday well in hand. Death List to Reach 1000 By RICHARD FRIZELL (Associated Press Correspondent) (Copyright 1931 by the Associated Press) Managua, Nicaragua, April 1 (4)—Stunned by the destruction of their city by earthquake and terrified by constantly recurring tremors, the people of Managua feverishly carried on rescue work today against terrific odds. The day broke bleakly in the stricken Nicaraguan capital with fire still raging in many sections of the city. Estimates of the dead from yesterday’s shocks and flames have reached 1000. The number of injured tentatively was placed at 2,000. The entire population of about 60,000 was homeless. Hardly a building remained standing. Fire threatened to complete the catastrophe. The Tropical radio operator in Managua reported that the cable office there was in ruins and that the Tropical company was operating from a plant five miles outside the city. The seismograph at the canal zone registered the quake which appeared of unusual intensity centering in Central America. A complete reading of the record had not been made, but officials said that it was very distinct. The quake was felt at 10:10 a. m. Managua time (11:10 a. m. EST). Chicago, Ill., Mar. 31 —The defense in Leo Brothers' trial for the slaying of Alfred “Jake” Lingle, Tribune reporter, rested today without putting the defendant on the stand. The defense took less than a day to present its case which consisted, like the state's, of testimony of persons who were in or near the pedestrian tunnel the day Lingle was shot. Eight witnesses for the prosecution had identified Brothers as the man who threw down a pistol near Lingle’s body, or as the man who ran from the murder scene. Today, seven persons, two of them women, took the stand for the defense and asserted just as positively that Brothers was not the man.

1931-09-13.text: New York, Sept. 12—(AP)—Pan American Airways Inc., announced receipt of a report today from its radio station at Belize, British Honduras, that unofficial estimates now place the total dead in the hurricane disaster at 700. The message also stated that a request had been broadcast for 500 pounds of medicated cotton, twenty pounds of iodine, and a large quantity of bandages. Relief Ship Arrives Washington, Sept. 12 (AP)—The first American relief ship arrived at Belize, British Honduras, today to aid in caring for the hundreds of persons who were injured in the hurricane swept city. The American Red Cross headquarters here was informed that the navy’s minesweeper, Swan, reached Belize from Rujillo at 8 o'clock this morning. The gunboat Sacramento also is on its way to the stricken city with additional supplies from Puerto Cabezas, Nicaragua. The Red Cross also was arranging for the purchas

LONDON, Sept. 12. (AP) — Mahatma Gandhi arrived in London from Folkestone this afternoon and went directly to the headquarters of the Society of Friends in Euston Road. Riding with him in the automobile was the Rev. John Haynes Holmes of New York, who had met him at the pier in Folkestone. Dr. Holmes, although he has introduced the Mahatma to America through his writings, never had met Mr. Gandhi until today. There was a pelting rain, but Gandhi did not seem to mind it. “I am not going to take part in Monday’s meeting of the federal structures committee,” he said, “but I shall be there listening. Monday is my day of silence.”

LONDON, Sept. 14—(UP)—The federal structure committee of the Indian round table conference met today to consider a constitution for India, holding one-fifth of the population of the world. The meeting convened at St. James palace. Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, leader of the Indian nationalists, arrived 12 minutes late. He was observing his regular weekly day of silence. Gandhi was accompanied by Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, popularly known as India’s Joan of Arc and the only woman ever chosen president of the nationalist congress, and his secretary, Nahadeo Desai. He rode to the palace in the back seat of a small car. The Mahatma said, before his day of silence began, that if his opinion was needed at today’s meeting he would communicate it by note. Mrs. Naidu carried a thermos flask of goat's milk and Desai, a package, apparently containing nuts and fruit. Gandhi smiled when his car was driven into Amb

Belize, British Honduras, Sept. 12. (4)—More than 1,000 of the 16,000 inhabitants of Belize perished in Thursday's hurricane, it was estimated tonight after a survey. Authorities tonight were seriously considering abandoning the town in which almost every house was damaged by the storm and moving the site to the higher plains along the pine ridge. Unable to keep up with the rising death toll, the government applied the torch tonight to burn areas where the destruction and death took the highest toll. The funeral pyres were lighted to ward off the menace of disease, made more threatening by the broiling sun which beat down upon the ruined city. Fire lanes were then cut around the grimly burning area to protect the rest of the city. Food Supply Short The food problem was becoming pressing tonight. Several small food riots occurred during the day, but all were quashed immediately by authori

I. Dunten, operations manager here. Martial law to prevent looting has been established in Belize, according to information received here today by Ellis McLane, amateur wireless operator. McLane reported he had established communication with an amateur American operator in Belize known to him only as "V2BA." Residents are being forced to depend on rain caught in a downpour last night for their water supply as all water tanks were destroyed, he reported. All boats in the Belize vicinity suffered severe damage, according to the messages, and in some instances vessels and crews disappeared entirely. CALSHOT, England, Sept. 12.43 The Schneider cup airplane races were postponed today because of heavy rain and a driving wind which kicked up high seas in the Solent channel between the Isle of Wight and the British mainland. If the weather is favorable the race will be held tomorrow.

FOLKSTONE, England, Sept. 12—UP—The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi reached England here today at 1:15 P. m. on his way to London. On landing from the channel steamer, Gandhi walked to a waiting motor car in a drizzling rain, clad in his inevitable loin cloth. He had two white shawls thrown over his thin shoulders and wore sandals. The automobile was driven by F. A. M. Vincent, social secretary at the Indian conference. Before they drove off for London, Gandhi gratefully accepted an automobile rug which he spread over his lap. Gandhi's secretary, Nahadeo Desai, accompanied him. A motor car carrying agents from Scotland Yard followed.

1931-04-20.text: Alfonso of Spain will establish the seat of his exile at Fontainebleau, a little more than 15 miles from Paris, putting up his family at the Hotel Savoy there for the time being. He will go to London on business Tuesday, perhaps motoring down to Calais for the Monday night boat. Among other things he will arrange to place the infante Juan, his son, in an English school near London, and other business will keep him in London for a few days. The queen is leaving for Fontainebleau Tuesday and Alfonso will join her and their children when he comes back from London. These arrangements were disclosed Monday by the Duke of Miranda, chief of the Spanish royal household. The last of the Spanish royal family was on its way into exile Monday aboard a train from Madrid to Irun and the French frontier where they will change for a Paris train. Paris, April 20 (UP)—Former King Alfonso, of Spain, will leave Paris at noon Tuesday for London, accompanied by the Duke of Miranda, it was said today. The deposed monarch will make his plans for the week today and will go to London to confer with his bankers. Later he will return to rejoin the queen here. The president of the municipal council said no effort will be made to persuade the king to leave Paris and that no restrictions will be placed on his activity, except the usual rules applicable to political exiles.

WASHINGTON, April 20 (AP)— New navy construction to the London naval treaty limit was advocated today by Mrs. Lowell F. Hobart, President-General of the Daughters of the American Revolution. At the opening session of the annual D. A. R. convention here, she said “there is every justification for our building up to the London naval treaty requirements.” Mrs. Herbert Hoover planned to attend and more than 3,000 delegates were expected. Stressing perils of unemployment, Mrs. Hobart asked for a definite program in the United States to “unite the people of this nation for Americanism.” She called attention to the Russian government's five-year plan; lauded the army and navy as “peace institutions,” and urged enlistment of youth in patriotic movements. “You have all experienced disagreeable events in your separate states, based upon the leadership of Communists who have come to this country to

By The Associated Press. Lendon, April 19.—Great Britain's ancient blue laws, which the high courts have interpreted as banning Sunday movies, will provide the House of Commons with a spectacular free-for-all fight tomorrow. If the "Sunday Performances" bill is rejected about the only institutions which will be open in England on Sundays other than churches will be the "pubs"—English saloons. The bill legalizing Sunday entertainments was introduced by Home Secretary Clines, but it is not actually a government-sponsored measure and party lines will be disregarded. The issue has stirred public excitement to a pitch that is almost unprecedented.

CEPALU--A story: of cruel and brutal activities of Nicaraguan insurrectionists—including beheading—was told Saturday as 30 American refugees returned to the United States. Twenty-two of these, the Cefalu, putting into the port of New Orleans, were women and children. They shuddered as they told of the atrocities of the insurrectionists who have killed 10 persons in Nicaragua in the past few days. The flag of the Cefalu, vessel of the Standard Fruit and Steamship Co. whose properties were the subject of the insurgent attacks near Puerto Cabezas, was at half mast when the steamer entered the mouth of the Mississippi on her way to New Orleans. The bodies of two of 10 known dead were on board. The refugees were forced to retreat aboard the Cefalu when marines.

London, April 20.—(A. P.)—Most of western Europe, which switched yesterday to summer time, today was getting almost its first real taste of winter weather this year. There was heavy snow in Switzerland and northwestern sections of the continent; gales whipped up the English Channel and gave mail boats a rough crossing; airplanes were held up at Le Bourget and Croydon; shipping was driven to harbors along the north coast of France. In the London area, rain fell the day long. There was hail in many parts of southern England. Heavy crop damage is feared from a 40 hours rain, averaging nearly two inches, which has fallen over the western part of central and southern Italy.

PARIS, April 20.—Alfonso XIII. De Bourbon, King of Spain a week ago and now perilously near to being a man without a country, will journey to London tomorrow for the reported purpose of liquidating some of his holdings in England, it was learned today. As the “Duke of Toledo,” the exiled Monarch will make the trip incognito and accompanied only by his cousin and chief aide, the Duke of Miranda. It is understood he will travel by one of the ordinary train and boat routes to the British Capital. To Dispose Of Estate While in England, Alfonso will dispose of his estate there, apparently postponing indefinitely his plan of seeking sanctuary in that country. He will remain in France for the time being, hoping that the parliamentary elections in Spain in June 28 result in a majority for Monarchistic candidates and place him in a position to effect a restoration. Because of his refusal to abdic

Port Darwin, Australia, April 19. —(P)— The Australian airmail liner 'City of Cairo' crashed at Kupang, Timor, Dutch East Indies, this afternoon within 500 miles of the end of its experimental London-to-Port Darwin flight. No one was injured and the cargo of mail was salvaged. The plane left Croydon airdrome near London April 4.

1931-05-10.text: WASTINGLUN, May 4.—Republican party leaders have cast expectant glances London-ward in the hope that the forthcoming international wheat conference may offer some solution to a pressing economic and political problem in this country. Two things might conceivably result: 1—An avenue for future disposal of the enormous wheat stocks owned by the grain stabilization corporation, a farm board agency, and 2—some means of bolstering the depressed price of the commodity. Should one or both develop from the conference of leading exporting nations, no one would be more pleased than members of the republican agricultural advisory council formed to “sell” the tariff and the farm board in the middle west. Representation at the London meeting was urged upon President Hoover by Senator McNary of Oregon, the assistant party leader and chairman of the senate agriculture committee. Discusses Methods McNar

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, May 9.—(P)—The German steamer Esstrom, formerly the Hugo Stinnes, collided today in the Baltic with the British steamer Pacific, which was badly damaged. The crew of the Pacific took to the boats and were picked up by the Esstrom, which took the Pacific in tow and proceeded toward Kiel. So far as could be learned no lives

BUCHAREST, May 7—Queen Helen of Rumania was hastening home from Belgrade tonight and reports here said she would be reconciled with King Carol tomorrow after a year's estrangement. She and the king, the report said, will appear together in a grandstand tomorrow with Crown Prince Michael to review a military parade celebrating the 10th anniversary of the enthronement of King Carol I. Although police denied the story, it was reported today they had uncovered a plot to assassinate the king, arresting a man who had concealed himself under the grandstand with a loaded revolver. The prospective reconciliation between the king and queen is believed to have originated Monday when King Carol met with King Alexander of Jugo Slavia in a motorboat on the Danube. Carol, the story goes, gave his brother-in-law, the Jugo Slavian king, a message for Queen Helen, proposing the terms of the reconciliation

Brussels—(f)—The seven great sugar exporting countries of the world today signed the Chadbourne international sugar contract which, they hope, will assure producers fair profits and at the same time guard the consumer against unduly high prices. The plan calls for rigid restriction of exportation by the signatory nations and will result in an increase of the price of sugar to a point which will make export profitable. The present surplus stock of 2,599,000 tons will be segregated and if the price goes too high part of it will be released to world markets, thus bringing the price down for both producers and consumers.

PARIS, May 9.—(UP)—Aristide Briand’s eloquence repulsed a bitter attack on his conciliatory foreign policy today and won an overwhelming parliamentary victory, which may, paradoxically, end the foreign minister’s long career at the Quai D'Orsay. Briand, with the word “peace” on his lips, appeared certain of election to the presidency of France next week. Briand maintained his silence concerning his candidacy for the presidency, but it was understood that he was willing to consent in the election if the left and center groups of the chamber and senate consult him and urge him to accept. The groups decided last night to take such action.

VIENNA, May 5—(INS)—Discovery of an alleged communist plot against King Carol I, of Romania, was claimed by Bucharest police today, it was reported in Central European radio dispatches from the Rumanian capital. Numerous arrests have been made, the dispatches said, including that of a heavily armed man found hiding under the royal platform from which King Carol plans to review a parade of troops tomorrow, which is a national holiday. The man fled when police discovered his hiding place, but was captured after a gun battle. Bucharest police said the plot was directed against the life of the king, the dispatches reported.

LISBON, May 9.—Bad weather in the South Atlantic has made necessary postponement of the flight of the German seaplane DO-X from Africa to South America at least until tomorrow, the colonial office announced tonight. Commander Christiansen and his crew are guests of the German Colonization Company which is developing plantations on the island of Bubaque, about 100 miles off Bolama, Portuguese Guinea.

MADRID, May 9.—(AP)—A court martial today quashed charges against Former Premier Damaso Berenguer, who was arrested shortly after the establishment of the Spanish Republic. The former premier was released from jail on the court martial's order.

1931-11-30.text: London, Nov. 29.—(#)—The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi before dawn today revealed as he walked the streets his plans to renew the struggle against Great Britain for India’s freedom. “There is going to be hell,’ he said. The little man, with his head bowed, his shoulders drooping and his homespun shawl pulled tightly around his scrawny body, said: ‘I leave Saturday for Bombay. There we shall take up again our weaponless battle against England.’ His Mission Fails His voice sounding almost spectral as it came waveringly through the thick fog to the listener at his side, he remarked mournfully: “I came here expecting nothing and I leave with nothing.” From behind him came the solicitous words of Miss Madeline Slade, his devoted disciple, ‘“This way Baaboo (father)’ and Gandhi paused while the daughter of a former British admiral picked up the end of his trailing shawl and put it as if he were a child

Tokio, Nov. 30. (UP) — The “Stimson incident” appeared closed today both as an international affair and a domestic political issue, as the story behind the incident became known. War Minister Gen. Jiro Minami said after a cabinet meeting at which he asked Foreign Minister Baron Shidehara for details of his conversations with Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes regarding the Japanese agreement not to attack Chinchow that he, Minami, considered the matter closed. This was interpreted to mean that efforts of the opposition to embarrass the foreign minister over the Stimson incident had ended. The foreign office retracted its statement denouncing Stimson after it became known that a news agency blunder misquoting Stimson was responsible for what threatened to be the most serious international incident in the Manchurian problem. TOKYO, Nov. 30—The Japanese foreign office Sunday revoked its criticism of Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson for statements on the Manchurian situation "which had been misconstrued as his," and said the situation had been entirely clarified. "Mr. Stimson assures that he did not make any such statement as I thought from press dispatches," said a spokesman for the Japanese foreign office, which Saturday accused the American secretary of state of "losing his head" and "flying into fulminations." "Therefore I consider my impulsive expressions Saturday entirely uncalled-for," the spokesman continued. "I desire to state that any part of my statement which was not proper is hereby revoked. The assurance given by Mr. Stimson to Ambassador Debuchi clarifies the situation entirely to our satisfaction. The incident is closed." By The Associated Press. Paris, Nov. 29.—A committee of the League of Nations council renewed today its efforts to draft acceptable terms for a neutral inquiry into the Manchurian strife between China and Japan, with indications of little progress toward finding an acceptable formula. Its work will be continued tomorrow, therefore, while league quarters await further information regarding Japan's military policy toward Chinchow and Tientsin. Dr. Alfred Sze, Chinese spokesman, again pressed for inclusion of something more definite about evacuation of Manchuria by Japanese troops. It was understood the Chinese representative now is urging that the commission be charged with responsibility to determine in the course of its inquiry when the evacuation should be completed. The Chinese are anxious that the evacuation date should not be left entirely to the Japanese. A French observer at Chinch

Paris, Nov. 30—(AP)—The proposal of the League of Nations Council to send neutral observers into Manchuria to pave the way to peace does not constitute an “interposition of third parties” to which the Japanese government objects, Chairman Briand replied today in a note to Ambassador Yoshizawa. M. Briand expressed the belief that a misunderstanding exists regarding the council’s plan. “Exceptional measures” for saving human life are contained in the council’s proposal, he said, and these “may be taken without prejudice to wider proposals which your government may wish to submit to the Chinese government.” The council's proposal provided for sending observers to Manchuria for two purposes. They were to examine the possibility of establishing a neutral zone between the Chinese and Japanese troops or initiating any other system calculated to prevent a clash, and they were to cooperate to con

Mt. Vernon, O., Nov. 30—(4)— Ohio’s second hiccup sufferer of the month, Carl Horlacher, 39, today entered his 18th day of convulsions. Dr. Julius Shamansky, however, said he had cured Horlacher of a similar attack that lasted three weeks in 1929, and said he would try the same treatment again. He declined to say what the treatment is. Horlacher, a news dealer, cannot retain food and is growing weaker from the strain of his constant hiccuping, his physician said. Horlacher’s condition, however, was not regarded as serious as that of Ira A. King, of Mansfield, who hiccoughed for nearly three weeks until the attack was stopped by removing his gall bladder.

Paris, Nov. 30.—(UP)—Japan clung to her demand for direct negotiations with China in the Manchurian dispute today in rejecting the League of Nations council's proposal for a neutral zone in Manchuria. China accepted the proposal aimed to remove the threat of further hostilities in the area between Chinchow and the Great Wall. “The policy of the Japanese government, so far persistently pursued in the true interest of good relations between China and Japan, has not been to resort, in disputes capable of direct settlement with China, to the interposition of third parties, and it cannot but pursue this line of contact in the present case,” a Japanese note delivered by Kenkiechi Yoshizawa to President of the Council Aristide Briand said. Briand’s reply to Yoshizawa indicated that presumably there was a misunderstanding regarding the council’s aims. “The measures in question were exceptional m

oe | ND 5B Staff Correspondent. TOKYO, Nov. 30.—The Japanese war office today took a hand in the controversy between Washington and Tokyo over statements made by American Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson concerning Japanese policy in Manchuria. Although the foreign office revoked its criticism of Stimson, holding that he had been incorrectly quoted by a Japanese news agency in declaring that the Japanese army had “run amok,” the war office charged that either Stimson or W. Cameron Forbes, United States ambassador to Japan, had given out inaccurate accounts of Japanese military policy with respect to the status of Chinchow. The war office declared that no promise had been made to Stimson, as was indicated by the state department in Washington, that Japanese troops would not occupy Chinchow. 1931-03-02.text: Paris, March 4. — The French cabinet today decided that the tri-partite naval agreement reached last week by Great Britain, Italy and France was “satisfactory” it was announced after a meeting of the ministers, presided over by President Doumergue. Thus France's adherence to the arrangement which must now be submitted to the United States, Japan and the British dominions was virtually assured. The point which seemingly created the greatest interest was that one which some newspapers alleged would ask the United States and Japan to agree not to build capital ships larger than 23,000 or 26,000 tons, whereas the maximum fixed by the Washington treaty and unchanged by the London document was 35,000 for battleships.

Franco-Italian naval race, one of the most serious threats to the peace of post-war Europe, appeared today to have been eliminated with definite agreement of Great Britain, France and Italy on a naval relationship to be maintained during the next five years. The terms of the agreement were withheld pending transmission to Washington and Tokyo, but it was understood today that they were constructed around the actual needs of France and Italy until 1986, rather than on the basis of specifying a proportion between the navies. The agreement, if acceptable to the United States and Japan—and there was no doubt here on that score—will broaden the London naval treaty, which never was more than a three power pact in its important phases, to a five power instrument, limiting until 1986 the navies and naval construction programs of the great maritime nations of the world. PARIS, March 1.—An agreement on limitation of naval armaments which involves modifications of last year’s London naval treaty was concluded in Paris this evening by France, Britain and Italy. The text of the agreement will be cabled immediately to Washington and Tokyo, as both the United States and Japan were signatories to the London naval pact. It also will be sent to Canada and other British dominions which participated in the London conference. The accord which was reached by foreign and naval ministers of France, Britain and Italy, will be submitted to the respective governments with a recommendation that it be approved.
