Paris, March 2 (UP)—The naval accord reached between France, Italy, and Great Britain regulating construction until 1936 and avoiding a building race between France and Italy was approved today by the council of ministers. The accord will be submitted to parliament as soon as the United States and Japan adhere to the clause limiting the construction of future warships to 25,000 tons or less. "I am very well satisfied with the conclusion of the accord," Premier Pierre Laval told the United Press. "It will have much to do with our future relations with Italy." It was understood that the accord might be summed up as a modification of the Washington naval treaty. The totals of tonnage allotted to capital ships at Washington and incorporated in the London naval treaty will need to be rearranged. Lopdon, Mar. 2—(4)—The greater part of Europe and the British Isles were under snow today. A biting wind piled the white blanket high in places and in others swept the ground bare. Bitter cold prevailed. Extreme winter conditions prevailed over most of the continent from Urria to France. Sheep farmers suffered severe losses of stock. The gale which accompanied the snow raised dangerous seas in the channel and North Sea which claimed several victims. Sixteen were believed to have perished near Fraserburgh, Scotland, when a Dutch trawler turned over offshore and conditions were too bad to attempt a rescue. One body was washed ashore.

LONDON, March 2—Northern Europe looked for an abatement today of violent weather that caused numerous deaths in storms and blizzards and harassed shipping during the weekend. The entire crew of 16 aboard a Dutch fishing trawler from Ymulden was believed drowned off Reshearty, Scotland. The trawler was seen wallowing, bottom up in tremendous seas. Assistance was impossible although the ship was not far from shore. One body was washed up on the beach. Three fishermen were drowned in Seaton Sluice, Northumberland, when their boat capsized. Violent gales in the Irish Sea and the English Channel handicapped continental steamers and kept smaller boats in port. The gale reached 70 miles an hour in the Irish Sea. Heavy snow storms were general in the British Isles. Four inches of snow was recorded in many parts of the London area. Heavy blizzards were reported in Denmark. Several towns were floo

PARIS, March 2.—(UP)—March brought the winter’s worst storm today. An area extending from Russia to Central Italy was whipped by snow, wind and rain. Snow covered most of the British Isles and half of France. Many mountain villages were isolated. According to reports received here, two thirds of Italy was in the grip of the storm. Railroads were blocked in Denmark and Russia and trains were delayed in Germany, Holland, Belgium and France. Twenty fishing ships were reported missing in the North Sea and the English Channel.

BAIN APN, RET. moet eae” of fifteen was feared today in the wake of a weekend storm over the Irish Sea. A Dutch trawler was found floating bottom up off Robehearty on the Scottish coast. An Aberdeenshire crew of twelve men was reported missing. Three men fishing from a motorboat off the Northumberland coast drowned when their boat capsized during a blizzard.

1931-11-14.text: LONDON, Nov. 14 (Saturday)—UP)—A desperate battle for capture of the Nonni bridge in Manchuria is in progress, a Harbin dispatch to the Daily Herald said this morning. The dispatch, sent Friday midnight, stated the Japanese started the attack with an aerial bombing and then employed cavalry in a flanking movement. Aided by a Russian brigade, the Chinese repulsed the attackers and hurled their own infantry into the enemy lines, the Herald correspondent said. He reported the Japanese right wing was gravely imperiled. Both sides put up a fierce artillery bombardment, the dispatch

LONDON.— (AP)—Mahatma Gandhi repudiated the communal agreement between Muslims and smaller Indian minorities Friday, and announced that on Thursday he intends to leave London because he has abandoned all hope of obtaining independence for India. At a meeting of the Minorities Committee of the round table conference Mr. Gandhi took sharp issue with Prime Minister MacDonald, who presided. The Nationalist leader expressed astonishment that the prime minister should have said the minorities agreement reached Thursday was acceptable to 46 per cent of India’s population. Asserting that his Nationalists are at least 85 per cent of India, Gandhi said he would renew the anti-British campaign rather than permit an arrangement under which the “untouchables” would remain a separate caste. When the meeting was over Gandhi told questioners that only a drastic change in the government's attitude toward

Washington, Nov. 13.—The navy's highest officer said today it never was intended to build the fleet up to London treaty limits by the time that pact expires in 1936. Admiral William V. Pratt, chief of naval operations, made the statement. He was explaining that President Hoover's reduced budget plan, announced yesterday, means a substantial number of vessels will be placed in reserve. “Certainly not, we never intended that it should be,” was the admiral’s reply when asked if the navy could be built up to treaty tonnage by 1936. “Why, no right thinking American naval officer would want such a thing. We are suffering now from having rushed construction all at one time so that our ships become over age all at once,” he added. British Built to Limit The British fleet is substantially up to the treaty limit. The United States fleet, at the present rate of construction, will be 250,000 tons sh

London, Nov. 13 (UP) — Great Britain will not take the initiative now on war debts and reparations but “at the proper time” will present her proposals to the world, Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, declared in an important statement in the House of Commons today. Baldwin, debating the King’s Speech, said the Hoover moratorium was not sufficiently long to restore confidence and hence the future is most uncertain.

MOSCOW. (Saturday). (P). Moscow newspapers Friday published dispatches from Peiping saying a white guardist named Ushakov had been arrested on his arrival from Harbin and documents in his possession were proof that provocative action against Russia was being prepared by Japanese military authorities. White Russians are cooperating with the Japanese in these purported preparations, the dispatches said. Ushakov was declared to have had a letter from a Japanese military mission addressed to a Japanese military agent in Manchuria named Meddo. The White Russian, the dispatches said, described himself as a member of the "Kharbine active group of Amur Cossacks" controlled by white guardists. In Moscow the reported arrest of Ushakov caused a sensation and official publication of the documents he carried, as well as the statements he is said to have made to the Chinese authorities, was expected.

Japanese cavalry clashed with Chinese in frequent minor engagements, but the Manchurian army of Gen. Ma Chan-Shan and the 10,000 troops of Gen. Cheng Hal-Peng, Chinese ally of Japan, bore the brunt of the skirmishes. The Japanese described the situation as “increasingly threatening.” The fall of Tsitsihar is expected soon as a result of artillery bombardments and cavalry clashes between Chinese and Japanese on the Nonni front. A Japanese ultimatum, delivered to Gen. Ma Chan-Shan, demanded withdrawal of the Chinese troops opposing Japanese in the Tsitsihar area by November 25 on threat of “effective measures” by Japan's army. It was believed by neutral diplomats

TORONTO, Ont., Nov. 13, GAP— The red coat of a Royal Canadian mounted policeman was an ironic symbol to eight followers of the red Flag who faced sentence today as members of an unlawful association and parties to a seditious conspiracy. They were convicted yesterday, largely upon the testimony of Sergeant John Leopold, who doffed his red coat seven years ago to sit on the councils of Canadian Communists and rise to an official in the organization as "Comrade E. W. Esselwain." The Crown counsel said he would ask for confiscation of their property and for the deportation of any of them who can be compelled to leave the Dominion under the immigration.

MUKDEN, Manchuria, Nov. 13 (#) — Twenty thousand Chinese troops, with field guns and trench mortars are holding a strong front line south of Tsitsihar, the Japanese intelligence department reported today. General Mah Chan-Shan is in command, his force includes infantry, cavalry and artillery and additional reinforcements were arriving. Already there have been cavalry skirmishes, a telegram from the Nonni bridge sector to Japanese headquarters here said. On Wednesday a squadron of Chinese cavalry working around the Japanese right flank attacked an outpost, killing four Japanese and carrying off some prisoners. The outpost appeared to have been taken by surprise and routed. Chinese cavalry also penetrated the region behind the Japanese line, menacing communications with Taonan. From Tsitsihar

1931-11-02.text: London, Nov. 2—Japanese military advances against two points within “the Russian sphere of influence” in Manchuria and a “secret Chinese-Russian” treaty were reported today in alarming dispatches to the London newspapers concerning war threats in China. The Daily Express correspondent at Tokio said the Japanese infantrymen en route from Kirin to Taoman were moving with “extreme caution” and under protection of strict censorship on news dispatches. The Soviet, warned last week by Japan against mobilization of its troops in Manchurian territory, was reported “in a belligerent attitude.” The Daily Mail correspondent at Tokio reported that the Japanese were threatening to advance northward from Kirin province because Chinese troops in northern Manchuria had defied a Japanese ultimatum to repair a damaged railroad bridge. The bridge was wrecked last week by Japanese aviators who said Chinese

NORTH BEND, Wash., Nov. 2 — A week-end hunting trip into eastern Washington ended in tragedy, late yesterday when five men and an English setter dog were killed in the crash of their airplane near Snoqualmie Pass. Four of the men were prominent in Seattle professional circles. The fifth was the pilot. The victims were Dr. Russell J. McCurdy, president of the King County Medical Society; Arthur Hoge, president of the Hoge Piston and Ring Co.; Ray Sutherland and Harold De Spain, salesmen for a real estate firm, and Pilot John Blum. Apparently in perfect working order as it left the Okanogan region where the five had been hunting, the plane passed over Snoqualmie Pass on its way to Seattle when the nose suddenly tilted earthward. Eye witnesses said the pilot seemed helpless, and the large ship plunged directly downward to crash with terrific force. Flames swept over the plane within a few s

CHURT, SURREY, England, Nov. 2 --- David Lloyd George, war-time prime minister and Liberal party leader, has declared himself for a policy of close cooperation between Liberals and Laborites in the new British parliament to prepare a bold program of reconstruction. The aggressive, white-haired Welshman was widely mentioned as leader of the Laborite opposition to Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald's national government. As a result of the cabinet’s overwhelming victory in the election, he will seek to mobilize all “advanced” Liberals, Laborites, and other progressive forces. He believed the government incapable of achieving reconstruction of the nation, he indicated to the United Press and the Manchester Guardian in his first interview since the election. Lloyd George emphasized, however, that he merely planned cooperation of the anti-government parliamentary factions and did not envisage

LONDON, Nov. 2. (AP) — A. J. Cook, once known as the “firebrand” of the labor party, for many years general secretary of the British Miners Federation and dubbed “Emperor Cook” during the general strike in 1926, died at a hospital in Hampstead today. Cook, who was 47 years old, entered the hospital in September and underwent an operation for a glandular swelling in his neck. The operation was successful and he improved considerably up to ten days ago when his condition took a turn for the worse. His right leg was amputated above the knee in January as a consequence of an injury suffered years before when he was shoved in a political meeting. Cook was born the son of a soldier and educated at the elementary school and Central Labor College, London. He preached in a Baptist pulpit when he was 17, (Continued on Page 6)

LONDON, Nov. 2.—(UP)—The general election was complete today when the combined English universities, with two seats, returned two pro-government candidates to parliament, giving the national government a total of 556 seats of the 615 in the house. The combined universities elected Miss Eleanor Rathbone, Independent, and Sir Reginald Craddock, Conservative. The new parliament contains 15 women, the same number as the old.

Londen. Nov. 2.-(14)—-A Reuters Agency dispatch from Tokyo today said Japan declared she is unable to accept China's proposal for direct negotiations on the Manchurian problem on the basis of the resolution adopted by the League of Nations Council October 24. The dispatch said the Japanese government insists on the recognition of its five fundamental points as a prerequisite to the withdrawal of troops from the area.

| CAIRO, Egypt, Nov. 1.—Miss Pegyg Salaman, 19-year-old society girl who is flying from England to Cape Town, South Africa, arrived here today from Athens, Greece. She left a half hour later for Aswan, Egypt.

MANCHESTER, Eng., Nov. 1.—(P)—David Lloyd George, leader of the remnants of the Liberal party, today suggested in an interview with the Manchester Guardian that "advanced liberalism and labor cooperate to attain their common ends." "Labor must now realize," Lloyd George said, "that their area of recruitment and the recruiting conditions they impose are too narrow for them to become a truly national party for at least a generation."

1931-04-24.text: SEAHURST PARK, Eng., April 23.—Air Vice Marshal Felton Holt, commander of the air defenses of Great Britain, was killed today in an airplane collision. His pilot, Lieutenant Henry Moody, was also killed but the occupants of the other plane escaped without injury. Marshal Holt was one of the pioneers of the Royal Air Force and received the distinguished service order for valor.

HESTON AIRDROME, England, April 23.—Capt. Frank Hawks, the American flier, arrived from France today, smashing two more European records to finish off his two days of flight between London and Rome. An official announcement said the American speed flier who yesterday set a mark of five hours and 22 minutes from London to Rome, had broken two records on his flight from Paris to London. Flying from Le Bourget, near Paris, he reached Croydon airdrome in 55 minutes to break the 56 minute mark recently set by Commander Glenkidston and then continued to Heston airdrome to set a new record of 59 minutes. Hawks arrived here at 12:51 p.

WASHINGTON, April 24.—President Hoover tomorrow will turn southward to take part in the celebration of an anniversary of one of the country’s historical events. He will join Sunday in a pilgrimage to Cape Henry, Va., where 324 years ago English colonists under the leadership of Capt. John Smith of Pocahontas fame, landed and stopped for a few days before journeying to Jamestown and establishing the first permanent English colony in America. Last October the president went to Kings Mountain, N. C., and made an address celebrating the battle of Kings Mountain, an important engagement of the Revolutionary War. The chief executive, Mrs. Hoover and a small party will go from Washington to Little Creek Inlet, about five miles from the cape, on a 140-foot inspection boat belonging to the Department of Commerce. There a special train will meet him.

AESION, England, April 23.— Finishing what he started yesterday, Captain Frank M. Hawks brought his record breaking monoplane to earth here today with the distinction of having flown from London to Rome and from Paris to London faster than any human. The speed ace of the American air lanes sped across the channel from Le Bourget airdrome in 59 minutes, clipping 37 minutes from the previous high mark of Commander Glen Kidston. The distance is 229 miles. He had streaked there from Poilly Les Gien, 87 miles to the south, in 24 minutes on an interrupted return flight from Rome. Climbs Over Alps Taking breakfast in London yesterday morning, Captain Hawks flung himself across the Alps—rising to 23,000 feet at one time in foggy weather—and set his plane down in the eternal city in time for lunch. NEW YORK, April 23.—(AP)—Alcala Zamora, provisional president of the new republic of Spain, is to address America by radio Sunday. He will speak in Spanish for about seven minutes over the combined networks of the National Broadcasting Company. His address will then be translated into English. The talk also will be relayed by the short wave stations associated with KDEKA and WGY. The program will last from 11 to 11:30 a.m. CST.

Lisbon, Portugal, April 23. (4)— Thirty thousand British rifles just arrived from England were being served out tonight to Portuguese troops as the government continued its drive against the revolt in Madeira and took precautions against any possible spread of Communism into Portugal from Spain. All leave for reserve officers not yet called into active service has been cancelled and President Carmona’s government apparently was determined not to be caught napping. The minister of marine sailed for Funchal today with 600 troops to put down the rebel junta there. He will do it without bloodshed if possible, but he is prepared even to bombard the city.

1931-12-25.text: The report of the Young Plan advisory committee meeting at Basel aroused comment in capitals throughout the world. Below are the "nutshell" reactions: Berlin—Satisfactory, although it fell short of being a large-minded solution of the finance problem. Paris—Not so bad as had been feared. London—Betters the outlook for the impending international conference on reparations. Geneva—The experts did their work well, but only the governments can work out remedies when political questions dominate the international situation so completely. Vienna—At least another step in the right direction. Washington—Despite the committee’s findings, congress has made it impossible for the administration to take any further action on debts. Berlin, Dec. 24 (4)—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening today said the Basel reparations report could be called satisfactory, considering what had been expected of the committee,

WHITELEATHER Basel, Switzerland. —(P) — The Young plan advisory committee report upholding Germany’s contention that she cannot pay conditional reparations at the expiration of the Hoover moratorium is regarded by bankers here as the beginning of the end of the Young plan. Those who have studied the document regard it as a carefully balanced statement of the German situation in the light of the world depression, and as remaining within the framework of the Young plan as France demanded, but at the same time they believe it sounds the death knell of the plan itself. The French victory, if such it was, came in omissions—in the shifting of the whole reparations problem to the international conference tentatively scheduled for next month, and in the achievement of the French delegation in forcing their colleagues on the committee to confine themselves strictly to the letter of

(Copyrighted 1931, Associated Press) SHANGHAI, CHINA, Dec. 24— Civil war in China by next spring was predicted today by Madam Sun Yat Sen, widow of China’s former revolutionary president, who a few days ago delivered a strong attack upon the present Chinese leadership. Referring to the recent changes in the government at Nanking, she said: “These changes will in no way alter the grievous conditions existing in the Kuomintang (national party). It is merely the squabbling of petty chieftains for additional spoils.’ The Kuomintang, she said, as a leader of China’s revolutionary movement is “dead.” Madam Sun Yat Sen has been a revolutionary leader in China ever since as a girl of 20, she returned after graduating from Wesleyan College for Women at Macon, Ga., and served in the Republican government of 1912 with Dr. Sun Yat Sen, whom she married three years later. She is now 41.

TOKYO, Dec. 24.—(G)—The United States government went on record here today as indicating renewed concern regarding the movements of Japanese troops in the Chinchow area of Manchuria. American Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes personally delivered to Premier Inukai a memorandum from Secretary of State Stimson. It followed closely similar communications from Paris and London, which the foreign office preferred to call “expressions of apprehension” rather than warnings. Forbes conferred with the premier for 40 minutes and read Secretary Stimson's memorandum to him through an interpreter. It was understood to have referred to threats in general, but did not specifically mention the Nine Power Pacific Pact. Secretary Stimson, it was understood, also called attention to the statement he made in support of the League council's resolution of December 16. The French and British communications likewise

BASEL, Switzerland, Dec. 24 (P)— Fifty-one pages of economics and politics interwoven in one document — the Young plan advisory committee’s report on reparations was given to the world here on Christmas eve. Summarizing the financial and economic situation of Germany and the world business depression in general, the experts’ report, extracts of which were given out yesterday, was accepted by authorities here as the best available collection of information about reparations questions and kindred subjects. Concluding with an appeal to the government to act immediately to alleviate the world depression, the document accepts Germany’s plea of inability to make conditional reparations transfers after the end of the Hoover debt holiday. It infers, also that the unconditional annuities provided by the Young plan should be reduced or suspended. While the document is valuable only as a guide for

Fort Elizabeth, Cape of Good Hope. | Dec. 24.—(9)—Twelve persons were believed to have been killed Thursday when the walls of a building in the course of demolition collapsed, burying a small store crowded with Christmas shoppers.

(Copyright, 1931, By The Associated Press) Berlin, Dec. 23—The year 1932 will be a landmark in German history. More than anything else the country hopes for a new deal in reparations. The Young plan does not and cannot work, the German people contend. The reparations burden is too heavy, and through every stratum of German society pervades the conviction that the war payments must be scaled down. There are, however, indications that the economic depression which already has caused so much misery has hit the bottom and that any change must be a change for the better. Production of iron and steel has increased steadily during the last months of this year. The textile industry is picking up. The latest in the series of Chancellor Bruening’s emergency decrees has cut prices slightly and thus increased the purchasing power of the working man. International relations are improving, if the crea

Ottawa, Ontario, Dec. 25. — A shortage of copper coins was reported in Canada yesterday, although the mint here has been coining at full pressure since September. The shortage, it was explained at the mint, will correct itself after Christmas, when a surplus normally exists. It is due in part to the withdrawal of United States l-cent pieces from circulation in Canada, a situation which officials said is temporary.

1931-12-11.text: President Hoover’s message to Congress, making recommendations on war debts and disarmament, brought ‘generally favorable reaction in Germany, England and Italy, but French newspapers gave little attention to it. Petit Parisien, widely read Paris daily, printed nothing whatever on the message and other Paris papers limited the space to short summaries. High parliamentary circles in London accepted the message as a sign of hope in the economic difficulties of the world and the belief was expressed that it indicated the United States, while not committing itself, recognizes that debt questions lie at the root of world economic problems. The Allgemeine Zeitung, Berlin industrial paper, described the message as “of the utmost significance to Germany.” All German newspapers gave prominent space to it. Official quarters were inclined to regard a little dubiously, however, the statement that “r

Tipton, Iowa, Dec. 11.—(AP)— J. W. Reeder, 95 years old, who held President Hoover's hat when Hoover was inaugurated, died at his home here last night. Reeder, who owned 1,000 acres of land near here, was one of the country’s best known pioneers and is believed to have been the oldest living graduate of Cornell College at Mount Vernon. He attended that institution when it was known as the Iowa Conference Seminary and was graduated in the second class in 1854. Reeder was a friend of the Hoover family and met the future president during the last presidential campaign. At that time he expressed a wish that he might hold Hoover's hat at the inauguration if the latter were elected. The president did not forget the incident, and Reeder was one of the honored guests at the inaugural. Reeder was born in Ohio and came to Iowa in 1850. He taught the first free school west of the Mississippi, at Ti
LONDON, Dec. 11, (F)—The house of commons adjourned today to Feb. 2, the motion providing, that the speaker may call an earlier session should the necessity arise.

MANCHESTER, ENGLAND, Dec. 11.—A proposal to dismantle or immobilize 10,000,000 spindles and 100,000 looms as a means of restoring prosperity to the British textile industry will be made to the trade immediately. The proposal was adopted at a meeting last night by a joint committee of employers and workers. It will be submitted to every branch of the trade, from raw to finished goods. The government also will be asked to introduce a bill in parliament to empower a special board of trustees to carry out the plan, which, it is estimated, will cost more than £2,500,000 (about $12,000,000 normally.) This sum, according to the plan, would be raised by a loan.

By the Associated Press Tokyo, Dec. 11 —The Japanese cabinet of Premier Baron Reijiro Wakatsuki resigned today. The resignation was brought about by criticism of its foreign and financial policies. With the resignation of the cabinet, Japan faced the possibility of a suspension of the gold standard and an embargo on gold. The cabinet crisis appeared to have been precipitated mainly by economic causes rather than diplomatic, and it was thought probably Korekiyo Takahashi, Japanese financial expert, would be asked to form a government in case Premier Wakatsuki resigned.

MADRID, Dec. 10.—(#)—Niceto Alcala Zamora, a farmer's son, was elected first constitutional president of the Spanish republic by vote of the national assembly tonight. The election was by secret ballot and Senor Alcala Zamora got 262 votes out of a possible 466. Thus the man who is called the Father of the Republic and served as provisional president after Alphonso XIII had been overthrown, becomes the first, and probably the last, president to be elected by this procedure. The new constitution, adopted yesterday, provides that hereafter the president shall be elected by a body composed of members of the assembly and electors chosen by the people in equal numbers. The new head of the state owes his election to the combined action of the minority leaders in the assembly who agreed to support him in the belief that since he was the man who headed the revolutionary movement which gave birth

TOKIO, Dec, 11. (U?)—The Cabinet of Premier Reijiro Wakatsuki resigned today. The resignation was tendered to Emperor Hirohito at 5:30 p. m. The formation of a coalition regime is forecast, as the fall of the Government was caused principally by the demand of Home Minister Kenzo Adachi for cooperation with the opposition party to meet Japan’s domestic and international problems.

PARIS, Dec. 10--Japan and China today accepted the compromise plan evolved by the League of Nations for settlement of the Manchurian dispute and the tangled issue was placed in the hands of a neutral investigating commission whose five members have not yet been selected. Approval by the two belligerents made acceptance of the plan unanimous and it also has been endorsed by United States Ambassador Dawes who watched the deliberations of the League council at a distance during the three and a half weeks of discussion. Kenkichi Yoshizawa reserved for Japan the right to take such measures as it considers necessary against bandits in Manchuria. Dr. Alfred Sze, China’s spokesman, stipulated that in accepting the plan China abandons none of its rights under existing treaties and expects that the Japanese will evacuate Manchuria with the greatest possible speed. 1931-12-12.text: Paris, Dec. 11. (4#)—The League of Nations was looking for five unbiased men tonight to bring them the facts on the Sino-Japanese dispute in Manchuria. The council has appointed a committee composed of Chairman Aristide Briand, of France, Lord Tyrell or Lord Cecil, of Great Britain, Salvador de Madariaga, of Spain, and Erik A. Colban, of Norway, to name the members of the neutral commission which will carry out the terms of its peace resolution. They are expected to be engaged for several days and they may have difficulty in selecting a personnel satisfactory both to China and Japan, each of whom will have a delegate on the commission. Those prominently mentioned include General Bernard Serigny, secretary of the French National Defense Committee; Former Finance Minister Carlo Schanzer, of Italy, and Vittorio Cerruti, Italian diplomat. When Ambassador Charles G. Dawes left today for Londo

SPURS VEEe London, Dec. 12 (UP)—The 32 members of the crew of the German steam trawler Venus were drowned when the trawler was wrecked in bad weather north of Floro, Lloyd agent at Bergen reported today. A lifeboat containing seven persons was reported missing. The trawler was reported a total wreck.

TOKYO, Dec. 12—Tsuyoski Inukai, following a summons to the imperial palace, today began the formation of a new cabinet composed exclusively of members of the Seiuykai party. Japanese military authorities have decided to submit to the new Japanese cabinet, as soon as it is formed, a proposal to send about 15,000 more troops into Manchuria, to be used as a threat against the Chinese at Chinchow. The proposal was outlined just too late to be placed before the Wakatsuki cabinet before it resigned yesterday and it is expected to be one of the first major problems upon which the new government will be called upon to pass. General Jiro Minami, minister of war, had the matter in his hands and was to have brought it before the old cabinet, but the resignation yesterday prevented it. He had discussed the plan with Finance Minister Junnosuke Inouye, however, and the finance minister disapproved of

By JAMES P. HOWE Tokyo, Dec. 11.—(4)—Premier Reijiro Wakatsuki’s cabinet turned in its resignation today in the face of internal criticism against its foreign and financial policies. Leaders of the Minseito (government) and Seivkai (opposition) parties went into conference at once to formulate a new ministry and the present government continued until they had reached an agreement. Fear for Gold The possibility that Japan might suspend the gold standard and levy restrictions on the exportation of gold was foreseen in authoritative quarters as one result of the turnover. MADRID. (UP). The Spanish cabinet resigned. Resignation of the cabinet, which has been administering affairs of the nation since formation of the new republic, came one day after inauguration of President Niceto Alcala Zamora.

Oslo, Norway, Dec. 12. —(AP)— Two half frozen seamen drifted ashore near the fishing village of MMaatoey today on a raft with the bodies of four who had been their shipmates in the German-owned trawler Venus, described by coastguard officials as a rum runner. The ship ran aground and sank, they said, after rescuers had carried them ashore. One lifeboat capsized as it was launched, drowning six men; a second boat also capsized but the seven men in it were clinging to the overturned craft when the raft bearing the two survivors and their four companions drifted out of sight. The captain, whose name was Visnaerotsky, was drowned and it appeared that in all seventeen members of the crew were either dead or missing. Fishermen picked up the men clinging to the second overturned lifeboat, but two of them died of exposure shortly after they were taken aboard. Coastguard officials said the Venus

Tokio, Dec. 12.—(U. P.)—Tsyoshi Inukai, leader of the Seiyu party which opposed the resigned government of Reijiro Wakatsuki, was commissioned by Emperor Hirohito today to form a cabinet. Until the new Premier selected the members of his cabinet it could not be determined whether the new regime would be a straight Seiyukai body or a coalition with representatives of the Minseito cabinet which resigned yesterday. A Seiyukai cabinet appeared more likely however. The appointment of Inukai was not in itself a victory for military elements with which the late government came into conflict over the Manchurian dispute. There appeared little likelihood that ex-Foreign Minister Baron Shidehara would participate in a coalition government if one was formed. Inukai is a former editor and war correspondent. He had been a member of the House of Representatives since 1890 and became leader of the Seiyu

BASEL, Switzerland, Dec. 11.—(# Following closely on President Hoover’s moratorium message to congress, strong indications came tonight from persons close to the Young plan advisory committee that the committee’s report will declare Germany unable to make the conditional payments which form about two-thirds of the total war reparations. The report is still in the making, but it has been discussed in detail among the committee members and probably will be ready for consideration by the full committee near the end of next week. The president's message, in its references to the debt moratorium, was interpreted as a proposal that some manner, and it was believed that without such an extension the committee's report would be somewhat different.

1931-02-21.text: LONDON, Feb. 21. — King George today conferred a knighthood on Captain Malcolm Campbell, the world's motor car speed king. The knighthood was in recognition of Campbell's accomplishment at Daytona Beach, Fla., where he set a world speed record by driving 245.73 miles an hour in his car, “Blue Bird II,” Feb. 5. The ceremony in which the racing driver, who came home to England from his conquests in America as a popular conquering hero, was at Buckingham Palace.

LONDON, Feb. 21. (W.P)—Twenty-five were killed, 14 were injured and three are missing in a mine blast at Eschweiler, it was officially announced today. The explosion was caused by black-damp, preliminary investigation revealed. Eschweiler is near Aix La Chapelle, on the German-Belgian border.

LONDON, Feb. 21, (/)—Captain Malcolm Campbell walked into Buckingham Palace this morning, spent 40 minutes with King George, and came out Sir Malcolm Campbell, his majesty having bestowed upon him the accolade of knighthood. The honor was in recognition of the captain’s feat of driving an automobile 246 miles an hour on the sands of Daytona Beach, Fla, on Feb. 5.

LONDON, Feb. 21.—One of Scotland Yard’s greatest chiefs, Sir Edward R. Henry, who brought fingerprints to their great importance in criminology, was mourned today by London “Bobby” and skilled detective alike. He died during the night at the age of 80. Sir Edward began his studies of fingerprints while a member of the Indian civil service many years ago and continued research during the years he was with Scotland Yard. He established that there was only one chance in 640,000,000,000 of two fingerprints being identical.

LONDON, Feb. 20. (P) Avalanches in the Alps today were reported to have taken 15 lives, including nine Sularen. At two separate places today. Advices from Berne, Switzerland, said a family of seven, including two children, were thought to have perished in an avalanche that hurtled down the mountainside, crushing and partly carrying away the Post hotel in Lukmanier pass in the canton of Grisons.

London, Feb. 21 WPi—Bodies of 14 dead and 14 injured have been recovered from the pit of a mine wrecked in a mine damp explosion at Eschweller, near Aix la Chapelle. The fate of 13 others known to be below the surface was unknown. More than 30 others believed to have been below when the blast snuffed out the lives of their companions escaped.

New York, Feb. 20 (4)—The stock market boiled up briskly today, sending share prices to fresh high levels for 1931. There were bright spots in the day's business news, particularly a report showing a cheering pickup in building contracts, but in addition, bulls used an old-time, and of late rather neglected expedient to blow up the speculative fires—merger talk. Since the market boiled over on Tuesday, it had merely simmered until today, when trading swelled to 3,800,000 shares, the largest for a rising market since the bear stampede early last week. Progress was rather uneven, such a traditional leader as United States Steel common ending the day with a loss of 37 cents at $147.87 a share, after reaching a new top for 1931 at $149. Rails and coppers also held back, but utility, communication, motor and chemical issues were bid up vigorously. Net gains of $1 or $4 were numerous, while a

VIENNA, Feb. 21.—(AP)—Precautions for the safety of King Zog I, 36, self-made monarch of Albania, were redoubled today as police investigated an unsuccessful attempt against his life as he left the opera last night. The king’s adjutant, Maj. Topolai, received one of the twelve bullets intended for the monarch and was killed instantly. Another bullet wounded an Albanian court official, M. Lipozova, in the hip. The two assassins, who gave their names as Asiz Cami and Nadk Tielezi, were captured by chauffeurs of other cars standing behind the royal vehicle. They were badly manhandled. Questioning brought no other explanation than they had acted through political motives. A blood feud exists among the Albanian mountaineers against the king and there have been frequent attempts to kill him. He rarely emerges from his palace at Tirana without clouding his movements. 1931-02-01.text: Las Palmas, Canary Islands, Jan. 31. Carrying 19 men and 180,000 pieces of mail, the Dornier DO-X, largest airplane in the world, today successfully completed the first leg of its long-delayed flight from Lisbon to New York by way of South America. She left the Tagus harbor at Lisbon at 8:08 a.m., the roar of her American motors echoed in the cheers of the crowds which lined the waterfront. She arrived here, 715 miles from her starting point, at 3:10 p.m. after an uneventful voyage. Preparations were begun immediately for the next stage of the flight—to Cape Verde, 845 miles away. Tonight the mechanics began filtering into the huge tanks of the flying boat the 4,160 gallons of gasoline which it is estimated will be required on the hop to the Cape Verde islands. Captain Christiansen said that he expected to be able to take off at dawn.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 12. (AP). Selection of one of two plans to give war veterans more cash on their compensation certificates was expected today as the House Ways and Means Committee moved to complete consideration of the pending proposals. Yesterday it eliminated all but the Bacharach plan to increase loans on certificates by approximately $500,000,000, and the Fish proposal to pay off one-fourth of the face value of the certificates at a cost of $850,000,000. Action by the committee will clear the way for consideration in the House Monday. Leaders were thinking of bringing up whatever measure is reported under a suspension of the rules which would cut off debate, bar amendments and make for speedy passage. Paving the way for the measure to stall further, House members have been consulting with senators in the interest of speedy action there. However, debate cannot be shut off easily in th

WASHINGTON, Jan. 30. (UP)— An open trial will be sought by Major General Smedley D. Butler, marine corps officer awaiting court martial for utterances derogatory to Premier Mussolini, for which the state department was forced to the navy department indicated today it did not expect to make an exception in Butler's case. Secretary Adams is known to be particularly anxious that Butler's letter to him admitting the truth of the reports of the marine general’s address at Philadelphia, and said to be couched in caustic terms, shall not become public. If the court martial decides on a secret session Butler will have no recourse except to President Hoover.

ANN ARBOR, Mich. Feb. 11.—(UP)—In the most extensive raid ever conducted on the campus of the University of Michigan, five fraternity houses were invaded today by Ann Arbor police. They said liquor was confiscated in each house. Warrants charging disorderly conduct have been issued for 70 students. The houses raided were those of Delta Kappa Epsilon, Kappa Sigma, Phi Delta Theta, Theta Delta Chi and Sigma Alpha Epsilon. The raids were made after police had arrested Joseph Looney and Shirley O'Toole, whom police say later admitted they had delivered liquor to the fraternity houses.

Washington, Jan. 31.—(AP)—Over a plea by Veterans Administrator Hines for unemployed relief instead of conversion of bonus certificates, service men’s organizations today raised persistent demands for cash in testimony before the House Ways and Means Committee. Estimating 200,000 to 300,000 veterans are jobless, Hines said a considerable number were in ‘dire need.’ He urged special efforts to find work for them. He said only 13,000 jobs have been found through cooperation of the veteran’s bureau and the labor department since summer. Billion Might Do Advocates of cash payments stressed that acceptable plans might be executed by the treasury’s raising $1,000,000,000. This they said was less than one-third of the figure on which Secretary Mellon and others calculated that conversion, even if possible, would shake the securities market. KANSAS CITY, Mo. (UP)—The business barometer is rising. Not speedily or suddenly, but rather slowly and steadily, and business conditions throughout the southwest, that great farming territory upon which the prosperity of the nation is in so large a measure dependent, are improving. Retail dealers, as represented by the more than 2,000 who this week have convened in Kansas City for the annual meeting of the Midwest Retail Merchants’ Association, are replacing depleted stocks. With restored confidence, they are looking forward to a year that will see a gradual but consistent upward trend for business men and farm folk alike. “We have weathered a period of doubt and depression and pessimism,” Earl J. 1931-12-04.text: LONDON, Dec. 4. (AP)—Sir Thomas Lipton, who made a fortune in tea, had a verse for a business motto. His autobiography, just published, reveals that his belief was: The man who on his trade relies must either bust or advertise.

PARIS (#) — Ambassador Charles G. Dawes today described as “absolute nonsense” reports from New York that a group of Republicans had decided to designate him as the party’s presidential candidate in 1932. He refused to discuss the matter further. - General Dawes is here from London representing the United States as unofficial observer at the League of Council’s sessions on Manchurian peace.

PARIS, Dec. 4.— (7) —On the frozen Manchurian plain, over which many weeks of effort by the League of Nations Council have been spent to bring peace, international observers here fear the world's dream of disarmament in 1932 may die. Even the news that the heads of three of Europe’s most powerful governments will attend the opening of the disarmament conference in Geneva in February has not dispelled the clouds of pessimism. In spite of what Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, Chancellor Heinrich Bruening of Germany and Premier Pierre Laval of France may do to lend the conference high authority, it is felt here that the persistence of strained conditions in Manchuria creates an atmosphere hostile to arms reduction. The Manchurian developments are looked upon as providing strong support for the French contention that further guarantees of security are essential before armame

TOKIO, Dec. 4 (P1)—New instructions believed to be Japan’s “last stand” for peaceful settlement of the Manchurian problem. Meanwhile, it appeared that the government would resort to arms rather than diplomacy to force Chinese troops to withdraw from Chinchow inside the Great Wall. The government did not consider the situation at Paris hopeless if the league would leave evacuation of the Chinchow area to direct Sino-Japanese negotiations and Japan's modifications to terms to settle the conflict with China. That, of course, is what Japan has insisted. Aristide Briand’s declaration as president of the league council regarding the right of Japanese troops to operate against bandits in a neutral Manchurian zone was described officially as especially unsatisfactory. One of the provisions to which Japan objected was that neutral military observers should accompany either Chinese or Japanese for

| Copenhagen, Denmark, Dec. 4—(P) |—Great sympathy was expressed by the press and public and in high official quarters today for Else Bang, young Danish woman who confessed having killed her mother, Baroness Von Dueben, to end the latter's agony from an incurable disease. “I can very well understand the wish to cut short the suffering of a dear and near relative,” said Minister of Justice T. H. Zahle. “To me there is no evidence of criminal temperament in this case but, on the contrary, love and pity for suffering.” ; He pointed out that the new Danish penal code contains a provision for reducing the punishment to a minimum in cases where the sufferer asked assistance to die. “Unfortunately for Else, however,” he said, “the new code does not come into force until 1933 and the code of 1866, which is still in force, is rather severe.” The Rev. TOKYO, Dec. 3 — Japan rejected the League of Nations Manchurian peace program on two scores today and drew up counter proposals to be submitted to the League Council meeting in Paris. The Tokyo government interpreted the League plan as restricting Japanese activity against bandits and as fixing a virtual time limit for the evacuation of troops outside the Manchurian treaty zone. Baron Shidehara, the foreign minister, and the other members of the cabinet drew up the counter proposals at a meeting which lasted most of the night. These proposals were to be dispatched to Kenkichi Yoshizawa, Japan’s spokesman at the League Council, along with new instructions. | Helsingfors, Finland, Dec. 3—The Finnish government tonight asked the Diet to authorize a referendum to determine whether prohibition shall be continued, repealed outright, or modified to permit medium strength wines and beer. With the referendum measure the government submitted a statement declaring that during the 12 years prohibition has been in effect none of the expected changes in the nation's habits has occurred. Contrarily, the government statement said, the conflict between the law and the predilections of the people has led to brazen and pernicious violations of the statute. Kills Respect for Law Destructive influences have been brought to bear against respect for law in general, the government statement asserted, because violations of the dry law have become so common. In addition to the prevalence of drunkenness, the government cited a considerable increase in crimes of vio

TOKIO, Dec. 4 (UP).—Hunho, south of Mukden, was invaded today by 28 Chinese bandits, some wearing uniforms resembling those worn by Japanese. They hoisted two Japanese flags. Japanese guards were sent to the scene.

1931-08-31.text: LONDON, Aug. 31. (*)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald flew down from Lossiemouth today to take up the task of his new national government where he left off Friday. Reiterating his pledge to steer the emergency cabinet through the financial crisis, he made it clear that he has no intention of submitting to the demand of his constituents in Seaham Harbor that he resign from the House of Commons.

WASHINGTON, AUG. 31. (AP).—Chairman Nye, of the Senate campaign funds committee, today renewed his suggestion that Bishop Cannon “explain under oath the record of his use of campaign funds in 1928.” Declining to take notice of Bishop Cannon's cable to the President from London last night, Senator Nye remarked that Bishop Cannon was informed last May that the Senate committee would make its inquiry at the time it did. Meanwhile, District Attorney Rover announced he would study the stenographic records of the committee's hearings last week with a view to possible contempt action against Miss Ada L. Burroughs and Dr. J. Sidney Peters, who refused to testify concerning the disposition of funds given Bishop Cannon for the 1928 anti-Smith campaign. Miss Burroughs was treasurer and Dr. Peters secretary of the Virginia anti-Smith organization headed by the Southern Methodist churchman.

BEVERLY COUNTRY CLUB, Chicago, Aug. 31.—(AP)—Favorites, including Harrison R. Johnston of St. Paul, the 1929 champion, and Cyril Tolley, the ex-British titleholder, fell by the wayside today as Jack Westland of Chicago occupied at least temporarily the first round qualifying lead in the national amateur golf championship with a 72, one over par. Johnston scored 83; Tolley an 85.

LONDON, Aug. 20.—(4)—Bishop James Cannon, Jr., of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, in a statement issued here today, charged the Senate campaign expenditures investigating committee with “deliberately” deciding to hold its recent hearings in his absence. The bishop also charged that the committee, which is investigating expenditures in the national campaign of 1928, was conducting “a fish expedition to secure, if possible, some evidence of criminal conduct on my part.” He added that he had never opposed a grand jury investigation but had insisted “and shall continue to insist that my rights as a citizen are infringed upon by the Senate committee which has no jurisdiction over the election of presidential electors.”

TOKYO, Aug. 31. (AP)—The most brilliant midsummer affair of its kind here in many years—a dinner given by Premier Wakatsuki—tonight brought to an end the ambitious round of official ceremonies in honor of Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh. At its conclusion the Lindberghs assumed the role of sightseers, which will keep them busy for several days and take them to points outside Tokyo. Tomorrow the Lindberghs will go to Karuizawa, where they will be guests for several days at the summer home of Ambassador W. Cameron Tarkow.

ROME, Aug. 31.—U.P)—The accord between the Vatican and the Italian government has been completed, it was announced today, and has been approved by Pope Pius XI and Premier Mussolini. The text of the accord was printed privately. It was sent to the members of the college of cardinals, many of whom are at their summer residences. Their approval is not necessary, however, as the pope took full responsibility for the negotiations. There was a marked lessening of tension between the Vatican and the Italian government this morning. Prelates and members of the government staff fraternized openly for the first time since the open break, caused principally by differences over education of the youth of the country. Provisions of the accord were guarded closely, but it was learned, however, both sides were satisfied with the formula for the education of youths through a system whereby special cleri

Tokio, Aug. 31 (UP)—Japan's official tribute to Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, a six day program of receptions and banquets, ends tonight with a dinner in their honor by Premier Rejiro Wakatsuki. Tomorrow the famous family flying team that made the first aerial vacation trip from the United States to Japan will be free to do as they please. The Lindberghs decided that the first thing they would do would be to visit the summer villa of United States Ambassador W. Cameron at Karuizawa. This morning Col. Lindbergh addressed military and civilian aviators. This afternoon he had his photograph taken as the model for a bronze statue. Col. and Mrs. Lindbergh were guests at a luncheon given by the Japan Air Transport company. Yesterday the commoners of Tokio paid formal honor to their distinguished visitors. A great crowd at Hibiya Park cheered the Lindberghs and heard the colonel predict t

SHANGHAI, Aug. 31.—-(P)— While authorities sought today to pierce the veil of uncertainty that cloaked the flood situation in northern Kiangsu province, another area placed its dead at 250,000 and its destitute homeless at 500,000. 1931-07-26.text: Tokyo, Aug. 26—(P)—Yuko Hamaguchi, former premier of Japan, who won the appellation, “warrior for peace,” by his espousal of the London naval treaty despite the opposition of influential groups of extreme patriots and militarists, died here today. He was 61 years old. Heading the government during the negotiations in London, Hamaguchi succeeded in obtaining Japan's adherence to the naval treaty only by a strenuous fight which incurred the displeasure of the ultra-patriots and advocates of a strong navy. On November 14, 1930, Hamaguchi was shot and seriously wounded by Tomeo Sagoya, 23, who was described as having been patriotically misguided or mentally deranged.

BERLIN, July 25.—(#)—The swift course of developing events in Germany did not slacken with the arrival of Secretary of State Stimson today and the homecoming of Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Julius Curtius from the seven power conference at London. While the Secretary of State, who specifically announced he had come for "an unofficial, friendly visit," was dining with Ambassador Frederick M. Sackett and members of the German cabinet at the American embassy tonight, the government made public the result of today’s conference with representatives of the Reichsbank and other leading bankers. It announced the establishment of an acceptance and guarantee bank designed to restore unhampered currency circulation and to put the crippled Darmstaedter and national bank back on its feet. Secretary Stimson had a long conversation immediately after the dinner, with the German defense minis

Lisbon, Portugal (AP) — Rebellion flared briefly Wednesday against the administration of President Oscar Carmona, but failed completely. After a battle between government troops and revolting soldiers of the third artillery regiment, in which several were killed and wounded, the rebels, who were completely beaten, hoisted a white flag and surrendered. The capital now presents a Sunday aspect.

BERLIN, July 25—Henry L. Stimson, American secretary of state, bailed here as President Hoover's “right hand man,” came to Berlin today for what is described as a purely unofficial friendly visit. While here he will renew acquaintances with Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius and will meet other German leaders. It was only this morning that the chancellor and foreign minister returned from the London seven-power conference, and this afternoon as Secretary Stimson's train rolled in they still were in the midst of what may prove one of the most important cabinet sessions since 1918. For it was the chancellor's task to lay before his colleagues the result of the London conference and endeavor to agree with them quickly on what can be done to hold the German economic structure together for the next few weeks in the absence of new international credits.

By The Associated Press. Leningrad, Russia, July 25.—The giant dirigible Graf Zeppelin, seeking new worlds to conquer, arrived here late today from Berlin on the second lap of a flight to the Arctic region. She flew over the city and then landed safely at the Novaya Deryavina airdrome forty-five minutes later.

By The Associated Press. Berlin, Germany, July 25.—The government announced late tonight that, with the Reichsbank and eleven leading German banking institutions, it had formed a new concern named "The Acceptance and Guaranty Bank" with a capital of 200,000,000 marks (about $50,000,000). The formation of the new bank was announced as the first concrete action toward bringing about a removal of the present banking restrictions in the country.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 26.—(AP)— The administration hopes to be able to inform Congress in December that relief funds raised locally through the country will be adequate to care for the unemployed during the winter months. This was emphasized today by arrangements for completing a nationwide drive for relief funds two weeks before Congress meets in regular session December 7. President Hoover's organization on unemployment relief, headed by Walter S. Gifford, selected the period from October 19 to November 25 for the appeal to obtain funds through city, state and county campaigns. It was announced this period had been determined upon "because of the fact that a majority of the fund drives in past years have been conducted between those dates." Gifford has emphasized the national organization is not planning to raise a fund, but will merely coordinate and encourage the raising of funds by polit

BOISE, Ida., Aug. 26. (AP)—The fire demon sweeping relentlessly through the forests of central Idaho today has added to its toll of destruction the lives of two fire fighters, a valuable gold mine and a dozen homes. The burned bodies of Nolan Warner, 28, Fillmore, Utah, and Howard Harvee, Boise, were found on the ridge between Pioneerville and the south fork of the Payette River late last night. Reports said the men were trapped between the main fire and a spot fire which broke out behind them. Earlier in the evening, the wall of flame raging on a 20-mile front broke through trenches on both sides of Grimes Pass, first sweeping the $250,000 Golden Age mine and a number of residences. The fighters fled as their efforts failed. Nearby, homes around the Mineral Mining Company mine were destroyed but the main mine buildings were saved. A group of national guardsmen, members of a band of 100

1931-12-19.text: | London, Dec. 19.—Dense fog throughout England today caused numerous accidents at sea and on highways and railroads with an estimated loss of approximately 20 lives. Air services were suspended. Two persons were known dead and about 50 Christmas shoppers were injured in a train wreck at Dagenham dock. Two coaches occupied mostly by women and children were telescoped. The crew of 15 of the trawler Girde-ness were believed lost when the ship went ashore and was broken in two by an explosion, near Thorshavn, Faroe Islands.

LONDON, Dec. 19—(U.P) Further payments of Europe’s $20,000,000,000 war debt to America are impossible under present conditions, according to British financial leaders and British newspaper opinion. Financiers and economists agreed with the newspaper editorial comment to the effect that because “you can’t get blood out of a turnip,” the Hoover moratorium “must be continued, and war debts and reparations must be revised.” The American House of Representatives last night approved the moratorium after a bitter contest which put the House on record at the same time as opposing cancellation of the debts in any manner. Most authorities declined to hazard an open prediction on possible revision pending action of the American Congress on the Hoover moratorium and the report of the advisory committee of the Young Plan studying Germany's capacity to pay at Basle. London, Dec. 18—If world governments take the proper fork, the greatest era of prosperity in history is just down the road, in the opinion of Sir George Paish. If they continue on their present course, the international economic and credit fabric will go to smash within two months, the noted economist warns. He Charts Course. In an exclusive interview with the Associated Press today this former advisor to the British treasury outlined the steps he believes should be taken to assure the one and avert the other. They were: 1. An international conference to consider rehabilitation measures, 2. Revision of Germany's reparations payments to insure eventual repayment of her commercial debts. 3. London, Dec. 18.—(/?)—Twenty-eight persons were believed to have lost their lives in three sea tragedies resulting from the violent gales that swept the North Sea and surrounding areas today. Meanwhile London and large parts of England suffered from cold raw fog or frost, which tied up traffic and generally delayed railway movement. A passenger train struck the rear of a freight train near Dagenham, Essex, derailing the locomotive and the first car. About 30 passengers were injured. Weather conditions contributed to the accident, railway officials said. The Hull trawler Girdieness was wrecked early today near Thars-haven, Faroe Islands. The vessel was at the mercy of heavy seas, which made rescue work impossible and it was considered certain the 11 members of the crew had perished. Trawler Gone Several bodies were seen near the wreckage of trawler No. 782, which went on the rocks near Su

KYO.—(#)—A dispatch to the Rengo News Agency from Mukden, Manchuria, Saturday said an ultimatum is to be sent to Chinese authorities soon demanding withdrawal of Chinese troops at Chinchow to a point within the Great Wall within a stipulated time. This Mukden report was virtually confirmed in authoritative quarters here. Two warnings will be sent, it was said, one by the Japanese government to Marshal Chang Hsueh-Liang, through the Peiping legation, and the other from General Honjo to Jung Chin, Marshal Chang's chief of staff. It is understood also General Honjo will issue a statement at the same time in which he will declare he will be compelled to resort to drastic measures if the Chinese fail to comply with the notice to withdraw.

A renewed military campaign against Chinese bandits in Manchuria was announced by the Japanese war office in Tokyo yesterday on strength of reports of a distressing situation in the Chinchow area. Strong measures will be taken against guerillas in the area of the South Manchurian Railway, a spokesman said, particularly West Oqrielbiao river and north of Chinchow. The killing of two Chinese civilians when Japanese planes dropped bombs in the vicinity of Tungliao was recounted in authoritative reports from Mukden. Lieut. Colonel Nelson E. Margetts, American observer, said there was no evidence to support Japanese assertions that Chinese troops were concentrating near Japanese positions. The Chinese government in Nanking employed regular soldiers to round up students who have been conducting a “reign of terror,” shipping them back to their homes. The capital was quiet for the first time in

| PARIS, Dec. 19.—(UP)—Police announced today that Albert Davin, 21, a Frenchman, had confessed to the murder of Richard Wall, 31, an American from Grampian, Pa. Wall also was known as John Craig and John Wall, police said. He was wanted in the United States for using the mails to defraud. He accused his former sweetheart, an American dancer, of robbing him of $40,000 last summer, but the charge was not substantiated. Police dragged the Seine river near Triel bridge for Wall's body without success. Prior to the confession of Davin, who was arrested today, detectives investigated Wall's private affairs on the theory that his many difficulties might have made it convenient for him to disappear.

Basel, Switzerland, Dec. 18.—(4?)—There was a growing belief tonight that the Hoover moratorium on reparations and international debts will be extended for at least two years as a result of the deliberations of the Young plan advisory committee now in session and of the international conference on debts tentatively scheduled for next month. In informed quarters, this was regarded as the best solution, in view of the refusal of the United States Congress to consider revision or cancellation of the war debts. Can't Pay Today the advisory committee, with the French delegates agreeing, admitted that the German railways will not be able to pay next year the 668,090,000 marks ($1,900,000) in reparations imposed upon them by the Young plan. 1931-04-26.text: WASHINGTON — () — President and Mrs. Hoover were enroute to Cape Henry, Va. Saturday night on the commerce department boat Sequoia to take part Sunday in a celebration of the 324th anniversary of the landing of English colonists who, later founded Jamestown. They expected to arrive at Little Creek inlet shortly after noon tomorrow and go immediately to Cape Henry. The English landed first at Cape Henry, journeyed to Jamestown a few days later and there established the first permanent English colony in North America. The landing at Cape Henry was made April 26, 1607.

Fort Worth, Tex., Apr, 25—Daisy and Violet Hilton, born in London but known now throughout the world as “The Texas Siamese twins,” were happier today to be "free from bondage” than they were to have won $99,000 in a lawsuit. “It is so wonderful to be free to go where we please, choose our own friends and appear in public as humans rather than freaks," declared the twins who yesterday won a $99,500 verdict from Mver Myers, their manager and guardian the first 23 years of their lives. The auburn-haired twins had charged that Myers and his wife refused to let them have friends or to ever appear in public except before paid crowds. They charged also that their guardians kept all their earnings and forced them to live every minute of their lives as “freaks in tents and theaters.

LISBON, Portugal, April 20 (4) Homeward bound from South America, the Prince of Wales and his brother George spent this day here on the way to Bordeaux whence they will fly to Paris and home. The steamer Arlanza slipped into the Tagus early in the morning under a British naval escort. The guns of Fort Sao Juliao thundered a royal salute and army airplanes roared overhead, but the prince slept through it for they had gone to bed late the night before.

ROME, April 25—(/)— Premier Mussolini, appearing personally before a great crowd of students demonstrating at the Venezia palace this noon, quieted their protests against anti-Fascist demonstrations in Brussels with a pledge of Fascist alertness against its enemies. Il Duce, holding his hand aloft for silence, shouted to the crowd, which had moved en masse from the university to the palace, intending later to go to the Belgian embassy. “The Italy of the students is always on its toes to defend the revolutionary regime and Fascism against the stupid calumnies of anti-Fascists,” he said. When Premier Mussolini had concluded his brief appearance before the mass of shouting humanity most of them dispersed but a number of groups with flags marched toward the Belgian embassy. They were stopped by large squads of soldiers and police who were stationed at every corner within a quarter mile radiu

ROME, April 25.—Italian resentment against anti-Fascist demonstrations in Belgium became a national affair today when Premier Mussolini, the parliament and the University of Rome took a hand. The premier stepped out on a balcony at the Venezia palace at noon when several thousand students of the university paraded in protest against an anti-Fascist demonstration at Brussels earlier this week which had its roots in the arrest here of the Belgian professor Leo Moulin on a charge of anti-Fascist activities. Mussolini quieted the demonstration by his appearance and a short speech. In the afternoon Moulin came up in parliament with the undersecretary of the interior justifying the professor’s arrest, Moulin, he said, “participated actively in a real attempt to organize a movement against the power of the state,” and letters of an incriminating nature were found in his possession.

CALGARY, Alberta, April 25 (AP)—Now come purple chickens. Just a matter of serum. Some people interested in such things injected the serum into the eggs by means of a hypodermic needle on the 19th day of incubation. Yesterday the chickens were hatched, some all purple. Others were all green. The serum people figure they can obtain a blue chick by a mixture of the serum. It was not explained why.

Swedish Crown Prince Gustaf Adolph was successfully operated upon today for rupture at Sophia Hospital. He was reported progressing favorably. The Crown Prince, 43, was admitted to the hospital 2 weeks ago. Stockholm, April 25 (UP)—Sxed-

1931-08-29.text: LONDON, Aug. 28. Well said Prime Minister MacDonald, who has devoted his life to building up the British labor party, today was stripped of its leadership and only his young son, Malcolm, among all of labor’s rank and file, defended his action in forming the national emergency government to deal with the nation’s financial crisis. Arthur Henderson, affectionately known as “Uncle Arthur” to British labor, was given Mr. MacDonald's mantle and will lead an almost solid force of 280 members to the House of Commons against the new government when Parliament assembles in special session on Sept. 8 to press through the economy program for Great Britain's financial salvation. Against that force of men and women Mr. MacDonald will marshal the combined conservative and liberal members. Tonight he appeared assured of success for the economy program which calls for a cut in the nation’s expenditures

NEW YORK, Aug. 29.—The most powerful banking interests in France and the United States combined Friday in offering credit of $400,000,000 to the British treasury as a measure of their confidence in Great Britain. J. P. Morgan and Company formally announced that a group of more than 100 American banks and banking houses had combined in the extension of half of the credit, while extension of a like amount was announced in Paris. The credit is believed to be the largest private banking credit to a foreign government in financial history. The negotiations were completed by cable and trans-Atlantic telephone in the extraordinarily short time of 36 hours. Doubt of Stability Banished. American bankers explained the credit was substantially larger than the British government had any thought of asking for, and was made of such huge proportions as to banish all doubts as to the stability of Britis

New York, Aug. 28 (#).-—J. P. Morgan and Company announced tonight that negotiations for the extension of a $400,000,000 Franco-American credit to the British Government had been completed and that the credit had become effective as of today. The credit, which is to run for one year, is being furnished in equal amounts by New York and Paris banking groups. The American banking group includes more than 100 banks and banking houses throughout the country. It is distinct from the $250,000,000 credit extended by the Federal Reserve and the Bank of France a few weeks ago, and the Federal Reserve is not participating in the credit. The credit has been negotiated by cable and transatlantic telephone within the past 36 hours.

CLEVELAND, Aug. 28.—On the eve of tomorrow's opening of the 1931 national air races, Flight Commander R. L. R. Atcherley of England, who holds the fastest speed record ever made by man, cracked up today in landing his plane with part of the landing gear. The Briton escaped with cuts on the head and a severe shaking up and air race officials said they expected him to participate in the exhibitions in a day or so. Fourteen stitches were taken on his forehead. Commander Atcherley came here as one of a group of states national representatives.

CAPE GRIS NEZ, France, Aug. 208. Spurred by the successful crossing of Karl Naumestnik Thursday, two men named Leibhardt and Konrad started across the English channel this morning for Dover on water skis. The men, who are Austrians like their predecessor, had proceeded 12 miles toward their goal, or about half way, at 10 a. m.

NEW YORK, Aug. 29.—(P)—A one year credit of $400,000,000 has been extended to the New British government by banking interests of this country and France. The announcement is made by J. P. Morgan and Company, who with 109 other American banking houses have placed $200,000,000 at the disposal of the Bank of England. French bankers have made the same amount available. The credit was arranged for the purpose of stabilizing sterling exchange. It will not be used to repay the existing credit of $250,000,000 extended by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Bank of France to the Bank of England August 1. That credit was drawn upon heavily to support sterling. The rate charged by the banking interests was not disclosed, but American bankers indicated that the $100,000,000 portion of the French credit which is to be offered to the public of that nation would carry a rate of 4 1/2 per cent.

LONDON, Aug. 29. — (INS)— Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy had two narrow escapes from death or serious injury today when the plane in which he was returning to Rome from Spezia was forced down twice at the mouth of the river Ombrone near Ostia, according to a Central News dispatch from Rome. Mussolini was accompanied on the flight by Gen. Italo Balbo, Italian Air Force minister. The premier and Balbo had been at Spezia for several days watching the Italian army’s aerial maneuvers, in which the entire Italian air force took part. As they approached Ostia, their plane encountered a terrific storm. The premier’s plane, according to the news, was badly buffeted, and twice the pilot was forced to

London, Aug. 29--(4)--Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald has been expelled from the Hampstead labor party "for joining an anti-socialist government formed for the purpose of forcing through parliament anti-working class legislation," it was announced today. Mr. MacDonald has his private residence in Hampstead, a suburb of London, and has been a member of the party there for several years, holding his membership in the labor party proper through that branch. His expulsion was decreed in a resolution passed by the party last night. London, Aug. 29--(4)--The Seaham Harbor labor party which Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald represents in the House of Commons, today recommended that he be asked to resign his seat. This action by the party executive which will be referred to a meeting of party delegates, followed soon after the Prime Minister had been read out of the party by the Hampstead division

1931-02-19.text: CHERBOURG, France, Feb. 19. —(UP)— Capt. Malcolm Campbell, who recently set a new world’s automobile speed record at Daytona Beach, was raised to the knighthood today by King George of England. The British vice consul communicated the king's desire to Campbell while the speed driver was still aboard the steamship Mauretania off Cherbourg.

PALM BEACH, Feb. 19.—Playing a sensational game, Helen Hicks, sturdy Long Island golfer today scored an international victory by routing Miss Diana Fishwick, British champion, six and five in the semi-finals of the Florida Woman's Championship tournament. Miss Hicks will contest the final match tomorrow with Miss Virginia Van Wie, of Chicago, who disposed of Miss Peggy Wattles, Buffalo, by the same score in the other semi-final match. The finals, at 18 holes, will be played tomorrow afternoon. Miss Van Wie has won the Florida title twice and another victory would have given her possession of the championship cup.

(By Associated Press) St. Just, Eng., Feb. 19:—All hands of a crew of 29 were saved from the Greek steamer Theotokos which sank after a collision with an unidentified steamer off Lands End last night.

NEW YORK, Feb. 18. — (#) — Edna Best, nostalgic English actress, sped toward New York on a fast train tonight to the husband for whom she left the films flat. “It's perfectly true my wife has run away from Hollywood,” said Herbert Marshall, who is playing in the Broadway stage success, “Tomorrow and Tomorrow.” Turning her back on what the cinema world said was her “big chance,” Miss Best boarded a train, leaving John Gilbert waiting at a camera and a frenzied director doing things to his hair. Her place in the picture, “Cheri-Bebi,” in which she was to have starred, was taken by Leila Hyams. “Please forgive me,” she telegraphed to the director when her train made a stop at Needles, Calif. “I am awfully homesick and besides I am just afraid I wouldn't be any good in the picture.” Marshall said he expected her to arrive tomorrow.
