Madrid, Feb. 18.—(4)—Spain tonight had a new government, peacefully formed, and was looking forward to a period of calm after the political turmoil of the last five days. Admiral Juan Bautista Asenar, staunch royalist and political neutral, heads the ministry formed today by King Alfonso in a successful effort to head off another military dictatorship like that of Miguel Primo de Rivera. People Quiet The king called for no participation by left, socialist and republican elements, and their attitude remained problematical tonight. The public generally, however, seemed to be waiting quietly until the program and policies of the new government could be formulated and put into effect. The cabinet which replaces that of Damaso Berenguer, which resigned last Saturday, because of widespread opposition to Premier Berenguer’s plan for parliamentary elections in March, includes Berenguer himself,

MADRID, Feb. 19,—Spain’s new cabinet headed by Admiral Juan Bautista Aznar y Cabanas met today to prepare a ministerial declaration outlining a new political era after eight years of government without a parliament. The confusion which followed the resignation of Premier Gen. Damaso Berenguer after a year as a dictator was resolved at least temporarily when the 70-year-old admiral obeyed the order of King Alfonso XIII to form a government.

HENDAYE, Spanish Frontier, Feb 19. (AP).—Reports were current along the frontier today that King Alfonso of Spain had purchased a chateau at Talence, near Bordeaux, France, for use in an emergency which might have caused him to leave the country over which he rules. While the general feeling here was that Alfonso never would run away from events in Spain, it was commented in Petite Gironde, a widely known Bordeaux paper, that “for Alfonso it is all or nothing. Each time he plays a card or makes a move he is justified in thinking of Charles I, Louis XVI, or Nicholas II.”

Paris, Feb. 19.—The French naval budget totaling 2,856,511,533 francs (about $114,260,461) was passed by the chamber of deputies early today after the legislators had been reminded that “Italy is rushing construction.” Marine Minister Charles Dumont declared “the navy is the guarantee of French security and colonial integrity. Therefore, we need a modern navy.” Recent efforts of Great Britain to persuade France to delay her building program appeared wiped out by the chamber’s decision. The only determined stand against the huge naval appropriation, exceeding that of last year by about $5,320,000, came from the Socialists who attempted to clip about $1,606,000,000 from the budget. The socialist amendment was rejected, 450 votes to 100.

1931-01-02.text: Cardiff, Wales, Jan. 1 (4)—There was little activity today in the great collieries of South Wales, where last night negotiations between miners, operators and government officials ended in a sort of combined strike and lockout. One hundred fifty thousand men are employed in the fields and most of them were idle today, although here and there small bodies of men went into the pits by special local agreements. As some workers already were idle because of industrial disputes, the number out of jobs in the area now ranges close to 230,000. The trouble results from a dispute over both hours and wages. At this the Miners’ Federation balked and ordered the 150,000 men not to report for work today. The owners countered with an edict that the mines should be locked to all who refused to accept their wage reduction offer.

Leige, Belgium, Jan. 1. (®)— Amy Johnson, who flew alone to Australia last year, landed here tonight on the first stage of a solo flight to Peiping, China. She took off at Hendon, England, at 10:40 o'clock this morning and reached here just at dusk. She plans to continue to Berlin, going thence to Moscow where

The proclamation of the treaty’s effectiveness came 24 hours after the last foreign signatory had completed ratification. It was not accompanied by comment, Mr. Hoover having already one on record as asserting the treaty would prevent “competitive building of navies with all its flow of suspicion, hate and ultimate disaster.” By signing the treaty proclamation Mr. Hoover accomplished the final formality putting the pact into force. ROME, Jan. 2-47, Benito Mussolini, Italian premier and “strong man,” spoke for 16 minutes into a microphone here last evening in English, to an audience of millions of Americans from Atlantic to Pacific coasts who listened to one of the most ambitious radio broadcasts ever attempted. Premier Mussolini, who is reputed not to have known a word of English when he rose to power eight years ago, took the occasion to wish America a Happy New Year, explain some of the tenets of Italy’s Fascist regime, and to declare that Italy never would start a war. Mussolini pointed out in his address that he himself had fought in the ranks and was severely wounded, and he asked how anyone with his experience as a man and a statesman could consider a future conflict without horror. WASHINGTON, Jan. 1.—(U.P) President Hoover began the new year today with a message of peace. He proclaimed the London naval treaty, ending battle fleet competition between America, Great Britain and Japan, fully effective. Twenty-four hours after the last foreign signatory had completed ratification of the document limiting building programs of great naval powers, the president signed his formal proclamation at 10 a. m. He informed the American people that he made the treaty public “to the end that every article and clause may be fulfilled in good faith by the United States.” The president's proclamation merely formalized putting into force the pact made last April when the United States, Great Britain and Japan agreed to restrict their navy building programs for six years. Tring, Hertfordshire, England, Jan. 2. (P)—A little gray donkey has provided the biggest thrill of the English hunting season and furnished huntsmen with many hearty laughs. A pack of drag hounds was being exercised near here yesterday when a donkey straying from a farmyard suddenly trotted into their midst, brayed loudly and took off across the country at a gallop. Off went the hounds in pursuit, chasing the ass hard into a wood. There he turned and faced the dogs, who instead of attacking the strange quarry lay down around him and watched to see what he would do next. By coincidence a fox suddenly broke over nearby and the hounds, forgetting the donkey, immediately gave chase to the more natural game. Then to the amazement of the huntsmen the ass joined the hounds, and galloped after the fox, leaping hedges and ditches in grand style, apparently enjoying the chase as much as the dogs,

New York, Jan. 2, ()—Heads of the four eastern trunk line railroads who reached an agreement last week on the major points of a consolidation plan were in conference here again today. There was no announcement as to the subject of the discussion, but it was believed that ratification of the agreement's terms, which have not been made public officially, was being considered. It is known that the executives desire their proposals before the Interstate Commerce Commission as soon as possible, perhaps by the end of this month.

PARIS, Jan. 1.—Clinging to life with the astonishing vitality which has marked his 12 days of desperate illness, Marshal Joffre lay tonight in a coma from which he had not aroused since 11 o'clock in the morning. His doctors, nonplused by the vigor of this rugged old hero, expected death at any moment and all Paris which had been plunged into grief by a premature report of his death this morning, was prepared for the end. He sank into unconsciousness an hour before noon and it appeared for a moment his gallant life was over. Even those at the bedside thought he was dead and the report flashed across the world. But a few minutes later the feeble pulse fluttered, the heart was beating and the marshal of France breathed. — Quickly the premature report was denied, but the denial was a long time in catching up with the first report and not until late in the afternoon was France convinced “Pap

1931-05-22.text: SIMLA, India, May 22, (#)— Nearly 500 persons are reported to have been killed and thousands wounded or captured in the current insurrection in Burma against British authority. American missionaries returning here say that the rebellion is in danger of spreading from southern Burma, its starting point, throughout the country and that colonial officials are rushing fresh troops from India into the upper section. The trouble is much more serious than earlier reports indicated, it was said, although martial law has not yet been declared. Business is nearing a standstill and rice, the national staple, is selling at half its normal price. The interior was described as unsafe for foreigners. Burmese Nationalists have been agitating for some years for a dominion status, separate from India. Guerilla detachments of natives have clashed with British troops frequently in the Tharawaddy and Theyetm

London, May 2—(AP)—The world wheat conference was forced to postpone today’s plenary session until tomorrow due to the inability of its sub-committee to complete work on the proposals for solution of the international grain crisis. While no official word was permitted to leak from the committee rooms, the general impression among observers was that the committee was deadlocked on the divergent plans suggested by Russia and the United States. The postponement emphasizes the diversity of opinion regarding export quotas and how they shall be calculated. Russia’s proposals were based on pre-war figures as a starting point in fixing the scale for new quotas. The American delegation opposes such a plan and the Russian insistence upon the pre-war basis is said to have found little support from the Argentine, Canadian and Australian delegations. Seat American as Delegate M. W. Thatcher of the Fa

Eric Smith of Cambridge University wins British Amateur Title. (By The Associated Press.) Westward Ho, Devon, England, May 23.--Eric Smith, little known golfer from Cambridge University, today won the British amateur golf championship, defeating John De Forest in the final 36 hole match one up. Smith, 22 years old, the son of a London banker, had never played in a national championship before, his play heretofore having been with college and club affairs.

LONDON, May 21.—(AP)—Russia's delegation to the world wheat conference today issued a statement definitely rejecting the American plan for restricted acreage as suggested by Samuel R. McKelvie, and proposing instead a broad scheme upon which Russia would be inclined to enter a world agreement limiting exports. The announcement enlivened an otherwise dull day of routine committee meetings but what its effect will be on tomorrow's open meeting of the conference was conjectural. Some of the delegates, although they refrained from commenting on the note itself, said they believed it would prolong the conference. The immediate result of the publication was to divide the conference into two camps, one supporting the quota system and the other holding (Continued on Page 2, Col. 1.)

London, May 21 (4)—The London Daily Express said tonight that Scotland Yard detectives will meet the French steamer Paris at Plymouth to see that Texas Guinan does not land in England on her way to France from New York. The New York night club hostess is definitely on Great Britain's list of barred aliens, the Express said, and immigration officers in every port have been instructed to turn her back if she attempts to enter the country.
SOUTHAMPTON, Eng., May 22 - Ambassador Charles G Dawes left today on the liner Bremen for the United States on private business. He expects to return about July 1.

WESTWARD HO, Eng. (UP) — Eric Martin Smith of Royal St. George's succeeded Bobby Jones as British amateur golf champion by winning the final 36-hole match with John G. DeForest of Addington, Friday. The score was 1 up. Smith led most of the way. He was two up at the end of the morning 18, and remained two up at the turn of the afternoon round.

London, May 22—-(?)—Substitution of a loudspeaker for the minister in some churches was reported by the Daily Mail today to be under consideration by bishops of the Church of England: Inasmuch as there is a serious shortage of clergy, it has been suggested that services in certain churches be broadcast with the hope that congregations would join in the prayers and responses as though they were led by a clergyman. Proponents were said to see no reason why the change could not be made.

1931-06-17.text: Croydon Airport, England, June 17 -(UP)—Capt. Frank Hawks returned at 5:58 P.M. today after having flown to Rome and return since his departure at 5:31 A.M. The round trip was approximately 1,600 miles. He took time in Rome for a leisurely luncheon. New speed records were established in both directions. Captain Hawks made his return trip from Rome to London in six hours flat.
- CROYDON, UP. Capt. Frank Hawks took off Wednesday at 5:30 a.m. on the first leg of a projected round trip flight to Rome between dawn and dusk.

ROME, June 17. (®)—Captain Frank Hawks landed here on a round trip flight from London at 10:15 a. m. (4:15 a. m. E. S. T.) today, completing the trip in four hours and forty-five minutes at an average speed of nearly 200 miles per hour.

LONDON. (UP) The mother of parliaments uproariously laughed off the political crisis that had threatened to overthrow the labor government. With the House of Commons all set for a big debate and a critical vote late Tuesday night, the presiding officer ruled the whole show out of order. Days and nights of anxious negotiations, conducted under the threat of a general election, terminated in an anti-climax. For a moment parliament was dazed. Then David Lloyd George started the chuckling. Ramsay MacDonald, grave chief of the ruling laborites, joined in. Laughter spread to the opposition conservative benches which had hoped for a definite break-up of the liberal and labor alliance and soon the whole chamber was rocking with laughter over the fiasco of Great Britain's latest political crisis. A liberal amendment to Chancellor Philip Snowden’s land tax proposals was declared out of order on a

CROYDON, England — Frank Hawks fulfilled the promise to his Eesha friends today by taking breakfast in London and lunch in Rome and returning to London in time for dinner. Leaving here at 5:30 A.M. he reached Rome at 10:10 o'clock, left there at 1 P.M. and landed at Croydon at 6 P.M. He averaged about 200 miles an hour on the southward trip, but the return journey in which he faced headwinds was a little slower. The weather was fine and skies were blue for the final lap of the flight across the channel to England.

By The Associated Press. ROYDON, England, June 17.—Captain Frank Hawks brought his fast monoplane down on the field here at 5:55 p. m. today completing a flight from Rome in 5 hours flat. CROYDON, England, June 17.—Frank Hawks fulfilled the promise to his British friends today by taking breakfast in London, lunch in Rome, and returning to London in time for dinner. Leaving here at 5:30 a. m., he reached Rome at 10:10 o'clock, left there at 1 p. m. and landed at Croydon at 6 p. m. He averaged about 200 miles an hour on the southward trip, but the return journey in which he faced head winds was a little slower.

Galway, Ireland, June 17.— A huge mass of black, malodorous mud which poured down the sides of Slievanenakilla mountain, in County Leitrim, blocking the headwaters of the River Shannon, has caused serious damage. Hundreds of tons of earth loosened by recent torrential rain in the upper Shannon country, plunged down the hillside and dammed the river which finally broke through the barrier and flooded the district. The mud spread for miles and drove farmers from their homes spoiling crops and threatening a winter of famine to hundreds of country folk.

Tokyo—(UP)—Tokyo and vicinity was rocked by a severe earthquake starting at 9:10 o'clock tonight. Authorities believed considerable property damage would be reported. Several sections of the city were in darkness due to the failure of power lines. Telephone and telegraph lines also were damaged. Some damage was reported at Yokohama, the seaport city, 18 miles from here.

1931-06-25.text: WASHINGTON, June 25. — President Hoover today rested the fate of his momentous war debt holiday plan on the shoulders of Andrew W. Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury. Mellon was ordered from London to Paris to negotiate with France in an effort to persuade her to relent from a stubborn desire to compel Germany to continue partial reparations payments during the year in which President Hoover proposes all payments be suspended. At the same time the United States Federal Reserve board joined with the Bank of England, the Bank of France and the Bank of International Settlements at Basle, Switzerland, in extending a credit of $100,000,000 to the strained German Reichsbank. The credit will be effective tomorrow. Of the major creditor powers involved in the Hoover Moratorium plan, only France remaining to be brought into line.

New York, June 24 ()—World financial markets read the news of France's qualified acceptance of President Hoover's war debt proposal with rose-tinted spectacles today. Security prices in New York, London and Paris surged up strongly, and the Berlin Boerse rallied after a moderate setback early in the session. Advances at New York rivaled those of Saturday and Monday, and stock sales were the largest in four months. On Wall Street, equity share values surged up $2 to $12, in the second 5,000,900 share day of the year on the Stock Exchange. The total quoted value of all shares listed on the New York Stock Exchange has increased roughly $5,000,000,000 since last Friday, price indices show. The advance was also resumed on most of the commodity market. Wheat and corn futures gained about 1/4 cent at Chicago, and New York cotton ended the day 5 to 7 cents a bale higher. Non-ferrous metals, rubb

- LONDON. cP. As unobtrusively as he came, Andrew W. Mellon, secretary of the United States treasury, is leaving England Thursday for France and there is much speculation as to his reasons for his visit there. Ostensibly he goes for a holiday, but he said virtually the same thing when he came here and had a whirlwind series of conferences with Great Britain's political and financial leaders prior to advising Washington regarding conditions in Europe. Observers feel certain that during the few days that he will be in Paris Mr. Mellon will consult the government and officers of the Bank of France in connection with President Hoover's proposal for a moratorium on war debts.

Paris, June 25 (U.P.)—Andrew Mellon, United States Secretary of the Treasury, was expected in Paris late this afternoon to take up personally the question of President Hoover's war debts plan with the French government. Mellon was due from London at 5:40 P.M. He has been cabled instructions by President Hoover to take urgent action toward obtaining France's unreserved acceptance.

By The Associated Press Southampton, June 24.---Captain Frank Hawks, who took the old world's breath away in his series of speed tours over Europe, sailed for Quebec today on the liner Empress of France. His Red monoplane left ahead of him yesterday from Liverpool on the Duchess of York and will be awaiting him at Quebec when he arrives.

St. Louis, June 24 (®)—The St. Louis Post-Dispatch today quoted Alanson B. Houghton, former ambassador to Germany and Great Britain as saying the “siphoning process to which Germany now is being subjected must be completely suspended, not for one or two years, but until Germany can recover her strength.” Houghton is president of the American Academy of Political Science. Houghton, who was ambassador to Germany during the difficult reconstruction years, 1922-1925, said that if adequate relief were not given, “there would shortly be no reparation payments to discuss.”

London, June 24.—(/)—Great Britain today granted a one-year moratorium to the Dominions for their war debts to the United Kingdom, thereby complying with what Chancellor of the Exchequer Snowden told the House of Commons was "the spirit as well as the letter" of President Hoover's debts proposal. This action of the British government will cost the already heavily taxed British budget about $55,000,000. "This is a serious sacrifice for the taxpayers of this country following on the heavy calls which have been made on them," Mr. Snowden said in his address in the House. The Hope "But we hope that the steps we have taken in cooperation with the United States will be more than justified by the help given in reviving confidence and prosperity." | Paris, June 25.—(P)—Franco-German conversations similar to the recent discussions at Chequers between Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain and German officials, probably will take place in Paris within the next few weeks. Foreign Minister Briand of France Thursday was reported to have sent word to Foreign Minister Curtius of Germany, through Ambassadeur Von Hoesch, that the French government would welcome an intimate conversation with the German chancellor and foreign minister. The invitation was said to have been discussed at yesterday's council of ministers and Briand was charged with the issuance of the invitation. With France's answer to President Hoover’s proposal for a war debt and reparations suspension delivered to the American government, interest centered today on the coming visit of Andrew W. Mellon, American secretary of the treasury, who left London at noon. While the

1931-01-15.text: London, Jan. 14.—-(AP)—-By the narrow margin of one seat in the Punjab provincial legislature, the Indian Round Table conference tonight failed to solve the Indian minorities problem, although Hindu and Moslem leaders reached a provisional accord which in itself may force a full agreement later. The evening session ended however, with the conference still deadlocked over deep racial and religious problems as they affect India’s political future under the proposed federal organization.

LIVERPOOL, Eng. Jan. 15-- (UP)—The steamer Oropesa, of which the Prince of Wales and Prince George will go to South America, departed today for La Rochelle-Pallice, France, carrying the luggage of the royal party. The Prince of Wales and his brother will proceed to Paris tomorrow, probably by airplane if conditions are favorable. They will go to Santander, Spain by train and board the ship there for the start of their 20,000 miles “salesmanship” trip through Latin America. The first halt on the trip will be at range on January-

SHANGHAI, Jan. 15—(UP)— Army bombing planes were concentrated today in the southern part of Kiangsi province in an attempt to rescue Khang Hu-Chan, nationalist government general, reported captured during the battle with communists. Hankow advices asserted General Chang was being held for 2,000,000 Mexican dollars ransom and that the 15th and 18th divisions, which he was commanding, had been routed. Other dispatches received from Changsha said a communist army numbering 2,000 had been defeated in an offensive drive against a division of government troops in the Hunan province. The repulsed communists, after heavy casualties, were believed withdrawing eastward.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 15, (P)—Fighting between government troops and marauding armies of Reds was reported from three south China provinces today. Amoy reported 200 Communist bandits had been slain at Yungting, southern Fukien province, when provincial forces drove the outlaws from that city. The Reds had held Yungting since Jan. 1. Reports from southern Kiangsi province said sharp fighting was in progress between Reds and the military near Ningtu, which Communists looted last December.

| PARIS, Jan. 15, (AP).—United States Ambassador Walter E. Edge told the American Club at Paris today that America’s “darkest age” of economic apathy and stunned business inertia was past. The ambassador, who was the guest of the club upon his return from the United States, said that the “dark age” followed “the most cataclysmic deflation of security markets in our history.” He added that it had been superseded by a period of courageous effort under the scientific leadership of President Hoover and Federal and State officials. Mr. Edge said that he had no desire to deny that American business, in common with world illness, was still ailing, but he declared that the crisis was past.

By FRANCIS M. STEPHENSON, Washington, Jan. 14—(AP)— The emergency appropriation of $45,000,000 for seed loans to drought-stricken farmers was finally approved today by Congress but in its wake arose a new dispute over relief legislation. Senate Democrats proposed a direct appropriation from the treasury of $25,000,000 for the Red Cross to administer relief and threatened an extra session of Congress in the spring, if necessary, to get it. Robinson Plan. Senator Robinson, of Arkansas, the Democratic leader, offered the 25,000,000 relief proposal as the minority party yielded to the insistence of the administration-controlled House for elimination from the drought relief measure of the $15,000 food loan provision sponsored by Senator Caraway, Democrat, Arkansas. Senator Black, Democrat, Alabama, joined Robinson in offering the new proposition as an amendment to the ending agriculture appro

LOS ANGELES, Jan. 15—The Richfield Oil Company was placed in receivership today by Federal Judge William P. James, on the petition of the Republic Supply Company of California. The petitioners estimated assets of the oil company at $12,000,000 and liabilities at $35,000,000.

MEXICO CITY, Jan. 14—-(AP)—The sharpest earthquake felt in Mexico City for 19 years caused at least one death and four injuries tonight, at the same time starting fires in two parts of the city, cracking buildings and throwing the inhabitants into panic. A woman was killed by a falling wall while four persons, one of them a small child, were injured by falling objects in houses. The shock began at 8:48 p.m. (EST) and for two minutes shook buildings with a rolling motion. Minor quakes continued for some five minutes after the principal shock. Electric lights went out, power lines were broken and telephone service was interrupted for some time. The fright of the inhabitants, who ran out of their homes in terror as they began to heave, was pathetic. Despite a downpour of rain, with vivid flashes of lightning adding to their consternation, they ran to the streets and prayed for divine protec

1931-01-16.text: LONDON, Jan. 16. (AP).—The Prince of Wales got off to a flying start today on his tour to South America. With his brother, Prince George, he left Hendon airport in a plane bound for Paris on the first leg of a tour which will take them over 18,000 miles.

LONDON, Jan. 16.—A wave of influenza swept Europe today while Britain was in the midst of the worst epidemic of grippe, influenza, and colds experienced since 1927. France, Germany, Spain, and Portugal reported unusual suffering. Severe cold in Spain and Portugal added to the discomfort of thousands; the military college in Lisbon was closed due to the illness of 370 cadets. Reports from Berlin estimated that 10,000 persons in Germany were being treated for influenza and colds. One-third of the patients were in hospitals. Approximately 200 deaths in England during the last fortnight were attributed to influenza; recent cold, foggy weather and the neglect of colds were considered responsible. It was estimated that bad weather, and consequent illness, caused the loss of 7,000,000 weeks of work in Britain during 1930. The epidemic of grippe in Spain was reported intensified by continued exc

London — (— An influenza epidemic, covering a large part of Europe, especially in the cities and towns, has put thousands in their beds and hampered business and transportation services through reductions in staffs. In some cases schools have closed. In 107 large towns of England on whose returns the country's vital statistics are based there were 191 deaths from the disease last week compared with 60 deaths the previous week. - England, Ark., Jan. 15.—The icy hand of winter that has spread over Arkansas added today to the suffering of this little farming town where the Red Cross is busy feeding hundreds of destitute sharecroppers and tenant farmer families. “The bread line,” as the natives call the crowd in front of the fire department headquarters, where food requisitions are handed out, was expected to increase greatly as a result of the cold wave. More than 250 persons received food orders yesterday. Since January 3rd, when a food riot was narrowly averted, 2,143 requisitions for food have been issued to impoverished families. Dr. W. T. Fuqua, chairman of the local Red Cross committee, said that school children had gone without noonday lunches in many cases, and soup kitchens in the schools would be opened today to prevent pupils from going hungry. Women from various churches will be in charge. England, a

| Mid-January means cold, and it is. Great ships of the sea ploughed to the refuge of their piers along the north Atlantic seaboard yesterday sheathed in ice. Biting winds whipped the plains states and New England buttoned up its overcoat against temperatures that had sunk to single figures. The ultimate of yesterday's cold spot and down in lesser degree into the midwest was in the Adirondacks, where Tupper Lake, NY, had a minus 22; but the Canadian northwest continued brewing cold which made itself felt in the Dakotas, Minne- (Continued on Page 10)

HENDON AIRDROME, Bng., Jan. 16.--The Prince of Wales and Prince George began their South American trip officially when they left Hendon for Paris at 1 P. M. today. The royal brothers travel in a private biplane piloted by F. Fielden. They will spend the night in Paris and proceed to Santander, from where they will embark for South America tomorrow. The Prince of Wales will travel as the Earl of Chester, and will be known by this title throughout the trip. Prince George is traveling as the Duke of York.

BIRMINGHAM, England, Jan. 15 (®)—Former Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin is broke—and is proud of it. In recent years shares in the iron trade owned by the Conservative leader have depreciated in value from three pounds (about $14.60) in 1923 to 20 pence (40 cents) now, he revealed last night.

LONDON, Jan. 16 (AP) — Mrs. William McKechnie of Gaven told a magistrate that she had been whipped by her husband every day for the past 18 years and was growing tired of the procedure. Magistrate Campbell, doing a lightning calculation, figured she had been thrashed about 6,570 times and placed William on probation for 12 months, promising a jail sentence if he used his razor strop on his wife again.

1931-10-11.text: By The Associated Press. London, Oct. 10.—The campaign for the general election October 27 has developed into a free-for-all fight unparalleled in the nation’s history. Bewilderment existed in scores of constituencies today as party groups pressed ahead with their plans for two weeks of high pressure electioneering to determine the fate of Ramsay MacDonald's national government. The campaign is settling into a fight for or against the national government with free trade or tariffs as the main immediate issue. In the background is the struggle between capitalism and the British labor party’s brand of socialism. One of the important developments today was the refusal by Conservatives to withdraw their candidate at Darwen in opposition to Sir Herbert Samuel, leader of the national liberals. This action is likely to precipitate more three-cornered fights among conservatives, liberals and lab

PARIS, Oct. 10.—The impending visit of Premier Pierre Laval was hailed today as an event of the first importance by two of France’s former ambassadors to the United States. Jules Jusserand, long the dean of the Washington diplomatic corps, and Julius Cambon, France’s envoy at the turn of the century, Jusserand declared that in Premier Laval, President Hoover “will find a man according to his heart”—a man who prefers to do things rather than talk about them. M. Cambon said in a similar statement that the Laval trip indicates Franco-American relations have never been more cordial. The French premier is sailing for the United States Oct. 16, taking with him Louis Aubert, expert on the armament, to report when the premier meets the President he will make.

GENEVA. (UP)—Hope of the League of Nations to bring about a compromise between Japan and China in Manchuria was lessened today when China served notice on Japan that her troops must be withdrawn at once from Chinese territory. On China’s request, Sir Eric Drummond, Secretary-General of the League, informed the council today that the Chinese minister at Tokio had notified the Japanese government that steps must be taken by Monday for immediate evacuation of Japanese troops and restoration of Chinese authority in Manchuria. Virtual Ultimatum Because of the time limit set, the demand was regarded as a virtual ultimatum. It was not specified here what steps China proposed to take in the event the demand was not met. Meanwhile, a score of Japanese warships were ordered to take up their positions off Chinese cities and Japanese troops held their positions in Manchuria.

WEST ORANGE, N. J., Oct. 10 (AP)—The world for Thomas A. Edison now is just one person—his wife. As the inventor lay in a stupor today, on the verge of a coma, Dr. Hubert S. Howe said Mr. Edison for days has been able to recognize no one except his white-haired wife, who has been at his bedside almost constantly. In the past, because of the peculiar timbre of her voice, her words have been clear to Mr. Edison despite his deafness. To this circumstance is partially attributed his ability to recognize her now. Other members of his family are maintaining a vigil near the sickroom but the last word of farewell between them and Mr. Edison apparently has been exchanged. How much longer he will be able to recognize Mrs. Edison was beyond prediction. But she, his companion of 45 years, remains close at hand to keep alive his last contact with the world. (Associated Press Sports Editor) SPORTSMAN’S PARK, ST. LOUIS, Oct. 10.—(CAP)—In a game that alternated thrills and chills, the home forces, the Cardinals recaptured the banner of the world baseball championship today, bringing it back to the National League and St. Louis after a lapse of five lean years. The National League champions, in a spirited comeback, conquered their nemesis, none other than George Earnshaw, and whipped the Athletics, 4 to 2, in the seventh and deciding game of the prolonged battle. It gave the Cardinals the decision, four games to three, duplicating their margin of triumph over the Yankees in 1926. Old Burleigh Grimes, the 37-year-old master of the spitball, was the hero of the final victory for the high-flying Red Birds. By The Associated Press Chicago, Oct. 10.—Philip D’Andrea, personal friend and constant champion of Al Capone at the scar-faced gang chief's income tax trial was ordered by Federal Judge James H. Wilkerson today to stand trial for carrying a pistol in the courtroom. D'Andrea, suave, nattily-dressed, and secretive appearing, was seized by three deputy United States marshals as he left the courtroom after today’s session. The marshals found a .38 caliber pistol tucked under his belt. Capone and his attorneys pleaded unsuccessfully for his release, and he was taken away to jail. Judge Wilkerson called his court into special session again this afternoon and ordered D'Andrea to be arraigned before him Monday morning on a rule requiring him to show cause why he should not be punished for contempt of court. (By Associated Press.) The United States government gave indication Saturday of early diplomatic action in the Manchurian situation, while the Chinese republic celebrated its twentieth birthday in a subdued, non-holiday spirit. Reports of further Japanese military activities were coupled with open demands from Tokyo that Chang Hsleh-Liang be removed by the Nanking government as governor of Manchuria, due to his alleged anti-Japanese attitude. An unconfirmed report from Peiping said Japanese airplanes which Friday bombed Chinchow, the temporary Manchurian capital, had crossed the great wall the rulers of China built so many centuries ago to keep out barbarians and had flown over Tangshan, an important coal mining center. Holzer, owner of the Gallipolis airport, Saturday night was investigating a report that a dirigible crashed and burned in the West Virginia hills south of here this afternoon. Dr. Holzer said more than a half dozen citizens had reported seeing the dirigible break in two and fall to the ground in flames. Several persons said they distinctly saw three occupants of the blimp jump with parachutes as the craft started to fall, Dr. Holzer said. Dr. Holzer, who operates a hospital here, said the ship passed over his hospital and that the persons who reported seeing it fall gave the time of the supposed crash at 2:50 p.m. The craft was said to have been from Akron, and to have been on the way to Huntington, W. Va. where it was to circle the field during a football game. Not a Goodyear Blimp AKRON, O.—(/)—Officials of the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. reported Saturday night that all company blimps

1931-08-08.text: TONBRIDGE, ENG., AUG. 8. (AP).—Brilliant handling by the pilot of the Hannibal, one of the largest passenger airplanes in the world, prevented an air catastrophe today. As it was, the Hannibal, bound with 18 passengers for Paris from Croydon, was forced down in a small field near here. In alighting, the plane barely missed a house top and sheared off its long tail when it got caught in telegraph wires. A telegraph pole was pulled down. None of the passengers or members of the crew was hurt. After a short delay, the passengers were taken by motor to Lympne, where they boarded another plane. Airways officials said one of the propellers broke in mid-air and fell off. In falling, it struck the propeller just beneath it and knocked it off, thus forcing the landing. The plane had four motors and a capacity for thirty-eight passengers.

[Associated Press Leased Wire]. FOREST HILLS, N. Y., Aug. 8— America regained the Wightman cup from England today as Helen Jacobs vanquished Phyllis Mudford, 6-4, 6-2, for the fourth straight and decisive victory of the international women's tennis competition.

By United Press CROYDON, Eng., Aug. 8.—An extraordinary accident disabling three of its four engines forced the 2200-horsepower air liner Hannibal—considered the largest and costliest plane in regular transport service—into a crash landing near Tonbridge today. None of the 18 passengers, who included two Americans, was seriously hurt. A statement issued by Imperial Airways, Ltd., after investigation of the affair said that one of the Hannibal's engines suddenly “locked.” This abrupt stoppage caused the rapidly revolving propeller to shatter, and pieces flew out and smashed two other propellers.

A message to Lloyds from Wick, Scotland, said that a plane giving the radio call letters KHVCX had been forced down by engine trouble and had asked for exact bearings and assistance. Radio Letters His. The plane in which Cramer has been making a leisurely investigation of the possibilities of a northern air route carried a radio with the call letters KHVCX. Associated Press Staff Writer Rome, Aug. 7, (AP).—Premier Mus- solini and Chancellor Bruening laid the groundwork today for a new friendship between Italy and Germany and started talking of practical measures for the common good of the world. The Italian Premier and the German Chancellor dealt frankly with European sore spots in their first meeting. Tonight they toasted each other at a dinner given by Mussolini to Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius, using words that, for all their generality of tone, promised sincere efforts to push or pull Europe out of the slough of despond. In his dinner speech the Duce paid tribute to German culture and expressed deep sympathy with the Reich in its present plight. Lindbergh took off from this Arctic trading post at 7:30 p.m., C.P.S. today for Point Barrow, Alaska, 536 miles away. Clearing weather permitted the flying couple to leave after being grounded for three days and two nights, the longest halt since they left Washington, D. C., 10 days ago. SHANGHAI, Aug. 8.—(4)—Declaring 10,000,000 dwellers in the flooded valleys of central China face starvation before spring unless aid is given them, John Earl Baker suggested today that part of the United States farm board's surplus wheat be poured into China under long term credit arrangements. Baker, adviser to the ministry of railways at Nanking, told the Associated Press correspondent the present floods probably constituted China's most terrible disaster in the present century. Baker directed international relief work in the Shensi and Kansu famine region in 1930. He estimated property damage of the present floods would total $300,000,000. He refused even to guess at the death toll.

He is recovering from injuries resulting when he was run down by an automobile last week. The driver of the automobile was this same young Mario Contasino. Every day since the accident Contasino, a 24-year-old mechanic out of work, has presented himself at the desk of the hospital and inquired anxiously concerning Mr. Churchill's condition. A nurse made casual reference to this in the presence of the injured man. Mr. Churchill was interested. He feared the young man might be worrying unduly and holding himself blamable. By The Associated Press. NEW YORK, Dec. 19.—Winston Churchill, British statesman, injured when struck by a taxicab last Sunday, will be able to leave the hospital Wednesday, his physicians, Otto C. Pickhardt and Foster Kennedy, announced tonight. Churchill will spend Christmas with his wife and daughter, Diana, in their hotel suite, meanwhile remaining under the care of the physicians. The pleurisy that complicated the injuries has cleared up satisfactorily.

TINOKIO, DEC. 21.—-(UP)—Japanese troops in the Mukden area began a general “anti-bandit” offensive today. Officials here expected the campaign to be concluded by Friday, after which there was the possibility of heavy fighting in the Chinchow area, where the last of Chang Hseuh-Liang’s troops are concentrated. The first Japanese detachments began operations out of Kaiyuan, on the Peiping-Mukden railroad north of Mukden, where Major General Mori established temporary headquarters. He is in charge of the Japanese punitive expedition. Major General Mori said he hoped to exterminate 7000 Chinese irregulars operating around Changtu, Kungping and Fakumen. The Japanese wrapped their helmets in white cloth to prevent the aviators from mistaking them for Chinese. +0820, Dec. 20--Japanese forces in Manchuria started raving southward toward Chinchow today, ostensibly to clean out lawless elements along the South Manchurian railway. Rengo dispatches from Mukden said the troops, which had been held for emergencies, departed from Nanling, Kirin and other points. Numerous reports mentioned engagements with bandits north and south of Mukden, and one referred definitely to troop movements. Chief of Staff Firo Minami, prior to his departure for Mukden, issued a statement saying all military operations in Manchuria had been completed with exception of that affecting Chinchow. His chief object in going to the scene, it was announced, was to effect closer cooperation between General Honjo’s headquarters and the war office and to assemble information as to how to rebuild Manchuria after troop movements have ceased. They weren't afraid to put an additional tax on big incomes; they forget politics when they are in a tight place. Republicans can't stay big incomes over here for they haven't got next year’s campaign budget yet. Democrats still owe for their last three elections. Somebody said that Al Smith wouldn't run next year but Al says it wasn't him that said it.

Four hundred persons, including eleven American Jesuits, were reported killed and hundreds were injured when a terrific hurricane swept out of the blue Caribbean late Thursday and demolished the west coast seaport of Belize. To add to the horror of destruction, a huge tidal wave followed in the wake of the 150-mile-an-hour wind, and washed many of the bodies of the dead out to sea, along with houses, churches and other buildings. - Miami, Sept. 12 (UP)—Two tropical hurricanes sweeping over the Caribbean, one leaving the city of Belize, British Honduras, in ruins, with 400 reported dead and 600 injured, the other striking with less force at San Juan, Puerto Rico, appeared to be losing their destructive power today. The Belize storm, which was accompanied by a tidal wave that sent a flood of water eight feet deep through the Honduran capital at its height, was reported spending itself in the area northeast of Vera Cruz, Mexico, the United States weather bureau announced. Won't Reach Florida Fear in Florida that the San Juan storm, which tore through the city at 100 miles an hour, unroofing houses and destroying communications, power lines and plantation equipment, might reach the southern coast of the United States with the intensity of 1926 and 1929, was set at rest by government assurances. A second intense storm, sweeping over San Juan, Puerto Rico, at a 110-mile rate, unroofed houses, destroyed plantations and resulted in the known deaths of two persons. They all studied at various times at St. Louis university here, which jobs Roman Catholic school systems in operation in Central America. MARSEILLES, France, Sept. 1 — Mahatma Gandhi rolled toward the round table conference in London tonight in a modest second class compartment aboard the Bombay-Paris express. He arrived in Marseilles today and was acclaimed only by Indian students and their young French contemporaries. French officialdom avoided him.

Belize, British Honduras, Sept. 12 —(P)— Belize, home of 18,000 persons, devoted itself today to burying the dead and ministering to the injured, victims of a hurricane that devastated the city Thursday. More than 150 persons were estimated to have lost their lives in the storm and ensuing tidal wave and bodies still were being unearthed. Seventy per cent of the city was levelled. Starting at 2:30 p. m., the disturbance raged for about three hours with a calm period of 30 minutes. It was immediately followed by a tidal wave that accounted for most of the dead and left water from five to nine feet high in the streets. The dead included 11 American Catholic priests and 18 native students who were trapped when St. John’s College, a Jesuit institution, was razed. The loss to American concerns was placed roughly at $250,000 and the total damage at well over $2,000,000. Wireless communications

1931-03-18.text: WASHINGTON, MAR. 18. (AP).—As a result of a long trans-Atlantic telephone conversation today between Secretary Stimson and Ambassador Dawes and Senator Dwight W. Morrow in London, the secretary said it would now appear unnecessary for the United States to participate in the work of drafting the Franco-Italian naval accord. In the talk which lasted about fifteen minutes, the ambassador and the senator gave the secretary a very favorable report on the progress made so far on the naval settlement.

Never before has the shamrock been worn so freely, many of the girls even wearing bunches on their dance frocks. Although the celebration was anew and quiet in Dublin, it was the gayest in years at Belfast. Schools and official offices were closed in Ulster, where the younger generation took the lead in the merrymaking. London, Mar. 18--(A.P.)—Widespread stories today of new British party alignments, which would lead David Lloyd George to the labor fold, and Sir John Simon to the conservative standard greatly excited political circles. The reports, published in the Daily Sketch and a liberal organ, appeared to be the outgrowth of the defeat of the labor government Monday night by four votes on a minor clause of the electoral reform bill principally because Sir John and ten fellow Liberals refused to follow Lloyd George in voting with the populists.

GLASGOW, Scotland, March 18 - The steamer Citritie was wrecked Tuesday night in a fog. The ship sank immediately. Two members of the crew swam ashore. The other nine were reported drowned, the announcement said.

LONDON, March 17—(AP)— A miniature naval conference was held at the foreign office this afternoon after Ambassador Dawes had rushed Senator Dwight W. Morrow, who arrived on the Leviathan to Downing Street to expound to Foreign Minister Henderson and A. V. Alexander, First Lord of the Admiralty, the American attitude toward the new Anglo-French-Italian naval agreement. It was understood that the meeting was satisfactory to all concerned and with Downing Street now officially informed of the American view that the tripartite accord is a matter of European concern only, it is expected the work of formally drafting the new agreement will begin Thursday as planned.

By United Press WASHINGTON, March 13.—A favorable report on the progress of his conversations with Great Britain regarding the Franco-Italian naval agreement was given by Ambassador Charles Dawes in London today in a 15-minute transatlantic telephonic conversation with Secretary of State Stimson.

London—()—United States Senator Dwight W. Morrow concluded his mission to London in connection with the tripartite-naval agreement today and prepared to continue with Mrs. Morrow on the European holiday which he interrupted to confer with British cabinet officials. The conversations in which Senator Morrow participated at the foreign office yesterday and today were considered from the British viewpoint to have had a satisfactory conclusion. The new Anglo-French-Italian naval agreement is to stand as a strictly European matter. Its formal drafting will be started tomorrow, but neither Mr. Morrow nor any other representative of the United States will be present officially or unofficially, and neither will Japan be represented.

A statement issued at the close of the conference, however, stated that the earnings of any adult male employee will not be reduced below 40 shillings a week. | LONDON, March 11—(AP)— Limitation of French and Italian naval programs until 1936 is definitely laid down in the terms of the British-Franco-Italian naval accord made public today. But even more important than its technical provisions, in the opinion of the three governments concerned, the agreement brings European peace measurably closer and provides a point of departure for the disarmament conference at Geneva next year. The accord covers building programs for battleships, cruisers, aircraft-carriers and submarines in substance as follows. Battleships—Both France and Italy are given the right to complete before December, 1936, two capital ships whose displacement shall not exceed 23,333 tons and whose gun calibre shall not exceed twelve inches. Cruisers—Both nations agree that after completion of the 1920 class they will build no more big cruisers with armament larger than six-inch g

LONDON, March 12 (UP)—A committee representing the United States, Britain, Japan, France and Italy will be formed to draft a new five power naval limitations agreement incorporating the new Franco-Italian accord, it was understood today in reliable American quarters. The committee would meet here possibly in April with Ambassador Charles G. Dawes as the probable United States representative. Dawes will visit the foreign office today regarding a matter separate from the naval accord, but probably will discuss the naval limitations question.

LONDON, Mar. 12. (4)—Winter still held most of Europe in a fierce, unrelenting grip today. Germany, France, Austria, Switzerland, Scandinavia, Holland and the British Isles suffered from storms which began last week and have continued with little pause since. The Zuyder Zee, Holland’s great inland sea, for the first time in several years, was frozen over and ferry service was suspended. Roads were either blocked by snowfall or made extremely dangerous for traffic in all the affected countries. Conditions in Great Britain were a trifle less severe than yesterday, although cold winds and frost continued. There was some anxiety in the Hill country at the prospect of melting drifts bringing floods.

Thousands of Homes Evacuated as Result of Floods and Freezing. PARIS, March 12.--(P)—Floods and freezing temperature spread suffering and death along almost every river in France today as storms which swept southward from the British Isles continued in Europe. Entire villages along the Seine, Loire, Rhone, Lot and Meuse valleys were evacuated and thousands of families were homeless.

LONDON, UP, Snow, high winds and bitter cold weather impeded traffic on land and sea Wednesday night as the worst late winter storm of recent years continued to rage in many sections of Europe. Ships were delayed, automobiles were stalled in drifts and many trains were far behind schedule. The blanket of snow covered much of England, France, Germany, Austria and other countries. Numerous accidents were blamed on the storm. The icy streets in Berlin alone caused more than thirty injuries and sent a dozen persons to the hospital with broken bones. Paris faced the menace of flood, since the snow was causing the river Seine to reach a high stage. In Munich and Berlin, scores of snow plows made little progress against the drifts. The street cleaning personnel was augmented by hundreds of unemployed.

(By Associated Press) CROESBECK, Tex, March 11—A jury today returned a verdict of death in the electric chair for Sonny Miller, Tom Henry “Armstrong” and Cai English, negroes, charged with robbery with firearms for the death of Charles Hunter, Lawrenceburg, Tenn., near Kosse, Feb. 13. Hunter and a brother, Rufus, were robbed and thrown from a moving freight train. Charles Hunter's neck was broken. In the middle of the afternoon, the three negroes were calm as the verdict was read. Armstrong was convalescing from a bullet wound received when he was shot by J. B. Piper, Southern Pacific Railway officer, near Denny, about three weeks ago. About 1,500 spectators were in the courtroom. Numerous handkerchiefs had been in evidence, as District Attorney Sam McCorkle described to the jury the robbery which resulted in Hunter's death. HONGKONG — The British navy has started open submarine warfare against roving Chinese pirates who prey on foreign and Chinese ships in the Bias Bay area. Four new submarines have been sent from Britain to reinforce the two now operating against the sea rovers off the South China coast, last stronghold of the pirates. The new submarines are of the “P” class, the latest things in underwater fighting ships. The Poseidon and the Perseus, two units of the new flotilla, are expected in Hongkong this month. Their sister vessels, the Pandora and the Proteus, are undergoing repairs after a collision in Gibraltar Bay and will arrive later. 1931-07-18.text: BUCHAREST, Rumania, July 16 (AP)—Queen Helen, tearfully leaving Crown Prince Michael with King Carol, was en route to London today on what may become a trip to the land of exile. When she passed the royal castle at Sinaia on the Orient Express she peered from the window in vain for a glimpse at the boy who is the only tie between her and her divorced husband. There was not even a royal salute to signify that her long-lasting marital troubles were nearing a climax. She left last night in tears—tears that were emulated by Dowager Queen Marie, her mother-in-law, and Princess Tieng who went to the station to bid her goodbye. Archduke Anton, Tieng’s fiancée, lingered in the background. She said she would first visit her mother in London and then go to Italy with her brother, former King George of Greece, before returning in the fall to see Crown Prince. PARIS, July 18 (AP)—France has decided to attend the London conference on Monday. This was the outstanding fact of today’s developments which centered on the meeting between French and German statesmen held this afternoon and to be resumed tomorrow. Official progress was made today to make it appear certain that some formula for agreement between Germany and France will be adopted tomorrow. This does not mean that any definite settlement, either financial or political, will be made in Paris, but that what amounts to the agenda for the London conference will be settled at tomorrow’s meetings which will include one of the representatives of all the countries now in Paris. It was understood the French, in deciding to go to London, have made it clear to the other powers they will not discuss the Young plan for disarmament at London. Paris, July 18 (UP)—Paris was the capital of Europe today, with leading statesmen gathering here for a hastily arranged conference on economic and political problems growing out of the German financial debacle. Members of the governments of five nations—the United States, Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy—will hold conversations over the weekend in an anxious effort to solve these problems. Seldom has so rare a spectacle of cabinet ministers hurrying from capital to capital been witnessed. Only a crisis of extreme importance, it was admitted, could have determined the governments, including America, to break away from the customary channels of negotiations through ambassadors. The United States was represented by Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson and Andrew W. Mellon, secretary of the treasury—admittedly two of the ablest members of the Hoover administration. Lancaster, Pa., July 18. (P)—Oliver C. Riggs, former assistant engineer of Sir Hubert Wilkins' submarine "Nautilus," said today that the undersea boat's crew "took an awful beating from the Atlantic" on the way to Great Britain, the first leg of the proposed journey to the North Pole. Riggs, who resigned when the Nautilus reached Ireland, said the ocean crossing was the worst voyage he had ever made. At one time, he said, all but four members of the crew were helpless with seasickness and the four had to operate the craft. Sir Hubert himself, though very ill, stood watch on two occasions when there was no one else to do it, and served as an oiler to relieve men too sick to work. "Three days and three nights of the trip were terrible," Riggs said. "The engines were not working properly, the fresh water tanks were turned over, and we suffered a lot from seasickness. Bucharest, Roumania, July 18. —(UP)— Helene, divorced wife of King Carol, was on her way abroad today for an extended tour away from the sad scenes of her shattered romance with the ruler of Roumania. She left for England, where she plans to visit her mother at Ascot, prior to proceeding to Italy. Neither King Carol nor the government was represented in the group which saw her off on the Orient Express. Dowager Queen Marie, mother of Carol, Prince Nicholas, brother of the King, Helene’s parents, the former King and Queen of Greece, and Princess Neana, Carol's sister, and her fiancé, Archduke Anton of Habsburg, were at the station to bid her farewell.

| By United Press | NEW YORK, July 18.—Catherine Kresge, $5,001,000 heiress of the 5 and 10 cent store family, has been married to Baron Carl Wijk, it has been learned here. The ceremony was performed at St. George’s Church in London June 8 and the couple now is honeymooning at Antibes, France. Wijk is the eldest son of Lady Reginald Barnes of Devonshire, Eng. The Baroness, who received $5,000,000 from her father, Sebastian S. Kresge, when he divorced her mother, Anna, was introduced to her husband by Rufus Clark Caulkins of Detroit, her sister Ruth's fiancé, it was revealed. Ruth and another sister, Ann, each of whom received $5,000,000 from the chain store magnate were present at the wedding, together with their mother. Ruth is expected to follow her blonde, 22-year-old sister to the altar before long. She was a friend of Ralph Barton, satirist and illustrator.

BOSTON, July 18 —(P)— Hundreds of men and women workers today walked the streets of southern New England textile centers, idle, not solely because of depression in the industry, but because of strikes. There have been strikes in the normally busy textile localities of Central Falls, Pawtucket, and the Olneyville section of Providence, in Rhode Island, and Putnam and New London in Connecticut. Three times last week mobs pitted their strength against police guarding the properties of the General Fabrics Corporation in Central Falls. In the adjacent city of Pawtucket, an extraordinary force of police was spread around the Royal Weaving Company, which opened some of its departments after two weeks of idleness. The Weybosset mill of the American Woolen Company in Olneyville has been silent for 10 days as a result of a walkout of its 600 employees. Wages were cut 12 1-2 percent last December.

WASHINGTON, July 17.—(#)—President Hoover today enlisted the assistance of Ambassador Dawes to strengthen still further America’s representation at the London conference of ministers. In addition, the chief executive has taken the position that active American participation must be confined to economic problems. This was made known after several transatlantic telephone conversations between Mr. Hoover and Secretary Stimson, at Paris. While a wide range of attending political questions is expected by the administration to be raised in connection with the formulation of a plan for economic relief for Germany, any suggestions which the American delegates may put forward on such issues will be wholly informal. PESHAWAR, India 26—(LP)— Eight persons were killed today and 50 others, including the superintendent of police, were wounded today when soldiers fired on a crowd of 500 ‘red shirts’ followers of Abdul Ghaffir Khan, head of the anti-British movement among frontier tribesmen. The ‘red shirts’ had gathered outside the Kohat Contonment. When they refused to disperse, police charged, wielding lathis (long bamboo sticks). The crowd drove the police back and the military then opened fire. Other Clashes Reported Many other clashes in the Peshawar district were reported today. A crowd stoned police yesterday at Baffa. A policeman and a soldier were wounded when a crowd interceded in behalf of an arrested ‘red shirt.’ ‘Red shirts’ appearing here and elsewhere in this vicinity are being arrested for violations of new ordinances outlawing frontier assemblages of Ghaffir.

Tokyo, Dec. 26.—(UP)—The Japanese government replied today to notes from Washington, Paris and London expressing apprehension over the possibility of a Japanese advance on Chinchow. At the same time, it was learned a declaration, placing responsibility for developments in the Chinchow area on the Chinese, will be published tomorrow.
