Paris, Dec. 25.—(4)—The newspaper Petit Parisien said today the French and British governments would propose to other interested powers the calling of a conference of nations on reparations, to meet at The Hague January 18. Other powers were expected to accept invitations to the meeting, which would precede the world disarmament conference at Geneva by only two weeks. The newspaper Temps warned that the attitude of the United States would be a decisive factor hanging over the reparations conference. “Without the aid of the Americans, the adjustment of inter-governmental debts cannot be usefully examined,” the Temps said, “and in that case one must proceed on the narrowly limited domain of the Young plan. The Germans deceive themselves if they imagine the question will be put otherwise at the governmental conference than at the consultative committee’s meeting at Basel.” Dangerous Situati

PESHAWAR, India, LOC. ae (AP) — British authorities were armed with three new ordinances today to combat the vexatious “Red Shirt” movement in the northwest frontier province. Abdul Chaffur Khan, called the “Frontier Gandhi,” and a dozen others have been arrested, along with threats to open a civil disobedience campaign. He was ordered expelled from the province because of his agitation as leader of the “Red Shirt” tribesmen. The provincial government was empowered by the ordinances to arrest, detain and control persons suspected of subversive activities, to take possession of property under suspicion, and to prohibit and limit access to certain areas.

MOSCOW, Dec. 26.—(UP)—Soviet political police charged today that Carl Wanek, Czechoslovakian diplomat, plotted assassination of Japanese Ambassador Koki Hirota, hoping to cause a break between the Tokyo and Moscow governments. Wanek is to leave Moscow. Wanek’s identity was revealed in dispatches from Prague. First charges were made against “a certain diplomat.” Czechoslovakia is without de jure recognition from Russia yet maintains a fully privileged diplomatic mission here. The Czech personnel is usually out of the diplomatic limelight.

PARIS (4) — A world conference to grapple with German reparations at the Hague on Jan. 18 was in prospect today on the authority of the French foreign office. While official comment was lacking, informed circles interpreted this development as growing out of the Young plan advisory committee’s report declaring that Germany would not be able to meet her conditional payments at the close of the Hoover moratorium on July 1. The French press looked upon the proposal as a climatic endeavor to settle for all time the problem that has been agitating the nations since the close of the World War. Petit Parisien said the French and British government would sponsor the conference and invite other great powers to participate. The parley would precede the world disarmament conference at Geneva by hardly two weeks. The attitude of the United States will exert a powerful if not a decisive influence on

1931-12-08.text: Less than a week after the second round table conference closed on London without providing, Mahatma Gandhi said, for “real freedom” for India, protests including a call for a revival of passive resistance and the boycott, have been registered in three important Indian centers. The provincial conference in Bengal urged a boycott of British goods, banks, insurance companies and shipping lines. The council of the All-India Muslim League at New Delhi expressed dissatisfaction with the British government’s failure to announce a decision concerning the safeguarding of Muslim rights. At Lucknow an agrarian sub-committee authorized local subcommittees to begin a no-rent campaign immediately.

LONDON, Dec. 8. (P)—At least one newspaper predicted today that Great Britain is “on the verge of a tariff war.” There were rumors, too, of a plan for a Franco-Belgian economic union, similar to the now abandoned Austro-German customs pact, as the British parliament considered the question of a 100 per cent duty on vegetables and fruits as part of the new tariff program. Conservative supporters of the national government pressed their demands for high protection rates in the face of a prospect of reprisals by continental Europe, including France, Germany, Belgium, Holland, Scandinavia, Spain and Portugal.

TOKYO, Dec. 1—(¥)—Rengo dispatches today confirmed the report that about 300 Chinese were killed yesterday as Japanese planes bombed Kungtapiu southwest of Mukden. Japanese said the affair was an attack on a thousand bandits. It was announced that Mukden headquarters is planning a new advance toward Chinchow. It is claimed the Chinese are concentrating troops and erecting defense works. If the drive is made it will probably last several weeks.

Paris, Dec. 8.—-(AP)—The league of nations council today appeared virtually to have abandoned the plan to establish an official neutral zone between the Chinese and Japanese armies in the Chinchow area, since agreement on its terms has been found impossible. Instead, its resolution, which may be ready for final adoption tomorrow, is likely to recognize the status quo and to express the hope that both sides will refrain from disturbing the comparative peace which now exists in southern Manchuria. In the view of the council, the neutral zone already exists in fact. The Chinese are left in possession of Chinchow and the Japanese have promised not to attack that city. The Japanese, however, have not withdrawn their demand that Chinchow be evacuated. The committee drafting the council’s resolution consulted Dr. Sze, the Chinese delegate, today and gave tentative approval to the inclusion by A

United Press Staff Correspondent. Copyright, 1931 by United Press PARIS, Dec. 7—U.P)—The end of “hard times” next summer and defeat of President Hoover next November were predicted today for the United Press by Madame Fraya, French seer. She foretold a year ago the slump of sterling, death of Joffre, war in Manchuria, overthrow of Alfonso and rise to power of Pierre Laval. By midsummer, Madame Fraya predicted, “Americans will be smiling again and happy days will be back on Wall Street.” “The United States will remain in an economic slump until summer but before the end of the year America will again be leading the world toward riches and prosperity,” she said.

VIENNA, Dec. 8 (#)—Friends of Prince Nicholas of Rumania said he stood ready today to renounce the royal purple and to play a commoner’s role in fustian with Mme. Deletj, his commoner bride. The third section of the supreme court at Bucharest yesterday formally declared the marriage of the young prince to Mme. Deletj “non-existent” and the declaration, it was reported here, forces on him the necessity of renouncing his membership in the royal family or abandoning his wife. His friends said he already had drafted the declaration of renunciation to submit to the court, the king and all political parties, as King Carol did under similar circumstances when he was crown prince and the way of his affections ran counter to the way of the king, their father. The court’s decision was interpreted as avoiding an annulment ceremony and leaving a means of escape from Carol who was furious over the ma

Rome, Dec. 8. — Foreign Minister Dino Grandi, with Signora Grandi and other members of his party arrived in Rome at noon today after their trip to Washington. The young foreign minister had already a long report of 100 pages to present to Premier Mussolini on his “most satisfactory mission” and his talks with President Hoover and Secretary Stimson. Signora Grandi’s report isn’t written yet, but she has a world of stories to tell little Franco and Simonetta, her two children, about the cheers their father received and all about the tall buildings and the subways and the big stores with escalators in New York. Most important for Franco and his sister, however, will be the huge cases of toys, sent by American friends, which will be given them in three installments.

BERLIN, Dec. 7. ()—Adolf Hitler, Germany’s fascist national socialist leader, is not ready to announce the economic reforms he intends to carry out if he comes into power, but the question of maintaining the gold standard, he said, will depend largely on the attitude of France. Nor does he plan a march on Berlin similar to the march on Rome by Premier Mussolini’s black-shirt bands a decade ago when the Italian fascists took over the helm of Italy. Instead of a coup d’etat, he indicated, he depends upon his national socialists to be invested with the governing power by way of the ballot box, in elections to choose members of the Reichstag. “The enemies of Nazism are lying of starvation, politically speaking,” he said last night. “That is, their adherents are dwindling while ours steadily increase. Wherever elections are held we land on top. Only today at Breslau in the university election

1931-09-11.text: WASHINGTON, Sept. 11. (AP)— Two hundred dead and unestimated property damage was reported today in the wake of two tropical hurricanes that were sweeping in almost opposite directions out of the Caribbean. The first, after lashing Belize, British Honduras, where 200 were reported killed, was described as moving into the southern part of the Gulf of Mexico, near Yucatan, with somewhat diminished intensity. The second had killed one person in San Juan, Puerto Rico, caused considerable property damage and cut off communication with the rest of the island. It was sweeping toward Haiti with Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic, almost directly in its path. The weather bureau expected it to pass near that city late today. With communication disrupted by the tropical storms, meager reports came from the stricken areas. From brief messages to the Red Cross, the navy department, t

Meagre Reports Indicate Disastrous Results In Honduras. TO GULF OF MEXICO. Hundreds Of Houses Blown Down; Number Injured Not Known. Two hurricanes were sweeping the Caribbean today. One was reported to have killed 150 to 200 at Belize, British Honduras, last night and today menaced the southern part of the Gulf of Mexico. The other killed at least one at San Juan, Puerto Rico and today was sweeping toward Haiti. Shortly before noon various weather bureaus on the Atlantic coast issued warnings of the San Juan hurricane over to pass near Santo Domingo late afternoon or early tonight. Belize, which is the capital of British Honduras, were put out of order by the storm. A flash from Tela, Honduras reported dead, and half the population homeless. Another message to Pan-American Airways from Belize field manager fixed the dead at 200. The Red Cross at Washington was advised by the manager of t

MARSEILLES, France, Sept. 11.—(AP)—Mahatma Gandhi, leaving Europe for the first time in 15 years, said the British government was facing such staggering domestic problems it was unlikely to refuse India self-government. A refusal would mean a renewal of the civil disobedience campaign and a boycott on British goods. Frenchmen stared at his loincloth. He told customs inspectors he had no tobacco, alcohol, firearms or narcotics; nothing but spinning wheels, goat milk, loincloths and reputation. His companion, the Pandit Malaviya, 70, had only mud and water from the river Ganges. He makes sacred images from the mud.

Summer's dying fury continued to harass the continent with tropical heat yesterday. Ten deaths were reported. Waves of torridity stifled millions from New England to the parched southwest plains and from the groves of Florida to the wheat fields of the northwest. And the weatherman’s forecasts indicated relief was not to be expected soon. Fleet mercury raced up 10 degrees in two hours in Charleston, W. Va., Friday to establish a record 103, and Chippewa Falls, Wis., and Ironwood, Mich., reported 98. New York roasted under 95, five degrees higher than the record September 11 of 1897, and the Central Park observatory, whose all-time September high of 101 was set in 1881, read 99 in the shade. Portland, Maine, with 92, reported the highest September 11 in fifty years. Schools were dismissed in Madison, Wis., Winona, Minn., and Omaha because of intense heat. Bathhouses were open and lifeguar

| London, Sept. 11.—(A.P.)—Philip Snowden's emergency taxation measures, producing $202,500,000 in additional revenue, went into force today as the British people from Mayfair to Limehouse cinched up their belts for the sake of national solvency. Cabinet members, school teachers, policemen and other government employees and the unemployed faced with resignation the fact that their remuneration would be sliced on Oct. 1 to effect a savings in administrative expenses of $350,160,000. The defense services, education and the road fund will contribute to this figure. Of all the drastic changes discussion centered chiefly around the measure increasing the tax on incomes to about $1.25 on $5, or 25 per cent and reducing the exemption limits.

LONDON, Sept. 11.—Philip Snowden, chancellor of the exchequer, searched the pockets of his countrymen Thursday, taxing rich and poor alike with $202,500,000 in new levies to balance the 1931-1932 budget and restore world confidence in British finance. His emergency budget, presented to the House of Commons, bristled with drastic assessments. The income tax standard rate, for instance, was boosted by six pence (12 cents), which means that every payer of the tax must turn one-fourth of his income over to the government. The Commons adjourned after agreeing to the tax increase resolutions without a vote, and next Tuesday was set for the debate on the budget. The acceptance of the budget resolutions on the first night is according to custom. The general rule is that government budget proposals are given immediate effect when they are made and challenged and debated later if at all. Great Ova

By RICHARD D. McMILLAN (United Press Staff Correspondent) MARSEILLES, France, Sept. 12— (UP)—The Mahatma Gandhi, the "great soul" bearing the blessings of millions of Indians, arrived here on Friday en route to the Indian round table conference at London. The Mahatma, clad in his customary loin cloth, with a scarf thrown loosely across his shoulders and a watch dangling from his waist, traveled second class from Bombay on the P. and O. liner Rajputana. He traveled across France by train to a channel port and continued to London. Gandhi was welcomed by a huge crowd. There were hundreds of telegrams and other messages for him. Officers and stewards of the Rajputana, officials of the steamship line, and local police had difficulty keeping the mob behind police lines. "I am going to London as a prisoner of the British government, but a willing prisoner," Gandhi said. "I cannot say anything a

London, Sept. 11. — Prime Minister MacDonald, opening the debate on the government's drastic economy bill in the House of Commons today, defended Procedure by orders in council as essential for speedy solution of the financial crisis. Mr. MacDonald promised that the power to issue orders in council would last only one month. He said the crisis temporarily had subsided, but the nation’s position must be entrenched before every measure that had been taken could be thrown to the winds. The financial position of the country must be sound as well as the budget balanced, he declared, and his duty in applying the national economy resolutions was no less difficult and unpleasant than that of Chancellor Snowden's yesterday.

1931-03-21.text: .PLYMOUTH, England, July 28 “Pi—The submarine Nautilus, in which Sir Hubert Wilkins plans to cross the North Pole under the ice, left today for Bergen, Norway, en route to the Arctic. Hundreds of Americans witnessed the departure of Sir Hubert, in his little craft as she passed alongside the Mauretania, just in from New York. Passengers aboard the liner cheered lustily.

WASHINGTON, March 21. (AP). Award of the distinguished flying cross to First Lieut. I. A. W., army air corps, of Enid, Okla., now stationed at Rockwell Field, California, for exceptional service in flying the Japanese ratification of the London naval treaty from Vancouver, British Columbia, to New York City, was announced today by the war department. Two planes assigned to rush the document across the continent in order that it would reach London in time for the formal ceremony of deposit set out from Vancouver. Lt. William

BUENOS AIRES, Mar. 21 ()—The Prince of Wales and Prince George who came here a fortnight ago to open the British trade exposition reached the end of their visit today. Three Argentine navy planes and two British corsair planes were primed to take them and their party shortly before noon down the River Plate to Montevideo, Uruguay, the next stop on their long journeys homeward, via Brazil.

New Delhi, India—(?)—Departing from his traditional attitude of non-cooperation with the government, Mahatma Gandhi today joined what might be termed a miniature round table conference which is to pave the way for the second round table conference to be held in London soon. Attired only in his loin cloth, which cost about a shilling, he sat at a massive walnut table in the sumptuous viceroy’s palace with blue-blooded Indian princes clad in resplendent silk and gold robes, stunning turbans and glistening jewels around him. At his right sat Viceroy Lord Irwin, who a year ago had him thrown in jail for his challenge to the British crown. Today's conference with the congress of Indian princes, which has been in session at New Delhi for several days, is for the purpose of preliminary work to the second round table conference at London and to measure the possibilities of cooperation between th

Glasgow, Scotland—#—The inbound Canadian Pacific liner Montclare ran aground Saturday afternoon on the Arran side of Little Cambrae Island, in the Firth of Clyde, in a dense fog. Six tugs were sent from Greenock to the liner’s assistance. The Montclare developed a dangerous list as the tide receded and lifeboats were lowered to carry the passengers ashore. The tugs which went to the scene picked up 200 passengers who had been landed on the rocky island. It was feared the Montclare had a bad hole. It struck a hidden reef.

ST. JOHNS, N. F., Mar. 21.—(#)— Search for the missing and completion of the rescue of survivors of the wreck of the steamer Viking depended today upon an improvement in weather and ice conditions. Bernt Balchen, skilled Arctic flier, with two companions was at St. John, New Brunswick, 686 miles away, waiting for weather which would permit them to fly their Sikorsky amphibian plane over the ice-filled wastes of White Bay in search for Varick Frissell, New York motion picture producer, and 25 others missing since the Viking blew up last Sunday night. The finding of two bodies has accounted for two of the 28 missing out of 155 aboard the Viking. A few miles off Horse Island, in White Bay, the rescue ship Sagona, with 110 survivors aboard, was fast in the ice. On the island where Captain Abram Kean, Jr., master of the Viking, and seven of his men, who must wait until ice conditions will per

BERLIN, March 20,—(AP)—Hermann Mueller, twice chancellor of the German Republic and one of the leaders of the revolution in November, 1918, died tonight after a prolonged illness. The political leader's wife and two daughters were at his bedside when he died at 10:45 p.m. The 54-year-old statesman had been in a coma for hours and his physicians had given up hope for recovery. Herr Mueller, who headed the sixth and nineteenth post-revolution German Cabinets, underwent an operation on Saturday for removal of a bladder abscess and gallstones after several days of acuteness. His condition improved somewhat, reviving hopes he might recover, but he suffered a relapse Monday night and steadily became worse. He became so weak yesterday that blood transfusions were resorted to. Inflammations of the right lung set in and he was conscious only momentarily since yesterday. Despite his robust appeara

BERLIN, March 21. (AP).—The band which, unflinching, wrote the principal German signature to the treaty of Versailles, was stilled today in death. Succumbing to a long illness, Dr. Hermann Mueller, twice German chancellor and one of the two or three most influential men of German postwar politics, passed away last night. He was 54 years old. He was in a comatose condition for several hours preceding the end which was brought about by thrombosis of the liver, complicated by pneumonia. A bladder operation last Saturday failed to aid him. Dr. Mueller first was a German chancellor for three months in 1920. He came to power the second time in June, 1928, remaining in office until March, 1930, when the present chancellor, Dr. Bruening, succeeded him.

1931-02-08.text: Brisbane, Australia, Feb. 7—(P)—All available police were rushed to the south side of the city during the night to warn residents of an impending flood. Rains have ceased but an enormous quantity of flood water up country had to find its way seaward. Coastal districts within 100 miles north and south of Brisbane were flooded. Seventy miles south of this city an automobile collided with a motor boat which was traveling on the flooded main stream. More than 1,000 people in this city were homeless today as a result of the floods. When the ground floor of the telephone building was flooded out, a plucky girl operator dressed in a swimming suit climbed through an upper window of the exchange and kept the lines open for several hours.

Berlin, Feb. 7.--(#)--Three times today Chancellor Bruening turned back the opposition in the Reichstag and the government whose fate seemed to hang by a thread before the Christmas recess emerged in full control, firmly entrenched in power and with a substantial majority in the parliament. Political observers saw this coming last Thursday when the chancellor, in a quiet but firm exposition of the country’s economic situation, told the deputies he was opposed to invoking the ‘dictatorship clause’ of the constitution and that the Reichstag must assume full responsibility for adopting the 1931 budget as speedily as possible. The Vote Today’s three-fold defeat took the starch out of the Communists and the National Socialists. A joint no-conference motion by both parties was defeated by a vote of 293 to 22.

PARIS, Feb. 5—(UP)—Bare legs, bare feet and painted toes protruding from scant sandals, all part of Jean Worth’s evening gown ensemble, created a sensation in the Paris fashion world today. In contrast, Worth’s models also wore long suede gloves and huge fur collars in the same ensemble. Long afternoon and evening skirts were slashed at the knee, revealing the leg during the process of walking. The skirts were reminiscent of the “sheath” skirts popular in 1910. There was a scarcity of printed silks in the display. There was much wool, wool lace, tweeds, jersey tussors, crepes satin, georgette, chiffon and lace. Pastel colors predominated, in chartreuse, champagne, shell pink, almond, green, grape, black and white. Navy blue was favored for day wear.

Rome, Feb. 7, (4)—Thomas Tittoni, one of the most active of Italian statesmen in the pre-Mussolini era, died here today. Tommaso Tittoni was one of the most prominent exponents of the pre-Fascist regime in Italy to rally to the cause of Mussolini. Few of his contemporaries in the kingdom had the wealth of experience in foreign affairs possessed by Tittoni. He was four times foreign minister, premier for a brief period, ambassador to London and Paris and in addition president of the senate from 1919 to 1929. He also served as first president of the Royal. In the summer of 1922, Tittoni visited the United States, being Italy's spokesman at the Institute of Politics at Williams College, Williamstown, Mass. Upon the adjournment of the institute he gave a number of lectures in different (Continued on page two)

Chicago, Feb. 7.—(A.P.)—Favored by nature with moisture, farmers in many sections of the parched middle west were hopeful today that the backbone of the three months’ drought had been broken. Reports from various sections of middle America last night told of rain or snow and the weather man held out further hope with a prediction for more moisture today. The prediction was for rain or snow in many parts of Illinois, Michigan, Indiana, Wisconsin, Iowa, Minnesota and North Dakota, with a possibility of showers in some sections of Missouri, Kansas and South Dakota. Illinois Gets Downpour, There was a veritable downpour in some localities in Illinois and it was welcomed particularly in the southern part of the state, where 250,000 residents in more than a score of communities have been apprehensive of a serious threat to their water supply. Farmers at Lerna, in the central Illinois region, s

LOS ANGELES, Feb. 7.—An underground explosion in front of the Orpheum theatre last night injured thirty-one, two seriously, in a crowd straining police lines at the Los Angeles showing of a talking picture. The film had just been completed and Fred Niblo, Hollywood director, was introducing members of the cast from the stage when the theatre and nearby buildings were rocked. The explosion was believed by authorities to have been caused by ignition of sewer gas caused by faulty electric wiring. A huge section of pavement shot into the air, lifting a taxicab with it and throwing men, women and children to the street. Two Badly Hurt. Two men, William Urquhart, aged 28, and Dave Freeman, aged 21, suffered concussions of the brain. Arthur Camp, chauffeur suffered cuts and bruises. George Delk, aged 28, driver of the demolished taxicab, miraculously escaped death. He was found to be only cut a

BUFFALO, N. Y., Feb. 7.—(AP)—At least 25 fishermen were carried out into Lake Erie today when a northwest wind broke off a huge section of the ice on which they were fishing. Identity of the men could not be determined immediately, but marine officials began compiling a list of those probably adrift from the license numbers of automobiles parked along the shore. The men were drifting in the open lake about three miles off the Buffalo harbor. It was feared the wind and waves soon would smash the floe to pieces beneath the men. When the ice floe broke away, four of the men on it leaped ashore and from their stories coast guards gleaned meager details of the accident.

NEW YORK, Feb. 7. (AP) — Amelia Earhart, transatlantic flier, and Geo. Palmer Putnam, publisher and explorer, were married today at the home of Mr. Putnam’s mother, Mrs. Frances Putnam, at Noank, Conn. Announcement of the marriage was made by Mr. Putnam’s secretary in New York and confirmed by relatives at Noank. Judge Arthur Anderson performed the ceremony, which was witnessed by the groom’s mother and Judge Anderson’s son Robert. The bride said she would retain her maiden name and continue her executive position with an aviation company operating hourly planes between New York, Philadelphia and Washington. She said she would be at her desk Monday and that her husband would be at work as usual in the New York publishing firm of Brewer and Warren with which he is associated.

1931-12-31.text: Wellington, N. Z., Jan. 1 (Friday)—(UP)—Some two hundred shepherds and fishermen on the Chatham Islands, 414 miles southeast of here, celebrated the arrival of 1932 today while milkmen in the United States were making the rounds on the last day of 1931. This small British colony in the southern Pacific was the first place in the world to welcome the new year for which the bell in the little church on Hanson Island pealed out midnight the great boom of Big Ben in London struck twelve, noon, and 7 a. m. risers in New York were just throwing back the covers. The Chatham Islands are the nearest point to the starting line of time. This starting line is the admiralty's date-line. It is made to curve east and west of the 180th meridian in such a way that it lies always in the ocean. The Chatham Islands lie just to the east of this line. From the islands the new year is now racing westward along

Calcutta, India, Dec. 30 (P)— Viceroy Lord Willingdon in unmistakable terms today laid the gage of battle at Mahatma Gandhi's feet but adorned it with an olive branch. In an address before the European association he said British authorities would invoke every means within their power to resist a possible renewal of the civil disobedience campaign by the Indian Nationalist Congress and expressed the hope that Gandhi would call off its activities "even at this eleventh hour." "I want to make it perfectly clear," he said, "that we are determined to go ahead as rapidly as possible with the work of constitutional reform and that non-cooperation will not be permitted." Appealing to the whole of India to put aside distrust and suspicion he said, "I venture to hope that even at this eleventh hour Mr. Gandhi will call a halt to his activities and I will agree to cooperate with his powerful influ

LONDON, Dec. 30 (#)--Great Britain took the initiative in attacking the reparations problem today by asking 10 European governments to meet at Lausanne, Switzerland, January 18, for a conference which will attempt to tide over the present German economic and financial crisis. "Without American participation there can be no permanent solution," one government official said, explaining the way still was open for the United States to send either an official or an unofficial observer.

HOLLYWOOD, Cal, Dec. 30.—(# Tyrone Power, 62, descendant of one of England's most famous stage families and himself a dramatic actor of renown, died suddenly from a heart attack here today in his club rooms. He succumbed but three weeks after his arrival here from New York to re-enter films after 45 years before the footlights.

London, Dec. 31.—(A. P.)—A Reuters’ dispatch from Heisingfors said today that the vote of rural constituencies of Finland in the prohibition referendum showed 78,958 for repeal, 18,868 for maintenance of the present law, and 905 for modifications.

NEW YORK, Dec 30. (U®)—Names were called and threats made before the opening of tonight's session of the Culbertson-Lenz contract bridge match at the Waldorf-Astoria hotel. Sir Derrick Wernher, an English nobleman, was waiting in the press room when Eli Culbertson and his wife, Josephine, arrived. Wernher, who weighs 230 pounds and stands a head taller than Culbertson, asked Culbertson when he intended to accept a challenge made last summer. Culbertson denied issuing the challenge and suddenly the Englishman yelled: "You're a yellow backslider, a cheap nobody." Culbertson clenched his fists, advanced on the huge man and screamed: "You call me yellow, I'll knock your teeth down your throat, you yellow remittance man, you lopsided slab of beef-steak." Friends separated the would-be combatants and Culbertson proceeded to the tournament room.

LONDON, DEC. 31. (AP).--A Reuters dispatch from Helsingfors, Finland, today said the count of votes cast in the capital city on the national prohibition referendum showed 65,900 in favor of abolishing the dry law to 13,000 for continuing prohibition. Only 600, it said, voted for legalized wine and beer. A later dispatch from Helsingfors said that the vote in 88 rural constituencies showed 78,953 for repeal, 18,858 for maintenance of the present law and 905 for modification, giving the wets a majority of 59,190 in those districts.

HELSINGFORS, Finland, Dec. 31. (/P)—Tabulation of about one-sixth of the total votes in Finland’s prohibition referendum indicated today that proponents of repeal would have the endorsement of at least half the ballots. At 7 p. m. 122,122 votes had been counted. Seventy-eight per cent of them were for repeal, 21 per cent for continuing the present law, and only one per cent for modification to permit light wines and beer. What surprised observers most was the fact that 60 per cent of the repeal votes were cast by women. The vote in the capital does not determine the national outcome, but supporters of repeal were confident that their large vote here was an indication of how the rest of the Finnish cities would go, and their prediction was that the prohibition laws are doomed. Government officials apparently thought so, for T. M. Kivimaki, minister of justice, began drafting a bill for go

1931-10-31.text: ‘London, Oct. 31—The story of 20 industrial revival in Great Britain since the suspension of the gold standard occupied a prominent place in the newspapers today. The pick-up was said to be especially noticeable in the cotton and textile industries, with iron, steel, coal and pottery showing improvement, though to a less extent. ‘The Daily Mail, which made a special feature of the revival story said a considerable increase was noted in the number of employees at the Bolton Cotton Mills, while at Bradford and Nottingham full time has replaced part time in a number of textile mills affecting several thousand workers.

LONDON, Oct. 30. (49)—Stanley Baldwin, whose conservative party has 472 of the 616 seats in the next house of commons, already has given assurance he will not attempt to run the government, it was learned today. Mr. Baldwin agreed, it was understood, to a suggestion that conservatives get no more than 12 of the portfolios in the next cabinet. That cabinet is expected to have the usual 21 members, and 12 is considered a modest total for the conservatives in view of their overwhelming parliamentary strength.

LONDON, Oct. 30. UPH-Mahatma Gandhi and other delegates to the second round table conference were invited by the lord chamberlain today to attend a party at Buckingham palace next Thursday. Commenting on his mode of dress, Gandhi said “I will wear my habitual dress of loom cloth, shawl and sandals. If the king or the government prescribe European or any other form of dress I will be obliged to decline the royal invitation.”

LONDON, Oct. 31—(4)—Nearly 15,000,000 pounds in bar gold, worth $75,000,000 at the normal rate of exchange, was withdrawn today from the Bank of England—the greatest total ever taken out in a single day. The withdrawal constitutes the first step in carrying out arrangements which the bank just completed for paying out two-fifths of the $250,000,000 credit jointly extended last August by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Bank of France to support the pound sterling. It is assumed that the remaining 5,000,000 pounds needed for the payment which has been arranged will be met from the bank's reserve of foreign currencies.

TOKYO, Oct. 21—(UP)—An unfavorable impression has been created in Japan by the reported conclusion of a treaty between the British minister at Nanking and the Chinese Nationalist government dealing with abolition of extra-territorial privileges. Japanese newspapers are becoming increasingly outspoken in criticism of Great Britain's policies in the Far East, and several have accused the British government of "intrigues" with China.

PY AetcrTom, Oct. 30, U.P)—Revelation that Herbert Hoover opposed creation of a separate American expeditionary force in France and recommended infiltration of American troops with French and British armies is contained in a book entitled “Newton D. Baker: America at War,” by Frederick Palmer, just issued. Mr. Hoover's recommendations, made just before the United States entered the war, were rejected. President Wilson, Secretary of War Baker and General Pershing were strongly in favor of maintaining a separate army. Mr. Hoover, it is disclosed, also later urged class exemptions from the draft for agriculturalists of the “foremen, manager and ownership type,” but his plan was rejected as being “too indefinite for practical application.” Under the heading “Herbert Hoover’s Military Plan,” Palmer said: “Abstractly, the infiltration of our man-power in small units into the veteran European a

Lympne, Kent, England, Oct. 31. —P)—Miss Peggy Salaman, 19-year-old society girl, took off last night from Lympne airport in an attempt to set a distance record on a flight to South Africa. “Cheerio, Mummy,” she said as she stepped into the cockpit. Miss Salaman is a pretty fair-haired girl, product of a Mayfair drawing room, who has always enjoyed everything money could buy. Suddenly she tired of it all, took up flying and only last night informed her family of her South African plan. It was the surprise of their lives. With her she took a revolver as a precaution against dangers in case of a forced descent in the wilds of the dark continent. Gordon Store accompanied her to take his turn at the controls.

FARIS, Oct. 31.—(7)—A prospect of immediate activity on the question of European finances, especially debts and reparations payments, as soon as Premier Pierre Laval arrives Monday was evident today. Petit Parisien printed a dispatch from the liner Ile De France on which the premier is returning, saying that an international conference on debts and reparations may be held in December. The premier’s first public appearance after his return from Washington will be at a luncheon at the American club Thursday. He accepted an invitation by radio and it is believed he will speak on his mission to the United States. The Petit Parisien also said the premier will see the German ambassador, Dr. Leopold Von Hoesch, as soon as he returns and that he may telephone directly to Chancellor Bruening at Berlin. Goes To Berlin Ambassador Von Hoesch has gone to Berlin to receive the chancellor’s instruction

1931-09-14.text: Vero Beach, Fla., Sept. 13.—(AP)—Three men were killed as an airplane carrying pictures of hurricane scenes in Belize, British Honduras, crashed in a citrus grove at Oslo, near here. The bodies of G. R. McBroom and George H. Gibson, pilot and co-pilot, and of E. A. Edwards, Miami newspaper photographer, were found in the wreckage. The plane was making a chartered night flight from Miami to Atlanta when the crash occurred.

Belize, British Honduras, Sept. 14. —(U. P.)—(By Radio to the United Press.) —Between 1,500 and 2,000 persons are dead in the hurricane-crushed city of Belize, it was believed today. The survivors, moving swiftly among the ruins, burning the debris—and bodies—to prevent an epidemic, were too pressed with the immediate demands for relief and prevention of further disaster, to engage in an authoritative check. Reports made of another storm of hurricane intensity which was reported veering towards the north of this city lent desperation to the situation. There is little left here, however, to engage the grip of a new storm. Nothing but a few concrete houses are left standing. Today the small supply of water was diminishing. All of the regular supply, stored in tanks, was destroyed in the storm, and the rain water gathered by survivors will last only a short time. Fear of a cholera epidemic

CALSHOT, Eng., Sept. 13.—-(4)— Flight Lieutenant G. H. Stainforth set a new world's record of 386.1 miles an hour in a seaplane over a three kilometer course here today. Great Britain also won permanent possession of the Schneider cup when Flight Lieutenant J. N. Boothman flew another seaplane 271 miles at an average of 240.08 miles an hour over a 31-mile course. LONDON, Sept. 13 (4%—Breaking a tradition of 50 years, Mahatma Gandhi gave up his usual prayer period today in order to address the American people by radio in an international broadcast. Although it was the first time in his eventful life that the Mahatma faced an invisible audience of so many millions, he approached the microphone like a veteran actor, betraying no nervousness, never faltering and never having to search for an appropriate phrase. The tiny “cell” in the east end settlement house, from which Gandhi spoke, was so cold his teeth chattered as he stood before the microphone. He was bundled up in thick, homespun shawls. Complete silence prevailed as Gandhi said:

LONDON, Sept. 14 (UP).—Flight Lieutenant G. H. Stainforth's official average time in winning the Schneider cup was 379.05 miles an hour, the Royal Aero Club announced today. Stainforth was timed by stop watches at the race course off the Solent as reaching his highest speed at 404.275 miles an hour. The official times clocked by the automatic timing device for the best four of six runs were: 373.85, 388.67, 369.87, and 383.81 miles an hour.

ALSHOT, ENGLAND, Sept. M—England held the world’s speed record of the air today, 388.67 miles per hour, established by Flight Lieutenant G. H. Stainforth in the Schneider cup races. Driving a supermarine Rolls-Royce S-6 seaplane, a tiny machine that shot like a bullet over the race course along the Solent, Stainforth attained a speed never before equaled by man. Six times the plane swept over the course. The young English flier set a world record of an average of 379.05 miles per hour for the best four of six successive trials. The best times, counted as record achievements, were: 373.85, 388.67, 369.87, and 383.81 miles an hour. England had a walk-over in the races due to the withdrawal of France and Italy, and obtained permanent possession of the Schneider trophy when Flight Lieutenant J. H. Booth established a record of 340.1 miles an hour. His speed of 343.1 miles an hour on the firs

By United Press; LONDON, Sept. 14.—Rumors that Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald might become British ambassador to Washington or viceroy of India were current today in political circles. The News of the World, owned by Lord Riddell, a close friend of David Lloyd George, understood that MacDonald might go to Washington "in circumstances which would enable him to discuss with full authority the question of war debts." The Sunday News-Chronicle predicted that the premier would be made Lord MacDonald of Lossiemouth, and viceroy of India. Philip Snowden, chancellor of the exchequer, will become Lord Snowden of Tilford, the newspaper predicted. Stanley Baldwin was expected to become prime minister in time to introduce a tariff budget early in May.

Tegucigalpa, Honduras, Sept. F)—The Honduran Consul at Belize, British Honduras, reported today that a plague has broken out in that city following the hurricane and tidal wave. Two unidentified Honduran schooners were reported caught in the hurricane area between Puerto Cortez and Belize and sunk with the loss of crews and passengers. President Mejia Colindres has ordered North Coast authorities to dispatch several small ships with doctors, foodstuffs and medicines to Belize to help the stricken population.

1931-02-24.text: PARIS, Feb. 24.—France and Great Britain today reached an accord, in principle, on Naval Limitation. Foreign Minister Briand announced the accord which was merely verbal and will not become definite until after the British representatives have consulted Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy.

NEW DELHI, INDIA, Feb. 24—(?)— Behind the scenes of the present political drama in India is an English woman, Miss Madeline Slade, daughter of Sir Edmund Slade, for many years commander in chief of British naval forces in India. Renouncing all the pleasures, comforts and amenities of everyday existence, Miss Slade has embraced asceticism and the mysteries of Hindu life and has become the ardent disciple of Mahatma Gandhi, who took her to the Sacred City of Benares and after immersing her in the holy Ganges river, initiated her into the mysteries of the Hindu religion. She has shaved her head in monastic fashion, given all her money to the poor, goes barefooted, burned all her European attire and wears only the cheapest homespun Hindu garments. She has taken the Hindu name of “Mira Bai.” When asked by her British friends if she is “Miss Slade” she replied: “No. Miss Slade has been dead an

PARIS, Feb. 24—(P)—An agreement between the French and British foreign ministers, Aristide Briand and Arthur Henderson, on the conditions under which France will adhere to the London naval treaty was virtually reached this afternoon. Mr. Henderson and A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, will probably leave for Rome tonight in an effort to obtain the adhesion of Italy to the accord. If they succeed, the London tripartite treaty between the United States, Great Britain and Japan will become a five-power treaty.

New London, Conn., Feb. 23.—Coast guard boats scurried through the waters of Narragansett bay and the Atlantic ocean today in running fights with at least two rum boats and on two salvage missions. Reports which had been received here tonight at the destroyer force headquarters, still incomplete pending the arrival of the service boats involved in the wide flung activities, told stories of the sinking of one rum boat and the escape of two other rum runners under heavy coast guard fire. A speed boat, identified by Commander M. J. Ryan, chief of staff of the coast guard destroyer force, as the Monolola, was one of the two rum runners which escaped after being hammered by one-pound shells in Narragansett bay. One of the service boats which engaged the Monolola, reports received here indicated, also encountered the British liquor supply vessel Accuracy in Narragansett bay, but the rum ship e

PARIS (Feb. 23.—(AP)—Arthur Henderson, British foreign secretary, and A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, came here tonight from London to take a hand in the Franco-Italian naval negotiations which hitherto have been carried on between R. L. Craigie, the British expert and Count Rene Massigli for France. They went into conference immediately with Aristide Briand and Charles Dumont, minister of the navy. Should France and Italy fail to reach an accord on their naval program, a building race between those countries might ensue, such a race, it is felt in naval circles, would imperil the London treaty and might oblige Great Britain to invoke its safeguard clause and build in proportion to Italy and France. Such a course on the part of Great Britain, it was said, might entail similar activity by the United States and Japan and thus destroy the whole London agreement. These possibil

HOLLYWOOD, Calif., Feb. 24, H —It is a brave man who would attempt to name the six most beautiful women in motion pictures, yet Cecil Beaton, London artist, came forth today with his selection as friends advised him to lay low to escape the aftermath. Here, in Beaton’s opinion, are the six most beautiful women of the films: Norma Shearer, Marion Day, Greta Garbo, Marlene Dietrich, Lilyan Tashman and Ina Claire.

LONDON, Feb. 24—A momentous battle of wills in which the Mahatma M. K. Gandhi has pitted himself against the government of Great Britain entered its critical stage today with the future of the great subcontinent of India at stake. Whether the 320,000,000 Indians shall go forward peacefully toward the set goal of Federal Government or shall renew rebellion and bloodshed for complete independence from British rule will be decided by the outcome of conferences between the slight, bent man who is called “the great soul” and the tall, stately representative of King George, Viceroy Lord Irwin. Already stirred to tense feelings by fresh disorders and fighting in Bombay after almost a year of riots, battles and wholesale arrests growing out of the civil disobedience movement, the natives awaited a decision with great uncertainty. Lord Irwin has consulted the home government by telegraph as to fu

LONDON, Feb. 26--Sidney Chas. G. Dawes today set at rest reports that he intended to resign as ambassador to the Court of St. James and return to America, either in connection with the forthcoming world’s fair at Chicago or political work. The fair, he said, was a year ahead of itself so far as preparations were concerned and everything was progressing so very favorably that his presence at Chicago was not needed. “Unless some unforeseen circumstances arise,” he told the Associated Press, “I expect to serve my full term as ambassador. (This would mean another two years). “I see no reason now why I should have to leave here.” He paused and then added: “I am 65 years old. What more should I want to do?” The general made it clear, however, that there was a period last year when it seemed possible that he might have to resign to devote his energies to the fair. 1931-05-27.text: LE BOURGET, FRANCE, MAY 27. (AP).—Captain Frank Hawks landed here at 6:10 p. m., winning a bet that he could have breakfast in London, luncheon in Berlin and dinner in Paris in the same day. He left Paris at 2:20 a.m., going first to Croydon, Eng., airport, then to Berlin.

LONDON, May 27.—Russian airplanes and warships today circled above the spot where Soviet submarine No. 9 of the Baltic fleet sank Friday in a pool of oil. Although the Soviet government remains silent on the tragedy, dispatches from Riga, Latvia said it was understood the craft went down after an explosion, presumably with all hands, about 100 miles from Helsingfors, Finland. Moscow dispatches said the submersible failed to rise after making a dive during maneuvers with other vessels of the fleet. Auxiliary ships were sent to the scene, it was said, but were unsuccessful in attempts to raise it. Destroyers and planes stood by in hope of being of assistance. The fact that the water's depth at that point is from 60 to 110 fathoms led experts here to say that it would be an extremely difficult task to recover the vessel. The number of the crew or the extent of the casualties was unknown.

BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., May 27.—At a conference in London on what to do about the world’s surplus wheat, it broke up as usual. They even eat cornbread during the conference. Russia proposed exporting wheat on a quota basis. We wouldn't agree to it, so another conference breaks up with us being the “goat.” Will we ever quit sending delegations off to conferences? We just wait for a conference to get in wrong with somebody: There should be a heavy export duty on “good will” groups and delegates to conferences. We have had so many conferences that we are even sore at each other here at home. Yours, . ut. a ge.

LAINDON, England, May 26 — (AP) Brief dispatches from Moscow and Riga brought to London tonight the news that the Russian submarine No. 9, of the Baltic Fleet, had sunk last Friday during maneuvers in the Gulf of Finland. The sinking of the submarine was supposed to have been due to an explosion aboard. There was no indication as to how many men made up the crew of the submarine or how large the casualty list might be.

LONDON, May 26 (#)—Radio messages received at Lloyd’s Land End station near midnight tonight said a steamship believed to be the Portuguese Corretora Primeiro was afire at latitude 45 degrees 40 minutes north and longitude 7 degrees 55 minutes west, and the fate of the crew was uncertain. The British steamship Dunkwa, which gave the first report, said the steamer was badly afire from end to end and that there had been several explosions. Mystery over fate of the crew resulted from conflicting, and apparently garbled, wireless reports from the Dunkwa and the German steamship Ubena, both of which seem to be nearby. The Dunkwa was reported as messaging it was alongside and had lowered a boat. The Ubena gave the name of the ship as the Corretora Primeiro. It reported the ship was entirely in flames and that it carried a cargo of gasoline. Another message from the Ubena which the receiving st

WASHINGTON, May 27. (AP) Its position explained to the world at the London international wheat conference, the farm board will intensify its campaign for domestic acreage reduction this summer and next fall. The board, which has repeatedly said the cure for low prices lies in growing wheat equal to home consumption needs, has set as its goal a cut of 20 to 25 per cent in winter wheat sown next fall. Such a reduction, board officials believe, plus a cut of 12 to 14 per cent in spring wheat planted this year which may be further reduced by adverse weather, would be a remarkable stimulus to improved prices. Samuel R. McKelvie, — grain member and one of the United States delegates to the London meeting, held up acreage reduction as this country's solution for the over-production crisis and opposed all proposals for export agreements. PARIS, (UP).-—Frank M. Hawks, American speed flier, returned late Wednesday after an all-day flight around Europe and announced himself ready for a big meal. He had taken his breakfast coffee in London; his beer and venison for lunch in Berlin and he had beefsteak and wild strawberries in Paris for dinner. “I worked up a bigger and bigger appetite all day long and now I’m ready for a good dinner,” he said on arrival. “There was almost perfect flying weather throughout, with the exception of a few local thunderstorms which I avoided.” Official timers said he took off from Le Bourget field near Paris at 8:16 a.m., arrived at London at 9:35 a.m., left London at 10:18 a.m., arrived at Berlin at 1:36 p.m., left Berlin at 3:12 p.m. and was back at Le Bourget at 6:07 p.m.

SANDRINGHAM, England, May 26—(f)—While the villagers of Sandringham displayed flags to mark the occasion, Queen Mary today quietly celebrated her sixty-fourth birthday with Members of the royal family and a few friends. Messages of congratulations from many parts of the world poured into the village and the queen personally opened birthday gifts from her children and grandchildren. There was no public ceremony.

1931-11-24.text: Threat of “real war” in Manchuria in event President Chiang Kai-Shek of China combines his forces with the Manchurian troops of Chang Hsueh-Liang, as indicated in reports, came from Tokyo today. A Peiping dispatch to the London Daily Mail said Japanese troops in Manchuria were moving southward toward Chinchow with a view to crushing all military and political forces hostile to Japan. A new proposal to deal with the Manchurian conflict was evolved Monday in Paris. It contained only a vague provision for the withdrawal of Japanese troops, and so was expected to prove unsatisfactory to China. The Tokyo government instructed its Washington ambassador to reassure the United States that Japan had not violated the nine-power treaty, the Briand-Kellogg pact or the covenant of the League of Nations. The ambassador had informed Tokyo the United States was evidencing concern about Japanese military

LONDON, Nov. 24 — (INS) — Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, exhausted by his extended labors here in connection with the Indian round table conference, is threatened with a nervous breakdown, it was learned today. Gandhi had been sleeping only three hours out of 24 since his arrival in London, but during the past few days has begun to sleep for an hour or two each afternoon. His associates, fearing that he might suffer a stroke, have insisted that his automobile be supplied at all times with first aid equipment, The Mahatma and those who accompanied him here from India are scheduled to sail from either Trieste or Venice, on December 11 or 12 on their return voyage.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 24.—(UP)—The United States government intends to take no action one way or the other on the proposed rise in British tariffs, it was indicated authoritatively today. The tariff problems of Great Britain were felt in administration quarters to be purely a domestic concern in which the United States cannot become involved.

(International News Service) LONDON, Nov. 24.—The first thing in the nature of a threat to reach Mahatma M. K. Gandhi since he came here for the Indian round table conference was delivered at his headquarters today. It was a package containing 4 strong ropes accompanied by a letter telling the champion of Indian independence to go hang himself in Hyde Park. The writer offered to assist. Gandhi is being heavily guarded by police and detectives. Wherever he goes one police car precedes that in which he rides and another follows it. The Mahatma, exhausted by his extended labors here, is threatened with a nervous breakdown, International News Service learned today.

Moscow, Nov. 24--(i—Rusiaia prepared today to return to a National day of rest on December 1, by authority of the council of the people's commissars. The Holiday “Slagger system” under which industry kept going continuously, Sunday, Monday and every day, while the “day off” for the workers varied with the individuals’ preferences, or the arrangements among trades, is to be abandoned. Except for co-operative stores, dining halls, transportation and other agencies serving the cultural and living needs of the people, the holiday for everybody will fall every sixth day. It will not fall on a fixed day of the week, however, and Sunday will be recognized no more than under the present regime. The sixth, twelfth, eighteenth, twenty-fourth and thirtieth days of the month will be the holidays. Working hours will be reduced, at the same time, from 6½ to 6 hours a day. TOKIO, Nov. 24—(AP)—A “real war” in Manchuria was predicted in authoritative circles here today if Chiang Kai-Shek, Chinese president, goes to the north to join forces with Chiang Hsueh-Liang, former Manchurian governor and friend of General Ma Chan-Shan. The statement was prompted by reports received here that such a plan is under way. The reports, official circles said, indicate Chiang already is moving his troops northward and that he has reached Honan. A belief prevailed here that the president might establish himself at Peiping if the League of Nations made a decision unsatisfactory to the Nanking government. The Japanese reaction to such a move, it was said, would be an increase in the military force at Tientsin, such as authoritative circles claim is allowed under the Boxer protocol. OO A Metter) drive into the rough country southwest of Mukden in Manchuria was begun today by several battalions of Japanese railway guards, it was announced today, against a force of Chinese bandits believed to be in the area and which has been estimated as high as 12,000. Military authorities here said they considered the drive "a local affair to stamp out banditry" which has threatened the South Manchurian railway and it was emphasized that the move has no bearing on the reported concentration of Chinese troops at Chinchow. The Japanese forces have orders to drive the bandits west of the Liaohio river. Perhaps half of them, it was reported here, are gypsy soldiers who have been raiding villages and living off the country. By The Associated Press Paris, Nov. 24.—The 12 members of the League of Nations council after another session this morning made no progress toward a solution of the Manchurian problem and a disposition was to show to await a purported new plan of Dr. Wellington Koo, new Chinese foreign minister, is said to have forwarded from Nanking today.

1931-06-02.text: CARNOUSTIE, Scotland, June 2. (AP)—Paced by MacDonald Smith, returning to his homeland in search of his first major golf title, nine leading American professionals competing in the British Open golf championship today qualified for the tournament proper, beginning tomorrow. Smith’s record-breaking 71 at Old Carnoustie, in the sunshine, added to his record-breaking 70 at Panmure, Barry, in the rain yesterday, gave him medalist honors with a 36 hole total of 141. Seven strokes back of Smith came Horton Smith and Johnny Farrell each with 148. Tony Manero scored 149, Gene Sarazen 151, Joe Turnesa 152, Joe Kirkwood 154 and Willie Hunter and Tommy Armour 155. The two qualifying rounds were played at Old Carnoustie and at Panmure, 18 holes at each. The tournament will be played on Old Carnoustie, one of the stiffest golf tests in Scotland, at 72 holes of medal play, the first 36 tomorrow and Th

QUEBEC, June 2. — (UP) — A new page was written in the history of St. Lawrence shipping when the Empress of Britain, newest, largest and fastest liner in the Canadian Pacific fleet, glided into the new wharf at Wolfe's Cove, above Quebec, at 10 p. m. last night, 5 days, 13 hours and 25 minutes after she had left Southampton. The trip from Cherbourg was completed in 5 days, 5 hours and 25 minutes, both of these times being St. Lawrence route records.

HAVRE, France, June 2. (AP)— Texas Guinan, New York night club hostess, was confronted today with a shower of marriage proposals. One of them was from Harry Sleet, of London, who offered to marry her so that she could enter England as an Englishman's wife and later obtain a divorce. She said she was willing to marry either an Englishman or a Frenchman if “it helps me out of this mess.” Judith Dean, toe dancing member of her troupe, and Ralph Cook, comedian, tried to obtain permission of the American consul to be married with a license obtained in New York but he refused on the grounds that three days would be required to get the necessary French legal papers. As the last hope vanished that they would be allowed to go to Paris, the entertainers’ spirits sunk to a new low. Huddled in the bar dining room of their emigrant hotel, they listened mournfully to the plunk of a guitar and a dancer

(By the Associated Press) ROME, June 1.— Premier Mussolini has dissolved all organizations of Catholic youths in Italy by decree and according to good sources tonight Pope Pius XI is expected to recall the papal nuncio to Rome. It is said the pontiff may even sever diplomatic relations with Italy. Regarded as Violation Since the pope regards the concordat with Rome as violated and as he holds this concordat and the Lateran treaty to be inseparable, many observers believe there might arise the question of denunciation of the Roman settlement. This might result in the pope's returning to the state of “voluntary prisoner” in the Vatican. This new development followed an order from the Vatican that the editor of the semiofficial newspaper Osservatore Romano should discontinue its anti-Fascist editorial campaign and a similar order to editors of Fascist papers to stop publishing anti-Catholic

HAVRE, FRANCE, June 2.—()—Texas Guinan not only will have to leave France tomorrow afternoon, but she will have to pay her own fare back home, the director of the French Lines said today. “Her visa stipulated that she and her girls were not coming to France to work,” he said, “and it’s not our fault that she has to go back. They can go any way they want to, but it will not be at the expense of this line.” The Broadway entertainer spent this afternoon posing for an American news reel photographer and sorting out several proposals of marriage which she said she had received. She said nothing regarding reports that she had been offered a job at Monte Carlo and word from the Casino management there said no official offer had been made.

Ottawa, June 2. (UP)—Approximately 200 products in wide general use and manufactured in the United States and other countries for exportation into Canada were subject today to the new, higher tariff rates—some as high as 40 per cent—announced by Premier R. B. Bennett. Many of the rates strike directly at the pocketbooks of the American farmer, as well as the manufacturer, and are intended to aid industry and employment in this country. The increases, which went into effect immediately upon being read in the House of Commons by the premier except in stipulated instances, are radical in nature and affect nearly every product produced for export from the United States. Although many see the new tariff as a retaliatory measure against the tariff wall placed around the United States with passage of the Smoot-Hawley measure, Premier Bennett in his budget speech indicated the increases were a r

ROME, June 2.—(UP)—The split between the Vatican and the Fascist government over Fascist charges of political activities by Catholic lay organizations reached a deadlock today. A truce prevailed, but formal negotiations to prevent a rupture of the concordat establishing the Vatican as a sovereign state were suspended. Only unofficial negotiations were proceeding, since the pope's protests against anti-Catholic organizations in Italy were made as the Bishop of Rome, not as the temporal head of the Vatican state. Efforts to arrive at a peace agreement were being made through persons having no diplomatic rank, although fully conversant with Italian-Vatican relations. The government decided to regard the Knights of Columbus playgrounds, which are run by Americans, as part of the whole question of Catholic clubs. The playgrounds therefore were still closed today. PARIS, June 2.—-(UP)—The ministry of interior today ordered the deportation of Texas Guinan and her company of show girls, who were barred from landing in France when they reached Le Havre last Friday on the liner Paris. They will be sent back on the Paris tomorrow. The ministry urged the police to take extra precautions against any plot to liberate the girls and smuggle them into Paris. Miss Guinan, her girls and her white horse, Waco, were barred under the labor laws, on the ground that they would deprive unemployed French cabaret performers of a livelihood. Miss Guinan had planned to open a cabaret in Paris in partnership with Harry Piicer. England also has barred her entry.

1931-11-06.text: By the Associated Press LONDON, Nov. 5.—Clothed only in a loincloth and shawl, Mahatma Gandhi attended a formal reception today at Buckingham Palace and stood before the emperor from whom he has been trying for years to wrest all of India. It was the first time the humble ‘little Nationalist leader, who claims to represent 60,000,000 untouchables and 300,000,000 other Indians, had met George V, and he seemed to like it immensely. “The king and queen were most friendly and gracious,” he said. “I also liked the Prince of Wales.” The prince had come by airplane from Liverpool to attend the stately tea party at the royal palace to which 600 guests were invited. Before the function was half over, Mr. Gandhi abruptly left the palace, for he has no patience with social gatherings and the conversation usual on such occasions bores him. The Mahatma showed none of the signs of awe frequently manif

DEAL, England, Nov. 6. (INS)—Lifeboats and tugs were rushed today to the assistance of the United States shipping board steamer Hybert, which went aground on Goodwin sands and was reported in a dangerous position. The vessel was close inshore, looming mountain-like through a grey mist. The sea was calm, and it was believed that part of the cargo was being thrown overboard in an effort to get the ship refloated. The Hybert is a freighter of 6,500 tons, built for the United States shipping board in 1920.

CAPE TOWN, Union of South Africa, Nov. 5---(AP)—Peggy Salaman, 19-year old British society girl, stepped out of her airplane here today after a flight from England in the record time of five and one-half days and apologized for arriving so soon to beat the “silly old records.” “The nearest approach to hell I have experienced,” was her characterization of the flight over Africa. Although she and her co-pilot, Gordon Store, cut a whole day off the previous record set by the late Glen Kidston, they loafed on the last 500-mile lap from Kimberley. The pair were given a rousing welcome by a large crowd at the airdrome, many of whom had been waiting for hours.

London, Nov. 6—(4.F.)—Japan’s side of the story of severe fighting in Manchuria, contained in a dispatch to the London Daily Mail from Mukden, places the responsibility on the Chinese troops under General Ma Cheng-Shan and charges that the Chinese forces attacked after first hoisting the flag of truce. Many Japanese were wounded in the engagement, the dispatch said. Japanese troops, it added, arrived at the bridge over the Nonni river and found it destroyed. Crossing the river by ferries, they found two smaller bridges also destroyed. They then crossed marshes toward the hills of Hsingan, three miles to the north of the main bridge, and countered the main line of General Ma's army, which included 5,000 infantry, 20 guns, 12 French mortars and 50 cavalry troops guarding the flanks. There was a brief skirmish, the Japanese reported, and the Chinese raised a white flag, but as the Japanese

London, Nov. 5—(7)—A Reuters agency dispatch from Tokyo today said the Japanese Rengo news agency received a message from Mukden, Manchuria, saying Yaan-Chin-Kal, enemy of the Manchurian governor, Chang-Sueh-Liang, had formally established a new government in the province of Mukden, independent of Chang. The dispatch to the Rengo News agency said only three Japanese companies bore the brunt of the severe fighting north of the Nonni river, which began Wednesday. They opposed Chinese forces more numerous and possessing cavalry and artillery. Considerable losses appeared to have been suffered by the Chinese. The war office here asserted the Japanese force in the Nonni river area, including today’s reinforcements, was about 900 men, including three batteries of artillery. In Complete Control. Portsmouth, U., Nov. G.---(A’)-- psi Marguerite Clark Tidd, 35, alone was responsible for an embezzlement of $2,115 from the municipal court funds, a jury has decided acquitting former Municipal Judge William R. Sprague of a charge of aiding and abetting her. Sprague, who was arrested and indicted on the strength of testimony by Mrs. Tidd, former clerk of the court, was found not guilty after a jury of four women and eight men considered his case three hours yesterday. The 55-year-old jurist denied he had anything to do with the shortage in the court funds, but testified he attempted to borrow money to cover up the missing funds to prevent court proceedings which would reveal his intimate relations with Mrs. Tidd.

DOVER, England, Nov. 6. (UP)— The American Steamer Hybert, owned by the United States Shipping Board, was ashore off the English coast today, Lloyd's agent was informed. The Hybert is of 6501 tons and 395 feet long. It was built in 1920 and Wilmington, N. C., is its port of registry.

MOSCOW, Nov. 6 ()—An appeal to its members to support the “Chinese Proletariat” against Japanese occupation of Manchuria and a warning that war against China is “a step toward war against Soviet Russia” was issued today by the executive directorate of the Communist International. The appeal was made on the occasion of the celebration today of the fourteenth anniversary of the revolution in Russia. “The leaders of all the capitalistic countries,” the statement said, “are wandering about, searching for an outlet and afraid of complete bankruptcy before the mounting swell of the proletarian revolution. The class fight is becoming more acute. The imperialists have already begun war in the east in the hope of attaining this outlet.” “This war against the working classes of China,” it said, “is a war against us. Let us organize revolutionary barriers against it, in the interest of a united, in

1931-10-17.text: YORKTOWN, Va., Oct. 16—(%)—The glory that was Yorktown's, heralded as a triumph of the English people for the right of self-government, was reviewed today in pageant and in story. And among the thousands who came to participate in the four-day sesquicentennial of the battle that ended the American Revolution was Lord Cornwallis, descendant of the English earl whose forces surrendered to Washington and Lafayette 150 years ago. "We feel that it would be as agreeable to him as it is delightful to me that a member of the family can be here today," Lord Cornwallis said, "War is behind; peace is in the future, let us hope, forevermore." He spoke at the dedication of a bust of his distinguished ancestor, dedicated by Virginia as a memorial to the affection for the other country. As the British flag was pulled aside to reveal the bust, it was Major Rochambeau, great-great grandson by adoption of

VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Oct. 16 (®)~Labor started swiftly after its mug of mild beer today. The modification committee of the American Federation of Labor announced it would ignore “threats of the army of gangsters and abuse of dry fanatics” in its drive for 2.75 per cent brew. Meeting a day after adjournment of the American Federation of Labor convention, the modification of Volstead Act committee laid plans for carrying out the demand of the convention for legalization of beer without the return of the saloon. Chairman Matthew Woll and Secretary I. N. Ormburn of the committee said they accepted the convention’s beer resolution as “an order to work harder for real temperance, for law and order and the protection of public morals and health.”

(International News Service) YORKTOWN, Va., Oct. 17—The sun flashed out of the broad sweep of the York River here today and called to action the illustrious sons of France, England and America: the governors of the thirteen original states or their representatives, who awoke to continue their part in the celebration of the 150th anniversary celebration of the battle which made the colonies free. Lord Cornwallis, descendant of the English Earl, found himself here yesterday at the dedication of a memorial to his ill-fated ancestor. "War is behind, peace is in front, we hope for ever more," he declared. It had been intimated he would find some delicacy in taking part in the exercises. "I assure you such delicacy never crossed my mind," he said. "Forty-eight hours after Yorktown, General Washington entertained Lord Cornwallis, and from that moment all animosity was forgotten." Havre, France, Oct. 16. (A’)—Premier Pierre Laval sailed on the Ile De France today for his conferences with President Hoover, taking with him the assurances of Ambassador Walter E. F. Edge that the American people eagerly await his arrival. At his side as the big liner pulled out was his daughter, Jose, just under 20 years. The premier received an enthusiastic send-off from Havre, with Ambassador Edge, who accompanied him on the train from Paris, he was accorded a reception at city hall and then he proceeded through lanes of demonstrative well-wishers to his pier. “I am convinced I am working for Franco-American collaboration,” he said, “I am aiming at world peace.” At the city hall reception Mayor Leon Meyer of Havre told the premier that, so long as he was at the head of the government, France might be confident she would sacrifice nothing. The members of the premier’s party are Profe

Tokyo—While the War Department and Foreign Office staffs worked throughout a national holiday today, army authorities were quoted by the press as characterizing the attitude of the United States in the Manchurian situation as "extremely meddlesome." Most other government offices were closed in keeping with the national holiday, but dispatches saying the League of Nations Council had decided to permit an American representative to participate in discussions over Manchuria created such concern that the War and Foreign departments continued activity. Rengo News Agency said the statement of army authorities was made after a meeting at which they voted to uphold Japan's stand. Army authorities, according to the agency, contended that since the government repeatedly had stated the recent difficulties in Manchuria should be settled without the intervention of a third party "it is extremely medd

Geneva, Oct. 16.—America took her place tonight at the horseshoe table of the council of the League of Nations to assist in bringing about peace between China and Japan in Manchuria. Japan fought to the last ditch against inviting the United States to participate, but was overruled in a new vote today when the question was formally settled. The other 13 members of the council lined up against. When the American representative—the youthful Prentiss B. Gilbert, consul-general at Geneva—joined the 14 members of the League's executive board, the event was hailed as historical and highly auspicious for organized efforts to strengthen international security. Menaces World Peace The presence of Mr. Gilbert meant that the Briand-Kellogg pact, formulated in large part through American effort, was linked with the covenant of the League in the effort to solve the Sino-Japanese problem. GENEVA, Oct. 17—(#)—Strengthened by America’s participation, the council of the League of Nations returned to private negotiation today to restore peace in troubled Manchuria. Consul General Prentiss B. Gilbert, the American delegate, was the center of attention as efforts went forward under the direction of Chairman Aristide Briand to persuade China and Japan to compose their differences for the sake of world security. Mr. Gilbert took part in the council’s discussion for the first time last night and will again take his place when it meets Monday. To Send Commission Although Japan opposed the project when first suggested, it was believed likely the council would formulate a neutral commission to go to Manchuria and examine the situation at close range. Such a body would be empowered to arrange for the withdrawal of Japanese troops and the protection of Japanese lives and property again

Paris, Oct. 17—-(A P)—Premier Laval, en route to America, was represented by the newspaper Le Matin today as having been advised to propose to President Hoover a fifty per cent reduction in intergovernmental war debts in place of a possible extension of the one-year moratorium. His experts urged him also to suggest progressive reduction in armaments on the basis of budget costs rather than the idea of equality, the paper said, and with the stipulation that the Kellogg-Briand peace pact be amended to provide that in the event of war the United States would consult with other powers and agree to deprive the aggressor of all assistance. If he follows their advice, he would oppose renunciation of Germany’s unconditional reparations payments, it was said, but would accept the substitution of payments in kind for payments in money.
