Monday was the center of diplomatic activity in which the friendly hopes and determined efforts of three nations converged on a solution of the acute problem of Germany's distress. Arthur Henderson, the British foreign secretary, arrived from England in the morning and immediately began discussions with Julius Curtius, the German foreign minister. Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson, accompanied by Ambassador Frederic M. Sackett, talked for half an hour with President Von Hindenburg, then started for Amsterdam by airplane on the way back to London. MacDonald Welcomed. Soon afterward Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald stepped off the train from London into the wildest welcome a German crowd ever gave a foreign statesman. Meanwhile bankers were arriving from several points to confer with German financiers as recommended by the recent seven power conference at London. Oliver Sprague, American

By United Press LONDON, July 30.—David Lloyd George, Liberal leader, may go on a tour of the world, visiting the United States, before attempting to return to his parliamentary duties, it was indicated today. Physicians attending him said it may be two or three months before he has recovered completely from his operation yesterday. The doctors and relatives, however, were delighted with Lloyd George's response to the operation. He slept peacefully and was believed on the road to convalescence. Before taking the anesthetic, he insisted on dictating a message to his daughter, Megan Lloyd George, a member of parliament, to be read at the opening today of the Liberal party's summer school at Cambridge.

1931-05-03.text: | REYKJAVIK, Iceland, May 2. — Misfortune dogged today in the wake of the expeditions which are endeavoring to reach Augustine Courtauld, British scientist, who is marooned on the interior of the Greenland ice-cap. Captain Albin Arenberg took off in a plane early this afternoon, hoping to reach his base at Lemon Camp by dark, but he was forced to return less than two hours later because of unfavorable flying conditions and the need for readjustments of his motor.

| LISBON, Portugal, May 2.— | Harassed on all sides by Portugal's ‘available military and naval forces, and deserted by the comrades on whose support they had counted, the rebels who set up a junta gov- ernment at Funchal, Madeira, just one month ago capitulated today. General Souza Dias surrendered unconditionally to Magalhães Cor- teia, the minister of marine who commanded the attacking force, winding up a month of “warfare” in which the casualties on both sides were small and during which no civilian or foreign resident was injured. By land, sea and air the federal troops bombarded the rebels, but despite the natural fortifications of the island the junta forces were outnumbered and tonight govern- ment troops took control while the (Continued on Page 2, Col. 5.)

NEW YORK, May 2. (?)—George T. Baker, 91, dean of New York financiers, died at his home tonight of pneumonia. The aged financier died at 8 p. m., his secretary, Frank Rysavy, announced. He had been ill since Thursday. George F. Baker Jr. and other relatives were with the banker at the residence, 258 Madison avenue, when death came. A formal statement was issued some few minutes later which said: “George F. Baker passed away peacefully tonight at 8 o'clock.” The banker, regarded as the third richest man in the country, lapsed into unconsciousness late in the day. Three doctors remained constantly at his bedside to the end. Spends Thursday at Desk Baker returned a few weeks ago from his winter home on Jekyll Island, off the Georgia coast. He then was apparently in the best of health. After spending Thursday at his desk in the First National (Turn to Page 2, Column 1)

WASHINGTON, May 2.—(#)— The United States Chamber of Commerce was charged today by republican independent senators with failing, at its recent Atlantic City convention, to present a program for solving the nation’s economic problems. Senator La Follette, republican, Wisconsin, said the industrial and financial leadership represented at the meeting attempted to shift the blame for the economic depression from its own shoulders to ‘“politics and politicians,”’ Senator Borah, republican, Idaho, remarked that ‘“no Moses appeared.” Meanwhile democratic leaders attributed great political significance to the speech of Julius H. Barnes chairman of the board before the chamber, advocating reductions in the Hawley-Smoot tariff rates to benefit foreign trade and aid in the revival of business. Revision of tariff rates was opposed, however, by Chairman Smoot of the senate finance committee and Senat

Washington, May 2—(A P)—“It's almost as hard to leave here as it was to leave home.” Bryan Untiedt, of Towner, Colo., who had been the guest of President and Mrs. Hoover for four days, was standing on the platform of the westbound Liberty Limited as he spoke. There was a warning whistle and the train slowly began to gather headway. The thirteen-year-old boy, whose heroism during a Colorado blizzard attracted the attention of the president, was on his way home.

DALLAS, May 6. — David Sink, 61, and his son, Miles F. Sink, 32, were shot to death late today at Cedar Hill, 20 miles from Dallas. Floyd Plummer, 25, came to Dallas and surrendered a short time later. He was charged with murder in two complaints. The shooting, said to have resulted from a dispute over $1.50, occurred near the Cedar Hill post office just after Plummer had emerged from a barber shop where he had had his hair cut. Will Lay, a barber, said the Sinks came into the shop while he was cutting Plummer’s hair but left before he finished. After Plummer left, he said, he heard the men talking outside and then heard four shots. Automatic Used A .25 caliber automatic was used. One bullet struck the elder Sink in the neck and two struck his son in the abdomen. The elder man was killed instantly, his son dying a short time later. There were several eye witnesses but they were reluctant

| WASHINGTON, May 2.—(P)— Efforts of Bishop James Cannon, Jr., to obtain a postponement of next Wednesday’s hearing by the Senate campaign funds committee on his 1928 anti-Smith campaign expenditures today met with failure. Chairman Nye announced the meeting would be held with or without the presence of the southern Methodist churchman. The North Dakota senator made public correspondence with the bishop in which the latter said it was important that he attend the sessions of the general board of missions of the Methodist church at Nashville next week and asked that the committee meeting be delayed a day or two. Replying, Nye said the committee felt the bishop's presence would not be required at the hearing, that it would forward a transcript of the proceedings to him, and that Wednesday was the only date satisfactory to all committeemen. The committee is investigating the disposition of

Nashville, Tenn., May 2—(A-P.)—Having no power to remove a bishop the college of bishops of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, Saturday received but took no action on petitions seeking the ousting of one of its members, Bishop James Cannon, Jr. of Richmond, Va. The bishops likewise took no action on requests that Bishop Cannon be prevented from becoming president of the college but he asked that he not be considered for the post to which he was eligible last December. He laid a statement before the college, asking that the election of a president follow the regular order.

1931-03-22.text: GREENOCK, Scotland, March 21. —Aj—Two hundred passengers from the Canadian-Pacific liner Montclare, including 20 mothers and their children, were brought here tonight from the little island of Cambria after the Montclare ran hard aground on a reef in the Firth of Clyde. The crew stayed aboard and it was believed the Montclare might be floated tomorrow although her bows were badly damaged.

PUTNEY-ON-THAMES, England, March 21. ()—Cambridge defeats Oxford today in their 83rd annual eight oared boat race on the Thames. It was the contest's eighth straight victory in the historic event, which had been competed intermittently since 1829. Cambridge took a lead at the start, never relinquishing the advantage during the four and a quarter mile stretch from Putney to Mortlake. The victory gave Cambridge a margin of two races in the series, the light blue having triumphed 42 times to Oxford's 40 wins. The race of 1877 was a dead heat. The official time was 19 minutes and 26 seconds, almost a full minute behind the record set by Oxford in 1911 at 18 minutes 29 seconds. Cambridge’s margin of victory was two and one quarter lengths.

New Delhi, India. — (PF) — Mahatma Gandhi agreed today to participate in the second round table conference at London this fall if he succeeds in settling the Hindu-Moslem communal question. He told Viceroy Irwin today he believed this question could be solved by granting universal adult franchise. This and other important decisions were reached today at a miniature round table conference at the vice regal palace in which Lord Irwin, Gandhi and the congress of Indian princes participated. Attired only in his loin cloth, which cost about a shilling, he sat at a massive walnut table in the sumptuous viceroy's palace with blue blooded Indian princes clad in resplendent silk and gold robes, stunning turbans and glistening jewels around him. At his right sat Viceroy Irwin, who a year ago had him thrown in jail for his challenge to the British crown.

LONDON—A report from Dublin this afternoon stated that Timothy Healy, famous Irish statesman, was seriously ill at his home. He was the Irish Free State's first governor-general in 1922 and is one of the most notable figures in Irish-English political history in modern times.

LONDON, March 21.—Concern was felt today for Arnold Bennett, English author, reported in a critical condition. Bennett suffered complications after an illness of six weeks. He first was forced to go to bed with an attack of influenza.

Glasgow, Scotland, March 21—Two hundred passengers were landed safely on Little Cambrae island in the Firth of Clyde today after the Canadian Pacific liner Montelare, inward bound for Greenock, was grounded on a hidden reef on the northwestern side of the island today in a dense fog. The passengers were taken off the liner in lifeboats and were picked up by tugs which landed them on the island. They will be taken to the mainland late tonight or early tomorrow morning. The crew remained aboard the Montelare. Some was lying at a 45 degree list and was believed to have been badly stove in.

GLASGOW, Scotland, March 21.—(7)—The Canadian Pacific liner Montclare, with a bad hole in her bow, lay fast on a reef off the little island of Cambrai in the Firth of Clyde tonight while her 200 passengers crowded the island cottages waiting to be brought to the mainland. The liner struck the rocks in a dense fog today while she was bound in from Greenock. She settled to a 45 degree list and it was feared she had been badly stove in. The crew remained aboard. Tugs scuttled out to her assistance at the first word of her distress, but when it was found that she was hard aground the boats were put over and the passengers loaded in. The tugs convoyed them to the island where it seemed likely they would have to remain overnight. U. S. S. ARIZONA, March 21.—(®)—Cheers for President Hoover reverberated today from the throats of 800 gobs in white massed in the forecastle of the warship Arizona.

Montevideo, Uruguay, March 22. --(P)—The Prince of Wales and his brother Prince George left here today for Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on the steamer Alcantara. They flew here yesterday from Buenos Aires where Wales recently officially inaugurated the British trade exposition. The brothers will make a tour of several states of Brazil before returning home.

1931-05-17.text: PHILADELPHIA, (Sunday Morning) May 1-7 (4)—Department of Justice agents said they arrested Green, alias Callow, sought on charges of swindling British subjects, including the prince of Wales, of $7,000,000, early today. He had been sought in Chicago, Los Angeles, Miami and other cities after Godfrey Haggard, British consul in Chicago, had asked federal aid. Green is said by police to be an associate of "Jake the Barber" Factor, accused of being the ring-leader in a confidence game that duped hundreds of prominent persons. Green fled his home in Los Angeles, officials said, last week a few minutes before his home was raided. He also narrowly escaped arrest in New Orleans, they added. He was arrested as he entered a Germantown apartment house with his wife who landed in New York early yesterday after leaving her home in England two weeks ago. London, May 16.—(AP)— Russia has sent three of her best men here for the international conference of wheat exporting nations beginning Monday. They are: Isidore Lubimof, Soviet trade representative in Berlin; Abraham Kissin, probably Russia’s leading wheat expert, and Saul Bron, trade representative in London. All have had wide experience in Russia and abroad and are familiar with problems which this conference will face. They are saying nothing before the meetings begin, but Russia has an equal stake with other nations in the conference. G. Howard Ferguson, Canadian high commissioner and temporary chairman of the conference, said today the first few sessions will be secret so delegates may have opportunity for free discussion. One issue which may be decided early is a request by importing countries that they be permitted to send unofficial observers. On Bread Basis The conference, said

By The Associated Press, Madrid, Spain, May 16. Extreme left elements are demanding the expulsion of the Jesuits from Spain by Provisional President Alcala Zamora, himself a Catholic, who already is perplexed over the religious situation. The periodical “Gerisol,” representing the staunchest republican circles, joined communist organs last night in demanding that the Jesuits be banished. “The diplomatic flight of Cardinal Primate Segura gives the public the utmost satisfaction,” the newspaper said. “This healthy measure, however, will constitute an injustice unless the Jesuits have the same fate, and with the Jesuits must go other archbishops and bishops who have been distinguished for their hostility to the republic. But above everything, expulsion of the Jesuits constitutes the most peremptory demand of liberal and democratic Spain.” Presents Confusing Aspects The religious situation p

GENEVA, May 16 — Probing Europe’s economic difficulties today, the commission for European union developed, in its discussions, three remedial schemes and emphasized the sharp conflict between the French and German attitudes toward the proposed Austro-German customs union. The Austro-German proposal was defended in general terms by Foreign Minister Curtius of Germany and in specific terms by Vice Chancellor Johann Schaber of Austria. It was attacked on legal and political grounds by Foreign Minister Aristide Briand of France, and on economic grounds by his colleague François Poincaré. Foreign Minister Dino Grandi of Italy approached the subject of the Austro-German accord with reserve but said the existence of legal factors in connection with it was significant. The general discussion of the European economic situation — which brought out these opinions was adjourned until Monday, when i

WASHINGTON, May 16.—Firemen tonight quickly extinguished a small blaze in the north wing of the capitol. The private alarm box in the senate wing was sounded, drawing four engine and two truck companies to the scene. Extinguishing the blaze was but a matter of a few minutes. The fire recalled the spectacular blaze of early last year, which shrouded the capitol dome in smoke and flames. The fire tonight was in a basement room used as a janitor’s store room. A wooden wall of the room was found burning about 9 o’clock by an officer of the capitol police force, who reported the blaze. Dense clouds of smoke filled two long corridors in the basement. A considerable crowd gathered on the capitol plaza but nothing of the fire could be seen from the outside. Only one hose line was run into the basement room.

By The Associated Press. Fairfield Depot, Dayton, O., May 16. All army flying forces took to the air today under one command for the first time in history. Squadron by squadron they wheeled up from neighboring Wright field and Fairfield air depot on orders of Brig. Gen. Benjamin D. Foulois, assistant chief army air corps, until 600 ships were on the wing. Once in the air they separated into five groups and headed in as many directions from Dayton to practice formation flying and group maneuvers, to which residents of Chicago, New York, Boston, Washington and other seaboard cities will thrill within next two weeks. The most gigantic show, however, is planned for tomorrow. Aerial reviews will be held in both the morning and afternoon. By eliminating some of the department’s activities and deferring some work which may be necessary ultimately but can be postponed for the present, Mr. Hoover hopes to make these savings. NEW YORK, May 15-7). Ruth Nichols, who is planning a solo flight to Paris, received official recognition today from the National Aeronautic Association as holder of the world’s speed record for women. Flying at Detroit April 13 in the monoplane in which she will attempt to cross the Atlantic, she attained a speed of 210 miles an hour. The previous record, 181 miles an hour, was held by Amelia Earhart.

1931-04-12.text: LISBON, Portugal, April 11. () Martial law enforced quiet in the Portuguese capital tonight and strict censorship on communications from Madeira and the Azores made it extremely difficult for citizens here to follow developments in those islands, where a military revolt has been in progress for several days. Amusement houses in Lisbon are closed and private citizens find themselves accosted in the streets by soldiers with fixed bayonets to examine their papers. From the third artillery barracks where President Carmona and his cabinet have taken shelter there came a statement today that the Portuguese interior was quiet and that the loyalty of the home army has never been questioned. There were unconfirmed reports also that numerous arrests had been made in an effort to block the island rebellion from spreading to the mainland.

BERLIN. —(?)— Paul Heylandt’s latest rocket motor, claimed by the inventor to be capable of hurtling itself in projectile form from Berlin to any point in Europe in 12 minutes, was shown to newspaper men at the Heylandt liquid oxygen plant on Saturday. Although the motor, which looks like a small cannon, weighs only 15 pounds and could easily be adapted to projectile shape, the engineers declared they were more interested in perfecting it as a “vest pocket” airplane motor. Heylandt himself sees it as the logical motive power for airplane flights from Europe to America, through the stratosphere. The rocket motor demonstrated by Heylandt and the late Max Valier last year would seem a toy alongside this successor, which is not only far larger and more powerful but much more efficient and smoother in operation than its predecessor. CAIRO, Egypt, April 11—(9P)—Having completed a tour of the near east, the Graf Zeppelin churned the skyways tonight on her homeward journey to Friedrichshafen, scheduled to arrive Monday. As the great gray shape streaked across the Palestine sky and over historic biblical terrain, enroute here, thousands of Jews and Arabs forgot their animosities and gazed intently at the dirigible. Returning here about 5 p.m. (about 9 a.m. E.S.T.), the Graf Zeppelin moored for a short while and departed. A host of government officials and British representatives bid farewell to Dr. Hugo Eckert, wishing him “tail winds.”

NEW ORLEANS, April 11—(AP) The federal government struck a death blow today at a gigantic band of bootleggers and rum smugglers with the arrest of eight men and the seizure of a radio station here. Authorities said they had evidence the ring was supported by interests having millions of dollars and operated from the Mississippi gulf coast, Canada and British Honduras. Flushing of the band after weeks of investigation by a large corps of federal agents has uncovered, in the opinion of prohibition officers, the largest existing illicit liquor ring in the world. It represented, they said, a curious liaison between the underworld, Canadian distillers and Mississippi officials and business men. Seize Radio Station. (City The Associated Press) Columbus, Ohio, April 11 Forced down here by motor trouble at 5 o'clock p.m. today, Captain Ira Eaker, army test pilot who was attempting to set a speed record, tonight announced he would abandon the attempt to better Captain Frank Hawks' mark at this time. Captain Eaker decided to abandon the attempt when he learned the clutch of his supercharger was slipping and that it would be necessary to dismantle the entire motor to make repairs. He said he would remain here overnight and would summon army air mechanics from Wright Field, Dayton to remove the motor from the red and blue plane and make the repairs. He was undecided whether he would try for an east-west transcontinental air speed record when his plane is in flying condition again. WASHINGTON, April it — (AP)—The navy department was informed tonight that Captain Harlen Pefley of the marines had been killed in a clash between a Nicaraguan guardia detachment and insurgents today in northeastern Nicaragua. Captain Pefley, a native of Idaho, was leading the guardia detachment, the dispatch to the navy said, when the insurgents were encountered. An enlisted man was wounded but the navy was not advised whether he was a marine or guardsman. The clash occurred near Logtown, which is about 12 miles from Puerta Cabezas, base of the guardia patrol. There were about 50 in the insurgent band and the dispatch made no mention of its casualties.

More than 800 prohibition advocates earlier listened to the broadcast of a composite dry law report drawn up by 22 women comprising an “unofficial national law enforcement commission.” The chief recommendation of this document, delivered yesterday to President Hoover as a “woman's postscript” to the Wickersham report, was for a nation-wide education campaign in behalf of prohibition, fortified “by good example in the home.” The plea that the drys vote in 1932—“as in 1928, for the great protagonist of prohibition,” by Mrs. Shaver, wife of the former chairman of the democratic national committee, was cl

WASHINGTON, April 29.—(AP)— Four Nicaraguan insurgents were killed and three were wounded in a skirmish on April 23 with a patrol of the native guardia under Capt. O. A. Inman of the marine corps. The navy department was advised of the battle today by Rear Admiral Arthur St. Clair Smith, in command of naval forces in Central America. The guardia suffered no casualties. The skirmish occurred at Lacus Creek. Afterward the patrol proceeded to Lin and thence down the Coco river to Cape Gracias a Dios and from there to Puerto Cabezas without incident. Lacus Creek is in the northeastern portion of the department of Jinotega and flows northwesterly into the Coco river. Capt. Inman is a resident of Oakland, Calif.

1931-09-27.text: TOKYO, Sept. 24. (UP)—Foreign office spokesmen announced last night that movements of troops into Manchuria from outside the south Manchurian railway zone was to end. The announcement was made after the foreign minister, Kijūrō Shidehara, had conferred with the war minister, Minami. It was announced that reports of Japanese occupation of Chinese territory had been greatly exaggerated. An official statement was expected either Thursday or Friday. No date was mentioned for the withdrawal of troops from occupied cities but it was expected that troops would return to Japanese concessions when assured that property and life would be protected.

| WINDSOR, Ont., Sept. 26—(}—The Borter Cities Star today published the following: “Beer by the glass will be announced by the Ontario government within a month, according to word along the border. The date of the system’s inauguration is not yet mentioned. “Breweries throughout Ontario are paving the way for the action by sending agents throughout farming districts, particularly the areas where ordinarily a heavy dry vote can be commanded. They are contracting for large acreages of barley for next year. The breweries are agreeing to pay 50 cents a bushel for the grain provided it is up to quality. That much is definitely known.” The Star says those who are “in the know” say that after Oct. 31, when the present beer and wine permits expire, no more beer permits will be issued as they will not be required for the purchase of beer by the glass. THOROLD, Ont., Sept. 26 (UP).— A middle-aged man and his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Peter Holouchuck, the parents of five children, were shot to death today as they hastened from the Kozub grocery store after an argument over an unpaid bill. The proprietor, Nick Kozub, 48 years old, was arrested and taken to St. Catharines, Ont., where he was arraigned on a charge of first degree murder, and remanded to jail for one week. Police Chief Dennis Harold of Thorold said Kozub admitted the slayings, in a signed statement to police. The shootings occurred in front of Kozub's store on crowded Main street, in view of dozens of persons, including Police Constable Richard Hughes. Five shots were fired, three going wild. NEW YORK, Sept. 4 — Plans for a revolt against the Soviet commissars, for communist-led revolutions in all capitalist countries, and for reseating a monarch on the throne of Russia are being mapped out nightly behind the locked doors of secret societies here in the largest Russian colony in the world. Every shade of political thinking is represented among the thousands of émigrés who have come to this city since the revolution in their own country, but only the communists stand on soapboxes and give street corner crowds an inkling of their ideas. The monarchists are particularly secretive and for that reason there has been no public comment on this week’s reports that Archduke Cyril Vladimirovitch, pretender to the throne and cousin of the late Czar Nicholas, is coming to the United States to take part in a conference at which plans will be made to restore Czarism. PEIPING, China, Sept. 26 (UP). —Thousands of refugees streamed into Peiping from the “war” zones of Manchuria today. Hundreds were destitute. They roamed the narrow streets of the ancient capital seeking shelter and food. Railways and roads leading from Manchuria to the northeast were filled with fleeing men, women and children. Renewed clashes were feared in the trouble area between Japanese and Manchurian (Chinese) forces. The peasants and small shop owners—worst hit by the Manchuria crisis—deserted their properties and sought safety within the great wall of China. Tense anti-Japanese feeling here was heightened by reports that Japanese army planes had bombed three passenger trains south of Mukden. A communique from Manchurian army headquarters said the Japanese airplanes had flown low over the trains and opened fire with machine guns, endangering lives of non-combatants. The communiqu

By The Associated Press. New York, N. Y., Sept. 26. Another link in Mrs. Benjamin P. Collings’ story of the “pirate” murder of her husband on Long Island Sound a fortnight ago bobbed up today in the form of a faded, white linen bag. The bag, which District Attorney Blue said closely resembled one described by Mrs. Collings, was found on the beach at Lloyd’s Neck approximately two miles from the point at which Collings’ body was washed ashore. Mrs. Collings had said that one of two men who killed her husband and abducted her threw papers overboard from a bag as she was being taken away from the yacht Penguin in a canoe. Blue said the bag found on the beach contained clothing and cloth.

| LA PAZ. Bolivia, Sept. 26. (U.P)— | Reports of an engagement between Bolivian and Paraguayan troops in the disputed Gran Chaco region were received by the general staff today from Fort Munoz. The advices said 200 Paraguayan soldiers with rifles and machine guns attacked Agua Rica, retiring after eight hours of fighting and leaving six dead and many wounded. No Bolivians were killed or wounded, the messages said. The Bolivians captured some Paraguayan wounded, but did not pursue the main body which retired towards Nanawa. The official report said the Paraguayan troops belonged to the Second of May regiment and included cavalry.

1931-07-27.text: | BERLIN, July 27 (4)—Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson left for Amsterdam today by airplane on the way to London shortly after an audience with President Von Hindenburg. He maintained to the last his policy of extreme discretion, and when an American correspondent asked him to give his impressions of the audience with the president he replied: “As an American citizen you know that one never quotes the president. That’s my answer here, too. In my position one must be especially careful.” Then, after a pause, “needless to say, the visit was most pleasant.” Hope of early resumption of formal bank payments today lent a bright hue to the new workaday week for Germans who have been laboring under the depressing influence of the financial crisis for the last fortnight. The new Acceptance and Guarantee Bank, through which such resumption is to be attempted, was to be officially launched today
By The Associated Press. London, England, July 28—(Tuesday.)—Amy Johnson, Great Britain's foremost woman flier, took off from Lympne airdrome at 1:30 a. m. today for Berlin on a flight to Tokyo.

Berlin —(P— Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain reached Berlin Monday evening, several hours behind Arthur Henderson, his foreign minister, and was accorded one of the most enthusiastic receptions a visiting foreigner has received in recent years. Cheering Germans packed the big Friedrichstrasse railway station, jammed the surrounding streets and kept the whole district in an uproar of acclaim. Mr. Henderson and Premier MacDonald will discuss the German financial crisis with the heads of the Reich, Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson left for Amsterdam Monday by airplane on the way to London, shortly after an audience with President von Hindenburg.

New York, July 27—The United States and France have become the plutocrats of the nations. More than half the supply of gold in the world has been accumulated in the vaults of the two countries, and in the last two weeks, it has been flowing into France in a yellow stream, brought swiftly from London, Berlin and other centers by airplane and express. More than $7,000,000,000 in monetary gold stocks now rests securely in the vaults of the Bank of France and the federal reserve system. This amounts to more than 60 per cent of the world’s monetary gold stocks and threatens to upset the economic stability of many countries. The United States holds just another $5,000,000,000 of the precious metal and the Bank of France the balance. Foreign Minister Julius Curtius was at the station to greet him and as the two walked to their automobile there were cries of “Long Live Henderson—hoch the friend of peace—three cheers for the friend of Germany.” One national socialist ventured to yell the “Nazi” slogan, “Wake Up Germany,” but someone hustled him out of the way. Cheering Germans packed the big Friedrichstrasse railway station, jammed the surrounding.

London, July 27.—(®)— Gold withdrawals from the Bank of England, which amounted to 32,000,000 pounds sterling (about $160,000,000) in 11 days, were believed checked Sunday. During the 11 days in which gold has been taken out, most of it to Paris, there have been no withdrawals from New York, indicating an understanding between New York and London banking authorities. A hopeful sign was the recovery in Paris exchange on London to 123.95 francs and the New York sterling rate of $4.85 13-16, both slightly above points at which gold exports were profitable. It was stated when Paris started withdrawing gold in the early days of the German financial troubles that the Bank of England could stand a fair-sized loss of gold with equanimity.

Soviet Russia, July 27. —(UP)—The Graf Zeppelin was well on her way toward the frozen Arctic wastes today on a flight over the North Pole. The great German dirigible, commanded by Dr. Hugo Eckener, veteran of all her major flights, left Leningrad at 11:20 a. m., yesterday on the most perilous lap of the present polar cruise. The airship famous for its world girdling tour in 1929 and other notable flights—carried 16 passengers and 30 members of the crew. The course lay over the ice fields of the Arctic which brought disaster to Gen. Umberto Nobile’s airship ‘Italia in 1928. Dr. Eckener admitted that weather conditions would tend to alter the course but scientists aboard hoped to make extensive experiments and perhaps discover areas of unknown land. CARDIFF, Wales, Jan. 1—(AP)— New Year's day dawned bleak and cheerless in the great South Wales coal mining area with 150,000 miners thrown out of work by a general strike edict which became effective at midnight. Simultaneously with an order by the miners federation for its members not to report for work today, the owners issued directions for the mines to be locked to all workers who refused to accept the owners’ terms. Unless new negotiations which the South Wales conciliation board hopes to open Saturday between owners and workers are successful, the 150,000 miners and their families, estimated to number more than half a million persons, face hardship and suffering. It has been suggested that the government, if it cannot force an agreement, may declare a state of emergency and take over the pits temporarily. CARDIFF, Wales, Dec. 31—(AP)—A general strike in the great South Wales coal mine area, involving approximately 150,000 workers, was ordered tonight by officials of the miners' federation (effective at midnight). The decision of the miners’ leaders came after an evening of hurried conferences. Directly affected are the 150,000 miners who work in the area with their families, while a spread of the situation to other British coal fields is possible. Even as the South Wales meetings were being held, mine leaders in the Bristol area were debating stopping work tomorrow.

WILL ROGERS -_-.. ’ HOLLYWOOD, Calif., Jan. 1.— Was going to write my New Year resolutions yesterday, but right in the midst of Einstein landing here among us mathematicians, why along comes a guy from Harvard, and jerks the horse out from under Paul Revere. He claims the British tackled Paul behind his own scrimmage line before he could even get off a punt toward Concord. Now to keep even with Harvard some bird from Yale will yank the cherry tree out from under Washington’s hatchet, take the axe away from Lincoln, confiscate Grant’s quart bottle of rye, and find where Pocahontas was Jewish. It’s just as well some of us didn’t go to school. Yours, WILL ROGERS

WASHINGTON, Jan. 1—U.R—President Hoover today signed a proclamation informing the American people that the United States has entered into a treaty with Great Britain and Japan for the limitation of naval armament. His action formally promulgated the London naval treaty in the United States. Mr. Hoover was able to announce the impending proclamation because of the Irish Free State’s deposit of ratification yesterday. This enabled the United States to open the New Year with the proclamation declaring the treaty effective. Secretary Stimson declared the completed treaty "effectively eliminates competition among the greatest navies of the world." To Stimulate Peace This happy augury for peace and this example of the limitation and reduction of armament by agreement," Stimson said, "will, I am convinced, serve to stimulate further peaceful endeavors during the coming year. From London, where the majestic tones of Big Ben above the parliament buildings tolled the hour of midnight, to remote hamlets where the whistles of trawlers or the gaiety of villagers bore tidings that a new leaf was turned, the countries of the old world frolicked. In the capital of the British empire lords and ladies choked the streets along 'arries and arriets, drinking, laughing and making merry in general, while the same spirit reigned everywhere under the Union Jack. Iowa City, Ia, Jan. 1 (#)— When Margaret Adel Smoke and David Fuller Ash met, the flames of love were kindled. Miss Smoke, daughter of Mrs. Nettie Smoke of Iowa City, and Mr. Ash were married here today at the home of the bride's mother. Mr. Ash is an instructor in the English department of the University of Missouri, where his bride is a graduate student. They will make their home at Columbia, Mo.

LONDON, Dec. 31—(AP)—Unless millions of British radio fans were "disgusted" tonight, they probably soon will be shelving "fancy that" and other exclamatory expressions for "sho-sho!" For Amos and Andy, the blackfaced pair familiar to American dial twisters, were heard in Great Britain tonight for the first time. Reception was excellent and officials of the British Broadcasting Corporation estimated that a potential audience of 12,000,000 was available to hear the pair dissect the King’s English, across the Atlantic.

1931-06-22.text: WASHINGTON, June 22. (AP)— Upon France's response, more than any other one thing, rests the future of America’s offer for a one-year holiday from war debt and reparations payments. Up To France Great Britain is sympathetic toward the plan; Germany is appreciative; republican and democratic party leaders forecast that the next American congress will pass the necessary legislation. World-wide reaction, for the most part, is favorable. So, diplomatic circles in Washington believe, responsibility for the next step is with France. President Hoover has reason to think the French attitude will be favorable. Secretary Mellon, now in England, has conferred informally with French representatives as well as those of other European nations, and it is reported these discussions brought encouraging comment from all involved. CORK, Irish Free State, June 22. (AP) — The submarine Nautilus under command of Sir Hubert Wilkins arrived at the other harbor this morning in tow of the U. S. S. Wyoming. The arrival of the Nautilus concluded a gruelling 17-day trip across the Atlantic on the first lap of a projected underseas cruise to the North Pole. She lost a member of the crew overboard even before she got underway. Things went smoothly for about ten days and then trouble began. One of her motors was disabled and her batteries ran low. She was taken in tow by the battleship Wyoming a week ago when she still was 1,000 miles from her destination. Subsequently, her bridge and periscope were washed away by storms. Part of her crew was taken sick and all were sealed inside for strenuous efforts to repair her machinery.

(By The Associated Press) These are some facts and figures about war debts which would be affected by President Hoover's proposed one-year moratorium: Great Britain pays the United States approximately $165,000,000 a year in principal and interest. Allied war debt payments to Great Britain total $88,750,000 in 1931 and 1932 and $91,250,000 a year thereafter. Germany pays Great Britain $80,000,000 a year in annuities, and thus Great Britain collects from her creditors enough to cover her annual debt payment to the United States. France pays the United States increasing amounts each year, installments of principal rising from about $31,000,000 in 1926 to $115,000,000 in 1937. Interest did not begin until last year, and until 1940 will be at the rate of only one per cent. Italy pays the United States about $15,000,000 a year, increasing to about $80,000,000 in 1937. QUEENSTOWN, Ireland, June 22. —(UP)— The submarine Nautilus, towed by the U. S. S. Wyoming, arrived at Cork harbor early today. The Nautilus broke down while crossing the Atlantic on the way to England and thence northward on a projected cruise under the ice to the North Pole. The expedition is commanded by Sir Hubert Wilkins.

London, June 22.—(AP)— Prime Minister MacDonald told the House of Commons this afternoon that the British government cordially welcomed the striking declaration on war debts and reparations payments made by President Hoover.

London, June 21.—(AP)—Europe today welcomed possible relief from her economic burdens through the plan of President Hoover to postpone for a year payments of intergovernmental debts and World War reparations. Tomorrow her unemployed are expected to seek jobs with a new hope and her governments will turn to the task of solving their pressing financial and industrial problems with renewed zeal. Boston, June 22.—(4)—Dr. George Jameson-Carr, physician of the steamship Franconia, arrived here from England Sunday with information which he believes will aid New York state authorities in solving the mysterious death of Starr Faithfull. The physician, a former friend of the girl whose lifeless body was found on the sands at Long Beach, Long Island, on June 8, arrived here aboard the Franconia, and remained aboard the liner when it left late Sunday for New York. There he will submit to questioning by officials investigating the girl's death and will turn over to them three letters which he received from her. He declined to disclose the contents of the missives but he said: 'I wouldn’t waste my well-earned leave if I did not feel I could aid the grand jury and help clear up the 72 hours before Starr Faithfull’s death.' COBH, Irish Free State, June 21 (P)—The Rush-Brooke dockyard has offered all its available facilities for repairing Sir Hubert Wilkins Arctic submarine Nautilus, when it arrives here with the U. S. S. Wyoming tomorrow. ‘The entire town has taken much interest in the vessel, which became disabled on its voyage from America. Officials have sent Wilkins messages of greetings and the invitation to make use of the repair facilities here. The Cobh town clerk today received a message from the Wyoming saying the Nautilus was to arrive tomorrow morning.

London, Dec. 17 (UP)—The Daily Herald said today the government was considering temporary suspension of the entire naval building program for 1932, with the exception of submarines. Permanency of the suspension, it said, would depend on the results of the world disarmament conference at Geneva. The newspaper understood that the government hoped to give the British delegation a strong weapon for pressing naval and army reductions in Europe and save millions of pound sterling. — According to the Daily Herald, the admiralty is agreeable to the plan. Ships involved in the suspension were said to be two 7,000 and one 5,000 ton armored cruisers, one flotilla leader, eight destroyers, four sloops, one gunboat, and two auxiliary craft.

DALLAS, Texas, Dec. 16—(UP)—Henry Holden Colpus, self-styled King Henry IX of England, claims right to the British throne but is willing to settle for a pension. Colpus, a veteran of the Spanish-American War, asserted tonight he has legal proof to show he should be wearing the crown of King George V. He is 69 years old, and believes the royal family should pension him. According to Colpus, Edward VII fell in love with a young and beautiful Quaker girl in Farmcombe, Surrey, England. They were married by Quaker ceremony but the then Prince of Wales’ mother, Queen Victoria, frowned upon the match. She said the Quaker girl, though charming, was far below her son in station. Victoria had the marriage annulled, according to Colpus, and three weeks after Edward married his second wife, Alexandra, Colpus was born.
