London, Dec. 16. ()--Storm and flood were reported from widely scattered parts of Europe today and a cold wave gave many areas their first taste of winter. A blizzard tearing down the Baltic Sea imperiled shipping and caused minor damage to coastal districts. A sailing ship was torn from its anchorage and was wrecked in the roads at Liban, Latvia, the crew of seven being drowned. A fishing vessel was sunk in the Stockholm archipelago with the loss of one life.

Basel, Switzerland, Dec. 16.—Germany’s plea for reduction in reparations received several severe setbacks today. - A sub-committee of the Young plan advisory commission discovered, it was understood, that Germany’s foreign trade balance should be more than sufficient to pay unconditional reparations annuities of about $150,000,000. French Busy The reference to the foreign trade excess was understood to have been included in the report at the request of the French, who wished to combat arguments that (Continued on Page 10)

SHANGHAI, Dec. 17 (UP) — Gen. Chiang Kai-shek, resigned head of the China National government, left Nanking by airplane today while Canton leaders were nearing the city for a conference with him. Advices reaching here said Chiang's departure was accompanied by threats of new student demonstrations which officials claimed would develop a state anarchy unless checked. Gen. and Mrs. Chiang Kai-shek went to their native place in Chekiang Province. The Cantonese, escorted by an armored train from Shanghai, received an impressive welcome when they arrived here.

PARIS, Dec. 17.—(UP)—Pierre Laval, president of the council of France, declared today that if he is able to leave office before or at the occasion of the legislative elections next May, he will sail for the United States with Madame Laval and their daughter, Jose, for a tour from coast to coast. Friends have written to Senator Borah suggesting that Laval would like to see the western states in company of the Idaho leader. During their short interviews in Washington, they did not reconcile their widely divergent views, but Laval formed a keen liking for his opponent on international policy. Laval admitted that he personally expects the elections to show a swing toward the left which would revive the old cartel and perhaps turn the power over to the radical-socialists. In that case, he would be free to undertake the voyage which has interested him since his hasty voyage to Washington. He p

1931-03-26.text: Karachi, India, March 25 (?)—Turmoil broke out again in India today as Mahatma Gandhi, here for the Nationalist Congress meeting, was jeered and threatened by Communists. British troops at Cawnpore shot down at least 30 rioting Nationalists. These disorders grew out of the execution last week of three Indians convicted of the murder of a 21-year-old police official in 1928. Gandhi was taken off a train 12 miles outside of town, but the thousands gathered here for the Congress meeting spotted him as he rode into town in an automobile. A group of 30 or more young fellows, known to be of Communist leanings, even made as if to attack the frail little man with a flagstaff. Some carried a tray with a gruesome mess of mud and blood. “Here is the blood of our brothers who were murdered,” they cried, referring to the three executed Indians, “take it back with your truce to Delhi.” Gandhi's men dr

PARIS, March 26 (AP)—The Italo-French-British naval treaty conference ended today without any announcement of what decision had been reached by the representatives of the three countries on the final details of the treaty. It was understood, however, that the points discussed and solutions suggested must be referred to British naval experts in London.

London, March 26.—(U. P.)—David Lloyd George, Liberal party leader, announced in the course of a speech at Caxton Hall today that he favored “giving the Labor government another chance” with the understanding that Prime Minister J. Ramsay Macdonald’s cabinet will be ousted if it fails “to retrieve the situation.” Lloyd George warned that defeat of the government is inevitable “if the affairs of the nation are handled nervelessly and without vision or courage.” Lloyd George said the Liberal party which holds the balance of power in the House of Commons, would precipitate the defeat of the cabinet if “we are convinced there will be no improvement.” Unless the government leaders avoid reaction “they are headed for disaster” and will bring down with them “the whole force of progress” Lloyd George said in outlining the aims of the Liberal party. If the government fails in the future, the Libe

| Berlin, March 26,—(AP)—Despite a British suggestion that Germany and Austria take their projected economic union before the council of the League of Nations, the two governments were represented today as firm in their intention to carry out plans to which most of the nations of Europe have taken exception, Chancellor Bruenin, a government statement said, told the British ambassador that the proposed customs accord was within the bounds of the Geneva protocol and the treaty of St. Germaine, which pledge Austria to maintain its independence, and that in the opinion of the two governments there was no reason for the league council to take up the matter, The chancellor informed the ambassador, however, that such was the detail connected with the accord that it probably would be two or three months before it could be made effective, He further stated that, if other governments wished to exa

DUBLIN, Irish Free State—The condition of Tim Healy, veteran Irish statesman and first governor-general of the Irish Free State, who has been ill for some time, took a grave turn for the worse this afternoon. His son, who is an attorney and was arguing a case in court, was summoned to the bedside.

| PARIS, March 26 (CP) — The Austro-German customs pact will be submitted to the council of the League of Nations for its judgment, it was agreed today by Foreign Minister Arthur Henderson of Great Britain and Aristide Briand, no matter what attitude Germany and Austria may take. His information was contained in a statement to the press today by a spokesman for the French government, following a meeting between Henderson and Briand.

Berlin, March 4 (47) Chancellor Bruening today told Sir Horace Rumbold, the British ambassador, that the projected customs union between Germany and Austria is entirely within the bounds of the Geneva protocol of April 1922 and that, in his opinion, there is no reason for taking the agreement before the League of Nations council. If other governments want to examine its legal aspects, he said, Germany and Austria will not object and there is no reason for them to fear the outcome of such an examination. The proposed accord is purely an economic matter, Bruening said, and the German government considers it inadmissible to submit the agreement to examination from a political viewpoint. Herr Bruening told the ambassador, but it will probably be two or three months before the agreement is concluded. Sir Horace had come with a formal inquiry as to Germany’s intentions, at the direction of Art

| PHILADELPHIA, March 20. (7) The Italian freighter, Ruta, owned in Genoa, Italy, due here today with a cargo of chrome ore, sank last night in the Atlantic 420 miles northwest of the Canary Islands, a dispatch from Lloyds of London to the maritime exchange today reported. The 40 officers and men aboard were rescued by the French steamship Verdun Monday night.

1931-04-10.text: BRISBANE, AUSTRALIA, April 10.—(UP)—C. W. A. Scott, youthful aviator, broke Commander Charles E. Kingsford-Smith’s record for flight from London to Australia today, setting a new mark of nine days, two hours and 55 minutes. Scott started his flight from London to Port Darwin at 4:55 a.m. G.M.T. on April 1, departing from Lympne airdrome. He landed at Port Darwin at 5:50 p.m., local time (7:50 a.m. G.M.T.) after flying from Sumatra yesterday. Kingsford-Smith’s record flight, made after his trans-Atlantic venture, was made in nine days, 21 hours and 49 minutes. Scott flew a Gypsy Moth plane, making the flight on a regular schedule and without any spectacular incidents. Scott, who had been considered likely to lower Kingsford-Smith’s record by a few hours if he was not delayed by accidents, took almost a full day off the trans-Atlantic flier’s mark.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, April 9 (P)—Germany's Graf Zeppelin, with Dr. Hugo Eckener in command, took off today for Cairo with 25 passengers, including Commander R. &. Booth, who piloted England's R-100 to Canada. Two years ago the British government withheld permission for a flight over Egypt, but this time the Graf will land and its passengers will debark. The French government disappointed the sightseers by stipulating that no photographs be made of French territory, so the Zeppelin crew collected all cameras from the passengers. The Graf is due back in her hangar Monday morning. — Oe

WINDSOR, England, April 10.— King George will remain in his room at Windsor Castle several days longer as a precautionary measure to assure a complete recovery from an attack of sub-acute bronchitis. An official announcement said he continued to show steady progress. The weather was warm when phy- Lord Daw:

| FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, April 13, (#)--The Graf Zeppelin landed here at dawn today after a 97 hour journey to the Southern Mediterranean, Egypt and Palestine. While she was gone the dirigible landed twice Saturday at Cairo, Egypt, to debark and embark passengers.

Garrisons on two islands, in addition to Funchal, repudiate allegiance: Army's loyalty wavering LISBON, April 10 (Friday) (AP)—President Carmona and members of his cabinet took shelter Thursday night in the barracks of the Third Artillery behind barbed wire entanglements and a battery of machine guns as the danger of rebellion in the army at home appeared menacing. There they intend to stay for the period of the emergency. Meanwhile Lisbon has taken on the appearance of an armed camp. Soldiers are on sentry duty and armored cars rumble through the streets. Guns are mounted in the nearby hills and the batteries of naval vessels in the harbor are trained on the city. These extraordinary measures were taken when it became known that the revolt at Funchal, Madeira, where an army junta has taken over the island government, has spread to the Azores. Garrisons on the islands of San Miguel and A

MADRID, Spain, April 10 — The Portuguese military garrisons at Ponta Delgada and Angra, in the Azores islands, were reported today to have revolted and joined the Funchal military movement against the government. The Lisbon government refused to confirm or deny the reports which said the mid-Atlantic islands were in rebellion. The Portuguese government ordered troops to encircle the Amadora airfield near Lisbon after the escape of an aviation corps inspector. Another plane, carrying Lieut.-Col. Brita Pais and Capt. Sarmento, also escaped. It was forced to land at Beixa but resumed its flight and crossed the border into Spain.

h, I1.—(A—Developments in a fight to determine if Clarence Spierling and his family can continue to make their home in the Hickory Corners Methodist church, appeared to be rapidly approaching a climax today. Plans were announced whereby the trustees, worshipers and a pastor, will try next Sunday to enter the church, into which Mr. and Mrs. Spierling and the family dog moved more than a month ago after their own home, across the street, had been burned down. The Spierlings claim the right to occupancy on the ground that the church trustees violated provisions of ownership which held that, unless regular services were held, the church site shall revert to the estate from which it was willed. The matter was referred to a court and Spierling was charged with malicious mischief. Meanwhile Mrs. Spierling was halted into Justice court and freed Thursday on bond on a charge of disorderly conduct
Tokyo, April 10. (Friday) (—A dispatch from Rengo News Agency said that at least 100 fisherfolk drowned off Zen Korea, in storms Tuesday and Wednesday.

1931-09-04.text: ABOARD THE S. S. RAJPUTANA, Sept. 3 (#)—Mahatma Gandhi, leader of India’s swarming nationalist millions, has spurned the first class stateroom placed at his disposal by the British government for his trip to the round table conference in London and sleeps on a wooden bench in the stern of this liner. Covered by a white sheet, he slept unconcernedly today while deck-patrolling passengers gazed in amazement. “Who is it?” they asked, and an attendant answered courteously, “that is Mr. Gandhi, but this is his day of silence, and so he is sleeping.” There are many strange things for the uninitiated aboard the Rajputana—for instance, the half ton of mud brought from the sacred Ganges by Pandit Malaviya, Mr. Gandhi’s companion. The pandit converts the mud into miniature gods for purposes of worship. When darkness falls each evening the Mahatma Gandhi rises from his wooden bench and summons his

WASHINGTON, Sept. 4 — The celebration of the 150th anniversary of the surrender of Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, October 19, will be attended by President Hoover. The chief executive will deliver an address on the site where the commander of the red-coated British forces surrendered his sword to Washington, terminating the war of the revolution. In making known his intention to speak at the celebration, President Hoover issued a proclamation calling for the observation of October 19 as a holiday.

By United Press LONDON, Sept. 4.—Britain's aerial speed kings will attempt to drive their sea planes at 400 miles an hour in the Schneider Cup races September 12 with no other nation competing. The Royal Aero Club, sponsors, announced that British pilots would try for a record in absence of French and Italian competition.
, UR—The clearance of tobacco from bond was restricted by the government today. The action indicated that an increase in the duty on tobacco was imminent.

Cleveland, Sept. 4—(#)—British herve, and an unexpected sense of humor, are appealing mightily to crowds at the 1931 national air races. These two human attributes are being displayed in large doses by Flight Commander Richard L. R. Atcherley, British Royal Flying Corps and a member of the 1929 record-making British Schneider Cup team. Still bandaged about the head as a result of a serious crack-up a few days ago, the lanky British speed ace Thursday plowed furrows in the ground with his wing tips before 58,000 wildly-shouting spectators. Major Ernst Udet, German ver ace, has been cutting grass with his wing tips for a week, but Commander Atcherley put on a display of brilliant stunting that took the crowds by storm. The wing tips on his Curtis two-seater are scratched and worn, like the cuffs of trousers frayed by hard wear. He has flown mostly on one wing, and once he dashed about the

Chicago, Sept. 4.—{INS}—A report which may spell a long penitentiary term for Walter E. Wolf, pious embezzler, is forwarded to Lloyd's of London. That will have to pay $2,000,000 insurance to cover Wolf's thefts. Auditors meanwhile inspected the books of the Continental Illinois Bank and Trust Company to determine the exact loss. They were assisted by Wolf. Officials of the bank continued their efforts to discover any possible accomplices in the embezzlement. Wolf asserts he played a lone hand. How Wolf filched gilt-edged securities from the bank's repository to lose a fortune on the market was told by David D. Weiss, a tailor who turned broker. Weiss said that Wolf speculated with him to the extent of $1,000,000 in three years. “Wolf asked me to trade some bonds for him,” Weiss said, “and told me he didn’t want his name used. I bought stock for him on margin at his request. Sometimes he

OSLO, Norway, Sept. 4 (AP)—Premier Kolstad announced today that the government probably would send a relief expedition in search of Sir Hubert Wilkins’ submarine Nautilus, unheard from for five days on a cruise to the Arctic. The sealer Vieding or the sloop Fridtjof Hansen will be sent, it was said, and the plans will be worked out during the day. Captain Riiser Larsen, noted North Polar airman, discussed the advisability of a search with polar experts last night and the opinion was expressed that there were no grounds for anxiety but preparations should be made in view of the lateness of the season. Sir Hubert said before he left August 18 that it would be unnecessary to send an expedition even if communication with the submersible was broken for some time. He stressed the fact that he had no intention of endangering the lives of the crew by taking a foolhardy risk. The public has begun

OSLO, Norway, Sept. 2 — Concern for the safety of Sir Hubert Wilkins’ submarine Nautilus was felt today. The last radio message from the Nautilus was received Aug. 29, despite nightly calls to the submarine from Bergen.

1931-10-21.text: / OTTAWA, Oct. 20.—(4)—The wild man raging through the bush of northern British Columbia wasn't so ferocious, after all. He only had a toothache. Word reached the Liard post of the Royal Canadian Mounted that a lunatic was wandering the wilderness living the life of a wild thing. Two corporals were sent to investigate. They found the “maniac” to be Charlie Carlson, a trapper they knew as a sane, industrious citizen. He opened his mouth and disclosed two throbbing teeth, each a couple of inches long, growing along the roof of his mouth. In a territory where dental surgery is unknown, Carlson had suffered for 12 months, losing most of his normal sleep because of the pain. Finally, fearing himself insane, he had taken to the bush to avoid an asylum. The troopers pulled the teeth.

VICTORIA, British Columbia, Oct. 20 (VP)—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh will take off from the Victoria airport early Thursday, Vance Breese, pilot who brought a monoplane here for the Lindberghs to fly East, said after inspecting the field today. Breese's inspection was prompted by reports the Victoria port was closed and all markers removed. The pilot said it was in condition to be used. He left here, after going over the field, for Seattle, but will return late tomorrow to await the arrival of the famous pair, whose aerial vacation in the Orient was cut short by the sudden death of Senator Dwight W. Morrow, Mrs. Lindbergh's father. The Lindberghs are expected to dock early Thursday.

London, Oct. 21—(P)—A Reuters dispatch from Tokyo today said that Japan is willing to accept the advice of Aristide Briand, acting president of the League of Nations council, and forego her insistence on specific recognition by China of Japanese railway rights in Manchuria as a preliminary to opening negotiations provided China is prepared to agree to the general principle of recognizing treaty commitments. The dispatch said it was expected Kenkichi Yoshizawa, Japanese representative at Geneva, would be instructed accordingly. Will Be Step Forward If M. Briand is able to accept, it said, it would mark a great step forward and would clear the way for opening negotiations which

Geneva, Oct. 21.—League of Nations quarters became outwardly impatient today at the delay in approaching a solution of the Manchurian dispute. Adjournment of the league council was discussed. It was admitted that the situation was growing worse, despite hopes aroused through President Aristide Briand’s private conversations with Chinese and Japanese delegates. The situation was aggravated by unconfirmed reports that Secretary of State Stimson, who in September opposed sending a league commission of inquiry into Manchuria, which Japan also opposed, now was supporting the Japanese demand for no fixed date for withdrawal of troops from Manchuria. Council members who demanded a solution of the question this week believed it impossible and suggested immediate adjournment, with a meeting in two or three weeks at Paris. League leaders maintained that Japan had made the issue between the league

Calcutta, Oct. 21—(44)—At least 150 persons were drowned today, and 2,000 made homeless by floods which reached a depth of 30 feet in the Vizianagaram area of India. About 90 percent of the cattle in the area were drowned and considerable damage done to the jute crop.

GENEVA, Oct. 21.—(7)—Japan renewed her insistence today that she cannot take her troops out of Manchuria until China provides definite assurance that Japanese in Manchuria will be protected. The principal members of the League of Nations council could not shake the determination of Kenkichi Yoshizawa, the Japanese representative, at a long meeting this afternoon, and Lord Reading, of Great Britain said there probably would be an open meeting of the full council tomorrow. It was during today’s session that the Japanese distributed to the press another long memorandum setting forth their position, Ask Security “Something will have to be done,” the memorandum concluded, “to reestablish an atmosphere of relative security in order that living conditions in Manchuria may get back to normal. “Japan considers it essential that China give assurance that she wishes to put an end to illegal, hostil

Burlington, Iowa, Oct. 21—With more than six hundred men, women and children gathered at the farm of their leader with the avowed purpose of battling administration of the state bovine tuberculin law, an air charged with dread hung over Des Moines county today. Since before dawn farmers arrived at the home of Jake Eversman, president of the county chapter of the Farmers’ Protective Association, their spirit and their movements indicating that an offensive not equaled in three previous battlefronts of the testing war would be started. Meanwhile, the alarm of cavalrymen and liaison workers was awaited, and at the fairgrounds near here where four companies of Iowa national guardsmen now are quartered, officers spent a period of watchful waiting. At Des Moines, orders for another contingent of 1,300 men were issued by Adjutant General W. H. Bailey. All possible speed was indicated in moving
-CALCUTTA, India. Oct. 21 (UP)--One hundred fifty persons were drowned by floods in the Vizinagram area of Madras today and thousands were reported homeless and in need of food.

1931-01-26.text: NEW LONDON, Conn., Jan. 26. (AP)—With a full load of liquor, the British motor vessel Temiscondua from St. Johns, N. F., was captured today in Fort Pond Bay by a coast guard patrol boat. A one pound shell from the patrol boat tore through a fuel tank aboard the rum vessel and caused the engine room to be flooded with gasoline.

' As the British parliament prepared today to begin debate on the government's policy in India, the eastern empire itself seethed with excitement, for Mahatma Gandhi, the idol of millions, was about to be released from prison after nearly nine months. The viceroy had definitely ordered his release, but it was possible that Gandhi might refuse until the thousands of other political prisoners also were liberated. Several arrests were made in connection with the celebration and the Mayor of Calcutta was one of the prisoners. Several of the congress party leaders were released from prison today but the government had given no indication of its stand on general political amnesty. At Bombay Indian nationalists celebrated the first anniversary of their declaration of independence with parades and salutes to the nationalist flag,

New London, Conn., Jan. 26.— Coast Guard gunfire disabled the alleged British rum runner Temiscouda of St. Johns, Newfoundland, in Fort Pond Bay, Long Island, today. The vessel, carrying approximately 1,000 cases of liquor and a crew of six, was captured by the CG-288 after a one-pound shot had punctured its gasoline tank. The patrol boat fired three warning shots which were disregarded.

J Press Staff Correspondent, DON, Jan. 28, —Great Britain has taken the first step forward gaining the support of Mahatma Gandhi and his millions of Nationalist followers for the proposed Indian constitution framed at the round table conference, at which the Nationalists refused to participate. The government's decision to free more than a score of the principal All-India Congress leaders, including Gandhi, and to withdraw the outlawing of the committee, will be regarded here as a shrewd tactical move towards Gandhi's party and moderate elements, inasmuch as it forces the Nationalists' hands and impels them to make a decision soon on the proposed constitutional plan. Gandhi faces the most momentous decision in his career for whatever he decides to do is likely to split his followers into two camps. The great question now is whether Gandhi can control the movement that has started. He is

STOCKHOLM, Jan. 26. (AP)— One of the storybook's most appealing tales, that of the pretty girl who marries a prince, appeared today about to come true in Sweden. The principals in the romance are Prince Linnert, grandson of King Gustave and son of the monarch’s second son, William, and Karin Nisswandt, daughter of a prominent industrialist of Stockholm who is of Dutch descent. Court circles deny that stories of impending announcement of engagement of the two are correct, but the newspaper Degblad says, apparently with some authority, that an official announcement will be made shortly.

NEW DELHI, India, Jan. 25—(AP)—The unconditional release from prison of Mahatma Gandhi and other members of the nationalist congress working committee was ordered today by the Viceroy, Lord Irwin. Although no time was set in the release order, it is expected to take effect by tomorrow evening. Gandhi, leader of the nationalist movement, has been in jail at Poona since May 5. The Viceroy also issued an order establishing the lawfulness of the congress working committee. In his statement, the Viceroy said: “In order to provide an opportunity for consideration of the statement made by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald on January 19, my government, in consultation with the local government has thought it right that members of the congress working committee of the all-India congress should enjoy full liberty of discussion between themselves and with those who have acted as members of the commit

NEW DELHI, India, Jan. 26. (UP) — Millions of Indians awaited the release from prison today of their revered nationalist leader, Mahatma Gandhi. Unconditional freedom for past and present members of the All-India National Congress executive committee was ordered by Viceroy Lord Irwin. Orders which outlawed the working committee of the congress were cancelled. The release of such important native politicians as Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhai Patel, Mrs. Sarojini Naidu and Sen Gupta, was expected sometime today. The Indian civil disobedience leaders thus will have an opportunity to meet and discuss the proposals of the Indian round table conference. Upon his release, Gandhi will resume active command of the congress movement, which since he was imprisoned May 5, has had a score of leaders all of whom were arrested. Gandhi, a frail vegetarian, has been weakened by his long imprisonment

PARIS, Jan. 26.—(AP)—Senator Pierre Laval expressed confidence today that he would have a cabinet to replace that of Premier Theodore Steeg, which resigned Thursday, before tonight, and would be able to read his declaration of policy to the chamber of deputies Thursday. His optimism was in the face of a renewal of old antagonisms between the radical socialists, a powerful left group, and the rightist colleagues of Louis Marin. Yesterday the radicals voted to collaborate with their 135 chamber votes with the new premier designate, but their resolution was ambiguous and today it was understood that they maintained their old refusal of collaboration in any cabinet in which the Marinists were represented.

1931-02-05.text: PLYMOUTH, Eng. Feb. 4—A giant seaplane of the Royal Air Force, while engaged in practice, plunged into the waters of Batte Bay today with a loss of nine lives and injuries to two. One man escaped unhurt. The surface of the smooth bay, which was bright as a mirror, apparently caused the pilot to misjudge his distance above the water in landing. The craft dived full tilt into the water and before it could level out disappeared below the surface. A loud explosion was heard as the plane struck with terrific force. It brought small craft in the nearby waters to the rescue. The plane overturned and only the pontoons were visible. All except four of those in the plane were trapped in the submerged body. Divers were sent down in an effort to recover the bodies of the missing, among whom was Wing Commander C. G. Tucker, who had a splendid war record. After the accident, Flying Officer F. K. Wood

LONDON, Feb. 5.—(AP)—Disturbing reports that Ramsay MacDonald, British prime minister, had suffered a breakdown in health and would take an immediate vacation to recuperate were discredited at Ten Downing Street today. The prime minister, despite an all-night session of the House of Commons, was at his desk this morning. His presence was not required in all of last night’s debate which kept the Commons members on their benches for 17 hours and it did not greatly interrupt his schedule. Authoritative statements were made that he was in no danger of a breakdown in health and that his doctors had not advised a few days of complete rest, as reported generally here last night.

KINGSTON, Jamaica, Feb. 4 (P) — The Prince of Wales and his younger brother, Prince George, left the last British outpost in this part of the Caribbean at 7 o'clock tonight and their next stop will be in American territory. The liner on which they are ordinary passengers, the Oropesa, is scheduled to reach Cristobal, Canal Zone, sometime Friday.

BALTIMORE, Md., Feb. 5. (1)— John F. Dandy, 40, a Lieutenant in the British Royal Flying Corps during the World War, committed suicide on a street here, early today, after seeing a moving picture which dramatized the part aviators played in the war, police reported. His mother, Mrs. Mary Dandy, with whom he lived, said her son had been despondent recently because of ill health. A motorist, who summoned the police, told them he saw Dandy walk across the street and, as he reached the curb, draw a pistol and shoot himself in the head.

London, Feb. 5. (INS)—The British air ministry to-day ordered a complete inquiry into the flying accident in Plymouth Harbor yesterday when an R. A. F. tri-motored all-metal flying boat dived into the water and exploded, killing nine and injuring three. Eye witnesses of yesterday's accident said the pilot of the bomber was apparently trying to come down on the water when the accident occurred. The plane was returning to its Plymouth base after bombing practice. Bright sunlight dazzled the pilot, who apparently did not realize he was so close to the water. One wing touched the water and the next instant there was a violent explosion. London, Feb. 5. (INS)—Martial law has been declared at Hastings, New Zealand, one of the two cities razed by Tuesday's earthquake, according to a Central News dispatch from Auckland. This action was taken to prevent looting. Sunday has been declared a day of

LONDON, Feb. 1.—Martial law has been declared at Hastings, New Zealand, one of the two cities razed by Tuesday's earthquake, according to a Central News dispatch from Auckland. This action was taken to prevent looting. Sunday has been declared a day of mourning throughout all of New Zealand for earthquake victims. A sharp quake rocked Gisborne, 100 miles northeast of Napier, late tonight, sending most of that city’s 11,000 inhabitants scurrying to the streets. Little damage was done. According to a message to the Evening News from Christchurch, martial law has also been declared in Napier where marines are patrolling the streets to prevent looting. Desperate hungry men and women are ransacking the ruins of the city in search of food.

London, Feb. 5 —(UP)—Scotsmen stood in line and waited their turn to contribute to charity today. Londoners gasped to see the Scotch myth exploded. The occasion was the opening of an exhibition of Scottish antiques and historical relics. Proceeds went to charity. Scotch lads and lassies saw the chair in which Bonnie Prince Charlie sat as a boy. Kilted Scots filed past such relics as the rosary of Mary Queen of Scots, the first Bible printed in Scotland, and the hunting flask of the famous sheep thief, John Armstrong. Exhibits were loaned by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, Hugh (Continued on Page 2)

* U8 tailed ress.) PLYMOUTH, Eng, Feb. 5,--The bodies of Wing Commander, C. G. Tucker, and one aircraftsman had been recovered Thursday from the wreck of a Royal Air Force sea- plane which fell into the harbor here Wednesday. Eight men were drowned and one other died of in- juries. The others were injured severely.

1931-08-14.text: Associated Press Staff Correspondent BOMBAY, India, Aug. 14.—()—Mahatma Gandhi, apostle of India’s inarticulate millions, today placed on the shoulders of the British government the decision as to whether or not he would go to the second round table conference in London. “I will dash to London the moment the government makes the way clear for me,” he told the Associated Press. “The position is still retrievable by the local authorities implementing the terms of the truce.” Tired but not despondent after the ordeal through which he has passed in striving to obtain guarantees for the peasants, he added: “I claim for the Delhi settlement such sanctity and protection as are claimable for any ordinary contract. But if for this solemn contract one contracting party can be both prosecutor and judge it’s not worth the paper on which it’s written.”

Simla, India, Aug. 14—(4)—The British provincial government stands ready to examine alleged breaches in the Delhi pact and is making fresh overtures to Mahatma Gandhi in the hope of persuading him to attend the round table conference, it was learned today. Viceroy Lord Willingdon, while he is willing to examine the more serious breaches of the Delhi pact which Gandhi charges, is not disposed, however, to set up the arbitration board which the Mahatma demands, nor is he likely to return any taxes already collected from peasants, contending that these were collected under the ordinary tax laws and not by duress. Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, the Hindu lawyer who distinguished himself at the last round table conference, and who is generally credited with saving the negotiations between Gandhi and Lord Irwin, former viceroy, from collapse, is once more playing his role as peacemaker. When he arrive

GLASGOW, Scotland, Aug. 14—Police seeking three men who held up the Clydesdale Bank last Wednesday, killing two tellers and escaping with a considerable sum of money, today believed the crime was committed by American bandits. Their theory is supported by information from persons who passed the bank at about the time of the incident.

BOMBAY, Aug. 13 (AP)—Mahatma Gandhi, ‘the frail, loin-cloth-clad leader of India’s nationalist millions, decided today to remain aloof from the second round table conference on Indian affairs to be held in London this fall. At a meeting of the working committee of the Indian national congress, a resolution, drafted by the mahatma and calling for abstention from the London parley, was The committee took this decision because of “repeated serious breaches of the Delhi pact by the provincial government.” This pact, signed last March by Gandhi and Lord Irwin, then viceroy of India, provided for abandonment of the civil disobedience campaign by the followers of the mahatma and for correction of alleged abuses against which the nationalists had long complained. It stipulated also that the Gandhi party would take part in the second round table conference. Review Tribunal Refused The mahatma sai

Simla, India, August 14 (AP).—At the end of a long special meeting of the viceroy's executive council today it became known that the government authorities believe a way may be found to enable Mahatma Gandhi to attend the round table conference at London. The working committee of the Indian National Conference decided yesterday it would have no part in the conference. Long Willington is disposed now to examine the more serious charges regarding breaches of the pact but he is willing to set up a board of arbitration at Gandhi's demand and be opposed to returning any taxes already collected from peasants on the ground these were collected under the ordinary laws and not by duress. The Mahatma himself has charged that the British government has failed to live up to the Delhi agreement.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark (P)—A body dressed in an aviator’s suit was seen floating near Foula Island in the Atlantic, reports reaching here Friday said. The reports confirmed similar advices reaching Oslo, Norway, which said a body had been seen in the vicinity of the route supposedly taken by Parker D. Cramer, American transatlantic flier, lost since last Sunday. A Norwegian fishing vessel reported sighting the body late Sunday, drifting west between 20 and 30 miles northwest of the islands. The weather made it impossible to recover the body. Cramer and Oliver Pacquette, his Canadian radio operator, disappeared while on the last lap of their trip from Detroit to Copenhagen. They were mapping a proposed air mail route from America to Europe.

OSLO, NORWAY, Aug. 14—()—The submarine Nautilus, plowing northward through heavy seas, passed Bear Island at about midnight on the way to Spitzbergen, a wireless message from a Norwegian whaler said today. The message said the polar undersea vessel reported all hands well.

Copenhagen, Aug. 14--(UP)— Capt. Wolfgang von Gronau, German flier who left Iceland yesterday for Greenland, landed last evening at Scoresby Sound, a deep indentation in Eastern Greenland. Von Gronau departed for Greenland from Germany yesterday. He reached Iceland without incident. Von Gronau made the east-to-west flight via Iceland and Greenland in August last year, landing in New York Harbor. He was accompanied then by three students. They started from the Isle of Sylt in the North Sea, off the coast of Germany.

Mellon, American Secretary of the Treasury, and Premier Laval spent two and one-half hours conferring this afternoon in an effort to iron out the issues raised by President Hoover's war debt moratorium proposal and the French government's reply. The first tangible result of the Mellon-Laval conference was an invitation, issued as soon as the meeting was over, to Chancellor Bruening and Foreign Minister Curtius of Germany to come to Paris. At the conference table in addition to Mr. Mellon and the French premier were United States Ambassador Walter E. Edge, Foreign Minister Briand, Finance Minister Flandin, Budget Minister Pietri, Andre Francois-Poncet, undersecretary for finance and economy and J. Theodore Marriner, counselor to the American embassy. The portion of the French reply believed to have come in for the major part of the discu

BLAGOVESHCHENSK, Siberia, June 27.—()—With their plane bogged down in a mud hole, Wiley Post and Harold Gatty faced a possible delay tonight in their record-shattering flight that has taken them three-fifths of the way around the globe in four days and three hours. It was with a shower of mud and water that the American fliers greeted the gentry of this town when they landed this evening from Irkutsk. Step Out with Smile. They had a smile through it all, and stepped out of the plane with word they were in perfect condition. The landing field was in bad shape and the mud hole was softer than at first thought, however. Gradually the monoplane Winnie Mae settled down into the Siberian mud and “all the king’s horses and all the king’s men,” in the form of patient plow horses and peasants, could not free it. It was the first mishap of the flight. Hub-deep the staunch plane rested tonight and

BLAGOVESHCHENSK, Siberia. (AP) After an enforced delay of fourteen and one-half hours here, Wiley Post and Harold Gatty, the "American 'round the world fliers, roared away at 9:50 p.m., Saturday. Their next scheduled stop was Khabarovsk, 350 miles distant, which they expected to reach within two hours and a half. At Khabarovsk, they said, they would refuel and take off immediately for Nome, Alaska, probably the most hazardous leg of their record breaking flight. From Khabarovsk to Nome is an air line distance of more than 2,000 miles, fraught with danger of high mountains and seas, and the possibility of storms and enshrouding fog. The fliers landed here at 7 a.m., Saturday (e.s.t.). The landing field was in bad shape and their plane, the "Winnie Mae," settled down into Siberian mud. Throughout the night the monoplane rested in the muck. It was removed Sunday morning, however, and the fl

(By The Associated Press) Ottawa, Ont., June 27.—J. H. Marshall, 22-year-old student pilot of the Ottawa flying club, was killed today when the airplane he was flying crashed from a height of 3,000 feet. He had obtained his pilot's license only yesterday.

(By the Associated Press) The central valleys of the nation were parched again yesterday as a blistering sun kept steadily at work. Thermometers flirted with the 100 degree mark, serious damage was reported to crops and the number of deaths from the heat for the week exceeded 90. The Missouri and Mississippi valleys suffered principally, but other isolated areas felt blasts almost as hot. Some sections in the Arkansas and lower Ohio valleys had temperatures of 100 or more. Storm Rising The Texas coast was keeping its eye on the Gulf of Mexico, where a tropical storm with high winds was swirling eccentrically towards land with northeast winds and gales in prospect for the area around Port Aransas. A drizzle which the weather bureau had predicted might bring relief to the northernmost sections started falling at Duluth Saturday -(Continued on Page 6)

OTTAWA, Ill., June 21 (A') -- Howard Smith, 16, high school student, was being kept alive by air compressors tonight while a mine rescue crew was digging desperately to reach him at the bottom of a 24-foot well where he was buried under rocks and dirt by a cave-in. He told county officials at the top of the well through a speaking tube that he was not injured. A crowd estimated at 5,000 persons thronged the farm of Frank De Bolt, the boy's grandfather, where the well is located. Because of the fear of further cave-ins, miners and mine rescuers who were summoned from La Salle, Ill., could not dig directly into the debris covering the boy but had to sink a 24-foot shaft a considerable distance from the well. From there they were tunneling toward the well.

NEW YORK, June 27.—Wilbur C. Whitehead, 65, noted bridge whist expert, died today on the steamship Ile de France, on which he was bound for Europe with his granddaughter. Mr. Whitehead was one of the country’s most prominent bridge authorities, author of numerous books on whist. He was a native of Cleveland, Ohio. He was at one time president of the Knickerbocker Whist Club of New York and a pioneer in the field of contract bridge.

Washington, June 27 (4)—Tedious details tonight stood in the way of a Franco-American reparations moratorium settlement. Confidence of an ultimate agreement expressed by Secretary Stimson before sailing from New York for conferences with European leaders, was reflected throughout the day by his subordinates at the State Department. Acting Secretary Castle interpreted the vote of the French chamber of deputies as one of confidence in the government itself. It was not, he said, an expression of parliamentary support for an unalterable step on the French counter proposal to President Hoover's proposal for a one-year suspension of intergovernmental debt payment. Meanwhile Washington officials turned their attention to the economic situation in Latin America where Bolivia and Peru have defaulted in a total of $154,000,000 in loans. These include federal, state (Turn to Page Four)

1931-09-25.text: Washington, Sept. 25.—(A.P.)— Senator Reed of Pennsylvania, after advocating to President Hoover today his proposal for a sales tax, said he believed the United States should follow Great Britain's example and “face the music.” Reed said he believed that unless additional money were raised by taxation the treasury’s deficit would reach beyond $1,506,000,000. The Republican senator called upon the president principally to congratulate him upon his address to the American Legion which Reed said, “apparently has killed the bonus move.” “If the legion does not bring up the bonus,” he said, “I don’t believe it will ever pass congress. Reed said he was opposed to such methods of raising funds as decreasing the salaries of congress and federal workers. Senator Reed did not amplify his reference to following the example of Great Britain, which was in connection with recent drastic measures initi

LONDON, Sept. 25.—(#)— Directors of four Lancashire cotton mills, two of which have been idle for four years, announced today they would resume operations immediately employing 1,500 workers. Two blast furnaces will be opened at Barrow on Monday and steel works will be opened a few days later. Liverpool reports record sales of cotton and Birmingham and other industrial centers report business improvement.

LONDON, Sept. 25. (AP) — King George was understood today to be opposed to the movement for early dissolution of parliament and a general election on a protective tariff issue. He was said on good authority to be averse to terminating the tenure of the national government at least until it had put its economy program into effect and restored world confidence in the British pound. It was felt that his opinions would effectively stifle the call for an appeal to the people this fall. The king has played an influential role in politics since the financial crisis was recognized some weeks ago. He rushed back from Balmoral, Scotland, and personally took a hand in the formation of the emergency government to succeed the labor ministry. Several newspapers said Prime Minister MacDonald would interrupt his rest cure in the country and return to London to discuss the question of an election with hi

LONDON, Sept. 24.—(AP)—Undaunted by threats against his life from Lancashire workers who blame his “message of the spinning wheel” for the desperate state of the textile districts, Mahatma Gandhi will go tomorrow to a village near Manchester to spend the week-end in the heart of the factory district. Accompanying him will be three or four British government detectives, but authorities believe the leader of the Indian independence movement will be unmolested and his message listened to with nothing more than a few taunts. Gandhi's own attitude is that the people will not harm him when they understand that in boycotting British cotton goods he meant no harm for Lancashire, but good for India.

Boys who kept the world safe for democracy and who now are making Iowa safe for cows, today had yet another element essential for any self-respecting war. Mud. Mud of the kind some of the 1,785 guardsmen here to protect veterinarians while testing cattle for tuberculosis sloshed through at Vimy Ridge. Mud that supposedly was outlawed when Iowa embarked on its $100,000,000 paving program. Mud as muddy as that of the Argonne. And so today veterans of the A. E. F. had long stories to tell of previous days and of other climes: "Say, boy, you shoulda seen the mud at Shatto Terry ..." They used tractors to pull trucks and men to push tractors at the Iowa national guard camp. They put straw in the company streets for a dry place to walk on and then put straw on the muddy straw. It rained during the night, and it was cold. (Say, Buddy, you shoulda seen the rain at Poitiers ...). Mobilization at

UTICA, N. Y.—(U.P)—West Utica residents today hoped for early frosts to end almost three weeks of suffering from an insect plague identified by state entomologists as hordes of English crickets. Cold weather, advices from Albany said, would kill millions of young crickets, breeding in the West Utica dumping grounds and nearby hay fields, and check the plague, which has caused several families to desert their homes. The insects, a cross between a grasshopper and a cricket, have descended upon homes here in thousands, destroying rugs, clothes, home furnishings and food. Residents have been attacked. Many reported they could not sleep at night because the crickets bit them. Attempts by the local fire department to fire the breeding grounds drove the winged creatures into houses.

London, Sept. 25.~(AP)--The stock exchange committee announced today that, from tomorrow, all dealings must be for cash and may not be continued from day to day. No fresh option business may be transacted, the committee announced. Contracts already entered into on account will be settled in the ordinary way on October 8.

LONDON, Sept. 25, (#)—Prime Minister MacDonald returned to his residence at Ten Downing Street today, appearing greatly refreshed after a few days holiday in the country. It was made clear that his return was not in the nature of an official recall and that he was bound for his country home at Chequers for the weekend as originally planned. He had to pass through London en route from his unnamed retreat, it was said, and he decided to seize the opportunity of going to the House of Commons before leaving.

1931-04-22.text: WYNDSOR, Ont, April 22,--(COP) —Lady Mary Heath, famous British aviator, failed to appear in magistrate’s court here today to face trial on a charge of drunkenness and her bail was declared forfeited. Booked as Mary Heath, she spent six hours in the jail before she was released on bail of $16.50. When she failed to appear, Magistrate D. M. Brodie took brief testimony. “She was in a very drunken condition,” Constable Alfred Carter, who with another constable made the arrest, testified. That concluded the testimony and the fine and costs were entered against her. Reginald G. Williams, New York, her secretary, who was with her, was arrested, too, but subsequently was released without charges being filed. At her hotel room Lady Heath was informed of the forfeiture of her bond. “Honor bright,” she said, “I wasn't drunk. Why, I wasn’t even cheery. It is just a mean dirty old trick.” Lady Heath

Phea, Italy, April 22.—Capt. Frank M. Hawks, on his return flight from Rome to London, landed here at 3 p.m. and left 15 minutes later after refueling. Rome, April 22.—Capt. Frank Hawks departed on his return trip to England at 1:41 p.m. today from Venticello airdrome. Rome, April 22.—Captain Hawks, American flier, arrived at 11:48 a.m., after a record-breaking non-stop flight from London to Rome. Hawks said he had averaged 174 miles an hour on the flight, despite the fact that he encountered unfavorable weather. “I had to fight wind and rain along the route,” the American flier told the United Press correspondent. Hawks required only five hours and 22 minutes for the flight from Heston Airdrome, London to Rome. The former record for the London-Rome flight was 12 hours held by Commander Charles E. London, April 21. (—Alfonso XIII, king without a country, came to England tonight on a short business trip and was greeted by cheering thousands at Victoria station. A mighty roar of “Viva el rey” came from the throats of royalist followers as Alfonso stepped from the Paris express, tired but smiling whimsically at the ovation. He was hustled into an automobile and whirled away to the Claridge hotel, his favorite hostelry for many years. With him were 14 retainers.

Rome, April 22.—(A. P.)—Captain Frank Hawks, aviation speedster, took off from the Centocelle airport at 6:42 a. m. (central time) for Paris on a return flight to London, where he was due “about tea time.” “So long, boys,” he shouted above the roar of his motors as a group of Italian aviators, including a member of the air ministry, cheered him on his way. The low-winged monoplane which carried him across the American continent faster than any other man had ever made the flight rolled down the runway, gathering speed as it went, took off smoothly, circled in a bank and darted off to the north. Hawks intended to fly along the coast toward Paris, possibly halting there for fuel if headwinds deplete his supply, but he would rather race right through to London without stopping. It seemed more important to him than anything else that he be on time for a dinner to be given in his honor by the

LONDON, April 22.—Alfonso de Bourbon, exiled monarch of Spain, took his place today as one of the most popular visitors to London in recent years. Arriving from Paris a few hours after the British government had announced recognition of the Spanish republic, the former king’s “business visit” began with a roar of welcome at Victoria station and developed into something like an American Fourth of July celebration that continued until late at night. The usually staid old capital admitted today that it had never taken Alfonso to its heart in such a manner in the past, when he was a ruling monarch. His last visit to London only a few weeks ago was unostentatious, although the former king has always been popular here in social and sporting circles.

London, April 22.—(Wednesday)—UP)—Capt. Frank Hawks, American flier, took off at Heston Airdrome at 12:26 A. M. E. S. T. today in an attempt to make a record non-stop flight to Rome. Hawks planned to reach Rome within five hours and to arrive back in London, after a stop in Paris, by nightfall.

WASHINGTON, April 22 (AP) — American recognition of the new provisional government of Spain today was expected to follow closely that of Great Britain, France and Germany. With the announcement by the London foreign office that the British Empire was willing to begin diplomatic relations with the new government, it was felt in Washington that the principal nations of Europe and Latin America were now agreed in regarding the change of government as an accomplished fact. Diplomatic Slip Under these circumstances, it was considered likely that Ambassador Living B. Laughlin would notify the Spanish government the United States was ready to resume formal relations soon after Sir George Graham, the British ambassador, has notified Spain of the willingness of his government to recognize the new regime. The state department today had not been approached with regard to the appointment of Salvador

WASHINGTON, April 22. (AP)—Two blind British war veterans placed a wreath on the tomb of the Unknown Soldier today in the name of their 3,500 comrades who lost their sight in the world conflict. They were Captain Jaf Fraser, who served for five years in the English Parliament, and Clutha Mackenzie, a former member of the New Zealand parliament.

1931-11-18.text: Paris—()—The foreign affairs committee of the French Chamber by a vote of 16 to 11 Wednesday directed its vice president to call on Premier Laval and tell him that his explanation of his recent visits to Washington, London and Berlin was insufficient. | NEW YORK, Nov. 17.—(AP)— J. P. Morgan unexpectedly broke his usual silence upon his return from Europe tonight to observe that “things are looking a good deal better in England.” The financier spoke briefly as he neared port on the fog-delayed liner Mauretania. In response to a question: “How are conditions in England?” he said: “Things are looking a good deal better in England. It was a marvelous election and it looks as if the Nationalist government will be in for a long time. No party has ever had that majority before. The government is stable.”

London, Nov. 18.--(AP)—A preference tariff to unite the dominions of the British empire into economic unity, for which Lord Beaverbrook, noted newspaper publisher, fought for more than a year, seemed assured today with the passage of the government's tariff measure through its first stages in the House of Commons yesterday. Lord Beaverbrook, with his powerful newspaper, the Daily Express, demanded during the campaign a policy of free trade within the empire as a means of building up a British economic unity that would be comparable with the United States, between whose states no tariff barriers are known. The bill, as it was pushed through the first stages of House of Commons procedure, provides for several tariff duties, up to a maximum of 100 per cent, for hundreds of manufactured articles imported into Great Britain, most of them from the United States. Wellesley, Mass., Nov. 18—(A.P.)— Rosemary Pamela Gilding's adventure is ended. The homesick young English girl who disappeared from the home of Professor Hamilton C. MacDougall Saturday was due to sail from New York today to join her father, a London banker. Professor and Mrs. MacDougall, who accompanied the girl to New York, planned to secure passage for her on the S. S. American Trader. She was located yesterday at Springfield, where she sought work to earn her passage money home. Lonely, anxious to see her parents but afraid to ask them for passage money because she didn't want to "embarrass" them, she left the MacDougall home, where she had been a house guest for 14 weeks, to seek work in a strange American city. A few days at the Clinton hotel, a day in a Springfield rooming house and a round of the employment agencies in Springfield was the sum total of her adventure. She was loca

LONDON, (UP).—Reports that King Carol of Roumania had resigned in favor of his 10-year-old son, Crown Prince Michael, were ridiculed in official circles in Bucharest Wednesday. The reports were current in Berlin Tuesday night. The resignation was also rumored in Vienna, where it was believed it had become confused with a report from Budapest that Foreign Minister Count Julius Kar-Olyi intended to resign.

LONDON, Nov. 17, 4 -- Mahatma Gandhi talked across the Atlantic ocean over a telephone for the first time in his life today. He bestowed his blessings on the American people and said he would visit them “in God's appointed time.” He was hurrying to keep an appointment with Lady Astor when the phone rang and the operator announced that St. Paul, Minn., was calling. The Rev. Fred Pisher, pastor of the First Methodist Episcopal church at Ann Arbor, Mich., and a former missionary in Calcutta, was on the line and he wanted to invite Gandhi to come to America.

"NEW YORK, Nov. 18. (AP) — J. P. Morgan, back from Europe, is optimistic concerning conditions in England. He granted one of his rare interviews to ship reporters yesterday as the liner Mauretania waited for the fog to lift sufficiently for her to come up the harbor. “Things are looking a good deal better in England,” he said, “it was a marvelous election and it looks as if the nationalist government will be in for a long time. No party has ever had that majority before. The government is stable.” “Isn't unemployment in England decreasing?” he was asked. “Yes,” he said, “I think that is the case.” He declined to comment on economic conditions or American affairs.

Gandhi, heartened by talks with Prime Minister MacDonald, today reconsidered his decision to leave India Thursday and agreed to remain until the round-table conference ended. Lord Sankey, chairman of the conference, decided to prolong the session another week after several delegates had protested that the view of the principal representatives must be heard before a constitution could be drafted for India. "This leaves me in a fog," said Gandhi. "But I am ready to spend winter in England if necessary to secure some tangible results from these meetings." The Mahatma told the federal structures committee, charged with formulating a constitution, that India must have full control over her own army. "We will go through fire and storm and distress," he said, "and if it be God's will, through a shower of bullets to obtain our independence. "The nation whi

1931-08-23.text: LONDON, Aug. 22. (4)—Great Britain tonight began one of the most fateful weekends of her history, probably the most critical since the end of the war. Upon developments tomorrow or immediately after, the life of the MacDonald labor government seemed tonight to depend, and also the future of efforts to lead the United Kingdom from a growing economic crisis into greener fields of prosperity. The importance of the situation was brought home with considerable force to a slowly awakening British public this afternoon by an announcement from Buckingham Palace that King George was returning by special train from Balmoral, Scotland, where he arrived only yesterday for a vacation. At the same time Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader and principal opponent of the labor government, was hurrying back from a vacation in France. LONDON, (UP)—The king sped back to London by special train from Scotland tonight, prepared to be on hand during the grave political and financial crisis which threatens to overthrow the Labor government. The fall of Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald and his cabinet was widely predicted, but the government, after tedious hours of conferences, issued a statement indicating it had hope of finding a solution. Late in the day, an official statement was issued at No. 10 Downing Street which said: “The cabinet has been putting the finishing touches to a scheme which it is believed will meet the situation, and they will meet to hear the results tomorrow.” The problem which confronted

By The Associated Press NEMURO, Hokkaido Island, Japan Aug. 22—Fog over volcanic Iturup island Saturday again interrupted the vacation flight of Charles and Anne Lindbergh, marking the major weather delay since they left New York July 29. The Lindberghs were forced to descend on a swampy lake near Shansa, Iturup, after covering about half the 400 miles from Muroton Bay, Shimushiru Island, to Neumuro, their objective. Shansa, where the Lindberghs spent Saturday night, has a population of about a thousand; various phases of the seafood industries occupy its inhabitants. By The Associated Press. Hankow, Aug. 22.—An appalling picture of human misery and death confronted the American Asiatic fleet as it mobilized today to lend all possible assistance to the flood-stricken cities of Hankow, Wuchang and Hanyang, submerged by the swollen Yangtse River. Acting on orders from the navy department at Washington, the various units of the fleet, some already here, prepared to give what aid they could to the hundreds of thousands of homeless natives. A survey revealed that no Americans were in immediate need of assistance, although many American business men remained to carry on. The Yangtse, which already has engulfed a rich and populous territory of thousands of square miles, continued to rise and reached the level here of 53 feet, 5 inches. NEW YORK, Aug. 22. (®— With six persons dead and two more believed dying as a result of New York’s latest and most sensational gun battle, a harried police department Saturday sought new means to curb crime. The sixth victim, Gloria Lopez, three-year-old daughter of a fireman, died Saturday morning. Two Others Near Death The two in precarious condition are a 13-year-old messenger boy, shot from his bicycle, and a taxicab driver who was among the scores taking part in Friday night’s wild 15-mile pursuit of two murderers of a policeman seeking to shoot their way to freedom with a $4,619 stolen payroll. Dozens of patrolmen doing clerical work volunteered Saturday for extra duty after their regular working hours and were assigned to precincts where the danger of more holdups and gang war was deemed greatest. Havana, Aug. 22. (4)—Back in the palace here tonight after a fortnight in Santa Clara directing his troops, President Gerardo Machado said that he believed the revolution had been successfully stamped out and that action had ceased on all fronts. It became known tonight, however, that President Machado yesterday put into effect for Oriente province the state of war decreed in all the republic August 10. Fighting in recent days has centered in the far eastern section. Worn by loss of sleep, the president retired immediately after arriving and napped for three hours before dining with his family. Army headquarters denied reports there was still firing in many parts of Oriente—reports which were circulated by revolutionary leaders here today. The anti-Machadoists had asserted that some progress was being made by the rebels in the eastern province and that loyal troops had been unsuccessful

BOISE, Idaho, Aug. 22. (#)— Three more settlements, Pioneer- ville, the Golden Age mine and Grimes Pass, were evacuated tonight in the path of the fire thundering in the timber of Boise basin. The attack of the blazing demon on this new front forced dozens more families out of their homes and formed the second refugee camp in the basin,

Detroit, Aug. 22, (4) — Senator James Couzens of Michigan, today offered $1,000,000 for the relief of unemployment in Detroit during the coming winter. The Michigan senator, who said it was “more important to me that the unemployed be properly cared for this winter than it is to have my views adopted,” made his offer in a letter to Mayor Frank Murphy, and attached a provision that $9,000,000 more be raised by private subscription before his gift of $1,000,000 be made. The mayor, who has been hampered by lack of funds in his attempt to aid 18,000 families through the welfare department, characterized the senator’s offer as a “fine and noble deed,” and said he would take action at once to form a committee to raise the $9,000,000.

1931-04-19.text: (Associated Press) NEW YORK, April 14—Beginning time after midnight next Saturday, more than one-fourth of the population of the United States will lose an hour of darkness to gain an hour of daylight when 17 states will observe daylight saving time in some form. Clocks in all parts of the country will be pushed ahead one hour to conform with the new time which officially begins at 2 a.m., Sunday, April 26. In most localities, daylight saving will end at 2 a.m. Sunday, September 27. The Merchants Association of New York which has just completed a survey of the observance of Gaslight conservation throughout the United States and Canada, reveals that in 1941 the plan will be used by 437 cities and towns in the United States. This marks an increase of five communities over 1940. In Canada, 47 cities will observe daylight saving. Despite attempts of rural legislators in Connecticut to prohib

By The Associated Press. BUCHAREST, Rumania, April 18. —Dr. Nicholas Jorga, leader of the People’s Party, succeeded in forming a new Rumanian cabinet today and it was sworn in by King Carol tonight. The organization followed the failure of Nicholas Titulescu, former ambassador to Great Britain, to draw up a ministry satisfactory to the king. The latter insisted M. Argetoianu be appointed minister of the interior, but Former Premier Julin Maniu refused to serve with him. Dr. Jorga becomes prime minister and minister of education.

PARIS. April 18 (4)—Still resting from their hurried trip from Madrid into exile, King Alfonso and the Spanish royal family kept close to their hotel suite today and, as much as possible, out of the public eye. They planned to spend a quiet weekend. Whether or not Alfonso was considering his plans for the future could not be learned definitely. A press conference which had been tentatively arranged by the Duke of Miranda, the King's spokesman, for today was cancelled. That the king has plenty of money, it was being pointed out, is evidenced by the fact that the royal family is occupying the entire second floor of one of the most expensive hotels in Paris. There was a rumor, which could not be confirmed, that the king had deposited several million dollars in banks in the United States before his exile began.

BOMBAY, India. To the roar of 31-gun salutes, India bade affectionate farewell to retiring Viceroy Irwin Saturday and formally inducted Lord Willingdon as his successor for the next five years. Replying to an address from the municipality of Bombay, Lord Irwin adopted a grave tone concerning India’s future but tempered his remarks with expressions of hope and confidence. “The stiffest part of the hill is yet to come,” he said, “to none of us is it given to cast a true horoscope of the future or to foresee clearly the final shape of the great design for which we are set to labor. “The ultimate issue of that for which we are jointly striving lies indeed in other and wiser hands but I know my own hope and confidence in its attainment is shared by that old, trusted friend of India to whom I am now handing over my duties and responsibilities.
