HORTA, Fayal, Azores, April 14 (UP). Rebellious troops on the Island of Terceira surrendered today in the face of attack of naval vessels sent here from Lisbon. The garrison at San Miguel remains in revolt but the government appears to have the situation well in hand.

Vienna, April 18. (4).—Maria Jeritza, Metropolitan Opera company prima donna, tonight won a libel suit against Roderich Mueller Guttenbrunn, whose novel, “Riff-Raff,” she charged was a thinly veiled cartoon of herself. The author was convicted and sentenced to a month in prison after a trial which lasted two days and was attended by many of Vienna’s social leaders.

ABOARD ROYAL TRAIN, U.F. King Prajadhipok of Siam, with his consort, Queen Rambai Barni, enjoyed the scenery of the Canadian Rocky mountains as their special train bore them eastward to West Chester, N. Y., where he will undergo an operation for a cataract on his eye. The day was clear and bright and the king, refreshed by a good night's sleep and improvement in the bronchitis trouble which he suffered aboard the steamer, was better able to appreciate his journey thru mountains. The train made only brief stops to operations. No functions will be held until it reaches the American border at Portal, N. D., Sunday night where the Siamese royalty will be welcomed by representatives of the United States government.

NEW ORLEANS--Thirty Americans, men, women and children, tragic and nerve-shattered, arrived in American waters aboard the steamship Cefalu, Saturday, refugees from the latest outbreak of banditry in Nicaragua. Many of them penniless and with nothing left save the clothes they wore, they docked at New Orleans last night, bringing with them tales of massacre and guerilla warfare. The bodies of two of the nine Americans killed in the Nicaraguan bush during the past week lay in the hold of the Cefalu, whose pennants flew at half staff as she steamed up the Mississippi River. These were Marine Capt. H. O. Peffley, of Philadelphia, slain at the head of a detachment of Guardia Nacional trying to beat off a bandit attack on Puerto Cabezas; and William B. Selser, formerly of Jackson, Miss., standard fruit and steamship employee, who was killed from ambush. Sandino forces fell on a group of planta

1931-01-11.text: Windsor, England, Jan. 10. — King George stood with bowed head today before the scarlet and gold high altar in St. George’s chapel, Windsor castle, to bid a last farewell to his eldest sister, the princess royal, who died last Sunday. The service was simple and solemn, but the scene itself was one of color and pageantry. The coffin was borne from Albert memorial chapel, where it had rested overnight. It was carried between ranks of the Military Knights of Windsor, clad in blue capes and plumed hats, and the king’s life guards in scarlet uniforms and flashing breastplates. Two pipers playing a Scottish dirge preceded the coffin, and behind it walked the king, Queen Mary, the two daughters of the princess and other members of the royal family. It was laid at the foot of the altar during the brief service and then was lowered into the vault. While the ceremony at Windsor was in progress the

SHANGHAI, Jan. 10.—(#)—Sweeping down out of the barren steppes of Mongolia, a blizzard and sand storm that started Thursday had brought death and desolation to a wide area of North China tonight. Hundreds were reported to have died in the dust and snowstorm that raged southward as far as the Yangtse river. Temperatures suddenly dropped 40 degrees to an average of 15 below over the region most affected. Misery and suffering came to thousands of the poor people in the storm’s path. Peiping police gathered from the streets the bodies of 100 persons who perished in the last 24 hours. In outlying districts 18 more bodies were found in unheated shacks. Penniless, these victims were unable to buy fuel. Twenty froze to death in Tientsin. In both Peiping and Tientsin the Salvation Army and Chinese organizations set up gruel kitchens. They also built temporary shelters for many. The vast area from

LEBOURGET, France, Jan. 10.—(P)—All seaboard aviation posts from Biarritz to Nantes were instructed today to be on the watch tomorrow and thereafter for the monoplane Tradewind, which left Bermuda today on a flight to Paris by way of the Azores. The plane left Hamilton at 1:16 a.m. E.S.T. tomorrow. Should the pilots, Mrs. Beryl Wart and Lieutenant William S. MacLaren, push right on after refueling they should reach Paris some time after midnight Sunday. Authorities today made preparations at both Suresnes Fond, in the river Seine near Paris and at Enghien lake to receive the ship, which is equipped with pontoons for coming down on the water. The Montvalerien searchlight, near Suresnes, will flash intermittently as she comes and the river will be lighter if the weather is clear. Enghien lake will be lighted should it be foggy.

Guayaquil, Ecuador, Jan. 10.—(/) Little hope was held tonight for the rescue of any of the 170-track workers who were buried when a huge landslide roared down upon them without warning. The accident occurred near Huigra, seventy-three miles from Guayaquil, at about 5 a.m. The men were engaged in removing the debris of another slide, which had occurred about 10 p.m., when the great mass of dirt and rocks poured down upon them. Men who rushed to the rescue and attempted rescue work said they found no signs of life. Heavy Rains Blamed. The two slides were believed due to torrential rains which have flooded the country for the last few days. The Chanchan river has become a torrent, menacing the town of Huigra, and landslides have broken telephonic and telegraphic communications. From reports that reached here, it appeared a whole hillside fell upon the line of the Quito-Guayaquil railway whe

Bermuda, Jan. 11—Mrs. Beryl Hart and Lieut. William S. MacLaren, American aviators, headed eastward for the Azores Saturday in their Bellanca monoplane on the second leg of a commercial flight to Paris. They carried a load of more than three tons, including 300 gallons of gasoline, 20 gallons of oil and 250 pounds of varied cargo, the first ever carried in an ocean jump of such magnitude. The start was made at 12:15 p.m. local time (10:15 a.m. Decatur time). Weather conditions were excellent, although the roughness of the harbor waters forced the plane to taxi for nearly a mile before it got up in the air. The fliers expected to take about 21 hours for the flight to the Azores, arriving there about 7:15 a.m. Decatur time, Sunday morning. The distance for the hop, the longest in their journey toward Paris, is 2,045 miles.

OAKLAND, Calif., Jan. 10—(AP)—Through an opening too small to accommodate his companions, one of the 20 men imprisoned in Camp Mitchell tunnel since 6:30 p.m. Friday crawled to safety tonight. The other 19 were safe and could be touched by rescuers. Hope of getting all of the men out immediately led to the erroneous report that the 20 were freed. After Oscar Nelson, the smallest member of the trapped crew, crawled through, another tried to follow but the opening was too small. Some obstacle, which the rescuers could not cut through, necessitated a detour of the four-foot rescue tunnel and delayed releasing the other 19 who had been imprisoned more than 24 hours tonight. The men, part of a crew digging a tunnel for San Francisco’s Hetch Hetchy water project, were trapped by a cave-in at 6:30 o'clock last night, owed their lives, perhaps, to the “kid trick” of Welby Morgan, 28, a workman w

NEW YORK—(*) — About 150 persons were injured last night when a grandstand collapsed in a Brooklyn armory where a basketball game was about to begin between two college teams. There were about 1,000 persons in the stands... The stands were temporary structures extending from the balcony and held in place by steel clamps. There were about 3,000 persons in the hall. Scenes closely approaching a panic followed upon the crash, Police reserves were called and ambulances from several hospitals were sent to the scene.

Washington, D. C., Jan. 10.—Liberia, founded as a refuge for freed men upon whom the scars of bondage still were fresh, was pictured to the world today as a nation in which slavery was imposed by whip and chains. Piteous appeals from ignorant black natives ran through the pages of a report of an investigating commission sent there at the request of the state department. The department made the report public tonight. The commission consisted of Cuthbert Christy, chairman, appointed by the League of Nations; Charles Spurgeon Johnson, appointed by the United States, and Arthur Barclay, appointed by Liberia. The committee recommended radical changes in various government institutions to bring to an end the conditions. U. S. Takes Hand Severe pressure has been brought to bear by the United States upon Liberia to meet the commission’s recommendations, but so far the department considers the st

1931-09-06.text: Barcelona — It was officially announced this afternoon that leaders of the general strike, which began here Thursday and resulted in at least four deaths, had reached an agreement with the authorities to send their men back to work. Meanwhile, the disorders which occurred here yesterday and today had spread to several smaller towns in the vicinity, but no serious fighting was reported.

SHANGHAI, Sept. 5.—(P)— The China flood relief commission said today that wheat purchased from the American farm board would be less than half the foodstuff needed this winter by 10,000,000 starving Chinese. The commission was seeking to augment the 15,000,000 bushels of American wheat with huge amounts of millet and beans. (Continued on Page 8, Col. 6.)

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, Sept. 5.—(AP)—The Graf Zeppelin, homeward bound from Pernambuco, in a radio message received here at 11:30 p.m. (5:30 EST) gave her position as latitude 24.54 north, longitude 24.33 west. The position indicates the ship was flying northward some distance off the west coast of Africa and was nearing the Canary Islands. BERLIN, Sept. 6 — (AP) — A message direct from the Graf Zeppelin to the Wolff agency tonight said the airship flew at an altitude of 4,000 feet during the afternoon to permit scientists aboard to make a series of experiments. The message said the Graf was encountering strong headwinds and making a speed of 60 miles an hour.

BARCELONA, Spain — (#)— Mayor James Ayguade announced shortly after midnight that all syndicalists, including the “extremists,” had agreed to halt violence and to resume work. The mayor's announcement followed upon a Saturday night during which scattering pistol shots resounded in various parts of the city and the strikers had threatened further action. The subway, streetcar, bus and taxi branches, which early in the evening announced they would continue their strike until Governor

Monticello, Ky. Sept. 4 (P)—A long standing feud between members of two mountain families flared again here last night and Lon Guffey, 35, and Otho Lovelace were fatally wounded in a pistol fight at the Wayne County fairgrounds. Guffey, who slew Lovelace's brother, Lyle, July 12, encountered Otho Lovelace at the fair. Few words were spoken before pistols were drawn. Guffey, struck three times by Lovelace’s fire, fell, but lifted himself on his elbows and fired five shots into Lovelace. The shooting threw the fair crowd of several thousand into panic. Guffey died after reaching a hospital here and Lovelace succumbed early today. Officers said the bitter feeling between the two families dated back many years.

SANTIAGO, Chile —(>)— An official bulletin issued by the government Saturday night indicated that the “zero hour” for bombing the rebel fleet from the air, originally fixed for 6 p. m., had been postponed until Sunday. Although the government made no specific announcement of any change in the time, the bulletin said that nine additional planes would join the air force at Ovalle Sunday with a number of flyers with absolute orders “to

CLEVELAND, Sept. 5 (4P).-—-Maj. Jimmy Doolittle, yesterday's maker of a new trans-continental speed record, flashed through the air at 272.034 miles per hour today in a speed trial at the national air races here, but Lowell Bayles, Springfield, Mass, made plans tonight to go faster tomorrow. Bayles intends his flight to be the races’ first officially-timed assault on the world’s speed record for land planes, 278 miles per hour. He will fly his Gee Bee monoplane, which took him 286 miles per hour Tuesday with a 20-mile wind behind him. Doolittle, in his speed trials today, used the same Laird biplane in which he yesterday flew from Burbank, Cal., to Cleveland, to New York, and back to Cleveland again.

According to a telegram received at the office of the State fish and game commission from Washington D. C., Iowa will have one month of hunting migratory water fowl this fall, the month of October, in place of three months heretofore. This restriction of the open season for water fowl has been made necessary owing to disastrous drought conditions which exist in Canadian breeding areas. The Iowa season will be from 12 o'clock noon Thursday, October 1 until sunset Saturday, October 31. This applies to all surrounding states. This governmental edict is effective in the United States and Alaska and it is anticipated that Canadian authorities will soon take similar action. Although the open season is limited to one month and there will undoubtedly be a great curtailment of the flight, yet it is anticipated that there will still be a fair bag for hunters in those sections where ducks are usual

1931-04-06.text: Brooklands, England, April 6.—(A.P.)—Sir Malcolm Campbell, world's motor car speed king, looked death in the eye for a few seconds today while an almost unmanageable racing car carried him along the steeply banked track at Brooklands at 100 miles an hour. Competing in a handicap event at the opening day of racing on the Brooklands auto racing club program, Sir Malcolm was just completing the first lap of a 12-mile race when the rod holding the front wheels in position broke. As the spectators lining both sides of the track gasped in horror, Sir Malcolm fought the careening car along the steeply banked track as the other competitors roared past, and brought it to a halt without mishap. If the car had gone off the track it probably would have meant death both to himself and many spectators. Campbell said it was one of the closest calls he'd ever had.

| NEW DELHI, April 6.—(AP)— Mahatma Gandhi has decided to dispense with the aid of erstwhile colleagues at the forthcoming round table conference at London and will represent the nationalist cause there by himself. His decision has taken India and the Indian government entirely by surprise and has added fuel to the flame of his critics who have complained increasingly recently that he was assuming the role of a dictator of the nationalist movement. It was Gandhi's first intention to take twelve persons with him to England for the round table conference, at which a future constitution for India is likely to reach well rounded form, instead of the fifteen delegates to which the All India National Congress is entitled. Last week he whittled the number who would go to five, explaining that more would make an unwieldy group. Since then he has informed his congress co-workers that since he had

LONDON, April 6. (P)—An exchange telegraph dispatch from Tokyo said four persons were killed, 60 were injured and 13 airplanes were destroyed by a wind storm which wrecked the military airdrome at Kyushu with damages estimated at $5,000,000.

Washington — (%) — Montagu Norman, governor of the Bank of England, conferred today with Eugene Meyer, Jr., governor of the Federal Reserve Board, Secretary Mellon and members of the board. No official would discuss the nature of the conferences. Although it had been said upon his arrival in New York that no particular importance was to be attached to his visit there was much speculation and suggestion that he would bring the situation in the silver-using countries of the world to the attention of government officials, it was also suggested that the governor would discuss the world’s gold supply with administration representatives.

LISBON, Portugal, April 5. (AP) — Rebellious troops at Funchal, Madeira, succeeded in wresting control from civil and military representatives of the Lisbon government, it was learned today. An emergency session of the cabinet here directed that troops be ordered to Funchal immediately. A strict censorship has been clamped down on all messages between here and the island. Reports reaching here despite the censorship said two army officers, both Lieutenants, had incited the mutiny. They raided the military barracks and arrested Colonel Silva Leal, the high commissioner, and other officers who refused to join them. They took over the town without resistance and radioed the government here its representatives had been overthrown and the military junta in control would take orders only from a legally constituted "national" government at the capital. TOKYO, April 5 - Four persons were killed and 12 injured by a terrible whirlwind which early today swept the army aviation station at Cachiaral, on the island of Kyushu. Twenty-one airplanes were destroyed and 50 others were damaged. A number of houses also were destroyed by the wind, which was accompanied by hail. Damage was estimated at approximately $5,000,000. The whirlwind swept a path only about 35 yards wide. It leveled all the hangars at the air station except one. Those killed were women and children, crushed beneath falling walls.

LAS PALMAS, Canary Islands. April 6.—(UP)—The flying boat DO-X will start her new trials about April 16, officials said yesterday in commenting on progress toward repair of the ship, which was damaged here while en route to South America and New York. The German craft, largest in the world, probably will resume its voyage about April 29.

Tokyo, April 5. (®)—Japan was cheered tonight by the announcement of surgeons that the condition of Premier Yuko Hamaguchi was entirely satisfactory. The 61-year-old premier underwent an operation shortly after midnight for the removal of an obstruction in the abdomen resulting from a wound inflicted last November by a young Japanese whose mind had been deranged by opposition to Hamaguchi's acceptance of the London naval treaty. Surgeons said the premier was feeling so well he probably would be allowed to see a few callers tomorrow and predicted he would leave the hospital within ten days or a fortnight.

1931-04-25.text: London, April 25—(A.P.)—Frightened by preparations by a Portuguese expeditionary force for an attack on Funchal, Madeira Island capital held by a rebel junta, 100 British subjects yesterday took the advice of their consul and boarded the liner Armadale Castle for England. A dispatch to The Daily Express from the liner said there was every indication that the rebel leaders intended desperately to resist the expeditionary force. Funchal, their stronghold, is defended by American naval guns, left there after the war, and strong natural fortifications which made it difficult of access. Every available man on the island has been mobilized for the rebel defense force and it is believed an army of 3,000 rebels will be available to resist the Lisbon troops.

PARIS, Apr. 25.—1;—Clothed in the sombre corded robe of a sister of the order of Saint Francis of Assisi, the body of the 79-year-old Infanta Isabel of Spain, who died in exile here Thursday, was borne to its tomb today. Three masses were said in the mortuary apartment of the Ladies' home where she died. Then, with less pomp than accompanies the funeral of most humble citizens, the body was taken to Pere Lachaise cemetery, where the family vault of Don Jose Marts Quinones de Leon, monarchist ambassador in Paris, was opened for it.

(Associated Press Correspondent, ROME, April 24 (AP)—Pope Pius XI, for the second time in his reign, unexpectedly left Vatican City today and participated in the dedication of the new Propaganda Fide College, built largely with American funds. It was the first occasion since 1870 in which a Pope had officiated in a public ceremony outside the Vatican precincts. The Pope presided at the inauguration of the new structure, being assisted by Cardinal Mundelein of Chicago and 15 other Cardinals. He personally blessed the four points of the chapel, the auditorium and kneeling throngs which included many American students for the priesthood. Two hours later he was back in the Vatican, Surprising the Catholic world and even his own associates, he left the Vatican City this morning by a side portal and traveled the short distance to the college grounds in his own car. LENOX, Mass, Apr. 25 (UP)— A disastrous fire swept the fashionable summer resort colony in the Berkshire hills here today, destroying the largest hotel, several cottages, and a large stretch of woods before it was brought under control. Damage was estimated by the police department at a million dollars. Hundreds of volunteer firefighters from Lenox and other villages battled all night against the blaze which at one time threatened to wipe out the entire resort. The fire started in the hotel and soon spread to several surrounding cottages. Only a few persons were living at the resort since the regular season does not start until June 1.

LOS ANGELES, April 24 (P)— An earthquake that lasted five seconds shook Los Angeles and the suburbs at 10:28 a. m., today but with the exception of a few shattered store windows and some broken chinaware the sole result was a highly excited populace. The epicenter apparently was in the Santa Monica bay district. Several store windows fell in, plaster in offices and homes was cracked and dishes broken. From offices, homes and apartments alike, people, disregarding the warnings of earthquake experts, fled in the streets, In Hollywood, the shock was slight but it was more pronounced in Los Angeles. Redondo Beach, Compton and Torrance felt it almost as strongly as in Santa Monica and small amounts of damage were reported. By The Associated Press. Washington, April 24—Daughters of the American Revolution called for special police protection today after adopting resolutions denouncing communism. Officers were stationed at every door of the hall with instructions to allow no one to enter except business and plain clothesmen were scattered throughout the audience. With the meeting place of the organization's annual convention thus protected, the delegates listened to an address late today by Rep. Fish, New York, chairman of the House communist investigating committee. Fish, whose address had been blue-penciled by the organization with his consent, said the department had not co-operated fully with his committee's investigation of communism. Perry, alias George Parker, slain last night in South Bend, Ind, was put to death by two associates in the Edward Litsinger-Myrtle Blacklidge $50,000 “faro swindle” at Springfield, IL. SALEM, Ore., April 24 (AP) —Major General Smedley D. Butler of the marines is coming to Oregon to organize a new state police force designed to suppress crime. The noted marine officer was granted a leave of absence today and is expected here next month to direct consolidation under one superintendent of all law enforcing agencies of the state. Agencies to be consolidated into a state constabulary include two divisions enforcing fish and game laws, the fire marshal’s office, state traffic department and the prohibition department. The constabulary, provided for by the last legislature, will give Oregon a mobile police force with a superintendent responsible to the governor. “I am sure the general will be able to give us many valuable suggestions that will aid in putting the new state police law into effect,” Governor Julius L. 1931-10-13.text: NEW LONDON, IOWA, Oct. 12 —(AP)—Hospitality of southeastern Iowa farmers to the state compulsory Bovine Tuberculin Test law again burst into open rebellion today as veterinarians sought to begin inoculating county cattle. About 500 embittered men marched on the New London jail and freed Roland Hart, 20, arrested for scoffing at Iowa National Guardsmen dispersing farmers gathered to hinder work of the testers. The soldiers were attempting to disperse the crowd near the McKinnon farm near here, some of the protesters returned here. With more than 400 farmers from Cedar, Muscatine and Des Moines counties they gathered at the city park and paraded to the jail. There they overran the fire hall forming the front part of the municipal building and broke jail locks and cell bars to free the young man. Easington, Durham, England, Oct. 12 ()—In one of the most eloquent appeals of his career, Ramsey MacDonald tonight asked Durham miners to send him back to the House of Commons as a common laborer to help build the dam against national and world chaos. “Who dares point the finger of scorn at me?” the prime minister demanded. Whether MacDonald won the support of the nearly 2,090 miners and their womenfolk no one could say, but, judged from the applause, he carried his audience with him. The prime minister made this speech to his constituents, whose Labor party organization has repudiated him, on his sixty-fifth birthday. Hecklers interrupted him but he silenced them with strong words. “You be quiet, my friend,” he told one of the interrupters. “You'll be a wiser man.” The prime minister bared Great Britain’s problems to his simple hearers, reducing the complex problems of national and inte

NEW LONDON, Ia., Oct. 13 (UP)—Iowa's cattle testing has spread to a new county and state troops again stood guard today while veterinarians worked to the accompaniment of boos and catcalls. About 500 enraged farmers broke into the New London jail yesterday and released Ronald Hart, a young man who had been arrested for heckling veterinarians who were carrying out state orders to test all cattle for tuberculosis. The farmers, many of whom were said to be from neighboring Cedar county, stormed the jail, twisted bars, battered doors and carried Hart off by force of numbers. Soldiers were rushed here immediately and set up machine guns in the village square. Children and farmers booed. There was no serious physical resistance, however, and the soldiers

Ramsay MacDonald, three times prime minister of Great Britain, stumped the coal mining region of Durham today, continuing his three-day struggle to defend his parliamentary constituency against a 47-year-old schoolmaster. He spoke to 2,000 miners and their families at Easington last night in an effort to justify his leadership of the national government and his economy measures against the attacks of William Coxon, secretary of the labor executive that rejected him and his only opponent for reelection. Reducing complex problems of national and international import to “simple problems of housekeeping—government housekeeping,” he asked his hearers to “return him to the house of commons so that he might finish the job of reinstating Great Britain in her place in the sun. He talked for an hour. The Communists continually interrupted with hisses, laughter and angry cries of “dictatorship” and “inflation.” The Nationalist opposition members, including the National Socialist faction of Adolf Hitler, did not enter the chamber until after the chancellor had finished his declaration. GENEVA, Oct. 13.— (AP) —The League of Nations council, which convened in extraordinary session today to consider the Sino-Japanese conflict in Manchuria, listened to a statement by Dr. Alfred Sze, the Chinese delegate, and adjourned until afternoon. Dr. Sze, asserting that the hope for world disarmament depends upon the League taking action now, denounced Japan’s “violence and military aggression” and demanded that the League direct immediate withdrawal of Japanese troops from Manchuria. He emphasized that quick action is essential if “most unhappy results” are to be avoided. While he spoke the diminutive Renkichi Yoshizawa, Japan's representative, sat impassively on the other side of the council table. TOKIO, Oct. 13.—(UP) —Japan sought direct negotiations with China today as the League of Nations council convened at Geneva in an attempt to prevent war. Baron Kijiro Shidehara, Japanese foreign minister, swept aside his diplomatic corps in suing for a closer contact with Nanking government authorities. China already has refused to deal directly with Tokio, preferring instead to keep the league between them.

1931-02-13.text: London, Feb. 13—(AP)—Bucharest society reports that Queen Helen, unable to hold the love of her handsome Prince, now King Carol, plans to marry a Rumanian officer, Colonel Skeletti, were published here today. Helen is said to have written Carol, whose friend in Paris, the red-headed Magda Lupescu, is understood to be lodged now near the royal quarters, that she will resist all his efforts to nullify the divorce she obtained from him in absentia in 1928. While the Holy Synod of the Rumanian Orthodox Church declared that divorce null and void shortly after Carol became king last June, it has been explained that this made it only morally non-existent, since legal annulment would have to come through the courts. “Such a marriage as is reported to be contemplated by Helen would be almost unheard of in European royal circles.

LONDON, Feb. 13—(4’)-—The House of Commons by a vote of 187 to 18 today rejected the bill introduced by Edwin Sorymgeour, prohibition member from Dundee, Scotland, which would have prohibited the use of alcoholic liquors as beverages throughout the United Kingdom. The vote came after a lengthy debate in which Lady Nancy Astor, Virginian born member of the house, played a leading role by her slashing attack on alcohol. ~ Rave and girls basketball
| MANCHESTER, Eng. Feb, H- gi. The long drawn out tie-up in the Lancashire cotton industry ended today, and 300,000 weavers who were locked out last month will return to work on Monday.

LONDON, Feb. 18—Lady Astor, American-born member of the House of Commons, brought a heated debate on prohibition to a climax today by reiterating her prohibition sentiments but stating that she would not support Edwin Scrymgeour’s anti-liquor bill because she believed in local option. The House of Commons, by a vote of 187 to 18, rejected the second reading of the prohibition bill. The rejection did not constitute a governmental defeat. “You might as well call it the ‘peerage’ as the peerage,” said Lady Astor, referring to the House of Lords. “That would be a very good name for it.” Scrymgeour previously had denounced titled members of parliament who are brewers as “engaged in producing national degradation.” The speaker intervened to halt Lady Astor’s remarks, reminding her of the rule against saying anything disrespectful. LONDON, Feb. 12 (4)—Harsh gales which have lashed the English channel and the Irish sea for 24 hours swept up to the north of England tonight, the fiercest storm of the season. The winds abated somewhat, however, in both the channel and the Irish sea, and ships prepared to resume the journeys that had been held up for two days. No casualties were reported to shipping, but tugs took in tow the British steamer Swiftway, which called for help while wallowing in the high seas off the southwest coast of Ireland.

Lima, Peru, Feb. 13 (UP)— A Missouri girl won the favor of Prince George, youngest son of the king of England, at a dancing party last night when the leaders of the capital society circles were guests at a reception and dance in honor of the prince and his elder brother, the prince of Wales. She is Miss Virginia Harris, private secretary to United States Ambassador Fred M. Dearing. Miss Harris’ home is in Columbia, Missouri, where she attended the University of Missouri.

Melbourne, Feb. 13. - Violent earth shocks occurred in the Hawkes Bay region of North Island, New Zealand, today, where several towns were virtually destroyed and about 200 lives were lost in an earthquake a short time ago. Minor shocks were felt throughout the north and south islands. No casualties were reported. Communications with Napier, the center of the first earthquake, were re-established late today. Officials there, in charge of rehabilitating the ruined city, reported that the latest shocks were violent, but did little. Reports received here said that the earthquake was felt as far north as Hamilton, north of Hawkes Bay on North Island, and as far south as Invercargill, on the southern tip of South Island.
Cadiz, Spain, Feb. 12. (4)--Heavy police patrols guarded the streets tonight after a series of disturbances in which four striking workmen were wounded when civil guards broke up a demonstration.

1931-05-09.text: By The Associated Press. Copenhagen, Denmark, May 8—After a cold winter spent in an isolated meteorological station on Greenland ice-cap, Augustine Courtauld, 27-year-old British scientist, tonight was on his way back to his expedition’s base at Sermelik Fjord with his rescuers. While airplane searches were being organized to remove the young explorer from his marooned igloo, a group of his companions led by H. G. Watkins, chief of the British Arctic air route expedition, located Courtauld, who had volunteered to observe meteorological conditions alone on the ice cap. Behind a dog sledge the three rescuers and Courtauld are slowly making their way inland. Their tedious journey is expected to require nearly a week. News of the rescue was brought from the interior yesterday by Capt. Albin Ahrenberg, noted Swedish flier, who had flown to the meteorological station in an effort to rescue the

PARIS, May 8, — Aristide Briand, whose foreign policies were vindicated by a smashing vote in the chamber of deputies yesterday, declined to be stampeded into declaring himself a candidate for presidency of the republic. Shortly after noon he received a delegation from the chamber which asked that he make a formal declaration of his candidacy, but he declined for the time being to make any statement of his position. It was understood that he told the delegation considerations of courtesy made it necessary that he await the action of various groups in the senate which will not meet before Monday. The presidential election is on Wednesday. Some of Briand's friends believe he may not make a formal declaration of his candidacy at all. They think he wants the support of the right and center groups as well as of the left so that his election, if it should come, would be a real expression of th

(By the Associated Press) Berlin, May 8—A Union dispatch tonight reported that the giant German flying-boat DO-X had departed from the Bissagos Islands for a long flight to the Americas. “The dispatch said the great sea-plane had headed for Fernando Noronha, 200 miles off the Brazilian Coast. The distance to this island is some 1,600 miles. Officials of the Dornier works here had received no word of the takeoff from the plane. Express Some Perplexity Some perplexity was expressed by the company officials at the absence of direct news from the airship. It was pointed out that she has radio equipment and communication can be made with the Berlin office while the plane is in the air. It is estimated that approximately 30 hours would be required for the huge flying-boat to make the hop from the west coast to Fernando Noronha. It is possible the officers of the DO-X might continue on to Natal

The doors of the Elysee palace were opened wide to Foreign Minister Briand early Saturday, when the chamber of deputies by an amazing vote of 430 to 52 endorsed his six years of indefatigable labor in the cause of world peace. Briand’s friends expressed the belief that any lingering hesitation he may have retained over his own presidential candidacy can only continue after such a tribute to his accomplishments. His candidacy was put forward officially by radical and moderate supporters under conditions such that political observers generally consider it would be difficult for him to refuse. During the debate which preceded the vote and lasted until a late hour, the foreign minister defended his policies and also described his proposed European economic union. He was frequently applauded during the address, which required more than an hour. “Every step I have taken has been a step toward

PARIS, May 9. ()—The way to the French presidency was open today for Aristide Briand, veteran foreign minister, if M. Briand decided finally that he wants that office of much dignity and little power. By a vote of 450 to 32 the chamber of deputies last night recorded emphatic approval of his foreign office policies after a fiery debate in which a few of M. Briand's enemies made a determined but futile stand in opposition to him. It was as convincing a testimonial of popularity as any French statesman has had in many years, and in the lobbies there remained little doubt that the man to whom it was meted may have the highest office of the French republic in succession to Gaston Doumergue if he wishes. The left groups of the chamber and senate joined today to send a delegation to M. Briand to request him to announce his candidacy for the presidency, to which someone will be named by the nat

Madrid, May 9.—(4)—Compulsory religious education in the schools was abolished in a decree issued by the minister of public instruction, Marcelino Domingo. If the parents wish, children may attend classes conducted by priests without charge, the decree says.

Frankfort-on-Main, Germany, May 9.—(P)—The belated coming of spring has brought a series of unprecedented storms and floods to Germany, taking at least seven lives. The water ruined crops, inundated villages and cities and washed out roads, railway tracks and bridges. Southwest Germany was hit the hardest. The Main, Neckar, and Fils rivers and their tributaries have overflowed their banks, causing a shutdown of factories and schools. Residents of Bruchsal, near Karlsruhe, are using boats and the city is without gas or light. A prolonged cloudburst over Westphalia last night washed out crops and drowned livestock. Another struck Hamburg this morning and flooded cellars. Torrential rains swelled the Bavarian mountain springs, causing lowland inundations and numerous landslides.

Nemuro, Japan, May 9.—(UP)—Seiji Hoshihara, Japanese aviator who is flying from Tokyo to the United States by easy stages, took off from here at 8:38 a.m. today for Muroton Bay, his next scheduled stop, 280 miles away. Stormy weather forced the flier back Thursday when he first attempted to fly to Muroton Bay. Storms have kept him on the ground since he returned here. Today's flight will take Yoshihara for the first time away from Japan proper. Nemuro is at the extreme north of Hokkaido Island. Muroton Bay is in the Kuriles group of islands. Yoshihara plans to fly next to Petropavlovsk, at the southern end of the Kamchatka Peninsula. Then he would soar 372 miles over the Bering Sea to Nikolski, thence to the Aleutian Islands and Alaska. He left Tokyo Monday at the start of his 6,000-mile trip. At the start, he said he expected it would require 26 days for him to reach San Francisco.

1931-05-30.text: New York, May 27.—(AP)—Holding sway for its second day, a pre-seasonal heat wave continued throughout the East today, causing nine deaths in the two-day period and discomfort to sweltering humanity. In New England three deaths yesterday were added to three of the previous day. Two persons died in West Virginia and one in New York City. In New York, with a temperature of 88 degrees, an estimated million persons hastened their holiday exodus in search of cooling breezes at seashore and mountain resorts. Schools Closed In New England the thermometer flirted with the 90 mark, schools were closed in Boston and the municipal bath houses were thrown open a month ahead of schedule. At Boston, the temperature reached 94; and as far north as Portland, Maine, it was 91. The highest figure reported was 97 at Greenfield, Mass. The heat wave was felt as far west as Pittsburgh, where a temperature of 8

PARIS, May 30. (AP)—Texas Guinan and her “gang” of 30 Broadway blondes cannot enter France for business or for pleasure. The director of the Surete Generale, responsible for policing France, told the Associated Press today that the French government had refused admission to the American night club hostess and that the decision was final. No reason was given. * * Officials of the French line telephoned from Havre that they had received instructions from the government to send the party and their white horse back to the United States on the first boat. They probably will sail on the liner Paris Wednesday for New York. Havre police said they understood that the contract under which the entertainers were to perform in a Paris cabaret had not been visaed by the ministry of labor before they left New York. Le Guinan and her “pals” will be allowed to remain in the waterfront, emigrant hotel in

HAVRE, France, May 29,—Texas Guinan, sometimes called the “Queen of Night Club Hostesses,” and her troupe of 30 Broadway girls, tonight were unwilling guests of a hotel customarily used for third-class emigrants. Yielding to the impassioned plea of Miss Guinan and her friends, the head of the intelligence service of the commissariat allowed the New York entertainer and her “gang” to come ashore to spend the night in “the bunk house” which the French line maintains. Even Miss Guinan herself admitted there was nothing “fancy” about her present quarters when landed from the liner Paris; however, the hostelry is clean and wholesome. Earlier French authorities had refused to allow the troupe to land on the grounds their working contracts were not in order. This brought a strong protest from Miss Guinan, who declared, “I am an American citizen and I have never been convicted of a crime. There

(Copyright, 1931, By Associated Press) Ober Guregl, Austrian Tyrol, May 29. (P)—A slim bespectacled scientist stood bareheaded under the Tyrolean sun here this afternoon telling a dusty audience of newspaper men what he had found out about the stratosphere on his balloon flight of Wednesday to an altitude of almost ten miles. Although Auguste Piccard is professor of physics at the University of Brussels, there is little of the professorial in his manner when interviewed. Questions about Wednesday's balloon trip into the outer layer of the earth’s atmosphere were met with impatient snorts or with boyish enthusiasm, depending on whether they appealed to him as intelligent. Never once, however, did he revert to the tone of the classroom. “What color was the daytime sky as it appeared to you 50,000 feet up?” was one of the questions. “It was a deep dark blue,” he replied, “but no stars whate

HOULN, France, May 5 (AFP)— In honor of St. Joan of Arc, the girl in her teens who liberated fifteenth century France, and who was burned at the stake for heresy, the high clergy of the Catholic church and the leading civic and military authorities of France today united in a pious procession of atonement. For the first time in a quarter of a century, since the separation of church and state in this country, 60 ranking prelates, each accompanied by two canons, trod their solemn way through the streets of Rouen in full ecclesiastical regalia, before crowds of men who bared their heads, and women who made the sign of the cross. After them came the representatives of the central government, the Municipality, the “constituted corps” such as the magistrates, generals, admirals, mayors of nearby townships and patriotic societies. Six cardinals, in “Cappa Magna” or ceremonial capes, led the lin

MADRID, May 29 (4).—After one of the longest sessions since the republic was established, the cabinet tonight emphatically denied persistent rumors Niceto Alcala Zamora would retire as provisional president and be succeeded by Foreign Minister Alejandro Llorente.

WASHINGTON, May 29 (7) — President Hoover today reappointed Wm. F. Schilling of Minnesota as a member of the Federal Farm Board. The announcement of Schilling’s reappointment came coincidental with the completion of Charles C. Teague of his duties as vice chairman and fruit and vegetable member of the board. Teague submitted his resignation to President Hoover last week and it is expected to be accepted shortly.

WASHINGTON, May 24.-— War birds of the nation saluted the capital today in preparation for a massed Memorial Day review, bringing to a close the unprecedented maneuvers of the army air corps. Tomorrow more than 550 planes will make a sky march up the Potomac and over the city, while distinguished government officials look on from the new Arlington Memorial bridge.

1931-11-29.text: LONDON, Nov. 27—()—An Exchange Telegraph message from Tokyo today said Japanese airplanes had bombed the city of Chinchow, Manchuria. The message said the attack from the air was in retaliation for an attack by a Chinese detachment on a Japanese force which left Mukden to reconnoiter early this morning.

BUDAPEST, Hungary, Nov. 28 P.--A plot to overthrow the Hungarian government was revealed today with the dramatic suicide of one of the alleged leaders. The conspiracy, aimed at establishment of a dictatorship, officially was announced by the Hungarian press bureau. General Raice of the Hungarian army committed suicide in the Budapest police station while he was being questioned tonight in connection with the plot.

| TOKYO, Nov. 29. (4)—(Saturday)—An explanation by Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson that he never said some things which it had been assumed in Japan he had said was received in official circles here today with much satisfaction in view of a previous misconception of dispatches from Washington. | The American secretary of state had been accused by the Japanese foreign office, on the basis of statements attributed to him, of “losing his head” and “flying into fulminations.” The secretary of state Friday made public portions of an exchange of notes on the Manchurian situation between Japan and the United States. Japan had disclaimed any intention of attacking Chinchow and in view of this Secretary Stimson said it was difficult for him to understand press reports the Japanese were advancing toward Chinchow. Other statements were misconstrued in Japan as coming from him. Official quarters

The Japanese foreign office, acting yesterday on the basis of statements incorrectly attributed to Secretary of State Stimson, accused him of “losing his head” and “flying into fulminations.” In Washington the secretary reiterated that he found it difficult to credit or understand dispatches telling of a Japanese advance on Chinchow in view of assurances Japan had given against hostilities in that quarter. The Japanese ambassador conferred with Colonel Stimson, and the secretary of state received renewed assurances of Japan's good intentions. Senator Hiram Johnson of California called on the state department to publish all notes bearing on the Manchurian situation. The Japanese ambassador informed Secretary Stimson he did not expect a Japanese attack on Chinchow. Vienna, Nov. 28.—A Budapest dispatch tonight said 151 persons, including several young officers, had been arrested in connection with a revolutionary plot in Hungary. The conspiracy appeared to have been organized by right-radicals in an effort to obtain election of a King to fill Hungary's vacant throne. Motor trucks loaded with prisoners have been arriving from Budapest from the provinces, the dispatch said. All important public buildings in Budapest were guarded tonight by military cadets. Vague but sensational reports of an attempt to overthrow the government of Premier Julius Karolyi previously had leaked out of Hungary.

TOKIO, Nov. 29 (Sunday)—(AP)—An explanation by Secretary of State Stimson of the United States, regarding statements erroneously attributed to him in Japanese press dispatches, was received by official circles today with much satisfaction. TOKIO, Sunday, Nov. 29.—(UP)—The Japanese foreign office’s denunciation of Secretary of State Stimson was given out in an attempt to allay public indignation after Japanese newspapers had displayed a dispatch from Washington quoting Stimson as saying that the Japanese army had “run amok” in Manchuria and put Japan in the position of violating the nine-power pact. That was the explanation at the foreign office today of developments which caused the foreign office spokesman to declare that Stimson was “losing his head at a critical moment.” When the copy of the Associated Press Washington dispatch reached the Rengo News agency here early Saturday by way

| Berlin, Nov. 28.—(P)—Dr. Oscar Mulert, considered to be Germany's best-informed specialist on municipal problems, today protested against accusations by Premier Laval of France that German municipalities are guilty of lavish expenditures. “Nobody is more ready than I to admit individual cases of prodigal municipal expenditures,” he said, “but it is unfair to generalize from those instances. Instead of needing 5,000,000,000 marks a year, as before 1930, our cities operate now on a budget of 4,000,000,000 and this sum would be much lower but for unemployment. “Of 6,000,000 jobless Germans, fully one-third must be directly supported by the communities. Nobody can charge prodigality in doles, for these averaged 25 cents a day per man.” “Not Prosperous Dr. Mulert expressed doubt that anyone abroad realizes how economically German cities are operating. McGrath, Alaska, Nov. 28—(F)—The missing brothers George J. Feltes and Merial Lapeyre, Jesuit missionaries who had not been heard from since they left here a week ago to fly to Holy Cross, were located from the air today camped at the head of Ganes Creek. The two apparently had been forced down, wrecking their landing gear. Pilot Harry Blunt and Deputy Marshal Stanley J. Nichols reported on the return of their plane here. “We circled a number of times over their camp,” Nichols said, “and dropped a sack of food to them.” “Both flyers walked around their plane and waved to us. “They had a fire going.” Brothers Feltes and Lapeyre left here last Sunday on the 150-mile flight to Holy Cross, on the Yukon, but had not been heard from after they were sighted over Takotna, about 20 miles west of here. With wintry weather over the section, concern was felt for their safety and Blunt, flying here f

1931-03-15.text: WASHINGTON, March 14.—(?)— Conference which Senator Dwight W. Morrow of New Jersey will have with Ambassador Dawes in London at the suggestion of Secretary Stimson may result in a change in present plans to place the Franco-Italian naval accord in final form. Secretary Stimson said today he had wirelessed the senator, who is en route with Mrs. Morrow to Europe on the Leviathan, asking that he discuss the entire question with Ambassador Dawes upon his arrival in London. The secretary, in studying the basis of agreement resulting from the British-Franco-Italian negotiations, has reached some conclusions which he desires communicated to Ambassador Dawes and which eventually will reach the British foreign office in the form of suggestions. In the event these suggestions are accepted, it was considered highly probable here tonight that the proposed conference of experts of the five principal

BUENOS AIRES, March 14 (P)—The Prince of Wales delivered a salutation today for the British empire in an inaugural address which dedicated here the largest trade exhibition the empire ever sponsored outside its borders. In a speech which was radiocast to England, the United States and British dominions, he called attention to the vast display of British goods assembled in Palermo park as proof of a spirit of revival in British industry. He reached the climax of his address with reference to the two Spanish words which make up Argentina's name for foreign trade— "Intercambio Comercial." Translated literally into English, he pointed out, the words mean “commercial interchange.” The world’s depression, the prince said, probably is mainly due to its failure to recognize trade as an interchange of products. Britain and Argentina, alike, he said, are vitally concerned with foreign trade.

NICE, France, March 14.—Charlotte Nixon-Nirdlinger, who killed her husband last Wednesday night at the end of a bitter quarrel, is the calmest person the jail warden here ever saw. "She hasn't asked to see her children since the night they brought her here," he said. "She doesn't want to exercise, she won't read books, but spends her time manicuring her nails. It seems to me there is something unnatural about her." The examining magistrate today set at rest reports that she would be liberated without a trial by announcing that she would go before the court of assizes which reconvenes next August. WASHINGTON, March 14. (®—A conflict of opinion among those who sponsored the recent progressive conference developed today to preclude the probability of their participation as a political unit in the 1952 presidential race. Several of the group showed in their comments, both public and private, a decided disinclination to follow Senator Norris, Republican, Nebraska, chairman of the conference, in looking toward the Democratic Party for a progressive presidential candidate. One of the prominent participants in the conference said he could see little progressive hope in the Democratic Party as long as it was connected in any way with Tammany Hall or led by Chairman Raskob.

FORT MYERS, Fla., March 11 — Henry Ford today described the nation as prosperous, despite high prices, but unable to realize its good fortune. ‘The manufacturer predicted another term for President Hoover. He cautioned the government not to enter business through utility ownership. He said appreciation of present good times will not come until the people understand the cause of the business depression, which he said was the mental dishonesty of a speculating public. Mr. Ford declared so-called prosperity of the inflated values period preceding the 1929 stock market crash probably will not return.

EAST ST. LOUIS, DL, March 14— Two women and a 13-year-old girl were criminally attacked last night and four homes terrorized by two negroes who forced their way into the home at pistol's point. They were not apprehended. One of the women was seized while kneeling before her bed in prayer and attacked while her husband, bound to a chair and gagged, was forced to look on. The other woman and the girl were assaulted in a room where two women and a 13-year-old girl were held prisoners by the negroes. The husbands of three of the women were gagged and bound with wire in another room. In each of the places the negroes ransacked the house, stealing jewelry, table silver, and cash. The first public knowledge of the crimes came at noon today from Chief Deputy Sheriff Mike Doyle of St. Clair County. At the same time, James Leahy, chief of police here, and George Byrnes, chief of detectives, said t

Kansas City, March 14. ()—Paul Cline, Communist party district organizer, today charged members of the Ku Klux Klan with abducting and flogging of Lewis Hurst and C. J. Coder, Communist organizers, at Dallas, Texas, last Thursday. He alleged the police had connived with the mob. + Cline said Hurst and Coder had reached Kansas City yesterday and were under the care of a physician in private homes here, recovering from a beating administered by "fourteen armed klansmen," who, he said, kidnapped them as they were released from jail. "Coder and Hurst state that the motive behind the attack was the hatred of the klansmen aroused by the Communist speeches against Jim Crowism, lynching of Negroes and race discrimination," Cline said. Both men intend to return to Dallas to continue their work, the organizer declared, as soon as they have fully recovered. William Craw, district attorney at Dallas

WASHINGTON, March 14, — President Hoover is to embark next week on a ten-day trip which will take in Porto Rico and the Virgin Islands. The reconditioned battleship Arizona will carry him from Norfolk, Va., on the trial run it must make before being placed in active service. The journey has the dual purpose of rest and work. After relaxing on the ocean trip into the Caribbean, the president plans to confer on administrative affairs with Governor Theodore Roosevelt, Jr. in Porto Rico and with Governor Paul M. Pearson in the Virgin Islands. The exact date of departure soon will be announced. The Arizona's cruise was scheduled to begin Tuesday, but Mr. Hoover's decision to go along may mean a slight deferment. After returning, the president will direct his attention to a series of eight speeches starting at the annual Red Cross meeting here April 13, and ending with the dedication of the Li

1931-02-15.text: Boston, Feb. 14, (P) — Major General Clarence R. Edwards, commander of the 26th (Yankee) division in France, has “gone West.” The veteran commander of New England's own division in the World War died soon after daybreak today at the Massachusetts General Hospital. He was 71 years old. A spirit of mourning descended upon all New England with word of the passing of the beloved leader. Thousands of his military subordinates and friends, who hoped for his return to health after he became ill from intestinal trouble a month ago, were grief-stricken. A second operation to remove an obstruction which caused his illness was performed yesterday. Although attending surgeons held hope for recovery, he never rallied and died after having been unconscious for several hours. Tributes from those who served under him in France, military and naval officials and a host of public officials led by Governor

MADRID, Feb. 14.--The year-old cabinet of Premier Damaso Berenguer resigned today, forced to this action by countrywide opposition to its electoral program, and King Alfonso set about the difficult task of forming another ministry. He met with a serious obstacle, however, when the powerful constitutional party announced that it would not participate in any government that did not include all political factions. The king had at first planned a “concentration” ministry of royalist leaders. Thus, unless Alfonso agrees to a “nation” cabinet embracing Republicans, Socialists and other groups, he apparently faces a ministry composed largely of Liberal party leaders with perhaps some conservatives. This would leave the Socialists, Republicans and Constitutionalists as disgruntled as they were when Premier Berenguer was in power, according to political observers. Some military groups were even r

LISBON, Portugal, Feb. 14—An earthquake in the Azores alarmed the inhabitants today, but did little damage. Reports from Ponta Delgada said furniture was banged around and walls were cracked somewhat, but after a moment of panic the people went about their ordinary lives as the shock subsided.

by The Associated Press Washington, D. C., Feb. 14.— With Speaker Longworth determined to force the veterans’ 50 per cent loan proposal through the house Monday, administration opposition in both branches today apparently crumbled. Quick action was assured in the senate also, an agreement having been reached by proponents of both parties to jam it through unchanged in time to prevent a possible pocket veto. It will have to reach President Hoover's desk February 23 to remove this possibility. While not disputing Secretary Mel- Jon's statement denouncing the proposal, expected to call for an outlay ranging from $700,000,000 upward, Longworth declared the Bacharach compromise would give relief to the veterans and that no one could do more than guess how much money would be involved. Warnings were issued by Chairman Smoot of the senate finance committee and Chairman Hawley of the house ways

(By The Associated Press) Allahabad, India, Feb. 14.— Peace in India tonight seemed measurably nearer than at any time since the present civil disobedience movement began nearly a year ago. Mahatma Gandhi, the Indian Nationalist leader, made a dramatic gesture today, when it seemed that India would be torn with strife, agitation and economic decline definitely, by announcing that he had written a letter to the viceroy, Lord Irwin asking for an opportunity of talking the whole situation over in a spirit of candor and friendship. It was expected here that Lord Irwin would invite Gandhi to New Delhi on Monday or Tuesday and that the ensuing conference might prove the prelude to a permanent peace. Asked by the correspondent after today’s conference what the conditions for peace would be in his conversation with the viceroy, Gandhi reduced them all from his previous elaborate eleven points to

WELLTON, Ariz., Feb. 14.—The 200 inhabitants of this little Mormon settlement floundered in the mud tonight, gazing ruefully at what was left of their belongings after a torrential rain loosened a protecting dike, releasing a six-foot wall of water. The body of the one known flood victim, Mrs. E. P. Llewellyn, of Stockton, Cal., was taken to Yuma, Ariz. She was drowned last night when the raging flood swept from the highway the automobile in which she was riding with her husband and daughter. The body was found a mile and a half from the scene of the accident, half buried in silt and debris. Wellton experienced another near panic late today when a second downpour of cloudburst proportions fell to the west. While flood waters cut again through the highway leading to Phoenix and drove back repair crews, the torrent left Wellton virtually untouched. Sheriff J. C. Hunter of Yuma County said

© Associated Press. Chicago, Feb. 14.— Legal approval of police censorship of Earl Carroll’s “sketch book” was postponed at least until next Thursday by municipal court Judge Justin W. McCarthy today. Three male principals of the cast and 25 chorus girls arrested in a police raid upon the show last night were arraigned this morning before Judge McCarthy, who, combining first hand theatrical experience with judicial knowledge, decided to attend the performance and determine for himself whether the police charges of obscenity were warranted.

Washington, Feb. 14.—(AP)—Running contrary to administration wishes, a majority of house republicans and the democrats plan to pass the 50 per cent veterans loan proposal Monday. Word that quick action is desired in the senate came from Senator Couzens, republican, Michigan, in blocking a proposal to consider the nomination of Eugene Meyer as governor of the federal reserve board next Saturday. Filibuster Threatened Couzens said he would object to all unanimous consent requests for the remainder of the session pending disposition of veterans relief legislation. Previously he said he understood there was a move toward holding up the legislation and subjecting it to the chances of a pocket veto. 1931-09-07.text: LONDON, Sept. 7.—A crowd of several thousand persons staged a demonstration in Hyde Park Sunday, while political leaders were preparing for the opening of Parliament this week, and announced its intention to attempt to see Prime Minister MacDonald at the House of Commons Tuesday to protest against cuts in the dole and in wages. The crowd was made up of members of the Independent Labor Party and a contingent under the National Unemployment Workers’ Movement. It converged on Oxford Circus from all parts of London and, headed by a band of unemployed men, marched to Hyde Park.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 6.—(M)—Returning from a visit to Europe, Representative Beck of Pennsylvania cited “the fate of England” as a reminder to the coming congress of the danger of strangling prosperity by excessive taxation. The deficit could be wiped out, Beck said, if “all unnecessary and meddlesome government bureaus were abolished and if congress would declare light wines and malted liquors non-intoxicating in fact and impose a heavy excise tax upon these luxuries. “If we adopted this simple expedient, we could easily cut the necessities of taxation by two billions of dollars,” the republican said, “There would then be no deficit, but, on the contrary, a larger surplus; business would be less burdened and take heart, and the wheels of industry, now sunk in the mire of industrial prostration, would again move.”

(Associated Press Staff writer) SHANGHAI, Sept. 6—()—Fresh tidings of disaster reached Shanghai tonight from widely separated areas, emphasizing the nationwide character of China’s flood calamity, but confirmation was still lacking of the reported holocaust at Kunghsien, Honan province. The Kunghsien alarm was found to be based on a message received at Peiping from the Honan Relief Association, appealing for immediate aid because “about one million persons were drowned around Kunghsien,” by recent floods which were reported to have ruined all houses in the district. The figure was interpreted as merely another case of Chinese carelessness with ciphers, especially since the total population of the six surrounding counties including Kunghsien barely exceeds 1,000,000. Reports of further distress were received from the provinces of Shensi, Honan, Kiangsu while a new dark spot in China's flo

GENEVA, Sept. 7.—(UP)—The 12th assembly of the League of Nations convened here today for a month's session. The first act of the assembly was to elect Nicolas Titulesco, delegate from Rumania, to the presidency. “The entire world is suffering a terrible crisis,” Titulesco said, as he took office. “The assembly of the league will fail in its duty if it does not demonstrate that the sacred fires of Geneva are able to help in overcoming the situation. That must be our principal task.” With both the league council and Briand’s European economic union commission in session, the league expects to stage one of the busiest scenes of international activities it has yet held.

By United Press SHANGHAI, Sept. 7.—China’s acute distress from floods that scourged 11 provinces was revealed today in a survey that showed at least 180,000,000 persons are suffering. The number of deaths was impossible to calculate although a Chinese news agency estimated at least 1,000,000 were drowned in the Yellow River basin floods. The Yellow River has proven an even greater menace than the floods in the Yangtze River valley several weeks ago. Refugees in these sections need at least 1,000,000 tons of food to maintain them until spring, and the proposal to supply American wheat was regarded as only a temporary means of relief. Constantly increasing political complications have made the situation worse. Despite pledges of Chiang Kai-shek, head of the National government, that there will be no war, the Canton army is advancing in Hunan Province. A dispute between Manchurians and Japa

Clarksburg, W. Va., Sept. 7—County prisoners today were to begin digging beneath the home and small store of Harry F. Powers, confessed slayer of two women and three children. The hunt for other possible victims of the matrimonial agent was prompted, police said, by an odor pervading rooms on the lower floor of the building. Mrs. Asta Eicher, well-to-do widow of Park Ridge, Ill., and her three children and Mrs. Dorothea Pressler Lempke, North Cambridge, Mass., were found buried in a ditch near Powers’ garage, six miles from here a week ago. Belongings of the two women were discovered yesterday in Powers’ home. Mrs. Luella Powers, Powers’ wife, and her sister, Eva Belle, are under technical arrest in their home here, heavily guarded.

CLARKSBURG, W. Va., Sept. 6.—(AP)—The wife and sister-in-law of Harry F. Powers were placed under technical arrest today as officers continued investigation of the slaying of two women and three children here. The arrests followed discovery of silverware and clothing identified as the property of Mrs. Asta Eicher, Park Ridge, Ill., and Mrs. Dorothy Pressier Lemke, Northbridge, Mass., two of the victims. Mrs. Eicher’s three children also were slain. A quantity of silverware identified as the property of Mrs. Eicher was found in the Powers home today. Clothing marked with the names of both slain women was found last night. Plans were made to dig beneath the home and the small store occupying part of the structure to trace the source of a foul odor pervading the rooms.

Cleveland, Ohio, Sept. 6 (AP)--A near fatal crack up, the fastest race of the meet and the women’s free for all championship put thrills into the National Air Races today. Walter J. Hunter of Sparta, Ill. was forced to jump from only 200 feet when something went wrong with the gas line of his plane and it caught fire. Hunter escaped with minor burns but his plane which he was testing for the Thompson trophy race tomorrow, was wrecked. The Sunday crowd of 64,000, the largest of the week-old races, did not see Hunter ‘bail out,’ but they saw last year’s time for the Thompson trophy race bettered by 20 miles an hour and watched Miss Maude State of Springfield, Mass., win the annual Aerol trophy race with a speed of 187.574 miles an hour. The fastest closed course race ever run in the National Air Races was won by Robert Hall, of Springfield, Mass., in a black and yellow Gee Bee monoplane at

LONDON, July 3 (P)—A startled house of commons listened this afternoon as David Lloyd George hurled taunts and jibes at his former lieutenant, Sir John Simon, who recently severed his official connection with the Liberal party. It is many years since parliament members have heard a speech manifesting such personal virulence. Lloyd George received enthusiastic acclaim from the Labor side but from the Conservative benches came angry retorts. Referring to Sir John's intolerable “self-righteousness,” the fiery Welshman said “greater men have changed their opinions in the past, but at any rate they did not leave this slime of hypocrisy in passing from one side to the other.” He likened his dissident Liberal to a teetotaler who “looked with wrathful disdain on anyone who had a drop of alcohol, however, did— and suddenly, when he was approaching his seventh decade, took drink and you saw him ro

Uncle Sam, still leader of the world despite business ills, pauses this July 4 to celebrate his 155th birthday and to honor those brave forefathers who sacrificed their all for liberty’s cause. As 126,000,900 Americans celebrate the Nation's founding, pages of history turn back to 1776, when patriotic men and women gave their personal fortunes and, some, their lives for our freedom. Statesmen heroes they were, but as brave as those who carried muskets. One brave patriot rose from a sick bed and rode 80 miles through a blinding storm to cast a needed vote for independence; another risked death as a traitor, went to prison and died from the harsh treatment; others saw their homes looted and their families in ruin; one fired the cannon that destroyed his own mansion, then the estate. | OTTAWA, ONT, July 8. (4) - Capt. Frank Hawks went after one of Wiley Post's laurels Friday, but failed by four minutes to win it from the round-the-world flier. In his tiny aero-speedster plane, Hawks flew the 225 miles from Toronto to Ottawa in one hour, six minutes, just four minutes longer than it took Post to do it during the 1929 Ford reliability air tour.

San Antonio, July 3. (AP)— Suits seeking $1,008,000,000 damages for the slaying of Emilio Cortes Rubio, kinsman of Mexico's president, and Manuel Gomez, Mexican college students, slain several weeks ago in Oklahoma, were filed against the state of Oklahoma and the sureties on the bond of the sheriff of Ardmore, M. C. Gonzales, San Antonio attorney, said today. He represented the Mexican government at the recent trial in Ardmore, Okla., of W. E. (Bill) Guess, former sheriff, on a charge of murder in connection with the slayings. Guess was acquitted. The attorney said he was awaiting word from relatives of the youths preparatory to filing in federal court here two suits, each for $500,000, on behalf of the respective families of the slain youths.

SEATTLE, July 3 (®)—With the monoplane Fort Worth checked today for its proposed nonstop flight from Seattle to Tokyo, Reg L. Robbins and H. S. Jones, Texas aviators were impatiently waiting here for their refueling plane to reach Fairbanks, Alaska, to permit them to get under way. Word from J. J. Mattern and Nick Greener who are in Edmonton, Alta. with the tri-motored refueling machine, that they could not start for Fairbanks until tomorrow, forced Robbins and Jones to postpone the start of their perilous journey until at least Sunday. Mattern and Greener who are to refuel the Fort Worth over Fairbanks and again over the coast of Siberia, had planned to leave today for Alaska. Reports from Alaska and in Bering Strait indicate that excellent flying conditions prevail at least to the coast of Siberia and the aviators are anxious to get started.

New York, July 3 (AP)—The world fliers, Wiley Post and Harold Gatty, sought the quiet of Long Island Sound today for a peaceful weekend with their wives on the yacht of William H. Todd, wealthy shipbuilder. Early this morning they were up and away to Roosevelt Field to see how their famous plane Winnie Mae stood the rigors of the flight around the world. Hopping the plane over to the Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn, where it was placed on public view, they found it in perfect condition, but still grimy with the stains of travel. Navy personnel at the field promised to scrub it down. Returning then to Manhattan, Post and Gatty drove to Stamford, Conn., to board the Todd yacht, where they will talk over the possibility of removing some of the Winnie Mae's gas tanks so the wives can fly to Oklahoma with them. If this is done a third passenger will be Miss Viola Gentry, disabled endurance fl

Philadelphia, July 3.—(A.P.)— From historical Independence Hall where 155 years ago colonial leaders signed the Declaration of Independence, Philadelphia’s celebration of the anniversary of that event will be broadcast over a nation-wide hookup tomorrow. Patrick J. Hurley, secretary of war, will represent the government and deliver the principal address. Preceding exercises in the hall thousands of regular army and national guard troops will pass in review while squadrons of airplanes under the command of Major J. Sidney Owens maneuver overhead.

1931-06-21.text: Boulogne-Sur-Mer, France—(A.P.) Robert Kronfeld, a German, Saturday, made the first round-trip crossing of the English Channel in a motorless airplane, winning the $5,000 prize posted by the London Daily Mail for the first man to make the trip across and back in the same. It took him two hours to fly from an airdrome near Calais, France, to the Swingate airdrome near Dover. He stayed in England only an hour or so, then hitched his glider to an airplane which pulled him off the ground. Out across the water, he cast off the tow-line and continued on his own. The plane turned back and he finished his flight at about 10:30 p.m., flying through the night most of the way.

LONDON, June 20. (P)—President Hoover's announcement that America was considering stretching a helping hand to Europe in her economic extremity was looked upon by England Saturday night as having much of the significance of the entry of the United States into the war. Officially the British government had "absolutely nothing to say" but in authoritative quarters a comparison was drawn between America’s advent into the war at a critical juncture and the possibility of her jumping in now to help bridge the economic crisis. Seized with Approval Mr. Hoover's announcement, while containing no promises, was seized upon with eager approval in official quarters where the belief was stressed that to have delayed much longer would have been to court even worse economic distress for Europe and the world. ROME, June 20—A declaration by the Pope that no accord is in sight with Premier Mussolini's government made a dark picture today of what the government yesterday described as a fairly optimistic situation. The Pope said “odious” spying, persecutions, accusations and “continual menaces” have been reported by the bishops of Italy. He gave a much different view of his negotiations with the government than the one coming from government sources. The Pope resumed his policy of saying blunt words about Mussolini's “persecution” of him, of the church and of Catholic youth. To a group of seminarians he declared that not only Catholics but nearly the whole world was “with and behind the Pope” in his “bitter sorrow.” As for the negotiations with the government, he declared they are not even really started. To this government officials replied only that the exchange of notes was proceeding normally

Toronto, Ont., June 20.—(AP)—A Windsor, Ont., dispatch to the Toronto Daily Star says "liquor exporting on the grand scale is to be resumed to the United States early next week, liquor runners believe." The dispatch says the liquor runners claim to have found a loophole in the law prohibiting export to prohibition countries and today every rum runner on the border waterfront is preparing his boats for high speed work again, after a year of idleness since the liquor export act became law on June 1, 1930. The plan, according to the dispatch, is based on legal opinions holding there is no means of preventing breweries and distilleries from selling their products for exports by small boats, to non-prohibition countries, such as the French island of Miguelon, and issuing liquor export certificates for the goods.
